en: *Exegesis of the Verses of the Lotus Sutra*, by the Śramaṇa Guangzhao of Mount Huo in Qiantang, Shi Wendaifu.
Those who read the sutra must skillfully grasp the Buddha’s intent; having grasped the Buddha’s intent, they may then initiate practice, like a person with clear vision.
Those who do not understand the intent of the teachings will merely exhaust themselves in vain and ultimately be unable to know the realm of the Buddha, as described in the sutras.

One should know that the various meanings and principles—such as wisdom (*prajñā*), skillful means (*upāya*), parables, and causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)—which are perfectly integrated as a unity of three, are all manifestations of the mind alone.
It is only because of delusion that one wanders through the boundless cycle of birth and death; yet, when one suddenly attains awakening, [all these are seen as such].
The karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty; one must attain the state of non-action by letting go of everything. Right and wrong are both discarded, and defilement and purity are both forgotten.
When even the mind that forgets has vanished, true awakening is perfectly luminous. At such a time, though no intentional effort is made, the unobstructed clarity constantly manifests before one.
If you seek it in old scrolls, when will it ever appear? Therefore it is said: "The true mark of all phenomena is not..."

It can be said that only those who possess true wisdom are able to know this; when it comes to such a discourse, one must directly recognize its point of arrival before Śākyamuni has even opened his mouth.
If you can clearly realize it and avoid being deceived by him, what harm is there in stepping back three paces?
It is not necessary to snap the fingers; see into the fundamental mind of your own, and you will have accomplished the great matter of beginningless time.

The causal conditions are truly not difficult; as for tracing the origin and examining the end, grasping the main framework and shaking loose the knots, these are fully detailed in the Preface and the "Diagram of Pointing to the Palm.
The present explanation of the meaning of the characters is intended for those who are beginners, like preliminary warm-up exercises before practicing a craft.
I hope you will not become mired in this; you should instead spur yourself forward.

An Exegesis on the Phrases of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and an Exegesis on the Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
By the Śramaṇa Guangzhao of Qiantang, Shi Wenda.
Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The five characters "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra" constitute the title of this scripture; the three characters "Preface to the Propagation" were established by [Zhi] Nan-shan.
"Propagation" (*hongchuan*) means to widely disseminate and transmit. "Preface" (*xu*) refers to the account of the origins and circumstances of this scripture’s propagation.

Furthermore, selecting the wondrous meanings from within the sutras and elucidating their great purport by placing them at the beginning of the scripture—vowing to propagate and transmit [this teaching] throughout the turbid age so that all sentient beings may ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment—is what is meant here.

"Wondrous Dharma" refers to the Buddha's knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), which is the fundamentally enlightened wondrous mind. This knowledge and vision is equal throughout the dharma-realm; the Buddha and...
Because sentient beings are fundamentally non-dual, it is said that the wondrous mind is inherently present, like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction. Furthermore, one should know that although their nature is equal, there is a difference between delusion and awakening.
Because the Buddha has awakened, he dwells within this [nature], and all his daily enjoyments are none other than the four virtues. Sentient beings, however, are deluded and turn their backs upon it.
Awakening to the union with sense objects, one has wandered through saṃsāra for long kalpas, wherein nothing is not one of the eight inversions.

Out of compassion for the deluded masses, the Buddha appears in the world and employs various skillful means to subdue their minds; all of this is solely for the purpose of enabling them to attain the wisdom of the Buddha. As the Sūtra says:
"The reason the Tathāgata appears is to expound the Buddha-wisdom. Because this wondrous Dharma is inherently possessed by the mind itself, it is said:

Because the Buddha commanded that [beings] be opened, shown, awakened, and entered [into the truth], thereby transforming the mundane into the sacred and realizing the wondrous Dharma-body, the Sūtra says:
"If there are those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not realize the meaning of the Buddha-Dharma. Is this not truly marvelous?
As for the lotus flower: when viewed by those of superior faculties, it is none other than the *Svabhāva-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*; for those of middling and inferior faculties...

The mechanism of this [teaching] is to provide analogies that draw forth the object [of understanding]: the fundamentally existing awakened mind and its pure, wondrous principle. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to attain purity, I appear in the world.
Furthermore, there are three meanings: first, because those of dull faculties are unable to receive the Great [Vehicle], the provisional means establish the Three Vehicles for them.
To guide and assist them, the former sutra stated: "The faculties of sentient beings are dull; how can they be saved? Now that I have attained the Way, I shall preach the Three Vehicles.

The reason for preaching the Lesser Vehicle was to accommodate those with provisional capacities, serving as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of the Great Vehicle—just as one produces lotus flowers in order to obtain the lotus seeds.
Since the two have been harmonized for a long time and their faculties have become mature, [the time has come] to reveal what was previously hidden.
All skillful means are the Buddha-vehicle; those hired laborers are none other than one's own children. As the Sūtra says: "The path you all practice is the Bodhisattva path;
you gentlemen should know that these are my children. This is like the opening of flowers so that the lotus seeds within may be seen.
Thirdly, for those of great capacity, the previous skillful means are set aside, and he speaks using provisional names, teaching only [the ultimate truth].
The unsurpassed teaching of the One Vehicle is as the Sūtra says: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the unsurpassed Way.
In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle; it is like flowers falling away while the lotus seed alone remains.

The above refers to the Trace Gate, while the following refers to the Origin Gate, which also contains three meanings. The Sūtra says: "I left home at a young age and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Attaining" (ti) refers to the manifestation of the traces of original giving; "I have truly been a Buddha since time immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas" reveals the fundamental reality by opening up the traces.
"For the sake of sentient beings, there is extinction and non-extinction"—in truth, there is no passing into extinction—this establishes the fundamental by setting aside the traces.
Because it combines both the Dharma and the analogy to encompass all these meanings, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma).
The *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan) states: Question: Is the "Lotus Samādhi" the Lotus Samādhi of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or is it the lotus flower of the plant kingdom?
Answer: It is certainly the Lotus of the Dharma (*dharmapuṇḍarīka*). Because the Lotus of the Dharma is difficult to understand, the plant lotus is used as a metaphor.

Those of sharp faculties immediately understand the principle and do not require a simile; they simply form an understanding of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. However, those of middling and inferior capacities have not yet... [text ends]
One must rely on analogies to realize that the lotus flower—a metaphor for easily understood phenomena—is used here to illustrate the lotus flower of samādhi, which is difficult to understand.

Therefore, there are three cycles of teaching (tripartite dharma-wheels) to accommodate the three faculties of sentient beings: for those of superior faculty, it is designated by its actual name (*dharmābhidhāna*);

for those of middling and inferior faculties, it is designated by its metaphorical name (*upamābhidhāna*). When discussing the three faculties together, both the dharma and the metaphor are presented. As for what is called a "sūtra" (*sūtra*), it is defined as "dharma."

The "Constant" (常) refers to the path of the knowledge and vision of the Buddha *Śāśvata-sad-dharma-padma-rāja*, which is followed equally throughout the three periods of time and remains unchanging from beginning to end;
hence it is called "Constant. The "Dharma" (法) refers to the rules and regulations that gather and sustain beings, transforming them so that they may attain Buddhahood;

hence it is called "Dharma. Regarding its wide propagation, there are four points: first, the compilation and translation as clarified at the beginning of the text; second, the transmission and universal dissemination by ancient Buddhas; third, [its arrival] in this land...
Regarding the fourfold upholding, our current master’s extensive praise of the words and meanings is exceedingly clear; by examining the text, one may see it for oneself.

The various intentions clarified therein are intended to cause students to broaden the paths of meaning and transmit the Dharma of the mind, so that they may inherit the established school without falling into empty pretenses.

As for the preface, it is like the wall at the entrance of a hall; if one wishes to enter the inner sanctuary, one must pass through the wall and the preface. If one wishes to explore the scriptural text...
One must clarify the introductory purpose.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Zhongnan.
Zhongnan is the name of a mountain; it is located south of Chang’an City in Jingzhao Prefecture. This mountain extends from afar...
The auspicious energy of this capital city finally coils and gathers here in the south; it is the seat of the Sage King.
The Grand Master formerly resided in these mountains. Regarding "Śākya," the translators explain that it is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren);
because he was able to benevolently nurture and transform sentient beings, it is the ancestral surname of the Tathāgata. Those who have left the household life take the Buddha’s—
As for the master’s surname, he followed that of his teacher; thus, the *Āgama* Sūtras state: "The four rivers enter the sea and no longer retain their original names.
Likewise, those of the four castes who leave the household life are all equally called Śākyas. "Xuān" (宣) was the master’s personal name (*hǔì*).

Because he left the household life following the Buddha, practiced the direct path, and proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to benefit sentient beings, he received this title. "Shù" (述) means to narrate.
This preface is intended to bring about the understanding of those who seek it.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the fundamental essence of all Buddhas’ descent of their spiritual power. The first phrase titles the scripture;
the second phrase provides a comprehensive judgment on the general purport of the entire sūtra, exhausting every aspect without exception throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The original intent of the appearance of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in this world is solely for the sake of the one great matter;
that is to say, to open, reveal, awaken, and lead sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

This "Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers precisely to the Great Wisdom of equality of the One Buddha Vehicle, intended specifically to distinguish it from the various knowledges and visions of the three vehicles and five vehicles. To speak of them separately:
When this is in the mind, it is called "knowledge"; when it is in the eye, it is called "vision. Furthermore, one must distinguish between what is experienced by oneself and by others.
Regarding one's own portion, the heart of true wisdom is transparently clear and the eye of pure wisdom perceives the five aggregates as empty.
Regarding the portion of others, the Buddha knows that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) of sentient beings is equal, and the Buddha sees sentient beings as the object [of his compassion].
Because they are to be delivered, the Sūtra says: "He knows the thoughts and mental inclinations of all sentient beings," and it also says: "With the Buddha-eye, I see all sentient beings.
For this reason, he employs skillful means to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to all, causing them all to awaken and enter [into it].
It is for this purpose that the Buddha appears in the world; therefore, it is said that his appearance is solely for the sake of this one great cause and condition. It is nothing other than this.
Because one reality alone is true while the other two are not, it is said that "the gate of skillful means is opened to reveal the mark of ultimate truth.
Therefore, Many Treasures praised, saying, "Excellent, excellent! All that has been spoken is indeed the truth. This single Dharma is what the Buddha has realized;
it is that which all Buddhas constantly protect and keep in mind within their hearts. Out of compassion, they turn it over to reveal it to the multitudes.
Because it has arisen, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the teaching for Bodhisattvas through the Great Wisdom of Equality, which is protected by the Buddhas;
when he preached it for the great assembly, sentient beings who heard it gave rise to great courage regarding the One Buddha Vehicle—this is called "opening the *Dharmapuṇḍarīka* through faith.
By the power of this faith, the jewel of the mind shines forth—this is called "opening the *Dharmapuṇḍarīka*. In all places...
Universally manifesting [the truth] is called "Manifesting the Lotus Sutra"; seeing with complete clarity and attaining certainty without doubt is called "Awakening to the Lotus Sutra";

the depth and distance of the place of vision being no different from that of the Buddha is called "Entering the Lotus Sutra"; and never departing from the stage of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) at every step is called "Realizing the Lotus Sutra.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the two characters "knowing" (jñāna) and "seeing" (darśana) are concise in expression yet comprehensive in meaning, fully encompassing all aspects.
One should say "seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing" (*darśana-śravaṇa-vedanā-jñāna*); only then will the meaning correspond fully to the six sense faculties. How is this known?

It is according to the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, which states that the luminous nature (*prabhāsvara*) possesses six thousand [qualities]: seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, and smelling, tasting, and touching with the nose, tongue, and body—these three are collectively termed "sensing" (*vedanā*);

that which is in the mind is called "cognizing" (*jñāna*). The Sūtra mentions only the first and the last—the two faculties of the eyes and the mind—and does not speak of the remaining four: the ears, nose, tongue, and body.

The body and the treatise, regarding their merits and defects, are clearly shown in four thousand [verses]; this indicates that the text is abbreviated. If one asks whether the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are the same as those of ordinary beings, the answer is:

the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are fundamentally no different. Furthermore, the Buddha’s teachings were opened for the sake of ordinary beings, not for the sake of Buddhas themselves.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the Buddhas of the ten directions, with one voice in harmony, addressed Ānanda, saying:
If you wish to recognize and know the innate ignorance that causes you to wander through birth and death—the very root of your bondage—it is none other than your six sense organs;

there is nothing else. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that will swiftly lead you to realize peace, liberation, and the wondrous, eternal stillness, it is likewise your six sense organs and nothing else. Thus, one knows that the six sense organs are pure.

Purity is identical to the Buddha; only then can it be called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because all sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-nature, which is no different from that of the Buddha.
Since beginningless time, they have been mired in delusion, unaware and unawakened, flowing along in the cycle of birth and death with no prospect of liberation.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, behold this with their path-eye and cannot bear to see them sink into such depths; thus, from the realm of truth...
Because he arises to manifest in the world, it is called the descent of the spirit. Through various skillful means, words, and parables, he expounds all dharmas;

this is for the sake of those sentient beings whose delusions are heavy and whose Buddha-nature is obscured, opening them up so that even dragon girls within the realm of animals may attain Buddhahood, Devadatta in the path of hell may receive his prediction, and those with wrong views [may likewise be transformed].
In the "Chapter on King Yanyan of the Ghost Realm Attaining the Dharma Master’s Degree," it is recorded that the asuras and the eight classes of beings shall all attain bodhi.

Human affairs and livelihoods are themselves the true aspect (*dharmatā*). Giving, precepts, meditation, recitation, snapping the fingers, and scattering flowers are originally the karmas of the heavens;
all shall achieve the Buddha-way. [The Buddha] addressed the assembly of śrāvakas and those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle in the presence of the Buddha.

It is taught that one should give rise to great faith and resolve; the Dharma for Śrāvakas is the king of all sūtras, for it causes all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, which is the single true path without duality or triad.

The Bodhisattvas open the net of doubts regarding the Dharma, and within the "Chapter on the Removal of Discrimination," the World-Honored One bestows predictions of attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment upon as many Bodhisattvas as there are motes of dust, thereby opening up the nine previous paths.
This is precisely the Buddha-vehicle: the Dharma-realm is equal, without distinction or partiality, forming a single, perfectly interfused, pure, and wondrous essence.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Wondrous Sound realizes this samādhi, it is called the "Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body.
It is illustrated by the metaphor of a high, vast, and great palanquin adorned with myriad jewels; it is revealed by the bright pearl within one’s garment—this is the ultimate state of True Suchness.
Furthermore, before the jewel was revealed, the various vehicles were separated and distinct, which was truly a provisional concealment—just as a bright pearl is hidden within a king’s topknot.
That which resides upon the king’s head is the object of veneration for the ultimate fruit. Once the faculties are purified, the provisional is opened and the real is revealed;
thus all shall attain the Buddha-way, just as that valiant general, having achieved great merit, is recognized by the king.

Having bestowed upon him the bright pearl from within his topknot, he opened it to reveal extensively the places where all Buddhas have practiced, as well as the immeasurable and innumerable merits of samādhi, thereby instructing him.
Having thus instructed him, he exhorted him to strive in cultivation and advancement, not wasting even a moment of time, desiring that he attain clear awakening.
Once awakened, he further required him to nurture and sustain this realization, never abandoning what had been attained before.
Merit advances toward Bodhi and enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), becoming equal to all sentient beings as they together attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Because all Buddhas desire to cause all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they appear in the world.
Therefore, the Patriarchs have stated: "One must understand that this encompasses the fundamental reason for the descent of all Buddhas into the world."

The significance of this Dharma is perfectly integrated; while each stage encompasses all stages, it is taught as having a sequential order, yet in principle there is no before or after, as they manifest one another in layers like a net of Indra’s jewels.
"Accumulating [the teachings] in Great Xia and emerging after those thousand years.

"Great Xia" refers to the Western Regions. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda accumulated the sublime meanings and compiled them into chapters, which were transmitted to that land and emerged more than a thousand years later.
It has been transmitted to China for over three hundred years.
Because the Dharma came from the West, it is called "transmission to the East" (Dongchuan Zhendan);

it is also called Zhendan, which is a slight variation of the Sanskrit sound, here translated as Shenzhou (Divine Continent), as this land is so excellent that many divine beings are produced there; the region of Donghua spans five thousand li.
It is but a single island of water within the great ocean, also called "Chixian" (the Red District) because it lies to the south; thus it is near the flourishing brilliance of the *Li* trigram.
From the Yongkang era of the Western Jin, when the Lotus Sūtra was transmitted here, until the Great Tang, more than three hundred years have passed.
Some claim that from the Han to the Jin there were over three hundred years, but this is not because the *Lotus Sūtra* existed prior to the Western Jin.
The period prior to this is also like the preface by Zu Wen to the *Four-Part Vinaya* (translated during the Yao Qin dynasty), which states:

"It had been compiled in Central India for over a thousand years, and its translation and transmission to the Eastern Xia [China] have been for nearly four hundred years. This is based solely on the number of years since the scripture first appeared in this land.
The *Gantong Zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance) states that from the Jin to the Tang dynasties there were over three hundred years; the meaning of this is also the same.
This [text]:
during the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin dynasty, the Dharma-protector Zhu Fahu, a bodhisattva from Dunhuang, first translated this sutra in Chang’an’s Qingmen Gate,
titling it *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma).
The capital of the Later Wei was Luoyang; therefore, it is called Western Jin Chang’an. Chang’an is the ancient Xianyang. Qingmen is the southeastern gate of the capital.

Dunhuang is a place name located in Longxi Commandery. "Bodhisattva" is fully rendered as *Mahā-bodhi-sattva*, which translates to "Great Path-Mind Being who Accomplishes the Teacher of Sentient Beings.
His secular surname was Zhu and his given name was Fahu (Dharmarakṣa). He was a man of Pingyuan.
Residing in Dunhuang, his transformative influence spread to the capital, where people revered his virtue; thus he was titled the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva.
Initially, he translated the Sanskrit original of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, completing it in ten fascicles.
During the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty, and during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin, the śramaṇa Kumārajīva from Kucha subsequently translated this sūtra,
titled *Miaofa Lianhua* (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma).
The Central Plains were in turmoil, and Emperor Yuan fled east to establish his capital at Jianye; thus it is called the Eastern Jin.
As for Later Qin, this refers to the Yao clan who usurped the title [of kingship]; their surname was Yao and their name was Chang. "Hongshi" is the era name of the Qin dynasty.
Since the Jin was the orthodox lineage and the Dharma Master translated the scriptures during the Qin period, both are mentioned. Qiuci is a kingdom in the Western Regions.
His name was Śramaṇa; this is translated as "Diligent and Quiescent. He left home to practice the Way, diligently cultivating all manner of goodness and extinguishing all evils.
His clan name was Kumārajīva; this is translated as "Child-Longevity. By nature he was exceptionally brilliant and his refined talent was transcendent;
though he had the age of a child, he possessed the wisdom of an elder. His virtue flourished in that region, and his fame spread to this land. Former Qin [Emperor Yao] Xing held him in deep esteem.
I have respectfully dispatched General Lü Guang as an envoy to the Rong kingdom to raise an army;
subsequently, I have translated these seven fascicles of this sutra into their final form within the Xiaoyao Garden in the ancient city of Chang’an.
Translated later by the Śramaṇa from North India, Jñānagupta, at Daxingshan Monastery during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty;
the title is the same, *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The ruler’s surname was Yang, the state name was Da Sui, the era name was Renshou, the monastery was named Daxingshan, and [the origin] was North India.
Some say that "Shendu," "Xiandou," and "Yintu" are slight variations of the Sanskrit sound; here it is translated as "Yuezhi.
Because the land is numinous, it produces many sages and worthies, like the moon which is pure, clear, cool, and illuminates the world.

The territory of the Western Regions spans ninety thousand *li* in circumference, roughly divided into five regions according to the cardinal directions. Here, we designate the northern region for the sake of brevity.
They differ from the other four *jñāna*s; *Jñānagupta* means "Possessor of Supreme Virtue" (*zhìdé*) and *Dharmagupta* means "Treasury of the Dharma" (*fǎzàng*).
Both were masters from South India who, during the Renshou era, traveled from the Western regions of India to the East, reaching the Sui dynasty.
They subsequently translated this sutra at Xingshan Monastery, and their accounts are likewise the same.

Kumārajīva’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in eight fascicles was composed as a refined literary work; however, between the two versions—the Qin and the Jin—there were considerable additions and deletions, and it is rarely heard being recited.
As for the three overlapping sūtras whose textual themes are presented alternately, those currently venerated and upheld all follow their respective original texts.
The translations were made three times, and the phrasing and intent of each differ; whichever was most esteemed at the time has been transmitted as the "Qin edition.
For those who wish to consult them, the sutra is contained within the Tripitaka, while the *Bai* [commentary] is in three fascicles.
As for the remaining chapters, sections, and individual verses, they are not without their own traditions; as these are fully detailed in the introductory catalogs, they are not recounted here.

The twenty-eight chapters of the Jin translation, the twenty-eight chapters of the Qin translation, and the twenty-eight chapters of the Sui translation differ significantly in the titles of the chapters and sections, as well as in their wording and individual verses; such variations are extremely numerous, yet they do not lack a coherent lineage.
Since the calendar preface contains a full account of this, it is not explained here.
Now, as for the descent of spiritual power upon the Sacred Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), no great sage could have brought about its transformation without such an event.

*Vana* means "forest" and *gṛdhrakūṭa* is translated here as "Spiritual Vulture Peak" (*Língjiù*). Because vultures gather on this mountain and its nature is spiritual, it is named "Spiritual" (*Líng*).

Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak), also known as the Mountain of the Vulture’s Shape because its form resembles a vulture, is the place where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Located approximately fifteen *li* northeast of Rājagṛha, it is now called Lingyue (Numinous Mountain) because of the mountain’s spiritual power. Here, the multitude of spirits were born with talent and insight so sharp and refined that they surpassed their peers;
were it not for a Great Sage who could have enlightened them, how could such excellence have been revealed? This Great Sage is [the Buddha]... who has reached the ultimate.
Ultimately, when the fruit is perfected, the Great Awakened One is called the Tathāgata. If we represent this through the Dharma:
the mountain is the Dharmakāya, the spirit is Prajñā, and the vulture is Vimukti. The mountain possesses the spirit, and the spirit arises from the vulture;
the vulture relies upon the mountain. Thus, nature possesses wisdom, and wisdom arises from practice; practice manifests within nature. The mountain is immovable, for nature is without [change].

The transformation is manifested through the mountain, which represents nature; nature is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which, though devoid of movement or stillness, is not obscure regarding its numinous awareness.

This numinous awareness is manifested through the vulture, which represents wisdom; wisdom is itself *prajñā*. Numinous awareness arises from the Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), and wisdom arises from practice;

the Vulture Peak thus represents practice, and practice is itself liberation (*vimukti*). These three virtues are perfectly integrated and inconceivable; only then can they be called "wondrous contemplation. Such is the reason why.
If one wishes to perceive the objective realm to clarify the mind during daily activities and enter the Way through hearing, one does not depart from names and forms to realize the Dharma-body.

When this is true for a single dharma, it is so for all dharmas; thus, the boundless and wondrous realms of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses will simultaneously manifest upon the tip of a single hair.
As practice continues long-term, the samādhi becomes refined and pure, emerging from within oneself.

Yet, it is not through deliberate mental effort that the hands guide the scrolls so they are never grasped, nor that one constantly reads this sutra with the mouth remaining silent while reciting all the scriptures universally.
Were it otherwise, it would be like the chirping of spring birds by day or the humming of autumn insects at night—driven merely by the winds of nature, devoid of any meaningful intent.
Since the clear instructions of the former masters are as earnest and repeated as this, how could one fail to realize this inconceivable truth?
The reach of appropriate transformation cannot guide the mind without the conditions of former causes.
When transformation suited to the time reaches sentient beings, only those who have planted deep roots in the past are able to awaken and enter.

If there were no fundamental affinity, by what means could they be inspired and guided? As in the Trace Gate, during the time of the Buddha Mahāvyūha, the sixteen princes served as the four [leaders].
The assembly further expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, saying:

"Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were converted at that time, are none other than you, O bhikṣus, and the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa—just as it was described in the 'Expedient Means' chapter [of the Sūtra] regarding the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging during the time of Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. Regarding the four [classes of followers]...
"Planting the seeds of the Mahāyāna among the multitude" refers to what the Sūtra says: "At that time, was the one who constantly disparaged this Bodhisattva anyone else?
It was none other than these five hundred bhikṣus in this assembly who have now attained non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding this, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus) states that there are three ways of encountering [the teaching]: first, encountering it by meeting [the teacher]; second, constantly receiving the Mahāyāna; and third, among such a group...

Throughout this interval, they have already achieved [liberation] and have not reached the present day. Had they encountered one another, and had those who had encountered the Great Vehicle been met instead with the Small, these individuals would still not have been fully exhausted by now.

Now that they have returned to hear the teaching of the Mahāyāna, if we were to consider only their encounter with the Small and disregard their encounter with the Great, then those who were not yet liberated during the interval would not have been fully exhausted even until today. Would it not be so?
This refers to those who first received the Great [Vehicle] up until those who attained the Way after his parinirvāṇa.

Thus, at the completion of the Rșipatana Garden, the capacities were distinguished as Small and Great; and at the Bequeathed Charge by the Golden River, the teachings were differentiated into the Half and Full [Vehicles].
Regarding the "Garden of the Immortals": formerly, two sages resided within this grove;

one was named Ārāḍa Kālāma, who had attained the concentration of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*), and the other was named Udraka Rāmaputra, who had attained the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
When the Tathāgata first studied their teachings, he practiced them until he attained realization; however, knowing they were not the ultimate goal, he then departed for the Nairañjanā River.
It is here that one cultivates the path to Nirvana and attains perfect enlightenment without rising from one's seat; it is also called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva).
In ancient times, this grove was a place where herds of deer gathered in competition, governed by two leaders of the deer—one good and one evil.
The good leader’s body was the color of the seven precious jewels. At that time, there was a king named Brahmadatta who, in the course of a hunting expedition, arrived at this place.
When he wished to shoot at the herd of deer, the Good Deer Lord informed the king of the situation and begged for his compassionate mercy.

Moved by these words, the king vowed never again to eat meat; thus, the herd of deer was able to preserve their lives. The Good Deer Lord is now the Tathāgata, and the Evil Deer Lord is now Devadatta.
As stated extensively in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), it is also said that the Nava Grove originated from this.
The tree is named "Completion" (Gaocheng) because from ancient times he has cultivated the practices of loving-kindness and patience, and in his final body attained Buddhahood;
having realized the Way, he immediately went to this grove to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude to repay this debt of gratitude.

Some say it should be called the "Immortal Garden" (Xianyuan), but it should rather be called the "Tree of the Way" (Daoshu), as the Buddha attained the Way beneath this tree; thus it is now so called.
To report the fulfillment of his great success, although it occurred at the Bodhi Tree, there were differences in the capacities for awakening when preaching the True Doctrine;

thus, one must speak of the "Garden of the Immortals" (*xiānyuàn*) to clarify both meanings within a single phrase. If one speaks only of the "Bodhi Tree," then because the capacities differ, the meaning of the Garden of the Immortals would not be manifest.
Regarding the division of capacities into small and great, the *Tiwai jing* states: "Initially, at the Deer Park, he preached [the teaching of] birth..."
The Dharma of cessation was attained by the five Kālāmas and others as they became Arhats; eighty thousand devas resolved their minds upon the Great Way.
As for the Golden River: when the Tathāgata manifested illness, he was between the śāla groves west of Kuśinagara;
that location was near the Jambūnada River. "Jambūnada" is the name of a tree; when its fruit ripens and falls into the river, it dyes the sand golden.
Regarding the "Bequeathed Testament" (*chengjin guling*): when the Tathāgata wished to enter parinirvāṇa, he gave instructions for the future and charged his disciples with his final affairs.
As for the distinction between the "Half" and the "Full": "Half" refers to the meaning of the Hīnayāna, as its principles were not yet complete;

"Full" refers to the meaning of the Mahāyāna, as its principles are perfectly fulfilled. At the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Mahāyāna was originally taught, yet Subhadra instead realized the [Hīnayāna].

As a result, all other listeners realized the intent of the Dharmakāya Buddha; although the underlying capacities and conditions varied, [the Buddha] specifically cited the Garden of the Immortals and the Golden River to mark the beginning and end, thereby encompassing the intermediate stages within their meaning.
Is it not the case that when the teaching is applied according to the capacities of those who ride upon the vehicles, there is no basis for scrutinizing their ultimate, sublime convergence?

Since the vehicles upon which those of inferior knowledge and vision rely differ according to the timing of the teaching and the capacities of the recipients, what is the use of scrutinizing or exhausting the inquiry into the ultimate, supreme convergence?
As the Sūtra says: "Those of little wisdom who delight in the lesser Dharma do not believe themselves to become Buddhas."
Thus we know that those who withdrew from their seats numbered five thousand because they were a class of people whose pride had increased;
these individuals of inferior capacity, having engaged in superior practice, considered themselves satisfied with minor gains.

Upon hearing the Buddha praise the Tathāgata’s wisdom as being profoundly deep and difficult to understand, they felt a sense of despondency and unconsciously withdrew. The Buddha, too, [perceived this].

There are five reasons why [the Buddha] remained silent and did not restrain him: first, if he were allowed to remain in his seat, those of inferior capacity would be dull and weak, unable to overcome their own limitations;
second, upon hearing the sublime Dharma, they would surely give rise to doubt and slander, falling back into the cycle of birth and death;
third, by waiting until he has departed before speaking, the Buddha manifests his knowledge of the capacities of beings; fourth, it serves as a reprimand conveyed through words.

He rebuked them so that they might repent and advance toward the Buddha Vehicle; fifthly, he desired that others would know their faults and surely reform them, thereby avoiding the arising of overweening pride.
The bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred disciples was a manifestation of his joint veneration for the traces of esoteric transformation.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was a bhikṣu under the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, whenever he encountered the fourfold assembly, he would always proclaim:
"I do not slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. At that time, those who heard him were unable to believe or accept his words, but instead gave rise to contempt and slander.
Because of this lack of faith, they sank for a long time into the cycle of birth and death. Once the karma of their slandering the sutra was exhausted, they were able to be born among humans.
Because he had previously heard the Mahāyāna Dharma, his wisdom was superior; when the Buddha came, he constantly followed the Buddha’s transformation.
Although he later regressed from the Mahāyāna and practiced the Hīnayāna, he has now received the Buddha’s prediction that he shall attain Bodhi. As stated in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging":
"Those who at that time constantly disparaged this bodhisattva are these five hundred bhikṣus in the present assembly. And as stated in the "Chapter on the City of Illusion": [the same applies].
Regarding the karmic conditions from past lives between myself and you, my disciples numbering five hundred shall all receive their predictions of enlightenment.
You should know that having now received this revelation, all of these are the manifest traces of the secret transformations through which we revered the Buddha in the past.

As it is said in the sutras: "Among my disciples, there are various skillful means—some concealing within while manifesting without—that are not of a single kind. If I were to describe them in full...
If one speaks of the assembly, doubt will inevitably arise; yet this serves to further clarify that even the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was but a proximate condition.

To investigate its ultimate origin, it truly stems from King Bimbisāra. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "They are all but the lingering dust of Jñānabhibhū, and together they are the remaining achievements of King Bimbisāra."
Therefore, the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious omens served as the source for the teaching that inspires and requests [the Dharma].

Upon entering meditative absorption, he emitted light, rained down flowers, and shook the earth; the fourfold assembly was filled with doubt, Maitreya requested a resolution, and Mañjuśrī led the response.

This was the initiation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to awaken the minds of the multitude. Their earnest requests increased all the more, through which they came to know that the manifestation of omens gave rise to the teaching.
Source. Emerging from meditative absorption, he extolled his virtues and set forth the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Knowing that the time had come, the Buddha arose from samādhi and praised the profound wisdom of all Buddhas, desiring to fully expound its fundamental nature.

He harbors the aspiration to manifest the Great Matter, to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, and further to demonstrate that the Way is the same throughout the three periods of time and that compassion is uniform and equal;
thus, his every appearance in the world is nothing other than for the purpose of enabling others to attain the Buddha-wisdom. This is the general outline.
The decaying house is brought into the universal system of the Great Way.
When the decaying house is set ablaze, the sons do not perceive it; out of pity, the father skillfully provides three carts.

Although these carts were originally non-existent, he leads them out of the house. Once they know they have escaped, he bestows upon them equally the great carts, filling the realm so that sentient beings find no further restlessness.
Because the Buddha is stained with compassion, he skillfully expounds the three vehicles; yet these vehicles are fundamentally non-existent, his intention being merely to lead beings forth.

Once they have realized their own limited selves, they are equalized through the great transformation. He uses the house to accommodate them, the vehicles to suit their capacities, and the vehicles to connect them to the truth.
His practice of civilizing through teaching is like the ruts of a carriage; thus, he employs the small vehicle as a means for entering the Great Vehicle.
The phantom city preserves the legacy of past conditions so that they do not fall into oblivion.
In the past, the Great Transformation Buddha intended for all sentient beings to ascend to perfect enlightenment;

however, because the faculties of sentient beings were dull, they regressed midway. Knowing their capacities, the Buddha taught the existence of *nirvāṇa* along the way, causing them to rest for a time.
Having known that they have ceased [their toil], he leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.
It is like a caravan leader who wishes to guide a multitude out of a perilous path and toward a place of treasure;

when the people become weary and wish to turn back, the leader perceives their disposition and, midway along the road, conjures a city for them to rest. Once they have attained peace and security, he causes them to proceed once more.

The manifestation of evolution illustrates the provisional establishment of cities as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, leading those of the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle without causing them to fall away from their former conditions.
The parable of the tied jewel clarifies that the fundamental nature is ever-present;

for those who have left the household life, the Dharma serves as their kin, following the instructions of teachers and friends. This principle is like a perfect sphere, yet the poor lack the merit [to perceive it].
Wisdom is like that impoverished son who seeks a teacher for instruction, as if visiting a close acquaintance; the admonitions enter his ears like a jewel tied within one’s clothing.

Because he was deluded in the interim, he was like one intoxicated and unaware; now, having received this revelation, he is like one suddenly awakened from sleep, finally realizing that the jewel of his nature has always been present.
Some say that the two characters "li-xing" (principle-nature) should be changed to "su-zhong-li" (the principle of past seeds).

This is the "original existence" (pūrvabhava), illustrated by the parable of the tied jewel. Now, although the principle is inherently complete within one's nature, it is not manifest unless it is opened.

Opening [the mind] is for the purpose of manifesting the nature; the nature is itself the principle. The principle is not something external to phenomena, and phenomena do not transcend the principle.

Since cultivation arises from nature, and complete cultivation is identical to nature, one should seek this profound significance rather than letting one's emotions remain as cold and distant as ice. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Suddenly encountering a wise person..."

When he was instructed regarding that jewel and his wishes were fulfilled according to his heart, bringing about great abundance, he finally realized that the divine jewel is not obtained from without.
This illustrates how awakening is achieved through various means, such as digging a well until the source is revealed.
The mind cannot be moistened by the Dharma like one who is parched with thirst; studying the teachings to clarify the mind is like digging a well.

Keeping the mind focused on the realm of the Buddha is like excavating a high springhead; the mind is not easily awakened, for as with a well that requires much labor, it must be accomplished through many skillful means.
The phrasing and meaning are vividly present; the metaphors and explanations are profoundly remote.

This concluding praise draws upon the eight preceding sections of the sūtra, wherein the words and meanings are clear and manifest, forming a coherent composition, while the metaphors and expositions are exceedingly deep and far-reaching.

Were it not for Great Compassion that universally rescues those submerged in the stagnant currents of delusion, and the Single Ultimate Compassion that saves those whose natures have become obscured and lost—
Great Compassion and the Single Ultimate Compassion being but different names for the Buddha— if this wondrous scripture were not the result of the Great Sage’s vast pity and mercy...

Practicing compassionate relief with single-minded perseverance and tireless effort, exhausting the depths of one’s compassion, how could one fail to pull out those mired in stagnation and deliver them from the stream of birth and death?
How could one fail to rescue those in a state of stupor and restore their original luminous nature? Thus, while compassion can bestow happiness, it is pity that can extract suffering;

if we follow the intent of this present sutra regarding the world-transcending original aspiration, it is to extract the suffering of the two deaths and bestow the bliss of the three virtues upon those in the six realms.
As long as karma and afflictions have not been forgotten, birth and death remain entirely present;

even for those of the Two Vehicles who have emerged from the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm, the *parināmika* (transformative) rebirth still persists, let alone those who sink into empty quiescence and have not yet realized the perfect and eternal. As for the minor Bodhisattvas, they merely suppress their afflictions while practicing the causes, yet they are not yet free from fault.

Now, [the Buddha] completely uproots these for them and causes them to realize Nirvana. This is precisely what the Sūtra says: "The Buddha sees that sentient beings are poor, lacking in merit and wisdom."

Because they have entered upon a perilous path, this sutra is preached so that when Bodhisattvas hear the Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed, and all Arhats shall surely become Buddhas.

From the Han to the Tang dynasties, over six hundred years elapsed; throughout this time, more than four thousand fascicles of various scriptures were examined, yet the one most widely upheld was this.
There is no sūtra that surpasses this one.

Since ancient times, throughout the period from the Han to the Tang dynasties, although other sūtras were numerous, those who transmitted them were rare; yet this Lotus Sūtra alone has been recited and practiced most extensively.

This is truly because its teaching is sublime, exhausting the profound and subtle depths of the Buddha’s wisdom, and furthermore, because the timing, the circumstances, and the karmic seeds of sentient beings have converged.
Because [the time] was ripe,

it was not that the capacity of the recipient and the teaching did not strike one another; rather, this was the lingering dust of the excellence of [Master] Ji (Jizang), and both were heard with deep reverence as the remaining achievements of King Wei (Weijing).
The teaching arises for the sake of those with capacity, and that capacity awakens through the teaching; when the teaching accords with the capacity, reverence arises upon hearing it.
Is this not perhaps the remaining capacity left behind from the world of the Great Penetrating Buddha, or the residual power of the transformation of King Vairocana of the Dust-Aeon? It is indeed so.
I have immediately prefaces and synthesized them at the beginning of each scripture.

Since the Supreme Vehicle of Perfect and Sudden Enlightenment cannot be lightly discussed, I have now woven together the origins [of these works] at the head of the scriptures; hence, it is said, "immediately."

May we soon purify the six sense faculties and look up to the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One; may we swiftly accomplish the four virtues and follow the profound path to the Land of Bliss.

This vow of our ancestors is precisely based on the scriptural passages from the two chapters of the *Bhaiṣajyarāja* and *Samantabhadra* in the Lotus Sūtra, concerning how the six sense faculties perceive their objects.

Having given rise to various faults, I now uphold this wondrous scripture to wash away all defilements; through faith and veneration of the Compassionate Honored One, may I participate in the sublime assembly and be born in Tuṣita.
May I swiftly fulfill the four kinds of ultimate virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and ascend to the highest grade to be born in An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Because of realizing the true and eternal, may I remain unchanging and non-transmigrating, dwelling in immovability like Mount Sumeru.

Because Mount Mi possesses the virtue of permanence, it attains peace and bliss, and is thus forever free from all suffering; this is the virtue of sound, for like the resonance of a gong within a vessel that issues forth, it is joyful.
Because it realizes the true self, it attains great sovereignty, being without obstruction like the wind in space;
this is the virtue of the self. Because it returns to original purity, its radiance penetrates everywhere, and it views all worlds as a dream.

The "Middle Matter" refers to pure virtue. Those who aspire for the Land of Bliss enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realize the Light of Eternal Quiescence (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*).
"Eternal" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Light" is Prajñā; "Quiescence" is Liberation (*vimukti*). Whichever single body one mentions, it is endowed with these four virtues;
whichever single virtue one mentions, it is endowed with the three bodies. If the four virtues are individually correlated with the three bodies, "Eternal" is the Dharma-body.
Purity does not abide in signs; the cessation of feeling and perception is Prajñā-wisdom, which corresponds to the *Sambhogakāya*.
My [attainment of] mastery corresponds to *Vimukti* (liberation), which corresponds to the *Nirmāṇakāya*. The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into numerical categories.
One, four, four, three—perfectly interfused and sovereign, there is no fear; nirvāṇa is bliss. "Mysterious Way" (*xuányóu*) means profound and remote.
This Dharma is profound, far-reaching, subtle, and inconceivable; only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust its depths.

Nevertheless, though it is thus, it does not depart from daily life; within the slightest flicker of the mind, it is perfectly complete. A single thought-moment is perfectly luminous—what is distant is near.
To turn one's back on this and pursue elsewhere is to lose it by a thousand miles. Someone said: "The Southern Mountain..."

The introduction discusses primarily the meaning of the provisional traces (*jia*) and does not speak of the fundamental gate (*benmen*), as previously cited in the cases of Bhaiṣajyarāja, Samantabhadra, Aśoka, and the King of Majestic Power regarding the *Nirmita-āyuṣpramāṇa* (Life Span) chapter. Whether these refer to the traces or the fundamental, please reflect upon this yourself.
The promotion and praise [of this teaching] are inexhaustible.

The Buddha’s intent is profound and subtle; his wisdom is as deep as the ocean. Now I shall speak of it, for it is the foremost among all sutras in its wide dissemination and its supportive exaltation, such that no one can exhaustively fathom it.
"To be perpetually bequeathed to all future generations" means this.
"Perpetually" (*yǒng*) means eternally; "bequeathed" (*yí*) means to present as a gift; "all future generations" refers to those who come to study hereafter.

It is said that by now composing this preface to widely praise the *Lotus Sūtra*, it shall remain inexhaustible throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and he vows to attain perfect enlightenment together with all sentient beings.
The meaning of what was stated in the Preface is as follows:

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Volume One, it is said that the mind-dharma is wondrously luminous, possessing the fruit within the cause; as the lotus flower is fragrant and pure, with a lotus within its stamens, so too does Buddha-nature abide therein.
The dust of delusion cannot stain the lotus; though it is in turbid water, the lotus cannot be defiled. The flower represents the cause, and the lotus represents the fruit.

Within the soil of the mind, which is subject to afflictions, there exists the Tathāgata-body; within the low-lying mud, there is the seed-nature of the lotus. Through wisdom, the lotus is revealed; facing the sun, it blooms.
As the cause is purified, the fruit becomes luminous; as the flower opens, the lotus appears. Thus, the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
The petals fall and the lotus is formed; the Dharma-nature is primordially true, and the lotus is fundamentally pure.
These meanings are elucidated by the text, which is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The scroll may be rolled up or unrolled, and its chapters are designated in sequence.
Hereafter, whenever the terms "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka" and "sūtra scroll" appear, they shall be treated according to this precedent and will not be explained again.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the sovereign was surnamed Yao and named Chang; he established his capital in the region of Guanzhong, which was called Daqin (the Great Qin).

The Buddhist Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are termed the Tripiṭaka. "Piṭaka" means a "storehouse," for it stores the mind, nature, consciousness, as well as the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the Buddha.
Because he practiced the true and eternal Great Meaning and was able to penetrate the Dharma-nature, serving as a teacher for the world, he is called a Dharma Master.
Kumārajīva—translated here as "Child-Longevity"—was originally from Kuci; his innate nature was clear and敏捷 (nimble), and even at the age of a child, he possessed the wisdom of the long-lived.
By imperial decree of the Qin King, he translated the Sanskrit texts into Chinese.
The Introduction to the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Chapter One.
"Introduction" (*nidāna*) means to relate; it relates the intent behind the arising of this *Lotus Sūtra*. "Chapter" (*parivarta*) refers to a section.
Thus have I heard. Ānanda said to himself: "Such is the wondrous meaning expounded in this wondrous sutra, which I have received from the Buddha."
"Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha—beginning from the initial inception of his resolve and ending with the conclusion of his teaching—is called "at one time.
"Buddha" is translated as "the Awakened One," meaning one who has fully realized the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
He was staying in Rājagṛha. The Tathāgata was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of King Bimbisāra in the kingdom of Magadha.
This [mountain] is called "Spiritual Vulture" because vultures possessing spiritual nature gather upon this mountain.

Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—“bhikṣu” being translated here as “mendicant,” for they beg for food to sustain the body and beg for the Dharma to save the mind—the assembly numbering twelve thousand people was gathered together. “Together” (jù) means assembled in one place.

All are Arhats. This means they have attained non-arising (*anutpāda*), severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), and emerged from the suffering of saṃsāra so as not to be born again within the three realms.

All outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted. That which constantly flows forth as various evils is called "outflow" (*āsrava*); since Arhats have completely departed from these, they are called "those who have already [departed]" (*kṣīṇāsrava*).
Exhausted.
No further afflictions remain. The three poisons are already exhausted and will not arise again.

Having attained one's own benefit, one is free from old age, sickness, and death, and has escaped the triple world; yet, while one is merely able to benefit oneself, one has not yet attained ultimate benefit.
He exhausts all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*).

When the karma of the three realms of existence is simultaneously exhausted, his mind attains mastery and is no longer bound by the birth and death of the triple world; his mind wanders in empty tranquility, which is called "self-mastery" (*ātma-vaśitā*).
As for their names: the former praises their virtues, while the latter reveals their personal names.
Ājñātakauṇḍinya means "One Who Has Realized the Fundamental Limit," because he has seen the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
Mahākāśyapa: "Mahā" means "Great. "Kāśyapa" is the clan name, translated as "Great Drinker of Light" (Dīpamkara).

Because his light swallows all other kinds of light so that the radiance of others cannot manifest, it is called "Pippala," which is the name of a tree; he prayed to the deity of this tree and thereby obtained a son.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa: "Uruvilvā" is translated here as "Pawpaw Grove" (*kōmoku-rin*); he was named after his place of residence.
Gayā-Kāśyapa: "Gayā" is translated here as "River"; because he obtained this son by praying to the river deity, [he was so named].
Nadīkāśyapa—this is translated as "City Prayer," for he was obtained by the city deity through prayer.
Śāriputra—this is translated as "Son of the Body," for he is the son of a mother with excellent physical bearing.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana—this is translated as "Bean-Gatherer," which is his ancestral clan name; his personal name was Nyagrodha, which means "Banyan Tree.
Because he prayed to the tree deity and thereby obtained a son, [he was so named].
Mahākātyāyana—this is translated as "Fan-Rope. He lost his father at a young age; because his mother raised him, he no longer served another man.
The son was bound to his mother like a rope tied to a fan.

Aniruddha; alternatively, he is called Anuruddha, which translates as "Free from Poverty. This is because he offered a meal of wild rice to a pratyekabuddha ninety-one kalpas ago, and as a result of that karmic retribution, his provisions have been fully sufficient ever since.
Kapphiṇa means "the lunar mansion Kṛttikā"; because he obtained this son through prayers to the Kṛttikā star, he is so named.
Gavāmpati means "the cow-chewer"; having formerly been a cow, his residual habits still remain, such that after eating, he chews his food over again.
Revata; this means "Star Chamber," as he was obtained through prayers to the constellation Revatī.
Piṅgalavatsa; this means "Residual Habit," for despite five hundred lifetimes as a Brahmin, his residual habits were not eliminated, and he remained arrogant toward others.
Bakkula means "Good Appearance," so called because his physical form was beautiful.
Mahākoṭṭhila means "Great Knee-Cap," named after his physical characteristics.
Nanda—here translated as "Joyful"—was originally a cowherd who questioned the World-Honored One regarding the matter of tending cattle.
The Buddha’s response was that his mind was liberated through joy, and he thus left the household life.
Sundarananda—*Sundara* here means "lovely" or "beloved," which is the name of his wife; *Nanda* here means...
Nanda was the Buddha’s own younger brother; because his lustful mind was heavy, he took pleasure in his wife.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: *Pūrṇa* here means "Full"; it refers to having obtained a son through prayers, thus fulfilling the heart's wish. *Maitrāyaṇī* here means "Compassionate" (*maitrī*).
*Putra* (the word for "son") here means "daughter," indicating that she was the daughter born of Maitrāyaṇī. This refers to the one produced by Maitrāyaṇī. She was "Compassionate."
The daughter of a woman and her mother are collectively called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Subhūti is here translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kōshō), because from the moment he was first in his mother's womb, he knew emptiness and stillness;
he is also called "Venerable Well-Appearing" (Zen-gen), because auspicious signs appeared at the time of his birth.
Ānanda: This means the Venerable One of Joyous Celebration; when he was born, all manner of celebrations gathered and the entire nation rejoiced.
Rāhula: This means "The Obstructor"; he is the son of the Buddha. When the Buddha desired to renounce the world, his father, the King, said:
"If you have obtained a son, you shall follow your own will. Thus, being obstructed by his son, he did not immediately renounce the world.

Thus, those who are widely known and recognized—those whose perfect knowledge and wondrous discernment are honored, and whom the multitude reveres as virtuous—are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This refers to the great Arhats and others; since the assembly of twelve thousand raised [their voices] and the remaining twenty-one were not named, it is so stated.
...and so forth.

Furthermore, there were two thousand individuals, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). These two thousand also belonged to the assembly of bhikṣus; however, their names and virtues are not mentioned here, as the text merely cites their number.

Those whose afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted—namely, those who have attained the first, second, or third fruits—are called persons in training (*śaikṣa*). Those who have attained the fourth fruit are the noble ones (*ārya*).
When a person has seen that craving is forever exhausted and what was to be done has been accomplished, they are called one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī— *Prajāpatī* here being translated as "Loving Path" (Ānandā)— was the Buddha’s maternal aunt.
He was accompanied by six thousand followers; these six thousand nuns were all his attendants.
Among them was the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula. Yaśodharā means "Flower-Color" (Huase) in this language;
she is the mother of Rāhula.
Sixth, together with his retinue; the term "retinue" here also refers to the assembly of nuns.
There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. "Bodhisattva" is translated here as "one with the mind of the Way," and "mahāsattva" is translated as "great being."
All have become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. *Anuttara* is translated here as "unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*);

*samyak* is translated as "rightly equal" (*zheng-deng*). The term "rightly equal" serves to distinguish it from "erroneous equality," meaning that the nature of the Buddha and that of sentient beings are non-dual.
*Saṃbodhi* is translated as "right awakening" (*zheng-jué*), for it is the ability to correctly awaken to and comprehend all phenomena.

There are three types of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression in terms of sequential stages; second, non-retrogression in terms of courageous practice; and third, non-retrogression in terms of right mindfulness.

In all these cases, one attains *dhāraṇī*—which here means "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). It protects the good by causing it to arise and obstructs evil so that it does not occur. It is a comprehensive synthesis.
Because they maintain [the Dharma], they possess the eloquence of joyful speech; their wisdom and talent are swift and their joyful speech is inexhaustible.
They turn the irreversible wheel of the Dharma; these bodhisattvas of sharp faculties are the wise ones capable of turning it, possessing the quality of non-retrogression.
The wheel is the sublime Dharma that is turned.
To reverently serve and comply with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas with a profound mind is called making offerings to the Buddhas.
To plant the roots of all virtues under the various Buddhas and extensively sow the causes of goodness is called planting the roots of virtue.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas; because their virtue is weighty, they always receive the Buddhas’ mention of their names and praise of their merits.
They cultivate the body with loving-kindness (*maitrī*); loving-kindness can bestow happiness, and thus they cultivate the body thereby.
One skillfully enters the Buddha’s wisdom. The mind of the Buddha is great compassion; to be able to cultivate great compassion is to skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
One penetrates great knowledge.
Among all forms of knowledge, the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme. To penetrate great knowledge is precisely the vision of the Buddha.
He knows;
he has reached the other shore, having ultimately attained the other shore of bodhi.
His fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and his name and reputation are renowned in distant lands.
They are able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings; their realization is most profound and those they transform are most numerous.
Their names are as follows: the former part praises their virtues, while the latter part sets forth their names.

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: This is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). The *Siyi jing* states that although he expounds all dharmas, he does not grasp at the marks of dharmas; thus, he is named Wondrous Virtue.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: The *Lengyan jing* states: "Because I do not observe the auditory faculty itself, but rather observe the observer."
Therefore, whenever sentient beings suffering in the worlds of the ten directions hear his voice, they all attain liberation.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta is also named Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"When this bodhisattva walks, the worlds of the ten directions all tremble; when he sits, the lands of the seven jewels shake simultaneously."
Therefore, this bodhisattva is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Great Power Attained).
Regarding the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent (*Sadāprarudita*), the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"For the sake of a single sentient being, this bodhisattva follows them for immeasurable kalpas without abandoning them; even if that being does not accept transformation, this bodhisattva never abandons them for even a single thought-moment."
This mind is called "constant diligence" and is the "unresting Bodhisattva.
The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "A period of Ganges-sand eons constitutes one day and night;
thirty such days constitute one month; twelve such months constitute one year. Throughout immeasurable eons, one encounters innumerable Buddhas and cultivates all [virtues]."

The name "One Who Receives Prediction Only After Completing the Holy Life" (*brahmacarya*) refers to the two aforementioned bodhisattvas who, though similar in meaning, each have their own specific intent:
"Ever Diligent" (*sadā-vīrya*) means that for the sake of sentient beings, whether they be kin or strangers, one never abandons them;
"Unceasing" (*anikṣipta-dhura*) means that for the sake of the holy life, one has long cultivated wholesome causes without ever allowing the mind to become lax.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the *Pǔchāo jīng* (Sūtra on Universal Transcendence) states: "He constantly uses his sincere mind to penetrate the nature of all wisdoms and expounds them for others.
Because he has no greed or attachment toward any precious things and extends his hand to assist others, he is named Ratnapāṇi."
Regarding the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that since beginningless kalpas he has acted as a Great King of Physicians to save all from suffering and affliction;
in the Bhadrakalpa, he shall later attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Rocana.
The Bodhisattva Courageous Giving (*Vīradatta*) signifies that the bodhisattva arouses a courageous mind, opens the gate of great giving, and universally benefits all beings.
The Bodhisattva Jewel Moon (*Ratnacandra*) signifies that the bodhisattva cherishes the supreme jewel to benefit sentient beings, like the clarity of the moon.
"Coolness" can remove the affliction of heat;
as for the Bodhisattva Candraprabha (Moonlight), the meaning is that the Bodhisattva possesses great wisdom which, like the light of the moon, shines coolly upon the world.

The Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra: in terms of meaning, this refers to a bodhisattva who has long cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), whose defilements are exhausted and whose wisdom is luminous, like the pure, full moon.
The Bodhisattva Mahābala: in terms of meaning, this refers to a bodhisattva who possesses all merits and great power, capable of delivering and rescuing [sentient beings].
He is the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Power (*Amitabala*). In terms of its meaning, this refers to the boundless and incalculable power of the bodhisattva’s profound and great compassion.
The Bodhisattva *Trailokyavikrāmin*. In terms of meaning, this refers to a bodhisattva whose merit is profound and who possesses great wisdom that transcends the world.
The Bodhisattva *Bhadrapāla* means "Good Protector" (*Śubharakṣita*). The *Suyāmasaṃparigraha Sūtra* states that he is well able to protect [the Dharma].
If all sentient beings hear his name, they will certainly attain *sambodhi*.

Maitreya Bodhisattva—here translated as "The Kindly One" (*Maitreya*)—is described in the *Suyāmasūtra* as follows: "If there are sentient beings who see this bodhisattva, they shall immediately obtain the *maitrī-citta-samādhi* (the samādhi of the mind of loving-kindness) at that very moment."

Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa: in terms of its meaning, it refers to a bodhisattva who, throughout successive kalpas, diligently practices various samādhis until the Dharma-jewels are accumulated.
Although the number of texts concerning this in the Indian scriptures is extremely large, when transmitted to this land [China], not even one in ten has survived;
consequently, for the most part, no etymological explanations have been produced.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Guide (*Nāyaka*): the *Suyāma-sūtra* states that one who gives rise to great compassion for those with wrong views and causes them to enter the right path is called a "Guide.
Together with such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering eighty thousand, there was a multitude of eighty thousand; of these, ten are briefly enumerated.
Eighth, for this reason, the conclusion states: "Thus, all these together.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra—here called Tiandi (Heavenly Lord) or Dishi (Lord Śakra)—is the designation combining both the Chinese and Sanskrit names for the king of the second heaven of the desire realm, the Trāyastriṃśa. The term Trāyastriṃśa means "thirty-three," [derived] from the *sūtra*...
On the summit of Mount Meru there are four peaks, each with eight celestial palaces where the Eight Heavenly Kings reside; collectively, these are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
It is accompanied by its retinue of twenty thousand devaputras. This retinue of twenty thousand refers specifically to the various devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, there is the name "Renowned. This single title generally refers to the various devaputras mentioned below.
"Moon Devaputra" refers to the deva of the lunar palace.
"Universal Fragrance Devaputra" is alternatively said to be the deva of the stellar palace, who dwells in the North Star (Beichen) at the center, with all the stars surrounding him like a court.

The Devaputra Ratnaprabha (Treasure Light) is also called the Devaputra Suryamandala (Sun Palace). Because his radiant jewel-flames shine down upon those of lower station, he is called "Treasure Light.
The *Guanfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samadhi of Contemplating the Buddha) states: "The Sun King’s blazing flames emit a thousand rays of light.
These three devaputras are internal ministers of Śakra-devānām-indra, similar to the prime ministers and high officials of today.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings— Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, Virūpākṣa of the West,
and Vaiśravaṇa of the North— each lead their respective retinues and dwell in the four directions as external ministers to Śakra,
much like modern-day military governors.
Together with his retinue of ten thousand devas— namely, the multitude of devas who are the retinues of the three higher devas and the four heavenly kings— the Deva Īśvara,
the lord of the fifth heaven of the desire realm, the Nirmāṇarati, manifested [this] through his own supernatural power.
Because they enjoy their sensory realms according to their own minds, they are called "sovereign" (*vaśavartin*).
The Great Sovereign (*Maheśvara*) Son of Heaven is the lord of the sixth heaven of the desire realm, the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

All things that are superior and exquisite are manifested by others for his enjoyment; he does not expend his own effort. This is superior to the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*).
Therefore, the Palace is called the Abode of Maheśvara.
It is accompanied by thirty thousand devaputras as its retinue; these are the hosts of devaputras belonging to the celestial lords of the two higher realms: Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
The Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World. "Sahā" is translated here as "Endurance," meaning the capacity to endure and tolerate all suffering and affliction.

"Not knowing how to depart" refers to the world as a process of constant flux; that is, the past, present, and future are called the "three periods of time. "World" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation:
east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below are called the "worlds. Thus, the three periods of time and the ten directions are capable of... [end of fragment].

The realm of patience (*kṣānti*) belongs to that which is governed by the Brahmā King; therefore, he is called "King. This indicates his royal status, and it is only in the following passage that the name of the king is specifically pointed out:
Śikhin Mahābrahmā. In the Sanskrit language, *Śikhin* is translated as "Fire" (*jvālā*). The Honored One, the Great Brahmā, having cultivated... [the path].
The Fire-Light Samādhi transcends the realm of desire and constitutes the state of Brahmā-rāja, who is the sovereign of the Sahā world-system within the trichiliocosm.

Regarding "the Great Brahmā of Radiance" and so forth: "radiance" refers to the gods of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) from the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha) upward—including the Heaven of Infinite Light (Apramāṇābha) and the Heaven of Luminous Sound (Ābhāsvara)—as well as these celestial kings and their retinues, whose karmic fruition is exceptionally sublime.

Because his body possesses radiance, he is called Mahābrahmā, the Great Brahmā; likewise, Maheśvara at the summit of the Form Realm heavens is also named Maheśvara because he has attained mastery within the Brahma heavens.
He was accompanied by twelve thousand sons of gods from his retinue— namely, the assembly of sons of gods belonging to the various Brahma kings.
There were also eight dragon kings, including Nanda Dragon King (which is translated here as "Joy"), whom the people of Magadha heard of.
Their names were all Sarvananda (meaning "All-joyful").
Upananda the Dragon King—here translated as "Good Giver"—was the elder brother of Nanda.
Sāgara the Dragon King—here translated as "Salt Sea"—was so named after his dwelling place within the ocean.
The Naga King Sāgara (Andhaka); here translated as "Many-Headed," he manifests many heads upon a single body to symbolize that from within a single dharma, immeasurable dharmas emerge.
The Naga King Takṣaka; here translated as "Manifesting Poison," he manifests poisonous forms to transform sentient beings.
The Nāga King Anavatapta; this is translated as "Without Heat. At the summit of the Snowy Mountains, there is the Lake Anavatapta, where this dragon dwells.
The Nāga King Manasvin; this is translated as "Great Body," for by means of his exceedingly virtuous mind, he manifests great supernatural powers to protect the Dharma.
Benefiting sentient beings.
[The names of] the Nāga Kings such as Utpala and others; "Utpala" here translates as "dark-colored lotus pond," and the nāgas dwell within these ponds, manifesting their virtues through the lotuses.

Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues. Among the hosts commanded by the eight great nāga kings were four kiṃnara kings—here translated as "song deities," for the celestial king employs these deities for his music and song.
