The Dharma Kinnara King: When the Buddha preached the Dharma, the various devas sang with stringed instruments to praise the Buddha;
the Sublime Dharma Kinnara King performed sublime musical performances to praise the Buddha.
The Great Dharma Kinnara King extols and chants the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna;
the Dharma-Holder Kinnara King maintains the True Dharma by disseminating it through music.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues. There were four classes of *gandharva* deities and their followers;
there were four *gandharva* kings—here translated as "Fragrance-Smeller" (*xiu xiang*)—who subsist on fragrance and provide music for the Heavenly Emperor.
"Lè Qiāntuópówáng" (樂乾闥婆王). "Lè" (樂) means *zhòng* (橦)—pronounced with the initial *dào* and the rhyme *jiāng*—referring to acrobatic feats such as performing on a pole or being tossed upside down.
"Lèyīn" (樂音) refers to the Gandharva King; it refers to those who perform drum music.
The Gandharva King Surūpa performs the most beautiful acrobatic feats;
the Gandharva King Susvara plays the most exquisite music.

Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues. Among the hosts commanded by the four kings of music, there were four asura kings—so called because they lack upright features and their appearances are hideous.
The Asura King Bāli; here it is translated as "Most Victorious," because he is able to overcome all objects of sensual desire.
The Asura King Kharaskandha; here it is translated as "Broad Shoulders," because he is able to bear the Dharma.
Vemacitrin, the Asura King— here translated as "Pure Mind"— is the father of Śacī, the consort of Śakra. Rāhu, the Asura King—
here translated as "Obstructing"— possesses a body of vast length and breadth, and with his hands he obstructs the sun and moon.
They shrouded the radiance.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers; these were the four kinds of assemblies of asuras.
There were four garuḍa kings—so called because their feathers are golden in color.
The Garuḍa King Mahātejas possesses the greatest majesty and power, surpassing all his peers.
The Garuḍa King Mahākāya dwells atop a great tree spanning the four continents;
when he spreads his two wings, they extend three million three hundred and sixty thousand li apart.
The Great Full Garuḍa King fans the waters with his wings to part them, entering the sea to devour nāgas until he is fully satisfied.
The Wish-Fulfilling Garuḍa King has a wish-fulfilling jewel upon his neck.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
There were also the retinues of the four garuḍas, as well as King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī. (Vaidehī means "Reflection";
Ajātaśatru means "Broken-Finger," so called because his little finger was broken; thus, this "Broken-Finger King" is the son of "Reflection," and the two are referred to together as mother and son.)
Together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues— the various attendants of the human kings—
they each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, grasping his feet with their hands and paying homage to the Buddha.
Having bowed, he withdrew to one side and sat down.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly; monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen circled around him.
As the sutra describes the causes for the Buddha’s emission of light, Śāriputra and the assembly gave rise to doubt and made their request, thereby initiating the discourse. Mañjuśrī... [text ends].
Ānanda assisted the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of sentient beings], like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound;

this refers to the assembly of those who have attained realization and received predictions of enlightenment upon hearing the Dharma from the Buddha according to their capacities. As for the others, although they heard it in advance, their minds were not yet clear;
thus, they serve as the distant cause for those who will form karmic connections [with the Dharma] in the future.
To offer worship and respect means to serve and provide offerings with solemn reverence and prostrations; this signifies that the meaning extends to the three karmas and the six sense objects.

Joining the palms and bowing at the crown of the head, rising with diligence and kneeling at the feet, constitutes physical worship (*kāya-pūjā*). Narrating their merits and speaking words of praise constitutes verbal worship (*vāk-pūjā*).
Never for a moment forgetting the Buddha’s benevolent virtues constitutes mental worship (*citta-pūjā*). Thus, one serves the six sense objects.

The aforementioned matters constitute offering; the single nature in accord with suchness constitutes offering according to principle; the perfect interfusion of principle and phenomena constitutes offering of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

To revere and praise is to hold them in the utmost sincerity and veneration; to be moved by their profound virtue is to hold them in deep respect; to discourse upon their Way is [the practice of] respect.
"Virtue" is praise; "alas" is an exclamation of being beyond reach.
It refers to the assembly of all bodhisattvas.
To expound the Mahāyāna sūtras is called "expounding the sūtras"; to discourse upon the true reality (dharmatā) is called "discourse."
That which possesses great power and can carry [beings] is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
It is named the "Infinite Meanings. Within a single Dharma, it gives rise to infinite meanings; as the *Sūtra of Infinite Meanings* states: "Two Dharmas, three paths, and four fruits.
The two Dharmas are the gradual and the sudden. The three paths are the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The four fruits are those of the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha.
It awakens to the four stages of noble fruition—those of the bodhisattva and the Buddha.
It is the teaching for bodhisattvas; it instructs bodhisattvas in the meaning of the Mahāyāna through all these aforementioned dharmas.
It is that which the Buddhas protectively keep in mind; all Buddhas protectively keep in mind this *Anantārtha-sūtra* as it teaches bodhisattvas.
The Dharma is that which is to be protected and kept in mind.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra—having finished preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*—he sat down cross-legged.
As for the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), he first placed the right foot over the left foot, and then [the left foot over the right].
Placing the left foot upon the right foot is called *paryaṅka* (the full lotus posture).
He entered the *Anantārthaviṣaya-samādhi*. "Samādhi" here is translated as "right concentration.

If one merely speaks of it in empty words without practicing it, how could one ever accomplish the ocean of immeasurable meanings and the various gates of samādhi? Therefore, the Buddha entered meditative absorption for this purpose.

The person acts as a model; body and mind are unmoving. The body being unmoving is the concentration of form (*rūpa-samādhi*); the mind being unmoving is the concentration of nature (*dharmatā-samādhi*).
At that time, *māndārava* flowers rain down. "Rain" is pronounced with a departing tone, falling from the heavens. *Māndārava*—this...
*Sumana* (Cloud-like Delight) is also called the Small White Flower;
*Mahāmandārava* is translated here as Great Delight and is also called the Great White Flower;
*Mañjūṣaka* is the Small Red Flower.

The *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers are great crimson blossoms. The rain of these four kinds of flowers symbolizes the forty stages of practice: the stages of abiding, progress, and penetration (*sthiti-prasthāna-abhimukha-bhūmi*).
Their scattering upon the Buddha symbolizes the cultivation of the causes of merit within the realm of the Buddha.
Together with the great assembly, this represents making offerings to all beings so that they may all attain Buddhahood.
Throughout all Buddha-worlds, pervading the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, the earth shook in six ways.
This signifies that when the ground of the mind’s essence moves through wholesome thoughts, the six sense-faculties are all transformed.
"Excellent.
At that time, in the assembly, there were immeasurable numbers of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs from the Assembly on the Meaning of the Immeasurable, as described above.
Upāsaka means "pure-faith male"; upāsikā means "pure-faith female.
[This includes] devas, nāgas, yakṣas, various heavenly kings and their retinues, as well as various dragon kings and their retinues.
The yakṣas— here translated as "valiant spirits"—
the gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, are all explained as above.
"Human beings" refers to those of the human world.
"Non-humans" refers to great seers (*maharṣi*), asuras, those in the hells, hungry ghosts (*preta*),
and so forth, as well as minor kings— those minor kings who are like scattered grains throughout the world.
The Wheel-Turning Sage Kings are those of the four wheels—gold, silver, copper, and iron.
This great assembly, as listed above, has attained what they have never before experienced.
They say that while the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth were things never seen in the past, they have now witnessed them; thus they speak of the "unprecedented."
There were those who, filled with joy, joined their palms; beholding these signs, they rejoiced, joined their palms in reverence,
and gazed upon the Buddha with single-mindedness, focusing their entire hearts as they looked up to the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.

Between the Buddha’s eyebrows was a single white tuft, one zhang and five chi in length, its color like white jade or snow; it curled between the brows and had eight facets with a hollow center like a tube.
From within this, a great radiance was emitted. Thus, the two eyebrows represent the two extremes of existence and non-existence, while the tuft between them represents the Middle Way.
It illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction. Since the east is the locus of movement, the number eighteen thousand symbolizes the eighteen realms (*dhātus*).
There was nowhere it did not pervade; its light was so magnificent that there was no place it did not fill.
Below, reaching as far as the Avīci Hell— where "Avīci" means the Hell of No Interruption, and where sentient beings constantly undergo various sufferings without cessation—
and above, reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven— where this is translated as the Ultimate of Form— down to the hells and up to the realm of form.
There is nothing that the light from the center of his crown does not illuminate universally.
Within this world and all worlds above it,
he sees the entirety of those lands and the realms of desire and form.
The sentient beings of the six destinies— devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals— are divided into six according to their karma,
each proceeding toward its own destination. Furthermore, one sees eighteen thousand lands in that realm.
The Buddhas of the present; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who currently preach the Dharma;
and "hearing" refers to hearing with the ear the sūtras and dharmas spoken by those Buddhas, for the Buddha is the one capable of preaching the Dharma, and these are what is preached.
And he also saw those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, the monastics— both monks and nuns— from other worlds,
as well as the upāsakas and upāsikās, the lay men and women from other worlds.
There were those who had practiced and attained the Way, who, having cultivated and restrained their minds, practiced the noble conduct and entered the Path;
furthermore, he saw the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the Great Vehicle.
"Various causes and conditions": "cause" refers to the wholesome mind and "condition" refers to the wholesome object; because the mind and its objects are not identical, they are called "various.
"Various faiths and understandings": one gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding toward all phenomena.
There are various characteristics; the gateways of the Dharma have immeasurable and differing characteristics.
To practice the bodhisattva path—wherein the six perfections and the myriad practices constitute the "path," and their actual implementation is termed "practice"—is to walk this way.
Furthermore, one sees various Buddhas; that is, the Buddhas of other directions who have entered parinirvāṇa.
Here, "parinirvāṇa" is translated as "extinction. When the fuel of the karmic conditions has been exhausted, the fire of the response accordingly perishes; this is called extinction.
Furthermore, one sees various Buddhas, as well as Buddhas from other directions,
after their parinirvāṇa and following their passing into extinction,
by means of the Buddha’s *śarīra*— here translated as "bone-body."

He erected a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels. In the Sanskrit language, *stūpa* is translated here as "a high and prominent place"; it is a monument for the Buddha constructed from seven kinds of rare treasures.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought. It was because he saw the land through the light that he gave rise to this reflection.
Now, World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, you have manifested signs of spiritual transformation and displayed the miraculous power of manifesting a purified land.
By what causes and conditions? For what cause and for what reason?
Yet there is this auspicious omen; there is this manifestation of a marvelous and extraordinary sign.
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One—meaning Śākyamuni Buddha—has entered into samādhi, having entered into right concentration after preaching the sutra.
This is inconceivable. These auspicious signs cannot be fathomed by the mind nor discussed by the mouth;
they manifest rare events, extraordinary occurrences that do not exist in the world.
"To whom should I ask? He reflected within his own mind, considering whom he should question and who might be able to answer.
Continuing his search for one capable of answering, he further thought and spoke thus:
This Mañjuśrī is the foremost among the great bodhisattvas in the assembly;
he is a son of the Dharma King. The Buddha is named Dharmarāja, and this bodhisattva is the Teacher of the Buddha, thus he is named Dharmarājaputra (Son of the Dharma King).
Having already drawn near and made offerings; for a long time, he has personally attended upon, approached,
and served with physical and mental reverence and offerings past immeasurable Buddhas— those who were the objects of his close attendance.
One must surely have seen this rare phenomenon. Having served the Buddha for so long, he must certainly have witnessed such a miraculous sign.
I shall now ask; I shall now ask one who can understand this.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all formed this thought;
these various people likewise formed the same thought.

This is the light of the Buddha; it is the light emitted by the Buddha, the manifestation of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the manifestation of the application of his transformative spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
Whom should I now ask? I am reflecting on whom I wish to question.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva wished to resolve his own doubts. Although Maitreya Bodhisattva’s rank was that of Equal Enlightenment (Sambodhi), he remained obscured by doubt regarding the auspicious signs he had perceived;
desiring to seek clarification and resolution, he [addressed the Buddha].
Furthermore, he observes the fourfold assembly— namely, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
as well as the gods, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others, who constitute the eight classes of beings.
The minds of the assembly are as previously described; now, whom shall we question?
Thus he questioned Mañjuśrī, asking both for himself and on behalf of the assembly.
For what reason and by what cause did he ask the Buddha about the manifestation of auspicious signs?
For what reason was there this manifestation— namely, the emission of light and the signs of supernormal power (ṛddhi)— referring to those which had appeared above?
He emitted a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows,
which illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction; within those illuminated realms,
he saw all those Buddhas— indeed, he beheld all those Buddhas.
The adornment of the realm and the embellishment of the external environment.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning— having already fully described the doubts of himself and others—
now once again proclaims his previous intent in verse.
He asked in verse: "O Mañjuśrī, Guide, for what reason do you utter these verses? By what causes and conditions do you utter these verses?
Why does the white tuft of hair between your eyebrows emit a great light that shines everywhere, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds throughout the entire universe?"
It rained *māndārava* flowers; the verse says it rained two kinds of white flowers.
It rained *mañjūṣaka* flowers; the verse says it rained two kinds of red flowers.
There was sandalwood-scented wind, which did not exist previously.
It gladdens the hearts of the multitude. The manifested signs are so pleasing and appropriate that they accord with the minds of the great assembly.
For this reason, it refers to the signs of the mental objects manifested above.
The earth was entirely adorned and purified; through supernatural transformations, it became majestic and clean.
Furthermore, this world, this Sahā world, shook in six ways—namely, first shaking, second shaking everywhere, and third shaking everywhere equally—but it shook in only one place.

It is called "moving" when it moves the four continents; it is called "universally moving" when it moves a great trichiliocosm; and it is called "equally and universally moving" when it performs each of the six modes—namely:
first, rising; second, surging; third, shaking; fourth, roaring; fifth, awakening; and sixth, vibrating—with each individual term possessing three distinct meanings.
At that time, the fourfold assembly—referring here to the aforementioned four groups—all rejoiced.
Beholding the auspicious omen, their hearts were filled with joy;
their bodies and minds felt refreshed and at ease, experiencing within them a sense of exhilaration and delight as before.
I have attained what has never been attained before; such a thing as this has never existed in the past.
The radiance from between his eyebrows and the light from the hair-tuft in the center of his brow shine toward the east.
Although light is fundamentally all-pervasive, it first illuminates the eastern direction.
The eighteen thousand lands within the range illuminated by it all became like the color of gold;
such was the illumination of the Tathāgata’s light from the tuft between his brows.
From the Avīci Hell above to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) below, throughout all worlds, he alone universally manifested the upper, lower, and middle regions.
Pervading the sentient beings of the six realms as described above,
they pass through the cycle of birth and death, dying here and migrating there.

The causal conditions of good and evil karma—the causes and conditions of the good and evil deeds performed by sentient beings, and the resulting retributions of beauty and ugliness—how they receive retributions that are excellent or wretched according to their karma:
all of this is seen here; it is all clearly perceived within the light of a single hair-pore.
Furthermore, he beheld all the Buddhas; moreover, he saw the Buddhas within eighteen thousand lands.
These Holy Lords, Lions, Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones, and Sovereigns among the Sages, were like lions, the sovereigns among the hundred beasts.
He expounds the sūtras, flowing forth and explaining the words and principles of the scriptures with supreme subtlety;
his meanings and logic are foremost, subtle, profound, and far-reaching.
His voice is pure, and the sound of the Dharma he preaches is clean, bright, and immaculate.
They emit a soft and gentle sound; from this sound issues compassion, gentleness, and kindness.
They instruct the various bodhisattvas, and the assemblies instructed by each individual Buddha number in the hundreds of millions, so vast that they cannot be calculated.
The Brahma-voice is profound and subtle; "Brahma" signifies purity, while the meaning is deep and the words are exquisite,
causing people to delight in hearing it and inspiring them to wish to hear it throughout the eighteen thousand lands of the various worlds.
He expounds the True Dharma; he elucidates the correct and true Dharma of liberation.
Through various causes and conditions and innumerable skillful means, he reveals the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood.
By means of immeasurable parables, he cites countless events as metaphors.
It illuminates the Buddha-dharma; through the light of wisdom, it clarifies phenomena just as light illuminates objects.
It awakens sentient beings, bringing enlightenment and clarity to all classes of living beings.
If a person encounters suffering or meets with worldly calamities and distress, [it provides relief].
They grow weary of old age, sickness, and death; they weary of and abandon the four marks that cycle again and again.
For them, he preaches *nirvāṇa* and preaches the supramundane bliss of cessation, which brings an end to all suffering.
The attainment of the four fruits of sainthood and the transcendence of the three realms is called "the end of suffering."
If there is a person who possesses merit, who has a measure of merit,
who has previously made offerings to the Buddha, who has had a karmic connection through having cultivated offerings to the Buddha in the past,
and who aspires to the supreme Dharma, being resolved to seek that most excellent Dharma.

For them, he teaches the Pratyekabuddhas. To these [beings], he teaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination so that they may contemplate the world and realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If there is a son of the Buddha—a Bodhisattva who practices the Great Name is called a "son of the Buddha"—[he is included here].
They cultivate various practices; they resolve their minds to practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds, seeking unsurpassed wisdom and seeking the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
For them, he expounds the pure path; for these beings, he teaches the pure way of the Buddha.
Mañjuśrī, as for the person to whom I am speaking, I abide here;
I abide in this Sahā world. What I see and hear is such as this:
my eyes behold the realm of the Buddha, and my ears hear the voice of the Buddha; such are its characteristics.
And there are thousands of millions of matters, as well as various characteristics of phenomena;
such are the many things seen and heard, their signs being exceedingly numerous.
Now I shall speak briefly. It is difficult to describe them in full, so I shall provide a concise explanation.
I behold that land; my eyes behold those pure buddha-fields of the various Buddhas and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— many bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
through various causes and conditions, and through various wholesome mental states conditioned by their respective objects.
They seek the Buddha-way; they cultivate the causes of Buddhahood in order to achieve the Buddha-way.

Some practice giving, or perform acts of relinquishment, such as gold, silver, and coral—treasures from the ocean formed by the condensation of sublime vapors, their color red and lustrous like that of trees.
Their forms are called coral, pearl, and maṇi.
Pearls and maṇis of the oyster and conch varieties are harvested from the moon’s radiance and formed into true pearls and maṇis;
this is translated as "Nengsheng" (Capable of Sanctity), which is the Cintāmaṇi (Wish-fulfilling Jewel).
Tridacna shells and agate; great sea shells like the *śakaṭamukha* (cart-mouth), which are large marine conchs;
and the refined essence from within stones, its color red and lustrous like the brain of a horse.
Vajra-treasures: hard and sharp vajras and various precious gems;
slaves and mounts: male and female servants and vehicles for transport; jeweled palanquins and litters:
those pulled by beasts are called *nan* (palanquins), and those carried on the shoulders are called *yu* (litters), all adorned with jewels.
They give with joy; with a joyful mind, they scatter and bestow their gifts, dedicating them toward the Buddha-way.
They turn the merit they have cultivated toward the Buddha-way, vowing to attain this vehicle—vowing to obtain this Great Jewel of the True Vehicle.
The foremost in the three realms; the most supreme among the three realms;
praised by all Buddhas; one who is constantly extolled by all Buddhas;
or there may be a bodhisattva who is able to practice giving.
"Four-horse precious carriage": a carriage drawn by four horses adorned with jewels;

"railing and canopy": that which runs horizontally is called a *lán* (railing), and that which stands vertically is called a *shǔn* (fence)—referring to the railings of the carriage—and the jeweled canopy decorated atop the precious carriage.
Adorning one's carriage and giving it away— this refers to such acts of giving as providing carriages and the like today.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas, and one sees givers who give their own flesh,
hands, feet, and personal wealth as offerings.
Giving away one's wife and children constitutes the gift of internal wealth.
Seeking the Unsurpassed Way means seeking the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattvas who, having previously given away their hands and feet, now give their heads and eyes.
Rejoicing in giving. With joy and aspiration, they wish to give to sentient beings, seeking the wisdom of a Buddha. The reason they give is to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
Mañjuśrī—[the Buddha] addressed Mañjuśrī.
I have seen various kings; I have seen those kings of men in that world and others who went to the presence of the Buddhas,
each going to the abodes of those various Buddhas to inquire about the unsurpassed path,
requesting instruction on the unsurpassed path from the Buddhas.
He then abandons the blissful land—the land where one enjoys the pleasures of the five senses—and the palaces and ministers and concubines;
for the palaces are that upon which he relies, and the ministers and concubines are that which he loves.
He shaves off his beard and hair; even that which is most cherished, the beard and hair, is likewise shaved away.
He dons the Dharma robes, leaves the household life, and receives the full precepts, wearing the three Dharma garments.
Or, seeing a Bodhisattva acting as a bhikṣu, he leaves the household life to become a member of the Saṃgha.

Dwelling alone in leisure and tranquility; dwelling by oneself in a solitary, empty, and quiet place, one delights in reciting the scriptures, meaning the mind finds joy in reading and reciting Mahāyāna sūtras.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who are courageous and diligent; being resolute is called "courageous action," and being vigorous is called "diligence."
Advancing without retreating,
he entered the deep mountains, distancing himself from the clamor and dust of the world to dwell in seclusion within mountain valleys.
There he contemplated the Buddha-way, contemplating with right mindfulness the sphere of the Buddha’s practice and observing the illumination of dhyāna.

Furthermore, he saw those who were free from desire; he also saw people who were weary of and detached from the five desires, constantly dwelling in seclusion and always residing in empty, quiet, and peaceful places, deeply cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is translated here as "quiescence" (*śamatha*); they have entered deeply into the gates of samādhi and abide in meditative absorption.
The essence of tranquility is true dhyāna.

One attains the five supernormal powers (abhijñā): the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, and the power of miraculous transformations; these are called the five supernormal powers, excluding the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
Furthermore, he saw Bodhisattvas sitting in meditative absorption with palms joined;
dwelling securely in dhyāna, they sat upright with palms joined, reciting ten million gāthās—“ten million” being a vast number—and gāthās are here translated as "verses" (頌).

He praises the Kings of Dharma. Having spoken of meditative stillness (*dhyāna-śama*), he further praises the Kings of Dharma: "Without meditation there is no wisdom; without teaching there is no realization.
Thus, to settle in meditation while praising the Dharma is to teach through silence; to praise the Dharma while settling in meditation is to remain silent while teaching.
Furthermore, he saw that the Bodhisattvas possessed profound wisdom and firm resolve; their wisdom was deep and far-reaching, and their character was steadfast.
They were able to question the Buddhas; with wisdom both firm and deep, they skillfully questioned the Buddhas.
Having heard it, they receive and uphold it all; according to what they hear, they remember it firmly and are able to receive and uphold it completely.

Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha—here, "sons of the Buddha" and "bodhisattvas" are used interchangeably—who are fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Meditative concentration serves to gather the distracted, while wisdom serves to dispel dullness; the equal maintenance of concentration and wisdom is called being "endowed."
He was sufficient in employing immeasurable metaphors and using countless matters as illustrations to preach the Dharma for the multitude;
he elucidated for others the Dharma that he had attained.
They delight in preaching the Dharma; having attained the profound joy of the Dharma, they preach it tirelessly.
They transform bodhisattvas and guide all the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
They shatter the hosts of Māra—those who oppose the True Dharma and lead others astray are called the hosts of Māra—and by means of the True Dharma, they bring them back to the right path.
The eyes blaze away all evils, which is called "destroying Māra.

Furthermore, one strikes the Dharma drum. Within the intersection of the four great elements, a sound is produced that expounds the meaning of the Great Dharma; this is called "striking the Dharma drum."
Furthermore, he saw the Bodhisattva sitting in tranquil silence, seated in peaceful stillness, with devas and nāgas showing him reverence;
all the celestial kings and nāga kings came to pay him homage, yet he did not feel joy.
Even when great nāgas came to show respect, he remained in accord with the nature of phenomena; the Bodhisattva dwelt in emptiness from the very beginning and was not affected by it.
Joy is the abandonment of dhyāna.
Furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest emitting light; dwelling peacefully in the forest, he radiates pure light to rescue those from the sufferings of hell.
To deliver others from the pains of hell with a heart of great compassion is the dhyāna of compassion.
Causing them to enter the Buddha-way; transforming the body of the path of suffering and entering the Buddha-way. Briefly, "to be weary" is called sleep, and "deep sleep" is called slumber.
Sons of the Buddha, you have never been so diligent before.
Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha who never sleep, walking in the groves; they practice the Way in the forest as straight as a sūtra,
diligently seeking the Buddha-way, and with tireless effort they seek entry into the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he saw those who possessed the precepts, fully receiving and upholding the pure great precepts, their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) being without flaw.
Their conduct of body and speech was called "dignified deportment"; they were sincere, meticulous, and pure, without any transgressions or violations.
Pure as a precious jewel; their observance of the precepts is as clean and pure as a precious jewel, as they seek the path of the Buddha.
Through the merit of upholding the precepts, they seek the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, they see the sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience, able to endure humiliation while dwelling in that power of patience.
Those who possess overweening pride, those who treat with contempt those who practice superior cultivation,
those who revile and strike them, those who utter evil words from their mouths and carry out blows with their hands—
all these he is able to endure. He is able to endure all the afflictions caused by wicked people.
They seek the Buddha-way through the power of patience; they seek the Buddha-way through the power of forbearance.
Furthermore, they see that Bodhisattvas are free from all frivolous laughter; when the mind is scattered by frivolous laughter, its departure leads to tranquility.
As well as the retinue of delusion. To deny cause and effect is called the retinue of delusion.
"To draw near to the wise" means to stay close to those possessed of wisdom.
"To single-mindedly eliminate confusion" means to single-mindedly remove the obscurations of confusion that hinder the Path.
He concentrated his mindfulness in the mountain forests, practicing the cultivation of right mindfulness while dwelling in the mountains for hundreds of millions of billions of years—
a phrase used to indicate the great length of time—
in order to seek the Buddha-way; that is, he sought to attain Buddhahood through the practice of wisdom that is free from delusion and distraction.

Alternatively, one may see Bodhisattvas with various delicacies, foods, and drinks: "delicacies" (*yáo*) refers to mixed dishes, while "fine food" (*shàn*) refers to excellent meals; "drinks" (*yǐn*) refer to various syrups, and "food" (*shí*) refers to rice and flour products.

There are also a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions; "a hundred" is a general designation and does not necessarily mean exactly one hundred types, such as those medicines made from *artemisia* (*shù*) and *notoginseng* (*cán*). "Decoction" (*tāng*) refers to the rounded [preparation] of these medicinal ingredients.
Distributed.

Offered to the Buddha and the Sangha. Providing for the Buddha and giving to the Sangha refers to renowned garments and superior robes—garments that are famous and robes that are of excellent quality.
"Price worth ten million" means a high price.
Or it refers to "priceless robes," meaning robes so exceedingly precious that they have no price in the world;
these are offered to the Buddha and the Sangha as the objects of veneration.
There were ten million billion kinds, including all the various items below:
sandalwood jewel-houses, houses adorned with precious sandalwood incense wood,
and many exquisite bedding sets— numerous wonderful and fine sets of red bedding.
He offered it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; he gave it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
It was a pure grove, with gardens for strolling and viewing and forests for providing shade.
Flowers and fruits flourished there, and such were the features of the grove.
Flowing springs and bathing pools— springs for drinking and pools for washing—
are objects offered to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Such offerings as these collectively encompass all the various items mentioned above.
Various and subtle; each individual object is refined, exquisite, and beautiful.
One rejoices without weariness. If one gives with vigor, joy will be without end, and thus it will endure for a long time.
Seeking the unsurpassed path, one delights in renunciation without weariness in order to seek the ultimate Way.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescence. Although the Dharma of quiescence is fundamentally inexpressible, they preach it through skillful means out of compassion.
They provide various instructions, preaching various Dharmas to teach, admonish, and inform others.

Among the countless sentient beings in the assembly being transformed, some saw the Bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena. With wisdom, he observed that the essential nature of all phenomena is devoid of dual characteristics;
fundamentally, they possess no distinct characteristics, being uniformly empty and quiescent.
It is like empty space; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally quiescent, like the great void.
Furthermore, one sees that the sons of the Buddha have minds free from attachment, their minds unstained by any conditions.
By means of this wondrous wisdom—wherein a mind free from attachment is called wondrous wisdom—one seeks the unsurpassed path; one seeks the unsurpassed path by means of wondrous wisdom.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, [reside] within those various lands where the Buddha has passed away.
Afterwards, they made offerings to the śarīra—here referred to as the "bone-body. Internally perfumed by precepts and meditative concentration, it was not shattered by the pestle and mortar;
with single-minded reverence and veneration, it was as if the Buddha were present in person.

Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha constructing various stupas and temples; those containing relics are called stupas, while those that merely provide an image for veneration are called temples.
They are as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers—this is said to describe their great multitude.
He adorned the boundaries of the realm and constructed stūpas and shrines to beautify the land.

The precious stūpa was sublime and magnificent; made of jewels, this Buddha-stūpa rose high and surpassingly wondrous, reaching five thousand yojanas—here [in China] a yojana is approximately forty li. The height of the body of this precious stūpa was five thousand [yojanas].
This represents the fivefold Dharma.
Its length and breadth are equal, and its height, length, and width are precisely symmetrical, measuring two thousand yojanas.
The base of this precious stūpa is eight thousand li square.
In each and every stupa and temple—indeed, in all those countless stupas and temples—there were a thousand banners and streamers for each;
that is, one thousand precious banners and precious streamers were suspended for each.
There were jeweled canopies, meaning canopies for the stupas formed by interlacing pearls.
Precious bells chime in harmony; when the wind moves these precious bells, their sound is harmonious and elegant.
There are the eight classes of beings: devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
There are fragrant flowers, musical instruments, and the performances of various arts and music.
They constantly made offerings, never failing to do so at any time.
Mañjuśrī addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O sons of the Buddha, you are truly capable of making offerings."
For the sake of making offerings to the śarīra, and for the sake of the śarīra, they adorn the stūpas and temples and embellish the sacred sites.
The realm becomes naturally so; the wondrous boundaries of the kingdom emerge spontaneously.
"Extraordinary and exquisitely beautiful. "Extraordinary" means exceptionally great; "exquisitely beautiful" means excellent and fine.
It is like the king of celestial trees: in the garden of Śakra, there is a king of trees whose branches and leaves cover fifty *yojanas*.
Its flowers bloom; the stupas and temples adorn the land as if tree blossoms have opened.
When the Buddha emits a single ray of light, the Buddha refers to Śākyamuni, and that light is his white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*).
"I and the assembly" refers to myself, Maitreya, and the great congregation.
He beheld these world-realms— eighteen thousand lands,
each diverse and exquisite, with their environments and inhabitants both wondrous and sublime—
through the spiritual power of the Buddhas, the supernatural might of the Buddhas dwelling in those lands.
His wisdom is rare; his wisdom is profound and distant, seldom found in the world.
He emits a single pure light—a single ray from the white tuft of hair—which illuminates immeasurable lands, shining throughout countless realms in the eastern direction.
"We have seen this"—referring to what was observed above—"and we have attained what we have never before experienced. Since the Buddha attained enlightenment, such a thing has never occurred.
O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly. Thus they entreated Mañjuśrī to resolve the doubts of the multitude.
The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy; monks, nuns, men, and women look up to you with joyful admiration.
Behold us, both you and me! We look to you and me to resolve this for us.
For what reason, World-Honored One? By what cause does the Buddha [act thus]?
He emitted this radiance. When asked about the cause for emitting the light, the Son of the Buddha then replied;
Mañjuśrī was requested to respond and answered immediately according to the occasion, resolving doubts and bringing joy.
He resolved the doubts of the assembly, causing them to give rise to great delight.
What is the benefit? For what purpose does he provide such nourishment and benefit by emitting this radiance and causing these rays to flow forth?
When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, when the Buddha was seated at the site of enlightenment in Magadha.
The sublime Dharma that has been attained; the subtle and wondrous Dharma realized within the mind.
It is for the sake of wishing to preach this that he wishes to preach this unsurpassed sublime Dharma.

It is for the sake of bestowing a prophecy—that is, wishing to bestow upon the assembly the prophecy of Bodhi—it is because his mind is hesitant and undecided regarding this that these two [questions] are posed together.
Question:
"Manifesting all Buddha-lands" means that within the light, all Buddha-lands are manifested as adorned and purified by various jewels; these jewel-lands are thus magnificent and pure.
And they shall see all the Buddhas; and within that light, they shall see those Buddhas.
This is no small occasion; the manifestation of these auspicious signs is not due to minor causes or conditions.
Mañjuśrī, you should know this! I pray that Mañjuśrī will understand this intent.
The fourfold assembly, the nāgas and spirits, the monks and nuns, the men and women, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas gazed upon the Benevolent One;
they looked up with reverence and observed the Benevolent Mañjuśrī, wondering what he would say.
Regarding the two matters asked above, which one will he explain?
At that time, when Maitreya was seeking a definitive resolution to his questions, Mañjuśrī spoke to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya; "spoke" here means he addressed him directly.
As well as the various great beings and the assembly gathered here—
good sons and others— I praise this great multitude as "benevolent and compassionate good sons.
As I contemplate, and as I, Mañjuśrī, reflect and deliberate upon it:
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One; now the Honored Śākyamuni, desires to proclaim the Great Dharma. He truly desires to proclaim the Great;
he rains down the rain of the Great Dharma, letting fall the great rain to moisten all sentient beings.
He blows the great Dharma conch to issue a proclamation and summon sentient beings;
he beats the great Dharma drum, thunders the great Dharma thunder, and disciplines the great assembly of the Dharma;
he expounds the great Dharma meaning—expounding the Mahāyāna Dharma meanings never before taught.
"Sons of good family, I tell you all in this assembly:
regarding the Buddhas of the past, in the presence of those Buddhas of former ages, I have previously seen such an omen;
I have previously seen various Buddhas manifesting such auspicious signs."
Having emitted this light, and having emitted the white light, he immediately expounded the Great Dharma—the various Mahāyāna teachings.
Therefore, you should know; for this reason, you should understand my present intention.
Now the Buddha manifests light; now Śākyamuni Buddha manifests a great radiance, which is likewise the same as in the past.
He desires to cause sentient beings—meaning the Buddha intends for all sentient beings—to [attain this].
All shall hear and know; all shall hear and understand it as it truly is.
"All worlds" refers to the three worlds: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
This is a Dharma difficult to believe, a perfectly sudden teaching that the world finds hard to trust;
therefore, this auspicious sign has been manifested. To preach this wondrous sutra, he first manifests these auspicious signs.
"Good sons," he says, referring to the assembly present.
Just as the past was immeasurable and boundless, taking up a time in former ages that was inconceivable—
a duration so long that it could not be reached by thought or discussed by speech.
"Anasamkhyeya kalpas"—this is translated as "an incalculable period of time.
At that time there was a Buddha; that is to say, in a past kalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp).
"Sun" symbolizes the light of wisdom that thoroughly illuminates the Dharma-realm; "moon" symbolizes the settled nature that has completed its journey.

The extinguished lamp signifies that the light of precepts and wisdom illuminates all conditions; the three trainings are fully cultivated, the three bodies are perfectly realized, the three virtues are completely endowed, and the three wisdoms are perfectly luminous.
Thus, the Tathāgata—indeed, all Buddhas—possess both general and specific names; "Sun-Moon-Lamp-Light" is one such [specific name].
The ten titles from "Tathāgata" to "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) are the common names shared by all Buddhas.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. This refers to the Tathāgata of the Dharmakāya, which is neither born nor extinguished.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "His light of wisdom shines immeasurably, and his lifespan lasts for incalculable kalpas; he has long practiced [the path]."
That which is obtained through karma is the *sambhogakāya* Tathāgata, perfected through the fivefold cultivation, who has birth but no cessation.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Riding upon the path of reality, one comes to achieve perfect enlightenment"; this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata, who has both birth and cessation.

The Worthy One (*Arhat*): The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses a body endowed with ten thousand virtues and is worthy of receiving the respectful offerings and veneration of gods and humans.

The Fully Enlightened One (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*): Also called the Equal and Perfectly Awakened One. Because the Buddha’s nature of perfect awakening is equal to that of sentient beings, and because he is able to correctly awaken to and fully comprehend all mundane and supramundane phenomena without exception, he is titled the Fully Enlightened One.
One perfected in knowledge and conduct (*vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna*): one who is fully endowed with clear understanding and pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
One who has gone well (*sugata*): "well" means skillfully; "gone" means having departed from the land of delusion and proceeded to the ground of wisdom.
Knower of the World: He is well-versed in understanding the intentions of all beings in the world.
Supreme Being: Among the bodhisattvas and others whose ignorance is not yet exhausted, those who have a Buddha above them are called "beings with a superior";
the Tathāgata, having realized the ultimate, is called the "Supreme Being."
The Tamer of Men: one who tames, harmonizes, and controls those among gods and humans—like elephants and horses—through compassion and skillful means, is called a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa).
The Teacher of Gods and Humans: both gods and humans alike receive his instruction and awakening, serving as a model and guide for the world.
"Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language; *buddha* here means "the Awakened One," for he is fully awakened to all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
"World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) refers to one who possesses the aforementioned ten titles and is revered by all the worlds.
He expounds the True Dharma; he expounds the true, authentic, and unsurpassed Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Practicing the Path from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment is called "good in the beginning.

From that point onward, engaging in practice during the intermediate stage is called "good in the middle. Finally, reaching the ultimate consummation and accomplishing the unsurpassed path is called [good in the end].
It is good in the end.
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching; the Dharma taught from beginning to end is deep, firm, and subtle.
Its phrasing is skillful, and its eloquence is so refined and exquisite that it causes people to delight in hearing it.
It is pure and unadulterated. The One Vehicle is purely immaculate, without duality or triality.
It is fully endowed with clarity and purity; it is completely equipped with the characteristics of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), which are clean, white, and pure.

Cultivation arising from these characteristics is called the "factual Brahma-faring" (*vastu-brahmacarya*); the illumination of the essence as empty and quiescent is called the "principle Brahma-faring" (*tattva-brahmacarya*).
As for those who practice as seekers of the śrāvaka path, for those who seek the śrāvaka path out of weariness with the fruits of suffering,
he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths. The Dharma taught by the Buddha corresponds to the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

One crosses over birth, old age, sickness, and death. By practicing the aforementioned Four Noble Truths, one transcends birth and death, attains ultimate nirvana, and, having completely severed and departed from the fruits of suffering within the three realms, enters the bliss of nirvana without remainder.

For those who seek to become *pratyekabuddhas*: *pratyekabuddha* is here translated as "enlightened through conditions" (*yuanjue*), because they enter the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination;

they are also called "solitary enlightened ones" (*dujue*) because they appear in an age when no Buddha is present, and without relying on a teacher, they alone are able to awaken to the truth through observing the transformation of phenomena.
It is taught that one should explain the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination. The Dharma taught by the Buddha corresponds to each of these twelve links individually;
as for the "twelve," they are: first, ignorance; second, volitional formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form;
fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation; eighth, craving; ninth, clinging; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth; and twelfth, aging and death.
The successive arising of old age and death is called "cause" (*hetu*); their mutual dependence is called "condition" (*pratyaya*).
For the sake of the bodhisattvas—beings of great capacity—it is taught that they should practice the six *pāramitās*.
These are called "reaching the other shore. Birth and death constitute this shore, while the afflictions (*kleśa*) are [the waters].

Nirvana in the intermediate stream is the further shore; by cultivating the six kinds of brahma-conduct—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—one crosses the great ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions to reach the further shore of bodhi and nirvana.
As it has been taught, the capacity of the recipient and the teaching correspond.

May they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. May these great-rooted bodhisattva practitioners realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is said that there are three types of wisdom: the wisdom of all (*sarvajñatā*), which is the wisdom of emptiness; the wisdom of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), which is the conventional; and...
It is wisdom; it is the wisdom that realizes the non-duality of emptiness and conventionality regarding all modes of knowledge. To realize this perfectly is called "accomplishment" (siddhi).
Furthermore, there are Buddhas; after the first Buddha, another Buddha appears.
He was also named Candrasūryapradīpa, a name identical to that of the first Buddha.
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa, likewise identical to the first.
In this manner, twenty thousand Buddhas appeared in succession; in total, there were twenty thousand Buddhas.
They all shared the same single name; "name" here refers to their personal designation.
Their title was Candrasūryapradīpa. These twenty thousand Buddhas shared this identical name, and they also shared the same clan name; their lineage was likewise the same.
His clan name was Bharadvāja; this is translated as "Sharp Faculties" because his contemplation is preeminent.
Maitreya, you should know that Mañjuśrī said:
"O Maitreya, you should know that from the first Buddha to the last of the twenty thousand Buddhas."
They all shared the same name.
That name was Candrasūryapradīpa, complete with the ten epithets, as has already been explained previously.
Regarding the Dharma he taught, he never spoke of the inconceivable, tranquil extinction in an easy or casual manner.
The Dharma is good in the beginning, middle, and end, as has already been explained.
As for that final Buddha, he is the very last of twenty thousand.
Before he left the household life, when he was first still a layman, there were eight princes; the king had eight sons.
The first was named Yiyi (Intention), who possessed the great resolve for the Path.
The second is named Good Intention; he possesses the great intention for the Great Way.
The third is named Immeasurable Intention; he possesses great wisdom and understands immeasurable intentions.
The fourth is named Jewel Intention; he skillfully understands the nature of jewels and is endowed with the true path.
The fifth is called the mind of increasing resolve; it is the great resolve for the path that increases the cultivation of superior practices.
The sixth is called the mind of removing doubt; it is the mind that removes doubt through the increase and excellence of wisdom.
The seventh is called the echoing mind; it understands that the nature of phenomena is empty, like an echo responding from a valley.
The eighth was named Dharmamati; he thoroughly understood the meaning of the profound Dharma.
These eight princes were the eight sons of the Superior;
they possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, and through their spiritual power and merits, they attained great mastery.
Each took charge of the four continents; each assumed his office and ruled over the four continents.
These princes—the eight sons—heard that their father had renounced the world;
they heard that their father, the wheel-turning monarch, had abandoned the kingdom and gone forth.
They attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as previously explained.
They all renounced their royal positions; the eight sons likewise abandoned the status of human kings.
He also followed [the King] into the homeless life; he followed his father the king to leave the household and practice the Way.
He gave rise to the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, courageously generating the mind set on the path of Mahāyāna Bodhi.
He constantly cultivated pure conduct, perpetually practicing the pure and white *brahmacarya*.
They all became Dharma masters; the eight sons all became Mahāyāna Dharma masters.
They had already served ten million buddhas and previously attended upon hundreds of billions of buddhas.
They planted the foundations of all that is wholesome and cultivated roots of merit.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, the final Tathāgata, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra; such was the Dharma he taught.
It is named "The Teaching of Innumerable Meanings. Its name is established based on the meanings it elucidates.
It is the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas; it is the method for guiding bodhisattvas of great capacity.
It is that which the Buddhas protect and keep in mind; this Mahāyāna Dharma is constantly protected and sustained by all Buddhas.
Having spoken this sutra— having finished speaking the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings—
he sat cross-legged right there in the midst of the great assembly, within the crowd at the great dharma-gathering,
with his feet joined together in the full lotus posture.
He entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meaning. Entering meditative concentration in accordance with the sūtra, his body and mind were unmoving;
his body was tranquil and his mind was settled.
At that time it rained from the heavens; as he entered this samādhi, the devas rained down flowers.
Mandārava flowers—small white flowers;
Mahāmandārava flowers—large white flowers;
Mañjūṣaka flowers—small red flowers.
They scattered mahāmañjūṣaka flowers and great red flowers over the Buddha;
they scattered them upon the crown of the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa and over the entire assembly,
including all those present in the gathering who were hearing the Dharma.
Throughout all Buddha-worlds, pervading the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
the earth shook in six ways, as previously explained.
At that time, within the assembly, there was the Assembly of Immeasurable Meanings.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas,
yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all the minor kings and universal monarchs—
this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; filled with joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
These and other such meanings are all to be understood as explained previously.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as these various Buddha-lands are seen now. These are all to be understood as explained previously.
"Maitreya, you should know. Mañjuśrī said: 'Maitreya, you should know.
At that time, within the assembly at the *Anantārtha* gathering of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, there were twenty *koṭis* of bodhisattvas—ten million being a *koṭi*."
They desired to hear the Dharma; they aspired to hear the Dharma they had not heard before.
These twenty billion bodhisattvas, seeing this radiance—the light from the ūrṇā-kośa of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—beheld it.
It universally illumines the Buddha-lands; it universally illumines eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction.
It is something never before encountered; it is a sight never before seen.
One wishes to know this light; one wishes to understand this radiance of the white tuft of hair.
Regarding the causes and conditions for this, and what the purpose and basis were for the light shining so far and wide:
at that time there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light (Prabhāsa), who was none other than Mañjuśrī in a previous life.
He had eight hundred disciples, all of whom were students of Prabhāsa.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi; having entered the concentration on the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, he rose from his seat.
Because of the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light, the Dharma does not arise in isolation; its arising must depend upon a person.
He preached the Mahāyāna sūtra, and the Dharma taught therein is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma), as previously described.
The teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma; the instruction of Bodhisattvas;
that which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas; that which is cherished, guarded, and respectfully remembered by all Buddhas.
Sixty small kalpas—wherein one cycle of increase and decrease of the receptacle world constitutes a small kalpa.
He did not rise from his seat; for such a length of time, he did not leave this seat.
Those in the assembly who were listening, those who were hearing the Dharma, likewise remained seated in one place, never departing from the dharma-throne.

For sixty minor kalpas, the assembly remained for the same duration as the Tathāgata; their bodies and minds were unmoving, and they were serene both internally and externally as they listened to what the Buddha spoke,
hearing the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma teachings with focused attention as it passed through their ears.
That is to say, as if for the duration of a meal, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Dharma and was unaware that sixty minor kalpas had passed as if they were a single mealtime.
At that time, among the assembly, the listeners in the gathering—
There was not a single person— indeed, not even one person— who,
whether in body or mind, experienced weariness through the identity of body and mind;
nor did they ever give rise to a heart of sloth or fatigue.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, and having finished expounding the Lotus Sutra,
he was then surrounded by Brahmā, Māra, and the various Brahma-kings as well as the Mara-king.
"Śramaṇa" means "one who is diligent and at rest.
"Brāhmaṇa" means "one of pure conduct.
As for "gods and humans," this refers to the various devas and human beings.
Within the assembly of the asura hosts, he spoke these words among the gathered multitude, as follows:
"This very day at midnight, the path of the Tathāgata shall reach its ultimate end in parinirvāṇa."

It shall also be at midnight that he enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is called "quiescence" because the three delusions have been exhausted; yet, as long as a physical body remains, it is termed "with remainder.
When the capacity [of the faculties] is spent and the body should perish, it is termed "entering without remainder."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakara,
who possessed merits complete like a worldly treasure-store.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, entrusting him with this predictive declaration.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "At that time, among this assembly, this Bodhisattva Guṇagañja shall next become a Buddha, just as Maitreya succeeds the Honored One Śākyamuni;
his name shall be Viśuddhakāya, the Pure and Sublime Body."
*Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*).
*Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yinggong*).
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*Zhengbianzhi*). These constitute his ten original titles; the text here briefly cites three of them.

After the Buddha had bestowed this prophecy—having bestowed upon Dezhang (Guṇagañja) the prophecy of a pure body—he was born at midday and entered parinirvāṇa at midnight; for all Buddhas are thus: born in the light of day and passing away in the darkness of night.
He entered parinirvāṇa; he entered into quiescence.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, after his entry into quiescence, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, the disciple of Candraprabha—
He upheld the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma;
upholding this treasury of the Dharma for a full eighty minor kalpas,
he spent such a length of time expounding it for others and preaching it to people.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had eight sons. Before the Buddha renounced the household life, he had these eight sons, all of whom took Maitreya (Prabhāpāla) as their teacher.
They studied under Maitreya, who instructed, taught, transformed, and guided them.
He caused them to be firm and steadfast; he caused the eight princes to firmly uphold and guard Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, as previously described.
These princes were the king’s eight sons.
Having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and having served and attended upon immeasurable Buddhas,
they subsequently realized the Truth and all attained the Way of Buddhahood. Because they originally cultivated the causes for Buddhahood, they all became Buddhas.
Regarding those who will attain Buddhahood last: Prince Dharmamati will be the very last to attain Buddhahood;
his name shall be Dīpaṃkara. By virtue of his causal name Dharmamati, his resultant title is Dīpaṃkara, the Dharma King. He shatters existence like a lamp, continuing its illumination.
There were eight hundred disciples, the assembly of eight hundred followers converted by Prabhāsa.
Among them was one person, a single individual in that crowd, known as Yaśaskāma;
he had not yet forgotten worldly appearances and sought only fame and reputation.
They are greedily attached to gain and offerings. "Greed" refers to the mind, while "gain and offerings" refers to material things.
Although they may read and recite various sutras, even as they crave gain and offerings, they continue to recite the scriptures.
They are not proficient. Because they are attached to worldly conditions and their minds are not single-minded, they lack proficiency and forget much;
this is the fault of a lack of diligence, and thus they are called "those who seek fame. It is by means of this that they acquire their name.
This person likewise, by virtue of having planted various roots of goodness,
through the causes and conditions thereof— reciting and upholding the various sutras, cultivating various meritorious deeds, and planting the roots of goodness—
and because these virtuous causes have formed superior conditions.
They have encountered immeasurable and met countless hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas; through their past virtuous conditions, they have met many buddhas,
making offerings and showing respect, serving them with reverence and caution.
He honored and praised him; he esteemed, revered, extolled, and lauded him.
Maitreya, you should know this. [The Buddha] addressed Maitreya, saying:
"You should know that at that time, there was the Bodhisattva Candrasūryapradīpa’s Wonderful Light (Candraprabha)."
Could this have been anyone else? It was none other than myself.
Mañjuśrī himself declared that he was my former incarnation as the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame (Yaśaskāma).
Nor was the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame anyone else.
It is your very body; it is indeed your own body.
Beholding this present omen today—this mark of a marvelous and auspicious sign—is no different from before;
it is no different from the auspicious signs of Candrasūryapradīpa.
Therefore, I reflect and deliberate: "Today the Tathāgata—now Śākyamuni—is about to preach a Mahāyāna sūtra.
As it was with all Buddhas of the past, so it is with the Buddha of the present."

It is titled *The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas. These twelve characters above constitute the full title of the Lotus Sutra.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, within the great assembly, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke the preceding prose and the subsequent verses.
Therefore, it is said: "To proclaim again," and he spoke in verse. The characters of the verses are as before.
"I contemplate the past world" means that Mañjuśrī contemplates the worlds of the Buddhas of the past.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, for such a duration of time, there was a Buddha, a Honored One among Men;
a Buddha appeared in the world as a Honored One among Men, named Candrasūryapradīpa. This was the name of that Buddha.
The World-Honored One expounded the Dharma. After attaining Buddhahood, he expounded all dharmas and delivered immeasurable sentient beings;
immeasurable sentient beings received the Buddha’s transformation and deliverance.
Countless billions of bodhisattvas, a multitude of the Mahāyāna,
contemplate entering the wisdom of the Buddha, so as to cause all bodhisattvas to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Before the Buddha went forth from home, when he was formerly at home as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin):
The eight princes born to him— namely, Yaśas and the others—
seeing the Great Sage renounce the world and seeing their father renounce the world to become a Great Sage,
likewise followed him in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The sons also followed their father in cultivating all pure practices.
At that time, the Buddha was teaching the Mahāyāna.
At that time, Candrasūryapradīpa spoke the sūtra titled *Anantārtha*.
In the midst of the great assembly, within the great gathering, he taught the *Anantārtha-sūtra*.
He then provided a detailed analysis for the sake of the assembled multitude, explaining it at great length.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra and finished his discourse on the "Innumerable Meanings," he remained upon that very Dharma-seat— the seat of the "Innumerable Meanings."
He sat in the full lotus posture in samādhi; having assumed the full lotus posture, he entered the immeasurable concentration known by the name of the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meaning.
Then, from the heavens, māndārava flowers rained down—namely, the four types of flowers mentioned previously.
The celestial drums resounded spontaneously; the celestial drums in the sky resounded naturally.
The various devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits—the assembly of the eight classes—made offerings to the Honored One among Men, namely the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
At the moment Candrasūryapradīpa entered meditative absorption, all buddha-fields immediately shook with a great trembling,
just as the earth now shakes in six ways in the realm of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows;
he emitted light from the tuft of white hair between them, manifesting various rare and wondrous events and revealing all manner of unprecedented and extraordinary phenomena.
This light shone toward the east, first illuminating the eastern direction.
The eighteen thousand Buddha-lands represent the eighteen realms (*dhātus*).
They are shown to all sentient beings, and shown to the multitudes of the six paths of existence—
the places of birth and death as karmic retribution, and the places where one dies here and is born there according to the retribution of good and evil.

There are those who see various buddha-fields; some even behold the pure lands of the Buddhas, adorned with myriad jewels and embellished with a hundred treasures, possessing the color of lapis lazuli and crystal.

Lapis lazuli originates from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, its hue being translucent and pure; as for crystal— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly regarding the description of crystal (sphatika).*
It possesses these [features], yet their colors are not fixed; the light of the Buddha’s radiance makes the color of the land like that of various jewels.
This arises from the illumination of the Buddha’s light; all the various signs perceived are due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, he saw the various devas and humans,
as well as the eight classes of beings— nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras—
each making offerings to their respective Buddhas; each was making offerings to the Buddha of their own land.
Furthermore, one sees all Tathāgatas; in the lands manifested by their light, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas spontaneously accomplish the Way of the Buddha.

This Buddha-way is pure and fundamentally not a product of fabrication; by accords with principle and awakening to the truth, they immediately ascend to perfect enlightenment, which is called "spontaneous accomplishment."
The color of his body is like a mountain of gold; the color of his body is superior and wondrous, like a mountain of purple gold.
He is upright and majestic, exceedingly subtle and marvelous; he is handsome and well-adorned, refined, subtle, and exquisitely beautiful.
It is like pure lapis lazuli: the color of the lapis lazuli is pure, translucent both inside and out, and within it appears the image of true gold.
The body is like the golden image, while its nature is like the color of the lapis lazuli; this subtle and wondrous physical body manifests within that nature.
The World-Honored One was in the great assembly, and the Buddhas of other lands were also present among the multitude,
expounding the profound meaning of the Dharma and proclaiming and elucidating the subtle and wondrous significance of the deep teachings.
In each and every buddha-field— eighteen thousand such fields—
the assembly of śrāvakas was incalculable; in each field there were incalculable śrāvakas,
all illuminated by the radiance of the Buddha, specifically by the light of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
He saw all those great assemblies; he saw them all in other lands— those great assemblies,
including various bhikṣus and the followers of the two vehicles,
dwelling amidst mountain forests in secluded and tranquil places.

He diligently maintains the pure precepts; he upholds them with such vigor that he does not transgress, his moral essence remaining as pure as one who guards a bright pearl, like a dragon guarding its jewel.
Furthermore, he beholds the various bodhisattvas, the assembly of the Mahāyāna.
Practicing generosity, patience, and so forth constitutes the cultivation of the six perfections.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges; the number of bodhisattvas is likewise like the sands of the Ganges.
This arises from the illumination of the Buddha’s light, whereby, through the illumination of the Moon-Lamp Light, all marks are perceived.

Furthermore, one sees various bodhisattvas deeply entering various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Because the number of these sublime concentrations of the bodhisattvas is not one, they are called "various.
To collect the mind and abide in stillness is termed "entering."
Body and mind are tranquil and unmoving; internally and externally they are serene, body and mind unmoving, as he seeks the unsurpassed path.
He enters into profound meditative concentration to seek the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, he saw various bodhisattvas who knew the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena and thoroughly understood the principle of the quiescent nature of all phenomena;
each in their respective lands, each in their own native realm.
They preach the Dharma seeking the Buddha-way. Bodhisattvas from various lands each preach the Dharma and seek the Way within their own realms.
At that time, the fourfold assembly—those present in the assembly when the light manifested in those lands—[beheld this].
They beheld the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa. At that time, the fourfold assembly saw him manifest great supernormal powers;
all the manifestations were through the Buddha’s spiritual power, and their hearts were filled with joy.
Thus, the hearts of the fourfold assembly were entirely gladdened.
Each asked one another, inquiring of each other:
"What is the cause and condition for this? What is the cause and condition for the manifestation of these lands?
Who is the Honored One venerated by gods and humans? Who is the Moon-Lamp World-Honored One venerated by gods and humans?"
He had just arisen from samādhi. At that moment, Candrasūryapradīpa arose from his concentration and praised the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu.

Because the Buddha had entered samādhi and emitted light from the tuft of white hair between his brows while Prabhāketu was instructing his disciples, the Buddha, upon emerging from concentration, praised Prabhāketu.
You are the eye of the world; you are the human and celestial eye of the world.
You are that to whom all turn for refuge and faith; all humans and devas take refuge in you and revere you with faith.
They are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma; they are well able to uphold the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Dharma, just as I have taught it, and all dharmas just as I have taught them.
Only you are able to realize and know it; only you are able to realize and understand its meaning and flavor.
Having thus praised him, the World-Honored One—the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara—praised Prabhāketu.
He caused Subhāṣitaghoṣa to rejoice; desiring to gladden Subhāṣitaghoṣa’s heart, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He spoke it after emerging from meditative concentration, and he continued for as long as sixty small kalpas.
Without rising from this seat— without rising from this Dharma Lotus assembly—
he preached the sublime Dharma, the most supreme, excellent, and wondrous Dharma.
This Dharma Master Wondrous Light was able to receive and uphold it all; because he could believe, he received it, and because he could understand, he upheld it.
When the Buddha spoke this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it was the Buddha Pradīparāja who spoke this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Having caused the assembly to rejoice, and having enabled the great multitude to hear and attain joy,
he immediately on that very day, at the conclusion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
addressed the host of devas and humans— the fourfold assembly of devas and humans.
The meaning of the true nature of all phenomena—the sublime meaning of the true nature within all phenomena—has already been explained for you;
it has already been expounded for you in accordance with reality.
Tonight, during the middle watch of the night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa;
having completed my work of transformation, I shall enter the peace of nirvana.
"You must practice with single-minded diligence. Entrust yourself to the propagation of the *Miaoguang* (Wonderful Light); proceed with exclusive devotion.
You should remain free from negligence; you ought to distance yourself from indolence and heedlessness."
The Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter. By saying that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, one gives rise to reverence and mindfulness.
They are met but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas; within hundreds of millions of kalpas, they may be encountered only once at some time.
The sons of the World-Honored One, the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara, and the rest of the assembly, heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa;
they heard that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Each harbored grief and distress; each harbored in their hearts sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction:
"How swift is the Buddha’s passing! How rapid is the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa!"
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma; the Holy Lord, World-Honored One, King of All Dharmas.
He comforts immeasurable multitudes; the Buddha, out of compassion for the sorrows of the masses, soothes and consoles them all.
When I enter parinirvāṇa, when my conditioned existence is exhausted and I manifest final quiescence, you must not grieve or fear;
you must not harbor grief or fear in your hearts.
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja is a bodhisattva in his final birth before buddhahood.
Regarding the unconditioned true mark and the liberation of the true mark of unconditioned dharmas, his mind has already attained thorough penetration;
his mind has already attained complete clarity and realization.
The next shall become a Buddha. The Bodhisattva Guṇagañja shall next become a Buddha, named Viśuddhakāya;
the Buddha bestows upon him the prediction of enlightenment, naming him Buddha Viśuddhakāya.
He also delivered immeasurable multitudes. Just as the light of a lamp delivers beings immeasurably, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa this very night;
