having bestowed his prediction and entrusted the Dharma, he immediately entered nirvana.
Just as fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, once the fuel of the spiritual capacity is spent, the fire should likewise perish.
Regarding the distribution of the *śarīra*: after the cremation by fire, the relics were distributed.
They erected immeasurable *stūpas*. In the Sanskrit language, *stūpa* means "a place of high prominence"; it refers to the construction of various *stūpas* to enshrine the relics of the Buddha.
This concerns the two monastic communities: the *bhikṣus* and the *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges; this speaks of their great multitude.
They redouble their diligence; seeing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and their own task remains unfinished, they redouble their efforts, practicing with even greater vigor and progress.
He sought the unsurpassed path; thus he practiced with diligence in order to seek the Buddha-way.
This Dharma Master Wonderful Light was a disciple to whom the Tathāgata Lamp-Light transmitted the Dharma.

They shall uphold the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma; they shall uphold the lamp that illuminates the precious treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma during the eighty minor kalpas following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, throughout both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma periods.
They widely proclaimed the Lotus Sūtra; they extensively expounded and taught the Sublime Lotus Sūtra.
These eight princes, the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara, were those who had been opened, induced, transformed, and guided by Prabhāketu.
The Unsurpassed Way is firm and solid. The characteristics of the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing;
the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna is called the Unsurpassed Way, and that which is neither arising nor ceasing is called the firm and solid dharma.
They shall see countless Buddhas; they shall see immeasurable Buddhas in future ages.
Having made offerings to these Buddhas, and having served and attended upon countless Buddhas.
They practice in accordance with the Great Way; they follow in accordance with all Buddhas to practice the unsurpassed way.
Successively they attain Buddhahood; in continuous succession they attain the path of Buddhahood.
They were conferred in succession. One after another, they were granted the prediction of attaining the position of a successor.
Finally, there was the God among Gods; this final Buddha was most supremely honored among humans and devas, and was thus named the God among Gods (Devātideva).
He is titled Dīpaṃkara Buddha. This is the name of his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
He is the guide for all sages; the teacher who transforms and leads among gods and celestial seers.
He delivers immeasurable multitudes, transforming and liberating many so that they all attain complete emancipation.
This was the Dharma Master Wonderful Light, the transmitter of the Dharma.
At that time, he had a single disciple; at that time, this sole disciple of Wonderful Light constantly harbored indolence in his heart, and his mind was always filled with laxity and negligence.
They are greedily attached to fame and profit. With greedy minds, they grasp at reputation, wealth, and gain;
they seek fame and profit without satiety, and their greedy-seeking mind knows no contentment.
He frequents the homes of prominent clans; for the sake of fame and profit, he travels extensively among great families, noble lineages, and wealthy households.
He abandons what he has practiced and recited, and with many preoccupations in his mind, his studies become neglected and superficial.
They become neglected and forgotten, failing to be mastered.

Due to these causes and conditions—specifically, the condition of abandoning one's practice out of greed for fame and profit—they fall into neglect and forgetfulness, unable to achieve thorough mastery.
They are called "those who seek fame. Fame is not obtained without cause; it arises from habitual practice.
Thus, even while greedily seeking fame, they are also able to cultivate a multitude of wholesome karmas.
One attains the vision of countless Buddhas. Because of cultivating goodness, one is able to see all Buddhas and make offerings to them.
By encountering many Buddhas, one practices the cultivation of offerings.

They practice in accordance with the Great Path; following the requirements of all Buddhas, they practice the path of the Mahāyāna, being endowed with the six pāramitās and fully cultivating the practices of the six perfections.
Now I behold the Lion of the Śākyas; now, within this Bhadrakalpa, I behold the Honored One Śākyamuni.
Hereafter he shall become a Buddha. As for those who seek renown, they shall become Buddhas next after the final dharma period of the Honored One Śākyamuni.
His name is Maitreya, which in this language means "The Benevolent One" (Cishi).
He will extensively deliver all sentient beings, preaching the Dharma in three assemblies beneath the Dragon Flower tree to save immeasurable people.
Their number was immeasurable and beyond calculation.
After that Buddha had passed into extinction—that is, after the Buddha Dīpaṃkara had entered *nirvāṇa*—the one who was indolent at that time was you;
the one who sought fame then was none other than Maitreya now.
The Dharma Master Wonderful Light during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was none other than myself;
at that time, Wonderful Light was none other than I, Mañjuśrī.
I saw the Buddha Lamp-Light. In the past, I saw that Tathāgata Lamp-Light;
the original radiance was such as this, and the auspicious signs of the original light were such as this.
By this one knows that the present Buddha—verified by these past conditions—desires to preach the Lotus Sūtra;
this means he desires to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The present auspicious signs are like those of the original; the present auspicious signs of the Buddha are like those of the original Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara).
These auspicious signs manifested by all Buddhas are the skillful means (upāya) of all Buddhas. It is indeed the skillful means of all Buddhas to manifest such auspicious signs.

Now the Buddha emits light; now Śākyamuni Buddha emits a great radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and to aid in the opening and development of the gateway to the meaning of the true mark.
All you people, you should now know; all those present in this assembly, you should now know:
join your palms with a single mind and wait; join the ten fingers of your palms together and stand waiting with a single mind.
The Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma; Śākyamuni shall pour forth the great rain of the Dharma to satisfy those who seek the Way.

When sentient beings contemplate the Dharma as one who thirsts longs for a drink, the Tathāgata’s gift of Dharma falls like rain, universally moistening the hundred grains and all vegetation, fulfilling them all without exception.
Those who seek the three vehicles— namely, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who seek the three vehicles—
if there are any among them who have doubt or regret, or those who possess uncertainty, agitation, or remorse.
The Buddha shall eliminate and sever them for you. Śākyamuni shall uproot and sever the root of doubt, cutting away the net of views so that nothing remains;
he shall exhaust the three delusions until not a single trace is left.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Two: The Expedient Means.
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment for more than forty years, he did not expediently preach this sutra because sentient beings were not yet capable;
it was only at the very end, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, that he spoke it—this is the Buddha’s skillful means.
At that time, while Mañjuśrī was responding to Maitreya with these verses, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi;
he emerged with composure and careful deliberation from the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings,
rising from that wondrous concentration.
He addressed Śāriputra: "Among all my disciples, Śāriputra’s wisdom is foremost; therefore, I speak to him.

The wisdom of all Buddhas consists of what is called the knowledge of all things (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)—the wisdom of the Buddha."
It is also the Buddha-wisdom that eternally abides in the equality of the true mark (*dharmatā*),

a great wisdom that is profoundly deep and immeasurable. It is called "profoundly deep" because it is the realization of all Buddhas who have thoroughly fathomed the source and bottom of all phenomena, such that no others possess this knowledge.
Regarding this gateway of wisdom: above, it was praised as true wisdom being without limit or measure; here it is said that this gateway of wisdom cannot be entered without wisdom.
It is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; because it is profound, it is not easily understood, and because it is subtle, it is not easily entered.
All śrāvakas—those of the Lesser Vehicle—are called "hearers" (śrāvaka) because they awaken to and clarify the Four Noble Truths by hearing the Buddha’s voice.

Pratyekabuddhas—here translated as "those awakened through conditions"—are so named because they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken to the ultimate truth; they are also called "solitary awakeners."
It is not that they can awaken independently without the instruction of a teacher;

rather, there are things they cannot know. Because the wisdom and insight of the Two Vehicles are shallow and inferior, the sublime realization attained by the Buddha is beyond their capacity to know.
Why is this so? To inquire into the reason for not knowing:

it is because the Buddha was once closely attended. "Closely attended" means that he was personally served and remained in close proximity for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, even up to ten million times ten thousand *koṭis* of days.
Those whom he had attended for many eons under countless Buddhas— he has fully practiced all that those Buddhas practiced;
he has completely carried out all the spheres of action of the Buddhas,
as well as immeasurable dharmas of the Path and innumerable methods for practicing the Buddha-way.

Valiant and diligent: to dare to act is called "valiant" (yong); to exhaust one's wisdom is called "fierce" (meng); and for the mind to single-mindedly strive toward the fruit is called "diligent" (jin).
Its fame is heard everywhere; its good name and beautiful reputation are universally known and pervasive.

"Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the profound. To "accomplish" means to bring about; to "perfectly complete" is called accomplishment. Because the locus of accomplishment is sublime, it is termed "profound.
"Unprecedented phenomena" (*adbhutadharma*) refers to phenomena that have never before existed within the six destinies or the three vehicles.
These are spoken according to what is appropriate. Although the Buddha employs skillful means to expound all dharmas as is suitable for each case, their underlying intent is difficult to understand;
this intended meaning is fully realized only by the Buddha, while others find it hard to comprehend.
"Śāriputra," he called out by name and addressed him:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood— since I realized the fruit at the site of enlightenment—
I have, through various causes and conditions, explained for those of dull faculties the various causes and conditions of good and evil throughout the past, present, and future."

Using various kinds of parables, for those of middling faculties, he draws upon diverse things as analogies and metaphors to extensively expound the verbal teachings and to widely proclaim his instructions and admonitions.

Through countless skillful means and innumerable ingenious, subtle, and expedient methods, he guides and leads sentient beings, inducing them to transformation and instruction so that they may leave behind all attachments.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, greedily clinging to every matter; the Buddha provides skillful means to cause them to distance themselves from these attachments.
It is detached. Why is this so? To investigate the preceding thought: by what cause is it possible?

It is through the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata. The Greatly Awakened Tathāgata compassionately expounds the Dharma through analogies and causes and conditions; these are his skillful means.

The meaning is as follows: knowing and seeing the *pāramitā* is called the Buddha’s knowledge; realizing that the source and bottom of all phenomena are fundamentally empty is called the Buddha’s vision;
and reaching the other shore is called *pāramitā*.
All are already fully complete; their practice through understanding is entirely perfected and fulfilled.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—his correct knowledge and correct view—is vast and profound, thoroughly comprehending all phenomena; it is called "Extensively Manifesting Beyond All Sages. It is called... [name].
The Great Ultimate Limit of Reality is called "profound" because no one can reach it; it is called "distant" because it is immeasurable and unimpeded.
It is beyond calculation and thus lacks quantitative measure; its nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent, and thus it is without obstruction.
The powers and fearlessnesses. The ten powers of a Buddha and the four fearlessnesses.
Dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samādhi. Dhyāna is the cause, vimokṣa is the fruit, and samādhi—in the Sanskrit language, this is translated as "cloud-like concentration" (yún-dìng).

They penetrate deeply into the boundless. As described above, they exhaustively practice all the spheres of action of the Buddhas; through the powers of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they enter correctly and individually into that which is without limit or boundary.
They accomplish all unprecedented dharmas, as described above.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to perform various kinds of analytical distinctions. For instance, he extensively explains and distinguishes through manifold wisdom the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the myriad practices of the six perfections.
He skillfully expounds all phenomena. The names of the teachings he proclaims are skillful; their meanings are not singular, yet they are called by various names.
His speech is gentle and soft; the words and phrases he utters are mild, supple, and refined.
It gladdens the hearts of the multitude; it brings joy and satisfies the minds of all people.
Śāriputra, I shall speak to you by taking up the essential points; I shall summarize the most profound and subtle for your sake.
There are immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas; all such dharmas as those above have been fully accomplished by the Buddha, meaning that the Buddha has realized them completely.
"Stop, Śāriputra," [the Buddha said]. Since these dharmas are profound and subtle, they are difficult for people to believe and understand; it is therefore appropriate to cease [speaking of them].
There is no need to speak further; it is unnecessary to speak again.
Why? For what reason is it stopped and deemed unnecessary to speak?
Because of that which has been accomplished by the Buddha—namely, that which has been accomplished by the Blessed One.
"Supremely rare": it is supreme because it is realized by the Buddha alone; it is rare because it has never been heard before.
"A dharma difficult to understand": its principle is profound and its essence is subtle, which is why it is hard to comprehend.
Only Buddha and Buddha— only the Buddhas and Śākyamuni Bhagavān—
are able to exhaustively investigate and reach the very bottom of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This subtle and profound Dharma is called "real" because it understands that while phenomena appear to exist due to delusion, their fundamental nature is empty.

The marks refer to all phenomena. These ten "Thusnesses" constitute the essential core of this single sutra, intended to reveal the true mark (dharmatā) so that one may attain realization and understanding.
Such are the characteristics. "Characteristics" refers to appearances, which may be either true or delusive.

The "true" refers to that which is eternally abiding, without arising or ceasing—the true mark of *tathatā* (suchness), as the Sūtra says: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true mark of all phenomena.
The "delusive" refers to ignorance, characterized by arising and ceasing, a phantom-like appearance, as the Sūtra says: "Seeing all sentient beings [subject] to birth..."
The Tathāgata perceives clearly and without error that [beings] are scorched and boiled by old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;

this is called the "suchness" (tathatā) because it is the teaching of the Buddha regarding the causes and conditions of reality as it truly is. Upon hearing this, sentient beings realize that the meaning of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) has already been explained for them, as the Sūtra says:
"I have already taught you the meaning of the true nature of all phenomena."
Such is the nature of karma: it does not arise spontaneously, but truly originates from one's inherent nature.
The mind fundamentally possesses the natures of both good and evil, which manifest in various distinctions according to temporal conditions and causes.

Just as fire exists within bamboo and wood, yet cannot be ignited without encountering the necessary conditions, and must necessarily be produced by drilling and friction, so too when that which is good is brought forth, it is called the "Light of Wisdom."
When the accomplishment of wholesome deeds is incited by evil, it is called "poisonous fire.

When the nature of delusive conditions is fundamentally empty and quiescent, yet transforms according to conditions, this is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* means when it says: "The nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions."

Such is the essence (*tattva*). This essence has three meanings: it is called the "essence of principle" (*li-ti*) because it is equal for both the noble ones and ordinary beings; it is called the "essence of outflow-free cultivation" (*wulou-ti*) because it is accomplished through the fivefold path of practice;
and it is called the "essence of outflow-bound existence" (*youlou-ti*) because it refers to the illusory body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Such is "power. It refers to all functional efficacy inherent within the substance of karma, accomplished through the karmic power of the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants.
Such is "action": it is the process of movement and creation according to each respective power; by advancing toward the good, one obtains merit, and by committing evil, one invites calamity.

Such is the cause (*hetu*). By means of this cause, it is correctly pointed out that all good and evil within the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) are manifested solely by the mind, just as grasses and trees grow based upon the earth.
Such is the condition (*pratyaya*). The condition refers to immediate phenomena which are originally neither good nor evil; they necessarily manifest their characteristics through the mind.
Just as dry wood spreads when it encounters the power of fire, and ice melts when it sees the sun, so it is with results:
the beginning of an action is the cause, and the end of the action is the result. Both good and evil are entirely the gathering of causes that produce results.

Such is the retribution. Once the fruits of karma have been realized, one receives retribution according to that karma; awakening results in the Four Noble Ones, while delusion is termed the Six Classes of Beings.
Thus, from the beginning to the end, all is ultimately equal. Whether on the two paths of delusion or awakening, from the root to the branches, cause and effect are non-dual and ultimately equal.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma,
wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke in verse. For those who had not yet fully understood, he again summarized the preceding meaning and spoke it in verse.
The Hero of the World is immeasurable; the Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One, is of immeasurable wisdom.
This includes all classes of sentient beings within the nine realms: the gods and the people of the world—both the paths of humans and devas—and all other categories of living beings.
There is no one who can know the Buddha. Among the six realms and the three vehicles, none can know the Buddha’s intention.
The Buddha possesses the powers and the fearlessnesses—the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses—as well as liberations and various samādhis.
His inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous liberations comprise hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great [qualities].
Samādhi, as well as the other dharmas of the Buddha— the "other dharmas of the Buddha" here referring to the provisional three vehicles—
none can measure them; with the sole exception of the World-Honored One, no one else is able to fathom them.
Having followed countless Buddhas from the very beginning,
he has fully practiced all paths and fully cultivated the dharmas of the path of all Buddhas.
The profound and subtle Dharma refers to the unsurpassed, profound, and subtle Dharma that is the sphere of activity of the Buddhas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

It is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend; both its ontological essence (*tattva*) and its underlying meaning (*artha*) are profoundly subtle—it is not seen by the eye, nor is it grasped by the mind.
He was able to comprehend this.
Having practiced these various paths throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas,
and having performed all the aforementioned noble paths during countless hundreds of thousands of millions of time-periods, he was fully accomplished.

"One attains the fruit at the site of enlightenment. The place where one cultivates the Way is called the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); the attainment of supreme perfect awakening is called "attaining the fruit.
I have fully known and seen this all. The Buddha has fully known and fully seen all regarding the Dharma.
Such is the great fruit of retribution. Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment is called the "Great Fruit," and the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is called the "Great Retribution.
The phrase "the meanings of various natures and characteristics" refers precisely to the meanings of the nature and characteristics of the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
I and the Buddhas of the ten directions—only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this matter.
This "matter" refers to the subtle and wondrous Dharma. This Dharma cannot be demonstrated;
such a wondrous Dharma is fundamentally not of the nature of speech and cannot be revealed through words.
Regarding human beings, their verbal expressions are quiescent; the very nature of the characteristics manifested in their speech is quiescent.
This applies to all other classes of sentient beings, including those of the six realms and the three vehicles.

No one is able to understand it; it cannot be comprehended by the power of their own intellectual wisdom, except for the assembly of bodhisattvas—specifically, the great bodhisattvas whose power of faith is vast.
Those whose power of faith is firm and stable— except for those whose power is exceptionally solid, real, and firm— the profound and subtle Dharma-gate cannot be entered without faith.
This refers to the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, the disciples of the three vehicles within the assemblies of all Buddhas.
They have made offerings to various Buddhas. These pratyekabuddhas have also cultivated portions of merit by making offerings to various Buddhas.
All outflows are exhausted; the outflows and karmic actions of the three realms have been entirely eliminated.
Dwelling in their final body, they attain the state of a pratyekabuddha in that last existence.
Such persons as these [regard] such individuals as pratyekabuddhas.
Their strength is insufficient to endure it; though their power surpasses that of ordinary beings, they are incapable of hearing the Sublime.
Even if they were to fill the entire world, even if they were to fill the worlds of the ten directions.
Suppose everyone were like Śāriputra— each possessing the foremost wisdom of Śāriputra—
and they all exerted their minds together to deliberate, exhausting their spiritual faculties to calculate and measure it.
One cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom; none are able to measure or know the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even if the ten directions were filled—filling the worlds of the ten directions—with those like Śāriputra, all possessing great wisdom such as that of Śāriputra himself.
As well as the other disciples, and all other people, great disciples, and so forth,
they also filled the lands of the ten directions, filling even the countless buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.

Even if they were to exhaust their thoughts and deliberate together, they still could not know it. Previously, it was said that even those who lead with wisdom, such as the various disciples, cannot fathom it.
As for the Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom—those who are awakened through conditions and awaken alone—their wisdom is somewhat sharper than that of the Śrāvakas.

The final body free from outflows; having already eliminated all outflows, this final body of awakening also fills the worlds of the ten directions, just as the śrāvakas fill the worlds of the ten directions.
Their number was like that of a bamboo grove; this describes their great multitude.
These individuals were of one mind; these pratyekabuddhas shared a single mental focus for immeasurable billions of kalpas throughout that duration of time.
If one wishes to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom, or wishes to contemplate the Tathāgata’s genuine wisdom, one cannot know even a small portion of it;
even if one wishes to know a small portion, one cannot attain it.

Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, and all such bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon the path, have made offerings to countless Buddhas; they have already made offerings to countless Buddhas.
He thoroughly understands all meanings and purposes; he comprehends and penetrates the meanings and purposes of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Furthermore, he is skilled in preaching the Dharma, and is also well able to expound the Dharma for others.
Like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds—these four things are cited as metaphors for great numbers—filling the lands of the ten directions;
so too do bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve fill the worlds of the ten directions.

With a single mind and sublime wisdom; all together with a single mind and supreme, wondrous wisdom, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—throughout a multitude of kalpas equal to the sands of the Ganges.
They all deliberated together. All these people collectively conjectured that they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom;
they could not fully comprehend the Buddha’s insight.
Regarding the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas: previously, this was discussed in terms of those at the initial stage;

now, these Bodhisattvas at the stage of non-retrogression are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and those at the profound stage of non-retrogression are even more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.

Even if they were to contemplate and seek together with a single mind, they still could not know it. Although those who have ascended to the stage of non-retrogression possess profound power of wisdom, they cannot know the Buddha.
Furthermore, he told Śāriputra: "The dharma-nature is untainted and inconceivable; it is pure and free from all defilements of outflows."
It can be contemplated by the mind and discussed with the mouth.
This most profound and subtle Dharma—the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is profoundly deep, subtle, secret, and wondrous—I have now fully attained it;
the Buddha has now fully and completely realized it.
Only I know these marks. Only a Buddha can know such characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
The Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise; the Buddhas who have attained fruition in the ten directions are also thus.
Śāriputra, you should know this. I tell you, Śāriputra, you must understand:
the words of all Buddhas are not different; the words of all Buddhas are identical, and you should now give rise to faith.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, and regarding the Great Sameness of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, one should give rise to the power of great faith;
one should give rise to the power of vast and profound faith.
"Long after the World-Honored One’s Dharma": because the World-Honored One has taught the Dharma for more than forty years, it is called "long after.
He must speak the truth. Having previously taught the provisional teachings for forty years, when the faculties [of sentient beings] have matured long after, he must speak the truth.
I address the assembly of śrāvakas, as well as the śrāvakas present in this gathering, and the pratyekabuddhas seeking the vehicle of solitary awakening who are present in this assembly:

I have caused them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering; in the past, the Buddha taught and transformed them so that they attained liberation from the bonds of the suffering of birth and death.
"Those who have attained nirvāṇa" means those who have reached and realized the bliss of quiescence.
"The Buddha by the power of skillful means" means that the Tathāgata employs the power of skillful means according to the capacities of sentient beings.
He reveals the teachings of the three vehicles. He elucidates the provisional means of the three vehicles: those of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
Sentient beings are attached everywhere; wandering in delusion, there is no object to which they do not cling.
He leads them so that they may attain deliverance; the Buddha uses skillful means to lead them to liberation.

At that time, within the great assembly, there were twelve hundred śrāvakas, including the arhats who had exhausted all outflows, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others, just as described at the beginning of the sutra.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had resolved upon the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas each thought to themselves:
"Because the Buddha has praised the Dharma as profound and difficult to understand, we have given rise to doubts."
Now, for what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly, most earnestly, and with such profound gravity,
praise the skillful means and the wondrous vehicle that guides and receives beings?
He speaks thus of the Dharma attained by the Buddha— the Dharma realized by the Buddha at the site of enlightenment.
It is extremely profound and difficult to understand. Because the meaning of the Dharma is deep, it is difficult for those of shallow capacity to comprehend.
Regarding that which is spoken, the Buddha has already explained it;
yet its underlying intention is difficult to know, for its intended meaning and purpose are hard to discern.
It is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is beyond the reach of the intellectual power of the two vehicles.
The Buddha speaks of the single meaning of liberation; the Buddha speaks of the single meaning of the quiescent extinction of liberation in the Hīnayāna.
We, too, have attained this Dharma; we have attained this Dharma of liberation through true emptiness, reached nirvana, and realized the bliss of cessation.
Yet now we do not know it; that which you now praise, we are unable to understand.
This is the direction toward which this meaning tends; it is the direction toward which the meaning of the Mahāyāna tends.
At that time, Śāriputra knew the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly; he knew the uncertainties within the hearts of all those in the fourfold assembly.
Not having yet understood it myself, and not yet being clear regarding this Dharma, I addressed the Buddha, saying to Śākyamuni Buddha:
"World-Honored One, by what cause and by what condition? By what reason and for what reason [do you speak thus]?"
He praises with earnestness; he earnestly extols and lauds in his heart the foremost skillful means of all Buddhas—
the constant, conventional skillful means that guides beings toward the three vehicles— and the foremost, most profound skillful means of all Buddhas, not knowing what dharma it is.
It is profoundly deep and subtle; it is exceedingly profound, extremely subtle, secret, and supreme.
It is a dharma difficult to understand, for it is called "difficult to understand" because it is not known by those of the three vehicles.
"Since of old" means from the time I was at the Deer Park in the past.
Never before have we followed the Buddha, nor have we ever heard such a teaching spoken by him.
Having heard the Dharma praised by the Buddha in this way, the fourfold assembly now all harbor doubts; none among them understand, and all possess minds filled with uncertainty.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, will contemplate this matter and expound upon it; may you unfold and explain this point of doubt.
For what reason, World-Honored One, and by what causes and conditions?
He earnestly praised the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma. At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom! The Buddha’s wisdom shines everywhere like the sun.
The Greatly Awakened Holy Lord, the World-Honored One of myriad virtues!"
After a long time, he speaks this Dharma; only after a long time since attaining enlightenment does he speak this Dharma.
He himself declares that he has attained such a thing: the Buddha himself declares that he has attained such a supreme Dharma that is difficult to understand.
The powers, the fearlessnesses, and the samādhis; the ten powers, the four kinds of intrepidity, and the assembly of those rightly established in certainty;
the dhyānas, liberations, and so forth; the meditative absorptions, tranquil concentrations, and various deliverances, and so forth.
The inconceivable Dharma. This Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.
The Dharma obtained at the site of enlightenment; the Dharma obtained within the site of enlightenment.
There is no one capable of posing a question; there is no one at all who can pose a question.
My intention is difficult to fathom; the Buddha’s intention is subtle and difficult to measure.
Furthermore, there was no one capable of questioning him. It was not only that he was difficult to fathom, but also that there was no one who could question him.
Without being questioned, he spoke of his own accord; though no one requested it, the Buddha himself proclaimed this teaching.
He extols the path he has traveled; he praises the unsurpassed path he has practiced.
His wisdom is most subtle and profound; that wisdom is exceedingly refined, secret, and marvelous.

This is what all Buddhas have attained. Such profound wisdom is attained by all Buddhas, by all Arhats free from outflows, and by those who have attained the four fruits through the outflow-free noble path.
As for those who seek nirvāṇa— namely, those who previously gave rise to the two types of mind of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and sought quiescence—
they have now all fallen into the net of doubt. Those who have already realized the small fruits, as well as those who seek such realization, have now all fallen into uncertainty.
...this net.
For what reason did the Buddha speak this? World-Honored One, for what purpose did you say these words:
"Those who seek pratyekabuddhahood," and "those who seek to realize pratyekabuddhahood"?
The two assemblies of renunciants— the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs— and the eight classes of beings, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others,
looked at one another with hesitation. Each member of the assembly gazed at the others, indecisive and full of doubt.
Beholding the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings—beholding and gazing up at the World-Honored One who is fully endowed with merit, wisdom, and myriads of virtues—what is the meaning of this?
How is this matter to be understood?
May the Buddha explain this for us. May the Buddha, out of his great compassion, explain it for the sake of the assembly.
Among all the śrāvaka assemblies, and among the disciples of the Śrāvakayāna.
The Buddha declared me to be foremost; the Buddha has always said that I am foremost in wisdom.
Yet, regarding my own wisdom, I myself do not now understand the Buddha’s wisdom.

They were unable to resolve their doubts; harboring uncertainty within their minds, they could not reach a definitive conclusion as to whether this was the ultimate Dharma, or rather the great ultimate Dharma realized upon the fruition of the path.
This refers to the path practiced therein; alternatively, it refers to the pure path practiced at the stage of the causal ground.
Those born from the Buddha’s own mouth are called "sons born [of the Buddha]" because, having heard the Dharma of the Four Truths from the Buddha’s own mouth, they have entered the Noble Path.
With palms joined in reverence, they gaze up at the Buddha, awaiting his instruction;
may he utter a subtle and wondrous sound—may the Buddha bring forth the subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma.
At that time, he spoke according to reality; at one time, he spoke truthfully to the assembly.
There were gods, nāgas, spirits, and others—members of the eight classes of beings—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, indicating their great multitude.
The bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha, those many bodhisattvas seeking the path to buddhahood, are in great number eighty thousand; approximately, there is a multitude of eighty thousand.
Furthermore, from all the myriad billions of lands and all the nations of the world,
the wheel-turning sage-kings arrived; all these wheel-turning kings came to the presence of the Buddha,
joining their palms with a reverent heart, and gazing upon him with joined palms to manifest their devotion.
"I wish to hear the complete path; I wish to hear the complete and wondrous path through the power of my karma.
At that time, when Śāriputra had spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra.
"Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further. By repeating "stop, stop," it is shown that one need not speak of this matter.

If one were to speak of this matter—meaning to say "this matter"—it would refer to the supreme and wondrous Dharma. The first "stop" is merely a cessation, while the latter clarifies the intent of that cessation.
"All worlds" refers to the three worlds. The various devas and humans—the devas of the three realms and all worldly beings—shall all be struck with alarm and doubt.
Those in the world of shallow understanding who suddenly hear this profound Dharma shall all be terrified and give rise to confusion and doubt.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "I have already been rebuked previously, yet now I address you once more.
World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain this; I pray that you will explain it. I beseech the Buddha to speak for my sake."
Why is this so? To ask what the intention behind this request is:
there are in this assembly countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* beings; *asaṃkhyeya* here means "innumerable."
He has seen various Buddhas; he has already beheld many Buddhas.
His faculties are sharp and keen; his six sense organs are pure, courageous, and acute.
His wisdom is clear and bright; he is sagacious and thoroughly penetrating.
Upon hearing what the Buddha has taught—having heard the profound and subtle teachings spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One—one is able to develop reverent faith.
Fearing that [others] might be startled or doubtful, the Buddha did not previously speak; he now speaks because those with the clarity of wisdom can develop reverent faith.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One;
the Buddha-King who rules the three realms as the Great Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One within the world."
Please speak; do not have concern. I pray that you will speak; do not harbor any anxiety.
This assembly is immeasurable; within this gathering now are countless multitudes.
There are those capable of respectful faith; there are those capable of honoring the Dharma.
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra. Śāriputra requested the Buddha a second time, but the Buddha again stopped him, saying:
"If one were to speak of this matter, or if one were to further expound upon this matter of the wondrous Dharma..."
All those in the world—devas, humans, and asuras—will be filled with alarm and doubt. For devas and asuras to speak out of alarm and doubt is of no benefit.
As for the monks of overweening pride, they practice with excessive arrogance, looking down upon all others and claiming that none can equal them, thus giving rise to haughtiness.
Pride: it will cause one to fall into a great pit; it will cause those who are arrogant and ignorant to fall into the great pit of the conceit of self within birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. He stopped him a second time.
"My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive"; it is because it is difficult to conceive that he does not speak of it.
Those who possess overweening pride—those people who act with arrogance due to their superior conceit—will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing this;
such individuals will certainly not show respect or faith if they hear it.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "The Buddha has already twice restrained me, yet I have repeated my request a third time.
World-Honored One, I pray that you will speak of it; I pray that you will speak of it. To repeat the words "I pray you will speak" is an expression of the utmost earnestness.
Within this assembly now, within this great assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
those such as ourselves, resembling our own kind, number in the hundreds,
thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions; such is the multitude.
Throughout successive lifetimes, they have already done so; throughout past ages, they have already seen the Buddhas,
received transformation from the Buddhas, and heard the Dharma from the World-Honored Buddhas to receive transformation—
such people as these, like the various individuals mentioned above.
One will surely be able to respect and believe [the Buddha]. Having long followed the Buddha’s transformation, one will surely be able to believe the Dharma.
"The long night" refers to the darkness of ignorance; if one can respect and believe, one will surely transcend birth and death, which is called "peaceful stability."
It brings great benefit; it provides much that is gained, nourishing and advantageous.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings."
O Unsurpassed Compassionate Honored One, perfect in both merit and wisdom, pray teach the foremost Dharma; pray teach the foremost, most subtle and wondrous Dharma.
I am the eldest son of the Buddha; I am the World-Honored One’s eldest son who has attained the Dharma.
Please deign to explain this in detail; we pray that you will compassionately provide a detailed exposition.
This assembly consists of immeasurable multitudes; within this Dharma assembly are countless great congregations.

One who is able to revere and believe in this Dharma—speaking of these people who are able to revere and believe in the Dharma—the Buddha has already [done so] throughout successive lifetimes; the Buddha has already [done so] in past lives.
He thus taught and transformed such as these; he instructed and guided such multitudes as these, all of whom with single-minded devotion joined their palms.
The entire assembly, with single-minded reverence, joined their palms.
We wish to hear and receive the Buddha’s words; we intend to listen to, believe in, and accept the Buddha’s words.
We, the twelve hundred—twelve hundred great arhats.
And for others who seek Buddhahood—just as the various disciples and others were listed in the introduction—I pray for the sake of this assembly; I pray for the sake of all these great multitudes.
Please deign to explain this in detail. We pray that you will compassionately and analytically expound it.
May these people hear this Dharma; may this great assembly hear the sublime Dharma.
They will then give rise to great joy; they will be able to respect and believe, giving rise to great delight.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "You have already made your request earnestly three times. [The Buddha] said: "Śāriputra has already extended his request three times."
How could I not speak? Since your request is so earnest and repeated, how could I not speak?
Listen now attentively. As I am about to speak for you, first restrain your senses, focus your mind, and listen with earnest attention.
Reflect upon this well. Contemplate it thoroughly and keep it in reverent mindfulness.
For your sake, and for the sake of the assembly, I shall provide a detailed explanation according to the Dharma-exposition, the parable-exposition, and the causal exposition found below in the text.
When these words were spoken, at the time our Buddha, the World-Honored One, made this declaration,
there were five thousand people in the assembly— five thousand in total, comprising both monks and nuns, as well as laymen and laywomen,
whether they had left the household life or remained at home.
He immediately rose from his seat; rising from the assembly, he prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
He paid homage to the World-Honored One, joined his palms, and withdrew. Why was this so?
When the Buddha desired to preach the Dharma, the assembly withdrew from their seats—what was his intention?
The roots of sin of these people are deep and heavy. These five thousand individuals possess ignorance and deluded thoughts that can give rise to all manner of faults;
this is called the root of sin, where karma is profound and hindrances are heavy.
Furthermore, they harbor overweening pride and treat those who practice with superior diligence as negligent and indolent.
To claim what has not been attained as attained; to claim for oneself that there is attainment when there is none;
to claim what has not been realized as realized; and to claim for oneself that there is realization when there is none—such are the errors, such are the faults.
For this reason, he did not remain; he withdrew from his seat and did not stay at the Dharma assembly.
The World-Honored One remained silent;
the Buddha merely maintained his silence and did not restrain him, nor did he constrain or suppress him to make him stay.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine, those with overweening pride have now departed. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In this great multitude present before me now, there are no longer any branches or leaves;
those who left out of overweening pride are like the removal of branches and leaves."
They are purely of genuine substance; they are purely of solid and firm bodies.
Śāriputra, such people of overweening pride are precisely these five thousand members of the assembly.
It is well that they have withdrawn; it would have been best had they not stayed previously, for now that they have departed because of their arrogance, it is truly excellent.
Very well. Listen now attentively. Now, carefully restrain your mind and listen with close attention;
I shall speak for you. Having consented to speak for the assembly, I shall do so.
Śāriputra said, "So be it, World-Honored One. "So be it" (*vāḍha*) is a term used to express assent.
"I wish to hear with joy" means that his heart desires, delights in, and wishes to listen to [the teaching].
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such is this wondrous Dharma; such is the subtle and sublime Dharma that shall be spoken.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, preach it only at the proper time. This wondrous Dharma is inconceivable; one must wait for the right moment and the ripening of conditions before daring to speak it."
It is like the udumbara flower—here called the "flower of auspicious response"—which appears only once in a great while.
Just as the flower of auspicious response manifests only when its time has come, Śāriputra, you all must believe; you all must give rise to great faith.
That which has been spoken by the Buddha—believe that the sublime Dharma spoken by the World-Honored Buddha is not false.
The Buddha’s words are true and devoid of falsehood.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; they teach in accordance with the inclinations and preferences of sentient beings.
He preaches the Dharma, yet its underlying intention is difficult to understand; its meaning and purport are profound, subtle, and hard to comprehend.
Why is this so? In what way is it difficult to understand?
I employ countless skillful means; the Buddha employs various skillful means and wisdoms, various causes and conditions, as well as various mental causes and objective conditions.
Metaphorical expressions: speaking by drawing upon analogies and similes to illustrate;
expounding all phenomena. To flowingly expound all phenomena means that these dharmas are beyond conceptualization and discrimination;
their dharma-nature is empty and quiescent, free from all names and signs, and cannot be conceived by the mind.
It cannot be understood through verbal discrimination; it is beyond the reach of thought and reflection.
It belongs only to the Buddhas; indeed, only from Buddha to Buddha [is it known].
Only then can one know it; only then can one come to understand it.
Why is this so? For what reason is it thus difficult to comprehend?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the Honored Ones of the world—[are such].

It is solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition; that is, exclusively for the purpose of opening, revealing, awakening, and entering sentient beings into their own inherently existing Buddha-knowledge and vision—the primary correct cause and virtuous condition for the single great matter of transcending birth and death.
They appear in the world; they manifest supernatural transformations and emerge into the world.
Śāriputra, what is meant by saying that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter?
This question is raised here, while the answer is found in the following text.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Knowledge" refers to the Buddha-mind; "vision" refers to the Buddha-eye.
Before hearing the Dharma, the mind is constantly obscured; [the Buddhas] wish to expound it for them so that their minds may be opened.
It is for the sake of making [beings] pure; it appears in the world so that they may eliminate defilements and return to their original purity. It appears for this reason:
desiring to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it appears in the world. As for what was said above regarding "opening," it is like this:
The "opening" mentioned here is like pointing out and indicating all the objects within a room.

It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world. Thus, by opening and revealing true knowledge and true vision, he intends to cause them to realize and understand that the mind itself is the Buddha.

He appears in the world in order to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; although they previously attained awakening and possessed the Buddha’s insight and knowledge, he now desires for them to realize and enter and thereby obtain the Buddha’s wisdom.
Śāriputra, it is for this one great cause and condition that all Buddhas appear in the world.
These four phrases conclude and demonstrate the preceding passage, showing that the terms "opening, revealing, awakening, and entering" constitute the one great cause and condition.

The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas. This clarifies that the original intent for the appearance of a Buddha is solely to instruct all bodhisattvas so that they may enter the Buddha-way.

In all that he has done— from the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*— whatever actions or skillful means he has employed have always been for a single purpose;
they have constantly and solely been for the sake of this one great matter.
He reveals and awakens sentient beings solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this refers precisely to that single matter.
Śāriputra, it is because the Tathāgata relies only upon the Single Buddha Vehicle that, although he speaks of three vehicles, in reality there is but one.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

For the sake of sentient beings, he preaches so that they may attain the One Vehicle (ekayāna), such that there are no other vehicles—neither two nor three. There is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, with nothing else besides it, whether the two vehicles of Great and Small, or the three vehicles of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is also like this. It is not only the present Buddha who teaches the One Vehicle;
all Buddhas in the ten directions do likewise.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past— those Buddhas who have already passed away—
by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, that is, through the various gates of the perfections and their skillful expedients, [have taught].
Through various causes and conditions, through all causes and conditions of the retribution for good and evil,
through parables and expressions, and through similes, analogies, and verbal formulations—
for the sake of sentient beings, indeed for the sake of sentient beings.
He expounds all dharmas and all skillful means;

these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Although he teaches various dharmas for the purpose of entering the One Vehicle, there are these sentient beings among the assembly who hear the Dharma.
They hear the Dharma from the Buddhas; they obtain and hear the sublime Dharma from the presence of the Buddhas, attaining it all to the ultimate degree.
Although he initially speaks of three vehicles, in the end he causes all to attain the single vehicle path.
Regarding "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*): it is said that there are three types of knowledge. First, "all-knowledge" refers to the emptiness-wisdom realized by those of the Two Vehicles.

Second, "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgajñatā*) refers to the skillful means realized by Bodhisattvas. Third, "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*)—which integrates both emptiness and the provisional—is the Middle Way, the wisdom of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, as for the future Buddhas who shall appear in the world during the future time— those who will appear in the world— they too,
by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, will [teach] for the sake of sentient beings.
He expounds all dharmas because every dharma is for the sake of the single Buddha-vehicle. He demonstrates that the mind and dharmas of all Buddhas are identical.
He shows that these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Thus he instructs and leads the multitude.
The realization attained by those born [in these lands] is equal.
Śāriputra, while previously the past and future were clarified, here it is said that [this realization occurs] within all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions in the present.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently teaching the Dharma and dwelling in the world,
are compassionate Honored Ones who bring great benefit; through many skillful means, they provide nourishment, profit,
and peace for sentient beings, establishing all sentient beings in security and happiness.

These Buddhas—the Buddhas of the ten directions—likewise employ immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of expression to expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
all these teachings are for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Thus, they draw upon the deeds performed by the present Buddhas as being identical [to their own].

Thus, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). This demonstrates that the benefits gained by all sentient beings are equal.
Śāriputra, these Buddhas, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, teach and transform only bodhisattvas;
they do so solely for the sake of bodhisattvas and have no other vehicle.
This is because they desire to reveal to sentient beings the knowledge and vision of a Buddha. Know that these two characters [“Buddha”] are themselves the Buddha-mind.
The two characters "seeing" (ken) are the Buddha’s wisdom itself.
It is because he wishes to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because he desires to cause sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"Showing," "awakening," and "entering" represent the Buddha’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Those who realize this principle are sentient beings who are themselves the Buddha.
Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus. I encompass the three periods of time and know all sentient beings—
those things known by the Buddha’s wisdom,
their various desires, and the manifold inclinations within the minds of sentient beings.
Deeply attached in their hearts, they give rise to extreme craving and delight toward all sensory objects.
According to their own natures and the fundamental habitual tendencies of those who are deluded,
[the Buddha] employs the power of skillful means through various causes, conditions, parables, and verbal expressions— through all such skillful means and wisdom— ...
...and preach the Dharma for them, expounding it for them.
Śāriputra, all this is for the sake of causing them to attain the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes. Such is the seed.
Through countless skillful means, [the Buddha] acts for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain the One Vehicle.
Śāriputra, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, within all the buddha-fields of the ten directions...
There is not even the Two Vehicles; there is not even the Great and Small Vehicles, let alone three.
How much less could there be the teachings of the Three Vehicles consisting of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas?
Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

Just as when one throws dust into clear water and it becomes turbid and murky, they are called "turbidities"; likewise, when delusive false thoughts overturn the fundamentally pure mind and render it obscured and dim, this is called "turbid evil."
What is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) refers to the depravity of the times.
The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) refers to the mind being constantly sorrowful and troubled, unable to attain clarity.
The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers to the constant arising of manifold thoughts, remaining in a state of perpetual confusion.
The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): that which is seen by the mind’s eye does not depart from the conditions of sensory dust.
The turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*): the life-span of a single karmic retribution always remains within turbidity.
Thus, Śāriputra, these two terms refer to the aforementioned five turbidities.
During the turbidity of the kalpa, at the time of the confusion of the final kalpa and the darkness of the turbid world, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy;
the obstructions and impurities of the worldly beings are deep and grave. They are stingy, greedy, and envious.

To be parsimonious with wealth is called stinginess (*mātsarya*); to take more than one's share is called greed (*lobha*); to harm the worthy is called envy (*īrṣyā*); to harm others for the sake of beauty is called... [jealousy] (*mātsarya*).
Envy. Because it accomplishes all unwholesome roots, that which is shrouded by ignorance and produces various evil karmas is called an unwholesome root.
Through the power of skillful means, the Buddhas act; because sentient beings are deluded, the Buddhas manifest skillful means.
Within the single Buddha-vehicle, within the single true path of the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle, [the Tathāgata] distinguishes and teaches three.
Through skillful discernment, he provides the teaching of the three vehicles.
Śāriputra, whether they be my disciples, or disciples sitting beneath me, Śākyamuni—
Those who claim to be Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas— namely, those of the two vehicles who claim for themselves that they are Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—
do not hear and do not know; their ears cannot hear it and their minds cannot know it.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform beings solely for the sake of bodhisattvas. Not knowing that the Tathāgatas act only for the sake of bodhisattvas, they cling to the existence of the three vehicles;
such individuals are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they bodhisattvas.
They are not Arhats; rather, they are Arhats of the Lesser Vehicle and not Arhats of the Great Vehicle.
They are not Pratyekabuddhas; rather, they are Pratyekabuddhas of the Lesser Vehicle and not Pratyekabuddhas of the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—the two assemblies of the Hīnayāna—claim for themselves that they have already attained arhatship.
Like those who have entered the fourth dhyāna, these bhikṣus, who lack learning and insight, were originally ordinary persons;
yet they falsely claim to have realized the state of a sage, asserting for themselves that they have attained the fruit of arhatship.
This is the final body; it is the very last body for one who has emerged from the three realms.

Having attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*, they reckon the fruits of the outflow-free state within the tainted heavens and thus no longer aspire to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Within these minor benefits, they themselves...

If they believe that by not seeking great benefit they have achieved *sambodhi*, you should know that such people are all those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Merely because of their diligence, they engage in superior practice and attain a minor degree of joy;
yet, lacking deep learning and vision, they have in fact not attained any of the fruits of sainthood. Claiming to have attained what they have not attained is called overweening pride.
This concerns those who are conceited. Why is this? Because how could they have attained what they have not yet realized or entered?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship, yet he did not believe in the realization of the objectless (anālambana), [he would be conceited].
It is impossible that one would not believe this Dharma. If there were indeed realization, it would be natural for one to believe the Dharma upon realizing it;
for one to realize it and yet not believe it is impossible—except after the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa. Indeed, except after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha is not present before us; it is a time when the Buddha does not dwell in the world.
Why is this? For what reason is he excluded?
Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there is no enlightened teacher in the world.
Regarding such sūtras as these, and all other Mahāyāna scriptures of this kind, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain their meaning are called people of right faith.
Such people are difficult to find; indeed, such persons are rare in the world.
If one encounters other Buddhas, or if one happens to meet other Buddhas appearing in the world,
then within this Dharma, within this subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna Dharma, one will attain definitive understanding;
for it is only by encountering a Buddha that the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna is resolved.
Śāriputra, you all should believe and understand with a single mind. A mind free from divergent thoughts is called "one.
Receive and uphold the Buddha’s words: receive them because of faith, and uphold them because of having received them.
The words of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not false. The Buddha’s speech is true and real; it is certainly without falsehood.
There is no other vehicle; there is neither two nor three.
There is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. There is only this one Buddha Vehicle, the true path.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "There are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride;
they cherish a heart of excessive arrogance and contempt."
The upāsakas were arrogant, relying on themselves to despise others;
the upāsikās lacked faith, as did the fourfold assembly previously mentioned who lacked right faith.
Such was the state of these fourfold assemblies—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as the eight classes of beings and so forth.
Their number was five thousand. Altogether, such people as these did not perceive their own faults;
they were unable to recognize for themselves the error of their arrogance.
They possessed deficiencies and gaps in their precepts, and their practice of minor discipline was deficient, flawed, and leaking.
One guards and cherishes one's flaws. A flaw in jade is called *xia*; a flaw in a person is called *ci*. To defile the original received body is termed "flaw" (*xiaci*).
This indicates that a limited wisdom has already emerged; to delight in and cling to minor dharmas is what is meant by "limited wisdom. One must fortunately depart from this.
They were the dregs and chaff among the assembly. Their understanding was merely superficial, lacking the true essence and function—like the dregs of wine or the husks of rice.
They departed because of the Buddha’s majestic power; they departed out of fear and awe of his supreme majesty.
These people have little merit. These five thousand individuals all lack the conditions of fortune and virtuous conduct;
they are incapable of receiving this Dharma. Their power is insufficient to receive this Great Dharma.
This assembly is without branches or leaves. Now, in this great assembly, the branches and leaves of both views and afflictions have all withered and fallen away;
there remain only those that are pure and substantial, possessing exclusively firm, steadfast, and sincere roots and trunks.
Śāriputra, listen well. Tell Śāriputra, listen and receive this well:
the Dharma attained by all Buddhas, that which is attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, at their site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
By means of the power of immeasurable skillful means, and through the power of the wisdom of expedient skillfulness, he teaches for the sake of sentient beings;
for those of sharp faculties, he teaches in accordance with reality.
Regarding what sentient beings think in their minds, and the various paths practiced within the minds of those sentient beings,
he employs skillful means to teach the way of the five vehicles.
The various natures of desire; the various numbers of natures of pleasure and longing;
the wholesome and unwholesome karma of previous lives; and the wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed in the past.
The Buddha, having fully known this, and having fully known the various faculties and capacities of those beings,
[taught] by means of various conditions and parables, and by means of various causes, conditions, and parables.
Through the power of skillful means in speech and the power of wisdom in the skillful use of language,
they cause all to rejoice and ensure that the entire assembly attains joy and gladness.
Some speak of the *sūtra*, which here is called the *Kṣepaṇīya-sūtra* (Scripture of Concordance).
It refers to that which was spoken by the Buddhas, being in accord with the principle and suited to the capacity of beings. The *gāthā* and the *itivṛttaka*: *gāthā* is also called *geya*;
this is translated as "isolated" (*kuqi*), meaning verses spoken directly without preceding prose. The *itivṛttaka* refers to accounts of events performed in former lives.
The Jātakas and Adbhutadharmas: "Jātaka" refers to the accounts of the bodies born in former lives;
"Adbhuta" refers to the teaching of rare and unprecedented dharmas that have not been heard before.
It also speaks of causes and conditions: namely, the causes of good and evil, as well as the conditions for good and evil.
There are also parables and *geya*. A parable (*avadāna*) refers to an explanation that employs a simile.
*Geya* refers to verses that restate the preceding prose (*gadya*) in metrical form.
The *Upadeśa-sūtra* (Expository Sūtras), here translated as "Discussions," together with the preceding nine divisions, are termed the "Dharma of Expedient Means.
They are for those of dull faculties who delight in the Lesser Dharma—those of inferior and dull capacities who take pleasure in and are attached to the Lesser Dharma.
They are greedily attached to birth and death; their greedy minds are fondly attached to the conditioned phenomena within the realm of birth and death.
Toward all the infinite Buddhas, at the abodes of all the Buddhas...
They do not practice the profound and wondrous path; they are unable to receive and practice the profound and wondrous path.

They are afflicted and disturbed by manifold sufferings: their minds are constantly troubled by the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death; the suffering of encountering the hated and the disliked;
the suffering of being separated from the loved; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
For their sake, I speak of nirvāṇa; for those whose faculties are weary of suffering and seek the Lesser Vehicle, I speak of the two kinds of nirvāṇa:
that with remainder and that without remainder.
I establish these as skillful means. Thus does the Buddha bestow the teaching of such skillful means.
To cause them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom; to cause them to gradually enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
I have never said to you all—meaning, I have never said to you śrāvakas—that [you yourselves could attain it].
When I shall attain the Buddha-way, and furthermore when I shall achieve the Buddha-way, for that reason I have not yet spoken; for this reason, from of old, I have never spoken.

Because the time for speaking has not yet arrived; since the capacity of the audience is dull and inferior and the proper season has not yet come, now is precisely that time. Now is exactly the time when it ought to be spoken.
The Mahāyāna is taught as definitive. The provisional teachings of the past involved both opening and closing [the path], and were thus not definitive;
what is now taught is the Wondrous Vehicle, which is therefore called definitive.
"These ninefold teachings of mine" refers to the ninefold methods that I previously expounded.
These teachings are spoken in accordance with sentient beings; they are all expounded according to their individual capacities and dispositions.
Entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation. Only upon entering the single reality realm of the Mahāyāna does one reach the fundamental source.
For this reason, I preach this sutra; for this reason, I preach this wondrous vehicle.
If there is a son of the Buddha whose mind is pure—if there is a son of the Buddha whose mental ground is clear and pure.
"Supple and also of sharp faculties. Being disciplined, gentle, and soft, and furthermore possessing sharp faculties, refers to one of great capacity.
"In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas" means in the presence of those various Buddhas.
They practice the profound and wondrous path and cultivate the conduct of the Mahāyāna.
For these sons of the Buddhas, for these sons of the Buddhas with such great capacity, he preaches this Mahāyāna sūtra;
he preaches this perfectly wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
I bestow a prediction upon such persons; I grant a prediction to those of such capacity that they shall attain the Buddha-way in a future life, achieving the path of Buddhahood in the world to come.
One recollects the Buddha with a profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) delight only in minor fruits; their minds are shallow and near to the Great Vehicle.
Mahayana Bodhisattvas, however, desire directly to achieve the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood; their minds are far-reaching and thus called "profound.
To take the Buddha as an object of contemplation by means of this mind is termed "recollection" (*smṛti*).
Because they have cultivated pure precepts, among the three trainings, precepts are foremost; with pure precepts, concentration becomes clear, and one enters the Buddha-wisdom.
Such as these attain Buddhahood upon hearing [the teaching]; such as these, being of great capacity, attain the realization of Buddhahood upon hearing it.
Great joy pervaded his entire body; great rapture filled his whole being.
The Buddha knew his mental conduct; the Buddha knew all the dispositions and mental activities of that individual.
Therefore, I preach the Mahāyāna; for these very reasons, I preach the Supreme Vehicle for such as these—whether they be Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas, whether all Śrāvakas or even Bodhisattvas.
They hear the Dharma I preach; they hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma spoken by the Buddha, even down to a single verse, or at the very least, hearing but a single four-line stanza.
They will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood; they will all certainly and undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; within the Buddha-fields of the worlds of the ten directions.
There is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is only the perfectly wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
There is neither two nor three; that is to say, there is neither the duality of the Great and Small Vehicles, nor the triad of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles.
Except for what the Buddha has taught through skillful means, except for what the Buddha has compassionately taught through skillful means as three;
these are merely provisional names. Whether two or three, they are all but provisional designations.
He guides sentient beings. By the power of skillful means, he guides sentient beings by preaching the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, he speaks of the Lesser Vehicle to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
The Buddhas appear in the world; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest in the world.
This alone is the one true reality; this alone is the wondrous vehicle, the perfectly complete and true Dharma.
The other two are not true. The other two vehicles—the second and third—are merely expedient means and not ultimate reality.
One never uses the Lesser Vehicle; although two may be taught at the outset, in the end only the Great Vehicle is employed.
To deliver sentient beings; to rescue, succor, and liberate all sentient beings.
The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; the Buddha himself abides in the ultimate Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Dharma thus attained: it is the Dharma realized by the Buddha at the site of enlightenment;
it is adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, and adorned by meditative absorption, wisdom, and the ten powers.
By this, one delivers sentient beings; by this, one personally realizes [the truth] and delivers other sentient beings, personally realizing the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha has personally realized and attained the unsurpassed path.
The Mahāyāna Dharma of equality; the dharma of the non-duality and equality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
If one were to transform others using the Hīnayāna, or if a Buddha who has realized the Great Vehicle were to transform others by means of the Small [Vehicle].
Even down to a single person— if I were to teach the Lesser Vehicle to even one person out of a desire for small gain,

I would fall into stinginess and greed. If the Buddha were to conceal the Great [Vehicle] and preach the Lesser for their sake, he would fall into a greedy mind and a parsimonious attachment to the Dharma.
This matter is not permissible; this one thing is not permissible.
If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha; if a person, with a faithful mind, takes refuge in the Buddha.
The Tathāgata does not deceive. The Tathāgata is truthful and certainly free from deception.
Furthermore, he has no thoughts of greed or envy; nor does he have any thoughts of covetousness or jealousy.
He has severed the evils within all phenomena; he has severed all unwholesome karma within all phenomena.
Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout the ten directions—in the worlds of the ten directions—[is present].
Yet he alone is without fear. Because delusions and karma have not been exhausted, one cannot be free from dread; because the Buddha has thoroughly exhausted delusions, he alone is without fear.
"I adorn my body with marks" means that I adorn it with a body endowed with the primary and secondary marks.
His radiance illuminates the world; the light of his wisdom shines universally upon the world.
He is honored by immeasurable multitudes; he is revered and esteemed by immeasurable assemblies.
I shall preach the seal of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*). For these sentient beings, I shall preach the seal of the True Dharma of the true nature.
Śāriputra, you should know; Śāriputra, you should know my intention.
I originally established a vow; I established a great vow based on my original cause, desiring to cause all sentient beings to [attain liberation].
I desired to cause all living beings to [attain liberation].
They are no different from us; they are no different from the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Just as I have previously vowed, just as I have previously made my solemn aspiration.
Now it is fulfilled; now that my vows are complete, I have attained the Way of the Buddha to transform all sentient beings, to guide and convert all beings who remain lost in delusion.
May they all be led into the Buddha-way; may they all be led into the Buddha’s true path.
If I encounter sentient beings—if I should meet with all sentient beings—[I shall lead them].
They teach all by means of the Buddha-way; they transform and instruct them all through the Buddha-way.
Those without wisdom are confused; those without great wisdom have their minds inverted and disordered.
Deluded, they do not accept the teaching; being confused and full of doubt, they are unable to receive the teaching.
"I know these sentient beings"—I know these deluded sentient beings.
