They have never cultivated the roots of goodness; they have never cultivated or studied the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna.
They are firmly attached to the five desires, and with resolute minds they cling to the objects of the five desires: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
Affliction arises from delusion and craving; that is, affliction arises because of ignorant attachment.
It is due to the conditions of various desires, and because of the evil conditions of greed for those desires.
They fall into the three evil realms; they tumble, collapse, and sink into the three types of evil paths—those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
They transmigrate through the six destinies, where karmic fruits repay one another like the turning of a wheel, entering the six paths of the three good and three evil realms.
They undergo all manner of bitter poisons; they fully receive and take upon themselves the retribution of all bitter poisons.
They receive the subtle form within the womb, receiving birth from the maternal womb as a minute and insignificant form.
It constantly increases from lifetime to lifetime. From lifetime to lifetime, accumulated karma increases the retribution of suffering.
For those of meager virtue and little merit—those of inferior character whose virtue is slight and whose merit is scanty.
Oppressed by manifold sufferings, they are constantly tormented by various forms of suffering;
they enter the dense forest of false views, entering the dense forest of birth and death characterized by false views.
"Whether existent or non-existent" refers to various wrong views, such as those who cling to existence when things exist, or those who cling to emptiness when things are non-existent.
Relying upon these views means depending upon and dwelling within these improper views of existence, non-existence, and so forth.
The sixty-two [views] are fully present. Various non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings give rise to four kinds of views regarding the objects of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):
some say that the self is large and matter is small, and the self is within matter; some say that matter is small and the self is large, and matter is within the self;
some say that matter is itself the self; and some say that the self is distinct from matter. Since this is the case for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is likewise for the others.
The four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—each also have four propositions, totaling twenty.

If these are categorized according to the three periods of time—past, present, and future—there are twenty propositions for each period, totaling sixty. When combined with the two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two.
They are deeply attached to false and illusory phenomena. They harbor profound and heavy craving for the world’s deluded views and deceptive dharmas;
they cling to them firmly and refuse to relinquish them, grasping with a resolute mind and being unwilling to let go.
Arrogant and self-conceited, they give rise to great conceit, boasting, haughtiness, and self-importance while belittling others;
their minds are crooked, deceitful, and insincere—fraudulent, perverse, and dishonest, lacking integrity or truthfulness.

Throughout kalpas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, for such a duration of time, they did not hear the name of the Buddha; they did not hear the names of the myriad virtues of the Buddhas;
nor did they hear the True Dharma, nor even the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Such people are difficult to deliver. Because they lack the necessary conditions, such people are difficult to liberate.
For this reason, Śāriputra, it is for this cause.
I have established skillful means for them; I have established the skillful means of the three vehicles.
I have taught the paths that exhaust suffering; I have taught various Dharma gates, which are the paths that exhaust suffering.
I show them nirvana; I show them the dharma of the tranquility and extinction of nirvana.
Although I speak of nirvana, although I preach the dharma of tranquility and extinction for them.
This, too, is not true cessation; it is merely a skillful means and not the ultimate dharma of quiescent extinction.
All dharmas from the very beginning—all dharmas from the primordial source—[are thus].
It is eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction. The purity of the dharma-nature, being inherently quiescent from the beginning, is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Once the sons of the Buddha have practiced this path of the Buddha, [they realize it].
In a future life, one shall attain Buddhahood; in a future age, one shall indeed attain Buddhahood.
I possess the power of skillful means; I possess the power of skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
They reveal and teach the Dharma of the three vehicles; they open up, enumerate, and demonstrate the methods of the three vehicles.
All World-Honored Ones refers to all the Buddha-Bhagavāns of the world.
All speak of the path of the One Vehicle. Every Buddha speaks of the path of the One Vehicle.
Now, these great assemblies—this present assembly within this very gathering.
All should eliminate doubt and confusion. All should have deep faith in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching and not give rise to suspicion or hesitation that would lead to self-delusion.
The words of all Buddhas are no different; the Buddhas of the ten directions share the same Single Perfect Vehicle and have no differing words.
There is only the single vehicle; there is but one vehicle and no second dharma.
Throughout the countless eons of the past, within the world-systems of those bygone ages.
There are immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
These various Buddhas are so numerous that their count is immeasurable; they are exceedingly many, beyond all calculation or measurement.
In this way, these World-Honored Ones, through various conditions and parables, various causes and conditions as well as parables,
and by means of countless powers of skillful means— by means of countless kinds of skillful expedients.
He expounds the characteristics of all phenomena—the characteristics of all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
All these World-Honored Ones, those countless billions of Buddhas, all preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle;
they all preach the Way of the true reality of the One Vehicle.

He transforms immeasurable sentient beings; he transforms and delivers immeasurable sentient beings with whom he has a karmic affinity, causing them to enter the Buddha-way, causing them to enter the unsurpassed Buddha-way of the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, all the Great Holy Lords, and likewise all the Great Holy and Wise Masters of the Dharma, know all worlds;
through the Buddha’s wisdom, they perceive and understand the world.
The various classes of beings among gods and humans, and all types of sentient beings in the world—
whatever they desire in their deep-seated minds, and whatever they take pleasure in through their deeply attached deluded minds.
Furthermore, there are "other skillful means. The provisional paths of the Three Vehicles are called "other skillful means.
They assist in manifesting the primary meaning; by using the provisional to assist the real, they manifest the primary meaning.
If there are any classes of sentient beings— indeed, all classes of sentient beings—
who encounter the Buddhas of the past, or who have previously encountered the Buddhas of the past.
Whether it be hearing the Dharma and practicing giving, or hearing the Dharma and practicing giving;
or upholding the precepts and practicing patience, or being able to uphold the precepts and practice patience.
Vigor, meditation, wisdom, and so forth—vigor without slackening, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so on—are the six perfections and the myriad practices.
These constitute the various cultivations of merit and wisdom, and the various practices for the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom.
All such persons as these have already attained the path of Buddhahood. These individuals who practiced the pure life (*brahmacarya*) in past ages have all become Buddhas.
After the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas—whereas the previous passage referred to the time of the Buddhas' presence, this clarifies the period after their passing.

If there are people with virtuous and gentle minds, or again, those who are skillfully harmonious, refined, and mild—such sentient beings have all already attained the path to Buddhahood; they have all already attained Buddhahood, knowing that there is no distinction between vehicles.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa,
those who make offerings to their relics— those who reverently worship the Buddha’s relics—
shall erect billions of kinds of stupas, constructing billions of various types of stupas to enshrine the relics.
Gold, silver, and *sphaṭika*—the latter being crystal; *śaṅkha* and *aśmagarbha*, as before;
*musāragalva* and *vaiḍūrya*. Regarding *musāragalva*:
that which is exceptionally beautiful is called *musa* (stone), while that which is perfectly pure is called *garbha* (essence). Regarding *vaiḍūrya*: it is lapis lazuli.
The *li* is as previously described; it is a pearl (*muktā*).
It is pure and extensively adorned, being embellished with various pure and excellent objects.
It adorns the various stupas, serving as an ornamental chain for the various precious stupas.
Some erect stone shrines, while others build temples out of stone;
some use sandalwood and aloeswood, or else sandalwood timber and aloeswood incense.
Regarding *mukū* wood and other timbers: *mukū* is a fragrant wood found in Chang'an that can be used to fashion images as well as other various timber materials.
As for bricks, tiles, clay, and earth—one may construct halls and stupas using such materials.
If one piles up earth in a wilderness to create a Buddhist temple— like those made of earth in desolate wilds,
or even those fashioned as playthings for children— even during the playful laughter of infants and young children.

"Piling sand to make a stūpa for the Buddha": although it is said that piling sand to make a stūpa as a mere plaything is also a wholesome cause, all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
This passage encourages the production of faith by pointing to those who, in the past, performed various wholesome causes and have already achieved success.
"If a person acts for the sake of the Buddha," or "if there is another person who, for the sake of the Buddha,
establishes various images"— whereas the preceding section explained the construction of stupas and temple halls, this subsequent passage clarifies the making of images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Those carved and sculpted into various forms have all already attained the path of Buddhahood. Whether made of stone or wood, they are chiseled, engraved, carved, or incised into the forms of various Buddhas and other holy images;
or they may be made of the seven precious jewels, or fashioned through casting, assembly, or carving from precious materials.
Brass, pewter, red copper, and white copper; brass and pewter resemble gold.
White tin, lead, and tin—lead is soft while tin is hard and its color is slightly greenish-blue.
Iron, wood, and clay; cast iron, carved wood, and molded clay.
Or using glue, lacquer, and cloth—these three substances combined to fashion and adorn Buddha images;
by thus adorning the sacred images, all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood. Thus, all those who created images in the past [have likewise attained it].
"Having already attained Buddhahood" indicates the manifestation of the attainment of the fruit.
"Painting an image of the Buddha" means using pigments to depict the marks adorned with a hundred blessings;
that is, creating the marks of the World-Honored Buddha adorned with a hundred kinds of meritorious virtues.
Whether they create [images] themselves or cause others to do so, all have already attained the Buddha-way.
Whether they fashion images themselves or cause others to fashion them—even down to children playing in games, or even the playthings of young children.
Whether using grass, wood, or a brush; whether using grass, wood, ink, and a brush,
or using one's fingernails, or even using only the fingernails to draw an image of the Buddha—
these various methods constitute the creation of the form of the Buddha.

In this way, these people gradually accumulate merit; they gradually amass boundless merit, becoming fully endowed with a heart of great compassion and fully accomplishing a heart of great kindness and pity.
All have already attained the path of Buddhahood. Those who were thus in the past have all already realized the fruit;
they merely transform the various bodhisattvas by declaring that the Buddhas of the past had no distinct vehicles, but only the teaching of the One Vehicle to instruct bodhisattvas.
They deliver immeasurable multitudes; they rescue and liberate immeasurable sentient beings.
If a person [worships] at a stupa or a temple—a stupa being that which contains relics, and a temple being a place where an image is enshrined—then...
Regarding precious images and painted images— whether fashioned from various jewels or depicted in colors—
the flowers and incense represent virtuous causes, the banners represent virtuous qualities, the streamers represent the virtuous body, and the canopies represent virtuous fruits.
One should make offerings with a reverent mind; that is, one should cultivate offerings with a heart of respect.
Whether by having others perform music, or perhaps by having others produce various musical instruments.
Striking drums and blowing horns and conchs: one strikes the drum with a mallet or blows long horns and conch shells.

The *xiao*, flute, *qin*, and *konghou*: the *xiao* is made by weaving bamboo; the flute is made by hollowing out bamboo; the five-stringed *qin* was that of Shun, while the seven-stringed *qin* was that of the Zhou;
the *konghou* is likewise made of bamboo and is the music of the Han.
The lute, the gong, and the cymbals: the lute is made of wood and has three strings; the gong and the cymbals are as they are found in the world.
Such are the various wondrous sounds; such are the various wondrous musical sounds of these instruments.
They offer everything they possess as an act of worship;
they offer all that exists in the world as an act of worship, whether out of a joyful heart or because they have developed a joyful heart upon seeing the Buddha.
To chant and sing praises of the Buddha’s virtues: "chanting" (gebei) refers to the eternal words, while "praising virtues" (song) refers to the Sanskrit sounds.
This extends even to a single small sound, down to the very lowest, smallest sound.
All have already attained the path of Buddhahood. This cites the past to exhort the present:
if a person with a distracted mind, or even another who, amidst a distracted state of mind, offers so little as a single flower—this uses the few to illustrate the many.
By making offerings to a painted image, one gradually comes to see countless Buddhas;
for this reason, through such causes and conditions, one gradually attains the vision of countless Buddhas.
Some people perform prostrations by touching their heads to the ground, which is termed "bowing.
Others merely join their palms together, bringing the two palms in contact as a gesture of reverent etiquette.
Up to raising a single hand, down to merely lifting the hand to the forehead,
or slightly bowing the head, or even slightly lowering the head to pay respect.
By making offerings to this image, and by honoring the Buddha-image through these rites, one gradually beholds immeasurable Buddhas;
through these virtuous conditions, one gradually beholds all the Buddhas.
One spontaneously attains the Unsurpassed Way; this is the fulfillment of one's own practice through the accumulation of merit and virtue.
One extensively delivers countless beings; this means broadly liberating innumerable sentient beings.
He enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is the benefit of others, enabling them to attain ultimate, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
It is like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted; sentient beings are like the fuel and grass, while the Sage is like the fire in the hearth.
Once the fuel is spent, the fire must perish.
If a person with a distracted mind, or furthermore,
if someone with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple, or enters a temple or even a palace hall.

To once utter "Namo Buddha" and, with a single thought, call upon the Buddha for refuge and respect—by these means, all have already attained the Way of Buddhahood. How can it be that one attains Buddhahood in a single thought? If one does not resolve the mind [to seek awakening], one will never realize enlightenment. A journey of a thousand li begins with the first step; the merit of the myriad virtues begins with a single thought. To cite an analogy: *The Sutra on the Parable of the City* states: "Suppose there were a man who, having traveled for many years, arrived at a great city. He was weary and exhausted, yet he did not know the way back home. At that time, there was another man who, seeing him, felt great compassion and spoke to him, saying: 'Good man, you have come from afar and are weary and exhausted. I shall now show you the way back to your own country. The traveler said to him: 'How far is it from here to my home? The other replied: 'It is not far; it is only a hundred li. You need only proceed straight ahead, and you will reach it. The traveler said: 'I am weary and exhausted; how can I go so far? The other said: 'If you do not go, you will surely die here. If you go, you will certainly reach your home. The traveler said: 'I am indeed weary and exhausted, and I fear I cannot go. However, because of your compassionate instruction, I shall follow your words and proceed. Having heard this, he set out. After traveling for some time, he encountered a great river, deep and vast, with no bridge or ferry. Seeing this, his heart was filled with distress, and he feared he would not be able to cross. At that time, the other man saw him and again felt great compassion. He took a raft of wood and grass and gave it to him, saying: 'Good man, take this raft and cross over. The traveler said: 'How can I cross such a vast river? The other said: 'You must make an effort; you will surely be able to cross. The traveler said: 'I am weary and exhausted; how can I exert myself? The other said: 'If you do not exert yourself, you will surely perish in the water. If you exert yourself, you will surely reach the other shore. The traveler said: 'I shall now exert myself and cross over. Having heard this, he made an effort and crossed the river. Once he had reached the other shore, he sat down and reflected: 'I have come from afar and have endured much hardship. Now that I have reached this place, I should rest for a while. He then lay down and slept. Because he was exhausted, he fell asleep and died. What do you think? Has this person reached his home? The Buddha told Śāriputra: "This person has not yet reached his home. Why? Because he died after reaching the other shore. If he had not died, he would have reached his home. Śāriputra, the meaning of this parable is as follows: 'The great city' refers to Nirvāṇa. 'The traveler' refers to sentient beings. 'The other man' refers to the Tathāgata. 'The great river' refers to the ocean of birth and death. 'The raft' refers to the Dharma of the Mahāyāna. 'Reaching the other shore' refers to the stage of non-retrogression. 'Dying' refers to the exhaustion of the life-span of the body. 'Reaching the home' refers to the ultimate Nirvāṇa. Thus, it is known that although one may have reached the other shore, if one does not further cultivate the path, one will not attain the ultimate fruit. That all those who practiced even subtle causes in past lives have already attained Buddhahood proves that this is no empty proclamation.
Regarding the Buddhas of the past—regarding the countless Buddhas of the past world.
Whether during his lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa— whether while the Buddha is still in the world or after he has passed away—
if there are those who hear this Dharma, if there are those who hear this wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
All have already attained the path of Buddhahood. This illustrates that by hearing the Dharma, one attains the path of Buddhahood.
As it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it shall be with the World-Honored Ones of the future.
Their number is immeasurable; the names and numbers of the Buddhas are without limit.
These Tathāgatas, and these future World-Honored Ones as well—
They also teach the Dharma through skillful means, and they also expound all dharmas through skillful means.
This applies to all Tathāgatas of the past and all Tathāgata-Buddhas of the future.
By means of immeasurable skillful methods, all teachings of the Dharma are the Buddha’s skillful means for delivering all sentient beings and delivering all future sentient beings.
They enter the Buddha’s untainted wisdom; they enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha-vehicle.
If there are those who hear the Dharma—those who hear the sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha.
There is not one who will not become a Buddha; there is not a single person who shall fail to attain Buddhahood.
This is the original vow of all Buddhas: that when sentient beings hear the Dharma, they shall all attain non-retrogression and achieve Buddhahood through the power of the Buddhas' vows.
The Buddha-way that I practice; the path to Buddhahood that I enter.
I desire to cause all sentient beings—indeed, all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm—to [attain it].
They likewise attain this path; they likewise attain this unsurpassed Buddha-way.
As for all Buddhas of future ages—all Buddhas who shall exist in the future world.
Although one may speak hundreds of billions of times, and although one may expound hundreds of billions of kinds of dharma-gates,
countless skillful means, and countless gateways to the Dharma.
In reality, it is the One Vehicle; speaking according to the truth, all are the One Vehicle.
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, are fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.
Knowing that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature, the Buddhas have thoroughly realized that all dharmas are permanently abiding and immutable from the very beginning.
Emptiness and quiescence are fundamentally without self-nature.
The seeds of Buddhahood arise from conditions; the seeds of Buddha-nature—the fivefold merits—arise from conditions and thereby accomplish the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
For this reason, the One Vehicle is taught; for this reason, the Single Buddha Vehicle is taught.

This is the abiding of phenomena in their own position (*dharmasthititā*). That all phenomena are by nature empty and quiescent, such as they are and immovable—this is called "abiding in the position of phenomena."

The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. While the illusory characteristics of the world are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, the true characteristic is eternally abiding and neither arises nor ceases.

To realize that dharmas have no characteristic of arising is to be without characteristic; it is like the moon in water, which is empty yet visible, or like an image reflected in a mirror without a mind, which appears yet is always empty.
Having known this at the site of enlightenment, and having realized it at the site of enlightenment,
the Buddha— the Guide— teaches through skillful means. For the sake of sentient beings, the Guide of the World speaks by means of provisional words and expedient devices.
Worshipped by gods and humans; worshipped by all gods and humans. Regarding the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions:
whereas previously it was explained that past Buddhas practiced for themselves and transformed others, this teaching concerning the present is likewise the same.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges; the number of Buddhas is as great as the sands of those rivers.
They appear in the world; out of compassion, the Buddhas appear in the world.
For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, and desiring to bring peace and security to all sentient beings,
he likewise preaches such a Dharma, just as the Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma of the true marks of reality and quiescence.
He knows the supreme quiescence. The Buddha knows that all phenomena are pure, supremely and eternally quiescent by their very nature.
Yet, through the power of skillful means, although the Dharma is fundamentally ineffable, he provides various explanations for the sake of sentient beings by means of skillful means.
Although he manifests various paths, and although he reveals various gateways to the path, in reality they are for the Buddha-vehicle;
according to their true intent, they all lead to the Buddha-vehicle.

He knows the various conducts of sentient beings; he knows the diverse mental activities of all sentient beings, what their deep minds contemplate, and in which dharmas they deeply conceive attachment and affection.
Regarding the karma practiced in the past: what kind of karma was practiced in previous lives?

With regard to the power of desire, nature, and diligence—among what various inclinations and various habitual natures is one able to exert diligence, and in what pure powers of the path does one possess such capacity?

Furthermore, regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties— since capacities differ as superior, middling, or inferior, with the sharp being the superior faculty and the dull being the middling or inferior—
he employs various causes and conditions, such as the Jātaka and Avadāna tales, through countless kinds of causal circumstances.
An analogy is also a form of expression; it is an exposition using analogies to lead people toward understanding.
It is taught through appropriate skillful means, being explained according to whatever skillful means are suitable for each case.
Now I am also like this. As it is with all Buddhas, so it is with me now.
For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, and for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
By means of various dharma-gates and by means of various dharmas as gateways for entering the Path, he proclaims and reveals the Buddha-way;
he extensively expounds, demonstrates, instructs, and clarifies the Way of the Buddha.
By the power of my wisdom, and by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom and skillful means, I know the dispositions and natures of sentient beings;
I know the various faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings.
He teaches all dharmas through skillful means; he teaches the skillful means of the Three Vehicles so that all may attain joy.
Because he teaches the Dharma according to their faculties, they all rejoice.
Śāriputra, you should know this; Śāriputra, you should understand this intention:
with my Buddha-eye, I observe; with the eye of the Buddha’s perfect realization, I observe that Dharma-realm.
He beholds the sentient beings of the six realms. He perceives clearly those sentient beings within the six realms who are lost in delusion:
they are "poor" because they lack merit and wisdom; "lacking" means being destitute, while "extreme poverty" refers to the utmost state of deprivation.
Because of stinginess, they do not practice giving, and thus they lack merit; because of folly, they do not study, and thus they lack wisdom.
One enters the perilous path of birth and death. Birth and death are fearsome and are thus called the "perilous and evil path.
Suffering continues in succession without interruption. Due to past karma, one has brought about a present body;

within this present existence, being ignorant of the means of escape, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, thereby summoning future suffering that links together in succession without a moment's break.
They are deeply attached to the five desires; they develop a profound craving for the objects of the five desires, just as a yak loves its tail. By nature, a yak is excessively fond of its tail.
One is shrouded by craving and attachment. Because of craving and attachment, one's wondrous clarity is obscured;
being blind and dark-sighted, one sees nothing. To have no eyes is called "blind," and to be in darkness is called "dark-sighted"; thus, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing seen.

They do not seek the Buddha of Great Power; because they lack vision, they are unable to advance toward seeking the Buddha of Great Might, nor the Dharma that severs suffering, nor the Dharma of the cessation that severs suffering.
They have deeply entered into various false views; they have deeply entered the dense forest of false views regarding birth and death.
Seeking to abandon suffering through suffering, they perversely cultivate karmic actions of suffering in an attempt to escape the retribution of suffering.
For the sake of these sentient beings, and for the sake of those sentient beings with such wrong views, he gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness;
and the Buddha gives rise to a mind of great compassionate pity.
I first sat at the site of enlightenment. I first sat at the site of enlightenment in Magadha.
I contemplated the tree and also practiced walking meditation; I contemplated the past causes and conditions of the Bodhi tree and also practiced quiet walking meditation beneath that tree.
During the three periods of seven days, having already attained enlightenment, he maintained meditative stillness for twenty-one days,
contemplating such matters and deliberating upon such transformative deeds.
The wisdom I have attained—the unsurpassed wisdom realized by the Buddha—is subtle and wondrous, the most supreme;
it is profound, secret, perfect, and marvelous, the very pinnacle of excellence.
The faculties of sentient beings are dull; indeed, the natures of these beings are昏钝 (obscured and dull).
They are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance; because they cling to worldly pleasures, they are shrouded by delusion.
Regarding such types as these—how may this class of sentient beings be delivered?
By what means of teaching the Dharma may they be liberated?

"At that time, the various Brahma Kings": when the Buddha formed this thought, there were the various Brahma Heavenly Kings of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) as well as the various Śakras, Lords of Devas.
Within a single Buddha-field, there are three thousandfold world systems (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), each containing ten billion Sumeru Mountains;
since there is one Śakra for each Sumeru, they are referred to here as "the various [Śakras]."
The Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, the Gate-Keeper Kings who guard the four directions of the world,
and Maheśvara— the sixth heaven of the desire realm, known as "Sovereign" (*īśvara*) within the desire realm and "Great Sovereign" (*Maheśvara*) at the summit of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Together with the other hosts of devas, and the other hosts of celestial sages present in the assembly—
each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of followers— every single deva was joined by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions.

With reverence, they joined their palms and paid homage; with single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and prostrated themselves, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma, requesting the Buddha to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
I then reflected within myself; while seated, I reflected with my own mind:
"If one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, or if one were to extol exclusively the path of the Single Buddha Vehicle."

Sentient beings are submerged in suffering; indeed, these sentient beings are immersed in the ocean of suffering and are unable to believe in this Dharma, and ultimately they will never be able to gain faith in this sublime Dharma.
Because they destroy the Dharma and lack faith, and because they disparage and ruin the true teaching and cannot believe in it, they fall into the three evil realms.
Due to their destruction of the Dharma, they will inevitably fall into the evil paths; thus, it is not only useless, but it also harms them.
I would rather not teach the Dharma; it would be better for me not to speak at all and to quickly enter parinirvāṇa, to swiftly enter the tranquil nirvāṇa.

He called to mind the Buddhas of the past; he further reflected upon the power of skillful means practiced by those Buddhas of the past, and the power of skillful means employed in their transformative activities.
"The path that I have now attained—the path I have realized in this present life—should likewise be explained as the three vehicles;
it should also be explained as three through such skillful means."
While he was reflecting in this way—at the very moment the Buddha was engaged in such contemplation—the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared;
the Buddhas of the ten directions all manifested before him.
The Brahma-voice consoled me; with the sound of the Brahma-voice he comforted me:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni! Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!"
The foremost guide. Skillfully contemplating expedient means to lead and benefit sentient beings, he is the most preeminent among all guides.
He has attained this unsurpassed Dharma; he has attained this unsurpassed, right, and true Dharma.
Following all Buddhas and being able to accord with all Buddhas,
they employ the power of skillful means— that is, the power of the skillful means of the Three Vehicles.
We, too, have all attained it; we Buddhas have all likewise realized it—the most wondrous, foremost Dharma, the supreme, subtle, and foremost Dharma.
For the sake of all classes of sentient beings—for all such categories of sentient beings—he distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles;
within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three.
They possess little wisdom and delight in inferior teachings;
having little wisdom, they are attached to inferior teachings and lack self-confidence regarding their attainment of Buddhahood, being unable to believe that they shall become Buddhas.
Therefore, by means of skillful means— and for this reason, employing various skillful means—
he distinguishes and explains the various fruits; he extensively distinguishes and explains the fruits realized by those of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles.
Although the three vehicles are taught, and although they are explained with distinctions,

it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas; when its fundamental intent is examined, it is merely to guide those with the capacity for the bodhisattva path so that they may attain the Buddha-way.
Śāriputra, you should know this. Śāriputra, you should know that at that time, I heard the Holy Lion; I heard the Buddhas, the Holy Lords and Lions.
With a profound, pure, subtle, and wondrous voice— a deep, far-reaching, and pristine, subtle sound—
he utters "Namo to all Buddhas," vocally professing refuge and reverence to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Again he formed this thought; furthermore, he directed his attention and thought thus:
"I have emerged from a world of turbid evil; the Buddha has appeared during a time of turbid evil in the final kalpa."
Just as the Buddhas have taught, and according to the ritual procedures taught by the Buddhas of the past and present, I shall likewise practice in accordance with them;
I shall likewise follow the conduct practiced by all Buddhas.
Having reflected on these matters, and having reflected on the expedient means of the three vehicles, he proceeded toward Vārāṇasī; thus, from Magadha, he went to Vārāṇasī.
All phenomena possess the characteristic of quiescence; all phenomena are empty by nature and have the characteristic of quiescence.
This cannot be proclaimed through words; it can be realized through principle, but it cannot be expressed in speech.

By the power of skillful means; indeed, solely by the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, he spoke for the sake of the five bhikṣus, speaking for the sake of the five Kauṇḍinyas as mere provisional designations.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma; this is called the first turning of the wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park.
Therein arises the sound of Nirvana, the sound of skillful means regarding Nirvana.
As well as the Arhats—the five bhikṣus and others—all realized the four fruits.
Regarding the distinction between Dharma and Saṃgha: the Four Truths are called Dharma, and the Arhats are called Saṃgha.
Since time immemorial, throughout kalpas past, the Buddha has, from his long journey through the causal stages, praised and revealed the Dharma of nirvana;
he has extolled and elucidated the Dharma of quiescent extinction.
"The suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted; having distanced oneself from all the sufferings of birth and death, they are forever exhausted.
I always speak thus. The Buddha has always spoken thus throughout long kalpas."
Śāriputra, you should know this; Śāriputra, you should know the Buddha’s intention.
I see these sons of the Buddha; I see these sons of the Buddha present before me.
Those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way— those who set their minds on the vow to seek the path of the Buddha—
are immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis. This immeasurable great assembly,
all with hearts of reverence, at one and the same time, with hearts of reverence...
They all came to where the Buddha was; they all arrived at the place where the Buddha resided.
They had previously heard this from various Buddhas; they had already heard it from the presence of various Buddhas.
Regarding the Dharma taught through skillful means and the Dharma spoken with skillful mastery, I then had this thought:
"The Buddha, perceiving that the time has come, has formed this thought."
The reason why the Tathāgata has appeared, the reason why the Tathāgata has manifested in the world, is for the sake of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom;
it was originally for the purpose of proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now is precisely that time; now is the very time to proclaim the Buddha’s wisdom.
Śāriputra, you should know this: you must understand my intention in preaching the Mahāyāna.
Those of dull faculties and small wisdom; those of inferior, dull faculties and small wisdom and views;
those who are attached to signs and arrogant; those who are greedily attached to worldly appearances and self-conceited.
They are unable to believe this Dharma; they are unable to believe this Mahāyāna Dharma, which is why it was not taught to them.
Now I rejoice and am fearless; now I rejoice, for I have no such sorrow or fear.
Among all bodhisattvas, within the great assembly of bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means.
Previously, for those of inferior capacity, he did not yet escape the circuitous use of expedient teachings;
now that they have reached full maturity, he abandons his former expedients and teaches directly.
He speaks only of the unsurpassed path; he speaks only of the teaching of the single vehicle, the unsurpassed path.
When a bodhisattva hears this Dharma—when a bodhisattva of sharp faculties hears such a Dharma.

The net of doubt has been entirely removed. Having previously been undecided and entangled within the net of uncertainty, they have now heard the sublime teaching that tears asunder the web of all views.
These twelve hundred arhats were those whom the Buddha first converted: the five Ājñātakauṇḍinyas, the three Kāśyapas, Maudgalyāyana, and Śāriputra.

The entire assembly of Śāriputra’s disciples, totaling one thousand two hundred people— including five hundred disciples and those foremost among the arhats who have attained the stage of no-more-learning—
all shall likewise become Buddhas. Upon hearing this great news, the arhats’ [realization] shifted from being partial to being complete, and they all shall likewise attain ultimate perfection.
He brought it to completion,

just as the Buddhas of the three periods have done. He followed the ritual protocols for preaching the Dharma and the skillful means and ritual protocols for teaching and transforming beings, exactly as those Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods have practiced.
I am now also like this. The unsurpassed path I have now attained is likewise so.
I preach the Dharma of non-discrimination. While the paths of the three vehicles are called "discriminative teachings," preaching only the One Vehicle is precisely non-discriminatory.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world: the Buddhas of the ten directions arise with compassion in the world.
It is difficult to encounter them, for they appear after vast intervals of time; it is difficult to meet them because of the immense distance and long duration.
Even were a Buddha to appear in the world—even were the Buddhas to manifest in the world—it is difficult to preach this Dharma;
it is likewise difficult to preach the One Vehicle Dharma.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, across countless periods of time, it is difficult to hear this Dharma; it is not easy to obtain the hearing of this Dharma.
Those who are able to listen to this Dharma are those who can attend and receive this teaching within an assembly of the Dharma.
Such people are likewise rare; such individuals are not easily found. They are like the udumbara flower.
In the *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, this flower is translated as "Auspicious Response"; when this flower blooms, a Buddha appears in the world.
Thus, it is used as a metaphor for the fact that a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
All love and delight in it; all sentient beings without exception love and delight in it.
It is rare among gods and humans; it is seldom found in the heavens or the human realm.
It appears but once in a great while; it does not manifest when there is no path, but only when the opportune moment arises and the conditions are met can one hear it.
If one hears this Dharma and rejoices with praise—should one hear this Dharma and rejoice and offer praise—[one attains great merit].
Even down to uttering a single word, even down to briefly producing the sound of a single word, one has already made an offering;
one has already been able to perform the offering of Dharma.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time; all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—such a person is most rare;
such a person who possesses faith in the Dharma is extremely uncommon.
It is rarer than the udumbara flower; it is even rarer than the udumbara flower to encounter.
You all should have no doubt; you should not harbor any doubt regarding the Dharma.
I am the King of all dharmas. I am the World-Honored One, the King of all dharmas.

Upright and without guile; their nature is substantial, honest, and straightforward, free from all falsehood.

he will achieve the Buddha-way as the Honored One of Pervasive Wisdom.
His name shall be Flower Radiance (*Puṣpārāma*). He is a response-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*).
He shall deliver immeasurable multitudes; he shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to liberation.
He shall make offerings to countless Buddhas; he shall reverently serve and honor countless Buddhas.
They are fully endowed with the bodhisattva practices; they are fully endowed with the cultivation of the great bodhisattva deeds.

Regarding the phrase "the ten powers and so forth," this refers to the various merits such as the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Thus it is said "and so forth."
They shall realize the unsurpassed path; with their merits fulfilled, they shall enter the Buddha-way.
After immeasurable kalpas have passed—from this day forward, after immeasurable kalpas have elapsed—
The kalpa was named Great Jewel Adornment; during the time of the Buddha Flower Radiance, it was adorned with the great jewels of bodhisattvas.
The world was named Free from Defilement; because the world was pure, it was called Free from Defilement.
It is pure and free from defilement; because it is free from defilement, it is clear, and because it is free from blemish, it is pristine.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*); the clarity and transparency of the mind-ground is what is called "lapis lazuli.
Its paths are demarcated by golden cords; golden threads serve as boundaries along the sides of the roads.
There were trees of various colors made of the seven treasures; these rows of trees of the seven treasures had diverse names and forms, and they were always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The trees belonging to those bodhisattvas likewise constantly bore flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The bodhisattvas of that land—the great bodhisattvas of that Land of Flower Radiance—possess minds and thoughts that are always firm and steadfast;
their aspirations and virtuous reflections never falter or shrink back.
The perfection of supernatural powers—the six kinds of supernatural powers and all the perfections—are all fully complete;
their meritorious practices are profound and firm, with no dharma left unprepared.
In the presence of countless Buddhas, they have already well studied the bodhisattva path;
they are well able to cultivate and train in the bodhisattva path.
Such great beings as these, and the countless great beings mentioned above, were all transformed by the Buddha Flower Radiance;
they were all those whom Flower Radiance had transformed over the course of many accumulated kalpas.
When the Buddha was a prince, and when that Flower-Light Buddha was a prince, they both renounced their kingdoms and abandoned worldly glory;
they relinquished their royal succession and cast aside all worldly splendor.
In his very last body—after attaining equal enlightenment, it is called his final body—he leaves the household life to achieve the Buddha-way;
he departs from the mundane home to accomplish the path of Buddhahood.
The Buddha Flower-Light shall dwell in the world. While the Buddha dwells in the world, his lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas for the duration of one lifetime.
As for the multitude of people in that land—the entire population of all those within the realm—[it shall be vast].
The lifespan is eight minor kalpas; such is the measure of his life.

After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa—that is, after the Tathāgata Padmaprabha has entered final extinction—the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings. The True Dharma shall abide in the world.
He extensively delivers sentient beings.
After the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma remains for thirty-two [kalpas]. The Semblance Dharma likewise abides for thirty-two kalpas.
His relics are widely disseminated; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all his relics are distributed far and wide.
Devas and humans universally made offerings, causing all devas and humans to receive universal offerings.
These were the deeds performed by the Buddha Flower Radiance; specifically, they were the deeds performed by the Nirmāṇakāya (response body) of the Buddha Flower Radiance.
All such matters are exactly like this. All manifested activities and transformations are likewise so.
He is the Honored One among two-legged beings; he is the Great Sage whose merit and wisdom are complete.
Most supreme and peerless; most excellent, without equal, and beyond comparison—that is your very self.
That Flower-Light Buddha is none other than your own body.
"You should rejoice; you ought to be glad and consider yourselves fortunate.
At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen;
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras—[rejoiced].
The *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, and so forth— namely, the eight classes of beings as described previously in the Introductory Chapter—
beheld Śāriputra receiving the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddha before the great assembly.
When the assembly saw Śāriputra receive the prophecy of bodhi in the presence of the Buddha, their hearts were filled with great joy.
Witnessing this supreme event, their hearts rejoiced immensely;
they leaped for joy beyond measure, their feet and bodies quivering with boundless signs of delight.
Each one removed from their bodies the upper garments they were wearing— the exquisite robes currently upon them—
to offer as an offering to the Buddha and to all the Buddhas assembled at the Lotus Assembly.
Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devaputra, and countless sons of gods— namely, the celestial hosts enumerated in the preceding introduction—
likewise [offered] exquisite celestial garments and the finest robes from the heavens.
They offered divine *māndārava* flowers, small white flowers,
great *māndārava* flowers, and large white flowers to the Buddha;
they presented robes and scattered flowers as offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
The celestial garments scattered, whether robes or flowers scattered by the devas,
remained suspended in mid-air; manifesting signless giving (*animitta-dāna*) abiding in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*),
they whirled of their own accord, revolving spontaneously within the sky.

The various celestial musical instruments and the arts of music, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds, were all performed simultaneously in the void; the music from the instruments in the sky played in unison at once.
A rain of various celestial flowers fell, scattering all the flowers found among the heavens, such as the four kinds of flowers and others.
Then they spoke these words: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī; in the past, at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the Buddha [taught]."
When he first turned the wheel of Dharma, for the sake of Kauṇḍinya and others, he first turned the pure wheel of the Four Noble Truths;
now it is turned once more, as it is being turned again at Vulture Peak.
The unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma; the unsurpassed path of the teaching, the most wondrous, supreme, and ultimate wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to restate this meaning and proclaim the sense of its second turning, spoke thus.
And he spoke in verse: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī—here called the Deer Park—he turned the Wheel of the Four Truths;
that is, the Small Vehicle wheel of the Four Truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path, characterized by arising and ceasing, which was turned three times."

One analytically explains all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and various other dharmas.

Regarding the arising and ceasing of the five groups: the five aggregates—form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—combine and aggregate to form a body subject to arising and ceasing.

Now, once again, he turns the most wondrous [Dharma wheel]. At this assembly of the Lotus Sutra, he again turns the perfect and wondrous, unsurpassed Dharma wheel—the supreme Great Dharma wheel, the most honored and ultimate, beyond which there is no other greater, superior, or wondrous Dharma wheel.
This Dharma is profoundly deep and subtle; this perfectly wondrous Dharma is profoundly deep and mysterious.
Few are able to believe it; few possess the sharp faculties capable of believing and accepting it.
"Since long ago, we—these gods, since we first heard the Dharma at the Deer Park in the past—have frequently heard the World-Honored One speak;
for over forty years, we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One teach the Dharma."
I have never heard such a thing; indeed, I have never before heard of such a profound and wondrous supreme Dharma, such a deep, far-reaching, subtle, and most excellent Dharma.
The World-Honored One has preached this Dharma; the World-Honored One has preached this subtle and wondrous Dharma.
We all rejoice in it; we all follow it with joy and gladness.
The Greatly Wise Śāriputra, the foremost disciple of great wisdom, has now received the prediction of honor;
today he has been granted the prediction by the World-Honored One.
We, too, are likewise. We, the celestial seers, shall also be so;
we shall certainly attain Buddhahood; we shall surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within all worlds, among all the devas and humans in those worlds, he is the most honored and unsurpassed;
he is the most venerable and supreme, with none above him.
The Buddha-way is inconceivable; the way of all Buddhas is beyond thought.

They teach according to what is appropriate through skillful means. What was previously taught as the three vehicles is now taught as the one reality—all of these are the Tathāgata’s skillful means adapted to circumstances.
Whatever meritorious deeds I possess— whatever meritorious deeds of practice my body has performed in this life or in past lives,
whether cultivated in the present life or committed in past lives.
Furthermore, upon seeing the Buddha’s merits and attaining the vision of the Buddha’s manifold virtues, they dedicate them all toward the path of the Buddha;
dedicating all these roots of goodness exclusively toward the Buddha-way and not toward any other vehicle, they thereby attain the Buddha-way.
This is the explanation in terms of the Dharma; following this, the request for the Buddha to explain by means of a parable is made.
At that time, while the devas were presenting offerings and reciting verses, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret. Previously, before my awakening, I suspected that the Buddha was a māra;
now that the Buddha has revealed the truth to me, all my doubts and regrets have been entirely removed."
They personally received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha; they received the Buddha’s prediction face-to-face.
These one thousand two hundred are the same as the two hundred arhats mentioned in the preceding chapter.

Regarding "mastery of mind": one who has already destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-āsrava) and attained liberation from the three realms, such that the mind is free from defilements and burdens, is called a master.

Previously abiding in the stage of training (śaikṣa), the Arhat has already destroyed the fundamental fetters and is thus beyond training (aśaikṣa); whereas those who have not yet destroyed the fetters remain in the stage of training.
Position.
The Buddha constantly teaches and transforms. The Buddha constantly teaches, trains, and guides with compassion.
He speaks of "my Dharma," meaning the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths that I have taught.

One is able to transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death; by power, one can distance oneself from the four marks of the world and attain ultimate *nirvāṇa*, which is the final extinction without remainder of the Lesser Vehicle.

These are persons who are both learners and non-learners; these are the twelve hundred noble ones of the lesser fruits, both learners and non-learners, who have each individually abandoned the view of a self and each individually abandoned the grasping at a self.

As well as views of existence and non-existence: "existence" refers to the view of eternalism, while "non-existence" refers to the view of annihilationism; these include other sixty-two views throughout the three periods of time.
These consist of claiming to have attained *nirvāṇa*, or claiming that by severing afflictions (*kleśa*) and thoughts (*saṃjñā*), one attains true quiescence.
Now, before the World-Honored One, today on this Vulture Peak before the World-Honored One, we hear what has never been heard before;
we have heard the Dharma that was not heard on previous days.
They all fall into doubt; they have all fallen into the net of doubt.
Excellent, World-Honored One! Praise be to the World-Honored One, exclaiming "Excellent!
May you, for the sake of the fourfold assembly—first the community of monks, and now including both men and women—[speak].

He explains its causes and conditions. He explains the reasons why that which was small in the past is now again said to be great, so as to cause them to abandon doubt and regret, and to attain hearing and knowledge that removes the mind of doubt, hesitation, and remorse.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra. He spoke thus because of Śāriputra’s question.
"Did I not say it previously? Did I not indeed say it earlier in the preceding chapter?"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all the transformation Buddhas who come from the ten directions of the three periods of time,
employ various causes and conditions, using diverse primary causes, virtuous conditions, parables,
and verbal expressions to lead sentient beings through analogies or through words.
He teaches the Dharma through skillful means. He teaches all dharmas by means of the three vehicles as skillful means;
is it not for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it not for the sake of supreme, perfect enlightenment?
As stated in the preceding chapter: "Whatever is done always has but one purpose: solely to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Do you not hear how sentient beings have attained awakening?
All that has been spoken, all these dharmas taught through various skillful means, are for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas; indeed, they are all for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas.

However, Śāriputra, since you have not yet understood what was said regarding the preceding Dharma, I shall now further explain it by means of a parable; indeed, I shall now speak again by means of a parable.
To further clarify this meaning, the meaning of the Sublime Dharma is further elucidated through a parable.
Those who possess wisdom—those present here in this assembly who possess discernment—attain understanding by means of a parable;
it is through a parable that they achieve full comprehension.
Śāriputra, in a kingdom, city, town, or village— whether it be a nation, a district, a county, a hamlet,
or a settlement— there may be a great elder, a person who is a wealthy and affluent elder.
He was advanced in years; his age was ripe, decrepit, and far-advanced.
His wealth was immeasurable; his household property was abundant and beyond limit.
He possessed many fields and houses, and many gardens and dwellings for habitation.
As well as various servants, youths, and attendants;
his household was vast because his family was wealthy, and its dwellings were extensive, yet it had only a single gate.
The elder represents the Buddha, whose advanced age signifies that he is about to enter *nirvāṇa*; "wealth" refers to the wealth of the Dharma.
The abundant field where one may plant represents having great merit; the dwelling where one may reside represents abiding in nirvāṇa;
the servants and laborers are metaphors for the five faculties; the skillful master is a metaphor for the functioning of the Buddha-dharmadhātu;
and the single gate is a metaphor for the Single Buddha Vehicle, the place of transcendence.
There are vast multitudes of beings; sentient beings of the five destinies dwell together within the triple world.
One hundred represents the various heavens, and two hundred represents the human realm.
Up to five hundred people: three hundred are used as metaphors for hell-dwellers, four hundred for hungry ghosts, and five hundred for animals and asuras;
it is not said that they pervade all five realms of existence.
They dwell within it; the five destinies cohabit therein.
The halls and pavilions are decayed and ancient; the halls and pavilions are a metaphor for the head and face, while their decay represents senility.
The walls have collapsed and the plaster has fallen away; the walls are a metaphor for the skin, and the crumbling of the plaster represents the deterioration and movement of the skin.
The base of the pillar is rotten. In terms of lifespan, life is the base of the pillar; in terms of the body, the feet are the base of the pillar.
When one’s years have advanced and the feet tremble, this is called being rotten.

The beams and rafters are leaning and perilous: the beams, rafters, ridgepoles, and purlins are used as metaphors for the spine; when a person grows old, their back becomes hunched and they lean precariously forward.

"Simultaneously on all sides" refers to the four surrounding directions, which metaphorically represent the mind—namely, the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, along with the equal portion [of these].
The four unwholesome thoughts are likened to the body itself, which is simultaneously afflicted by the four unwholesome signs of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Suddenly a fire breaks out; in an instant, the internal and external poisons erupt.
It burns down one's house and residence. Consciousness relies upon the body, which is thus called a "house";
when evil thoughts arise toward various objects, fire breaks out from within, first burning the body itself.
The sons of the elder are all the children of the Buddha—beings of the three vehicles.
Whether ten or twenty, ten are used as a metaphor for śrāvakas and twenty as a metaphor for pratyekabuddhas.
Or reaching thirty, this represents the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
These three types of spiritual capacities within the five aggregates are like being inside this house.
The elder seeing this great fire is the Tathāgata seeing these blazing fires of karma.
They arise from the four directions; the four poisons and the four signs act simultaneously.
Thereupon, one is greatly terrified. Immediately, the mind is struck with great alarm, fear, and dread, and one thinks thus:
"It is as if the Tathāgata’s mind were to think these words."
Although I am able to do so here, and although the Buddha has practiced within these three realms,
he has emerged safely from the doors that are burned by fire— the doors of the house consumed by flames—
and has emerged with a settled mind, having carefully and securely exited the three realms.
And as for these sons— the children of the three vehicles—
within this burning house, amidst the abode being consumed by the fires of karma,
they delight in play and sport, craving and becoming greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires.
They do not perceive or know; they cannot reflect or understand.
They are neither startled nor terrified—startled because of delusion and terrified because of ignorance.
As the fire comes to press upon their bodies, the fires of karma approach and close in upon them.
Suffering cuts to the very core. The sufferings of the three realms cut to one's own person, yet the mind feels no weariness or distress;
the mind is merely deluded and never knows weariness or renunciation, even though it recognizes this as a disease.
He had no intention of seeking liberation, nor did he have any intent to search for deliverance.
Śāriputra, at that time, the Tathāgata reflected thus:
seeing one who was pitiable, he gave rise to a mind of rescue and protection.

My body and hands possess great strength. The body is a metaphor for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the hands are metaphors for wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). To lift [the child] up is the power of the Buddha.
One should use a garment-bag (*kośa*); the garment-bag is a metaphor for the Buddha’s patience (*kṣānti*) and insight (*jñāna*).
If one uses a small table— as a table is a metaphor for the Buddha’s powers and fearlessness that can be relied upon—
one emerges from the house. The Buddha wishes to use these dharmas, such as precepts and patience, to cause [beings] to emerge from the burning house.
He reflected further and pondered again:
"This house has but a single door; while all the other doors of this great burning house are ablaze, this one door alone has not been consumed by the fire."
Furthermore, it is narrow and small. Because the nature of the gateway to the sublime teaching does not admit evil, it is said to be narrow and small.
"The children are young and immature" means that the children of the three vehicles are still young and immature, which is a metaphor for their weak faculties and powers.
They have no true discernment; they lack the mature insight of the wise.
They are attached to places of play and clinging to the realms of sport and the five desires;
they shall either fall away or descend into the burning house.
They are being burned by fire; they are scorched and roasted by the fires of great karma.
I shall speak for them; the Buddha shall speak to them concerning matters of dread—the terrifying reality of the burning house of the triple world.
This house has already been burned; this dwelling is now being consumed by that fire.
It is fitting to emerge quickly; it is fitting to emerge all at once with great speed.
Do not let yourselves be [caught] by the fire; do not allow yourselves to be overtaken by the fire.
...that which is burned and harmed. Fire is that which can burn; the body is that which is harmed.
Having formed this thought, at that time the Tathāgata, having formed this thought, acted according to what he had reflected upon and according to what was deliberated within his mind.
He informed his sons fully and announced it to those of the three vehicles:
"All of you, come out quickly! You, my sons, must all come out of this burning house.
Though the father feels compassion, and though the Buddha feels pity, [you do not heed him]."
He exhorted them with kind words, using skillful speech to transform, entice,
and instruct them; yet these sons remained attached to their play,
greedily delighting in and clinging to their games and diversions.
They are unwilling to believe or accept it; they cannot, with a willing mind, believe, understand, or receive it.
They are neither startled nor afraid; they are deluded yet unstartled and ignorant yet unafraid.
They possess no intention to emerge from [suffering]; they clearly lack any mind of renunciation.
Furthermore, they do not know; they are deluded and ignorant, having no awareness or realization.
What is the fire? The three poisons are the fire.
What is the house? The five aggregates are the house.
What constitutes a loss? To fall away is the loss.

Merely running back and forth in play—here, the two characters "east" and "west" serve as metaphors for rushing about day and night between emptiness and existence; thus it is called "running in play."
He merely looked at his father; his eyes fixed upon his father with a steady gaze from below. This uses the analogy of a carriage to clarify the meaning.
At that time, the elder—when he encountered the fire, the elder was outside the gate.
He then formed this thought; immediately he further reflected:
"This house has already been so; this house of the five aggregates has already been scorched by the great fire of the five turbidities and ravaged by the great fires of the three poisons."
If I and my sons, as well as the elder and his sons,
do not go out at once, or if we are unable to go out all together,
we will surely be burned; we will certainly be consumed by the great fire.
I shall now employ skillful means. Today, I shall employ the provisional designation of the three vehicles as a skillful means to lead these sons, these thirty children within this house.
They were thus spared from this calamity; that is, they were enabled to escape this affliction within the triple world.
The father knew that his sons—the Tathāgata knowing his thirty sons—each had their own prior inclinations and that their desires and preferences were different.
Various rare treasures; all manner of rare, extraordinary, and delightful playthings;
strange and marvelous objects; and peculiar, wondrous, and lovely things—his heart will surely become attached to them, and his sons' hearts will certainly crave and delight in them.
And he spoke to them, saying: "Reflect upon this, and having reflected, speak thus:
'Whatever objects you may delight in, whatever things you may find pleasure in.'"
It is rare and difficult to encounter; it is exceedingly rare and difficult to find in this world.
If you do not accept it now—if you do not take it up today—you will surely experience grief and regret later;
henceforth, you will certainly be filled with sorrow and remorse.
Such various things, rare and wonderful in the world,
as the sheep carts, deer carts, and ox carts— the sheep cart being a metaphor for the śrāvaka, the deer cart a metaphor for the pratyekabuddha, and the ox cart a metaphor for the bodhisattva.
It is now outside the gate. This chariot has been set out here on the open ground by the gate for you to play with;
it can serve as a place for you to sport within the Buddha-fields of the Three Vehicles.
"You all, within this burning house; you, my sons, within this burning house of the triple world—should quickly come forth!
You should swiftly emerge from the triple world!"
"Whatever you desire; according to what your hearts wish for, I shall give it all to you;
I shall bestow all these things upon you.
At that time, the sons heard what their father said; they heard the elder father speak of the three vehicles.
Precious playthings and jeweled toys;
because they satisfy their wishes, and because he accords with the desires of his sons,
each of their minds becomes courageous and keen— each of their hearts becomes individually brave, fierce, and sharp.
They push and shove one another; drawing near to one another, they reason and urge each other to cast aside all other conditions.
They race together and compete with one another, vying to escape from the burning house, rushing out together in their haste to flee the burning house of desire and love.
At that time, the elder saw his sons; the father saw that all the people had emerged safely, having escaped from the burning house in peace, security, and composure.
All [of them] were at the crossroads, which is a metaphor for the path of the four gates of the expedient teachings.
They sat upon the open ground; dwelling in the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is called "sitting on the open ground."
There are no further obstructions; there are no longer the obstructions of the delusions and karma of the triple world.
His mind is serene, and his father’s heart is relieved of all anxiety.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, because his heart is filled with gladness, his body itself leaps up. This concludes the illustration of the search for the carriage from below.
Then each of the sons addressed their father, saying: "Sons see their father with joy and each addresses his father regarding what was previously promised by our father;
that which our father previously promised to us."
Toys for play and amusement; rare and exquisite articles for appreciation, enjoyment, and sport.
The sheep-cart, the deer-cart, and the ox-cart—these two types of expedient vehicles—we pray you will grant them to us at this time; we pray you will grant them to us all at once.
Śāriputra, at that time, when the elder requested the chariots,
he bestowed them upon his sons; to each and every one of his thirty sons,
he gave an identical great chariot— a precious great chariot, equal for all.
That carriage was high and wide; this wondrous jewel-carriage is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, being lofty in height and expansive in breadth.
Adorned with various jewels, the carriage represents the essence of the Dharma, while the jewels represent all manner of virtues.
It is surrounded by railings; the railings symbolize *dhāraṇī*, which prevents evil and protects the good.
Bells hang from all four sides, their sound of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) allowing all to hear.
Furthermore, upon it—on top of the chariot’s roof—there are...
A canopy and parasol were set up; the design on the top of the canopy symbolized the ultimate path of the One Buddha Vehicle and its unconditional great compassion.
Furthermore, it was adorned with various rare and precious jewels; because the meritorious achievements of the myriad virtues are of many kinds, they are called "various jewels."
And it is adorned and embellished; this is used to adorn the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The jeweled cords are interlaced; these jeweled cords are a metaphor for the interlacing of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) that guard against transgressions.
Various flower garlands hang down; the hanging of these flower garlands is a metaphor for the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).
A double-layered, elegant mat was spread; within the carriage, double cushions were placed to signify softness and suppleness.
A vermilion pillow was set out: the vermilion color of the carriage pillow represents wisdom (*prajñā*), while the pillow itself represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He is drawn by white oxen. "White" symbolizes pure wisdom; "oxen" symbolize the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

Their coats are full and clean, their flesh is plump, and their color is pure white—meaning that the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the clarity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are in perfect harmony within and without.
The physical form is beautiful; the body is exquisitely handsome, endowed with all virtues and further refined in its excellence.
Possessing great strength and vigor, he is capable of bearing heavy burdens and traveling great distances until he ultimately attains Buddhahood; thus he is called "Great Strength and Vigor."
His gait is level and upright. His conduct is "level" (ping) because it accords with the Dharma and is without partiality; it is "upright" (zheng) because it is without depravity.
His swiftness is like the wind; by the power of great wisdom, he reaches Nirvana as swiftly as the wind.

Furthermore, there are many attendants. The great number of these attendants is a metaphor for the practices that assist the Path, which serve and protect it. They wait upon and guard the primordially existing *dharmakāya*.
Why is this so? What is the intention behind such magnificent adornment of the Great Vehicle?
This is the great elder. Because of this great and wealthy elder, his material wealth is immeasurable;
his spiritual wealth is abundant and its quantity is likewise immeasurable.
His various treasuries consist of these five virtues: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.
The profound Prajñāpāramitā is called the treasury of wisdom;
it is completely overflowing. All manner of wholesome virtues have been fully cultivated, reaching a state of abundance and surfeit.
Then, he forms this thought: "The elder" is a metaphor for the Buddha, who speaks these words of reflection.
My wealth and treasures are inexhaustible; the riches of the Dharma are so abundant that their use is never depleted.
You should not be given inferior small carts; you ought not to be given inferior small carts drawn by sheep or deer.
I bestow [these things] upon my sons.
This young child—called "young" because his power of the Way is slight—is indeed my son.
Those with the capacities for the three vehicles are all sons of the Buddha.
Love is without partiality. The loving heart is impartial, free from biased views or private factions.
"I possess such [qualities]; I am already so wealthy, noble, and exalted."
The great carriage of the seven treasures: the sevenfold merits are called the "seven treasures.
Their number is immeasurable; because the substance of the mind in a single thought-moment is a great carriage and its pure practices are manifold, they are without measure.
One should maintain an impartial mind; one ought to be without distinction, with a single mind of equality.
Bestow upon each and grant to each;
it is not fitting to differentiate, nor is it fitting to cause them to be disparate or separate.
Why is this? For what reason do you wish to bestow these things equally?

By means of these items of mine, by means of all the accumulated wealth and possessions I have, you would provide for the entire kingdom, giving and distributing them universally to all the people of the land.
It was still not exhausted. Even with such extensive giving, it remained without depletion;
how much less so for his sons? How much less so for this equal distribution to these thirty sons? From this point downward, it clarifies their joy upon obtaining the chariots.
At that time, the sons all bowed in gratitude for their father’s gift and each mounted a great chariot.
This is a metaphor for those of the three vehicles who all realize the perfect principle;
they have attained what they never had before, having received a great boon such as they had never possessed in the past.
This was not what they originally hoped for. Those of the three vehicles abide in skillful means; from the beginning, they have had no mind to hope for the fruit of perfection.
Śāriputra, what do you think? In your own view, how do you consider this?
This elder, with an impartial mind, bestowed upon all his thirty sons precious great chariots—
great single-vehicle chariots filled with rare and diverse treasures.
"Is there not falsehood here? Previously you promised three carts, yet now you grant only one; since the promise and the granting differ, is there not the fault of falsehood?
Śāriputra replied, answering the Buddha’s question.
"No, World-Honored One. There is no fault.
This elder has no intention of erring;
he merely intends to ensure that these thirty sons [attain safety]."
One escapes the calamity of fire; one escapes the calamity of the burning house of the triple world.
One preserves one’s physical life and sustains one’s existence without falling away.
This is not false; it is indeed non-false.
For what reason? Why is it not false?
If one's entire life is preserved, or if one's safety is secured, that is already a gain; that is indeed a gain.

As for the objects of play and enjoyment, if one’s body and life are not destroyed and there is abundance of happiness, these are true objects of play and enjoyment; therefore it is said that they have already been obtained.
How much more so regarding skillful means, and how much more so regarding the skillful means of the elder’s compassionate mind!
From that burning house—that burning house of the triple world and of craving—He delivers them;
He pulls them out from the triple world and rescues them across the ocean of suffering.
World-Honored One, such is this elder; such is this great wealthy elder who saves others from peril.
He did not give them even as much as that;
he did not bestow upon them even the smallest single chariot—that is, the small sheep-cart, which represents the fruit of the Śrāvaka.
Yet it was not false; indeed, it could not be called false.
Why is this? For what reason did that elder first form this intention?
The elder first formed the intention to rescue those in distress, thinking:
"I shall use skillful means; I shall use the three vehicles as my skillful means."
He causes his sons to escape; he causes all the sons to escape from the burning house.
For this reason, and because of this causal intention, there is no falsehood;
there is no falsehood whatsoever.
How much more so for the elder, how much more so for his father!
