He himself knows that his wealth is immeasurable; in his own mind, he knows that he has acquired immeasurable riches.
He desires to benefit his sons; he intends to nourish, enrich, and bring them profit.
"I shall give them equal great chariots; with an impartial mind, I bestow upon them precious great chariots.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! Well done, Śāriputra, for you have been able to eloquently respond."
"It is as you have said; it is indeed as you have described. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this.
The above was an illustrative explanation; what follows below is the application of the Dharma to the analogy.
Thus, he is the father of all—the three vehicles and the six realms of existence;
the compassionate father of the world of the three realms of existence:
the desire, form, and formless realms—regarding all fears and the terrors of birth and death within the triple world.
Decay, affliction, sorrow, and calamity; the five signs of decline in the heavens and the four marks of change in the human realm—all manner of suffering, afflictions, sorrows, and calamities;
the obscuration of ignorance; and all dark obstructions, both fundamental and derivative, that prevent clear understanding.
"Permanently exhausted without remainder": suffering, afflictions, and karma—these three are all permanently exhausted with nothing remaining;
they are fully accomplished, entirely established, and perfectly realized.
Immeasurable knowledge and vision: although knowledge and vision are one, they are designated by various names according to their respective objects, and thus there are immeasurable [distinctions].
As for the powers and fearlessnesses: these are the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata.
He possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), being fully accomplished in the power of great supernormal faculties as well as the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
With the power of supernormal faculties he subdues Māra, and with the power of wisdom he destroys obstacles.
He is endowed with skillful means (*upāya*); the hundreds of thousands of various clever methods are collectively termed "skillful means."
The Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). All skillful means (*upāya*) constitute the Buddha’s provisional wisdom; because they can reach the other shore, they are called *pāramitā*.

Great Loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): bestowing the bliss of the three virtues is called Great Loving-kindness, and extracting the suffering of the two deaths is called Great Compassion.
Compassion.

He is always free from indolence and weariness; his compassion is ever-present, devoid of laxity or fatigue, as he constantly seeks virtuous deeds—specifically, those noble and wholesome deeds that transcend the mundane world.
Benefiting all; providing benefit and assistance to all sentient beings, he is born into the triple world for the sake of all.
He enters the triple world because it is dilapidated—the ancient dwelling of the fire of desire that has fallen into ruin.
It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings; it is because one desires to deliver and liberate all sentient beings from birth,
old age, sickness, and death— the four marks—
as well as from sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and from grief, despair, hardship, and anguish.
Obscured by the darkness of ignorance— foolish, deluded, and blinded by the gloom—
the fires of the three poisons, like the blazing flames of greed, hatred, and delusion, are all completely extinguished.

He teaches and transforms them so that they may attain it; he instructs, exhorts, and transforms them so that they may obtain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

He beholds all sentient beings. With the Buddha-eye, he observes those beings in the various realms who are being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, as previously explained;
they are collectively scorched and boiled by the eight kinds of adverse conditions.

Furthermore, for the sake of the five desires and material gain, one gives rise to a mind of attachment and delight toward the objects of the five sensory realms; this is what is meant by "the five desires and material gain.
Because of this, one undergoes various kinds of suffering, as an unwholesome mind invites and brings about all manner of misery.
Furthermore, because of greed and attachment in pursuit, and because the greedy mind clings to worldly appearances,
seeking and searching without ceasing,
one presently undergoes manifold sufferings; within the present body, one thus experiences various forms of suffering.
Thereafter, they undergo the sufferings of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Those who perform such deeds receive various forms of suffering as a "flower-retribution" in their present life;
subsequently, they fall into hell and endure great agony. When their retributions in hell are exhausted, they again fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
when their retributions as hungry ghosts are exhausted, they again fall into the realm of animals.
If one is born in the heavens, there is the suffering of the five signs of decline; likewise, among humans,
there is the suffering of poverty, hardship, destitution, and exhaustion.
The suffering of separation from the beloved: when those who were once intimately dear suddenly part, is this not suffering?
The suffering of encountering the hated: when those who are enemies and harbor mutual resentment constantly meet, is this not suffering?

Such as these. Furthermore, that which one seeks but cannot obtain is called suffering; the blazing intensity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitutes the suffering of birth, old age, and death.
There are various kinds of such sufferings. Because the characteristics of suffering are not singular, they are described as "various."
Sentient beings are submerged within it. Because sentient beings are deluded, they are submerged in manifold sufferings;
because their minds are deluded, they take pleasure and sport, failing to contemplate that future suffering involves being born again and dying again—therefore, it is said they "sport."
They are unaware and unknowing; they have never been awakened to it nor can they comprehend it.
They are not startled and not terrified; they do not give rise to alarm or fear, nor do they know dread.
Furthermore, they do not conceive of revulsion; throughout the day they indulge in desire, never giving rise to weary detachment.
They do not seek liberation, nor do they seek the skillful means to disperse, dissolve, or escape from this burning house of the triple world.
Although the three worlds differ and their suffering and pleasure are unequal, all possess the three poisons;
therefore, it is called a "burning house."
They gallop to and fro; being born in the east and perishing in the west is what is meant by "galloping.
Although they encounter great suffering—even encountering various kinds of great suffering—they do not regard it as a calamity.
Because their minds are deluded, they pass from suffering to suffering, unaware that this is a disease.
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha—having seen these manifold sufferings of sentient beings—then formed this thought;
at that very moment, he immediately gave rise to such a reflection.
I am the father of all sentient beings. Having emerged from the triple world, I am the Great Compassionate Father of all beings;
I ought to extract them from their suffering and distress, and I ought to eradicate all their manifold afflictions and calamities.
They grant the joy of the wisdom of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, the joy of the quiescence of the Buddhas' wisdom, causing them to sport therein;
they cause those sentient beings to sport within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further formed this thought; the Tathāgata further spoke these words:
"If I were to rely solely on my supernormal power, or solely on the power of my various meditative concentrations and spiritual penetrations..."
And as for the power of wisdom—this is the power of *prajñā*.

It involves abandoning skillful means; it abandons the gradual gate of the teachings on skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, specifically for those sentient beings who are dull, inferior, and lost in delusion.
He praises the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; he extols the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.

Regarding the powers and fearlessnesses—the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses—sentient beings are incapable [of attaining them], for all sentient beings shall ultimately never be able to obtain them.
By this they attain deliverance; by means of this wondrous vehicle they achieve liberation.
Why is this so? For what reason do they not grasp its meaning?
It is because these sentient beings—these sentient beings within the deluded realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)—are thus.
They cannot avoid birth, old age, sickness, and death; they have not yet escaped the four marks of the world—sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress—and all unpleasant matters.
Thus they are bound by the three realms and enveloped by the three realms.
Burning in the house of fire: the house of greed, anger, and delusion is like a conflagration.
By what means can it be extinguished? What causes and conditions allow for its understanding?
It is the wisdom of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the unsurpassed wisdom.
Śāriputra, he is like that elder. What precedes is the explanation of the Dharma; what follows below is the application of the analogy.
Although his body and hands possess strength, this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s physical power and fearlessness.
Yet he does not employ it; that is to say, he does not employ the Great [Vehicle].

He merely uses diligent skillful means—specifically, the skillful means of gradual instruction through diligence—to strive for the rescue of his children, exhorting and delivering those children of the three vehicles.
Regarding the calamity of the burning house: having been delivered from the sufferings of birth and death within the three realms,
they are each subsequently given the precious great vehicle— that is, the Single Buddha Vehicle— only after they have first attained their respective [lesser] realizations.
The Tathāgata is likewise so; this is the application of the analogy.
Although he possesses power and fearlessness as previously described, he does not employ them—meaning he does not employ [the power of] reality.
Relying solely on wisdom and skillful means; relying solely on the provisional vehicle, skillful means, and wisdom, [he acts] within this burning house of the triple world.
To deliver sentient beings; to rescue and ferry across those sentient beings who are lost in delusion.
For their sake, he expounds the Three Vehicles, preaching the three expedient vehicles:
the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Buddha Vehicle. The Śrāvaka Vehicle consists of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle...
This refers to the Buddha-vehicle of the twelve links of dependent origination, which is the Mahāyāna of gradual teaching.
He speaks thus within the context of the three vehicles:
"Do not take pleasure in dwelling [in these], O sons; do not insist upon them."
The burning house of the three realms. This is the dwelling place of the fires of karma within the saṃsāra of the three realms.
Do not covet that which is coarse and wretched. One must not harbor craving or attachment for the coarse, impure, and evil objects of the five desires:
forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. These are the sensory realms of the five desires.
If you become attached through craving, or if you again become attached and give rise to a mind of longing, you will be consumed; you will be burned by the fire of desire.
You must quickly emerge from the three realms. If you swiftly depart from the three realms, [you shall be liberated].
"You shall attain the three vehicles; you shall attain the three kinds of joyful conveyances:
the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha vehicle, as previously described.
Now, for your sake—I, on this day, shall act for all of you."
"Guard and maintain this matter; protect and sustain this matter of renunciation, for it shall never be in vain—it is ultimately true and will certainly not prove empty.
You, my children, should simply apply yourselves with single-minded devotion."
He diligently cultivates vigor; he practices with arduous effort and proceeds with refined progress.
By these skillful means, the Tathāgata employs this wisdom of skillful means.
He entices and advances sentient beings; he entices, guides, and urges on those of the three vehicles.
He further speaks these words: "The Tathāgata has also spoken thus:
'You all should know! You, my sons, must surely know this!'"
These are the teachings of the Three Vehicles; these skillful means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles are all praised by the noble ones. These teachings are all praised by all the sages.
Sovereign and unbound; originally sovereign and without bondage, they have nothing upon which to rely or seek. Regarding the signs of the world, they have no dependence or aspiration.
They ride upon these three vehicles—riding upon these provisional, transformative, and expedient three vehicles.
By means of the untainted faculties and powers, they employ the five untainted wholesome faculties and the five powers;
they awaken to the path through the factors of enlightenment, meditative concentration, the seven limbs of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, and the eight samādhis.
They enjoy themselves through the liberations, samādhis, and so forth— the eight liberations, the various right concentrations,
right wisdom, and so on— and they find delight and joy therein for themselves.

They shall immediately attain the immeasurable; at that very moment, they shall obtain that which is beyond calculation—peaceful bliss, the joy of serene seclusion, and the happiness of a tranquil mind.
Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings, such as those among the class of beings who delight in the wholesome...
Within, he possesses the nature of wisdom; within his mind, he possesses single-minded cultivation and progress.
Following the Buddha, the World-Honored One—the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One—he hears the Dharma and receives it with faith;
hearing the sound of the teaching, he accepts it with a faithful heart.
With earnest diligence; with profound gravity, tireless effort, and single-minded cultivation and progress;
desiring to quickly emerge from the three realms; delighting in the desire to quickly attain liberation from the three realms;
seeking nirvana for oneself alone; seeking only one's own deliverance without the intention to transform others.
This is called the Śrāvaka-yāna; this is what is termed the Śrāvaka-hīnayāna.
It is like those sons, like those young children within the house, who seek the goat-drawn carts, desiring to obtain small, minor goat-drawn carts.
"Emerging from the burning house" means emerging from the burning house of birth and death within the triple world (*tridhātu*).
If there are sentient beings— specifically those of a certain class who delight in the good—
and who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accept it with faith and apply themselves with earnest diligence (the first three phrases are as before).
He seeks the wisdom of spontaneity (*svayambhū-jñāna*). He deeply seeks the spontaneous wisdom regarding all phenomena.
He delights in solitary tranquility; he constantly delights in dwelling alone to authentically cultivate sublime stillness.

He profoundly understands the causal conditions of all phenomena; he is deeply able to comprehend the arising and ceasing of all phenomena through the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is called the Pratyekabuddhayāna; it is the vehicle for those of middling faculties among the pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers.
It is like those sons—like those young children within that house.

Seeking the deer-cart, the deer king frequently looks back at his herd while moving; because he exerts himself in the effort of solitary travel and cultivates meritorious deeds with the capacity to benefit others, he is likened to a deer.
They emerge from the burning house; they emerge from the fearful burning house of the triple world.
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, believe and accept it, and practice with diligent perseverance as described before.
They seek all-knowledge. They seek the wisdom of universal emptiness and quiescence.
They seek the Buddha-wisdom. They seek the pure wisdom of attaining Buddhahood.
They seek self-arisen wisdom. They seek the wisdom of the non-arising of natural principle.
Unlearned wisdom (*asatśāstrajñāna*): that which is able to be understood by oneself without depending on instruction is called unlearned wisdom.
The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision: the Tathāgata’s ultimate fruit of right knowledge and right vision.
The powers and fearlessnesses— the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses—
[consist in] compassionate mindfulness for peace and happiness, and benevolent, merciful, loving concern for the security, well-being,
and joy of immeasurable sentient beings and incalculable beings lost in delusion.
It benefits devas and humans; it brings profit and advantage to all devas and people of the world.
It delivers all beings and gathers in and liberates the entire multitude of sentient beings.
This is called the Mahāyāna. This is precisely what is called the "Water Buffalo Cart" of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna.
Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, the Bodhisattvas of Great Resolve who seek this ox-cart are called Mahāsattvas; this is translated as "Great Beings.
They are like those sons—like those young children within the house.
In order to seek ox-carts, and desiring to find great ox-carts, they emerge from the burning house;
they emerge from the burning house of the afflictions of the triple world.
Śāriputra, you are like that elder, like that wealthy elder of the village.
He saw his sons—seeing the thirty sons and the five hundred others—safely emerge from the burning house;
he saw them safely, securely, and with full composure emerge from the perilous burning house of the three realms.
He reaches the state of fearlessness; he reaches the state free from the terror of fire.
He considers his own wealth to be immeasurable; he reflects that the riches and treasures of his household are immeasurable.
He calculated by means of large chariots; with an impartial mind, he bestowed upon all his sons chariots made of the great jewels, granting them to all thirty children in the open space.
The Tathāgata is also like this; the intention of the Tathāgata is just like that of the elder.
He is the father of all sentient beings; he acts as the father of compassion for all sentient beings.
If one perceives him as immeasurable, it is because the Buddha is perceived as being without limit.
Hundreds of millions or thousands of sentient beings— those who cultivate the path—
by means of the Buddha’s gateway and through the skillful means within the Buddha’s teaching,
emerge from the suffering of the triple world; they emerge from the various sufferings of the triple world.
Fearing the perilous path—being terrified and apprehensive of the treacherous and evil road—they attain the bliss of nirvana; they attain the supramundane bliss of cessation.
At that time, when those sons of the Tathāgata thus realize cessation...
He then formed this thought; he immediately reflected and thought to himself:
"I possess immeasurable and boundless wisdom. Within my own body, there originally exists supreme wisdom that is neither limited nor has any boundary."
The powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth—the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and other such treasuries of the Buddhas’ Dharma;
the treasury of the Dharma-jewels of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
These sentient beings— all these sentient beings within the three realms who are lost in delusion—
are all my children. I regard all sentient beings equally as my own children,
bestowing upon them the Great Vehicle equally, granting them the ultimate Great Vehicle with impartiality.
He does not allow anyone to attain parinirvāṇa individually, nor does he permit any single person among them to achieve liberation alone; rather,
all are brought to parinirvāṇa by means of the Tathāgata, and all are brought to ultimate parinirvāṇa by means of the Tathāgata.
And he brings them to parinirvāṇa; he delivers them.

These sentient beings—these beings of the three vehicles within these realms who have escaped the three realms, those who have attained liberation from all the sufferings and hardships of the three realms.
He bestows them all upon the Buddhas; he grants them all to the Buddhas of the three periods of time:
meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and so forth; the pure and purified *dhyāna*, the great samādhi, supreme liberation, and all concentrations and wisdoms.
The instruments of entertainment—the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna—are all of one characteristic and one kind.
This "one characteristic" is the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and this "one kind" is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

To realize that all characteristics are entirely equal and to be without a mind of attachment or aversion toward self or other is called "one characteristic. All things are thus [of one characteristic].
That which is without distinction of kind is called "one kind.
It is praised by the noble ones; it is extolled by the Greatly Awakened Sages.
It is able to produce purity and excellence; it is well able to give rise to that which is pure, subtle, and wondrous.
The foremost bliss. The principle of cessation realized by all Buddhas is unsurpassed and is thus called the foremost bliss.
Śāriputra, he is like that elder; he is like that great and wealthy elder in the world.
At first, he used three vehicles—initially employing the three kinds of carts drawn by goats, deer, and oxen—to entice the sons;
that is, to entice the thirty sons within the house.
Thereafter, he gave them only the great vehicle; once this was done, he bestowed upon them exclusively the great precious vehicle drawn by white oxen.
Adorned with precious objects: it is embellished with various jewels.
It is the foremost in peace and security; because it is utterly immovable and most thoroughly examined, it is said to be "peaceful, subtle, and foremost."
However, that elder—that wealthy elder outside the gate—is free from the fault of falsehood;
granting three and giving one is without the error of falsehood.
The Tathāgata is likewise so; the intention of the Greatly Awakened Tathāgata is also thus.
There is no falsehood; there is not a single fault of falsehood whatsoever.
Initially, he taught the three vehicles; at the very beginning, he expounded the three expedient vehicles to guide sentient beings, leading and transforming those of the three vehicles.
Thereafter, one uses only the Mahāyāna; having thus established the three vehicles, one then delivers them by means of the single,
ultimate, true Mahāyāna, thereby rescuing and liberating them.
Why is this? For what reason is it that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom?
The Tathāgata has, from the very beginning, possessed an inconceivable and true wisdom-mind.
The powers and fearlessnesses: the ten powers of a Buddha and the four fearlessnesses;

the treasury of all dharmas, the secret and wondrous treasury of all true dharmas, which is able to bestow [benefit] upon all sentient beings and is well able to grant [it] to those sentient beings who study the Path.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the Dharma of equality—
though it is not that they cannot receive it at all, it is simply because the faculties and powers of sentient beings are weak that they are unable to receive it in its entirety.
Śāriputra, by this cause and condition, for those sentient beings whose roots are shallow and whose conditions are slight, you should know that there are Buddhas;
you should know that there are all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
By the power of skillful means— that is, through the power of wisdom and skillful means that accord with the capacities of sentient beings—
within the single Buddha-vehicle, which is the non-dual, non-threefold, and non-one Buddha-vehicle.

The three are explained through differentiation. This differentiation of depth and shallowness—based on the truths (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and means (*upāya*)—is taught as the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
The Buddha, wishing to reiterate this meaning, [intends to show that] Śākyamuni’s teaching of three within one is intended to unify them; thus, the three are identical with the one.
Such is the significance.
And he spoke in verse, composing the verses with intentional phrasing (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
For example, there was an elder; the Great Elder is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata.
He had a great house, which, when taken metaphorically, represents a single body and, in its broader sense, the triple world (*tridhātu*).
That residence is long-standing and ancient; the house of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), being long-standing, has become old and worn out.
It is dilapidated, leaning, and moreover ruined. The hall and chambers are high and perilous:
the "hall" is a metaphor for the face, and the "chambers" are a metaphor for the height of the body, which is lofty, leaning, and in danger of collapse.
The bases of the pillars are crushed and decayed. The pillars are a metaphor for the two feet, and the bases are a metaphor for the heels.
The beams and rafters are slanted; the beams and rafters represent the spinal column, which is said to be "slanted" because it becomes bent with the infirmity of old age.

The foundation steps have collapsed and crumbled. The foundation is a metaphor for the retributive life-span (*vipāka-āyus*), and the steps are a metaphor for one's destiny (*bhāgya*). This means the retributive life-span is diminished and one's destiny has decayed.
The walls and partitions have fallen into ruin; the skin of the body is like the walls and partitions of a house, and the damage to the skin is like the collapse of those walls.
The plaster cracks and the mud coating falls away; the body is wrapped in skin and the house is coated with mud, yet the body develops sores and toxins just as the wall-mud deteriorates.
The thatched roof-covering falls down in disarray. Those who are old have their short hair hanging down like the damaged grass-thatch of a house falling off its peak.

The rafters and eaves are askew and detached; the rafters are a metaphor for the bones and sinews, while the eaves represent the cotton-like fringe used as a fan to support the back when the body is bent over.
The slanting walls and partitions twist and turn;
within this enclosure, the large and small intestines coil and wind about,
filled everywhere with filth, and excrement and urine fill its interior.
There were five hundred people. These five hundred are a metaphor for the sentient beings of the five realms; the asura realm is dispersed among these five.
They dwell therein. Each individual sentient being resides within the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The *chī*, *xiāo*, *diāo*, and *jiù*. The *chī* is a bird that eats mice; the *xiāo* is the earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*), an unfilial bird whose offspring eats its mother;
the *diāo* has a red beak and is able to eat deer and roe deer; the *jiù* is tawny-yellow in color with red eyes, a bird that feeds on filthy things.
The crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the turtle-dove—among these eight birds, the old crow, the joyful magpie, the turtle-dove, and the pigeon feed on coarse and filthy things;
yet they consider themselves superior, being arrogant and boastful of their own abilities while looking down upon other feathered creatures.

This is a metaphor for those in the world who possess a mere modicum of wealth and power, who are conceited and self-exalting, and who recklessly treat all others with the eight kinds of violent arrogance and wanton insolence.
The *luán*, snake, *fù*, and scorpion: the *luán* is a venomous snake; the *fù* has a body three inches wide with a head like a large plum, resembling a spider, and its tail is poisonous.
The centipede and millipede: those with red necks are called centipedes (*wǔgōng*), which can eat the brains of snakes; those whose necks are not red are millipedes (*yòuyán*).
These are called centipedes; the six kinds [of insects] in this land are likely venomous caterpillars that injure people at the slightest movement, used as a metaphor for anger.
As for the gecko and the millipede: the gecko insect is the *kṛkalāsa*, which dwells among the eaves and walls; the millipede is a creature with a hundred legs.
The black variety is four or five inches long and can grow to a considerable size.

There are also the *yòu* (weasel), the *lí* (hermine), and the *xīshǔ* (musk-rat). The *yòu* is yellowish-red in color, its body is foul-smelling, and it has a large tail; it is capable of devouring mice and is colloquially known as the "yellow *dúzi*.
The *lí* resembles a domestic cat. The *xīshǔ*, or "sweet-mouthed rat," is a species that bites people without them feeling any pain.
The various evil insects refer to the five types [of fingers],

which run about crosswise and intersect; their crisscrossing and racing along the paths of the world is a metaphor for the foul and defiled realms of the mundane world, such as places reeking with excrement and urine.
Impurities overflow; at that time, the signs of impurity spread abroad.
As for the dung beetles (*śalabha*), also known as *gong-gong* (Sanskrit: *kṛkalāsa*; Chinese: 蛣蜣), they have black bodies with exoskeletons and are the very insects that roll dung.

They gather upon it. This is a metaphor for the deluded people of the world who, without distinguishing between the pure and the foul, greedily cling everywhere like insects attaching themselves to stench.
The fox is by nature full of suspicion; the wolf is by nature fierce and cruel; the jackal is a creature of demonic portents.

"Chewing and trampling. This is a metaphor for those in the world who are greedy and addicted to worldly flavors; "chewing" refers to their attachment to such tastes, while "trampling" refers to their destruction of others.
"Munching on corpses" means that, like those insects, they mouth and gnaw with their teeth upon foul and loathsome corpses.

The flesh and bones were scattered in disorder. To ruin an undertaking is like wounding the flesh; to harm the principle is like damaging the bone—just as a wolf, when eating its food, scatters it everywhere.
From this, there arose packs of dogs; that is to say, after this, there were groups of dogs.
They come vying with one another to seize and grasp; they all come at once to fight, strike, clutch, and snatch.

Starving and emaciated, they are terrified and distraught. Having no method by which to cultivate themselves, this is called "hunger. Their bodies and minds are parched and withered, which is called "emaciation.
They have never known any peace or security, which is called "terror and distraction."
Seeking food everywhere; all such matters are greed, like a hungry person begging for food, used as a metaphor for the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*).
They fight, quarrel, and seize one another; they struggle, contend, snatch, and drag each other about.
"Snarling, howling, and barking": like dogs fighting over food, they snarl with their mouths open, emitting sounds of howling and barking.
"His house is terrified": his house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is startled, terrified, and fearful.
Such are the manifestations of transformation; they appear in manifold ways to illustrate how the states of doubt and the latent tendencies of evil are like this.
They exist everywhere; in every single object of perception, each one is present.
"Chi-mei-wang-liang. The monsters of mountains and marshes are called *chi*; the monsters of dwellings are called *mei*;

the monsters of wood and stone are named *wangliang*. These kinds of spirits have shadows but no forms; they collectively symbolize how worldly people are driven by their own cleverness to afflict themselves and others.
"Yakṣas and evil ghosts": the yakṣa is a brave and powerful ghost; it is a metaphor for a mind that is turbulent and changes in an instant, like an evil ghost.
"Devouring human flesh": being attached to extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), regarding oneself as right and others as wrong, is like devouring human flesh.
The category of venomous insects refers to the aforementioned species such as snakes and vipers.
The various malevolent birds and beasts refer to the aforementioned owls, crows, foxes, dogs, and so forth.
Regarding "hatching" (*fu*) and "suckling" (*ru*): those born from eggs are called "hatched," while those born from a womb are called "suckled."
Each conceals and protects [their own]; each clings to their own views to constantly cherish and guard their own minds, just as those insects and beasts each protect their embryos and eggs.
Yakṣas come vying with one another; there are those who are clever and sharp, like those malevolent spirits who all come vying with one another at once.
They strive to devour it; with their perversity they harm what is right, just as a ghost devours its prey.
Once they have eaten their fill, they inflict further injury upon others while their own minds remain satiated.
Their evil intent grows more intense; their wicked and perverse minds reject cause and effect, becoming ever more inflamed.
The sound of contention: when existence and non-existence refute one another, it is called contention; the utterance of such disputations gives rise to this sound.
It is truly terrifying. Clinging to existence and clinging to emptiness both possess faults, for both are the root of birth and death; therefore, they are to be feared.

The *kumbhāṇḍa* demons— here translated as "demons of loathing and bewitchment"— serve as a metaphor for those in the world who, while practicing by clinging to signs, fall into the grasping of precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*).
Crouching on a mound of earth, that ghost’s male organ is shaped like a winter melon; when walking, he places it upon his shoulder, and when sitting, he crouches over it.

Because he strictly observed the precepts regarding this matter, his retribution is in the desire realm heavens, such as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, located atop Mount Sumeru, which is called a "mound of earth" (tǔduǎ).
At times they leave the ground; at other times, through the practice of dhyāna, they are able to transcend the realm of desire by one or two feet.
To leave the realm of desire and be born in the Brahma palace is called "one foot"; to further transcend the Brahma heavens and be born in the formless realm is called "two feet."

They travel back and forth; because they accumulate merit to be reborn in the heavens, and when that merit is exhausted, they decline and wander through the six realms of existence, they are said to "travel.
They indulge in wanton play, letting their minds run wild and becoming attached to worldly virtues while failing to seek the state of non-arising, just like children.

The "game" refers to seizing the two hind legs of a dog. The dog is a metaphor for the mind that clings to the observance of precepts; the two legs are a metaphor for the manifestations of body and speech as they engage with sensory objects.
To restrain various distracting thoughts and abandon the evils of body and speech is like the aforementioned ghost seizing the dog’s two hind legs.
He strikes him until he loses his voice; just as one cannot remain at ease under the lash, so too he does not realize he has lost his voice and begins to howl and bark.
He places his foot upon the dog’s neck. The neck is a metaphor for the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla*), which restrains the body and speech and abides in virtuous conduct—just like seizing a dog.
Placing his foot upon the neck of a dog, he delights in terrifying the dog.
That malevolent spirit strikes the dog until it loses its voice and manifests various strange transformations, desiring to terrify people while considering this a source of pleasure for himself;
such a person clings to precepts, restraining the evils of body and speech and abiding in what they deem purity.
One should constantly apply diligent effort, instilling fear of transgressions in the mind, and take this as one's own joy.

Furthermore, there are various spirits; these six phrases concerning the various ghosts and spirits serve as a metaphor for those who cling to the view of a self and are attached to the notion of "I."
Its body is long and great. It is called "long" because the body of ignorance and karma extends vertically through the three periods of time;
it is called "great" because it pervades all places horizontally, encompassing the five destinies.
They are naked, black, and emaciated. They are called "naked-bodied" because their minds lack a sense of shame; they are black because their vision is not clear;
and they are emaciated because they have lost the food of dhyāna-joy.
They dwell eternally therein—dwelling eternally within the wheel of suffering of the three realms.
The hungry ghosts emit great, evil sounds because of their hunger; human beings utter words seeking understanding because of their ignorance.
They cry out seeking food, like ghosts wailing and soliciting drink and nourishment.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts; these two phrases serve as metaphors for the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Their throats are like needles; the metaphor of the ghost being large while the throat is small illustrates that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only four aggregates (*skandha*), and the "throat" [of existence] is extremely narrow.
To regard the precarious as secure is not a calculation for longevity; to regard the impermanent as permanent is not a calculation for constancy.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like oxen. These eight subsequent lines illustrate the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
The dualistic attachment to the characteristics of the two extremes—emptiness and existence—is like the two horns of an ox.
Or they eat human flesh; destroying supramundane goodness is like eating human flesh.
Or again, they devour dogs; performing mundane karma is like devouring dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; the eighty-four thousand gates of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are like this hair, for they do not know how to penetrate them.
They block [the path] and act with perversion, like disheveled hair;
they are cruel and harmful, dangerous and perilous. Good and evil clash and destroy one another, inflicting injury and damage with ferocity and risk.
Pressed by hunger and thirst: that which lacks the food of dhyāna-joy is called "hunger," and that which lacks the moisture of the water of principle is called "thirst.
When the mind is parched and withered, lacking anything to sustain it, it is like being oppressed by hunger and thirst.
"Crying out and running about" refers to the act of speaking and disputing, which is called "crying out," and the inability to maintain self-control, which is called "running about.
Yakṣas and pretas— these six phrases summarize the unwholesome nature of the fire-house of afflictions within the desire realm.
As for the various evil birds and beasts— birds such as owls and the like, and beasts such as foxes and the like—
they are driven by hunger and rush in all four directions; tormented by hunger and thirst, they flee toward the four quarters in desperate haste.
Peering through windows and peeping at doors is a metaphor for seeking a path through the gates, vying with one another to escape and reach a place of warmth and satiety.
Such are the various hardships; these are the many afflictions and perils mentioned above.
There is immeasurable dread; the fear and terror are limitless.
This dilapidated and ancient house—these four lines clarify that the causes for the arising of fire are thus, and they express compassion for this decaying and afflicted dwelling.
It belongs to one person. That it originally belonged to one person refers to the elder, which is a metaphor for the three realms being the Buddha’s sphere of transformation.
That the person has recently departed and the elder has gone elsewhere is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature being concealed and the Buddha manifesting his *nirvāṇa*, which is "departing."
Not long after he had entered the residence, and not much time having passed since he turned his back,
the fire’s intensity within that residence became manifest; at this point, the eight lines [of verse] correctly clarify that the householder has emerged from the rear part of the residence.
Master, suddenly a fire breaks out; in an instant, the fires of the three poisons erupt simultaneously from all four sides.
These four sides are a metaphor for the four kinds of inverted views: perceiving the impermanent as permanent and the impure as pure.
The various emotional views—such as conceiving a self where there is no self, or conceiving pleasure where there is no pleasure—all gather together at once;
their flames blaze simultaneously, and the power of their fire blazes forth all at once.
The ridgepoles, rafters, beams, and pillars are metaphors for the four great elements of the body.

The sound of the explosion and the cracking represent the collapse of the house; the sound of the explosion and the violent trembling and splitting represent the destruction of the body and the clamor of groaning as all four great elements disintegrate.
They are crushed and fallen; the house collapses and crumbles, the wooden beams are damaged, broken, and shattered, falling down; the body is destroyed and the spirit departs;
the limbs are separated and the skeletal remains are scattered.
"The walls collapse" means that the body is destroyed and the skin splits open.
Regarding the various ghosts and spirits, these six phrases clarify the signs of being burned, namely those aforementioned black, emaciated, and evil ghosts.
They raise their voices and cry out; they immediately step forward, shouting and calling for food.
The vultures and eagles represent the eight kinds of arrogant birds;
the *kumbhāṇḍas* and others represent the squatting *yātudhāna* demons and the like.
They are utterly distressed, panicked, and terrified; they wander about in frantic agitation, startled and fearful.

This is a metaphor for the time of death, when the consciousness becomes chaotic and disordered, unable to emerge on its own. It falls into saṃsāra, lacking the power to escape by itself, and so forth.

Regarding "evil beasts and venomous insects": these fourteen phrases clarify that within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), fire breaks out and evil beasts—such as foxes and wolves—and venomous insects—such as vipers and snakes—hide in their burrows.
When these insects and beasts are forced out from their holes by the fire, they encounter the traveler who is practicing tranquility and sting him with their venom.
*Bhūta*: *Piśāca* spirits; here translated as "essence-eaters. This is a metaphor for those who crave tranquility: when their greedy minds arise, it is as if they were devouring vital essence.
They also dwell therein; they likewise reside together within this burning house because their merit is meager.
Those whose merit is profound and weighty do not encounter such circumstances, whereas those with meager and scant merit encounter them for this reason.
Pressed by fire, they are tormented and oppressed by the fires of the three poisons;
they harm one another, inflicting injury upon each other within this burning house.
They drink blood and eat flesh: their attachment to silent stillness is like drinking blood, and their attachment to applied and sustained thought is like eating flesh.
Furthermore,
as for the species of jackals— the beast of the jackal serves as a metaphor for those of shallow views—
they have all already perished; they have all already been consumed by fire, and all their various views have been extinguished.
The various great and wicked beasts refer to the pack of dogs mentioned earlier—the messengers of Māra—who compete to devour [the victim].
Their attachment to worldly flavors is like eating the flesh of a corpse.
The foul-smelling smoke billows forth because all things are being burned; there is a stench because the objects are consumed by fire, and smoke because the house has caught fire.
The fire’s intensity increases further, and the smoke becomes ever more oppressive and swirling. Because the mind is driven by poison, it emits foul vapors;
the body is agitated by the mind, and the color of the fire manifests externally. The inhalation and exhalation of the breath become coarse and heavy, like smoke.
It is filled on all four sides. The four kinds of inverted views fill their minds.

Centipedes and millipedes—these ten phrases clarify that in the formless realm, fire arises and insects hide in their burrows, serving as a metaphor for the gods of the formless heavens dwelling in the concentration of emptiness (*ākāśa-samādhi*).
The various kinds of venomous snakes—namely the aforementioned vipers and so forth—are scorched by fire;
being consumed by the fire of ignorance (*avidyā*), they struggle to rush out of their burrows.
The insects, driven by the fire, lose their nests; the people, impelled by the poison, lose their freedom.
As for the *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts: as before, they seize and eat [beings] at will.

Once meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is lost, one falls into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where existence and emptiness mutually incline; therefore, it is said that they "seize [at will]."
Regarding food:
furthermore, the various hungry ghosts (preta) are so named because they lack the means to sustain themselves and are constantly afflicted by hunger and emptiness.

Their heads are ablaze with fire; as they dwell at the summit of the three realms within the four formless heavens (ārūpyadhātu), they are enveloped by fire in mid-air, which is why it is said their "heads" [are burning].
They are scorched by the fire of the upper realms.
Because they harbor various calculations with a single moment of deluded mind, they are hungry and thirsty;
because they are constantly burned by the fires of the mind, they are tormented by heat.
They run about in confusion and distress, searching everywhere for an escape but failing to find its door; because their minds are bewildered and frantic, it is said they "run in confusion.
Such is that house. Within this, the four lines summarize the arising of fire in the three realms; therefore, it says, "Such is that house."
It is so. It is truly terrifying because of the extreme peril and difficulty.
There is the harm of poison and the calamity of the fire of the three poisons, which afflict the mind and the fires of karma.
The various hardships are not limited to one; the manifold calamities listed above do not end with a single aspect.
At that time, the master of the house refers to the elder who is the master of the house at the moment the fire breaks out within the triple world.
He stands outside the gate. Because the Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world, he stands outside the gate while establishing various skillful means;
thus it is said that he "stands.
He hears someone say: "The Tathāgata dwells in the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); fundamentally, he does not perceive any fire arising."
Within the context of the skillful means of mutual dependence, it is said that fire arises as if heard from another; thus it says, "I hear someone say:
'O you sons,' referring to the children of the three vehicles and those in the five destinies."
Previously, due to playfulness—wherein all suffering and pleasure arise not from causes but from the false thoughts of former causes—one played with the sense faculties and created various karmas.
Thus one entered this house; driven by karma and delusion, one entered this burning house.
"Immature and ignorant. This means that because one is young and immature, one lacks understanding— just as an ignorant person does not know this is suffering—
and thus delights in pleasure and attachment, giving rise to a mind of joy and clinging toward sensual desires.
Having heard this, and having seen this matter with his eyes of compassion, the Buddha was startled and entered the burning house.
Seeing his sons in such a state, he was unconsciously moved by alarm; arising from the Truth, he manifested a response by entering the burning house.

It is now appropriate to provide relief; it is now intended to establish relief according to what is suitable, so that there shall be no burning harm, and so that there shall be no suffering from the torment of the fires of karma.
He addresses and exhorts his sons—that is, he informs and instructs the sons of the three vehicles.
It describes various calamities and hardships, such as the characteristics of the following sufferings:
evil spirits and venomous insects. "Evil spirits" refers to *kumbhāṇḍas* and the like; "venomous insects" refers to vipers, snakes, and the like.
The fire of calamity spreads across the mats. The flames of disaster extend and draw along the mats.

The various sufferings proceed in succession; because suffering arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma arises from afflictions, and the retribution of suffering arises from karma—thus these three characteristics of affliction, karma, and suffering arise one after another, which is why they are called "successive."
The continuity is unceasing; karma produces afflictions, and afflictions produce karma, as these three paths revolve without rest.
There are venomous snakes, vipers, and various *yakṣas*, *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts, jackals, foxes, dogs, eagles, vultures, owls, and hawks.
The various species of centipedes—these six preceding lines likely reiterate the characteristics of the poisonous harm within the burning house of the three realms.
The urgency of hunger and thirst is most terrifying; the pressing distress of starvation is most fearsome.
This is a place of suffering and hardship; such a place of bitter affliction and peril.
How much more so when there is a great fire! The suffering of the house is already extreme, yet it is compounded by the breaking out of flames.
The sons are ignorant; these four lines describe how their intellect is inferior and they do not believe the words they hear.
Although they have heard their father’s instructions, and although they have heard the profound and earnest admonitions of their compassionate father,
they remain as before attached to pleasure; for the sake of desire, they remain attached and do not relinquish it,
never ceasing their frolics and refusing to stop their dalliance within the realms of sensory dust.
At that time, the elder— [the following thirty verses explain] the aspirations of the Śākyaputra within the prose section—
when his son did not accept his admonitions,
he thought thus; seeing that his son did not believe him, he further reflected:
Such are my sons; such are these young children, foolish and deluded.
They increase my sorrow and distress; they augment the sorrow and distress within my heart.
This house—this present abode of the five aggregates within the three realms—is like that.
There is not a single thing to be delighted in; everything therein is entirely suffering, and there is not a single matter that can be loved or enjoyed.
As for "my sons," these refer to those in the five realms of existence.
They are addicted to and immersed in play and sport; they are deeply attached to and submerged in merriment and diversion.
They do not accept my instruction; though I admonish and instruct them, they do not believe or accept it.
They will surely be harmed by fire; they will soon be destroyed by fire.
Even as he contemplated, he immediately further applied skillful deliberation and established various expedient means.
Having devised these various teachings of the three vehicles as expedient means, he addressed his sons.
Having reflected upon these expedients, he then spoke to his sons.
I have various kinds [of vehicles], namely the three types of precious play-vehicles mentioned below:
precious play-appurtenances, rare and wonderful articles for enjoyment,
and excellent jewel-carts— superior carts adorned with all manner of jewels.

The sheep cart and the deer cart: the sheep cart is a metaphor for using the Four Noble Truths to guide the sons of the Śrāvakas; the deer cart is a metaphor for using the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to guide the sons of the Pratyekabuddhas.
The great ox cart—that is, the water buffalo cart—is a metaphor for employing the Six Perfections and myriad practices to guide those of the provisional Mahāyāna.
He teaches the bodhisattvas;
they are currently outside the gate. Although the three vehicles differ, they are all dharmas of quiescent extinction beyond the realm [of saṃsāra], and therefore they are outside the gate.
"Come forth! I urge you with these chariots to leave the burning house.

For your sake—and I say this for all of you—I have fashioned these vehicles. Although the three vehicles were originally non-existent, they are said to be "fashioned" because they were provisionally established all at once.
"According to what you desire. Because the teaching of skillful means follows the capacities of others' faculties, it says, "according to what your hearts desire," so that you may play.
These three vehicles are true happiness; therefore, one may play [with them], but not with this house.
That one should indulge in the pleasures of the five desires within [this world] is what is not permissible.
When the sons heard this teaching, the following six phrases clarify the vows of the Śākyaputrīyas. At that time, the sons heard what their father had said.
These various chariots—these three kinds of sublime jeweled chariots—then rushed forward in competition.
At that very moment, they vied with one another to race out.
Hearing this, one develops reverent faith and practices with increasing intensity; this is called "rushing forth" (abhiprasthāna), which means liberation from the three realms.
The affliction of wandering through the realms of suffering is called "running about.
Upon reaching the open space—the state of nirvana’s emptiness and stillness—one is freed from all hardships and calamities.
Those of the three vehicles alike sever the views and afflictions, depart from the perils of defilement, and no longer give rise to delusions.
Due to being free from the karma of fetters, it is difficult not to be born within the three realms; due to being free from suffering, it is difficult to receive retribution.
When the elder sees his son, twenty phrases beginning from this point clarify the father’s joyful mind, showing how the Buddha beholds sentient beings with eyes of compassion.
They emerge from the burning house; they emerge from the perilous burning house of the triple world.
They abide at the crossroads; they abide at the four gates upon the thoroughfare that leads to the penetration of the paths of the three vehicles.
He sat upon the lion throne. Having enabled his sons to emerge [from the fire], the elder’s mind was at peace as he sat firmly upon the great precious lion throne.
Previously, he had employed provisional skillful means by establishing the three vehicles to entice them; this is why it was said earlier that they were standing outside the gate.
Now, having led them into the reality, he sits upon the precious throne.

He then spoke words of self-congratulation: "The reason the Buddha appeared in the world was to deliver sentient beings; that sentient beings have now emerged is the fulfillment of his original intent.
I am now joyful.
Previously, seeing them in suffering, my grief and distress only increased; now seeing them emerge from it, my spirit is at last relieved."
I cherish these sons; these sons of the three vehicles were very difficult to bring forth and raise.
Because they have been educated through skillful means since time immemorial, it is said that they were "very difficult."
Foolish and ignorant, with weak wisdom and no correct knowledge or vision, they enter a perilous house;
because of the conditions of their karma, they are drawn into the dangerous fire-house of the triple world.
The many venomous insects represent the poisonous mind;
the fearsome *chī-mèi* (goblins and specters) represent the deluded, false mind;
and the great fire with its fierce flames represents the intensely violent smoke and flames of the poisonous fire of afflictions (*kleśa*).
They arise simultaneously from all four sides; the four inverted views are produced at once.
Yet these sons—the sons within this house of the three vehicles—delight in play and revelry, becoming addicted to worldly pleasures and unaware that they are suffering.
I have already rescued them. By means of skillful expedients, I have protected and shielded them, enabling them to escape this calamity.
Now that they have been delivered from the disaster of the burning house, I am truly joyful. For this reason, I say to you all: "At this moment..."
"Daily they obtain happiness.
At that time, the various sons—these twelve subsequent lines clarify the metaphor of the sons emerging from [the house], seeking chariots from their father;
it illustrates the thirty sons seeking the fruit of the skillful means.
Knowing that his father was sitting at ease, and knowing that his father’s mind was settled in his seat,
the son went to where his father was— just as one approaches the presence of the Buddha—
and addressed his father, speaking virtuous words in common with him to the Buddha.

We pray that you grant us these. We pray that you grant my thirty sons the three kinds of precious chariots—the fruits of the three vehicles consisting of the sheep, deer, and ox chariots—just as previously promised.
It was precisely for the purpose of drawing them out that you promised to grant the three chariots.
"Come forth, my sons! I shall fulfill my previous promise;
I will provide three kinds of vehicles—specifically, three kinds of wondrous jewel-vehicles—according to your desires, according to whatever each of you, my sons, wishes for in your hearts."
Now is precisely the right time. Now that he has already left his home, it is truly the opportune moment.
I pray you will grant this; I pray you will bestow it upon me.
The elder is immensely wealthy. The following thirty phrases clarify the elder’s vast riches and his impartial mind in bestowing them.
The chariot of jewels has many treasuries and storehouses. The various faculties are like the storehouses; the myriad practices are like hidden treasures;
and wisdom and merit are likened to precious objects. Because their number is immeasurable, they are said to be "many."
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, and agate— among the seven treasures, these five types are briefly mentioned here, all of which are explained as before.
By means of various precious objects, the meaning of "various treasures" includes pearls and coral.
They construct various great chariots. These great chariots are white ox-drawn vehicles, which represent the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Because they are realized through cultivation, it is said that they are "constructed. The construction of the seven-jeweled chariot is a metaphor for the seven kinds of meritorious dharmas and wealth.
It is adorned and embellished; it is decorated and punctuated.
It has railings all around; its meritorious dharma-body is strictly guarded by vows and precepts, just like the surrounding railings of that great chariot.
Bells hang from all four sides; through the sounds of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), they cause all to hear as if bells were suspended.
Golden cords crisscross and interlace; using gold for the cords signifies that "cord" has the meaning of "black," just as the cords of the precepts (*śīla*) are interlaced.
The pearl net: the pearls of precept and the pearls of wisdom reflect one another like a lattice spread above;
this is illustrated by the metaphor of adorning the Dharma-body with various jewels, which are arrayed and displayed upon the chariot.
"Golden flowers and pearl tassels": the color of gold is yellow, which symbolizes the Middle Way;
arising from correct wisdom, the true and wondrous mind is called "golden flowers," while various jewels serve as tassels to adorn the body of the chariot.
It hangs down everywhere. Because the various unconditioned truths (anabhisaṃskṛta-satya) stoop down to accommodate the capacities of all sentient beings, it is said to "hang down.

Adorned with various jewels and interspersed with various colors, this great precious chariot is like the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) being collectively embellished by the myriad practices (sahasra-caryā).
They encircle it on all sides, spreading out and wrapping themselves around the top of the chariot.
They are soft silks and cotton-wool; these silken fabrics and cotton fillings are soft to the touch.

He used it as a mattress and bedding. A mattress and bedding are the coverings spread upon a carriage; with a mind of patience, one cultivates the various holy practices, which—like silk floss—are soft and fit to be relied upon as a support.
It was a superior, exquisite, fine *kṣauma* cloth. *Kṣauma* is fine linen; it was a cloth of the highest grade, exquisite, fine, and soft.
Its value is worth a thousand billion; this speaks of its noble substance.
It is fresh, white, and pure—fresh, fine, white, and moreover immaculate—with which it covers the top.
This great precious chariot is spread with cotton mattresses and further covered with white woolen cloth.
Taking the essence of the supreme Dharma-body as its foundation, it cultivates all myriad practices through the power of patience to serve as its adornment.
It possesses a great white ox: the ox symbolizes the power of the Way; "white" symbolizes purity; and "great" symbolizes magnificence. This greatness is threefold: first, greatness of essence;
second, greatness of attributes; and third, greatness of function.
They were robust and possessed great strength; because of their robustness, they were endowed with both physical luster and vitality.
Their forms were beautiful, their bodies exceptionally large and exquisitely handsome.
They drove precious chariots—chariots adorned with jewels that were lofty and wide.
He has many attendants; with great skillful means and the power of wisdom, they surround and follow him like retinues,
guarding and protecting him, serving and defending him.
With these wonderful chariots— chariots exquisitely adorned with various jewels—
he bestowed them equally upon all his sons, granting each son one of these foremost, most excellent, and sublime chariots.
At that time, the sons—by means of the six subsequent lines regarding the attainment of the chariots—were filled with joy.
They leaped for joy; their minds were gladdened and their bodies exulted.
Riding upon these precious chariots is a metaphor for riding upon the great jewel-chariot of the single reality.

To roam in the four directions and study all dharmas extensively is called "wandering. To traverse the forty noble stages of the *caryā*, *vihāra*, *mārga*, and *bhūmi* is called the "four directions.
To sport in joy and pleasure, traversing hundreds of thousands of samādhis and dharma-gates, is called "playful wandering," whereby one attains the Dharma.
Delighting in the flavor of dhyāna-joy is called happiness.
It is sovereign and unimpeded; the body attains sovereignty and the mind is free from obstruction.
[The Buddha] said to Śāriputra: "The following sixteen lines of verse constitute a collective metaphor."
I am also like this. This corresponds to the analogy of the elder.
Among the four types of noble ones—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas—the Buddha is the most honored.
The Father of the World. Because the Buddha is the common teacher of the world within the three realms and is the father who gives birth to the Dharma-body, he is called "Father.
This applies to all sentient beings—every class of living beings throughout the six realms of existence.
All are my children. I regard all beings equally, as if they were my only child.
Yet they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures; they are deeply attached to the pleasures of the five worldly desires.
They possess no wisdom of mind, nor do they possess the mind of supramundane wisdom.
There is no peace within the three realms. Although suffering and pleasure differ within these three realms, there is nothing that is not tainted by outflows (*āsrava*) or a place of instability.
It is like a burning house; it is like a dwelling consumed by a great conflagration.
Filled with manifold sufferings— the five sufferings and the eight sufferings— this realm is turbid and evil. Together with the aforementioned birds, beasts, venomous insects, spirits, and ghosts,
it is utterly terrifying, profoundly unstable, and most cause for alarm and dread.

There are always birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and affliction. One has not yet escaped saṃsāra, and thus there are constantly the sorrows and hardships of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Such are these fires; those listed above are these very fires of karma.
Blazing without ceasing; blazing day and night without ever resting, the Tathāgata has already transcended this.
[This concludes] the preceding section on the elder standing outside the gate. From the following twelve lines of verse, one sees how sentient beings are oppressed by suffering.
The burning house of the three realms: the Tathāgata has already emerged from beyond the three realms and dwells in tranquil seclusion.
He abides in cessation (*nirvāṇa*), with no desires stirring his mind and performing no manifold activities; therefore, it is called "dwelling in seclusion."
Dwelling peacefully in the forest wilds; dwelling serenely in the lush groves of the factors of enlightenment and the vast, empty wilderness.
Within this present triple world, amidst this burning house of the three realms.

"All these are mine. Because the Tathāgata, while on the stage of a bodhisattva, made a vow to deliver sentient beings within the three realms—the realm of the Buddha’s transformation—he said, "They are mine.
"The sentient beings therein" refers to all sentient beings existing within those three realms.
All are my children; all are children of the Buddha.
Yet in this place—this realm of the triple world and this locus of saṃsāra—there are many calamities and many matters of suffering, affliction, and hardship.
Only I alone; only the Buddha alone, am able to provide rescue and protection, and act as a teacher who delivers, protects, and mindfully remembers.
Although he provides such instruction, the following four phrases combine the analogy of the small table (*śayyā-pīṭha*), which the Sūtra states: "If one uses a small table... (or *śayyā-kaṭa*).
Although the Buddha issued such instructions as these to lead them out from their house, they did not believe or accept them;
specifically, they were unable to believe or accept the One Vehicle, the powers, and the fearlessnesses. As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter:
"If one were to praise only the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma."
Because their attachment to the defilements of desire and to the objects of the five sensual desires is profound,
and because their greedy minds are deeply attached to these desires, they lack faith.
By means of this expedient, the six subsequent phrases combine with the preceding account of rescuing the children by using carts to illustrate how,
because they do not believe in the true expedient,
he employs skillful means to preach the Three Vehicles, thereby providing the provisional teaching of the Three Vehicles.
He causes all sentient beings— those sentient beings within the realms who are lost in delusion—
to know the suffering of the three realms; he causes them to know that the pleasures experienced through unrestrained indulgence and arrogance within these three realms are none other than suffering.
To reveal and expound; to clarify, instruct, and proclaim in words the supramundane path—the path of renunciation and cessation from the world.
These six subsequent phrases collectively explain the aspiration of the sons, who are the disciples receiving the teaching.
...and so forth.

Whether the mind is determined, or if those of the three vehicles have their minds resolved and fixed, they are endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
As for the three types of clear knowledge: [the first is] the clear knowledge of past lives; [the second is] the clear knowledge of the present [leakage of defilements]...

The perfection of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that bring complete clarity regarding the future consists of: first, the power of the divine eye, which can see things both inside and outside of obstructions;

second, the power of the divine ear, which can hear all sounds, whether distant or near; third, the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), which can know the internal states of other people's minds;

fourth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), which can know the events of previous existences; and fifth, the power of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhividhi*), also known as the power of moving through space.

The supernormal power of the mind (*manojñāna-abhijñā*) can manifest various miraculous transformations; entering the earth or treading upon water is all according to one's will, and there is no obstruction regarding any object.

The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) means that the outflows of the three realms and karma are simultaneously exhausted, and one attains unimpeded penetration into the principle of true emptiness.
Those who resolve to develop the aspiration to be fully endowed with these supernormal powers and clarities are those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

There are those who attain the state of a pratyekabuddha; their minds desire to receive the teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination and the dharma of arising and ceasing, which is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
There are non-retrogressive bodhisattvas; their minds desire to attain the stage of non-retrogression within the Mahāyāna teaching, which is the bodhisattva [vehicle].
"Ride! You, Śāriputra, [and the others]—from these twenty subsequent phrases, all equally receive the great chariots.
'I' refers to sentient beings; 'the Buddha' refers to all sentient beings within the dharma-realm."
By means of these parables and these various words and metaphors,
he teaches the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekayāna). The reason he speaks of three vehicles is to manifest the One, desiring that all his children enter the Buddha Vehicle.
If you are able— if any of you, my sons, are well able—
to believe and accept these words, and with a faithful mind receive them, then this is indeed a word of singular truth.
All shall indeed attain it; all those of the three vehicles shall fully and rightly attain it.
They shall accomplish the Buddha-way, realize bodhi, and obtain the wondrous path of Buddhahood.
This vehicle is subtle and wondrous; this Single Buddha-vehicle is profound, secret, perfect, and sublime.
It is the foremost purity. Because it exhausts the three delusions, it is called "pure"; because it is supreme among them, it is called "foremost.
Among all worldly things—that is, among all phenomena within the three worlds.
It is unsurpassed; it is the most sublime Dharma, beyond which there is nothing higher.
It is that which the Buddha delights in; it is the seal of approval by which the Buddha expresses his joy.
It is for all sentient beings—beings of the three vehicles, the six paths, and the nine realms.
One should praise what is worthy of praise; one should extol and speak words of commendation;
one should make offerings and prostrate; one should provide various offerings, honoring and reverently prostrating to the extent of immeasurable billions.
These four subsequent lines clarify that the One Buddha Vehicle is complete with all dharmas, which accords with the preceding long passage.
Their wealth is immeasurable;
they possess the various powers and liberations, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the great samādhis, pure liberation, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Each of these various concentrations and various wisdoms is individually infinite in its hundreds of millions.
A thousand [pieces of gold], as well as the Buddha’s remaining teachings, and the Buddha’s skillful means and other truly pure dharmas—
by attaining such a vehicle, these twelve subsequent phrases together constitute the joy of obtaining the chariot; one thus attains such a [joy].
The Buddha’s wondrous vehicle causes all his sons— those seekers of the Dharma belonging to the three vehicles—
to spend days, nights, and kalpas; that is, near at hand for days and nights, or far off across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
They constantly enjoy sport; they constantly attain the Samādhi of Sporting therein.

Together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas—those who possess the capacity for the vehicle [of the Pratyekabuddhas]—they are endowed with the conditions for this; here, the two terms are stated in brief to encompass the intended meaning.
Riding upon this precious vehicle— riding upon this Great Vehicle of the Single Buddha’s supreme jewel—
one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment, proceeding straight to the field of quiescence of the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
For these reasons, by means of this wondrous cause and supreme, excellent condition,
one seeks with earnest scrutiny throughout the ten directions; within the realms of the ten directions,
one searches with diligent examination and finds no other vehicle and no other dharma outside of the One Vehicle.
Except for the Buddha’s skillful means— specifically, except for the Tathāgata’s provisional teaching when he addressed Śāriputra—
the fourteen phrases from that point downward, together with the preceding statement that there is no falsehood, [constitute this].
"You all, you seekers of the Dharma belonging to the three vehicles—all of you are my children.
Those who realize the truth through the three vehicles all become sons of the Buddha;
I am their father. Since you have been established as children, the Buddha is their father."
Throughout many kalpas, you have all been scorched by manifold sufferings and consumed by various afflictions;
I have rescued you all, delivering you all through the three vehicles.
I cause them to emerge from the triple world; I cause them to attain liberation from the burning house of the triple world.
Although I previously spoke, and although at that time I spoke through skillful means, saying, "You have attained parinirvāṇa," and "You have already attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
"Merely exhausting birth and death" means merely attaining the exhaustion of the segmented birth and death within the triple world;
yet in reality, it is not extinguished, and one truly does not attain ultimate nirvana.
That which should now be practiced, that which ought now to be undertaken for cultivation, is solely the wisdom of the Buddha;
it is solely the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
If there is a bodhisattva, then from the eighth verse below, all the various skillful means (*upāya*) are shown to be of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Thereupon, within this assembly, amidst this great multitude gathered for the Dharma-meeting,
there were those who were able to listen with a single mind; they were able to collect their minds and listen attentively to the true Dharma of all Buddhas— the reality of all Buddhas as it truly is.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones— the Great Enlightened World-Honored Ones of all Buddhas—
though they employ skillful means, though they utilize the provisional expedients of the three vehicles to transform sentient beings,
those beings whom they transform are the persons of the three vehicles.
All are bodhisattvas. In reality, they are all the children of the Bodhisattva, ultimately converging upon the single path of the Buddha-vehicle.
If people possess small wisdom, these following twenty-eight verses of praise were spoken as an expedient means out of necessity, according to their capacities.
Regarding the intent of the three vehicles: if there are those whose wisdom and vision are narrow and limited,
who are deeply attached to sensual desires, and whose hearts are profoundly bound by affection and lust—
for their sake, and for the sake of those of dull faculties— [the Buddha taught these].
He speaks of the Truth of Suffering; he speaks of the various sufferings within the three realms, declaring with certainty that this is reality and shall never be false.
The minds of sentient beings rejoice; those sentient beings of dull faculties, upon hearing his teaching, comprehend it and their hearts are filled with joy.
I have attained what I never had before. The worldly texts and commentaries could never reach this; through the Buddha’s revelation, I have obtained that which I had never heard.
The Buddha has taught the Truth of Suffering; the Buddha has taught the meaning of the Truth of Suffering within the three realms.
It is truly without difference. One knows with faith that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and there is no other teaching.
Whether it be sentient beings, or again, another class of sentient beings.
They do not know the root of suffering; they do not know what constitutes the causal basis for the fruit of suffering.

They are deeply attached to the causes of suffering; with deep-seated craving, they cling to the karma accumulated through those causes and cannot abandon them even for a moment, nor can they give rise to a mind of revulsion and renunciation even for a brief instant.
For the sake of these people, and because these people are deluded, he employs skillful means to speak the Way;
through the gateway of skillful means, he explains to them that which is the cause of all suffering—
the origin and conditions from which the various sufferings of the world arise.
Craving is the root; all things take craving as their foundation, which is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
If one extinguishes craving—if one can still the mind of craving—[then suffering ceases].
When there is no basis for dependence, then the fruits of suffering have nothing upon which they can rely to arise.
