All sufferings are extinguished; by the power of right mindfulness, one brings rest to accumulated karma and severs the various sufferings of birth and death within the three realms.
This is called the third truth, which is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
For the sake of cessation, and in order to accomplish the truth of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*), one practices the Path.
One cultivates and restrains body and mind so as not to let them run wild, and carries out the Tathāgata’s three trainings and eightfold [path].
The path of perfect reality is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
To be free from all bonds of suffering, and to swiftly be freed from the many bonds of birth and death, is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Because one practices the path, one is released from bondage and attains liberation; this is called the realization of the four fruits (*catur-phala*).
Furthermore,
in what does this person consist? As a practitioner of the path,
by means of what dharma do they attain liberation and enter the path to liberation from the world?

It is simply the departure from delusion. It is precisely the distancing oneself from the deluded mind of the two afflictions—viewing and thought—that results in emerging from the suffering of the segmented realm;
this is called liberation. Pointing directly to the transcendence of the three realms is what is meant by liberation.
In fact, they have not yet attained it. The following twelve phrases clarify that although they first employ skillful means and subsequently explain the general meaning,
regarding the Mahāyāna, they have truly never attained any liberation, any quiescence, or ultimate liberation.
The Buddha speaks of such a person. For this reason, the Buddha says that such a person has not yet truly attained extinction; they have never truly realized great parinirvāṇa.
Such a person has not yet attained it; because they have not yet attained it, [they are so described].
Because it is the unsurpassed path; because it is the path of supreme, correct, and true reality, it is my intention that I do not [desire this].
It is the Buddha’s fundamental intention that he does not desire this, so as to cause them to reach parinirvāṇa, to cause them to reach ultimate parinirvāṇa.
I am the Dharma King. The Buddha is the sovereign of all phenomena that transcend the world;
he possesses mastery over the Dharma, and regarding all sentient beings, he expounds the Dharma according to their inclinations with complete freedom in both contraction and expansion.
To bring peace and security to sentient beings, and desiring that sentient beings attain peace and security, he has appeared in the world.
For this reason, having appeared in the world—thus concludes the prose commentary on the preceding verses.
Hereafter follows the exhortation to believe and circulate [the teaching].
"Śāriputra, these six subsequent lines clarify that the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is intended to benefit sentient beings; for those capable of faith and acceptance, it is beneficial.
However, if the recipient is not such a person, hearing it will not produce faith; it is not merely useless, but also harmful.
Therefore, he charges you to examine this matter with great care."
This Dharma-seal of mine— this seal of the true nature of the supreme and wondrous Dharma—
is intended for the benefit of others, so that those who hear it may practice according to the teaching and achieve great benefit.
It is spoken for the sake of the world; it is spoken because of the world of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
In whatever direction one travels, and in every land where one wanders, do not propagate this recklessly.
One must first find the right person before proclaiming it; if they are not sincere, by no means speak of it recklessly.

The Tradition states: "If there are those who hear it"—this refers to the sixteen phrases that follow which clarify that one may preach it. Furthermore, if there are others who hear this sublime Dharma...
One should rejoice in and receive this with the crown of the head; one should fall into accord with it, receive it with joy, and wear it upon the head as a token of upholding.
It should be known that such a person—such a person who receives it with faith—is an *avaivartika*, which here means "non-retrogressive," signifying that they do not retrogress from the Right Path.
If there are those who believe and accept this sutra and its Dharma, those who believe in the supreme and wondrous Dharma of the Mahayana sutras, such persons have already done so in the past;
these people of the faculty of faith have already done so in their previous lives.
They behold the Buddhas of the past; they behold countless Buddhas of the past, paying them respect and making offerings.
In the presence of those Buddhas, with a profound mind of reverence, they practice the offering of the Dharma.
I have also heard this Dharma; I have also heard it taught that such a Dharma is established by inferring the cause from the fruit, according to the principles of logic.
If there is one who is capable, or if there is another person who can, with a pure mind—
I believe what you have said. To hear what you have said and give rise to right faith is to see me;
it is called seeing the Buddha, and it is also to see you, and it is to see your Dharma-body.
As well as the community of bhikṣus and the other assemblies of the bhikṣu-saṃgha— where *saṃgha* in the Sanskrit language is translated as "the harmonious assembly"—
if one can thoroughly understand that the Buddha and the Dharma are non-dual, this is called seeing the Saṃgha.
Together with all bodhisattvas, and together with all bodhisattvas practicing the Mahāyāna— for these,
this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom. These sixteen subsequent phrases clarify that this wondrous sūtra should not be taught to others,
but should be taught to those who possess deep faith and wisdom.
Those of shallow understanding who hear this—those whose wisdom and insight are superficial and who hear it for the first time—will be bewildered and fail to understand;
their minds will be deluded by doubt and they will be unable to comprehend it.
This refers to all śrāvakas, that is, those of the Hīnayāna śrāvaka vehicle.
As for the pratyekabuddhas and those who awaken through conditions,
they are beyond the reach of power within this sutra; within this wondrous Lotus Sutra,
their strength is insufficient and their capacity too meager to attain it.
"Śāriputra, you are foremost in wisdom among those of the Lesser Vehicle;
yet even you must enter this sutra—this sublime Mahāyāna sutra—by means of faith.
It is through the power of faith that you have entered the Dharma, for your practice is not yet complete and you have not yet attained direct realization."
How much more so for other śrāvakas, and how much more so for other śrāvakas of dull faculties?
As for those other śrāvakas— indeed, all other śrāvakas whatsoever.
Because they believe the Buddha’s words, having heard the Buddha speak of the sublime, they give rise to faith from those words.
They accord with this sutra, rejoice in it, and accept this sublime sutra;
yet it is not within the scope of their own wisdom, nor is it within the scope of the wisdom of others.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are eight points concerning arrogance and indolence that clarify how those of shallow understanding should not be taught this:
an arrogant person lacks right faith, and one who is indolent is unable to practice with diligence.

Regarding those who harbor views of self: if they are attached to their own views and are not yet vessels for receiving the Way, do not preach this sutra to them. Do not preach this sutra to the ignorant;
ordinary people possess shallow understanding, and inferior ordinary people have superficial insight and vision.
Deeply attached to the five desires, they develop a profound craving for the objects of those five desires.

If they hear [the teaching] and cannot understand it—meaning that even when it is explained to them, they fail to comprehend—it should not be taught to them; nor should it be expounded to them lightly.
If there are those who do not believe—hereafter follow one hundred and thirty phrases clarifying the offense of slandering the sutra, divided into three parts.
First, there are twenty-four phrases concerning how, because of slandering the sutra, one falls into hell. Furthermore, if there are people who hear [this] and do not give rise to faith...
To slander this sutra—that is, to speak words of slander against this sublime sutra—is to sever everything; it is to cut off all that exists:
the seed of the Buddha in the world, the seed for the attainment of Buddhahood by all sentient beings in the world.
Or they may frown; or upon hearing such an explanation, their brows may knit and wrinkle as they harbor doubts.
Their own minds are not pleased, and for this reason they furrow their brows, harboring hesitation and indecisive doubt.

You should listen as I describe the retribution for this person's transgression. Such is the retribution for the sin obtained by one who slanders this sutra, whether the Buddha is in the world or during the time when the Tathāgata is present in the world.
If, after his parinirvāṇa— that is, after the Blessed One has passed into extinction—
there should be those who slander, and there should be sentient beings who speak words of slander against such a sūtra, such a perfectly sublime Mahāyāna sūtra.
Seeing those who recite and chant; seeing sentient beings who, with a sincere heart, recite and chant, or who copy and uphold this sutra—
those who write it down and receive and maintain this scripture— they treat them with contempt and hatred,
looking down upon them with disdain and loathing, and feeling envy and jealousy toward them.
Yet they harbor resentment and bear grudges, giving rise to anger and hatred in their hearts.
Such is the retribution for this person’s sin; such is the retribution obtained by those who slander this sutra.
Listen now once more! You all should listen again as I speak.
When that person’s life comes to an end, having passed away after slandering the sutra, they enter the Avīci Hell.
"Avīci" is translated here as "Uninterrupted," meaning one constantly undergoes suffering without any interval.
It fulfills one kalpa. One day and one night in the Avīci Hell is equivalent to sixty minor kalpas by the reckoning of human years;
from this accumulation of months and years, it reaches a full kalpa.
When a kalpa ends, they are born again; after one kalpa has ended, they are born yet again.
Thus it continues in succession, increasing further and further until countless kalpas have passed; thus long is the retribution of suffering.
Emerging from hell, there are forty-two phrases below this that clarify how, upon finishing the sufferings of hell, one falls again into the realm of animals.
One is destined to fall among animals, falling into the midst of diverse species.
Whether they are dogs or jackals, or whether they become dogs or jackals again, their bodies are emaciated; their forms are hungry, weak, and withered.
They are dark-complexioned and afflicted with scabies and leprosy; their dark complexion refers to black skin, scabies, and the disease of leprosy.
Furthermore, they are harassed by others; they are provoked, disturbed, and vexed by others;
moreover, they are treated with contempt and disdain by others, being hated, loathed, and held in low esteem by others.
They are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst; they are perpetually beset by the distress of hunger and thirst.
Their flesh and bones wither away; their bones become parched, their marrow exhausted, and their flesh emaciated.
While alive, they undergo agonizing torment; throughout their lives, they endure various forms of bitter suffering and poison.
Upon death they are covered with tiles and stones; having died, they are further buried amidst tiles and stones.
Because they have severed the lineage of the Buddha, and because they have caused the severance of the Buddha-seed in the world, they undergo this retribution for their sins;
they receive this unwholesome retribution as members of the animal realm.
If it is made as a camel, it is a large-bodied animal found in northern regions;
or it may be born from among donkeys, its body constantly bearing heavy loads. Both camels and donkeys are capable of carrying burdens.
They are subjected to beatings with staves; they are forced to walk under the blows of clubs and staves, thinking only of water and grass.
Their every thought is fixed solely upon water and grass;
they know nothing else. Left to their own devices in ignorance, they possess no understanding whatsoever.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses; cause inevitably brings forth its fruit, just as a shadow follows a form.
Some become jackals, and at times they may even take the body of a jackal.
He has come to enter the village. This wild beast from the wilderness has entered the village with a body covered in scabs and sores as a retribution for his past destruction of goodness;
furthermore, he is blind in one eye because he destroyed the right view of others, which caused him to lose that eye.
They were beaten and pelted by young children; seeing them, the children would strike them with sticks or throw stones at them,
causing them to endure various pains and the agony of being beaten and pelted.
Sometimes they die; or again, they meet with death because of this.
Having died there, they undergo the state of a jackal, and further take birth as a great python.
Its form is tall and large, measuring five hundred yojanas; its body is exceedingly vast.
It is deaf and dull-witted, lacking feet. This serpent hears with its body and does not hear with its ears; it is foolish, ignorant, and footless.
They writhe and crawl on their bellies, twisting and turning as they move along with their abdomens.
They are devoured by various small insects; on every scale and shell, many worms swarm about, biting into their flesh and muscles.
They suffer day and night; throughout the day and night they constantly undergo pain without respite.
From beginning to end, there is never a time of rest.
Because they have slandered this sutra, they incur such retribution; this demonstrates the profound depth of their offense.
If one attains birth as a human, these following sixty-four phrases clarify that once the retribution for being an animal has ended, one is reborn among humans;
having escaped the animal realm and transmigrated to a human body,
one’s faculties are dull and obtuse, meaning the gates of the six sense organs cannot perceive clearly.
Dwarfish and deformed, hunchbacked and lame; short and ugly, with contracted hands and crippled feet; blind and deaf, with hunched backs;
if they have anything to say, whatever words they utter from their mouths—
People do not believe or accept it. People harbor feelings of disdain and contempt, thus they do not believe or accept it.
Their breath is constantly foul. Those who recite the sutras speak of it as having the fragrance of lotuses; because they slander the True Vehicle, their breath is foul.
One is possessed by malevolent spirits because one lacks right faith and allows the wicked to cause interference;
one is impoverished and lowly because one failed to cultivate merit and remains inferior and destitute;
and one is used by others and enslaved by others, lacking any autonomy.
Afflicted by many illnesses, they become emaciated; because their flesh and muscles have wasted away due to the suffering of disease and lack of nourishment, they become withered and parched.
Having no one to rely upon, and not depending on teachers or friends, they suffer from hunger and cold.
Although they may attach themselves to others, because there is no karmic affinity, even though they resolve to associate with them, those people do not take them to heart;
that is, the former person does not dwell upon them in their mind.
If there is something acquired, or if one has acquired even a small portion of the Dharma, it is soon forgotten;
the mind becomes clouded, wisdom is deluded, and one suffers from frequent forgetfulness.
Whether practicing the way of medicine or studying medical treatises and the principles of compounding medicines, [the same occurs].
Administering medicine according to the prescribed method, one should treat the illnesses of others in accordance with the medicinal prescriptions.
Yet, instead of increasing their ailments, one fails to cure them and causes further illness to arise;
or perhaps it leads to death. At times, the condition worsens so severely that it results in death—all of this is due to slandering the sutras and lacking wholesome conditions.
Therefore,
if one has an illness, or if one should have various ailments,
and there is no one to provide relief and treatment, no one to administer medical care and healing.
Suppose one administers excellent medicine; or suppose one follows the illness by taking and ingesting fine medicines, yet the condition worsens, becoming increasingly severe and distressing;
or if there is rebellion from another, or if it is due to the treacherous and rebellious acts of another.
Plundering, robbing, pilfering, stealing, and theft— such crimes as these,
such unlawful offenses, cause one to be unjustly ensnared by calamity;
through wrongful and perverse entrapment, one suffers such harm and ruin.
Such a person of sin, such a person who slanders this sutra and commits an act of rebellion,
shall never see the Buddha; they shall forever fail to see the Buddhas of the ten directions,
the Kings of all Sages, and the King of the Sublime Dharma within the fourfold assembly of noble disciples.
He preaches the Dharma to teach and transform others, expounding upon all dharmas to instruct and guide them.
Such a sinner—such a person who, through lack of faith, obstructs the Dharma—will always be born in difficult places;
life after life, they will always be born in places of suffering and hardship.
Mad, deaf, and mentally deranged; crazed, deaf-mute, and with a clouded mind, they shall never hear the Dharma.
For immeasurable kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they shall pass through kalpas as many as the sands of the Ganges, never attaining the opportunity to hear the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Born deaf and mute; from the very moment of birth, they are deaf and mute.
Their faculties are incomplete; the six sense organs are mostly not fully developed.
They constantly dwell in hell as if visiting a pleasure garden; because of their karmic obstructions, they perpetually reside in hell as if strolling through a park.
The places of gardens, palaces,
and pavilions are like their own homes to them in other evil realms; among the other hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras in the evil realms,
they are just like their own houses.
Camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs are their places of rebirth; driven by the power of karma, they move among these various species.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses; because they revile the Dharma of the sutra, they receive such evil retribution.
If they obtain human birth— this clarifies that once the retribution of the evil realms has been exhausted,
they are reborn as humans who are deaf, blind, mute, or suffer from diseases of the eyes, ears, throat, and pharynx.
They are adorned with all manner of misfortunes of poverty, with various calamities of destitution and suffering;
they adorn themselves with such evil retributions,
such as dropsy, consumption, edema, and emaciation from wasting away.
Scabies, leprosy, carbuncles; scabies, ringworm, white leprosy, boils, abscesses, and sores— such diseases as these,
and various other such grave and evil illnesses,
they take as their clothing, using them as ornaments and garments upon their bodies.
Their bodies are constantly in a foul-smelling state; their bodies always dwell amidst stench.
They are defiled and impure, stained and filthy, never being clean.
They are deeply attached to the view of self (*ātman*), and with deep-seated minds they grasp at and cling to their own views.
It increases hatred; the mind of anger becomes intense.
Lust blazes forth; one craves sensual desire as fiercely as a raging fire, making no distinction between humans and beasts, even to the point of engaging in debauchery and intimacy with animals.
Because one slanders this sutra, the offenses incurred are as follows: having accumulated karma through causes, one undergoes the retribution of suffering in a land of perverse results;
obstructed by the hindrance of wholesome deeds, one falls into evil states.
Śāriputra, these eight phrases below summarize and demonstrate that the explanation of such evil retribution cannot be fully exhausted; they are all subsumed herein.
The preceding text exhorted that one must carefully discern whether a person is worthy; if they are not the right person, one must not preach to them.

As for those who slander this sutra—those who slander this subtle and wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—if one were to describe their transgressions, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon. If one were to describe the sins incurred by slandering this sutra, they would endure for as long as the atoms of dust throughout all worlds.
Even throughout kalpas, they could not be exhausted.
For this reason, it is of no benefit and only causes harm to expound the doctrine of the causal conditions of karmic retribution to those who do not believe in it.
Therefore I tell you: for this reason I previously told you that among those without wisdom—among people who are ignorant and deluded—you must not preach this sutra.
Thus, the two preceding verses were admonitions to select the appropriate recipients and instructions not to preach it to them.

If there are those of sharp faculties, for these sixty-eight phrases from the preceding section, he uses the gate of great compassion to teach virtuous persons that their root-natures are universally sharp,
their wisdom is clear and lucid, and their nature of knowledge, vision, and insight is pure, clear, and luminous.
To those who are widely learned and possess strong memory, who have studied extensively, heard much, and possess broad knowledge;
to those who seek the Buddha-way, meaning those who resolve their minds to attain the path to Buddhahood—only for such persons as these may one preach.
When the capacity of the listener and the teaching meet, it is appropriate that one should preach.
If there are people who have previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas, who possess virtuous causes from past lives, who have encountered many buddhas,
planted various roots of goodness, made offerings, prostrated, and cultivated all manner of wholesome roots.
Their profound resolve is firm; they have generated the aspiration for enlightenment with far-reaching intent and steadfast vows.
To such persons as these, one may preach; for them, one preaches in a manner that accords with their capacity and is appropriate to their needs.
If a person is diligent, single-mindedly advancing toward the Buddha-way,
constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness, and always training their own mind through compassion and mercy;
if they do not begrudge their body or life, regarding life lightly and the Dharma as paramount, having no attachment or regret for their body, life, or wealth.
Only then may one preach for them; only when their faculties are such may one preach with them.
If a person is reverent, humble, respectful, and cautious, free from divergent thoughts, and with a mind devoid of distraction seeks the Buddha with single-minded resolve.
One who is free from all the foolish and ignorant, who has distanced himself from the many common,
deluded folk, and dwells alone in mountains and marshes— residing solitary within the empty forests and wetlands—
it is for such a person that one may preach; because one who detests clamor and gathers tranquility is a vessel for the Way, it is for them that one should preach.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who abandons evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends— where "associates" refers to those whose nature is diametrically opposed as being either good or evil—
and you see that one who has habitually practiced evil is called an evil associate, while seeing a virtuous person abandon such evil...
Such persons as these may be taught. For those whose minds delight in the good, teaching them is beneficial.
If one sees a son of the Buddha—by which is meant a bodhisattva of the right capacity—one should exclude the sons of the *śrāvakas* of the Lesser Vehicle.
Furthermore,
they maintain the precepts with purity. They firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts, which are clear, bright, and immaculate,
like a pure, lustrous pearl— just as a bright pearl is pure and free from any flaw or blemish.
One who seeks Mahāyāna sūtras, who aspires to the Vaipulya scriptures of the Buddha-vehicle—
such a person may be taught. One whose body and speech are pure and whose mind is vast may be taught.
If a person is free from anger, their mind is compassionate and devoid of resentment;
they are upright and supple, honest, straightforward, gentle, and mild.
They always take pity on all and constantly maintain a heart of compassion for all sentient beings.
They revere all Buddhas; they are able to show profound respect toward the World-Honored Ones.
To such persons as these, one may preach the Dharma. Because compassion, patience, and reverence are the conditions for receiving the Way, one should cause [the Dharma] to be preached to them.
Furthermore, there is a son of the Buddha who, as before,
in the midst of a great assembly and among the vast multitude of humans and devas,
preaches the Dharma for their benefit with a pure mind. This is called "the pure mind," which is free from all faults and far removed from impure states of mind.
Furthermore,
there are various causes and conditions, various virtuous causes, and various situational conditions;
there are parables and verbal expressions, as well as skillful words that employ analogies to guide sentient beings.
They preach the Dharma without impediment; they expound the True Dharma without any obstruction.
For such persons as these, one may preach. Their minds are clear regarding other teachings, and they well understand the meaning and flavor [of the Dharma];
for them, one may preach the sublime, for they will certainly be able to believe and accept it—therefore, it is appropriate to speak to them.
If there is a bhikṣu, a member of the renunciant Sangha,
who seeks the Dharma for the sake of omniscience and for the realization of the wisdom of universal emptiness and quiescence,
he searches in the four directions; in terms of actual practice, he travels toward the four cardinal regions to seek the Dharma of Nirvana.
The principle of the manifestation of dharmas consists of emptiness and existence, both together and the negation of both; these are called the four directions.
One should join the palms at the crown of the head to receive them, and with ten fingers joined, hold them upon the crown as a sacred trust.
They take pleasure only in upholding; they desire only to faithfully believe in, accept,
and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and the Vaipulya sūtras of the Great Bodhisattva Vehicle,
even to the point of not accepting a single verse from other sūtras, nor having faith in even a single verse within those other sūtras.

One may speak to such a person. For one who thus has faith and delight in the Great Teaching does not give rise to attachment toward the gateways of skillful means; therefore, it may be taught to them.
As for "a person with a sincere mind": suppose there is someone who gives rise to a most virtuous mind and seeks the *śarīra* of the Buddha.
The principle of quiescence (*śānti*) as expounded by the Great Teaching is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha;
it is like the marrow within the bones, which is called *śarīra* (here translated as "bone-body").
Thus one seeks the sutra; thus one seeks the Buddha’s wondrous sutra with a sincere heart.
Having obtained it, one receives it upon the crown of the head. When hearing the wondrous teaching, if one merely feels joy without deep faith, how could one be firm?
Only by having heard it and then receiving it with a profound mind—wearing it like a crown and receiving it with leaping joy—can one truly uphold it.
That person does not return; in that person’s mind, there is never again any further arising [of such thoughts].
They do not set their will upon seeking other sutras, nor do they resolve to seek other expedient teachings elsewhere.
Furthermore, they have never entertained such thoughts, nor have they ever once conceived them with a deviant mind.
The scriptures of the non-Buddhists— texts concerning killing, combat, marriage, and so forth, as well as the books of various non-Buddhists containing false views and false precepts—
it is for such people that one may preach [this teaching]. Such right view can be received and practiced by them, and they will not fall into error.
It can be explained only for those of the deluded yet perfect and sudden capacity.
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra: "From here below are eight phrases that conclude the brief demonstration; it can only be explained to such virtuous persons."
I have described these characteristics. If the Buddha were to explain these characteristics of attaining the Way in detail,
those who seek the Buddha-way— those who seek the unsurpassed way of the Buddha—
could not exhaust them even in an entire kalpa, nor could they reach their end even in a kalpa as vast as all the atoms of dust.
"Such persons as those mentioned above—these very individuals—will be able to believe and understand;
they will be able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding this sublime sūtra.
You should speak for them; you all should expound it for them in accordance with the Dharma."
The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma. This Lotus Sutra is the perfectly wondrous dharma of the mind.
Chapter Four, "On Faith and Understanding" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Previously, in the "Parable" chapter, the Buddha skillfully established three assemblies to lead them back to the single reality; this was for those of middle capacity regarding the teaching of the Dharma.

Those among them who had not yet attained awakening were enlightened to the principles of nature; having heard what the Buddha taught, the four great disciples gave rise to profound right faith in the path of the One Vehicle, and their wondrous understanding was fully revealed.
At that time, when the "Chapter on Similes" had been concluded, there was a preeminent disciple who sustained the Buddha’s life of wisdom named Subhūti—
this is translated as "Good Appearance" (Shanxian)— a venerable one who, at the time of his birth, manifested various auspicious signs and was thus named accordingly.
Mahākātyāyana means "Fan-String" (Śanreng) in this language.
Mahākāśyapa means "Drinker of Light" (Yinguang).
Mahāmaudgalyāyana means "Descendant of Maudgala" (Caishushi).
I have heard this from the Buddha; I have suddenly heard it from the presence of Śākyamuni.
This is an unprecedented teaching, a rare and marvelous dharma that the Buddha has never before disclosed during the forty-odd years since he attained enlightenment.
The World-Honored One bestowed upon Śāriputra the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Following the Discourse on the Dharma, at the beginning of the Chapter on Parables, he bestowed upon Śāriputra the prediction of becoming the Buddha Huaguang (Flower-Light).
They gave rise to a sense of rare wonder. Having heard in the "Expedient Means" chapter that the Buddha taught the Dharma such that these śrāvakas received predictions of enlightenment—
a thing never before known— and having further heard the parable of the burning house which elucidated the mind-ground, they exclaimed that it was truly marvelous.
He was filled with joy and exultation; his inner mind was joyful and his outward appearance was exultant.
He immediately rose from his seat, wishing to set forth before the Buddha what he had realized; thus, he raised his entire body and rose from his seat.
"Adjusting one's robes" means to arrange the three *kāṣāyas* to rectify one's outward demeanor.
"Baring the right shoulder" refers to the time of performing ritual actions; as the right hand finds greater convenience, baring the right shoulder signifies the appearance of one engaged in labor.
It is the ultimate expression of the disciple’s etiquette in serving the teacher.
Placing the right knee upon the ground, one unifies principle and phenomena within a single mind. Upon this single body, both left and right feet are present;
the left foot resting in space serves to manifest the emptiness of principle, while the right knee touching the ground symbolizes the reality of phenomena.
With single-mindedness, join the palms together; the unification of the two palms represents non-duality.
Bowing with reverence, the bending of the body signifies respect, and lowering the head expresses veneration.
Gazing up at the Honored Countenance—beholding and admiring the physical features of the World-Honored One—he addressed the Buddha with these words.
These eighteen phrases were narrated by Ānanda, the master of the compilation.
"We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha. Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "The World-Honored One regards us as the leaders within the assembly;
we are all advanced in years, our lives having reached a state of full decay and senility."
They claim for themselves that they have already attained nirvāṇa; they claim for themselves that they have already attained the quiescence of the Hīnayāna.
They lack any capacity for anything and are incapable of practicing the Mahāyāna path.
They no longer advance in their quest; they no longer have the resolve to progress upward in seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In the past, World-Honored One, when the Buddha himself had long been expounding the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā and had already taught the Mahāyāna Dharma for a great length of time,
I was then present in the assembly; at that time, I was beneath the Buddha’s seat.
The body is weary and lax; the physical form is scattered, exhausted, and indolent.

One merely contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). One thinks only of the three gates of liberation—emptiness, the true thusness of the Lesser Vehicle practitioners, non-self, the absence of the marks of persons, and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*)—which is wishless.
Regarding the bodhisattva-dharma— specifically the Mahāyāna bodhisattva-dharma—
they sport with supernormal powers; their minds roam through the dharma-nature with sovereign supernormal powers,
purifying buddha-fields and the eternally quiescent lands of the Tathāgatas.
To bring sentient beings to maturity and to purify the Buddha-land constitutes one's own cultivation; to bring sentient beings to maturity constitutes the deliverance of others.
"The mind does not find joy" means that there is no heart of aspiration or delight toward this Mahāyāna.
Why is this? What is the intention behind our lack of delight in the Great [Vehicle]?
Blessed One, you have directed us; Blessed One, in the past, you have only directed us.

They emerge from the three realms; they diligently seek emergence from the three tainted realms of desire, form, and formlessness, attaining the realization of nirvana—attaining the fruit of realization in the nirvana of partial emptiness.
Furthermore, we are now advanced in years; being old in age, we are unable to proceed toward the Great [Vehicle].
We are unable to turn toward the Buddhas' transformation of bodhisattvas, nor toward the Buddhas' teachings and instructions for the various bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they do not give rise to even a single thought of fond attachment, nor do they give rise to even a single thought of delighting in it.
We now, before the Buddha, at this assembly of the Lotus Sutra in the presence of the World-Honored One,
hear of the bestowal [of prophecy] upon the śrāvakas— specifically, we hear of the bestowal [of prophecy] upon Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the prediction of his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—the prediction of his attainment of Buddhahood—his heart was filled with great joy;
within his mind, he experienced profound and immense delight.
"It is unprecedented! Those who have now heard this have never experienced such a thing before.

We did not expect it today; we did not think that by mere chance at this present Dharma assembly, we would suddenly hear such a rare teaching. Because this wondrous Dharma is difficult to encounter, it is called 'rare.'"
I rejoice deeply within myself; from the depths of my heart, joy arises and I feel profound庆幸 (qìngxìng—gratitude/fortuitousness).

I have obtained great and wholesome benefit; I have gained the hearing of this great and wholesome benefit, which is like immeasurable precious jewels—namely, the names of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, such as the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the supernatural powers of the Way.
It is a rare treasure.
Not sought, it is obtained spontaneously; originally there was no intention to seek it, yet it is attained naturally.
World-Honored One, we who are now here—these of us śrāvakas present here now.
He delights in employing parables; he desires to cite illustrative examples to explain this meaning, thereby clarifying the sense that the śrāvakas lack the aspiration to seek great enlightenment.
It is as if there were a person in this world who,
being of tender age— still young from childhood—
abandoned his father and fled, leaving his father behind and departing for another place.
Dwelling long in another land is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who abandon the Great [Vehicle] and aspire to the Small, remaining in this defiled land of the five turbidities for ten,
twenty, or up to fifty years— ten representing the various devas, twenty representing humans, and fifty representing [the lifespan of] the *asura*s.
These are the five destinies.
Having grown old in years—meaning they have long been lost in delusion—their bodies have become large;
furthermore, being impoverished, their poverty and suffering increase all the more.
He roams the four quarters, using the four gates of the worldly truth as a metaphor for entering the Path;
he seeks clothing and food, seeking the Dharma through these four gates to adorn himself, just as that poor man begs for clothes to cover his body and begs for food to sustain his life.
Gradually wandering on, he gradually enters the Way like a pauper traveling;
encountering his way back to his native land, he is like discovering his original Buddha-nature; losing his hometown and returning from delusion to truth is like heading toward one's native land.
His father had arrived beforehand. "Father" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who extensively proclaimed [the teaching] with a great intention.
Seeking the son and not finding him is called "seeking and not obtaining," as he was unworthy due to his inferiority.
He stayed in an intermediate city. The Buddha spoke of two types of *nirvāṇa* in the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*), and also spoke of the Great *Nirvāṇa* in the Greater Teaching (*mahāyāna*).
He dwells between the two pillars of the Shared and the Realized Reward lands, like that elder who halted at the conjured city.
His household is immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures; the merit of the Buddha’s Pure Land is boundless, just as the wealth of that elder’s house was immeasurable.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, and pearls—these are the seven treasures. Lapis lazuli is produced from within stone;
coral is formed by the refined essence coalescing within the waters of the sea; amber is a transformation of *fuling* (tuberous fungus) a thousand years old;
crystal is of various colors and is also a type of jade; and "pearls" refers to *maṇi* jewels and red pearls.
If the jewel represents the Dharma, it is a metaphor for the seven treasures of Dharma.
As for the various granaries and storehouses: the grain such as rice and wheat accumulated in the granaries is a metaphor for the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) which sustains all virtues;
the wealth and silks accumulated in the storehouses are a metaphor for the practice of the six pāramitās within one's person.
All were overflowing, which is a metaphor for the treasury of the Buddha-dharma being filled with merit.
There were many servants, ministers, officials, and commoners; the class of young servants running in and out is a metaphor for the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*);

the ministers who provide assistance are a metaphor for the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*); the officials who manage records are a metaphor for the consciousness of discrimination (*vikalpa-vijñāna*); and the commoners performing service are a metaphor for the [five] sensory consciousnesses.
The analogy of the five sense organs represents the seven preparatory stages (saptaprayoga) as having the same essence as pure consciousness (*viśuddhavijñāna*).

The elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles— wherein elephants and horses replace the feet and the carriages proceed wherever directed with mastery— are metaphors for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Cattle and sheep are beyond counting. The merit and progress of those transformed into the three vehicles increase like the growth of cattle and sheep.

When the profits from these transactions reach other lands, it is called "outgoing breath" (出息). To give rise to the mind of cultivating goodness and extend its benefits to all is called "outgoing wealth" (出財);
to guide and benefit predecessors so that the merit of their transformation returns to oneself is called "incoming breath" (入息); and to spread horizontally across various lands is called "other" (他).
In this land, merchants and traveling traders are also extremely numerous. Those who travel are called "shang" (merchants), which is a metaphor for carrying out wholesome deeds;
those who sit remain are called "jia" (traders), which is a metaphor for maintaining stillness. Since their characteristics are not uniform, they are said to be numerous.

At that time, the impoverished son is a metaphor for one who has regressed from the Great Vehicle and remains on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); because he does not initiate transformative guidance and lacks merit, he is called an "impoverished son.
His wandering through various villages is a metaphor for traversing the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Passing through kingdoms and cities— traversing the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and experiencing the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) like a person traveling from town to kingdom—
he eventually arrived at the city where his father resided. Because his past roots of goodness had moved the Buddha to appear in the world, it is said that he "arrived."
The great city where the father resides.
The father constantly thinks of his son; the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings is like a father’s remembrance of his son.
Having been separated from his son for more than fifty years—from the stage of Buddhahood down to the five realms of ordinary beings—
The physical distance between us was over fifty positions apart,
yet I have never before spoken of such a matter to anyone. From the outset, I have never told the multitude that the śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna are the sons of the Buddha.
He merely reflects within himself; he constantly contemplates this solely with his own mind, harboring regret and resentment in his heart.
Thinking of his own decrepitude, he is like a Buddha who has appeared in the world and whose work of transformation is nearing its end.

Possessing abundant wealth and riches, he is enriched with the treasures of the Dharma—gold, silver, and precious gems—which are metaphors for the wisdom and merit of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
His granaries and treasuries overflow; by nature, his person is like a body that encompasses overflowing granaries and accumulated storehouses.
He has no offspring; though his household is wealthy, he lacks a son. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s abundant virtues yet still lacking a dharma-heir.

"In a single day, at the end of life" means that in the space of a single day, his karmic life-span perishes; this is a metaphor for the completion of the Buddha’s transformation, returning [to extinction] in a single day.
"True. When wealth and property are lost and there is no one to whom they can be entrusted, it is like the wealth of merit having no one to inherit it.
For this reason, one is earnest; for this reason, the mind becomes earnest."
Every time he remembered his son, he repeatedly called to mind the son he had lost;
he further formed this thought, and yet again gave rise to this thought:
"If only I could find my son; if only I could find the son who was born to me."
Entrusting the wealth: entrusting and consigning the wealth of the Dharma-treasure.
One becomes serene and joyful; with a mind that is level and even, one is naturally happy.
There is no further anxiety; there is no longer any more sorrowful reflection or deliberation.
World-Honored One, at that time, while the father was constantly thinking of his lost son, he prepared various means of employment and circulated [the news].
The impoverished son worked as a hired laborer for others, taking up various tasks and wandering through kingdoms and cities;
this is a metaphor for the disciples performing meritorious deeds and cultivating goodness, like servants receiving wages who travel everywhere in all directions.
He encountered his father’s house and arrived at the land where the Tathāgata dwells;
he stood by the side of the gate. Those of the Hīnayāna who are mired in the principle of biased emptiness fail to see the Middle Way, just like one standing by the side of the gate.

He saw his father from afar. Because the Buddha dwells in the realm of true retribution (*sambhoga-kāya*) while his father abides in the realm of partial emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they are separated by a vast distance; hence it is said he "saw him from afar.
He was seated upon a lion throne (*siṃhāsana*); "seated" refers to sitting firmly, as the Buddha sat upon a precious throne in the lion posture.
A precious footstool supports the feet; with manifold merit and wisdom as its causal basis, it is like a stool supporting the feet.
The various brāhmaṇas represent the "person," which is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings.
The kṣatriya householder—the kṣatriya of noble lineage being the royal caste—is a metaphor for the great bodhisattva;
the householder’s pure self-protection and abiding are a metaphor for the practitioner of the Brahma-faring life.
All paid homage and surrounded him. The fourfold assembly honored the Buddha just as those people had shown reverence to the elder.
With pearl necklaces—beads strung together like the adornment of the *dharmakāya* through merit and wisdom.
"Priceless" means of high value.
"Adorning the body" means adorning the Dharma-body with various merits.
"Officials, citizens, servants, and attendants" refers to skillful means and wisdom, which are like those officials and servants.
Holding white whisks in their hands—white symbolizing authority and purity—they brandish them as offerings;
they stand in attendance at the left and right, arrayed around the side to serve as attendants.
It is covered with a jeweled canopy; using jewels for the canopy to shelter its body symbolizes loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*).

Various flowered banners hang down; the splendor of the flowers represents the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), while the movement of the banners represents the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Sprinkle fragrant water upon the ground. Here, fragrance is used as a metaphor for virtue and water as a metaphor for wisdom; thus, through virtue and wisdom, one nurtures the fundamental principle of nature.
Scatter various famous flowers: these renowned flowers of myriad jewels represent the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
Precious objects are arrayed; the practice of the Dharma is distributed like an array of precious objects.
Bringing forth and bestowing, taking and giving—initiating teachings to benefit sentient beings is called "bringing forth";
withdrawing merit and returning it to oneself is called "receiving"; emulating the conduct of others is called "taking"; and extending oneself to others is called "giving."
There are various such ornaments as these. The names listed above refer to these various articles of adornment for persons.
Their majestic power is exceptionally sublime;
they possess a majesty that inspires awe and a virtue that commands reverence, and are thus uniquely honored.
The impoverished son seeing his father is a metaphor for a follower of the Hīnayāna seeing the *vairocana* (exalted) body.

It possesses great power and majesty; its virtues are such that it can subdue others, thus it is called "one of great power," and because all people stand in awe of it, it is called "one of great influence."
He was immediately seized with terror; having seen this, he felt fear and apprehension, regretting his arrival here.
He reproached himself for coming to this sublime place to behold the realm of actual retribution, his mind being ill at ease.
I privately formed this thought:
"This might be the King"—suspecting he was the Dharma-Buddha (the Buddha as the teaching);
"or it might be one equal to the King"—suspecting he was a Reward-Buddha (the Buddha as the fruition).
It is not that I employ labor; this is a metaphor for how the Land of True Reward naturally belongs to Bodhisattvas, whereas we of the Lesser Vehicle must apply effort.
Regarding the place where things are obtained: the view of those of the Lesser Vehicle—who admire the fruit and cultivate the cause—is like a hired laborer who first takes his wages.
The price is not as good as going to a poor neighborhood; it is not as good as going to a land of the poor and lowly. This is a metaphor for contemplating the partial emptiness of the Hīnayāna.
There is a ground upon which one may exert effort; there is a station where one may freely apply one's strength and advance.

Clothing and food are easily obtained: modesty serves as clothing, and the practice of the Dharma serves as food; because one practices in accordance with these supportive conditions, they are said to be easily obtained.
If one dwells here for a long time, or if the mind dwells for a long time fixed upon the true recompense (sambhoga-kāya), one may experience oppression.
This is because the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna does not permit attachment and provides no place of rest; thus it is called "oppression."
"Coercing me to act" means pressing and urging one until one believes;
having formed this thought, the impoverished son, having finished these secret reflections, fled quickly.
He advanced toward the gateway of the Mahāyāna, looking toward its further shore.
The wealthy elder represents the Buddha of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), who is honored for his merit and wisdom.
The lion throne represents the stage of the True Reward (sambhoga-bhūmi).
Upon seeing his son, he immediately recognizes him; likewise, upon first seeing the śrāvaka, he knows him to be a son of the Buddha.
His heart was filled with great joy. Seeing those with the capacity for deliverance, the Buddha’s heart rejoiced, and he immediately formed this thought:
"My wealth and storehouses—my own merit, the wealth of my wisdom, and the treasury of the Dharma."
"Now there is that which is to be entrusted. Now that I see this son, there is that which is to be committed to him.
I have constantly thought of this son; the Buddha, while at the stage of awakening, has constantly thought of the son to whom he would transmit the Dharma."
There is no means by which it can be seen; there is no cause or condition through which one may obtain a vision of it.
Yet, it comes spontaneously; it suddenly arrives from the Small Vehicle and gradually enters the Great Vehicle without being sought after—therefore, it is said to "come spontaneously."
This is most agreeable to my wishes; it perfectly accords with my long-held aspiration.
Although I am advanced in years—comparable to the Buddha in his later life—I still cherish [this teaching] with longing.
For over forty years, I have waited for the opportune moment, keeping it secret and not speaking of it; therefore, I say I "cherish" it.
"Pitying," he immediately dispatched an attendant; "attendant" refers here to a Great Bodhisattva. "Dispatched" means to employ them by way of the Mahāyāna designation.

He was pursued urgently to bring him back. "Yan" means a person of a quick temperament; "Jiao Yanming" (Teaching Name Pursuing) refers to the instruction given to pursue and cause him to be brought back to the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the messenger is a metaphor for a great bodhisattva acting on the Buddha's behalf.
He runs swiftly to seize him; this "swift running" refers to the application [of skillful means], and "seizing" refers to the gathering [of beings].
The impoverished son is struck with alarm; those of small capacity, upon hearing the Great [Teaching], are likewise startled and terrified.
He cried out in great lamentation, calling out loudly, "I am your enemy!
He shouted at the top of his voice, "I have not offended you; I originally had no intention of violating your great transformation.
Why have I been seized? For what reason do you suddenly arrest me?"

The messenger held him with increasing urgency. This illustrates how, within the *Avataṃsaka*, the great teaching for bodhisattvas involves a slow response from the sentient beings but an urgent response from the teaching itself.
He was forcibly dragged back; "forcibly dragging" refers to the great transforming the small, while "bringing back" refers to causing them to return to their original nature.
At that time, the impoverished son represents the capacity of those of the two vehicles within the Avataṃsaka assembly.
He thinks to himself that he is innocent; he thinks to himself that he has never transgressed against the Great [Vehicle].
Yet, he is imprisoned and seized. Being unable to hear the Great [Vehicle], hearing it produces distress, as if he were being confined and bound.
This body will certainly die. Because it is taught that by departing from signs there is no place for the mind to dwell and not even room to draw a breath, it is said to be a swift death.
He became increasingly terrified; he grew ever more restless, alarmed, and fearful.
He fainted and fell to the ground; he swooned, his breath ceased, and he collapsed upon the earth.
His father saw him from afar. Because the Buddha gazes upon the two vehicles from the perspective of true retribution, it is said that he "saw him from afar."
He spoke to the messenger, saying: "As for the turning of the mind toward its object, it is like instructing a messenger:

'There is no need for this person; do not bring him by force. Because he is seen to be one who cannot be transformed, it is said 'there is no need'; because he intends to enter the great sleep [nirvāṇa], it is said 'do not bring him by force.'"

Sprinkle cold water on the face to cause awakening. For the great sleep and the small sleep, guide them by means of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), like sprinkling water on the face to cause one to leave birth and death and realize the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*; this is called awakening.
Do not speak with him again; do not speak with him as if he were your superior. Why is this? What is the reason for it?
A father knows his son; the Buddha knows his śrāvakas.
Their aspirations are inferior; their intent lies in seeking the small, their minds are not lofty, and they dwell in base and lowly views.
They recognize themselves as noble and eminent, and the Buddha likewise recognizes them as being wealthy and honorable in merit, wisdom, and majesty.
It is difficult for the son; when the impoverished son’s wealthy father sees him, he is startled and suspicious, which constitutes the difficulty.
To "know with certainty that he is his son" means that the Buddha himself knows with certainty that he is his own Dharma-son.
Yet, by means of skillful means, because they were unable to bear the Great [Vehicle], he received them through skillful means;
he did not tell others, "This is my son," nor did he inform the rest of the assembly, "This śrāvaka is the Buddha’s son."
The messenger spoke to him. The messenger then explained the Buddha’s mind of skillful means:
"I now release you; let me rest from this great transformation as if casting you aside.
Go wherever you wish—whichever place your own mind desires to go."
The impoverished son rejoiced. Previously, he had feared the Great Teaching; now, seeing that the Buddha had ceased his grand display, he was filled with joy.
He attained what he had never experienced before, like one returning from death to life—something truly unprecedented.
Rising from the ground: formerly one lay prostrate in confusion, fearing the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); now having attained liberation, it is like rising from the ground.
Going to the quarters of the poor: turning one's back on the real and facing toward the provisional, one wanders through the principle of biased emptiness.
Seeking food and clothing is like seeking them for the sake of cultivating the Path and realizing cessation.

At that time, when the elder—that is, the Śrāvaka disciple—was about to withdraw from the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha’s intention was to entice his son back; it was his will to receive those of the Lesser [Vehicle] through skillful means.
He established skillful means; by means of the wisdom of skillful means, he established the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
He secretly dispatched two persons, secretly dispatching Bodhisattvas who manifested as those of the Two Vehicles.
Their forms and colors were haggard and they lacked majestic virtue; because they manifested inferior response-bodies with sunken faces and ash-grey heads, they are said to be "haggard."
He is haggard and does not manifest the marks and signs of a Buddha; because he appears identical to an ordinary person, he lacks majestic virtue.

You should go to him and speak gently to that impoverished son. Send a messenger to approach him and speak to him slowly using the teachings of the Hīnayāna, for this is different from the urgency of the past.
"If there is work to be done here, I shall pay you double wages. On this stage of the Śrāvaka, there is work to be done;
I shall pay you a price double [your current worth] and grant you the four fruits.
If the impoverished son agrees, bring him here to perform labor. If he is willing, bring him here and employ him as a servant."
[The father] acts. If [the son] asks, "What do you wish for me to do? or if the impoverished son says, "I now wish to hire myself out;
what work would you have me perform?", he may then say to him, "I employ you to remove dung," or he may tell him, "I now wish to hire you to sweep away the filth."
To realize the four fruits of the path is called "hiring," and to cause the severance of the afflictions of views and thought is called "removing filth.
We two shall likewise work together with you. The bodies manifested by Bodhisattvas as those of the Two Vehicles also jointly cultivate the practices of the Lesser Vehicle.
Then the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son. Having received their orders, they searched for the person to be transformed;
once they had found him, they fully reported the matter above. They provided this person with the means to present the details of the employment and the terms of service.
At that time, when the two messengers were instructing the impoverished son,
he first requested his wages; because his capacity was inferior, he first sought what he could obtain as labor pay.
He immediately began clearing away the filth; having received his wages, he then engaged in manual labor—this is a metaphor for those of the Hīnayāna who aspire to the fruit and cultivate the causes.
When the father saw his son, he felt pity and wonder; likewise, when the Buddha sees sentient beings abandon the Great [Vehicle] to take up the Small, he gives rise to compassion.
He felt pity for them and marveled at their strangeness.
Furthermore, on another day, from within his window, he thought: "The stage of the Dharma-body contemplates the days when the Deer Park taught the Lesser Vehicle;
the skillful means and knowledge-and-vision therein were not very vast, being like this window."
He saw his son from afar. Because the Buddha’s vision perceives ordinary forms from a great distance, he saw his son from afar.
He was emaciated and haggard; he was emaciated because he lacked the flavor of the Great Dharma, and he was haggard because he possessed no majestic power.
"Feces, soil, dust, and grime. "Feces, soil, and dust" is a metaphor for suffering, delusion, and karma obscuring the body; this is termed "grime.
"Filth, impurity, and uncleanness" is a metaphor for being entangled by hindrances.
He immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments of adornment. The necklaces and head-ornaments are metaphors for the Buddha’s merit and wisdom;
the fine garments that adorn the body are metaphors for the Buddha’s compassion and patience.

Furthermore, he dons coarse, tattered, and soiled garments, with dust and dirt covering his body; he discards his precious robes to wear these shabby ones, manifesting an inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
In his right hand he holds [an object], the right side symbolizing skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The "dust-removing vessel": the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles are called dust-removing vessels because they eliminate delusions and restrain evil;
their form suggests timidity, appearing as aged bhikṣus lacking in majestic adornment.
He addressed the laborers, informing the assembly of śrāvakas and those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle:
"All of you, work diligently and do not be indolent. You must apply yourselves with even greater vigor in these two vehicles."
By means of skillful expedients, he was able to approach his son. The Buddha, through the expedient of the inferior response of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), was able to receive the *śrāvakas*.
Later, once their faculties had been harmonized, he further addressed them, saying: [The text continues with the subsequent discourse].
"Hey, man! Hey!"—the exclamation "hey" is a vocal sound used to alert and awaken someone before one intends to address them:

"You should always do this; do not go elsewhere. This single word "this" refers to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while the instruction "do not go elsewhere" is a warning against following what is heterodox.
"I shall increase your wages. This is a metaphor for the successive advancement through the fruits of the śramaṇa.

Whatever is required—the requisites for practice, such as vessels, rice, flour, salt, and vinegar—the vessels used for storage are a metaphor for the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), while the rice and flour represent the sustenance [of that stage].
Hunger is a metaphor for precept and concentration; the seasoning of salt and vinegar is a metaphor for wisdom.

Do not harbor self-doubt or difficulty. This means that within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, all precepts, concentrations, wisdoms, liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are fully complete;
do not give rise to doubt or create difficulties regarding them.
There is also an old, decrepit servant. This "servant" refers to those who secretly harbor the two vehicles while appearing outwardly as such;
if you need one, I shall provide it to you. Whatever you require, I will surely give it to you.
"Be at ease with yourself; you shall naturally find peace of mind in this way.
I am like your father, for I have not yet personally pointed out that you are my son; thus, I say 'like a father. This is merely a provisional intention."
Do not worry further. Formerly, because you feared birth and death, you had much anxiety; now that you have something to rely upon, do not worry anymore. Why is this?
Because you have emerged from a state of anxious thought.

"I am old and great. In terms of appearance, because the Buddha possesses majestic virtue, he is called "old and great. In terms of principle, because the Buddha dwells in the ultimate fruit, he is named the "Old Great Man.
You, however, are young and vigorous; as you have newly entered the Way, your spiritual capacity is still immature, and thus you are called "young and vigorous."
"When you perform your regular duties— that is, during your ordinary tasks—
you are free from deception, indolence, anger, resentment, and complaints; you are without deceit, laziness, malice, regret, or words of grievance."
I do not see you possessing these various evils as other laborers do;
I do not see you at all possessing these various evils during ordinary times as worldly people who have not entered the Path possess their faults and evils.
"From this day forward, you shall be like a son born of my own body. Since the Buddha had already praised him to inspire joy, he further declared:
"From this day forward, you are indeed like a son born of my own body."
Immediately, the elder further gave him a name, calling him "son. He commanded those of the Two Vehicles to be called "sons of the Śrāvakas" and gave them names accordingly.
At that time, the impoverished son—when he was thus named—the impoverished son of the Śrāvakas.
Although they rejoiced at this encounter, and though they were indeed glad to have met him,

they still considered themselves capable of being born as lowly persons. Thus, although the Buddha spoke in this way, the śrāvakas still considered themselves to lack the capacity for bodhisattvas and persisted in their limited views.
For this reason, and for this cause, they did not yet trust one another.

For twenty years, he constantly had him remove excrement. Alternatively, the twenty years may be named after the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), which has one liberation and one non-obstruction, and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), which has nine liberations and nine non-obstructions;
or they may be named after the [abandonment of] views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa). Thus they are called "twenty years."
To cause one to wash away these faults is called "removing filth.

After this has been accomplished, the mental states come to accord with one another in essence; having severed the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), it is called "passing beyond the twenty minds," wherein the clear signs mutually correspond in essence and one attains understanding, faith, and acceptance.
Entering and emerging without difficulty—emerging from the realm of the śrāvakas and entering the vehicle of the bodhisattvas—there is no obstacle because of the presence of faith.
However, that which they dwell upon remains in its original place; yet, for those who are śrāvakas, although the mind that relies upon that place is joyful, [it does not transcend its state].
The "Great" [Vehicle] dwells as if in the Small Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One—because the elder was ill and knew he would not live much longer—manifested old age and sickness;
thus it is said he was "ill," and because the conditions for his retribution were about to end, it is said he would not remain "long."
He speaks to the impoverished son—that is, he addresses those of the Two Vehicles—saying:
"I now possess abundant gold, silver, and rare treasures, filling my storehouses to overflowing," as previously explained.
Regarding the quantity therein, it refers to the more than eighty instances [of teachings] within the *Prajñāpāramitā* where the Two Vehicles are empowered to become Bodhisattvas.
The categories of what should be taken and what should be given, you know them all; regarding those matters, you know all that should be taken and all that should be given.
"My mind is thus; you should embody this meaning. The Buddha says: 'This mind is fundamentally real in this way;
you should fully realize it and must not harbor doubt.
Why is this? For what reason do I command you not to harbor doubt?"
Now I and you are no different. Whatever I possess is now entrusted to your care; it is no different from my own.
You should apply yourself with diligence so that nothing is lost. You must take great care and attend to it closely, ensuring that nothing leaks away.
"Regarding the outflows and their cessation.
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instruction; when the great elder spoke these words, the destitute son immediately received his father’s command.

"To take charge of the various objects" means to take charge of and fully understand the many forms of Dharma-wealth, such as gold, silver, precious jewels, and all manner of treasuries; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom.
Yet, there is no intention to seek even a single meal, nor any hope or thought of receiving or accepting even a single meal;
this expresses the Mahāyāna state of being without a mind directed toward worldly aims.
However, that which they abide in remains in its original place. Since the basis upon which these śrāvakas rely still lies within the two vehicles, it is called their "original place.
Their inferior minds have likewise not yet been relinquished; though they hear the Great Teaching, they consider themselves small and are unable to abandon [that state].
After a short while had passed, having been refined by hearing the discourse on wondrous emptiness within the Prajñāpāramitā,
the father came to know his son's mind, just as a Buddha knows the minds of his disciples.
Gradually, they become open and unimpeded; gradually, their minds open up, becoming penetrating, peaceful, and secure.
They achieve great resolve and should give rise to the Great Mind, looking with self-disdain upon their former state.
They realize for themselves the base and lowly nature of their previous mind that clung to the Lesser Vehicle at the Deer Park.
When he was about to pass away— that is, when he was about to manifest his final extinction after the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings and was preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—
he summoned his son, called together the sons of the śrāvakas,
and assembled his kinsmen; these were the assembly of bodhisattvas who constitute his inner retinue.
The king and his ministers: in other lands, they manifest as kings; those who have attained awakening are called bodhisattvas and serve as ministers.
The kṣatriyas and householders: the kṣatriya great clans are the lineage of the Buddhas, while those who practice the Dharma are called householders.

They have all assembled. At this assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, where all capacities for awakening are gathered, he himself proclaims, as the Buddha did in the "Expedient Means" chapter when he addressed the multitude: [as stated in the sūtra].
"Venerable sirs, you should know. This address "Venerable sirs, you should know" is intended for the aforementioned great assembly.
"This is my son" means that this śrāvaka is a son of the Buddha.
Regarding my birth: during the time of the Great Penetration, I received transformation from the Buddha and gave rise to the Great Mind.
Yet, in such-and-such a city, within the Land of True Reward, you abandoned me and fled;
having forsaken the Buddha’s Great Teaching, you escaped into the Lesser Vehicle.
Lingering in hardship and suffering; wandering aimlessly and enduring destitution for over fifty years.
From the Buddha’s realm down to the common world, one dwells within the five paths of existence, separated by a distance of more than fifty stations.
His original name was so-and-so. Originally, he possessed the karmic capacity for this great Bodhisattva vehicle.
My name is So-and-so; I am now preaching the Perfect Teaching in my Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Formerly, I resided in the Original City; formerly, I dwelt in the Land of True Reward (*niṣyandaphala-bhūmi*).

Bearing this anxiety, he searched for [the truth]. Hearing of the Great [Vehicle], he did not believe it, which was why he harbored such anxiety. He sought out the original causes from the past, employing skillful means to guide him. Suddenly, amidst these very circumstances, within the gradual gates of the teachings of skillful means— [The text continues: ...he attained the stage of non-retrogression. Having already entered the path of the Bodhisattva, he was able to receive the prediction of future Buddhahood. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly: "If there are those who hear this Dharma and do not give rise to doubt, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. The Buddha further said: "If there are those who hear this Dharma and do not give rise to doubt, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable; it is not something that can be measured by the wisdom of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. It is only through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that he reveals this profound Dharma. Therefore, you should all believe and accept it. The Buddha then spoke a verse: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable; It cannot be fathomed by any in the world. Only through the power of skillful means Does he reveal this profound Dharma. Those who hear this and do not doubt Shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly: "If there are those who hear this Dharma and do not give rise to doubt, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable; it is not something that can be measured by the wisdom of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly: "If there are those who hear this Dharma and do not give rise to doubt, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable; it is not something that can be measured by the wisdom of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. It is only through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that he reveals this profound Dharma. Therefore, you should all believe and accept it. The Buddha then spoke a
They meet and find one another: the son comes and meets the father, and the father finds the son.
"This is truly my son"—these śrāvakas are truly the sons of the Buddha, and I am truly their father;
the Buddha-body is truly the father of the śrāvakas.
"Whatever I now possess— whatever exists within the body of the present Buddha—
all material wealth, immeasurable wisdom, and the Dharma-treasury of merit are yours; they are all that the śrāvakas themselves possess."
What was previously brought in and sent out—the management of income and expenditure of property—is what this son knows;
it is what the sons of the śrāvakas already know.
At that time, the World-Honored One was like the impoverished son, and the sons of the śrāvakas were like those to whom the wealth was entrusted.
Hearing these words from his father and hearing this voice of entrustment from the Buddha, he was immediately filled with great joy;
at that very moment, his heart rejoiced greatly, having attained what he had never experienced before.
From the past until now, he had never heard it said that a śrāvaka could attain Buddhahood.
And they form this thought; within their minds, they think to themselves:
"I originally had no mind. In the Great Teaching, I was originally without a mind.
Yet I have something to seek, something to hope for—seeking the fruit of Buddhahood."
Now this treasure store has arrived spontaneously. This wondrous vehicle, an invaluable treasure store, was opened and revealed by the Buddha himself, who said it had arrived spontaneously.
The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata. What was previously explained through parable is now applied to the Dharma.
"We are all like the sons of the Buddha. Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas are the true sons of the Buddha, while Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna are called "semblance sons.
The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons; yet the Mahāyāna teachings state that the Buddha regards all sentient beings as if they were one and the same.
"O Sons, we [speak] because of the three kinds of suffering. This phrase precisely reveals the cause for regressing from the Great Vehicle. Regarding the "three kinds of suffering":

to experience various sufferings upon a body that is itself suffering is called *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of suffering); to gradually wither and decay is called *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change).
The continuous flux of suffering karma is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Within the cycle of birth and death, within the ocean of birth and death in the three realms,
one undergoes various fevers and afflictions, and undergoes the heat-pressing sufferings and afflictions of a burning house.
Deluded and ignorant; because their minds are bewildered, they are confused by worldly phenomena and lack understanding of the unsurpassed path.
They take pleasure in and are attached to minor dharmas—the teachings of the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas—and out of weariness with old age, sickness, and death, they seek nirvāṇa.
“Venerable One, today at this Dharma assembly, our Buddha, the World-Honored One,
has caused us to reflect: that the Buddha, in the Deer Park, taught the vehicle of skillful means, thereby causing us to give rise to hearing regarding the gradual teaching.”
Contemplation and cultivation serve to eliminate the filth of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena. All the various dogmatic views held by the world are termed conceptual proliferation;
they are to be completely cleared away just as one would remove filthy excrement.

We have applied ourselves with diligent effort therein; within the Buddha’s teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, we have exerted ourselves through minor hardships and asceticism to advance toward the holy life (*brahmacarya*), obtaining the price of a single day’s labor upon reaching *nirvāṇa*.
We have sought the fruit by practicing the cause, attaining quiescence like a hired laborer.
A person receives a day’s wage;
having received this, and having attained the four fruits of the Hīnayāna,

their mind is filled with great joy and they consider themselves sufficient, for they have originally aimed to realize the small fulfillment of their aspirations, and thus their hearts are greatly [satisfied].
Delighting in minor gains, they consider themselves sufficient.
They then say to themselves, and such thoughts arise in their minds:
"Because of my diligent application within the Buddha-dharma, what I have attained is vast and abundant. [They speak thus] regarding the Buddha’s skillful means of the Hīnayāna.
