Although much is gained through diligent cultivation of effort, the World-Honored One already knew us beforehand. Indeed, our Buddha already knew our assembly when he was first at the Deer Park.
Their minds were attached to base desires; their minds were attached to the coarse and inferior five sensual pleasures of the world.
They delighted in the Lesser Dharma and delighted in the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus, the Buddha perceived their disposition and allowed them to practice the Lesser while setting aside the Great Transformation.
I do not differentiate by saying that you shall possess it, nor do I differentiate by teaching that we,
the śrāvakas, inherently possess our share of the Tathāgata’s treasury of knowledge and vision— the jewel of the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom and merit.
This is the portion of the treasury of the sublime Dharma.
By the power of skillful means, the World-Honored One has spoken of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

Out of compassion for us, the World-Honored One, through the power of various provisional gateways and skillful means, has taught by way of provisional names the profound wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

"We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day's wages for attaining nirvāṇa, which we consider a great gain. Having heard from the Buddha how to cultivate it, we have attained a minor nirvāṇa;
we are like those laborers who, having received the wages for a single day's work, consider themselves sufficiently satisfied."
They have no aspiration for this Mahāyāna; they have no vow or desire to seek progress and cultivation in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—this clarifies that at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha himself [relied upon] his own wisdom.
It is called the "cause" because the power of wisdom and spiritual authority was bestowed upon Subhūti and Śāriputra.
To reveal and expound for the sake of the bodhisattvas means that the Great Prajñāpāramitā is taught for the assembly of bodhisattvas;
this is termed "entrusting the lower to instruct the high," with the intent of supporting those below.

Yet they themselves have no aspiration for this; they consider themselves inferior, lacking the faculties of a bodhisattva, and thus have no aspiration or seeking for this Mahāyāna. Why is this so? What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha knows that our hearts delight in the lesser Dharma; because he knows our aspirations are inferior, we take pleasure in and cling to the lesser Dharma.
By the power of skillful means, he teaches us according to our capacities; by the power of wisdom and skillful instruction, he accords with us.
He preached according to our capacities,
yet we did not realize that we were truly the sons of the Buddha. We thought ourselves to be of inferior capacity and were unable to know that,
from the perspective of our original cause in the past, we were indeed the sons of the Buddha.
Now we finally know the World-Honored One; today we have only now come to know the Buddha.
Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, there is nothing he begrudges; regarding the unsurpassed wisdom realized by the Tathāgata, it is not something he holds back out of stinginess.
Why is this? It is because we wish to clarify for what reason the Tathāgata has no stinginess.
As before, we have from of old truly been the sons of the Buddha.
Yet they take pleasure only in the lesser Dharma; being of inferior wisdom, they delight only in the Hīnayāna.
If we possessed a mind that delights in the Great [Vehicle], if we possessed a heart that loves and rejoices in the Mahāyāna—
The Buddha then preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for me; the Buddha, with deep compassion, immediately preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for us.
Within this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle; within this wondrous Lotus Sutra, he expounds only this.
He preached the Buddha-way of the One Vehicle.
Yet, in the past, before the bodhisattvas, he disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in the inferior Dharma;
and in the assemblies of the Vaipulya sūtras of former times, in the presence of the great assembly of bodhisattvas, he censured the śrāvakas who were attached to the inferior Dharma.
It would be like burning seeds.
Yet, in reality, the Buddha teaches and transforms beings through the Mahāyāna. Thus, it is true that the Tathāgata, by means of the Mahāyāna, transforms only bodhisattvas.
Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind that harbored any aspiration. For this reason, we ourselves declare that originally there was no great resolve seeking the Buddha-dharma.

Now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously. Today, within this assembly, the unsurpassed great treasure of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, has come of its own accord without being sought.
All that a son of the Buddha ought to attain has already been attained; it is the very dharma that all Bodhisattvas should obtain.
"I have now attained them all.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse. Because he had already explained it in prose and now recites it again in verse, it is called "re-stating."
We, the śrāvakas, today at this Vulture Peak, have heard the Buddha’s voice and teaching;
we have heard the Buddha’s Dharma discourse, which employs skillful means, reveals the ultimate truth, and utilizes parables and verbal expressions.
They were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; their hearts were greatly delighted and their bodies thrilled with exultation.
They attained what they had never before attained and heard what they had never before heard:
that the Buddha has declared that śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood. Hitherto, it was only said that śrāvakas realize the Lesser Vehicle; today, suddenly—
Nevertheless, it is permitted that one may become a Buddha;

this supreme collection of jewels is obtained without seeking. This accumulation of the treasury of the supreme Dharma-jewel was not originally something I hoped for or sought, yet through the Buddha’s compassion, it has been revealed to me of its own accord.
For example, it is like a young child who is immature and lacks discernment; because he is of tender years, he has no power of discrimination.

He abandons his father and flees, traveling far away to another land. Previously, the Teacher [the Buddha] originally studied the Mahāyāna for the sake of wisdom, yet [this person] was inferior in intelligence.

Therefore, he abandoned the Great [Vehicle] to practice the Small [Vehicle], like a child who leaves his father and flees to another land; because the Great and Small are thus separated, it is said he "went far away.
He wandered through various kingdoms for over fifty years; because he circled through the five destinies, it is said he "wandered about."

His father, filled with anxiety, searched for him in all directions. The Master, mindful of his disciple as a father is of his child, sought him through skillful means throughout the four realms of birth.

Having grown weary from his search, he stopped at a certain city; though he sought the one with the capacity for the Mahāyāna, that person would not accept his teaching, and the Master was already exhausted.
Having rested from his weariness, he halted at a city along the way and established skillful means for transformation.

He constructed dwellings where he might enjoy himself through the five desires; yet, taking meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as the city and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) as the dwelling—because the fivefold meritorious virtues are a source of sublime joy—he dwelt securely within them to amuse himself. Since these were merely provisional constructs for the sake of those with spiritual capacities, it is said that he "constructed" them.
It stands;
its household is immensely wealthy with much gold and silver, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s abundance of various treasures of Dharma.
With carnelian, agate, pearls, and lapis lazuli, it is a metaphor for his various wisdoms and immeasurable merits.

Elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; litters, carriages, and vehicles—these four kinds of running beasts that draw the carts are used as a metaphor for the four kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
These four kinds of carriages and litters, which are what is mounted upon, are used as a metaphor for the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).
The vast fields, the numerous servants, and the many people represent the path of practice; the cultivation of the fields and the management of affairs are analogous to the path of cultivation;
the servants and attendants are analogous to the seven consciousnesses; and the planting and tending of the people are analogous to the five faculties.
The profit from the capital outflow and inflow extends throughout other lands. By means of the Dharma, one shows this to others, which is like the outflow of wealth;

yet the merit of transformation returns to oneself, which is like the inflow of profit. Because this occurs throughout the three lands—the land of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*), the land of true reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*), and the land of co-residence (*sahabhūmi*)—it is called "other lands."

Merchants and traders are found everywhere; "travelling merchants and seated traders" is a metaphor for the two kinds of virtuous causes—the concentrated and the dispersed—indicating that there is not a single place where wholesome dharmas do not exist.

Surrounded and revered by thousands of millions of beings—just as the fourfold assembly, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings all revere the Buddha—he is constantly cherished and remembered by kings.
The king represents the Buddhas; that which they preach is the meaning of the Middle Way, which is called the Dharma.
A king such as this is constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas;

his ministers and noble clansmen all revere him together. Here, the ministers represent the various bodhisattvas, and the noble clansmen represent the bodhisattvas of transformation who appear in all directions; this entire great assembly thus honors the Buddha.

Because of various conditions, many come and go. Due to the causal conditions for performing transformative deeds, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas constantly come and go with such great frequency.
A wealthy man of such great power and influence—noble, affluent, and possessing such characteristics—is so mighty that his authority overawes all quarters;
yet, as he grows old, his anxiety for his son increases.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha, who, being advanced in years and approaching the end of his life’s work, feels an ever-increasing concern.
He reflects upon his son:
"Night and day I think only that the time of my death is approaching; early and late I contemplate that my worldly affairs are about to conclude.
My foolish son has abandoned me for over fifty years; since that foolish and ignorant young son left me, more than fifty years have passed."

It is further illustrated by this analogy: if one dwells in the five realms of existence, separated from the Buddha-ground by more than fifty stages, what should one do with the various goods stored in one's treasury?
How should I regard my vast Mahāyāna treasury and its many precious stores, seeing that their heir has not yet appeared? What indeed shall I do?
At that time, the impoverished son— referring to the son who was destitute and exposed when the great elder thought thus—
and his seeking of food and clothing, is a metaphor for practicing various ascetic disciplines throughout all sensory realms.
From village to village, from kingdom to kingdom; from the five aggregates up to the six sense bases, from the twelve bases to the eighteen elements.
There may be something attained, or attachment to tainted wholesome states.
Alternatively, there are those who attain nothing and abide in the emptiness of annihilation (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
Because they are hungry for the Great Dharma and have lost its benefit, they are said to be "starving.
Because they do not cultivate merit, they are said to be "emaciated. Because their Dharma-body is inferior and weak, and its functional power is insufficient, they are subject to many faults.

Afflicted by the arising of sores and scabs, he gradually traveled on until he reached the city where his father resided. Wandering slowly through the spheres of the senses (āyatana), he eventually encountered the results of his past roots of goodness;
this place is called "Reaching the City Where His Father Resides."

Through successive rounds of hired labor, he eventually arrives at his father’s house; through the progressive advancement of his employment and wages, he reaches a place where he may receive the path of humans and devas—this is called arriving at his father’s house.
At that time, within the gate of the elder's residence— within the gateway of the Mahāyāna mansion in the house of the Tathāgata, the Elder,
where these śrāvakas had arrived in the land of his transformation— the Elder [spoke].

The great jeweled canopy represents the place where the lion throne is situated; the great jeweled screens represent the adornments of the Buddha, while the lion throne represents the emptiness of all phenomena.
Surrounded by his retinue, the Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body is like the moon enveloped by clouds.
The various attendants—namely the ministers, subordinates, servants, and the common people—some calculate gold, silver, and precious objects.
The sixth consciousness is that which performs the calculation and acts as the person who calculates;
wisdom and merit are what is calculated, namely the gold, silver, and so forth.

The recording of the issuing and receiving of property and assets. As previously compared and matched, the issuing and receiving of property and assets refers to the seventh *manas* consciousness transmitting [cognition].
"Property" (*cai*) refers to meritorious practice; "assets" (*chan*) refers to the station of the Dharma (*dharmapada*).

Abiding within the station of the Dharma and cultivating all pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is like managing property. The *Shuji* (Commentary) states that this should be understood as discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The "Record of the Contractual Deed" (*Shiqiquanwen shu*) refers to the scriptural teachings.
Just as a poor son perceives his father as wealthy, noble, and dignified, those of limited capacity perceive the Buddha as majestic, exalted, honorable,
and awe-inspiring.
This refers to a king or those like a king who, harboring doubts regarding the Buddha's deeds as they involve two paths, reflect that this king is the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha),
or that because his royal status and appearance are equal [to those of the Buddha], he is a metaphor for the Reward-body Buddha (saṃbhogakāya-buddha).
Startled and terrified, he wondered to himself why he had come to this place. He was seized with fear, thinking that such a realm as this was not a destination for him;
his heart was filled with self-reproach as he marveled at what karmic conditions had led him here.
He then thought to himself: "If I remain here for long, he will secretly form the intention that I stay in this superior place even longer;
perhaps he will see fit to coerce me into forced labor, or he may fear that I will be commanded to practice the Mahāyāna path where both vehicle and precepts are integrated."
Urgently pressed by me and driven with great force to advance further,
having reflected thus, the impoverished son fled in haste. Having thought this, the impoverished son ran away quickly.
He inquired of those nearby, intending to go to a poor neighborhood to work for hire.

"Inquiring of those nearby" is a metaphor for fearing the Mahāyāna and seeking with joy the Lesser Dharma, aiming for a partial emptiness. "Intending to go" refers to yearning for the fruit; "working for hire" refers to practicing the causes.
At that time, the elder was upon a lion throne, while the Buddha sat upon the seat of true recompense and the emptiness of dharmas.
From afar he beheld his son and silently recognized him. Because he looked upon the holy from the perspective of the mundane, it is said that he "beheld him from afar";
having seen him once, he immediately knew him to be his own son, yet because he did not speak of it to others, it is called "silent recognition."
He immediately commanded a messenger to pursue and seize him, bringing him back. He then commanded the Bodhisattva to act as his envoy to track him down, capture him, and bring him forward.

The impoverished son was startled and cried out; overwhelmed with confusion, he fell to the ground. This is because when the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate is revealed, its heights are so sublime that those of the Two Vehicles cannot hear it.
He describes his heart as being struck with such alarm and confusion that he is at a loss for what to do, like a person who has become dazed and tumbles to the ground.
This man seizes me, thinking, "I shall certainly be killed"; this bodhisattva seizes me, leaving me no room to set my mind at ease, certain that I shall be put to death.

"What use have you for clothing and food that you have brought me to this state? How could it be for the sake of providing clothing and food that you have caused my body to reach such a state of desperation?
The elder knew his son was foolish, ignorant, and narrow-minded; the Buddha knew that the disciple’s faculties were dull and weak, and that he was deluded and limited in his perspective.
Being narrow-minded, inferior, and weak, they are unable to prevail;
not believing my words is to disbelieve this father. Not following the Buddha’s teaching is called "disbelieving his words," and not knowing him as the Teacher is called "disbelieving the father."

He immediately employed skillful means to dispatch other people; that is, he concealed his true teaching and deployed the wisdom of skillful means to send forth those of the Two Vehicles to provide guidance and support.

Those who were blind, short-statured, and lacking in majestic virtue were seen nearby—those of inferior form were called "short and stunted," while those whose presence was hidden were called "blind."
"The various marks and signs are called 'ugliness'; manifesting these marks is called 'lack of majesty.
You may speak to him. You see that he is of limited capacity; you may speak to him."
"I shall hire you to remove all filth and impurities. To be hired by me means to attain the Lesser Fruit; to remove filth and impurities means to destroy delusions and karma.
I shall pay you double wages. From the First Fruit up to the Fourth Fruit, according to the merit of your realization and entry, the rewards shall increase twofold at each stage.
Because it was superior, he said, "I shall double your wages.

When the impoverished son heard this, he followed along with joy; because those of inferior capacity find delight in hearing the Small [Vehicle], which accords with their original inclinations, they follow along with joyful hearts.

To remove filth and purify the various rooms: destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts is called "removing filth," while cultivating the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) is called "purifying the rooms.
Just as the elder constantly sees his son through the window, a "window" (*yǒu*) refers to a slit in a wall and is not the main gate.
Furthermore, by means of the wisdom of skillful means, he constantly beholds his son;
mindful that the son is foolish and inferior, delighting in base matters, he probes for the Dharma-body and takes pity on this son who is deluded, narrow-minded, and inferior,
wishing to prevent him from performing menial tasks.

Thereupon, the elder—the Tathāgata—donned worn and soiled garments, took up a refuse-basket, and went to where his son was. The elder’s coarse, worn, and greasy clothing manifested the appearance of one who has responded to inferior capacities;
his taking up of the refuse-basket was precisely the grasping of the means for destroying delusions within the Hīnayāna Piṭaka.

The Teacher then went to the place where his son was stationed and, employing skillful means, approached him and spoke to encourage him to work diligently. By these means, drawing near and speaking with humble compliance, he said to him:
"You should apply yourself with diligence to the practice of the Dharma."
Since I have increased your wages and provided oil for anointing your feet—having thus augmented your labor compensation—it is sufficient that you apply this oil to your cracked and chapped feet.
This serves as a metaphor for the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): the cracks represent the locus of illness, while the oil represents the water of principle, which serves to moisten it.

"Abundant food and drink, and thick, warm bedding. Food and drink are metaphors for the lack of deficiency in what is required for precepts and meditative concentration; thus they are called "abundant.
Bedding and mats are metaphors for the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni), which can be relied upon as a support; thus they are called "thick and warm."
"You should diligently practice" with such words of admonition; one should urge them toward diligent cultivation using such piercing and urgent speech.
Furthermore, one should comfort and console them with gentle words, as if they were "like my own son.
This means that because a śrāvaka is like a bodhisattva who is a son born of one's own kin, he is referred to as being "like" [a son].
The elder possesses wisdom; the Tathāgata, as an elder, possesses manifold skillful means and wisdom.

He gradually causes [the disciple] to enter and exit household affairs for twenty years, training them step by step—from the coarse to the subtle, from dwelling in the Hīnayāna to perceiving the sublime marks (vairocana-kāya), and further hearing the names of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā for twenty years.
The Buddha’s power is bestowed upon them, causing them to act as bodhisattvas and expound the Mahāyāna teachings of Prajñā;
this is called "performing the work of the Buddha's household.
To them are shown the various treasures of the Dharma, such as gold, pearls, and crystal, as well as all manner of storehouses.
All the goods entering and exiting must be made known; likewise, the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis that enter and exit must all be made known.
This is like staying overnight in a grass hut outside the gate; one who has not yet entered the Mahāyāna is said to dwell outside the gate, abiding in the Hīnayāna.
The place was named Sokso Hermitage.

He thought to himself, "I am poor; I have no such things. He further reflected, "In this poor village, the matters of the Lesser Vehicle are common, but the wealth of the teachings of the Great Dharma is not something I possess."
The father, knowing his son’s intention had gradually become expansive, desired to bestow wealth upon him;

likewise, the Buddha, knowing that the śrāvakas have heard the Prajñāpāramitā, gradually opens their minds to the vast expanse of emptiness, intending to entrust them with the Dharma-wealth of wisdom.
He immediately gathered his kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders. He wished at once to have the multitude serve as witnesses;
those who were his kinsmen were the great bodhisattvas whom he had previously transformed and guided; the kings were emanations of the Buddhas;
the ministers were bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment (samyaksambuddha); and the kṣatriyas were the sons of the Buddhas.
The lay practitioner of the four preparatory practices who dwells in leisure is one who has attained tranquility;
among this great assembly, he is declared to be "my son. Within this great assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, it is said that even those of the Hīnayāna are sons of the Buddha.
Having abandoned me to practice elsewhere for fifty years, he left the Great Vehicle to enter the Small Vehicle, separated from me by the five destinies.

It has been twenty years since I saw my son return; although the father saw his son and had him taught the Small Dharma so that he might sever the views and afflictions, even after being commanded to teach others in turn, he still dwells in a grass hut—this is what is called "twenty years."
"Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son. Long ago, in the City of True Reward, I lost my son.

Wandering everywhere in search of him, I have come to this place. Having wandered through the five realms of existence seeking my son, I have finally arrived here at this city of transformation midway along the road."
All my dwellings, my people, and all things belonging to my person— my residences and even my followers—
I have now entrusted entirely to you, to be used as you see fit.
This is the transmission of the family lineage and the entrustment of the task, so that the lamp may continue to be lit and the Dharma may endure.
Cai freely expounded and disseminated [the teachings].

The son reflected that in the past he was poor and his aspirations were base; the followers of the Lesser Vehicle reflect that in the past they cultivated emptiness, yet their vows were inferior as they sought only the four fruits of arhatship.

Now, from my father, I have obtained a great and true treasure. Now, from the Buddha, having heard the sublime Dharma and received the prediction of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), it is as if I have obtained a great treasure, along with houses and all manner of wealth.
Here, the house is a metaphor for the principle, which is the locus of reliance; the wealth is a metaphor for... [the fruits].
This matter is that which is to be enjoyed;

he was filled with immense joy at having attained what he had never before experienced. In his heart, he felt great jubilation at having received the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood, something he had never received before.
The Buddha is also like this. This corresponds to the analogy of the elder:
knowing that we delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, he never said, "You shall become Buddhas. Knowing that our minds delighted in the Lesser Dharma, he never revealed, "You shall become Buddhas."
Yet you say that we have attained all the outflows-free states; you say that we have attained the dharmas of outflows-free wisdom and liberation;

you claim we have accomplished the status of a disciple of the Hīnayāna Śrāvaka vehicle and achieved the fruit of Arhatship according to the Lesser Teaching—this is merely a matter of name and reputation.
Regarding the disciples who have heard the skillful means:

the Buddha has commanded us to expound the supreme path; and regarding the sons of the Śrāvakas, the Buddha, within the Prajñāpāramitā, has commanded them to teach the unsurpassed Dharma to all Bodhisattvas.
Those who cultivate this shall attain Buddhahood. Those practitioners of this Mahāyāna who cultivate it shall achieve the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
I, receiving the Buddha’s teaching, am a great Bodhisattva; I, receiving the Buddha’s command, serve as a great-rooted Bodhisattva for the sake of those with keen faculties and benefit.
Sā. By means of various causes and conditions and diverse parables— such as the Tathāgata’s eighty-one categories of correct causes and virtuous conditions,
and various similes such as those of dreams and illusions— he [taught].
Various words are spoken regarding the unsurpassed path. "Various" refers to the approximate number of teachings on the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.
These sons of the Buddha—referring to the great bodhisattvas who are called "sons of the Buddha"—have heard the Dharma from me; they are distinguished from the śrāvakas.

When a person hears the Great Dharma, they contemplate it day and night, practicing with diligent effort. Without weariness, they contemplate and cultivate according to the principle throughout the day and night.
At that time, all Buddhas bestow upon them a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). During such a period, all Buddhas, with one voice, grant them the seal of approval (*mudrā*).
He bestowed upon him the prophecy of enlightenment:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha. In immeasurable ages to come, having perfected the bodhisattva path, you shall attain buddhahood."
The secret treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas; the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
It is expounded solely for Bodhisattvas to reveal its actual reality; it is expounded exclusively for those with the capacity of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas to reveal its subtleties.
Though the matters are wondrous and according to reality,
you have not spoken this essential truth for my sake; you have not imparted to me this true and most vital path.
Just as that impoverished son came into the presence of his father— the son representing the śrāvaka and the father representing the Tathāgata—
though he was aware of all the goods, his mind had no desire to take them; though he was aware of the Dharma-treasure, he considered it not his own and had no aspiration for it.
Although we speak of the jewel-treasury of the Buddha-dharma, we ourselves likewise lack any aspiration for it; this corresponds to the preceding metaphor.
We consider our own internal extinction to be sufficient; with the cessation of the inner mind, we claim that what has been attained is complete.
It is sufficient.
One understands only this matter and no other; one understands only the matter of attaining nirvana through [the understanding of] birth and death, and there are no further external Mahāyāna matters.
If we were to hear [this], yet our resolve were inferior,
and if we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings— where "purifying Buddha-lands" refers to the practice of self-benefit by eliminating all delusions and karma—

while "teaching and guiding" refers to the practice of benefiting others by initiating various forms of conversion and gathering in sentient beings; such a person who seeks the higher while transforming those below is a Bodhisattva.
They have no joy whatsoever in their karma; they fear birth and death and urgently seek only their own deliverance, finding no delight at all in the gateway of compassion and wisdom.
Why is this? What is the intention of those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle and do not seek the Great Benefit?
All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; within the Mahāyāna, one perceives that the characteristics and natures of all worldly and supramundane phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent.
There is neither arising nor ceasing. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally quiescent; since it has no point of origin from which it comes, it does not arise.
Since that which arises must cease, and its fundamental nature is originally without arising, it does not cease.

There is neither great nor small. Within the provisional teachings where the Great and Small Vehicles are distinguished, and within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, that which is coarse is entirely the subtle;
outside of the Great there is no Small, and the Small is itself the Great—there is only a single, perfect fusion, with neither great nor small.
It is untainted and unconditioned; because its nature is emptiness, it is primordially pure, without leakage and without conditioned activity.
One should contemplate in this way, contemplating with right mindfulness through such sublime understanding.
They did not give rise to joy or delight; from the very beginning, they never once conceived a single thought of fondness for it.
"We have wandered through the long night; we have been lost in delusion for as long as the darkness of night, knowing only how to delight in the small, fearing suffering, and seeking emptiness."
Regarding the wisdom of the Buddha, regarding the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha, World-Honored One,

they are without craving and without attachment. While "craving" refers to a mind of longing and stinginess, and "attachment" refers to being bound by it, because they are free from delusion, they possess no craving or attachment whatsoever.
They no longer have any aspirations; they have no further resolve to seek the Buddha-way.
Instead, they are personally deluded regarding the Dharma, clinging to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as being ultimate.
They claim to have realized arhatship and that the cycle of birth and death within the three realms has been entirely exhausted, such that they will not undergo further existence.

The body, then, is ultimately characterized by ignorance regarding that which lies beyond its realm; because even subtle ignorance has never been entirely severed, it is not the ultimate, unsurpassed Buddha-way of Great Parinirvāṇa.
For a long night we have practiced the dharma of emptiness; clinging to the small and being deluded regarding the great, we were obscured by the Perfect Vehicle.
This is what is meant by "a long night": we merely cultivated and practiced the one-sided, empty, untainted dharmas.

They attain liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the three realms; by severing the delusions of views and thoughts, they obtain the fruit of outflowlessness and are delivered from such afflictions as birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress within the three realms.
Abiding in the final body within *nirvāṇa with remainder*: having already realized the four fruits, one is called "in the final body.
Although the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted, the physical body still remains; this is termed "with remainder. The mind abides in emptiness and quiescence, which is termed "nirvāṇa."
The Buddha’s teaching that leads to the attainment of the Way is not in vain. Within this Lesser Teaching, the dharmas of arising and ceasing are what the Buddha has spoken;
practicing in reliance upon them, one has already attained the Noble Path, which is real and not false.

This constitutes having already received the Buddha’s grace; it constitutes having already attained compliance with the Buddha’s teachings and repaid the Tathāgata’s grace for his transformation and nurturing.
Although we have expounded the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sons of the Buddhas and others, within this Prajñā assembly, we have received the Buddha’s empowerment.
They have been taught Mahāyāna sūtras by various bodhisattvas in order to seek the Buddha-way,
so that those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna might employ them in practice to achieve the Buddha-way;
yet they have no aspiration or delight whatsoever for these teachings, and regarding this Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā dharma, they lack even a single [moment of faith].
Reflecting on our hearts of delight and attachment,
the Teacher has abandoned us; the Tathāgata, the Guide,
has forsaken us because he observed our minds and beheld that we were attached to and delighted in the practice of inferior dharmas.
From the beginning, he did not urge them forward by speaking of actual benefits; he never spoke a word of exhortation or encouragement to speak of true, unsurpassed benefit.
This was as a wealthy elder who, knowing his sons’ inferior intelligence, acts in accordance with the Tathāgata’s mind and understands the intentions of the assembly.
By the power of skillful means, he subdues their minds; by the power of wisdom taught through skillful means, he tames, softens, and subdues their deluded minds.
Only then does he entrust them with all his wealth, just as that elder first tamed his sons' hearts and subsequently entrusted them with his property.
Objects are like this; the Buddha is also like this. The Buddha’s skillful means are also like those of the elder.
Manifesting rare and extraordinary events is like the Buddha manifesting the power of his skillful means and wisdom—things that do not exist in the world and are called rare.
As for the matter:
knowing those who delight in the lesser [vehicle], that is, knowing those in the world who take pleasure in the Hīnayāna,
he employs the power of skillful means— the power of applied effort.
Having tamed their minds—having first disciplined and subdued their deluded minds—he then taught them great wisdom;
subsequently, he taught the Great Wisdom of the Buddha.
Today we have attained what we have never had before; today, at this Dharma assembly, we, the Śrāvakas, have obtained the secret [teaching].
My mind has never experienced such a thing before;

it is not what I previously hoped for, yet I have now attained it myself. It was not something my original mind had anticipated or expected, yet today, through the Buddha’s revelation, I have attained it spontaneously.
"Just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasure, so too do the śrāvakas receive the Dharma from the Buddha, just as that impoverished son received wealth from his father.
World-Honored One, we have now attained the Way and realized the fruit. Thus they addressed the Buddha, the World-Honored One: "Today we have heard the Buddha’s wondrous [teaching]..."
Having been taught to attain the path to the unsurpassed realm of Buddhahood, they will certainly obtain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood;
regarding the untainted dharmas, and regarding the single Buddha-vehicle, the wondrous untainted Dharma.
One attains the pure eye. Attaining the wisdom of the true mark is called the pure eye.
For a long night we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts; throughout the long night of our past ignorance, we have cultivated and maintained the Tathāgata’s pure conduct of the precepts.
Today, for the first time, they have obtained their karmic fruition. What was previously described as the Hīnayāna was the Buddha’s skillful means;
today, hearing the Buddha’s voice and teaching, they obtain the true fruition of attaining Buddhahood.
The Dharma King has long cultivated the holy life within the Dharma. The Buddha is the Dharma King who possesses mastery over the Dharma;
I have for many years practiced the pure holy life within the Dharma.

Now one attains the untainted, unsurpassed great fruit. The untainted state of the Hīnayāna is free from birth in the segmented realm (*prādeśika-jāti*), while the untainted state of the Mahāyāna is free from the suffering of the transformational realm (*pariṇāmi-duḥkha*);
that both forms of death are extinguished is called the unsurpassed fruit.
"We of today are truly śrāvakas. Whereas in the past we were called 'lesser śrāvakas' because we entered the Way by hearing sounds, we are now truly Great Vehicle śrāvakas."
By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear; by means of the subtle and wondrous voice that accomplishes the Buddha-way, we cause all people to hear and thereby attain Buddhahood.
We of today are true Arhats; whereas previously attaining the four fruits was being a Lesser Arhat, now we have entered [the Great Way].
Yuan was a true Arhat within the Mahāyāna;
among all the world’s devas, humans, māras, and brahmās— among the gods, worldly beings, māra kings, and brahma kings within the triple realm.
They should universally receive offerings therein; because they have cultivated the wisdom of the Tathāgata, they should all receive respectful offerings from the entire assembly of devas and humans.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness! The World-Honored One possesses great benevolence and virtue toward me.
By means of rare events and the unsurpassed Dharma—things seldom encountered—he has compassionately taught and benefited us.
Out of pity and compassion, he has skillfully instructed and brought us great profit.
Causing others to enter the wondrous Way—
throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could possibly repay this? Having diligently practiced austerities throughout immeasurable kalpas,
who could possibly repay the Buddha’s kindness?
To provide for them with one’s hands and feet; to serve and attend to them as a messenger;
to pay homage by bowing one’s head to the ground;
and to offer all forms of worship by means of every possible object.
None of these can repay it; all the various ways mentioned above are insufficient as repayment.

Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] upon the crown of one's head or bear him on both shoulders—bearing the Buddha with the crown of the head and carrying him with the shoulders—it still could not repay his kindness.

Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they exhaust their hearts in respectful devotion; even if they must pass through kalpas as many as the sands of the Ganges, they maintain single-mindedness in practicing such reverence.
Furthermore, they offer choice delicacies and exquisite meals.
Immeasurable precious robes and various bedding; that is, immeasurable kinds of costly precious robes and various implements for sleeping and reclining,
as well as various medicinal decoctions, or perhaps various superior and exquisite medicinal decoctions.
With *gośīrṣa* sandalwood— the wondrous fragrance of sandalwood from Mount Gośīrṣa—
and various precious gems, one should erect stūpas and temples; that is, using fragrant wood and various precious materials, one should construct various stūpas and temples for the Buddha.
Precious robes were spread upon the ground, serving as cushions and mats;
such things as these were used for making offerings, performing worship in the manner described above.
Even over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not repay [the Buddha's kindness]; though such kalpas may last for a long time, they are insufficient to express gratitude.
The Buddhas are rare; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is like that of the udumbara flower, manifesting but once in an age; therefore, it is said they are "rarely encountered."
The great supernormal power is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable. The Buddha’s supernormal powers cannot be measured and have no limit;
because they cannot be reached by the mind or discussed by the mouth, they are called "great."

The King of all dharmas, untainted and unconditioned: because the three delusions have been exhausted, there is no leakage; because one acts in accordance with the nature of reality, there is no deliberate effort;
thus, one is the Great Dharma King over both the mundane and the supramundane.
One is able to endure this matter for those who are inferior; out of compassion, one is able to patiently and gently teach this matter to those who are lowly, small, inferior, and weak.

For ordinary people who grasp at signs, the Buddha teaches according to what is appropriate. If he encounters base ordinary people who grasp at signs, the Buddha then employs skillful means to teach them accordingly.
All Buddhas have attained the supreme mastery over all phenomena; within the gates of the Dharma, all Buddhas may teach either gradually or...
He attains supreme mastery instantaneously,
knowing the various inclinations and aspirations of all sentient beings as well as their mental capacities. He skillfully understands the faculties,
karmic actions, diverse desires, and the power of sustaining wisdom and views of all sentient beings.
According to their capacity and according to the extent of their strength,
he preaches the Dharma using immeasurable analogies; he expounds the methods of skillful means through various and immeasurable parables.
In accordance with the roots of goodness of sentient beings from their past lives, and according to whatever roots of goodness they possess in those past lives;
furthermore, he knows those who are mature and those who are not yet mature, having known whose faculties are matured and whose are not.
Having thus deliberated, analyzed, and known [them], and having thus deliberated, weighed, and analyzed to know the nature of their various faculties,
he taught the One Vehicle path as three according to what was appropriate; through skillful means, he followed [the capacities of beings] within the unsurpassed path of the single Buddha-vehicle.
It is appropriate to teach by means of the three vehicles.
*Exegesis of the Phrases of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two.
*Exegesis of the Phrases of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Three.
The Śramaṇa Guǎngzhào of Qiántáng, Śākyamuni Wéndá, [translates] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Five: "The Parable of the Herbs.
The Tathāgata, through his great compassion, universally acts for the sake of the Dharma-realm, not allowing even a single person to attain parinirvāṇa alone; he does so by means of the Tathāgata...

Prior to his parinirvāṇa, in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," Mahākāśyapa—representing the class of śrāvaka disciples who enter the perfect [vehicle] from the gradual—explained the Buddha’s intention; however, his understanding of the Great Meaning was not yet complete.
Therefore, the World-Honored One further taught this chapter, wherein the three types of grass and two types of trees all flourish when rained upon.
Universally moistening all without exception, it manifests the comprehensive system of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to encompass the capacities of all sentient beings.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished teaching the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," he addressed Mahākāśyapa;
because his faith and understanding were not yet complete, the Buddha spoke to him.
As well as the great disciples—namely Subhūti, Kātyāyana, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the rest—he exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent!
repeatedly praising them for their ability to understand.
Kāśyapa has eloquently expounded the true merits of the Tathāgata. His words accord with the Buddha’s intent; thus, he is called one who "eloquently expounds the merits of the Tathāgata.
The term "true" distinguishes this from the provisional paths of the three vehicles, while "real" distinguishes it from the false, nominal teachings of expedient means.
It is exactly as you have said. It is indeed as you have understood and described.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits.

Although the Tathāgata’s merits fully encompass all that can be grasped through various understandings, it is said that "there are further [merits]" simply because they are beyond the reach of the śrāvakas and other assemblies.

If you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you could not exhaust it; even if those of the two vehicles were to speak of the Buddha’s merits with their own wisdom, they could not finish doing so even after passing through kalpas as numerous as atoms.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas. The title "King" signifies sovereign mastery;
the Tathāgata has attained supreme mastery over all dharmas.
Whatever he speaks is never false. Whatever Dharma he teaches at any time is entirely true.
It is truly without falsehood.
Regarding all phenomena— where "all" refers to both mundane and supramundane phenomena—
he expounds them through the skillful means of wisdom, employing the expedient means of sagely ingenuity.
The Dharma he teaches—the Dharma taught through the wisdom of skillful means—all reaches the stage of omniscience.
Omniscience is precisely the wisdom of emptiness; although the characteristics of phenomena differ, they all reach the state of wisdom.

The Tathāgata observes and knows; through the wisdom of a Tathāgata, he perceives and understands that all phenomena are where they ultimately converge: all phenomena tend toward emptiness and tranquility.

He also knows the deep-seated inclinations and practices of all sentient beings; regarding the various dispositions and preferences of sentient beings and the spheres of their conduct, the Buddha knows them all, penetrating them without obstruction.
The Buddha penetrates all things, free from any hindrance.

Furthermore, they have thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena; it is not merely that they give rise to the mind, but they have also reached ultimate realization regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
They demonstrate all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings, using the Dharma to instruct and reveal it to them, thereby leading them toward wisdom.
The earth enters into the Buddha’s wisdom.
Kāśyapa, it is like the trichiliocosm. This trichiliocosm is the sphere of transformation of a Buddha;
it is composed of one thousand small chiliocosms and one thousand medium chiliocosms, which together form the great chiliocosm—each being a single world-system.
Mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges are metaphors for the world and its objective spheres; "mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges" here metaphorically represent the objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
Regarding "the lands where herbs, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal plants grow": the land is the producer, while the grasses and trees are the produced.
"Herbs" refers to those of the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior; "trees" refers to the two types, large and small; and that which grows densely together is called a "forest."
There are various types, each possessing a corresponding number of seeds and affinities;
their names and forms are distinct, and their designations and characteristics differ from one another, analogous to the individual differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings.
Dense clouds spread everywhere. The cloud is a metaphor for the Buddha’s body; "dense" refers to the subtle response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

This response-body is like a great cloud extensively spread, universally covering the three thousandfold world system. One should know that the Buddha’s body responds universally, just as clouds cover everywhere.
At one time, [the rain] falls equally; the Buddha responds to all beings by raining down equally, so that its moisture universally saturates them.
"Moisture" is a metaphor for the flavor of the Dharma, which universally permeates and satisfies all.
As for the "grasses, trees, groves, and medicinal herbs": "grasses" refers to the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior, while "trees" refers to the great and the small.
When two trees grow together in a thicket, it is called a forest.
Those with small roots, small trunks, small branches, and small leaves refer to the two paths of humans and devas as the small roots and trunks.
Those with medium roots, medium trunks, medium branches, and medium leaves refer to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the medium medicinal herbs.
It has large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves. The root is a metaphor for the seeds of goodness; the stem, for virtuous vows;

the branches, for the gates of goodness; and the leaves, for virtuous conduct. Just as a worldly tree with large roots and stems will also have many branches and leaves, so too, because the wisdom and vows of a Bodhisattva are great, their practice and realization are likewise profound.

Regarding the various trees, both large and small, they are further divided among the Bodhisattvas into two categories: those who practice gradually are called "small," while those who practice all at once are called "large.
According to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities, each receives [the teaching] accordingly; each receives it differently according to its own measure.
The rain showered by a single cloud: the "single great cloud" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s body; the "thoroughly pouring down of sweet rain" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s teaching.
It plants their respective natures, according to the faculties, seeds, and habitual tendencies they have received.

Thus, flowers and fruits grow, and blossoms unfold to bear fruit. Just as rain moistens things so they may sprout, flower, and set fruit, so too does the Dharma-moisture nourish wisdom and bring about the realization of karmic results.
Although all things arise from the same ground—the ground being a metaphor for the nature that is fundamentally equal—the myriad things are a metaphor for the mind according to its desires.
Each is distinct.
Though moistened by a single rain, that single rain is a metaphor for the Dharma which universally benefits all;
yet the various grasses and trees each have their own differences, just as the faculties and natures of sentient beings are each different, like those plants.
The endowments of trees each differ.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so. What was previously explained by way of analogy is here applied to the Dharma.
His appearance in the world is like the rising of a great cloud; the phenomenon of the Buddha’s appearance and the rising of clouds share similar characteristics in meaning.
With a great voice, the Buddha’s sound preaches the Dharma like the roar of thunder;
it pervades the world of devas, humans, and asuras. All those in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—are able to hear it.
Just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm, so too does the Buddha’s body universally respond and cover all like a cloud.
Within the great assembly— namely, the aforementioned multitudes— [he appeared].

And he uttered these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavat. These ten titles above are explained as in the Preface Chapter.
"To cause those who have not crossed over to cross over" refers to the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
"To cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated" refers to the vow to sever innumerable afflictions.
"To bring peace to those who are not yet at peace" is the vow to study the immeasurable Dharma-gates.
"To lead those who have not attained nirvana to attain nirvana" is the vow to realize the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.

"In this world and in future worlds"—"this world" refers to the present life and "future worlds" refers to the lives to come—he knows these as they truly are. He knows each cause and its effect according to reality.
I am the All-Knowing One; regarding all phenomena, I am fully able to understand them.
The "one who sees all" possesses correct view that is clear and penetrating to the very source and bottom of the Dharma.
The "one who knows the Way" skillfully understands the characteristics of all obstacles and openings.
The "one who opens the Way" is well able to reveal and demonstrate the Way of the Buddha.
"The Speaker" refers to the one who expounds the unsurpassed path for the sake of sentient beings.
You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras—summon those whom you have transformed and guided;
all should come here to assemble at this Dharma assembly.
They have gathered for the sake of hearing the Dharma; the purpose of their assembly is to enable them to hear the Dharma.

At that time, there were countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings. While it is common practice to speak of ten classes of sentient beings, here "thousands of myriads of kotis" is said in reference to their various faculties and dispositions.
They came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma; they gathered at the Buddha’s presence desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, when the assembly of sentient beings had gathered, the Tathāgata—[the Buddha]—was present.

He contemplates these sentient beings; he observes each and every one of them, examining their faculties—whether sharp or dull, superior, middling, or inferior; whether they are intelligent or obtuse;
and whether they are diligent or indolent, pure in their application to the Path or lax, negligent, and remiss.
According to their respective capacities, he teaches through skillful means in accordance with what is appropriate for each being, preaching the Dharma as it should be preached for them;
these are manifold and immeasurable. Since the dispositions of beings are diverse, the teachings are likewise immeasurable.
May all be made to rejoice; may all hear [the teaching] and each find joy in their hearts.
May they swiftly obtain excellent benefit; may their spirits be refreshed and attain great, wholesome advantage.
These sentient beings—the immeasurable multitude of beings who have come here—[shall do so].
Having heard this Dharma, and having heard the Tathāgata’s exposition of these various dharmas,
one attains peace and security in the present life— the peace and security obtained by practicing and progressing in accordance with the Dharma within the present world.
They will be reborn in a favorable realm. After casting off the retribution of suffering, they will take birth in a favorable realm and experience happiness through the Path.
By practicing the Path now, they will later enjoy bliss, and they will also hear the Dharma—specifically, the True Dharma spoken by the Buddha.

Having heard the Dharma, they are freed from all obstacles; by virtue of past conditions, having heard it, they contemplate and cultivate it, thereby distancing themselves from the three obstructions and all hindrances.
Regarding all phenomena—within the teachings on humans, devas, and the three vehicles as taught by the Tathāgata—[they attain realization].
"According to one's capacity" means that by relying on one's own strength and according to one's ability,
one gradually attains entry into the Way. Because one leaves the four evil realms, is reborn among humans and devas, and enters the path of the Three Vehicles from the bodies of humans and devas,
it is called "gradual entry."
Just as that great cloud merges with the body of the Tathāgata and rains upon all;
and merges with the Dharma of the Tathāgata, [sustaining] the shrubs,
trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs— the three types of grasses and two types of trees.
According to their respective lineages, each one, in accordance with its own seed and habitual tendencies, receives full nourishment.
All things receive the moisture of the Dharma and are satisfied according to their respective capacities;
each attains growth, and each fulfills its own nature as it grows.
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like clouds pouring down rain;

it possesses a single characteristic and a single flavor. Because he regards all sentient beings with equality, it is said to have a single characteristic; because it universally moistens all, it is said to have a single flavor.
What is called the characteristic of liberation: it unties the bonds of the three realms to bring about release from birth and death;
the characteristic of detachment: it distances oneself from all worldly dust and afflictions;
the characteristic of cessation: it penetrates the principle of true emptiness to realize the bliss of nirvana.

Ultimately reaching all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), one first employs skillful means to temporarily guide those of initial capacity, finally returning them to the ultimate state of all-encompassing wisdom.
As for sentient beings— whatever classes of sentient beings there may be in the world— [they are all thus guided].
They hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata; they hear the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.
Whether they uphold, read, or recite it; or whether they both receive and uphold it while also reading and reciting it;
they practice according to what was taught, practicing in reliance upon what the Buddha has spoken.
Regarding the merit thus obtained—the merit acquired through the practice one has undertaken—one does not consciously perceive it;
because the mind is deluded, one is unable to know for oneself which dharma should be studied.
Why is this so? What is the intention behind the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world?
Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings; only the Buddha alone knows the various kinds of sentient beings within this dharma-realm.
The characteristics, essential nature, seeds, appearances, fundamental substance, and root-nature.
What matters does one keep in mind? What matters is bound to the mind?
What matters does one contemplate? What matters is contemplated within the mind?
What is the object of cultivation? What is the nature that is to be understood? What is the object of cultivation?
How is there mindfulness? How should one be mindful? What is volition? How should one exercise volition?
How is it cultivated? How should it be cultivated?
By means of which dharma is there mindfulness? By means of which dharma is the mind bound in mindfulness?
By means of which dharma is there reflection? By means of which dharma is one caused to contemplate?
By what dharma is it cultivated? By what means is the cultivation initiated?
By what dharma? By what kind of dharma?
What dharma is attained? What dharma can be attained?
Sentient beings dwell in various stages (*bhūmi*). Although their fundamental nature is originally one, their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) differ;
according to what they rely upon, these are termed "dwelling," and as each takes up its own position, they are called "various stages."

Only the Tathāgata knows and perceives it as it truly is. While the noble ones of the three vehicles perceive the truth partially, only the Great Sage Buddha realizes it according to reality, with clear and unimpeded comprehension;
he awakens to it with distinct clarity, free from all obstruction.
Just as those flowers, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs— whose natures as roots correspond to the aforementioned grasses and trees—

are unaware of their own superior, middling, or inferior qualities; and just as the grasses and trees, receiving moisture, each take what they need for satisfaction without knowing the magnitude of their own capacity.

The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor, as previously stated—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation, and ultimate nirvāṇa. What was previously called "all-knowledge" refers to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*);
what is here called "nirvāṇa" refers to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
It is the mark of eternal quiescence. That which eternally abides in the principle of nirvāṇic quiescence—the markless mark—is called "eternal quiescence.
It ultimately returns to emptiness. This so-called "emptiness" is precisely the aforementioned Great Parinirvāṇa of eternal quiescence; it is not annihilation.

Emptiness and partial emptiness are not merely emptiness; within emptiness itself there is the provisional and the empty, and the non-duality of the provisional and the empty is called ultimate emptiness.
The Buddha, having known this, knows such emptiness as the true meaning of reality.
Observing the desires of sentient beings, one views their inclinations with eyes of compassion and protects them;
thus, through skillful management and guardianship, one conforms precisely to their capacities and dispositions.
For this reason, he did not immediately teach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Since the knowledge of all modes is the Middle Way’s correct wisdom realized by the Buddha, he did not dare to teach it immediately because the disciples' capacities were as yet unable to bear it.
"You, Kāśyapas, are truly rare. Your faith and understanding are excellent; you have well penetrated the Buddha’s intention in a way that no one else can match, for such people are extremely few.
You are able to know how the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Thus he praised them as rare because they were able to act in this manner.
One is able to believe, able to accept, and able to know; because one knows, one understands thoroughly; because one believes, one has no doubt;
because one accepts, one does not forget. Why is this so? What is the intention behind this praise?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate. All Buddhas speak in accordance with the suitability of beings and in accord with their capacities;
there is no fixed dharma.

It is difficult to understand and difficult to know because the capacities of sentient beings are diverse, and the intentions of the Buddhas are profound, hidden, and subtle; therefore, its distinctions are difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, it is difficult to know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses. He spoke these verses because he wished to provide further proof by means of past events.
The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world; the Buddha, as the Dharma King appearing in the world, does so to destroy sentient beings' views that cling to existence.
He teaches the Dharma in various ways according to the inclinations of sentient beings, knowing their intentions and employing various means as appropriate to each.
He preaches the Dharma according to conditions.

The Tathāgata is revered; the Buddha possesses majestic virtue, his rank is exalted and his appearance dignified, and his wisdom is profound and far-reaching. The Buddha’s wisdom is deep and boundless.
This essential point has been long kept silent. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret and essential matter of all Buddhas;
since attaining the Way more than forty years ago, it has never been brought forth, and is therefore said to have been "long kept silent."
One does not strive for rapid exposition. Because what was previously taught did not involve discursive talk, it is said that one does not strive for rapid exposition.
If those possessing wisdom hear it, they will be able to believe and understand. Therefore, the reason for not yet teaching is precisely to wait for the appropriate capacity;
only after being able to believe and understand will one then teach it.

If one lacks wisdom, harbors doubt, or feels regret, one will suffer eternal loss. To speak of this wondrous sutra before those lacking wisdom is not only to fail to believe it, but to further give rise to slander;
such is eternal loss, for it constitutes turning one's back on awakening and aligning oneself with the defilements.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, I tell you: for this reason, I teach according to their capacity;
I teach according to their spiritual faculties.
Through various conditions, I may speak of the five vehicles or the three vehicles—all of which are expedient means.
It causes them to attain right view; it causes them to employ skillful means to attain right view.
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud: the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is likened to this, arising in the world.
From the Truth (dharmatā), the response arises just as a cloud is produced.
It completely covers all things, universally transforming all capacities like clouds that overspread the sky.
The cloud of wisdom contains moisture; the body-cloud of wisdom stores up benefit and profit.
The lightning flashes brilliantly; wisdom is like a bolt of lightning, its radiance shining forth with dazzling brilliance.
The sound of thunder resounds afar; the Dharma-sound responds universally like lightning flashing in the distance, causing the multitude to rejoice.
It is able to make the minds of the assembly joyful, delighted, and at ease.
The blazing heat of the sun is eclipsed, and the earth becomes cool and refreshing; the fierce glare of the sun is likened to various burning afflictions, while the clouds of compassion cover it.
Therefore, the mind-ground is cool and refreshing.
"Āi-dài" (靉靆) describes the appearance of dense, hanging clouds; the profound weight of the compassionate heart bends down for all living beings, like clouds lowering and spreading everywhere.

It can be understood as follows: "bearing upon the head" (*cheng*) means to support, while "grasping with the hand" (*lan*) means to take hold. Although the Buddha is most honored and supreme, he accords with the capacities of all beings;
out of compassion, he is easily approached. Thus, he is like clouds hanging down, appearing as if they could be borne upon the head or grasped by the hand.
That rain is universally equal; the preaching of the Dharma is like that rain, universally and equally falling from all four directions.
These four directions are a metaphor for the stages of abiding, practicing, advancing, and the bhūmis.
It pours down in immeasurable torrents; its flow is so vast and expansive as to be incalculable.
The entire realm is thoroughly saturated; there is no ground of sentient beings that is not moistened, just as the whole land is completely filled with moisture.
Mountains represent the nature of stillness, rivers represent the nature of movement, and steep valleys represent the evils of sentient beings.
Nature is that which arises from the profound and obscure; it is the product produced by the hidden and deep recesses.

Like various plants, trees, and medicinal herbs, the sentient beings of humans, devas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas possess superior, middling, and inferior faculties, just as there are diverse kinds of plants, trees, and medicinal herbs.

As for the category of grasses and the various trees, large and small: Bodhisattvas who receive sudden instruction are called "great trees," while those who receive gradual instruction are called "small trees.
Because they encompass immeasurable capacities, they are referred to as "various trees."
The sprouts and crops of the hundred grains; the sprouts and crops of the hundred kinds of wholesome thoughts and the *bodhicitta* can nourish life and allow one to realize the Truth.
Sugarcane and grapes: the sweet taste of sugarcane is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*gotra*), while the spreading vines of the grape are a metaphor for the various [wholesome] seeds.
As for the clans, they are moistened by the rain. The Dharma-rain is bestowed equally, such that all things receive an even distribution;
there is none that is not abundantly satisfied, and not a single thing that is not abundantly satisfied.

The dry land is universally moistened. Those sentient beings who have entered the Dharma, whose habits of desire are initially dried up but who have not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of the Dharma, are called "dry land";
now, having received the moisture of the Dharma, they too are universally and thoroughly saturated.
Medicinal trees flourish together, and the various capacities of beings receive nourishment as if all things were equally flourishing.
That which the clouds produce—the body-clouds produce—is water of a single flavor.
The Tathāgata benefits sentient beings with a single flavor, without any other thought, just as rain pours from the clouds.
Rainwater has no distinct flavors;

yet the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests receive its moisture according to their respective capacities. Although the flavor of the water is one, the degree to which the various plants and trees are moistened differs.
Likewise, although the flavor of the Dharma is one, the benefits received by the various faculties and vessels differ.
All the various trees are categorized by their kind; they are merely divided into large and small because the capacities of sentient beings are numerous. Thus, they are called "various trees.
The superior, middling, and inferior grades refer to the three types of grasses used as metaphors for the three vehicles (triyāna).
It corresponds to their respective sizes. This metaphor illustrates how the gradual, sudden, great, and small bodhisattvas each attain growth;
each fulfills its own nature through generation and development.
Their roots, stems, branches, and leaves are as described before.
Flowers, fruits, radiance, and color: flowers represent wholesome causes, fruits represent wholesome effects, radiance represents wholesome wisdom, and color represents wholesome deeds.
Wherever the single rain reaches, all things attain freshness and luster; being moistened by the rain of a single flavor, each and every thing is so transformed.
They attain a fresh, lustrous, and well-nourished appearance,
corresponding exactly to their physical form; it accords with their constitution and features,
and according to the magnitude of their inherent nature and disposition, whether great or small, they remain distinct within their own respective categories.
That which is moistened is one; the Dharma has no diverse flavors, yet each grows luxuriantly.
While the moisture received is not the same, the Buddha is likewise so. This concludes the preceding analogy.
He appears in the world, arising from the True as the Responsive,
like a great cloud; with his vast body as a cloud,
he universally covers all and responds everywhere to the capacities of sentient beings.
Having appeared in the world, his initial descent into birth was like the arising of clouds, and his turning of the Wheel of Dharma was like the falling of rain from those clouds,
for the sake of all sentient beings who were ready to receive the Way.
He expounds and analyzes them, teaching the three vehicles and the five vehicles separately.
Although he speaks of the reality of all dharmas through skillful means, in truth it is the Buddha-vehicle.
O Great Sage, World-Honored One, those who realize the three vehicles are called "lesser sages," while the Tathāgata, being perfectly consummate, is called "Great."
The Noble One,
amidst the assembly of all devas and humans— among those seeking the Dharma—
proclaimed these words; he made this proclamation.
I am the Tathāgata. I am the Tathāgata of ultimate fruition and virtue, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
Having long cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and being fully endowed with merit and wisdom, I have emerged from the world;
for the sake of sentient beings, I do not abide in nirvāṇa.
Just as a great cloud saturates and moistens all things, so too does the cloud of the body and the rain of the Dharma saturate and moisten all withered sentient beings.
There are no such things as "withered ones" who are not moistened by the rain of the Dharma.
May they all be freed from suffering— from the suffering of the evil realms and the suffering of the two types of death—
and attain secure bliss; may they attain the bliss of a secure body and mind,
as well as the worldly pleasures of the two rewards of humans and devas, namely the pleasures of the five desires.
And the bliss of nirvana; the bliss of cessation of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
All you hosts of devas and humans, all you multitudes of gods and men, listen with single-minded attention. With unified minds, listen well as I speak.
All should come here; having arrived at the assembly of the Buddha, they shall behold the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Unsurpassed Greatly Awakened World-Honored One.
I am the World-Honored One; I am the Honored One of all worlds.
There is none who can equal me; among all other sages and worthies, there is not a single person who can match me.
I appear in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings; I manifest in the world so that sentient beings may attain peace and security.

He preached the pure Dharma of ambrosia for the great assembly. As the Tathāgata expounded all dharmas for the multitude, those teachings were as pure as celestial ambrosia, none of which was not exquisite.
That Dharma is of a single flavor: liberation and nirvana. Although the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings differ, the Buddha’s intention is ever-blended;
he causes them all to attain the unsurpassed liberation and ultimate nirvana of this single flavor.
With a single sublime voice, he expounds this meaning. Based on the similarity of its distinctions, it is designated as "one" in intent;
what is called "expounding with a single voice" refers to the provisional being named real, which is termed the "sublime voice. This sublime meaning flows forth and is thoroughly elucidated.
They constantly act as the causes and conditions for the Mahāyāna. Thus it is said that the intention of the Lesser Vehicle serves to introduce [beings] to the wisdom of both the Great and the Small;
these small virtues are the conditions.
I observe that all things are universally equal; the Buddha-mind is unimpeded, viewing all sentient beings with equanimity.

There is no mind of love or hatred regarding self and other. While sentient beings possess such feelings of love and hatred toward one another, the Buddha’s mind is equal toward all, and none of these exist therein.
I have neither greedy attachment nor any obstruction; likewise, the Tathāgata has no greed, craving, grasping, or stinginess.
The mind also possesses no characteristics of limitation or obstruction;
it constantly teaches the Dharma equally to all, and always, with an impartial mind, preaches the dharma of signlessness to all beings.
As it is for one person, so it is for many; as it is for many, so it is for each individual, whether one or many.
He constantly expounds the Dharma and has never engaged in any other matter. Always with a single-minded focus, he expounds the Dharma for them, never allowing any other concern to entangle his mind.
In going, coming, sitting, and standing, he never grows weary; throughout the four modes of deportment, he remains ever diligent, never experiencing exhaustion or fatigue.
He satisfies the world like rain that moistens everywhere; by moistening the world with the Dharma, he brings all to fulfillment, just as the timely rains do.
The rain universally moistens all—whether noble or base, high or low; those of the highest wisdom or the lowest folly;
those who uphold the precepts or violate them. For those who uphold the precepts, there is absolute purity; for those who violate the precepts, there is absolute defilement.
Undefiled.
He is fully endowed with dignified deportment; that is to say, he is fully endowed with the observance of all the minor precepts, maintaining them without any deficiency or transgression.
And as for being incomplete: this refers to those who, although they have received and uphold the various precepts, are unable to maintain them in full purity.

Regarding right view and wrong view: one who knows causes and recognizes results is called a person of right view; one who turns their back on principle and is deluded regarding reality is called a person of wrong view.

Regarding those of sharp faculties and dull faculties: among the various vehicles, they are distinguished as superior or inferior; relative to what precedes them, they are considered dull, while relative to what follows them, they are considered sharp.
"Equally raining the rain of Dharma" means equally raining the rain of the Dharma of a single flavor.
Yet he never grows weary. His compassion for all beings is profound, and he never tires of it.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma—those sentient beings who hear the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Abiding in the various stages according to what is received through one's own power, they dwell in the positions of the five vehicles according to their faculties and strength—
whether in the realms of humans or devas, or in the vehicles of humans and devas,
or as a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*). There are four types of wheel-turning kings, which are the golden, silver, copper, and iron wheels, each produced by the influence of merit.
All others are likewise kings of men.
As for Śakra, Brahmā, and the various other kings: "Śakra" refers to Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; "Brahmā" refers to Brahmā, the Lord of the Rūpadhātu;
and this includes all other heavenly kings within the three realms.
These are the minor medicinal herbs. From the perspective of their own respective tracks, the two vehicles of humans and devas are called "minor medicinal herbs";
