yet from the perspective of the fundamental reality, those various heavenly kings are all bodhisattvas who traverse samādhi as the locus of their practice.

One knows that untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) can lead to *nirvāṇa*. One skillfully understands that the dharma of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) can lead to the partial emptiness (*prādeśika-śūnyatā*) and *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), whereby one gives rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*):
namely, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the power of miraculous transformation, and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The common characteristics [of the supernormal powers] arise because they are brought forth by the *Abhidharma-jñāna-prasthāna* (Jñānaprasthāna); thus it is said that they "arise.

Furthermore, one attains the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): the threefold supernormal clarity consisting of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Dwelling alone in the mountains and forests, he constantly practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Living by himself among the peaks and beneath the trees, he constantly maintained *samādhi* and abided in tranquil meditation.
He attained the realization of a pratyekabuddha; through awakening to conditions, he realized the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
Among these medicinal herbs, they are called "middle herbs" because they surpass those of humans and devas.

They seek the state of a World-Honored One, thinking, "I shall become a Buddha"; they seek the state realized by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, thinking, "I shall practice and attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
They practice the concentration of diligence and cultivate the supreme concentration of the tranquility of diligence;
these are the superior medicinal herbs. Because they aspire to attain Buddhahood, surpassing even the two vehicles, they are called the superior medicinal herbs.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha: those called "sons of the Buddha" differ from the śrāvakas;
they devote their minds exclusively to the Buddha-way and focus their single-minded attention on seeking the Buddha-way.
They constantly practice compassion. While those of the two vehicles do not give rise to the great transformation, the bodhisattva roots practice great kindness.
Compassion.
One knows for oneself that one will certainly become a Buddha without doubt; within the mind, one knows for oneself that one will certainly attain Buddhahood, free from any further uncertainty.

This is called a small tree. Because his power of meditative concentration increases further and his resolve becomes even greater than before—surpassing the previous stage of "growing grass"—it is called a "small tree.
A Bodhisattva at this stage is like one who has first resolved to attain enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*) as described in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Abiding securely in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they dwell at ease in the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.
They turn the wheel of non-retrogression; they are able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.

They deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. This refers to the great bodhisattvas who, through the sudden teaching, ascend to a stage from which there is no retrogression.
Because he is thus able to extensively deliver immeasurable sentient beings,
such a bodhisattva is called a "great tree. Since his power is great and his protective shade is increasingly vast, he is termed a "great tree."
The Buddha teaches with impartiality, like a rain of a single flavor. With a mind of equal compassion, the Buddha teaches impartially, like the falling of seasonal rain of a single flavor.
Although the Dharma is equal, what is received differs according to the dispositions of sentient beings; though the Dharma is equal, it accords with the faculties inherited by those beings.
The benefits received by their natures differ, just as the qualities received by various plants and trees each vary. The natures of sentient beings are like those plants and trees;
according to their size, what they receive and experience differs.

The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to provide instruction. By using grasses and trees as metaphors for all sentient beings, the Buddha provides skillful instruction for those who are deluded.
Through various expressions he expounds upon the single Dharma; by employing provisional verbal formulations, he collectively elucidates that one Dharma.

Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, it is like a single drop in the ocean. The essence of the Buddha’s nature is fully endowed with wisdom; what I have now preached as a single dharma is like a single drop in the ocean.
I rain down the rain of Dharma; the Buddha sends down the rain of Dharma.
It fills the world; it fills all worlds within the triple realm.
It is the Dharma of a single flavor; the flavor of the Dharma is fundamentally one.
Practice according to one's capacity, cultivating and upholding it in accordance with the power of one's wisdom.
Just as those forests of medicinal herbs and trees, through this analogy applied to the Dharma, grow increasingly lush and beautiful according to their size;
so too do they receive the Way according to their roots and gradually flourish.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is always of a single flavor. All Buddhas constantly employ the great Dharma of equal single flavor to cause all worlds to universally attain fulfillment,
and to cause the flavor of the Dharma of the three worlds to be entirely sufficient.
Through gradual cultivation, all attain the fruits of the Path. Those of the Three Vehicles cultivate the Path progressively and in sequence, causing them all to attain their respective fruits.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas dwell in mountain forests; because those of the Two Vehicles delight in tranquility, they reside in mountain forests.
Abiding in their final body, they attain the fruit of Arhatship; being called those in their final body, they are eternally liberated from the three realms and shall never be born again.
Hearing the Dharma, they attain the fruit; hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, their minds are able to comprehend and understand it, thereby attaining the state of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha.
As a result, these are called medicinal herbs that each attain growth. To draw the analogy to the dharma, this refers to the medium-sized medicinal herbs:
if the wisdom of various bodhisattvas is firm, and the power of wisdom of these bodhisattvas is firm, they shall never regress.
He falls [into the realization that] he has thoroughly understood the three realms. He clearly and completely penetrates that within the three realms there are no solid or enduring phenomena.
He seeks the Supreme Vehicle; among the three vehicles, the Bodhisattva vehicle is the most supreme.
This is called a small tree that attains growth. Although they seek the Buddha-way, they enter through the gradual gate rather than through sudden realization;
therefore, they are called "small trees.

Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and attain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Moreover, there are those of great capacity who, dwelling in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), give rise to and attain supernatural powers.
By the power of penetrating wisdom,
upon hearing that all phenomena are empty of self-nature, their minds are filled with great joy; upon hearing it explained that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent,
they attain clear awakening within their hearts and experience great joy.
They emit countless rays of light that illuminate all sentient beings. These rays symbolize wisdom; employing wisdom to gather in and transform living beings is called "emitting light.
Because this clarity of wisdom is not singular, it is termed "countless."
This is called a great tree that attains growth; this is a metaphor for the Great Bodhisattvas of the Sudden Teaching.
"In this way, Kāśyapa"—the two characters "in this way" refer back to the aforementioned five vehicles to address Kāśyapa.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha, the skillful means taught by the Tathāgata,
is like a great cloud that rains with a single flavor. The Buddha’s body universally responds and the Buddha-Dharma universally covers all beings,
just as a single-flavored rain has no distinction.

It moistens the flowers of human beings so that each may attain its fruit. It moistens the flowers of the hearts of those with wholesome minds of the five vehicles, causing them each to grow and bear fruit.

Kāśyapa, you should know that because what was previously explained through faith and understanding had not yet fully blossomed, it is now universally encompassed here, thereby causing [the fruit] to be attained.
He knows this through various causes and conditions, through the matters of the retributive effects of various good and evil karmas from past lives,
and by employing various analogies— drawing upon diverse phenomena of the world as metaphors.
"To reveal and expound the path to Buddhahood—this is my skillful means.
All such things are the skillful means of all Buddhas;
it is likewise for all Buddhas, and the skillful means of the Buddha are also thus."
I now declare for you the most ultimate reality: first, I taught the Three Vehicles to destroy all demons and externalists, which was called "the true reality";
now, furthermore, I lead you gradually into the One Vehicle, which is called "the most ultimate reality."

The assembly of śrāvakas has not all attained extinction; those of the two vehicles merely distance themselves from delusion and thus it is called "extinction," yet this is not the ultimate, quiescent, and unsurpassed nirvāṇa of the One Vehicle.
The path you are practicing is the bodhisattva path. The path practiced by you followers of the two vehicles is itself the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path.
By gradually training and studying, you shall all attain Buddhahood. Entering from the gradual to the perfect, there is only the single Buddha-vehicle; there are no three distinct vehicles.
Vehicle.

In the sixth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, titled "The Chapter on the Prophecy," it is said that "receiving a prophecy" means that through cultivation one attains the principle; it is thus that the Buddha provides authentication, like a worldly title of nobility.
According to their respective capacities, Mahākāśyapa and the others heard the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma; through the two chapters, their minds attained awakening.

Citing the parable of the impoverished son, they explained their own faith and understanding, which merely allowed them to grasp the dharma-meaning of those who enter the Perfect [Vehicle] gradually from the Two Vehicles.
To the Tathāgata’s Dharma, this was but a single drop in an ocean; the Buddha then preached it extensively once more.
Since the Dharma rain has universally moistened the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees so that all shall attain the Buddha-way,

and because the meaning of the Dharma has now fully reached all people, he at this time bestows upon his four disciples the prediction of their future attainment of Buddhahood as transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya).

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking these verses—the conclusion of the "Chapter on Medicinal Herbs"—he addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words and saying to those gathered there: "I declare this to you."
This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, as previously mentioned,
shall in a future age obtain the opportunity to behold [the Buddha]; from this point forward, in the future, he shall obtain the opportunity to pay respect to and behold him.
He beheld three hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
he made offerings to them with reverence, performing ritual offerings while honoring them with body and mind,
respecting and praising them, and expressing his praise through words of respect for the Buddhas.
They extensively proclaim the immeasurable Great Dharma of all Buddhas; they widely expound the boundless Mahāyāna teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
In their final existence, they attain Buddhahood. The Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment is named for the sublime realization attained in that final body.
Awakening is called "becoming a Buddha.
It is named "Radiance" (Prabhāsa). Because one uses the light of wisdom to illuminate the Buddha-dharma, one attains the fruit and is thus titled "Radiance."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—
these titles are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).
The land was named Prabhāśrī; it was so named because its radiant and magnificent virtue served as its defining characteristic.
The eon was named Mahāvyūha; at that time, it was pure and adorned by great bodhisattvas.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twelve small kalpas, which is the measure of his response-body (nirmāṇakāya) lifespan.
The True Dharma shall abide in the world for twenty small kalpas; because the faculties of human beings are superior, it is called the True Dharma, just as it was when the Buddha was present.
The Semblance Dharma will likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas. Because human faculties gradually become inferior during the period of the Semblance Dharma, it is called the Semblance Dharma.
The realms will be magnificently adorned, and the secondary environment will be pure.
It was free from all filth and evil; it was devoid of all inauspicious signs.
There were no shards, rubble, or thorns; no pits of debris, nor thickets of brambles and thorns.
There was no excrement or impurity—neither urine nor feces, nor any other forms of uncleanness, none of which existed at all.

That land is level and even, without elevations, depressions, pits, or mounds. Because the ground of the mind is level and even, free from the characteristics of high and low, the resulting stage of fruition attained through such realization is likewise so.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli. Because the mind is clear and penetrating both internally and externally, as a result, the ground of the fruition stage is made of lapis lazuli.
Precious trees stand in rows; because one cultivated precious practices that grow the Bodhi tree, as a result, precious trees stand in rows at the stage of fruition.

Golden cords serve as boundary lines for the sides of the path; because one maintains the right precepts and follows these lines to always practice the Middle Way, one reaches the fruit where golden cords mark the boundaries of the path.

Various precious flowers are scattered everywhere throughout the pure realm; because one universally cultivated the Brahma-conduct during the stage of the cause, upon reaching the fruit, precious flowers are scattered upon the ground, making every location solemn and immaculate.
In that land, there are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas; those who practice the Great Vehicle are exceedingly numerous.
The assembly of śrāvakas is likewise infinite, and the number of those of the Lesser Vehicle is also thus.
There will be no demonic activities; there will be no matters of demonic obstacles consisting of false views.
Although there may be Māras and the subjects of Māra, they shall all protect the Buddha-dharma. In the Sanskrit language, Māra Pāpīyān means "the Killer" or "the Lord of Slaughter";
he is named the Demon King (Mārārāja). Those who act according to the king's will are called the subjects of Māra. Whether king or subject, [they shall protect the Dharma].
Although they do not cease from killing, they are all able to love and protect the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses to address the bhikṣus and the assembly gathered there:
With my Buddha-eye and with my Buddha-heavenly eye, I see this Kāśyapa;
I see Mahākāśyapa in a future age. After the passing of incalculable kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood.
With the clarity of the Buddha-eye, I clearly perceive that his original time limit is fixed and not subject to the collective [uncertainty].
That which is known through the power of the mind of birth is called "incalculable eons.
In future lives, he shall make offerings to and attend upon three hundred trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as previously explained.
For the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom; desiring to accomplish the Buddha’s wisdom, they purely cultivate the brahma-faring.
Purifying body and mind, they practice all the brahma-farings.
Having made offerings to the Most Supreme among Two-Legged Beings, their minds are directed toward making offerings to the Most Supreme in the World, who is endowed with both merit and wisdom.
The Honored One is the object of offerings.
Having cultivated all unsurpassed wisdom, one’s virtuous mind was previously ruined by long-standing delusion;
now, having first awakened to it, returning to the essence of its original nature is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), and its gradual advancement is called "practice" (*abhyāsa*). All [phenomena]...
The wisdom realized by the Buddha is called supreme insight (*anuttara-prajñā*).
Having attained Buddhahood in his final body, he fully awakens and achieves perfect enlightenment.
His land is pure, devoid of any signs of defilement or evil.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, representing the clarity of the mind-ground.
Numerous jewel trees line both sides of the path, symbolizing the rows of Bodhi trees standing in dense formation along the side of the Right Path.
The paths are demarcated by golden cords. The firm and steadfast Dharma is called "the Golden Cords," which, by delineating the boundaries, causes one to walk upon the right path.
Those who see it rejoice; because the environment is sublime, all who behold it are filled with joy.
It constantly emits exquisite fragrances. There are three kinds of fragrance: first, from the pores of the body, there constantly issues the priceless fragrance of ox-head sandalwood;
second, from the mouth, there constantly issues the fragrance of the blue lotus; third, from the flowers and fruits of the jewel-trees, various kinds of fragrances constantly issue forth.
They scattered various famous flowers. By scattering these flowers of manifold names and colors, they manifested the practice of immeasurable, upright, and true goodness.
They were adorned with all manner of wonders; such were the various extraordinary adornments as described above.
Its ground is level and even, without mounds or pits, reflecting the mind’s flatness and equanimity.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is beyond calculation, and the number of disciples of the Mahāyāna is exceedingly great.
Their minds are harmonious and supple; being tamed and compliant is precisely the concentrated mind.
They attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); while those called Śrāvakas possess minor supernormal powers, Bodhisattvas attain the supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna.
To uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas and to reverently honor, uphold, and recite all the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas, those who possess the final body of no-outflows— the śrāvaka arhats of the Hīnayāna— are called "final."
The sons of the Dharma King are likewise incalculable; for the Buddha is the Dharma King and the bodhisattvas are his sons, and their number is difficult to reckon.

Thus, even with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one cannot calculate or know [them]. The term "divine eye" is common to all, yet with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the divine eyes attained by other noble ones (*ārya*) are unable to know their number.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas. One cycle of increase and decrease in the receptacle world is called one small kalpa.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty small kalpas, as explained above.
Such were the matters concerning the World-Honored One Prabhāsa; this concludes the reference back to the preceding text.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others—whose significance is as explained in the Preface Chapter.

They were all struck with awe and trepidation. The disciples of these three men, seeing that Mahākāśyapa had received the prediction of attaining the Way while they themselves were not included, felt uneasy and were seized with alarm, trembling, and horripilation.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms; unifying their minds, they pressed their ten fingers and palms together.

Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, they beheld and revered the World-Honored One’s features with eyes that never for a moment left him, seeking the Buddha with focused intent and unblinking eyes.
They then spoke these verses with one voice. Together they raised their minds and addressed the Buddha with a single voice:
"O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One! You are a hero, fierce and powerful, able to sever views and craving, and to subdue the afflictions; thus you are named the Great Hero."
The Dharma King of all the Śākyas; among all the Śākya clans, the Buddha is supreme.
Out of compassion for us; out of loving-kindness and pity for us.
And grant me the voice of a Buddha; I pray that you will bestow upon me the voice of a Buddha.
If you know my profound intention, and if you, the Tathāgata, would deign to know my deep-seated aspiration to become a Buddha.
Regarding the vision of being granted a prophecy: when one sees my mind and the one who grants the prophecy, it is like sprinkling nectar to remove heat and attain coolness;
it is like being drenched by celestial nectar, whereby the afflictions of heat are removed and the mind attains coolness.
It is like coming from a land of famine and suddenly encountering the meal of a great king; one’s heart desires to receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa) as one who starved longs for food.

Yet, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on the Perfection [of Wisdom], the mind still harbors doubts and fears, not daring to consume it immediately. Although one has received the Buddha’s permission, one has not yet heard the formal prediction.
Whenever he encountered the preparation of food, he did not receive any portion granted to him; his mind remained filled with doubt, and he did not dare to take anything on his own initiative.
Only after receiving the King’s instruction would he then dare to eat; it was only upon obtaining the King’s command that he would venture to accept the food.

We, too, are like this; we constantly contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna. Our disciples are like those hungry people who, by constantly reflecting on them, become habituated to the faults of the Hīnayāna.
They do not know how they shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha, nor do they know in their hearts how they should cultivate that which is capable [of attaining it].
They shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
Although they hear the Buddha’s voice saying, "We shall become Buddhas," this voice of the Buddha— referring to both the Dharma and the parables—
is heard by all śrāvakas and causes them all to become Buddhas.
His mind still harbored anxiety and fear, such that he did not yet dare to eat. He thought to himself with doubt:
"If I receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment, only then shall I find true peace and joy; if I receive the Tathāgata’s formal prophecy, only then shall my heart find swift and great bliss."
The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, constantly desires to bring peace to the world. The World-Honored One’s original intention is always to bring peace to all sentient beings in the world.
We pray that you grant us a prophecy, just as one who is hungry requires instruction on food; this is the appropriate way for this Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of his great disciples, spoke the preceding verse regarding what was contemplated in their deep hearts,
and addressed all the bhikṣus, announcing it to the entire assembly.
This Subhūti, in a future age, shall behold three hundred trillion nayutas of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them;
he shall constantly practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and fulfill the path of a bodhisattva, until in his final body he attains buddhahood.
"Nayuta" is a name for a large number in the Western Regions [India]; the rest is as explained previously.
He is designated by the name "Name-and-Form" (*nāma-rūpa*). The Venerable One, having realized that all phenomena are merely names and forms, is called the Buddha of Name-and-Form.
He is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi.
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, has already been explained as before.
The kalpa is named Possessing Jewels (*Ratnasaṃbhava*). Because there exists the empty and quiescent Dharma, it is called "Possessing Jewels.
The land is named Jewel-Born (*Ratnasaṃbhava*); that land is pure and possesses this "Jewel-Born" quality.
Its ground is level and even. Because the mind-ground is level, the ground of the world naturally becomes level and even.
The ground is made of vaidūrya; *vaidūrya* is translated here as "water-jade," which also signifies that it is transparent both inside and out.
The adornment of jewel trees represents the Bodhi tree adorned with all manner of virtues.
The absence of mounds and pits signifies the absence of an uneven mind.
Sand, gravel, thorns, and sharp stones that pierce the feet represent evil and poisonous thoughts that lead to killing.
There is no filth from excrement or urine; in that land, there is no malice or harmful intent toward the ground.
Jeweled flowers cover the earth, which is everywhere pure. Through various causes of goodness, the Buddha-land is adorned like those jewels.
Flowers completely cover the ground.
The people of that land—the entire multitude of inhabitants within the realm—all dwell in jeweled terraces;
the places where they reside have terraces made of jewels.
The rare and wondrous pavilions— the various precious, exquisite, and beautiful pavilions, terraces, and tiered levels—
serve as a metaphor for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The śrāvaka disciples are immeasurable and boundless. Because the multitude is so vast, their limit cannot be known;
they cannot be known through calculation or analogy. Whether by numerical reckoning or by material metaphor, none can reach them.
The assembly of bodhisattvas numbered countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas; the number of those in the Mahāyāna assembly was likewise.
The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve minor kalpas, which was the measure of his nirmāṇakāya’s lifespan.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas, as has already been explained previously.
That Buddha constantly dwells in the void; having realized emptiness, he enters the fruit of the Path and abides in the emptiness of dharmas.
He preached the Dharma for the assembly. He taught the assembly the Dharma of emptiness and quiescence, delivering immeasurable bodhisattvas.
Through great emptiness and perfect emptiness, he brought all bodhisattvas across.
And as for the assembly of śrāvakas: the *tathatā* (suchness) that pervades space delivers the assembly of śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse. [The preceding prose section restates the content in verse.]
O assembly of bhikṣus, the present community of monks, I now address you and admonish you so that all may know:
you should all be single-minded; you must still your discursive thoughts and unify your minds.
Listen to what I say; lend your ear and listen attentively to what I have to say.
When I refer to my "great disciples," I use the term "great" to distinguish them from other minor attendants and disciples.
Subhūti shall attain Buddhahood and be named Mingxiang (Renowned Appearance), as previously described.
He shall make offerings to countless millions of billions of Buddhas and shall be an object of their veneration.
Following the conduct of the Buddhas, one gradually perfects the Great Path; following the practices cultivated by all Buddhas, one gradually fulfills the path of the Great Bodhisattva.
In the final body, one attains the thirty-two marks; after the body of equal enlightenment, one becomes a Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, endowed with all the marks.
Excellent!
He is upright, beautiful, and exquisite like a mountain of jewels; majestic, well-proportioned, grand, and most wonderful, like the king of jewel mountains.
That Buddha-land is the most sublime and pure of all; compared to other Buddha-lands, this is the foremost.
Among sentient beings who behold it, there are none who do not find joy and delight, for they rejoice in the wondrous vision of both the primary and secondary adornments.
Within it, the Buddha delivered immeasurable multitudes; in this pure land, he delivered immeasurable people.
Within his Dharma, there are many bodhisattvas; indeed, within that Dharma, there are many great bodhisattvas.
All possess sharp faculties and turn the wheel of non-retrogression; their faculties are all keen and capable of turning the irreversible Dharma-wheel of all Buddhas.
That land is constantly adorned by bodhisattvas; it is always adorned by bodhisattvas.
The assembly of śrāvakas was beyond measure and exceedingly numerous;
they had all attained the three vidyās and were endowed with the six abhijñās, which constitute the fruits of the śrāvaka.
They dwelt in the eight vimokṣas—namely, the eight vimokṣas (or "eight liberations") that turn away from evil toward good, and from the coarse toward the subtle.
He is liberated and possesses great majestic power. He is well able to subdue internal and external enemies and māras; he has a majesty that is awe-inspiring and a virtue that is worthy of reverence.
When that Buddha preaches the Dharma, that World-Honored One manifests immeasurable supernatural transformations while teaching.
To those who possess faith, he need only preach the Dharma; for those who lack faith, he manifests supernatural powers to inspire reverence and belief, and thereafter teaches them the Dharma.
It is inconceivable. This is the Buddha’s wondrous power of non-action; how could it be grasped by the mind or discussed with words?
The gods and humans are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the assembly of the Dharma is even more vast.
They all joined their palms together to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words; the assembly joined their palms to listen with faith and accept the Buddha’s words.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas; this refers to the lifespan of his response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas, as previously stated.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus: "I now speak to you; let it be known to all."
This is Mahākātyāyana; he is designated as "Great" (Mahā) to distinguish him from other minor [Kātyāyanas].
In a future age, he will be able to serve as a worthy recipient for all manner of offerings.
He will make offerings to and attend upon eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, who constitute the objects of his veneration.

With reverence and respect, one is able to make offerings to the mind. The first part concerns the time when the Tathāgata was in the world; the second clarifies the making of offerings to stūpas and temples after his parinirvāṇa.
After the extinction of all Buddhas, stūpas and temples are erected, each reaching a height of one thousand *yojanas*, symbolizing the thousand Tathāgatas.
It is five hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, exactly equal; its height, length, and width are all precisely equal at five hundred *yojanas*, representing the fivefold Dharma.
It is adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby, as explained in the "Introductory Chapter."
It is composed of the seven treasures. The sevenfold merits are what are called "treasures.
There are various flower garlands, meaning various precious flowers and precious necklaces.
There is ointment, which refers to scented unguents for the body.
"Powdered incense" refers to finely ground incense.
"Burnt incense" refers to the incense that is burned.
"Silk canopies, banners, and streamers" refers to canopies and banners made of silk cloth.
After making offerings to these stūpas and shrines, one shall likewise again make offerings to twenty trillion buddhas;
the offerings cultivated during the buddhas' lifetimes as well as after their parinirvāṇa shall be no different from those previously described.
Having made offerings to these Buddhas, you shall be fully endowed with the Bodhisattva path. A mind of offering is wisdom; the act of service is merit.
To cultivate all practices is the Bodhisattva path.
You shall attain Buddhahood and be named Jambūnada-prabhāsa-golden-light. "Jambū" is the name of a tree, and "nada" means river.
The Cloud Island (Meghadvīpa) refers to a tree on the banks of a river in Jambudvīpa whose fruit, when ripe, falls into the water and stains the sand gold;

its color is supreme. Mahākātyāyana was foremost in debate, his nature being like the substance of gold which cannot be changed or destroyed, and his wisdom being like golden light that none can surpass.
For these reasons, it is called "Jambūnada-gold" (Yanfu Jin Guang).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān— these are explained as in the "Introduction Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).
That land is level and even. Because the minds of the bodhisattvas are without unevenness, the lands they bring forth are entirely level and even.
Its ground is made of vaidūrya; its substance is pure and adorned with jewels.
The jeweled trees represent the adornment of the bodhicitta vow and practice.
The golden cords signify the straightness, centrality, firmness, and rigidity used as a measuring line;
they demarcate the sides of the paths, dividing the area along the paths into eight sections.
Exquisite flowers cover the ground. The majestic Dharma-body is like these flowers covering the earth;
it is universally pure. Because it has completely severed all evils and universally cultivated pure practices, reaching everywhere without exception, it is called "Universal Purity" (Parishuddha).
Those who see it rejoice; among sentient beings, there are none who do not rejoice upon seeing it.
There are no lands of the four evil realms—the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras. Those with a mind of anger fall into hell; those with greed fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
those with delusion fall into the animal realm; and those with a mind of aggression and superiority fall into the asura realm. Within the causal stage of a bodhisattva, these do not exist.
As for the reason why there are no four evil realms within the fruits [of this land], it is because there are many devas and humans; both devas and humans are of virtuous nature.
Furthermore, there are the assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas—the multitudes who hear the Dharma belonging to the two vehicles, both Great and Small.
His land is adorned with immeasurable tens of billions of things; it is further adorned by immeasurable śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
The Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty.
A minor kalpa, as previously described.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse to explain the significance of attaining Buddhahood:
"All you assembly of bhikṣus, listen with a single mind. This is an exhortation to listen well.
What I have spoken is true and without deviation. The Buddha’s words are true; I urge you to believe and accept them.
Kātyāyana, you should offer various kinds of excellent provisions to the Buddhas, performing these offerings while the Buddhas are still in the world.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, one erects stūpas made of the seven precious substances and makes offerings of flowers and incense to the śarīra.
This constitutes the practice of making offerings after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.
Regarding his final body—that body which is equal to the stage of perfect enlightenment—[the same applies].
One attains the wisdom of a Buddha; delusions are exhausted and understanding is perfected.
One achieves Equal and Right Enlightenment and becomes a Nirmāṇakāya Buddha.
The land is pure, signifying the excellence of the *pariṇāmanopabhoga* (the environment sustained by the fruit of merit).
They deliver immeasurable billions of sentient beings; their deliverance of beings is vast.
They are all honored by those of the ten directions; they all receive the offerings of all humans and devas throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha’s radiance is unsurpassed; his brilliance, which symbolizes wisdom, has no equal.
That Buddha is named Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Jambu Golden Light), as described previously.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas sever all existence; though they differ in scale, both have utterly destroyed existence.
Their land is adorned with the immeasurable and innumerable. Within that buddha-field, the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas constitutes its great treasure.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly, saying, "I now speak to you. He further addressed the great assembly, speaking so that the multitude might know:
"This is Mahāmaudgalyāyana," as explained in the Preface Chapter.

One should, with various kinds of offerings and vessels capable of making offerings, worship eight thousand Buddhas—this refers to the objects of offering. To treat them with reverence and respect—this refers to the mind that offers.
The former section concerns the era when the Buddha was in the world; the latter clarifies the period after his parinirvāṇa.
After the parinirvāṇa of each of these Buddhas, stūpas and temples shall be erected, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth,
perfectly equal in all dimensions, composed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby— just as described before.
He made offerings with various flowers, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers;
such were the things he offered.
After this was concluded, he likewise made offerings to two hundred trillion Buddhas, and it was just the same. He was born...
The offerings and services practiced after his previous passing shall likewise be no different from those of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* and other [Prajñāpāramitās].

He shall attain Buddhahood and be named Tamālapatracaṇdanagandha. *Tamālapatra* here means "innately stainless" (*prakṛtyavimala*), while "excellent sandalwood" (*caṇdana*) refers to the *gandhamādana* or *gośīrṣa* sandalwood; his supernatural powers, wisdom, and merit will be sublime.
He is so named because his fragrance fills the Dharma-realm.
He is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān— just as explained in the Introduction Chapter (Nidānaparivarta).
The kalpa was named Joyful Fulfillment (*Priyapūrṇa*), for at that time, because the conditions were excellent, joy was fully pervasive.
The land was named Desired (*Manoratha*); the realm was pure, such that those who beheld it felt delight.
That land was level and even, with the earth made of vaidūrya, adorned with jewel-trees, strewn everywhere with pearls and flowers, and utterly pure.
Those who see him rejoice; the number of devas, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas is immeasurable, as explained previously.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twenty-four small kalpas. While the lifespans of the three former honored ones were twelve kalpas each, his is now twenty-four.
It increases twofold.

The True Dharma remains in the world for forty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for forty small kalpas. The number of kalpas for both the True and Semblance periods is also double that of the previous [period].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "This disciple of mine,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as before,
having cast off this body, shall cast off his present body on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and his final body as an arhat."
He beheld eight hundred and twenty billion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; first he made offerings to eight hundred [billion], and subsequently he again made offerings to two hundred and ten billion,
for the sake of the Buddha-way and for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
They shall offer worship and respect, honoring with material offerings and revering with their hearts;
they shall constantly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of all Buddhas, practicing the conduct that arises in the presence of all Buddhas.
For immeasurable kalpas they have upheld the Buddha-dharma; having passed through many years, they have reverently honored and received the Buddha’s True Dharma.
After the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas—from the time before the current Buddha up until after him—they have maintained it.
He erected stupas made of the seven precious jewels, constructing śarīra-stūpas with the seven treasures and raising tall golden *kīla* banners.
He manifested these banner-poles so that those who are lost might find a place of refuge,
and he adorned the halls and dwellings with golden *kīlas*.
With flowers, incense, music, and performances— whether it be incense, flowers, artistic skills, or musical instruments—
they make offerings to the stupas and temples of the Buddhas, as well as to the precious stupas containing relics, the statues, and the shrines.
Having gradually fulfilled the Bodhisattva path—now, since it is said that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is fundamentally without sequence, why speak of "gradual"?
This is "gradual within the perfect" (yuanjian), not "perfect through the gradual" (jianyuan). While the principle may be suddenly awakened to, phenomena must be cultivated gradually;
because they are cultivated gradually, one finally attains fulfillment.

He shall attain Buddhahood in the land of Manasvin (Intentional). It is named "Manasvin" because it is manifested through the power of the supernormal knowledge of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).
His title is "The Fragrance of Tamāla Sandalwood"; he is so called because his wondrous fragrance of supernormal powers universally perfumes the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Dāna. That Buddha’s lifespan was twenty-four kalpas.
During that period of his life, he constantly expounded the Buddha-way for devas and humans, preaching the Great Way of the Buddha to devas and humans.
The śrāvakas were as infinite as the sands of the Ganges. The number of bhikṣus was vast;
they possessed the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and great majestic virtue. The realization of the arhats was endowed with such great power of majestic virtue.
The Bodhisattvas are innumerable, their resolve firm and their diligence steadfast. The Bodhisattvas are numerous, their vows solid and their application to the path of practice tireless.
Regarding the wisdom of the Buddha, they all never regress; regarding the profound wisdom realized by the Buddha, they are all able to advance.
They shall attain the stage of non-retrogression.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for forty kalpas. The Semblance Dharma shall also abide in the world for forty kalpas.

My disciples are endowed with majestic power and virtue. Among my principal disciples who possess such majestic power and virtue, there are five hundred who shall all receive their predictions of enlightenment, just as described in the *Āyuṣparyanta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Names of the Arhats) regarding those five hundred arhats.
In future ages, they shall all attain Buddhahood; these five hundred who receive their predictions shall all share the same name, Samantaprabhāsa.

This account of my own and your past-life causes and conditions refers to the events of the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter, where the sixteen princes re-expounded the Lotus Sutra and established karmic connections.
I shall now speak; having granted permission for me to speak, you should listen well. I exhort you to collect your minds.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Seven: The Parable of the Phantom City.
For those of superior capacity, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Dharma was taught directly; Śāriputra received his prediction therein.
For those of middling capacity, it was taught through parables and the medicinal herbs; the four great disciples each received their predictions.

For those of inferior capacity who heard but did not yet realize, the Teacher again used the analogy of the "City of Transformation" as a skillful means to teach the five hundred disciples one by one.
At that time, the Buddha gave them their predictions. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, throughout the growth of successive eons..."
For a long time, even through mental reflection and oral deliberation, one cannot reach back to the past.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. Regarding the meaning of the name Mahābhijñā (Great Pervasive Wisdom):

as for "Great Pervasiveness" (*mahā-abhijñā*), it refers to the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of an Arhat which, by moving both forward and backward, know eighty thousand *kalpas* and, horizontally, perceive the three thousandfold world system from the first stage.

The Bodhisattva is able to know a hundred Buddha-worlds, perceiving their progression and regression across immeasurable kalpas; from the second stage onward, what he knows and perceives increases and surpasses [the knowledge of others] twofold at each step.

As for the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they extend horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time, knowing and seeing everything without exception or obstruction;
therefore, it is called "Great Pervasive Penetration. Regarding the superiority of wisdom, the wisdom of the two vehicles is... [incomplete source].

The wisdom of the Bodhisattva, who has severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and emerged from the three realms, although it severs the ignorance, dust, and sand (*avidyā-rajas*) beyond the realms, still possesses one final grade of subtle ignorance even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).

Only the wisdom of the Buddha is ultimately awakened, such that the three delusions are completely purified and the two deaths are simultaneously extinguished; because it surpasses those of the Three Vehicles, it is called "superior wisdom."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—
these titles are to be understood as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).

The name of that land was Supratishthita. The Buddha’s name was Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; because he had attained the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) appropriate for the land through his great supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), it was named Supratishthita.
The eon was named Mahālakṣaṇa. The lifespan of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five hundred and forty million *nayuta* kalpas.

"His lifespan is already thus long, and his kalpas are further extended; because the characteristics of time, the characteristics of phenomena, and the characteristics of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are each vast and great, they are called 'Great Characteristics.
O Bhikṣus! [The Buddha] addressed the assembled multitude."
It has been an exceedingly long time since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa;

that Great Penetrating Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) entered the past so long ago that it is as if one were to take all the earth-element within a trichiliocosm—the dust accumulated to form soil, the soil accumulated to form the ground—and take every single atom of that great element of earth to illustrate the vast duration of the kalpas; thus, he cites the entire earth of the great trichiliocosm for this purpose.
Suppose there were a person who ground it into ink; this is stated as a metaphor, saying "suppose, for instance,
a person grinds the earth to make ink."
Passing beyond a thousand lands to the east— traversing a thousand Buddha-fields of transformation and a thousand sets of trichiliocosms—
one drops a single speck, as large as a mote of dust; only after passing through that many lands does one drop another speck, like a mote of dust.
Great! Furthermore, passing beyond a thousand lands, one places another dot. A single dot of ink covers a thousand lands.
In this manner, proceeding successively until all the earth-element is exhausted by ink, one continues in this sequence, passing beyond a thousand lands and then another thousand.

If one were to exhaustively mark every single world-system within the three thousandfold world-system with ink ground from that [quantity of] water, what do you think? What do you, the bhikṣus present here, think?
Regarding these various lands and the lands marked by the passage of these [Buddhas]:
if a mathematician, a master of calculation, or a disciple of a mathematician—
whereas previously "mathematician" referred to a single individual, here we speak of their "disciples"— were to calculate their number...
They are numerous.
Can one reach the limit of their removal? Can one even reach the limit of the worlds from which they are removed?
Do you know their number? Do you know the number of the lands marked by them?
"No, World-Honored One," the great assembly replied to the Buddha, "it cannot be known. The Bhikṣus, the Buddha said to the great assembly,
"As for the lands this person has passed through, these are the places traversed by the person who [counted] those motes of dust."
Whether marked or unmarked, whether at the place where a mark was made or where it was not, all shall be rubbed away into dust;
all shall be reduced to fine powder and become minute particles.
Let one particle represent one kalpa; let each single particle of dust constitute one kalpa.
Since that Buddha passed into extinction, and since that Great Penetrating Buddha passed into extinction,
more time has elapsed than even this number, and moreover, more than the number of these atoms.
For immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas— so many that their number of kalpas is like motes of dust—
I have [attained this] by means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and by means of the power of the Buddha’s self-realized knowledge and vision.

He contemplates that which is far distant as if it were this very day; he views the past as if it were now—this is the Buddha’s supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse. He spoke again in verse because he wished to proclaim the meaning of what is remote.
I recall past lives. When the Buddha himself reflects upon past lives,
he sees that throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, across many kalpas, there were Buddhas,
the Honored Ones among two-legged beings— Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who were fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.
His name was Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, as described previously.
Suppose a person were to grind the three-thousandfold world system with great force;

suppose a person were to grind the entire three-thousandfold realm with great force until all the seeds of the earth throughout these lands were completely reduced to ink, and the entire substance of the earth within the three-thousandfold realm was likewise ground away.
Grind it into ink.
After passing through a thousand lands, drop a single mote of dust. After passing through a thousand Buddha-lands, drop another mote of dust.
In this manner, proceeding successively until all these motes of dust and ink are exhausted, travel from one thousand Buddha-lands to another thousand Buddha-lands.
If one were to mark each point in this manner until all the dust and ink upon the ground of the three thousandfold world-system had been exhausted—
whether such lands were marked or unmarked— and if one were to pass through thousands upon thousands of such lands,
whether they had been marked or not, these would constitute worlds as numerous as infinite atoms.

Furthermore, having completely ground [the earth] into dust, let one particle of dust represent one kalpa. Again, having completely ground all the realms into dust, let each single atom represent one kalpa.
The number of these atoms and the duration of those kalpas would exceed even this. Having thus exhausted the various kinds of earth above in this manner, its...
The kalpas that have passed since his departure exceed even this number.
Since that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such immeasurable kalpas have elapsed, as numerous as the particles of dust mentioned above.
The Tathāgata knows that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa through his unimpeded wisdom; Śākyamuni Tathāgata knows it by means of his unimpeded wisdom.
The signs of that Greatly Pervasive One’s parinirvāṇa,
as well as those of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas manifested by that Buddha,
were seen just as if they were currently entering parinirvāṇa, no different from what is seen this very day.
"O bhikṣus, you should know; I tell you, bhikṣus, you should know this matter:
the Buddha’s wisdom is pure, subtle, and exquisite, untainted and unimpeded. The Buddha’s wisdom is clear, pure, subtle, and exquisite, without leakage and without obstruction."
He has attained mastery over immeasurable eons; he is well able to penetrate all events that occurred prior to immeasurable eons.
Having spoken these verses, the Buddha further addressed the great assembly, saying to the bhikṣus: [He spoke] as follows.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was as previously described;

his lifespan lasted five hundred and forty million *nayuta* kalpas. If one were to express the lifespan of that Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in terms of the Dharma, the five hundred represents the five paths of rebirth and the forty represents the four modes of birth. It is for the sake of this desire that the Buddha appeared in the world.
Having delivered beings from the five realms and four modes of birth, he remained for such a duration of life and entered parinirvāṇa when his conditions were exhausted.
That Buddha originally sat at the site of enlightenment; that Buddha, in his original time, sat at the site of enlightenment.
Having defeated the armies of Māra, the great Māra kings, accompanied by their vast retinues, perceived that the Buddha’s Great Path and the fruit of enlightenment were about to be realized;
thus, through the power of his majestic virtue, he caused the world to tremble, and Māra and his subjects all came forth to battle.
Therefore, he employed this defeat of Māra so that only after Māra had retreated would he finally attain the Way.
He was on the verge of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "On the verge" (*chui*) means imminent; the rest is as in the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
Yet, the various Buddha-dharmas did not manifest before him. Because he had awakened to the Way, seeing the various Buddha-dharmas manifesting before his eyes is called "attaining the Way.
Now, because he was about to attain them, they had not yet manifested.
In this manner, for one intermediate kalpa up to ten intermediate kalpas, after having defeated Māra,
he remained seated in the full lotus posture, with his two feet joined together in the paryaṅka position.
Body and mind were unmoving: the body was unmoving, meaning its deportment was tranquil; the mind was unmoving, meaning deluded thoughts were extinguished.
Yet the teachings of all Buddhas still did not appear before him. Although he had long maintained such concentrated stillness, he had not yet attained the state of Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
Because he had not yet fully awakened,
at that time the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven— specifically those of the Thirty-three Heavens— when the Great Penetrating Buddha was about to attain the Way,
first acted as forerunners for that Buddha, pre-emptively serving as precursors for that Great Penetrating Tathāgata.

Regarding the Bodhi tree: the reason why the response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas attain enlightenment beneath a tree is that, during the causal stage, they gave rise to the bodhicitta and cultivated the practices of enlightenment;
just as the seed, root, trunk, branches, and leaves of a tree gradually grow, so too do they achieve the Way beneath the tree at the stage of fruition.
They prepared a lion throne one yojana high; because the Buddha’s body was large, the seat provided was likewise vast, forty li in height.
It was upon this throne that the Buddha was to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The devas had prepared the seat.
He resolved to worship the Buddha and requested that he attain enlightenment at this very spot.
Just as he sat upon this seat— just as he went to sit upon this seat of enlightenment—
the Brahma kings, the Brahma kings of the various Brahma heavens, [appeared].
A rain of various celestial flowers falls from the heavens of the four classes of gods;
each face [of the assembly] extends for one hundred *yojanas*, with each side likewise measuring one hundred *yojanas*.
From time to time, a fragrant breeze comes and blows away the withered flowers, and at other times, a fragrant breeze comes and sweeps away what has fallen.
Having scattered the withered flowers, he rained down new ones; furthermore, he separately rained down ever-fresh flowers.
In this manner, without ceasing, he made offerings to the Buddha for ten minor kalpas. For the sake of the Buddha who had not yet appeared, he prepared the Buddha’s seat for ten [kalpas].
Throughout the kalpas, the devas constantly scattered flowers as an offering;
even until his parinirvāṇa, they rained down these flowers. From the time he attained Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa, throughout many kalpas, they have constantly made offerings of flowers.

The gods of the Four Kings constantly beat celestial drums as an offering to the Buddha; likewise, the gate-keeping kings of the four heavens and all the other devas constantly beat celestial drums as an offering to the Buddha.
The other devas performed celestial music, and the various hosts of devas and immortals from the remaining realms of desire and form each performed heavenly arts, songs,
and music for ten minor kalpas; they beat drums and played instruments for a full ten kalpas.
It is likewise with his parinirvāṇa. From the first ten kalpas until his parinirvāṇa, for five hundred and forty million *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, it is also thus.
O monks, after the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had sat for ten intermediate kalpas prior to his final realization, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before him.
Only after those ten kalpas did he finally achieve the fruit of the Way. This is the way of all Buddhas.
All dharmas appear before him.
He attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is supreme, perfect enlightenment.
When that Buddha had not yet left the household life—when the Buddha was first at home and had not yet gone forth from the secular world.
He had sixteen sons. Of the princes born to him, there were sixteen;
the first was named Zhijí (Jñānakūṭa). Because the first crown prince’s wisdom was profound and vast, he was named Zhijí.
Each of the sons possessed various kinds of rare and extraordinary articles for play and enjoyment;
throughout their daily lives, each of these princes had his own personal collection of precious objects for use.
Hearing that their father had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and hearing that their royal father had achieved perfect enlightenment,
they all abandoned what was precious to them; they completely renounced all their habitual pleasures and delights.
They proceeded to where the Buddha was; they went to the place where their father, the King, had attained Buddhahood.

Their mothers followed and escorted them with tears and weeping. The mothers who had given birth to these princes, seeing their sons renounce secular life to follow their father into the homeless state, wept as each followed her own son to see him off.
His grandfather was a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), the father of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; because of his grandson, he was named the Grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King.
This refers to the stage of practice of a Bodhisattva.
Together with one hundred great ministers, those who assisted him were the hundred officials of the ministerial class.
Together with hundreds of thousands of millions of other people— all the multitudes of inhabitants within the kingdom—
they all surrounded him and followed him to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The princes, their ancestors, their mothers, the great ministers of the kingdom,
and the multitudes of people all completely encircled the prince and followed him until they reached the Great Universal Penetration Tathāgata.

They came to the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, all desiring to draw near to the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. The great assembly all desired to draw near to the Buddha, to make offerings, to pay homage, to revere, and to praise him;
they prepared offerings with the utmost sincerity and redoubled their respectful veneration.
He spoke again in praise.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet. Once he had reached the Buddha’s presence, he touched his head to the ground to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet.
Having completed the circumambulation, he performed the circumambulation as an expression of reverence.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms; stilling all deluded thoughts and maintaining a disciplined, focused mind, they held their ten fingers together in prayer.
Gazing up at the World-Honored One, they praised him with verses, looking upon him with their eyes and extolling him in verse.

The World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue; the World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and desiring to liberate all sentient beings.
Having practiced for immeasurable billions of years over such a long duration, one finally attains Buddhahood;
one finally attains the state of a Buddha of ultimate fruition.
All vows are now fully perfected; that vow made in the past while on the causal ground to attain the Way of the Buddha has now been fulfilled as perfect enlightenment.
All aspirations!
Excellent, auspicious, and unsurpassed! Praise, saying "Excellent, auspicious, and unsurpassed!
World-Honored One, you are most rare; the Honored One of the world is truly most rare.
Sitting for ten minor kalpas, his body, hands, and feet remained tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving—this praises the concentration of the body.
His mind was constantly serene and composed, never once distracted; his mind was perpetually tranquil and unconditioned, never clouded or scattered—this praises the concentration of the mind.

Ultimate and eternal quiescence; having ultimately and eternally severed the root of ignorance and delusion, one realizes great nirvana and dwells in the untainted dharmas, abiding securely in the sublime, untainted Dharma.

Now we see that the World-Honored One has attained peace and realized the Way of the Buddha. We have now been able to behold the World-Honored One, who dwells in tranquil stillness and has accomplished the Way of the Buddha.
We have obtained great benefit and rejoice with immense joy. Having encountered the Buddha and heard the Dharma, we have gained faith and understanding.
The Great Benevolent One and the Benefactor exchanged congratulations with one another, their hearts filled with great joy.
Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering; dwelling in delusion, they always harbor distress.
Blind and sightless, they have no guide. Like those born blind in total darkness, they find no kinship, for due to the absence of conditions, they do not encounter [the Way].
The teacher does not recognize the path to the exhaustion of suffering; he is unable to distinguish the ultimate path that brings about the cessation and extinction of all sufferings.
He does not know how to seek liberation, nor does he know how to seek the transcendence of and deliverance from [suffering].
The evil realms increase throughout the long night; just as one creates karma while lost in the darkness of the night, so too do evil retributions increase.
The hosts of devas diminish; because of karma, delusion, and the fruits [of such states], many beings are born in the evil realms, and the hosts of devas steadily decrease.
From darkness they enter into darkness; with a darkened mind they create dark karma and undergo dark suffering.
From delusion and darkness they enter into further delusion and darkness, never hearing the name of the Buddha, never even obtaining the opportunity to hear the name of the Buddha.
Now the Buddha has attained the supreme, secure, and untainted path. Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has realized the unsurpassed, secure, quiescent, and untainted noble path.
We, as well as the devas and humans, have obtained the greatest benefit. We and all other devas—
People who obtain this have attained the most supreme and vast benefit.
Therefore, they all bow their heads and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One; therefore, they all bow their heads and take refuge in the Unsurpassed World-Honored One.
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha with verses and offered the aforementioned eulogies,
they entreated the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma; although the Buddha had already attained it, they urged him further because he had not yet taught the Dharma he had heard.
They all spoke these words: "The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma brings great peace and security.

If the Buddha were to teach the Dharma, it would bring great benefit and cause beings to attain peace and security, out of compassion and for the welfare of gods and humans; out of pity and mercy, it would nourish and benefit the devas and sages."
The assembly and the people spoke these verses once more, restating their previous intent to entreat the World-Honored One:
"O Hero of the World, peerless one; O World-Honored One, Great Hero, without equal."
Adorned by a hundred blessings: one adorns oneself with a hundred kinds of merit.
Attaining unsurpassed wisdom: realizing and attaining the unsurpassed, true wisdom.
Please speak for the sake of the world; please speak for the sake of all sentient beings in the world.
Deliver us; please grant us liberation and deliverance.
And for all classes of sentient beings, and for every category of sentient beings,
he provides detailed analysis, reveals them clearly, and elucidates them for them.
May they attain this wisdom; may they attain such true and authentic wisdom.
Whether we ourselves become Buddhas, or whether we should ever attain the path of Buddhahood.
It is the same for all sentient beings; it is likewise so for all other classes of sentient beings.
The World-Honored One knows sentient beings; the World-Honored One, through his great compassion, is able to know sentient beings.
The thoughts held within the profound mind— arousing the aspiration to seek Buddhahood is called the "profound mind," and within this mind, one also knows what is being contemplated; furthermore,
one knows the path practiced and the causes from past lives of sentient beings, as well as the specific path they are currently traversing.

Furthermore, he knows the power of wisdom; furthermore, he knows the power of the wisdom of sentient beings, as well as their inclinations and the cultivation of merit—the inclinations of their minds and the merits they cultivate.
Regarding the karmic actions performed in past lives: the Blessed One fully knows all the past lives of sentient beings as well as their performed deeds of both good and evil.
Having thus fully known all matters concerning sentient beings, the Blessed One...
"You shall turn the unsurpassed wheel; you shall indeed turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it was as previously described."

In each of the ten directions, five hundred million *koṭi* of Buddha-worlds shook in six ways. The characteristics of these six ways of shaking are explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

The figure of five hundred million *koṭi* signifies that with the appearance of a Buddha in the world, all beings within the five destinies throughout the ten directions receive his light and benefit.
In the dark and obscure places within that land, and in all the secluded and shadowy regions of those various countries,
where the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not reach, there was now great illumination. Where the light of the sun and moon had never before reached in ordinary times,
the compassionate and wise light of the Buddha Tathāgata now shines upon it all, making everything clearly manifest.

Among them, sentient beings were each able to see one another; though there were sentient beings within that darkness who previously could not see each other, they all now saw clearly through the Buddha’s radiance.
They all spoke these words: "All sentient beings conceived this thought:
'How is it that sentient beings have suddenly arisen here? How is it that there are suddenly sentient beings in this profound darkness?'"
Furthermore, as for that buddha-field: the entire realm of the Great Universal Buddha,
including all the celestial palaces of the devas, the palaces inhabited by the devas of the desire realm,
up to the Brahma palaces, and even the eighteen Brahma palaces of the form realm.
There were six kinds of earth tremors, as explained in the Introduction Chapter.
A great light shone universally, filling the world; there was a great radiance that illuminated all things, pervading every world within the realm of transformation.
The Buddha’s radiance surpasses the light of all devas; how could it ever be equaled by celestial light?
At that time, the Brahma palaces within five hundred million koṭis of lands in the eastern direction trembled.
Dwelling in the palaces of the Brahmā heavens, their radiance shone twice as bright as usual; the Buddha’s light, where it shone, surpassed all other lights.
The various Brahmā kings then ascended five hundred [yojanas].
Each of them thought to themselves: "The radiance of these palaces now is unlike anything seen before. Such light among the palaces has never been witnessed previously.
By what cause and condition has this sign appeared? We do not know for what reason there is this auspicious omen."
At that time, the Brahma kings each went to one another and deliberated together on this matter. The various devas discussed the auspicious signs among themselves.
Then, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahma king named Sarvatra-trāyī (Savior of All). As for these Great Brahma kings...
The Honored One among the Brahmās, out of compassion, is named Savior of All.
For the sake of the assembly of Brahmās, he spoke these verses: "The radiance of our palaces is such as has never existed before;
what is the cause and condition for this? We should each seek it together. Seeing this rare wonder, he exhorted the assembly to seek it in concert.

"Is it because a Great Virtuous Deva has been born, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world? Is it because a Great Virtuous Deva has descended to birth, or is it because a Buddha has manifested in the world?
Thus, this great radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions. These latter two lines state that the light must necessarily illuminate [the world].
There was a holy seer born into the world.
At that time, the Brahmā kings from five hundred million trillion lands, together with their palaces, followed him;
the celestial abodes moved along with their palaces as they went.
Each took a fold of their robe as a vessel for holding incense,
filling it with various celestial flowers— specifically, all the wondrous blossoms found in the heavens—
and together they proceeded toward the west to investigate this sign; while the Buddha’s light came from the east, the gods traveled from the west.
They saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment, seated upon a lion throne beneath the bodhi tree.
The place where a Buddha attains the Way is called the site of enlightenment; because he attained bodhi there, it is named the bodhi tree.
He was respectfully surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, as is commonly understood.
Furthermore, he saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma; he saw them entreating the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Immediately, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, manifesting the ritual of reverence.
They then scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha; by scattering these flowers together with the Buddha, they manifested the sowing of virtuous causes.
The flowers he scattered were like Mount Sumeru; "Sumeru" in the Sanskrit language means "Wondrous High Peak," and the phrase "flower-accumulation like a mountain" describes their great abundance.
He offered them all to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, presenting the tree itself as an offering to the Buddha.
That Bodhi tree was ten yojanas high—four hundred li in height.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha; each offered the celestial palace they had been riding to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
And they spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us. We pray that the Buddha will take pity on us and bring us benefit.
May you graciously accept the palace we have offered; may the Buddha deign to accept this palace adorned with jewels as we have presented it."
Maitreya accepted them. Then the Brahma Kings,
before the Buddha, with single-minded focus and in unison, spoke in verse, maintaining a unified mind while speaking with different voices yet a single sound.
The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter. The Buddha’s wisdom, the Buddha’s virtues, and his marks and signs are rare in the world;
appearing only after the passage of vast eons, they are difficult to meet.
Possessing immeasurable merit, he is one perfected in knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*).
He is able to rescue and protect all; he is well able to universally deliver all sentient beings.
He is the Great Teacher of gods and humans, who takes pity upon the world; with compassion and mercy, he feels deep sympathy for the sentient beings of the world.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions universally receive benefit; those of the three vehicles and nine paths within the worlds of the ten directions all receive benefit.
From the five hundred million lands we have come, and through the five hundred million lands we have passed—
They have come from afar.

Having renounced the bliss of profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, the Brahma kings—all of whom dwell in the tranquil bliss of meditative concentration—have abandoned that bliss due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light and have come from afar to make offerings to the Buddha, saying: [as follows].
This refers to mental diligence.

"Our palaces were most magnificent due to the merit of our previous lives. For those such as us, because we cultivated meditative concentration in former times, the palaces manifested in this life within the Brahma Heaven are exceedingly beautiful and excellent.
I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will compassionately accept it. I now offer this celestial jewel palace, by which I travel, to the World-Honored One;
I only pray that you will look upon me with pity and graciously accept it.

At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they first extended offerings to manifest the practice of giving, and they praised him with verses to manifest their reverent devotion.
Each of them spoke these words: "We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma. They entreated the World-Honored One, wishing for him to act as a Great [Teacher].
He turns the sublime wheel of Dharma for the multitude,
delivering sentient beings by expounding the path to nirvana; he rescues and liberates all sentient beings,
revealing the path of untainted nirvana.
Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses: "The multitude all speak these verses with one mind to entreat you:
O Hero of the World, Honored One among bipeds, we pray that you will expound the Dharma. You are the majestic hero of the world, endowed with both merit and wisdom."
O Supreme Honored One, we pray that you will expound all dharmas for the sake of the assembly.
By the power of great compassion, deliver sentient beings from suffering; by the power of great kindness, bestow all happiness upon them;
and by the power of great pity, uproot all their pain so that all sentient beings may cross over the ocean of afflictions and suffering.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent. The signs by which a Buddha grants consent are manifold and differ according to the occasion:
sometimes he nods his head, which signifies consent with the body; sometimes he says, "I shall preach it for you," which signifies consent with the mouth;
now, by remaining silent, he signifies consent with the mind; or sometimes he says, "Stop, stop," which signifies non-consent.
Furthermore, the Great Brahma Kings from five hundred million billion lands in the southeastern direction each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as had never been seen before.
Overjoyed and leaping with delight, they conceived a sense of wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter.
They deliberated together regarding the auspicious light appearing in their palaces.
At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Mahākāruṇika. Because he compassionately delivers all beings, he is called Mahākāruṇika.
