For the sake of the host of Brahmās, he spoke these verses: "By what cause and condition does such a sign appear as this?"
We do not know by what cause this phenomenon has appeared—the matter of these wondrous lights illuminating our palaces.
Such radiance in our palaces as this has never existed before; such light in these palaces has never been seen before.

"Is it because a Great Virtuous Deva has been born, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world? Is it because a Great Virtuous Celestial Rishi has descended to birth, or because various Buddhas have manifested in the world?
We have never seen such a thing; we must now seek it together with one mind. Let us see what we have not yet seen and exhort one another to investigate it thoroughly."
They traverse thousands of myriads of kotis of lands, following the light together to seek it; they pass through distant lands, pursuing the light in unison.

In most cases, it is because a Buddha has appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings from suffering; for the most part, it is because a Buddha has manifested in the world to liberate all sentient beings from their afflictions.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces, all set out at once.
Each took a garment-bag (*kośa*) filled with celestial flowers; these garments served as bags for holding precious blossoms.

Together they went toward the northwest to investigate these signs. As the gods came from the southeast, the soil of the northwest was stirred as they sought to examine the auspicious signs of the light;
there they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon the lion throne.
First, he saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath the Bodhi tree,
respectfully surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; subsequently,
he saw these eight classes of beings surrounding the Buddha.
Furthermore, he saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma; on three occasions, he saw the princes requesting the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

At that time, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha with their heads at his feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times. Seeing the Buddha, the various Brahmas paid their respects and circled around him.
He immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha. Scattering flowers as an offering to the Buddha symbolizes planting various roots of goodness within the realm of the Buddha.
The flowers he scattered were like Mount Sumeru; their accumulation was vast.
They also used them to make offerings to the Bodhi tree of the Buddha; by offering the trees to the Buddha, they symbolized the forest of factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Having made offerings with the flowers, each presented their own celestial palace to that Buddha. Abandoning the celestial jewel palaces they had been riding, they offered them to the World-Honored One, performing a great act of giving.
And he spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us. We pray that the Buddha will look upon us with a heart of loving-kindness and benefit us with his merit and virtues."

"We offer these palaces; we pray that you will graciously accept them. Just as we have offered these celestial jewel palaces, we pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will hold us in kindness and graciously accept them.
At that time, the Brahma kings, before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse: "O Holy Lord..."
O God among Gods, the Buddha, the Great Holy Lord, the King among all devas, possesses the voice of the kalaviṅka.
"Kalaviṅka" is translated here as "wondrous sound"; the Buddha’s voice is as exquisite and beautiful as the song of the kalaviṅka.
We now pay homage to those who have compassion for sentient beings; we today respectfully prostrate to the Greatly Awakened Sages who have compassion for sentient beings.
It is most rare for the World-Honored One to appear even once in the long course of time. The World-Honored One’s compassion is exceedingly uncommon. Thus it was said in the sutra.
Only after a vast duration of time does one appear.

For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha; for these one hundred and eighty kalpas, no Buddha arose, signifying that the Buddha-nature within the eighteen realms was concealed.

The three evil realms will be filled and the hosts of devas will diminish. Because beings do not encounter a Buddha and perform many karmic acts that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies, these realms will become congested;
as they fail to cultivate wholesome merit, they will sink into oblivion and the hosts of devas will decrease.
Now the Buddha has appeared in the world to act as eyes for sentient beings. Those who do not distinguish right from wrong are like those without sight;
the appearance of the Buddha to transform and guide them is like the blind regaining their vision.
He is the refuge to whom the world turns, the protector of all; he is that upon which the world relies and toward which it inclines for salvation.
He delivers and protects all sentient beings;
he is the father of sentient beings, one who feels compassion and brings them benefit. He is the father of the world who can produce the physical body (*rūpakāya*);
the Buddha is the father of the Dharma, born from the transformation of the Dharma, the pure *dharmakāya*, who pities and benefits the world.
"By virtue of our past merits, we have now encountered the World-Honored One; by virtue of our past merits, we have today attained the joy of encountering the World-Honored One.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each spoke these words: "We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us."
"May all [beings] arise with compassion!
May you turn the Wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings; may you exhort them through the preaching of the Dharma.
Then, all the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses: "The Great Sage turns the Wheel of Dharma, manifesting..."
It reveals the characteristics of all phenomena; its operation is inexhaustible like the turning of a wheel, manifesting the signs of all that is wholesome and unwholesome.
It delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction, causing them to attain great joy; it frees them from pain and bestows happiness, enabling them to find delight.
Sentient beings who hear this Dharma attain the Path or are reborn in the heavens. Because sentient beings hear this Buddha-Dharma, some attain the Noble Path and others are reborn among the gods.
The various evil realms diminish, while those who practice patience and goodness increase; the multitudes in the evil realms gradually decrease through the cultivation of patience.
Those who endure and cultivate goodness will further increase their merit.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent. Having heard the request, the Buddha did not decline it, but expressed his acceptance through silence.
Furthermore, the great Brahma kings in five million billion lands to the south each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never seen before;
filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they conceived a sense of wonder,
each giving rise within their hearts to thoughts of the marvelous.
They immediately went to one another and deliberated on this matter together. As the assembly discussed it, they asked:
"By what causes and conditions does our palaces possess such radiance? Upon reflection, by what reason does this light exist?"
Now, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Subhadharma (Wondrous Dharma).
He was given this name because he skillfully expounded the sublime Dharma for all the devas.
For the sake of the host of Brahmās, he spoke these verses: "The radiance of our various palaces is most majestic and brilliant. Its majesty...
This radiance of virtue is not without cause or condition; it should be sought through appropriate means. This auspicious sign of radiant light did not arise without a cause;
all should with one mind seek its significance together.
For more than hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we have never seen such a sign. It is extremely rare and extraordinary that it has not been seen for so long;
it must be because a Great Virtuous Deva has been born, or a Buddha has appeared in the world, or a Great Virtuous Deva-Tīrthika has descended to be born.
It was at that time that the Tathāgata appeared in the world.
Then, five million billion Brahmā Kings, together with their palaces, each mounted a palace and came through the air.
Each taking celestial flowers in their robes, they went together toward the north. From south to north, they sought out these signs;
they searched and investigated for the signs of an auspicious omen.
They saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon the lion throne;
they beheld the Buddha.
The devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others paid him reverent homage.
They surrounded him. They saw the eight classes of beings, and they saw the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Seeing all the princes entreating him to turn the wheel of Dharma, at that time the Brahma kings bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, as if in deep reverence.
He immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha as a sublime offering.
The flowers he scattered were like Mount Sumeru in their accumulated height;
he offered them as well to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, requesting that the Buddha turn the Wheel of Dharma beneath it.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha, giving what they themselves had used as a gift to the Buddha.
They spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that the Buddha will accept us who seek the retribution of merit."
We offer these palaces; we pray that you will graciously accept them. We pray that the Buddha will graciously accept what we have offered.
At that time, the Brahma Kings, before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse, saying: "World-Honored One..."
It is extremely difficult to see; it is encountered only after a long time and is hard to behold.
"One who destroys all afflictions" refers to one who destroys all karmic afflictions.

Having passed through more than thirteen hundred kalpas, one now obtains a single vision of them. Whereas previously it was said that one passes through more than a hundred thousand kalpas, here it is said to be a hundred [thousand].
The difference in what is perceived over thirty kalpas is as stated in the sutra: "Only after a long time does one see the Buddha," which means that the Buddha is difficult to encounter.
Furthermore, regarding the "one hundred and thirty": the twelve cycles of rebirth constitute the realm of sentient beings; once one transcends these twelve, one sees the Buddha.

He fills all sentient beings who are hungry and thirsty with the rain of Dharma. To those sentient beings who are parched by the lack of the moisture of Dharma, he causes them all to be fully satisfied with the great rain of the Great Dharma.
Those immeasurable wisdoms never before seen, and those immeasurable, most profound [teachings] never before beheld—[he reveals them].
The wise encounter one like the udumbara flower only today; a Buddha is difficult to behold, like a rare and auspicious blossom,
which is encountered for the first time this very day.
Because our various palaces have been graced by this light, they have become magnificently adorned. Beholding this rare occurrence, we offer them as a gift through complete renunciation.
O World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, we pray that you will graciously accept them. We seek the Buddha’s acceptance so that merit may arise.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each spoke these words: "We only pray that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Having first extended offerings and praise, they then added this exhortation.
May all those in the world—gods, Māras, and Brahmās; Māra-kings and Brahma-kings;
śramaṇas, renunciants, and students;
brāhmaṇas, and householders of pure conduct—[be inspired].

All have attained peace and stability, and achieved liberation. Before hearing the Dharma, their minds were not at ease; having heard it, their hearts are now tranquil, and they have attained deliverance from birth and death.
Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse: "We pray that the Honored One among gods and men... I pray.
He who is revered by all devas and humans turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
its circulation is inexhaustible, and thus it is called "turning the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma," which is without superior.
He strikes the great Dharma drum; because the four elements strike one another to produce sounds that expound all dharmas, it is called the "Great Dharma Drum.

He also blows the Great Dharma conch; because the sound of the conch changes its designations according to the capacities of beings, turning them into the Buddha’s non-fixed teachings, it is called "blowing."
The Dharma Conch:
Universally raining down the great rain of the Dharma. The Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is like rain that universally moistens all, delivering immeasurable sentient beings.
Beating the drum and blowing the conch, turning the wheel and raining down the rain—may there be the universal vow to deliver and liberate all.
“Sentient beings!
We all turn to you in supplication: please manifest the profound and far-reaching sound. We all together take refuge and entreat you:
for the sake of the multitude, please manifest the profound and far-reaching Dharma-sound.”
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent; it was likewise so for the southwest and even down to the nadir.
Although there are ten directions, the sutra clarifies only the east, southeast, south, and zenith;
the remaining directions—the southwest, west, northwest, north, northeast, and nadir—are omitted for brevity.

Therefore it is said: "Even unto the various heavenly kings, upon seeing the light, they deliberated together and each came from their respective quarters to pay homage to the Buddha, scatter flowers, offer palaces, and entreat him;
each case was exactly like this. At that time, the Great Brahma Kings of five million billion lands in the upper direction all beheld their own abodes.
The radiance and majesty of their palaces were such as they had never known before; they leaped for joy and felt a sense of wonder.
Seeing these miraculous signs, their hearts were filled with delight.
They immediately went to one another and deliberated upon this matter: "By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance?"
To infer the reason for this:
at that time, there was among that assembly a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin—here translated as "King of the Fire-Brahmā Heaven.
Because of his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he transformed his many lustful thoughts into the fire of wisdom; therefore, he is called Śikhin.
For the sake of the assembly of Brahmās, he spoke these verses: "By what causes and conditions do we now [experience this]?
By what causes and conditions, for which we are currently unaware, have these palaces in which we dwell [come to be as they are]?"
The majesty, radiance, and splendor of his adornments were unprecedented; the various ornaments of his majestic radiance were such as had never existed before.
Such wondrous marks as these had never been heard of or seen before; such wondrous marks as these had never been seen before.

"Is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world? Is it because a celestial seer (ṛṣi) has descended into the world, or because a Fruition-Buddha (phala-buddha) has manifested among humanity?
At that time, five hundred trillion Brahmā kings, together with their palaces, each mounted a palace and departed from there.
They came from the void,
each carrying various celestial flowers in their robes, intending to scatter them over the Buddha.
Together they proceeded toward the lower direction to investigate this sign, searching for the miraculous omen from above down to below.
They saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne;
thus they beheld the Buddha.
The devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others paid him reverent homage.
They surrounded him and beheld the fourfold assembly.
They also saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, and they saw all the princes entreating the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

At that time, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha with their heads at his feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, manifesting their diligent and profound respect.
He immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha. Scattering flowers as an offering to the Buddha symbolizes the cultivation of pure merit within the realm of the Buddha.
The flowers scattered were like Mount Sumeru; the causes accumulated thereby are thus high and vast.
They also made offerings to the Bodhi tree of the Buddha, presenting the tree to the Buddha and requesting him to attain perfect enlightenment therein.
Having offered the flowers, each presented their own palace to that Buddha; by offering the flowers and the palaces, they cultivated their share of merit.

And they spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us. We pray that the Buddha, seeing us, will give rise to a heart of pity, accept our offering, and bring about merit and benefit for us."
"May you graciously accept the palaces we have offered as our dwelling place. May the Buddha, out of his great compassion, deign to accept the personal palaces we have offered.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma kings with one mind and in unison spoke in verse: "Excellent! To behold..."

The Buddhas, the holy Honored Ones who save the world. Excellent! The Tathāgatas of Right View, the great holy Honored Ones who protect the world, are able to urge all sentient beings out from the prison of the triple world, and to urge them within the prison of birth and death in the triple world.
He exhorts sentient beings to attain liberation.

The Honored One among gods and humans, possessed of universal wisdom, takes pity on the various classes of living beings. The Buddha, the Honored One among gods and humans, whose wisdom is universal, takes pity on the classes of living beings who are like sprouts of goodness.
He is able to open the gate of the ambrosia to universally deliver all beings. Ambrosia is the medicine of immortality for the devas;

the Buddha opens the gift of Dharma to enable liberation from birth and death, which is called "ambrosia. To provide impartial protection and succor for all sentient beings is called "universal deliverance."
In the past, immeasurable kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha. Throughout the incalculable number of kalpas in former times, they all passed away empty, with no Buddha appearing in the world.
When the World-Honored One had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness. When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, had not yet emerged in the world, the ten...
The various lands will remain perpetually shrouded in darkness;

the three evil realms will increase, as will the Asuras. In this world, lacking a teacher, sentient beings will fall into confusion, and evil retributions—along with the class of Asuras—will flourish.

The hosts of devas gradually diminish as deaths increase and many fall into the evil realms. Even though these devas indulge in sensual desires, when their merit is exhausted and they pass away, they are mostly reborn within the evil realms.
This is because they do not hear the Dharma from the Buddha and constantly perform unwholesome deeds; due to not hearing the True Dharma from the Buddha, they constantly...
Engaging in unwholesome deeds of the world,
their physical strength, wisdom, and so forth will all diminish; their complexion, vitality, and wisdom will all utterly decrease.

Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness. Because of these evil causes and conditions of various sinful karmas, they lose the retribution of happiness as well as the perception of happiness.
Abiding in the teachings of false views, they do not recognize virtuous conduct; they abide within the teachings of the heterodox paths and false views.
They recognize the rules for cultivating wholesome conduct and decorum;
yet, not being transformed by the Buddha, they constantly fall into evil realms. Not being transformed by the path of the Tathāgata, they perpetually fall and remain within the midst of evil realms.
The Buddha is the eye of the world; he appears only after a long, distant time. The Buddha acts as the eye for the people and devas of the world;
he manifests only after the passage of many kalpas.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he appears in the world; it is for the sake of pitying sentient beings that he has appeared in the world.
Transcending to achieve perfect enlightenment— transcending all three vehicles and the six realms of existence to accomplish unsurpassed,
right, and equal awakening— we are deeply moved with joy; we are truly delighted and offer our congratulations.

Furthermore, all other assemblies marveled at this unprecedented event with joy and praise. The remaining fourfold assembly, along with the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, rejoiced and extolled it as something never before seen.
Our various palaces have been magnificently adorned by the power of this light. We have come riding upon our celestial chariots and precious palaces, which have likewise been graced by it.
The Buddha’s radiance is thus adorned with exquisite beauty.
I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will compassionately accept it. I now present this palace to the World-Honored One;
I pray that you will compassionately accept it for my sake.
May all the merit from this— namely, the merit derived from these acts of prostration, reverence, scattering flowers, and offering to the hall—
be universally extended to all; may it reach everywhere to benefit all beings.
We and all sentient beings—we and all sentient beings within the dharma-realm—shall together attain the path of Buddhahood;
for the mutual benefit of self and others, we shall together achieve the path of Buddhahood.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, having praised the Buddha with verses, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma; we entreat the World-Honored One to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma."
It brings great peace and security; it grants peace to those whose minds were not yet at peace. It brings great liberation;
it delivers from birth and death those who have not yet been delivered.
At that time, the Brahma Kings spoke in verse: "The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma! The Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma to crush [the defilements]..."

It extinguishes afflictions and beats the Dharma drum of ambrosia. That which can remove the burning heat is called "ambrosia," and that which awakens those who are昏沉 (stupefied) is called "beating the Dharma drum."
He delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction. Turning the wheel and beating the drum, he does so entirely for the sake of delivering living beings.
He reveals the path to nirvana; he reveals the path of quiescence for devas and humans.
I only pray that you will accept my invitation; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my exhortation, with a great and subtle voice, with all manner of vast, subtle, and wondrous sounds.
Out of compassion, you have expounded it; out of pity for us, you have proclaimed it—the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable eons, the Dharma cultivated since time immemorial.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahma kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes;
the Buddha accepted the earnest and diligent exhortations of the multitude.

Thereupon, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects. Regarding the "three revolutions": first, the revolution of demonstration, which clarifies the Four Noble Truths as the law of cause and effect;
second, the revolution of exhortation to practice, which clarifies that the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is what should be studied;

third, the revolution of realization through testimony, which clarifies that the wheel of the Four Noble Truths has been cultivated and realized by him. Because these three revolutions of the Four Noble Truths constitute twelve aspects, it is called the "twelvefold aspect."
Because the characteristics of the Dharma revolve in a cycle like the turning of a wheel, it is called the "Dharma Wheel.
This applies to śramaṇas— the monastic community—
as well as to brāhmaṇas— lay practitioners of pure conduct.
Whether it be the gods of Māra, the Brahmās, or the various devas, the Lord of Māra, or the King Brahmā,
as well as others in the world and all other people throughout the world.
That which cannot be overturned—the supramundane Dharma—can only be turned by the Buddha and not by the world.
That is to say, it is suffering. One declares that all mundane phenomena are entirely suffering, shifting and passing away from moment to moment, without even a brief moment of peace.
This is the origin of suffering. The two types of accumulation—karma and afflictions—reside within one's person and are capable of summoning the retribution of suffering.
This is the cessation of suffering. Untainted nirvana is the dharma that brings about the cessation of suffering.

This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. The three trainings and the eightfold right path constitute the way to extinguish suffering. Knowing suffering and abandoning its origin, one cultivates the path toward cessation;
this is precisely the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, both mundane and supramundane. Suffering as the fruit and the origin as the cause constitute mundane cause and effect.
Cessation as the fruit and the path as the cause constitute supramundane cause and effect.
Furthermore, the detailed exposition of the twelve links of dependent origination states: ignorance conditions volitional formations; conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise.
Volitional formations condition consciousness; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). With consciousness as a condition, there arise the four aggregates (*skandha*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

these are "name" (*nāma*), which exists merely as a designation. Only the single aggregate of form (*rūpa*) is tangible, namely the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). When name and form are discussed together, they are termed the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). By means of the five aggregates as conditions, the six faculties arise that are able to enter into their respective objects.
The six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*). Depending on the gates of the six faculties, one comes into contact with the six objects.
Contact conditions feeling: because of the condition of contact, there arises feeling, which is the mind’s experiencing.
Feeling conditions craving: because of the condition of experiencing, there arises the mind of craving and delight.
Craving conditions grasping: because of the condition of craving and delight, there arises the mind of grasping and seeking.
Taking up clinging as a condition, there is becoming; because one seeks through clinging, karma arises.
With becoming as a condition, there is birth; because karma has accumulated as a condition, the form of retribution arises.

With birth as a condition, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; because birth has arisen as a condition, there consequently come about old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.

Affliction constantly follows that body; herein, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of the past; consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the fruits of the present;
craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are the causes of the future; and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the fruits of the future.

Furthermore, these five members—ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and becoming—belong to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, and birth belong to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Old age and death—these seven factors belong to the truth of suffering.
When ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if ignorance does not exist, no faults arise, and thus unwholesome conduct ceases.
With the cessation of formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) ceases. When unwholesome formations are not practiced, deluded consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases. Because consciousness enters the womb, name-and-form arises; when deluded consciousness does not arise, name-and-form ceases.

With the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) cease. From name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; when name-and-form does not arise, the six sense bases cease.

With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) ceases. Because the six sense bases exist, there is contact with external objects; when the six sense bases do not arise, contact does not occur.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; since contact does not arise, the characteristic of feeling ceases.
With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; without the mind’s grasping through feeling, the characteristic of craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*) ceases. When there is no mind of delight and the apprehension of signs (*nimitta*) ceases, grasping ceases.
With the cessation of grasping, existence (*bhava*) ceases. When there is no mind of attachment, how could karma exist? Thus, existence ceases.
When existence ceases, birth ceases. Since birth arises dependent on karma, once that karma has perished, the characteristic of birth ceases.
When birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Because old age and death exist dependent on birth, if one does not undergo birth, who would grow old and die?
Thus, with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. This is the first [link].

The former clarifies the principle of arising: that the production of phenomena has suffering as its condition, and they arise through mutual dependence. Now it clarifies the principle of cessation: that the cessation of phenomena has the Path as its condition.
By means of the Truth of the Path, one ceases the twelve links of dependent origination and realizes the bliss of nirvana.

Thus, the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination differ only in their mode of presentation—whether expanded or condensed. The twelve factors of arising are themselves the two truths of Suffering and Accumulation.
The dharma of cessation is the Truth of Cessation;

these are the two truths of the Path and Cessation. When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans—and when the Great Penetrating Buddha preached these Four Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination within that great assembly—
Six hundred trillion nayutas of people were those whose faculties were ready;
because they did not grasp at any phenomena, all afflictions— which arise from grasping— ceased, and because they did not grasp,
things did not obstruct their minds.

Their minds are liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). Having untied the bonds regarding all worldly objects associated with outflows, they attain mastery over their own minds and achieve profound, wondrous meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
As for the mundane, preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka-samādhi*) cultivated by ordinary worldlings—the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*)—they are merely...
Being unable to eradicate the underlying afflictions is called the coarse and shallow state of a noble one on the level of fruition;
whereas severing the delusions of views and thoughts to perceive the principle of the True Dharma is called the profound and wondrous bliss of meditative stillness.
He possessed the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, as described previously in the introductory chapter.
Regarding the second, third, and fourth occasions of preaching the Dharma, these refer to the assemblies present at those times of preaching.
The assembly of sentient beings who heard the Dharma— numbering as many as hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of *Gaṅgā* rivers—
likewise, by not grasping at any phenomena, from the second assembly through the fourth, just as in the first assembly,
remained empty and quiescent in their minds regarding the non-grasping of dharmas, perceiving nothing whatsoever.

Thereupon, his mind attained liberation from all outflows (*āsrava*). Within the three realms and amidst all phenomena subject to outflows, his mind attained sovereign mastery and was liberated from birth and death.
From that time forward, from the fourth assembly until the very end.
The assembly of śrāvakas—those members of the śrāvaka community who have attained the Way—are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; this speaks of their great number.
At that time, there were sixteen princes; these were the sixteen sons [the Buddha had] before he left the household life.
All of them left the household life as youths. With their bodies still in the state of childhood, they followed their fathers to renounce the world and became śrāmaṇeras.

This term [śrāmaṇera] is translated here as "one who rests from cruelty and practices kindness," referring to those who leave home with a beginner's mind to extinguish all evils and diligently cultivate benevolence and compassion.
Their faculties are keen and penetrating; they have attained sharp mastery over the gates of the six sense organs.
Their wisdom is clear and lucid; they possess great wisdom and a mind-ground that is perfectly enlightened.
They have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; in the past, they have already served many Buddhas.
They purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Through pure cultivation of the holy life, they sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Making offerings to the Buddhas and practicing, they deeply planted roots of goodness, aspiring for bodhi and seeking to attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
They all addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One," speaking with one voice to the Buddha:
"These immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great virtuous śrāvakas—this entire assembly of great śrāvakas endowed with majestic power."
All have already achieved it. Those six million billion who have attained Arhatship by not grasping at dharmas are called "those who have achieved it.
World-Honored One, you should likewise do so for us; we pray that the Buddha will also do so for us, the princes.
The teaching of the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— the method of practice for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
is precisely the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices.
Having heard this, we shall all practice and train together; having heard this Dharma, we shall all cultivate and study it within it.
World-Honored One, this is our aspiration; this is the vow established by us, the princes.

The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision: that which is intended by the profound mind for the sake of seeking the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision, and the resolve to seek the Buddha-way, is called "that which is intended by the profound mind. To seek within the Buddha and not other vehicles is what is meant by this.
The Buddha knows this through his own realization. By the power of his supernormal knowledges, the Buddha himself knows my mind and acts as my witness.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King was the grandfather of the Prince and the father of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.

Among the eighty trillion people in the retinue he led, the king, having approached the Buddha with his followers, saw that the sixteen princes had left the household life; upon seeing this, his heart was filled with joy.
He also sought to leave the household life and informed his king of his desire to renounce the world.
The king immediately granted his permission; at that time, the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) gave his consent.
Then, that Buddha, the Greatly Penetrating Tathāgata (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), [appeared].
He accepted the invitation of the śrāmaṇeras; he accepted the invitation of the sixteen sons who were śrāmaṇeras.
After two thousand kalpas had passed, he first preached the Three Vehicles and only thereafter spoke of the Sublime.
Then, amidst the fourfold assembly, the Buddha sat upon the lion throne in the midst of the multitude.
This Mahāyāna sūtra is spoken. The term "Mahāyāna" is used to distinguish it from the Hīnayāna teachings.
It is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas, as explained in the "Introductory Chapter."
Having spoken this sutra— having finished speaking the Lotus Sutra—
the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and desiring to achieve perfect enlightenment, [proceeded].
They all together received and upheld it; they received it by the power of faith and upheld it by the power of mindfulness.
They recited it until they were thoroughly proficient. To recite slowly is called "feng" (intoning), and to recite with a direct, clear voice is called "song" (chanting).
When this sutra was being spoken—that is, when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū spoke this Lotus Sutra—[they did so].

There were sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras. Although a śrāmaṇera typically receives only the ten precepts and belongs to the Hīnayāna, these are called "bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras" because they seek the Buddha-way and practice the path of the Mahāyāna.
They all received it with faith; they all accepted and took up the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* with a faithful mind.

Even among the assembly of śrāvakas there were those who believed and understood; although they were śrāvakas, upon encountering the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were some among them who gave rise to faith and understanding.
As for the remaining sentient beings, there are thousands of millions of billions of kinds. While it is commonly said that there are ten kinds or twelve categories of sentient beings,
this present sutra speaks of "thousands of millions of billions of kinds," which refers to the fact that the various capacities and natures of sentient beings are manifold and not uniform.

They all gave rise to doubt and confusion. Because these individuals were beginners whose faculties and powers were shallow, they could not understand the profound and subtle teaching when it was expounded;
thus, their suspicion was that this might be the teaching of a demon intended to disturb and confuse them, much like those who withdrew from their seats on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
When the Buddha preached this sutra—this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—it was never interrupted or ceased for eight thousand kalpas.

During the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the lifespan of human beings was long, and he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Wondrous Dharma, for a full eight thousand kalpas without ever having a moment’s rest. In contrast, during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, the lifespan of human beings is short.
He exhorted them to the sublime Dharma for only eight years; whether long or short, it depends on conditions, for the Dharma has no difference in flavor.
Having spoken this sutra—having finished preaching the Lotus Sutra—he immediately entered a quiet chamber.
This scripture clarifies the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and exhorts all sentient beings to dwell in seclusion and quietude to cultivate and restrain their minds.
Because the Buddha of the Mind appears in the world to serve as a model for humanity, he preached the sutra and immediately entered a quiet chamber.
He dwelt in *dhyāna*; in Sanskrit, *dhyāna* means "the meditative concentration of the skillful means of quiescence.
The previous mention of "entering a quiet chamber" refers to entering *samādhi*, while the present mention of "dwelling therein" refers to abiding in *samādhi*. Furthermore, in the passage below...

"To arise from samādhi" means to emerge from meditative absorption. However, according to the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), the great nāga-samādhi fundamentally has no entering or emerging.
Thus, the acts of entering, abiding in, and emerging from [samādhi] pertain to the provisional wisdom of the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).

For eighty-four thousand kalpas, his body remains in meditative absorption; if this duration were to be expressed through symbolic dharma, it is intended to encompass and pacify the eighty-four thousand afflictions and delusions.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his room; they knew that the Tathāgata had entered the chamber of tranquility,
where he sat in silent meditative concentration, with a concentrated mind, dwelling serenely in right samādhi.
Each ascended the Dharma seat; each person ascended the seat for preaching the Dharma.
This also lasted for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*. As for the śrāmaṇera ascending the seat, it likewise passed a vast duration. If this is interpreted as representing the Dharma:

the Tathāgata is the nature itself, abiding in meditative concentration and immovable; the śrāmaṇera is the mind responding to conditions through transformation—this "quiescence" (*jì*) signifies the meaning of cessation (*śamatha*).

Explaining this meaning of contemplation and preaching this Dharma is also for the purpose of illuminating and shattering the eighty-four thousand afflictions and defilements for the sake of the fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
He explained and analyzed it extensively; for the sake of the great assembly, he provided a detailed exposition of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Acting as a substitute lecturer for the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he preached the *Lotus Sūtra* and brought each and every one to liberation;
every single novice monk was completely delivered and emancipated.
There were six hundred trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
"Nayuta" is the name for a great number, and "sands of the Ganges" is a metaphor for the vastness of that number; "six hundred trillion" signifies the purification of the six sense faculties.
He instructs, exhorts, benefits, and gladdens them; he reveals and teaches, providing instruction that brings benefit and joy,
causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and encouraging them to give rise to the mind of the unsurpassed Great Way.
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from samādhi.

What was previously called "dhyāna-concentration" is here termed "samādhi," which is indeed dhyāna-concentration; the Buddha had long dwelt in concentration and has now arisen from that concentration.
He proceeded to the Dharma seat. Emerging from his private chamber, he went to the place of the Dharma seat and sat down with composure.
He remained calm and composed, free from all faults of restlessness or abruptness, and having fully perfected his dignified deportment, he then took his seat.
He addressed the great assembly, emitting a great sound that reached the fourfold congregation, saying:
"These sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras are truly rare; because they are able to preach the Dharma, I exclaim their rarity."
Their faculties are all-pervasive and sharp; the six sense organs are thoroughly proficient and keen.
Their wisdom is clear and bright; they possess great wisdom with clarity within their minds.
They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas; having long served the Buddhas, their past merit is profound.
Furthermore,
in the presence of all Buddhas— just as in the presence of the aforementioned Buddhas—
they constantly cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and perpetually practice pure conduct.
They uphold the Buddha’s wisdom. The Buddha’s wisdom elucidated in the sutras is that which all bodhisattvas are able to uphold;
they reveal it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein. By means of what they have themselves attained, they reveal it to others, enabling them to obtain it as well.
They have entered the path of the Buddha.
You all should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them. By drawing near repeatedly, you will become intimate with them;
by making offerings, you will generate merit.
Why is this? For what reason would one encourage others to draw near to and make offerings to bodhisattvas and śrāmaṇeras,
rather than to those of the śrāvaka or Hīnayāna,
or to pratyekabuddhas and those who follow the path of the solitary realizer?
And as for those bodhisattvas and followers of the Mahāyāna who are able to believe in this sūtra-dharma spoken by the sixteen bodhisattvas, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
and who receive and uphold it without disparaging it— those who with a sincere heart receive and uphold it without slandering it.
All such persons shall attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
all those who uphold this sutra shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
These bodhisattvas do not preach other dharmas; their minds always delight in preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
Each and every bodhisattva transforms six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
those beings who are thus transformed are so many in number that,
in birth after birth, they are born together with the bodhisattvas, constantly encountering one another due to their past affinities.
Upon hearing the Dharma from him, they all believed and understood it; because their faculty of hearing was matured, they easily attained entry into the divine.
By these causes and conditions, they have encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now this number is not exhausted.
Through the roots of goodness from hearing this Dharma, in the interim they encountered twenty trillion Buddhas named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), just as [the monk] Never-Despising did.
In this chapter, twenty trillion Buddhas named Candrasūryapradīpa are described, just as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta);
even up to the present day, they have not yet finished [their work], and in future ages, they shall continue to bring about liberation.
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you: these princes whom I have told you about have all now attained Buddhahood.
Those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha—those śrāmaṇeras who recited the teachings for Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha—"
Now they have all attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have all already accomplished perfect enlightenment and are currently preaching the Dharma in the lands of the ten directions.
The term "currently" serves to distinguish them from those of the past and...
The phrase "one who speaks the Dharma in the future" distinguishes this from one who has already attained Buddhahood but has not yet turned the wheel of Dharma.
He will have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as his retinue, each with their own immeasurable assemblies of the three vehicles.
As for those two śrāmaṇeras who will become Buddhas in the eastern direction, they are the first and second among the sixteen;
the first is named Akṣobhya, which translates as "Immovable Honored One.
He resides in the Land of Joy, which is the Eastern World of Wondrous Delight (Abhirati).
The second is named Sumeruśikhara. The Buddha’s merits transcend all others, just as Mount Sumeru stands at the summit of all mountains.
In the southeast, there are two Buddhas; the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa. The World-Honored One is so majestic and fierce that dragons and ghosts revere him.
The lion’s roar causes all beasts to fear;
this is the second, called the Lion-like Aspect, wherein his advancing and halting, his majestic deportment, are like those of a lion.
To the south are two Buddhas: the first is named Abiding in Space, who remains far removed from all states of existence, dwelling in the emptiness of the dharma-nature.
The second is named Constant Extinction (*nitya-nirvāṇa*). He does not falsely fluctuate, but dwells eternally in quiescent extinction.
To the southwest are two Buddhas; the first is named Imperial Sign (*rāja-lakṣaṇa*). His majestic virtue is solemn and awe-inspiring, manifesting the sign of the Lord of Devas.
The second is named Brahmālakṣaṇa (Brahma-appearance); he possesses pure conduct and manifests the appearance of a Brahmā deity.
To the west are two Buddhas: the first is named Amitābha, which in this language means "Immeasurable Life" and is also called "Immeasurable Light."
The second is named Savior from All Worldly Suffering and Affliction; by means of great compassion, he is able to deliver all beings from the world’s miseries and calamities.
In the northwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña (Divine Power of Tamāla-leaf Sandalwood Fragrance). Tamāla...

"Vimalacandana-gandha" (translated here as "Nature-Undefiled Worthy Sandalwood Fragrance") refers to the fragrant essence of ox-head sandalwood resulting from the Buddha’s supernormal powers and meritorious virtues;
because this wondrous fragrance fills the entire Dharma-realm and none can surpass it, he receives this name.

The second is named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa (Sumeru-appearance). His physical stature is vast and majestic, and his marks and signs of excellence are fully perfected, like Mount Sumeru appearing within the great ocean.
To the north are two Buddhas; the first is named Megheśvara (Cloud-Sovereign), who, with great clouds of bodies, pervades all things. In all...
He attained great mastery within the Dharma.
The second was named Meghasvararāja (Cloud Sovereign King). Like a cloud, he moved unimpededly and, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, became a king of the Dharma.
In the northeast is a Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears. Because worldly sentient beings experience much terror due to their attachment to the physical body,
this Buddha destroys their nests for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to be free from all signs of fear.
The sixteenth is I, Śākyamuni Buddha. "Śākya" is translated here as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren), so called because he is able to benevolently nurture and transform sentient beings;
this refers to the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Muni" is translated as "Silent Quiescence" (Jimo); this refers to the Tathāgata’s eternally quiescent Dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
When the true and the responsive are merged into one, he is named Śākyamuni Buddha.
Regarding the Sahā world-system: this refers to the great trichiliocosm manifested by the Buddha. "Sahā" is translated as "Endurance" (Kāṃkṣan), which has two meanings.
From the perspective of Bodhisattvas, it is called Endurance because they are capable of enduring all adversities and vexations without weariness while benefiting sentient beings.
From the perspective of sentient beings, it is called Endurance because, remaining in delusion, they are capable of enduring suffering without knowing how to escape it.
I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which means I achieved unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, it was due to the causes from our original ground.
Each of them shall convert immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those multitudes whom they deliver shall hear the Dharma from me and hear the teaching of the Mahāyāna Dharma from the Buddha.
For the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and desiring to accomplish supreme enlightenment,
these sentient beings are the multitude, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whom he previously transformed.

Now there are those who abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; even in this present life, there are still those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle and remain in the position of the Lesser Vehicle śrāvakas.
I constantly teach them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet for the sake of their specific capacities and conditions, I speak of various [vehicles].
The intention of the Tathāgata Dharmakara was solely for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle; as the Sūtra says,
"All that I do is always for one purpose," and thus he said,
"I constantly teach and transform these people," referring to all the śrāvakas.
One should, by means of these dharmas—the dharmas of the śrāvakas—gradually enter the Buddha-way;
from the gradual, one enters the sudden. Why is this?
For what reason does one proceed from the gradual? It is because the principle of the Buddha is profound and difficult to understand.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is what is called wisdom.
It is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. When the mind is enlightened in a single thought-moment, one immediately attains the Buddha-way; its merit is so sublime it is hard to believe.
This Perfect and Sudden Great Teaching explains that the meaning of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is profound and difficult to comprehend.

Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were converted at that time, were the beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who had been converted by the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras during the era of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
"You all, O bhikṣus— the assembly of bhikṣus at the assembly on Vulture Peak,
as well as the assemblies of bhikṣus during the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma after my parinirvāṇa."
In future ages, the Buddha will again manifest transformation bodies to deliver them;
these are the śrāvaka disciples. Such individuals as these śrāvaka disciples were all those previously transformed and delivered by him who had not yet attained final realization.
"After my parinirvāṇa—after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa in this world—there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra. As stated in the 'Expedient Means' chapter:
'Except for the time after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before them, those who can explain this wondrous sutra are extremely rare, and those who hear it are also few.'"

They do not know or perceive the conduct of Bodhisattvas; because they lack faith, there is no means by which they may know it, and because they do not practice it, for what reason could they awaken to it?
Thus, they remain deluded regarding all that Bodhisattvas rely upon and their conduct.
Regarding the merits they have themselves attained, and the merits attained through the practices of the Lesser Vehicle śrāvakas,
they conceive the thought of extinction and intend to enter nirvāṇa. Regarding the fruits of their skillful means, they give rise to thoughts and conceptions,
taking the nirvāṇa of an arhat that pervades space as the ultimate liberation.
I become a Buddha in other lands; these other lands are precisely my lands of transformation (*nirmāṇakṣetra*), though they have various other names.
The Tathāgata’s *nirmāṇakāya* has immeasurable alternative names.
Although these people give rise to the thought of extinction and enter into *nirvāṇa*, even though these śrāvakas thus give rise to [such thoughts]...
While perceiving that [the Buddha] had entered *nirvāṇa*, they sought the Buddha’s wisdom in that land and were able to hear this sutra.

Those of indeterminate nature, upon hearing the exposition of the Great Meaning, turn from the Small toward the Great; those of determinate nature, though unable to change their minds in this present life, [do so] in other [lives].
The kingdom seeks to study the Buddha-way and has been able to hear such a wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
It is only by means of the Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction; there is no other vehicle.
Relying solely on the supreme Dharma of the One Buddha-vehicle to advance in practice, one attains liberation; there is no longer any distinction between Great and Small, nor any Three Vehicles.

Setting aside the skillful means (*upāya*) by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma; setting aside the fact that the various directional *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgatas, for the sake of those with the appropriate capacity (*yathā-yogam*), skillfully teach the three [vehicles].
O Bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, or if the Buddha himself knows that the conditions and opportunities for [teaching] have already [arisen]...

When his work of transformation was nearly complete and the time for his parinirvāṇa had arrived, the assembly was once again pure; furthermore, the conduct and karma of those he had transformed were purified, their faith and understanding firm.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, they developed great right faith and well understood it, their minds becoming steadfast.
They thoroughly understand the dharma of emptiness; they clearly comprehend and penetrate the dharma of ultimate, tranquil emptiness;
they enter deeply into meditative concentration; they enter deeply into the dharma of Mahāyāna meditative concentration.

He then assembled the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them. By preaching this Lotus Sutra, he transformed the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, causing them all to enter the One Vehicle.
In this world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; in this world, there are no practitioners of either the Great or Small Vehicles who attain extinction.
There is only the Single Buddha Vehicle by which one attains extinction; there is but the single path of the vehicle of quiescent extinction.
"Monks, you should know this: fearing that upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, the monks might give rise to doubt in their hearts—

wondering why, if there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), he further speaks of the teachings of the Three Vehicles— I have declared, 'You should know,' in order to reveal my provisional intent and resolve their doubts."
The skillful means of the Tathāgata— the compassionate skillful means of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas—
penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings. They thoroughly know the natures, faculties, and karmic actions of all sentient beings,
penetrating to their boundless depths.
He knew that their aspirations were set upon the lesser Dharma; he knew that their minds and wills delighted in the lesser Dharma.
They were deeply attached to the five desires, and with deep intent they took pleasure in the objects of the five desires: forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles.
For the sake of these [beings], he speaks of nirvāṇa; for the sake of these individuals of lesser capacity, he speaks of the expedient means of the Middle Way as nirvāṇa.
When such people hear this, they immediately believe and accept it. These persons of shallow faculties, upon hearing the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, immediately exclaim:
They are able to believe and accept it through their spiritual capacity.

For example, consider a perilous and evil path five hundred *yojanas* long. The "perilous" metaphorically represents the various sufferings of the three realms, while the "evil path" refers to the cycle of rebirth within the five destinies.
As for the "five hundred *yojanas*," one hundred *yojanas* represent the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and two hundred represent the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The three hundred [yojanas] represent the five classes of sentient beings in the formless realm dwelling within the triple world;
Arhats who have transcended the wheel of suffering of the triple world are said to have traveled beyond these three hundred yojanas and reached the realm outside the land of *dharmatā*.

Bodhisattvas who subdue and shatter the sands of delusion and reach the stage of "skillful means with remainder" are said to have traveled four hundred [yojanas] and reached the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*). As for the [next stage], it represents the breaking of the delusions of ignorance and reaching the Land of Realized Retribution (*niṣyanda-kāya*).

The five hundred Tathāgatas simultaneously exhausted the three delusions and realized Great Nirvāṇa; this is called the "Jewel Place" (ratnasthāna), reaching the Constantly Quiescent Light (nityapraśāntaprakāśa).

It is a vast and remote place where no people dwell and which is free from fear. "People" is a metaphor for the Buddhas, while "sentient beings" refers to those lost in delusion who are separated from the Buddhas.
"Far away" refers to the perilous and difficult passage of birth and death, which is a place of terror.
"If there is a great multitude" is a metaphor for the multitudes of the five destinies who seek the Dharma;
"desiring to pass this path" is a metaphor for desiring to pass through this perilous path of birth and death.

It is like reaching a place of rare treasures. The merit and wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata are called "rare treasures," and the transition from the state of an ordinary being to that of a sage is called "reaching the destination.
There is a guide—this is a metaphor for the Buddha—and each has their own guiding teacher.
He is intelligent, wise, and discerning; his sharp wisdom is clear and penetrating.

He well understands perilous paths—that is, he is able to thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of obstructed and unobstructed ways within the treacherous and painful paths that lead to entering error and falling into suffering (which are called "obstructed") and those that transcend the mundane and enter the holy (which are called "unobstructed").
He will lead and guide the multitude; he will lead and guide the masses who are lost in delusion,
desiring to pass beyond this hardship, intending to cross over this perilous difficulty of birth and death.

The multitude of people he leads becomes weary and regresses along the way. The multitude of people is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles; the middle of the road is a metaphor for the limited nirvana.
Although they have followed the Buddha’s transformation, they fear the Great [Vehicle] and cling to the Small; this is what is meant by "becoming weary and regressing."
They spoke to the Guide; representing the assembly, they said to the Buddha:
"We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear. We of limited capacity are worn out and distressed, and we further give rise to a heart of fear toward the Great [Vehicle]."
They can no longer advance; they cannot rise again to proceed further toward the Great [Vehicle].

The path ahead is still far, and now they wish to retreat. Because ordinary fools perceive the Buddha as being separated from them by the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*), it is said that the distance is still great;
because it is beyond the reach of their power, they wish to retreat.
The Guide possesses many skillful means; this metaphor illustrates that the Buddha’s expedient wisdom is manifold and skillful.
He forms this thought out of compassion for those who have retreated from their resolve; such is the reason for his reflection.
These are pitiable. These beings of small capacity are truly to be commiserated.
Why do they wish to turn back, abandoning great treasures? Why do they wish to retreat midway, casting aside the great jewel of the Buddha-vehicle?
Having formed this thought, and having thus reflected with his mind,
the Buddha, through the power of skillful means— employing the provisional power of the three vehicles—
[acted] within the perilous path, that is, within the five perilous paths.
Passing beyond three hundred *yojanas*, one arrives at the Holy Abode outside the triple world (*tridhātu*).
There, a city is manifested through skillful means; this skillful designation of a manifested city is precisely the *Nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
He addressed the multitude, speaking thus to the lesser assembly:
"Do not be afraid; do not turn back. You of limited capacity, do not give rise to fear toward this Great Teaching;
do not grow weary or despondent, nor turn back midway."
This great city—this empty, tranquil, great city of Nirvana—is where one may dwell;
it is where one may find rest and peace of mind. One may act according to one’s will.
To know suffering according to the capacity of a lesser faculty, to abandon the origin, to realize the fruit, and to cultivate the cause is what is meant by "the object."
If one enters this city, or enters such a city of nirvāṇa, one swiftly attains peace and security.
Because one has attained a minor fruit, one’s mind is swiftly benefited; being free from birth in discrete segments is what is meant by "peace."
Yin: If one can reach the place of treasure beforehand, or if one can advance further to reach the Tathāgata’s jewel-light realm (śānta-prabhā-ratna-sthāna), then it is possible to go;
it is also possible that there is the principle of going forward.
At that time, the assembly who were utterly exhausted—those of small capacity who were weary of the Mahāyāna teachings—felt great joy in their hearts;
they rejoiced greatly because what they heard accorded with their own inclinations.
"How marvelous! How wonderful! This is a joy never before experienced.
We have now escaped this evil path; we have now escaped the evil paths of the triple world."
"May you quickly attain peace and security; may you quickly attain the peaceful state of nirvana.
Thereupon, the multitude entered the conjured city first. Having heard this, they initiated practice and entered the provisional, conjured city of nirvana.

Having given rise to the thought of having crossed over, the mind naturally gives rise to the thought of having already attained deliverance—meaning one has emerged from the three realms and reached nirvana.
One gives rise to the thought of security; the mind naturally gives rise to the thought of security, meaning one has already escaped from perilous difficulties and evils.
"Way. At that time, the guide is a metaphor for the Great Guide, the Buddha, during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* period;
he knows that this multitude of people has already attained rest, and he knows that this small group has already entered the illusory city to take their rest.
They rested;
there was no further fatigue, nor any more weariness of mind that had not yet reached this point.
Thereupon, the conjured city was extinguished, and the provisional teaching of the Lesser Vehicle was abolished as the One Buddha Vehicle was proclaimed.
He spoke to the multitude, saying: "I address the small assembly:
you all, come! You must not take pleasure in the lesser teachings; enter the Great Teaching of the Buddha’s Way—come!"
The place of treasure is near. Having now passed fifty yojanas of the five hundred, the Tathāgata’s place of treasure is indeed close at hand.
That great city of former times, that great city of Nirvāṇa on the middle path, is nearby.

I have manifested this through transformation. Seeing that you were weary, I employed skillful means to manifest it merely as a place of rest. It is for your sake, not as a final goal, but only as a temporary respite.
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise. Joining with the previous guide to manifest the Buddha’s intent, I now do so for you—for you, the assembly of śrāvakas."
He acts as a Great Guide. Guiding others out of the three realms is called being a Small Guide; guiding them to achieve the Buddha-way is called being a Great Guide.
He knows all births and deaths, and he knows the births and deaths within the three realms of all sentient beings.
The afflictions and evil paths: the various afflictions such as the thieves of views, thought, and ignorance, which are fearsome, poisonous, and harmful;
the perilous and difficult paths that are long and distant. They are called "long and distant" because one wanders through them for kalpas upon kalpas amidst calamities, dangers, and hardships.
They should go forth; they should be delivered. They must eliminate afflictions and must cross over birth and death.

If sentient beings hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle, even those of inferior faculties should not be taught anything shallow, but should instead be made to hear the wondrous vehicle of the Single Buddha.
Then they do not wish to see the Buddha; their minds take no pleasure in seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
They do not wish to draw near, for because he is so lofty and sublime, they do not wish to draw near.
Then they form this thought; that is, within their minds, they immediately conceive this thought:
The Buddha-way is long and distant. Because one must cultivate the myriad practices throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust before attaining the Buddha-way, it is said to be "long and distant.
One endures diligent suffering for such a length of time, patiently bearing hardship and fatigue over this duration.
Only then can they achieve accomplishment; only then can they realize and attain perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha knows these minds; the Buddha’s wisdom deeply understands such minds as being timid and inferior, cowardly and weak, and possessing base and lowly views.
By the power of skillful means: through the power of the Buddha’s compassion and skillful means,
while on the middle path— that is, midway along the path to Buddhahood—
for the sake of providing rest, and for the sake of allowing them to rest for a time.
Two types of nirvāṇa are taught. Those of the Hīnayāna have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts yet still possess a physical body; this is called "nirvāṇa with remainder.
When the fire of transformation consumes the body and both body and wisdom are extinguished together like the great void, it is called "nirvāṇa without remainder.
For those of lesser capacity, the Buddha expediently expounds these two as "nirvāṇa with remainder" and "nirvāṇa without remainder."
If sentient beings abide in the two stages, or if there are sentient beings who abide in the two types of stages within the Lesser Vehicle— the stage with remainder and the stage without remainder—
then at that time, when the Tathāgata sees them abiding in nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata [acts accordingly].
Even as I speak, even as I utter words to expound for you, what you have accomplished remains unfinished;
though you may claim that what you have accomplished in the Lesser Vehicle is complete, in the Buddha-vehicle it is not yet finished.

The ground upon which you dwell and the station in which you abide have already covered three hundred *yojana* to emerge from the triple world and reach the great city of nirvāṇa within the realm of dharmatā;
you are close to the wisdom of the Buddha. For an Arhat of the Lesser Vehicle, however, the stage of the Buddha’s fruition is separated by only two hundred *yojana*.
Therefore, it is said that they are "near.
You should observe and deliberate; you should observe, deliberate, and reflect that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality.
That cessation and stillness of mere emptiness which you have realized is not the true [nirvāṇa].
The true Great Parinirvāṇa is merely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means; it is merely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that accords with the capacities of you all.
Within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three; within the ultimate path of the single Buddha-vehicle, he skillfully distinguishes and provides the teaching of three vehicles.
He is like that guide—just as a teacher who points out the way through a perilous road.
In order to bring about rest, he manifested a great city; to alleviate their fatigue, he provisionally created this great city.
Once they had known that they were rested—once he knew that the assembly had attained repose—he [revealed his true form].
He then addressed them, saying, "The place of treasure is near. He urged them forward again, saying, "The place of treasure is near.
This city is not real; it is my own magical creation. Because this city of Nirvana is provisionally established for a single occasion, it is said to be not real.
Because existence is spoken of within non-existence, it is called a magical creation.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse. Desiring to restate the meaning of the skillful means of first employing provisional [teachings] and subsequently revealing the ultimate reality, he spoke in verse:

The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas. Although he had previously subdued the Māras and was seated at the site of enlightenment, the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not yet attain the Way of Buddhahood.
The untainted noble dharmas did not appear before him, and he had not yet become a Buddha of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
The various devas and nāga kings; the various devas, ghosts, spirits, and nāga kings;
the hosts of asuras and the eight classes of beings, including the asura kings.
Constantly raining down celestial flowers as an offering to that Buddha; constantly scattering various exquisite celestial jewel-flowers as an offering to that Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata;
and the devas beating celestial drums and performing various musical concerts. The devas beat the drums of the heavens and...
They perform celestial arts, music, and song.

Fragrant breezes blow away withered flowers and rain down fresh, beautiful ones; as the fragrant breezes come at times, they blow away the withered flowers and further scatter fresh, beautiful ones elsewhere.

After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the Way of the Buddha; ten intermediate kalpas later, when the Buddha-dharma appeared before him, he achieved the fruition of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
All the devas and the people of the world felt leaping joy in their hearts. The eight classes of devas and the people of the world beheld [him].
All were filled with exultation at the Buddha’s attainment of the Way.

Those sixteen sons of the Buddha, together with their retinues—the sixteen princes and all their followers—surrounded by thousands of millions of billions, proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was.
Surrounded by thousands of millions of billions of beings, the princes went forth.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling,
he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned. Placing his head upon the ground to cover the Buddha’s crossed ankles in salutation,
he spoke these words to exhort the Buddha to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
May the Dharma-rain of the Noble Lion satisfy me and all beings. May the Noble Lion rain down the great Dharma-rain to moisten us and all others.
It is extremely difficult to encounter a World-Honored One; he appears but once in a vast interval of time. The World-Honored One, the Awakened Father, is exceedingly difficult to meet.
Appearing but once in the course of vast eons,
he causes all things to tremble in order to awaken the multitude of sentient beings; for the sake of awakening all living beings,
he first causes the worlds of the ten directions to quake.
In five hundred million worlds to the east—since the east belongs to the trigram Zhen, the master of movement—the light first illuminated those five hundred million lands.
The radiance of the Brahma palaces was more brilliant than ever before; the splendor of the Brahma heavens’ palaces shone forth as never seen before.
It had never occurred before.
The Brahmās, seeing this sign, came one after another to the place where the Buddha was; the Brahmās went to the Buddha's presence because they saw this phenomenon of radiant light.
They scattered flowers as an offering and presented a palace; first scattering precious flowers, they then offered the palace.
They entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses. They entreated the Buddha to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma, again praising him together with verses.

The Buddha, knowing that the time had not yet come to accept the invitation, sat in silence. Knowing that the season for transforming sentient beings had not yet arrived, he accepted the invitations of the multitude and sat in silence.

It was likewise so for the three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir. [This occurred] nine times in the southwest, northwest, north, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
The devas of the Abhasvara Heaven likewise entreated the World-Honored One as those in the east had done;
they scattered flowers, offered palaces, and requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, performing all such acts of worship without any difference.

The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; we pray that you will exercise great compassion. A Buddha is difficult to meet; we pray that you will employ the heart of great compassion from your original ground as a bodhisattva.
Widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. The ambrosia of the heavens is the medicine of immortality; [this is] the Buddha.
"This Dharma-path is the gate of ambrosia; we pray that the Buddha will widely open it and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, so that all sentient beings may partake of the flavor of ambrosia.
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepted the request of those people. The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom and Ten Thousand Virtues accepted [the invitation].
May the assembly please grant their silent consent.

To proclaim the various teachings of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination— namely, the Four Truths for the Śrāvakas and the Twelve Causes and Conditions for the Pratyekabuddhas.
