From ignorance through old age and death, all arise from birth as their condition. Beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death, all sufferings exist because they arise from conditions.
You should understand these manifold faults and afflictions. Such are the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination.
"You should know that there are many faults.
When this Dharma is proclaimed—when such a Dharma-gate is being proclaimed—there were six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* [of beings].
(Note: One hundred million is a *koṭi*; one billion is a *nayuta*; ten billion is a *prabhedaka*; one hundred billion is a *kamkara*; and one trillion is a *vimbara*.)"
There were ten million.
They reached the end of all suffering; they reached the end of the suffering of birth and death in the world, and all became arhats.
Thus, this vast multitude all realized the four fruits of the path.

Regarding the second occasion of preaching the Dharma: at the time of the second assembly’s discourse on the Dharma, there were as many as ten million *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges sands) of beings;
such a multitude did not grasp at any phenomena, nor did they grasp at any of the five desires of the world.
They also attained arhatship, just as those who attained the four fruits at the first assembly did;
from that point onward they attained the Way, and from the second assembly onward, others attained the Way in subsequent assemblies.
Their number is immeasurable; indeed, their number is inherently without limit.
Even with calculations spanning ten billion eons (*kalpa*), one cannot reach their boundary; even if one were to pass through ten billion eons, one still could not know their limit.

At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras. Having renounced worldly life to enter the monastic order, they remained as śrāmaṇeras as they had not yet received the full precepts.
Together, they requested that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma; with one mind, they all resolved to join in requesting the Great Penetrating One to speak.
The Mahāyāna Dharma.
We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the path of Buddhahood. We, the princes and all our attendants, vow that we shall all achieve the realization of the Buddha-way.
"May we obtain an eye of wisdom as supreme and pure as that of the World-Honored One; may we obtain an eye of great wisdom as supreme and pure as that of the Buddha.
The Buddha knew the conduct of the youths in their past lives; the Buddha knew the thoughts of the princes, including the youth Candraprabha.
He departed from the karmic actions performed in past lives,
employing immeasurable causes and conditions and various similes— utilizing countless instances of past causes and conditions and diverse worldly objects as metaphors.

It explains the six pāramitās and the matters of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). "Pāramitā" is translated here as "reaching the other shore," which refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
The matters of the various supernormal powers refer to the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and so forth.
The path practiced by Bodhisattvas who discern the true Dharma; the path practiced by all Bodhisattvas, which he discerned and expounded as the sublime True Dharma.
He spoke this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He spoke this Great Vehicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* thus...
There were countless verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

After that Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber. Having preached the Lotus Sutra for eight thousand minor kalpas, that Buddha immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration.
He sat with a single mind in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas; he maintained that single-mindedness in one place for eighty-four thousand minor kalpas.
These śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had not yet emerged from his dhyāna; these śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha remained seated in meditation.
He emerged from meditative concentration and,
for immeasurable billions of beings, expounded the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha; for the great assembly, he expounded the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Each sat upon a Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra; each sat upon a Vaipulya-seat and expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the great assembly.
After the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation of the Dharma; after the Buddha had entered his chamber in silent repose, they [continued] to...
They propagate the transformation of the wondrous Dharma that assists the Path.
Each and every śrāmaṇera saves various sentient beings; these śrāmaṇeras, dividing their efforts, go forth to transform and save sentient beings.
There were as many assemblies as there are grains of sand in six hundred trillion Ganges Rivers.

By what causes and conditions does each of them preach the Dharma such that the number of those delivered is neither too many nor too few? You should know that sentient beings are themselves deluded thoughts; these six hundred trillion [assemblies] represent the purification of the six sense faculties.
After that Buddha had passed into extinction— after that Great Penetrating Buddha had passed into extinction—
all those who had heard the Dharma, all those śrāmaṇeras who had heard the Dharma.
In every Buddha-field they are always born together with their teachers; by the power of their past vows, in every land they always dwell in the same place as the Dharma-preachers.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras have fully perfected the practice of the Buddha-way; these śrāmaṇeras have fully perfected the cultivation of all [virtues].
The Way of the Buddha:

now, in each of the ten directions, they have attained perfect enlightenment; even now, in each of the worlds throughout the ten directions, they have each attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

At that time, those who had heard the Dharma were each at the abodes of their respective Buddhas; furthermore, those who had heard the sublime Dharma during the period of exposition were each at the places where their teachers had attained Buddhahood.
Among them, those who resided in the gradual teaching of the Śrāvakas for the sake of the Buddha-way, being weak in power, remained within the Śrāvaka vehicle as they gradually progressed.
I have gradually opened the way of instruction by means of the Buddha-way.
When I was among the sixteen [disciples], I once preached it for you as well. Śākyamuni was also among those sixteen, and he too once preached the Lotus Sūtra for you.
Therefore, by means of skillful means, I lead you toward the Buddha’s wisdom. Because you delight in the lesser vehicle, I lead you toward the Buddha’s wisdom through skillful means.
For these fundamental causes and conditions, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra; for the sake of these fundamental causes and conditions from that time, I now—
I shall preach the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma for you, so that you may enter the Buddha-way; do not harbor fear or dread. I shall cause you to enter the unsurpassed Buddha-way;
be careful not to harbor a mind of fear or dread.

It is like a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, with many venomous beasts. This is likened to the three realms, which are like a perilous and evil road—solitary, remote, and cut off, with many venomous beasts.
As for what are called "venomous beasts," they are as described in the "Fire House" chapter.
Furthermore, it is a place devoid of water and grass, which people fear; it is like a place lacking provisions where those in the great suffering of saṃsāra are terrified.
Countless tens of millions of beings wish to cross this perilous path, and immeasurable billions of people dread the three realms.
They emerged from the perilous path and reached a place of safety.

That road was exceedingly vast and distant, extending for five hundred yojanas. The path by which they traveled was most desolate and far-reaching, stretching five hundred yojanas toward the ground of the Buddha.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed strong memory and wisdom. The guide is a metaphor for the Buddha;
he is one whose learning is extensive, who possesses great wisdom, and whose mind is clear and resolute. Within this clear and resolute mind regarding all matters, there is no doubt whatsoever.

"Rescuing the multitude from perilous difficulties" is a metaphor for the Buddha manifesting his response in dangerous and evil paths to deliver sentient beings from the sufferings of birth and death.
The multitude, all weary, said to the Guide: "The multitude fears the distance of the road and has given rise to hearts of exhaustion. All together...
They raised their voices and addressed the Teacher, saying:
"We are now utterly exhausted here and wish to turn back; we are currently so weary and fatigued that we desire to withdraw at this midway point."
The guide thought to himself: "These people are truly pitiable. At that time, the guide further thought:
"These people of inferior capacity are most to be pitied;
how can they wish to turn back and lose the great treasure? How can they wish to retreat midway and fail to obtain it?"
Regarding the Tathāgata, who is a precious jewel of great value,
he immediately contemplated the means by which he should employ supernormal power; at that very moment, reflecting upon skillful means,
he resolved to manifest supernormal power for his sake.
They manifest as a great city with its walls and various adorned dwellings. Because these are not originally real but are produced through skillful means, it is said they are "manifested.

Here, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is taken as the city and ethical discipline (*śīla*) as the wall. The adornment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) by the powers of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom is called the "dwellings."

It is surrounded by gardens and groves; the gardens are for recreation and the groves are for resting, which metaphorically represent the various branches of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Canals and bathing pools represent the flowing waters of principle through channels, while the precepts (*śīla*) are called "pools" by the assembly of sages.
The place of bathing;
the heavy gates and lofty towers and pavilions: the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called "lofty towers and pavilions," and their successive ascent is called the "heavy gates."

It is filled with both men and women. Men are used as a metaphor for the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), whose function is movement; women are used as a metaphor for the nature of concentration (*samādhi*), whose function is stillness.
Among the various factors of the path (*mārga-dharma*), concentration and wisdom are fully present, just as a multi-storied pavilion is filled with men and women.

Having thus created this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying, "Do not fear. Relying upon skillful means, he preached of nirvāṇa to console and encourage the people, saying, "Do not be terrified.
You all should enter this city, each according to your own inclination. You all should enter this city of nirvāṇa, each..."
"You may do as you please.
Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were filled with great joy; once they had entered the city of Nirvāṇa, their hearts were filled with great delight.
They all conceived the notion of peace and security, believing they had already attained deliverance.
Regarding their minor fruits of attainment, they all gave rise to a sense of fearlessness and security, believing they had already crossed over the great ocean of afflictions within the triple world.

The Teacher, knowing that [the disciples] had rested, gathered the assembly and addressed them: "The Buddha, perceiving that those of limited capacity had attained the bliss of nirvana and found rest, then assembled the great multitude of śrāvakas and spoke to them, saying:"
"You all should advance; this is merely a conjured city. You people must continue forward and enter the Great Vehicle;
this small nirvana was created by me as a resting place for you to relieve your fatigue."

I saw that you were utterly exhausted on the way and wished to turn back; the Buddha saw that those of limited capacity conceived a sense of exhaustion regarding the practice of the Mahāyāna and desired to retreat midway.
Therefore, by the power of skillful means, he has provisionally manifested this city. For this reason, through the wisdom of skillful means, he has temporarily established the city of Nirvana.
You should now apply yourselves with diligent vigor;
you shall together reach the place of treasure. Since you have already realized the Lesser [Vehicle], you must now exert yourselves with diligence.
Together we arrive at the Tathāgata’s jewel-treasury.
I, likewise, am a guide for all; just as the metaphor of the guide applies to the Buddha, so too am I a guiding teacher for all sentient beings.

He sees those who seek the Way faltering and abandoning their efforts midway; he sees those who follow the Buddha in pursuit of the Way faltering midway and retreating from the Great Vehicle to the Small Vehicle.
Unable to cross over the perilous paths of birth-and-death and afflictions, they are unable to cross over the ocean of suffering of birth-and-death.
Because the afflictions are like thieves and the evil paths are perilous,
he uses the power of skillful means to preach nirvana for the sake of providing rest; thus, by the power of skillful means and wisdom,
he speaks of two types of nirvana for the purpose of cessation and repose.

He said, "You have extinguished suffering; all that was to be done has been accomplished. He told them, "All your sufferings have been extinguished, and the path of cultivation you practiced is entirely complete.
Knowing they had reached nirvana, he knew they had all attained arhatship. Thus he knew that all these people had realized nirvana.
At that time, they all attained the fruit of arhatship.

Thereupon, he assembled the great multitude and preached the Dharma of ultimate reality. Within the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, he gathered all the śrāvakas and preached for them the true path of the One Vehicle.

The Buddhas, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), distinguish and teach the three vehicles (*triyāna*). All Buddhas, by the power of skillful means, distinguish and teach the three within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
There is only the single Buddha-vehicle, which is the place of rest; therefore, they speak of two. In reality, there is only the single, wondrous vehicle of the Buddha.
To alleviate your fatigue, I spoke of "great" and "small" [attainments].
Now I shall speak to you of the reality: that which you have attained is not extinction. The Buddha now speaks to you of the true path;
the Arhatship you claim to have attained is merely a provisional bestowal, not the ultimate extinction.

For the sake of the Buddha’s omniscience, you should arouse great diligence. For the sake of seeking the all-encompassing wisdom of the Buddha-way, you should arouse the great mind and cultivate the practice of diligence.
You shall realize the Buddha-dharma equal to the ten directions through omniscience; you shall realize the knowledge of all modes.

The qualities of the powers, fearlessnesses, and the unshared [dharmas], as well as the possession of the thirty-two marks, constitute true cessation. Those of the Lesser Vehicle, weary of old age, sickness, and death, seek only their own nirvana;
they do not give rise to the aspiration to transform and guide others for the benefit of sentient beings. Because they lack the portion of merit, they do not possess the marks and signs of a Buddha.

Those who follow this Way cultivate both merit and wisdom, putting others before themselves and benefiting both self and others; ultimately attaining extinction (*nirvāṇa*) and being endowed with all the marks and signs—this is called true extinction.
The Teachers of all Buddhas preach *nirvāṇa* for the sake of bringing rest. All Buddhas, as teachers of the world, act for the sake of...
Because they find temporary rest, two types of nirvāṇa are taught.

Once it is known that this is merely rest, they are led into the Buddha’s wisdom. Having known that they have attained the peace of the Lesser Vehicle, he then teaches the Mahāyāna to lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom.
Phrase-by-Phrase Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Three;
Phrase-by-Phrase Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Four.
By the Śramaṇa Guangzhao of Qiantang, Shi Wenda.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Eight: "The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.

The "Expedient Means" chapter states: "If among my disciples there are those who claim to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas, yet have neither heard nor known that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas—these are not true disciples of the Buddha. For this reason...
For this reason, the various śrāvakas desire to receive a prediction of their future enlightenment and seek the path to Buddhahood.
However, in this chapter, the Tathāgata clearly states: "The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas; five hundred arhats are included among these.
Furthermore, in the sixth chapter, the Buddha says to the great assembly: "My disciples, numbering five hundred, are all..."
Since it was already clearly established that they would all attain Buddhahood in future ages when the prophecy was bestowed, for what reason did he again request that the Buddha grant a prophecy?
One should know that in the preceding chapter, the Buddha’s universal proclamation was a general prophecy (*sāmānya-vyākaraṇa*);

whereas in this present chapter, the request concerns the prophecy of the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is a specific prophecy (*viśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*). Following the "Expedient Means" chapter, Śāriputra attained realization and received the flower.

The *Guangji* (Commentary on the Light) states that the section from the "Exposition of the Dharma" (*Fashuo pin*) up to the "Herbs" (*Yaocao pin*) constitutes the "Cycle of Parables" (*Pishuo Zhou*). Following the "Herbs" chapter, the four great disciples receive their predictions (*jiji*) upon attaining realization;

this constitutes the "Cycle of Parables. Following the "City of Transformation" (*Huacheng pin*), the Venerable Pūrṇa receives the prediction of the "Light of the Dharma" (*Faming Ji*), while the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and five hundred arhats receive the prediction of "Universal Radiance" (*Puming Ji*). Subsequently, the twelve hundred followers also successively receive their predictions from the Buddha.
In the ninth chapter, the *Aṅgulimālīya*, Rāhula is also each given a prediction; thus the causal conditions for the two thousand śrāvakas who share the same name, Ratnākara, are complete.
Regarding the statement that "the Dharma has no diverse flavors," etc., it is because sentient beings have different capacities that their modes of awakening and entry [into the path] differ.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra— just as explained in the "Introductory Chapter"—
having heard from the Buddha this wisdom and skillful means, immediately referred back to the wisdom and skillful means of the "Transformed City" taught in the preceding chapter.
He preached the Dharma according to what was appropriate, teaching the Dharma in accordance with their individual capacities and inclinations.
Furthermore, he heard that he had bestowed the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon his great disciples;
specifically, the five individuals from the first two groups of disciples immediately received the prophetic decree of attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, he heard of the events concerning causes and conditions from past lives; specifically, he heard the account of the Prince’s previous lecture on the "Parable of the City of Illusion.
He also heard that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign spiritual penetrations, and he further heard that all Buddhas possess great wisdom.

With wisdom that acts with sovereign mastery according to conditions for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle, he employs skillful means to establish the three [vehicles], possessing unimpeded supernatural powers and universal penetration.
Attaining a state never before experienced, his mind leaps with pure joy. He beholds three kinds of unprecedented, supreme matters: first, hearing all...
First, upon hearing of the Buddha’s wisdom and skillful means, the śrāvakas receive the prediction of attaining the Way;
second, upon hearing of the great sovereign power of all Buddhas, their mental ground becomes pure, and for these reasons they leap with joy.
He immediately rose from his seat and went before the Buddha. Having something he wished to request, he first withdrew from his place and approached the Buddha.

He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to stand to one side. Having prostrated with his head in reverence and performed the ritual salutation by touching the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew.
He then stood to one side,
gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without ever averting his eyes; beholding and yearning for the Buddha’s majestic face with such profound attachment that his eyes did not blink.
And he had this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; the World-Honored One is most rare and sublime in his distinguished characteristics.
His deeds are marvelous; that which the Buddha does is most unprecedented."
He accords with the various dispositions of the world; he is well able to accord with the many and diverse dispositions of the sentient beings in the world,
preaching the Dharma through his skillful knowledge and vision, and teaching the various [vehicles] to sentient beings through his skillful wisdom.

The planting of the Dharma uproots the various attachments of sentient beings to their respective objects. Since the nature of sentient beings is such that there is no object they do not crave, the Buddha, out of his great compassion,
administers medicine according to their ailments and extracts the various poisonous roots from all places.
We are unable to proclaim the Buddha’s merits in words; because our wisdom is inferior, we cannot extol all the merits possessed by the Buddha.
Only the World-Honored Buddha—only our Greatly Awakened World-Honored Buddha—[can do so].
"You are able to know our deep-seated minds and original vows; you are well able to know the profound minds and great original vows with which I and this assembly sought Buddhahood.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, speaking these words to the assembly of bhikṣus gathered there.
"Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? He is named as in the 'Introductory Chapter'—is he not Maitreya’s son? Do you, monks, see this man?"
I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. Among my ten great disciples, Pūrṇa alone is the first in preaching the Dharma.
I have also constantly praised his various merits, and I have likewise always extolled the various kinds of wisdom cultivated by this man.
Possessing the merit of wisdom and supernormal powers,
they diligently protect and uphold my Dharma; with tireless diligence, they are well able to protect and uphold it,
assisting in its transformation and proclaiming the Buddha’s true Dharma.
He is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly; he is able to reveal, teach, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly of devas and humans.
He fully explains the Buddha’s true Dharma; he is completely capable of providing a thorough explanation of the Buddha’s teachings.
He brings great benefit to his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life; he is greatly able to benefit those who hear the Buddha-dharma and cultivate pure conduct.
Aside from the Tathāgata, no one can exhaust the eloquence of his discourse. From the time he left ordinary existence until he attained Great Enlightenment, the Tathāgata...
There has never been anyone else who could exhaust his eloquence.
You must not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming my Dharma;
you must not think that this son of Maitrāyaṇī, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming the Dharma spoken by Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas of the past, and also in the presence of Buddhas throughout long eons of the past,
he protected and upheld the true Dharma of those Buddhas; he cherished, maintained, assisted, and propagated the teachings of all the Buddhas.
Among those who preach the Dharma, he is also the foremost; among those who preach the Dharma as taught by the Buddhas of the past, he is likewise the most supreme.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma of emptiness taught by the Buddhas, and the emptiness and quiescence spoken from the golden mouths of the Buddhas—

Regarding the Dharma: they clearly understand and penetrate it, attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). They fully comprehend the nature of all phenomena and realize the four types of unimpeded knowledge:

first, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); second, the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); third... [the unimpeded knowledge of linguistic expression]...; fourth, the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
The fourth is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
One is always able to preach the Dharma with thorough discernment and purity, free from doubt.

Because of this wisdom, one is always able to explain the Dharma in accordance with reality, being precise, authentic, detached from defilement, and pure; thus, there is no hesitation, confusion, or delusion.
The mind is fully endowed with the power of a bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges; it is fully endowed with the power of all the wisdom and supernormal knowledges realized by Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.

Throughout his lifespan, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). In accordance with the life-span appropriate for each of those Buddhas, he constantly cultivated various pure practices in the presence of those Buddhas.
To the people of those Buddha-worlds, he was universally regarded as being truly a *śrāvaka*. Yet Pūrṇa was originally a bodhisattva.

Concealing his true reality while manifesting the provisional power of the marks of a śrāvaka, he was seen by the people of the world at the abodes of those Buddhas as merely following traces and deluded regarding the fundamental source;
they all claimed that the Venerable One was truly a śrāvaka.
Thus, through these skillful means and by manifesting such traces of expedient mastery,
Pūrṇa benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, providing nourishment and benefit for immeasurable capacities and conditions.
Furthermore, he transformed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people, causing them to establish themselves in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Moreover, he transformed and guided countless kinds of people, causing them to resolve their minds upon the cultivation of equal and perfect enlightenment.
For the sake of purifying the Buddha-field, and desiring to purify the Buddha-field,

they constantly perform the work of a Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings. Performing the work of a Buddha according to what the Buddha has practiced means transforming others by means of what one has attained oneself.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa was likewise, among the seven Buddhas of the past, the foremost among those who preach the Dharma;
his preaching of the Dharma was most sublime, and all acknowledged him as the first.
Now, among those who preach the Dharma under my guidance, he is likewise the foremost, no different from before.
Among all future Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa who preach the Dharma, he shall again be the foremost.
Śākyamuni is currently the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa; among those who preach the Dharma under that future Buddha, he shall also be the foremost.
First: they all protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma; this was so at every instance regarding each and every Buddha.
They shall likewise protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the immeasurable and boundless Dharma of all Buddhas in the future—not only for the present.
In future kalpas, at the abodes of boundless Buddhas, they shall likewise protect and uphold the True Dharma and assist in its proclamation;
they shall teach, transform, benefit, and edify immeasurable sentient beings, instructing and guiding the masses to bring them great advantage.
They cause them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, causing them to resolve their will upon seeking unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment,
for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields— that is, desiring to purify the lands where they shall attain Buddhahood.
Constantly and diligently applying effort to teach and transform sentient beings; always and tirelessly practicing the conduct of diligence to transform all classes of living beings;
gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva; thus accumulating through kalpas and progressively practicing until the bodhi is perfected.
The path practiced by this Bodhisattva will lead him,
after the passing of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas and through countless, incalculable kalpas,
to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this very land. This land is [the world-system of] Sahā.
In this Sahā world, he shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and be named Dharmaprabhāsa.
Because the Venerable One, while on the stage of a causal ground, clearly understood and thoroughly mastered all Buddha-dharmas, he attained the fruit and was thus named Dharmaprabhāsa;
his name was derived from his causal practices.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān— these ten titles above are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).
That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field.
To speak of the scope of his transformation, it is thus vast and expansive.

The ground is composed of the seven treasures; it is a land of supreme retribution resulting from the fruits of the merit of the sevenfold roots of goodness he cultivated, adorned with the seven treasures.
It was majestic.
The ground was as level as the palm of a hand; because the Buddha’s mind is level, the surface of the earth is likewise level.
There were no mountains, hills, streams, ravines, or gullies. The violent arrogance of the human heart is like the jagged peaks of a high mountain.
His greed and desire are as fierce as a mountain torrent swallowing all streams; he is as treacherous as a ditch and as deceitful as a ravine.
In his buddha-field, there is nothing at all that is level or upright.

The seven precious towers and pavilions fill its interior. Because the pavilions, terraces, and halls throughout the areas where one wanders are all accomplished through merit, they are called "treasures.
Since this is the case everywhere, it is said that they "fill" [the space].
The celestial palaces of the various devas are situated near the void. The superior grade of virtuous precepts gives rise to birth among the heavens of the desire realm;
the four immeasurable minds give rise to birth among the heavens of the form realm; and the four kinds of emptiness-concentrations give rise to birth among the heavens of the formless realm.
Referring to these aforementioned merits as the "celestial palaces" and "jeweled halls" where they dwell, it is said that they are "near" because one enters the Path by relying upon the void.

Humans and devas meet and are able to see one another. To speak in terms of phenomenal appearance (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it is like when the World-Honored One Śākyamuni descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, manifesting jeweled staircases that reached the ground so that humans and devas in both realms could see each other.
To speak in terms of principle (*tattva*), it is that humans who cultivate supreme goodness attain birth in the heavens, while the various devas, descending their virtues, are born among humans.
In that case, the characteristics of the realms are manifest, and both [the Buddha and his disciples] are able to see one another;

there are no evil destinies, nor are there women. While we dwell together in this defiled land where there are the four evil destinies and women, the Buddha Dharmaprabhāsa dwells together in a pure land, and therefore there are neither evil destinies nor women there.
All sentient beings are born through transformation and possess no sexual desire. Because they are born through the transformation of the Dharma, they have no lust;
because they cultivate and perfect the Dharma-body, this is not a path of suffering.

Having attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), his body emits radiance and he flies with mastery. By virtue of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he possesses these supernormal powers such that his body emits light;

arising from the three trainings of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration, and wisdom (*prajñā*), this mastery of flight is the supernormal power of the base of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*).
Their resolve and mindfulness are firm, and they possess diligence and wisdom; their aspirations and thoughts are all steadfast, and they are constantly diligent and possessed of great wisdom.
They are entirely golden in color and adorned with the thirty-two marks. The people within the kingdom are likewise all golden in body.

The color of gold is yellow, which is the color of the central region; because he practiced the pure and supreme conduct of the Middle Way, he consequently received the retribution of a true golden body, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Great Man.
The sentient beings of that land constantly subsist on two kinds of food, always taking two types as their pure sustenance.
The first is the food of Dharma-joy (*dharmaprīti*); hearing the Dharma with joy so that the mind-ground is fully satisfied is called the food of Dharma-joy.
Second is the food of dhyāna-delight. Cultivating the Buddha-concentration and attaining peaceful and blissful joy is called the food of dhyāna-delight.
There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas;
the number of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas is exceedingly vast.
They have attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), as previously explained.
They are well able to teach and transform sentient beings; because their supernormal powers are unimpeded, they are able to transform others skillfully.
The assembly of his śrāvakas is so vast that it cannot be known through calculation or reckoning; such is the extent of their multitude.
They have all fully attained the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā), and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), as previously explained.
That Buddha-land—the realm appropriate for the Buddha Dharmaprabhāsa—is such as this:
namely, the aforementioned two types of retribution, the primary and the secondary, which have been accomplished through the adornment of immeasurable merit; it is adorned by all manner of virtues.
The kalpa was named Ratnaprabhāsa. Because it abounded in many jewels and was further radiant, it was called Ratnaprabhāsa.
The land was named Suviśuddha. Because the land abounded in virtuous people and was further pure, it was called Suviśuddha.

The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Because the quantity known by the Buddha’s wisdom exists inherently, yet humans and devas cannot calculate it, it is called "immeasurable"; this is indeed an immeasurability that possesses measure.
The Dharma shall endure for a very long time; the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world for a very long time.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—following the passing of that Buddha Dharmaprabhāsa—stūpas made of the seven precious jewels will arise and fill his land. Many disciples will, with the seven kinds of rare treasures, erect [stūpas] for the Buddha.
Stūpas enshrining relics filled the land of the transformed, well-purified realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All bhikṣus, listen attentively!
I exhort the assembly to listen with a focused mind to what the Buddha has taught."
The path traversed by the sons of the Buddha, the path traversed by the son of the Buddha Rāhula,
is inconceivable because they have skillfully studied expedient means; because they have been well able to practice and learn the wisdom of expedient means,
it is beyond the reach of mental reflection or verbal deliberation.

Knowing that the assembly delights in inferior dharmas and fears great wisdom, and knowing that the assembly of śrāvakas delights in inferior dharmas while further fearing the great wisdom of a bodhisattva—
for this reason, the bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the bodhisattvas' transformation bodies appear as śrāvakas and...
By means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
he transforms all classes of sentient beings through countless skillful means; by means of countless tens of billions of skillful means,
he transforms and guides all classes of sentient beings.

They themselves say they are śrāvakas and that they are very far from the Buddha-way; they speak with their own mouths, saying that their nature is that of a śrāvaka and that they are indeed separated by a vast distance from the Buddha-way.
Yet, by means of this skillful means, they deliver immeasurable multitudes, causing them all to achieve accomplishment. Thus, through these expedients, they deliver immeasurable multitudes.
They shall attain the supramundane path;
though they may have few desires and be indolent, they shall gradually be led to become Buddhas.

As for the assembly they transform, although they delight in the Lesser Vehicle and grow weary of the One Vehicle path, he shall gradually entice and guide them with this Dharma so that they too shall become Buddhas.
Internally they conceal their bodhisattva practice while externally appearing as śrāvakas; internally they harbor the conduct of a bodhisattva while externally they manifest the form of a śrāvaka.

Having few desires and being weary of birth and death, they truly purify their own buddha-fields; externally they perform the practices of a śrāvaka and the dharma of minor aspirations, remaining weary of [saṃsāra].
Having transcended birth and death, their inner minds truly sport in supernatural powers and purify buddha-fields.

Yet they manifest the presence of the three poisons to the assembly and further display the signs of false views. Their manifestation of the three poisons is, for example, like Śāriputra harboring anger and Nanda being attached to desire;
their manifestation of false views is, for example, like the three Kāśyapas and Subhūti, who previously served as brahmin ascetics.
My disciples deliver sentient beings through such skillful means. Among the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this is the practice of "commonality of purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
By engaging in the same activities as them, they manifest the three poisons and the signs of false views to entice those who are deluded, making it easy for them to follow along.
If I were to fully explain the various matters of miraculous manifestations, or if the Buddha were to detail each instance of his skillful means and displays,
sentient beings who heard this would harbor doubts and confusion in their minds. Therefore, I shall now speak only briefly, not daring to exhaustively express everything, for fear that...
Because those who hear this will give rise to doubt and confusion.
Now, this Pūrṇa, in the past, [served] under a thousand billion Buddhas; indeed, this Pūrṇa has long been among the various Buddhas of the past.
Diligently cultivate the path to be traversed; diligently cultivate the pure path practiced by Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.
Proclaim and protect the teachings of all Buddhas; propagate and uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Seeking unsurpassed wisdom, seeking the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata,
they manifest as foremost disciples among all the Buddhas; among the teachings expounded by all the Buddhas,
they manifest as the foremost among all disciples.
Possessing great learning and wisdom; having studied extensively and heard much, they possess great wisdom.
In what they speak, they are fearless; the Dharma they teach attains the four kinds of fearlessness.
They are able to cause the assembly to rejoice; they are able to inspire a heart of joy in those who listen;
they never experience weariness, nor has any sign of weariness ever been seen in them.
And they assist in the Buddha’s work; they use minor transformations to aid and propagate the Buddha’s work.
They have already attained great supernormal powers; having transcended birth and death, they have acquired great supernormal powers.
Possessing the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge as previously described,
they know the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of all beings, and they know the sharpness and dullness of the dispositions of the faculties of all assemblies.
They constantly preach the pure Dharma, expounding upon such meanings, and constantly proclaim the flow of the pure, unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma.
He extensively expounded and elucidated such meanings,
instructing many billions of beings to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma, and teaching countless thousands of billions of beings to dwell within the Mahāyāna Dharma.
And they purify their own buddha-fields; though they manifest as śrāvakas, their minds are always pure regarding their own buddha-fields.
In the future, they will also make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas. Making offerings to these Buddhas is the cultivation of the portion of merit.

They protect and assist in proclaiming the True Dharma while also purifying their own Buddha-fields. Outwardly manifesting inferior forms to assist in proclaiming the True Dharma, they inwardly conceal their true mind to purify their own Buddha-fields.
They constantly preach the Dharma through various skillful means without fear, always employing many diverse and skillful expedients to teach.
Their minds have no fear regarding the sublime Dharma;
they deliver immeasurable multitudes and accomplish all-knowledge, causing all those delivered— beyond measure—
to achieve every form of wisdom.
He made offerings to all Tathāgatas and upheld the treasury of the Dharma-jewel. By making offerings to the Buddhas he cultivated merit, and by expounding the Dharma he cultivated wisdom.
Subsequently, he attained Buddhahood; his name was Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Light), which is the name of his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
That land is named Pure Excellence (*Suviśuddha*), composed of the seven treasures, as described previously.
The eon is named Jewel Radiance (*Ratnaprabhāsa*), also as described previously.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is exceedingly vast, numbering immeasurable billions; those delivered by them are many indeed.
All have crossed over, being fully endowed with great supernormal powers and majestic virtue;
they have all attained liberation, and their great supernormal powers and majestic virtue are complete, filling their land.
The śrāvakas are also innumerable; the assembly of śrāvakas is likewise innumerable.
They possess the two types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and have attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), as previously described.

Such individuals constitute the Saṅgha. By means of these and others, those who have realized the fruits of the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*) and possess untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*) are so named.
He became a monk.
All sentient beings in that land had already severed their lustful desires and were born solely through transformation. The land was devoid of evil realms and women;
having severed the marks of lustful desire, they were born purely through transformation.
His body is adorned with the marks of excellence; his body is of purple-gold color, naturally adorned with the thirty-two marks.

He feeds on the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna; that is, he takes the joy of the Dharma to open wisdom and the delight of dhyāna to settle the mind, thereby making concentration and wisdom his sustenance of the Dharma.
There is no further thought of food; there is no further thought of external, segmented food.
There are no women; all are born through transformation.
Furthermore, there are no evil realms; since even an ill repute does not exist, how much less could reality [of such things] exist?
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa has fully perfected all his merits; having achieved and fulfilled every virtue, he shall obtain this pure land;
he shall obtain such a pure land of common residence.
The assembly of noble sages is exceedingly vast; the multitude of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans is beyond calculation.
Such immeasurable matters I now describe only briefly. I have summarized them as stated above, for fearing that hearing them might give rise to doubt, I do not dare to set them forth in full detail.

At that time, there were twelve hundred arhats who were masters of their own minds; these twelve hundred persons had all realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and because their afflictions (*kleśa*) were already exhausted, they were called "masters."
They formed this thought; their minds formed this thought:

"We are filled with joy at having attained what we have never before experienced. We, all these people, have heard that Rāvaṇa has received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, and we ourselves also have our share [of this attainment]; therefore, we rejoice and exclaim that it is unprecedented."
"Would it not be a source of great joy if the World-Honored One were to grant us each a prediction of enlightenment, just as he has for the other great disciples?
If we were to receive from the World-Honored One a prediction of our own deep-seated original vows, just as he has for the aforementioned chief disciples,
would that not be most wonderful?"
The Buddha knew the thoughts in their minds. Through his knowledge of others' minds, the Buddha understood that this assembly was thinking of seeking a prophecy of their future enlightenment.
He addressed Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable Kāśyapa, those whom you previously prophesied, the Buddha now declares to be this very assembly."
For this reason,
these one thousand two hundred arhats consist of the one thousand disciples of the three Kāśyapas and the two hundred disciples belonging to Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra.
I shall now, in their presence, grant them the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in successive order.
"In their presence" means granting the prediction directly before them; "in successive order" means proceeding from one stage to the next;
and "*Anuttara*" and so forth refers to the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya— this great spiritual friend who was the first of the five men converted at Deer Park— is present here.
One should make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas. The number sixty-two thousand symbolizes the severing of sixty-two *koṭis* of ignorance and afflictions;
by following the words of the Buddha, one purifies all defilements, which is also termed "making offerings to the Buddhas."

Thereafter, he attained Buddhahood and was named Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance). Because he understood and realized the primordial limit of all phenomena during the causal stage and attained Buddhahood as the fruit, he was named Samantaprabhāsa.
He is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi.
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
As for the five hundred arhats—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—[they were as follows].
As explained in the "Introduction Chapter" (Nidāna-varga), Kālodāyin is so named because his complexion was dark;
Udāyin is so named because he appeared at the time of sunrise, as the Venerable One was born when the sun rose; he was a disciple of Ānanda.
Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, and Bakula are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-varga).
Cunda and Śagata are also called Cūḍapanthaka; he is also called Panthaka. This translates as "Small Roadside Mother.
She followed her husband on travels and, while about to return to her native country, gave birth at a place along the road.
Venerable sir, those for whom this name was established and so forth— namely, these five hundred—
all shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; all shall achieve supreme, perfect enlightenment.
They shall all share the same name, called Samantaprabha. His five hundred disciples shall likewise bear the same name.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable Buddhas.
In future ages, he shall behold immeasurable Buddhas, serving and making offerings to them."
After passing through incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Only after passing through innumerable kalpas does one finally achieve it.

One constantly emits great radiance and is fully endowed with all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The emission of light symbolizes wisdom (*prajñā*), while the supernormal powers symbolize meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
His fame pervades the ten directions and he is revered by all; his name and reputation fill the ten directions, and he is held in high esteem and veneration by all beings.
Because he constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path, he is named Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance). His preaching of the Dharma is precisely the universal emission of the light of wisdom.
Because it illuminates all things, it is called "Universal Radiance.
That land is pure; this refers to the excellence of the environmental retribution (*pariṇāmanavipāka*).
The bodhisattvas therein are all courageous and fierce; this refers to the excellence of the primary retribution (*mūlavipāka*).
All ascend the wondrous pavilions. All the factors of the path (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are called "pavilions," and the Bodhisattvas' progress toward them is termed "ascending.
They travel through the lands of the ten directions; the "ten directions" here represents the ten realms. They traverse the entire Dharma-realm and cultivate all [virtues].
Regarding merit:

to offer unsurpassed requisites to the Buddhas constitutes "merit. "Requisites" (pātra) refers here to the vessels [of offering]; for instance, the Bodhisattva’s self-sacrifice, King Bhaiṣajyarāja’s [offering of his] body, and the burning of one's own arm are all termed "unsurpassed offerings."
Having performed this offering, his heart was filled with great joy. Having thus performed the ritual and cultivated this sublime offering, his heart was refreshed and he experienced great delight.
In an instant, he returned to his own country; such is his supernormal power. He makes offerings everywhere throughout the ten directions and returns to his country in an instant. Why?
Its swiftness is due to the power of mental visualization; once a single thought-moment has pervaded [all], a single atom likewise becomes pervasive.

When the mind pervades and the phenomena pervade, it does not depart from a single kṣaṇa. This principle can be seen, for example, when performing a ritual of repentance: one visualizes incense and flowers pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and as the body follows the mind, it likewise reaches everywhere;
yet before a thought has even passed, one returns to the original place of practice. The logic of this is evident.
The lifespan of the Buddha is sixty thousand kalpas; the lifespan of his response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is the same.

The period during which the True Dharma (saddharma) remains is twice that lifespan—sixty-two thousand kalpas—and the period of the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpakadharma) is again twice that—seventy-two thousand kalpas.
When the Dharma perishes, gods and humans grieve. While the Buddha-Dharma remains in the world, it acts as the eye for humanity; when that Dharma perishes, both gods and humans all grieve.
These five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become Buddhas. The five hundred venerable ones, in turn, received my prediction.
Because you shall become a Buddha after my parinirvāṇa, it is called "successive transmission.
They share the same name, "Samantaprabha," and are given the prediction of enlightenment in succession: "After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha."
The intention is also as stated above.
The world he transforms is also like that of my own today. Since the one who occupies the place of succession performs the same transformative deeds as the previous Buddha, it is said, "also like me.
The word "one" (in "like me") refers specifically to the present day; this is the meaning of the five hundred [verses].
This is a statement concerning the future prediction [of Buddhahood].
The majesty and purity of the land refers to the Land of Utmost Purity (Sukhāvatī).
As for "various supernormal powers," this refers to the power of various transformations and masteries of the higher supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).

The number of kalpas for the lifespan of the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, the True Dharma, and the Semblance Dharma, as well as the names of the lands and the assemblies they convert, are all exactly as described above.
Since the succession of the five hundred honored ones appearing in the world, their kalpas and land-names, the beings they convert, their lifespans while remaining in the world,
and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma are all equal to those of the initial Tathāgata Samantaprabha without any difference, [the text] refers to them collectively.
"Everything is as previously explained.
Kāśyapa, you already know those five hundred who have attained mastery. The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "I have prophesied that these five hundred who have attained mastery—you already know this."
The remaining assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so. Of the twelve hundred who were previously prophesied, five hundred remain;
the rest of the śrāvakas shall also be so.
You should proclaim this for those who are not present in this assembly today. And as for those who have not participated in this assembly today...
"You, Kāśyapa, should proclaim this for them.
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions in the presence of the Buddha, leaped for joy.
The five hundred venerable ones were filled with exultation because they had received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood in the very presence of the Buddha.
He immediately rose from his seat and went before the Buddha. Desiring to set forth what he had understood, he left his original seat and approached the Buddha’s presence.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, repenting and reproaching himself for his transgressions; he bowed his head to the top of the Buddha’s two feet, confessing his former faults.
It was not that we reproached ourselves for our dullness and ignorance.
World-Honored One, we constantly held this thought: having spoken of what we ourselves had seen, we claimed to have attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, we attained the four fruits and then considered ourselves [to have reached the goal].
It was said that this is the ultimate path;
only now do I realize it as if I were one lacking wisdom. Although Arhats have attained awakening, they may fall back into delusion after having awakened, for they cannot penetrate the Mahāyāna;
hearing the Buddha’s teaching now, I am startled by my own lack of realization, as if I were one lacking wisdom.
Why is this? For what reason do we lack wisdom?
We ought to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata; through our practice, we should rightfully realize all the merits and wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata.
Yet they consider their own meager wisdom sufficient; thus, relying on the limited wisdom of a śrāvaka, they become complacent and do not seek the great benefit.

World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend and lay down, intoxicated by wine. "The person" is a metaphor for one's own self; "the friend" is a metaphor for the Buddha.

The friend is like the Buddha; intoxication is a metaphor for delusion; wine is a metaphor for the five desires. In the distant past, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, they were transformed by the Prince [Mañjuśrī] as if visiting a close friend, whereby they obtained entry into the Mahāyāna and the seeds of the Buddha-nature, like a pearl tied within a garment.

In the interim, they grew weary and regressed from the Great Vehicle to enter the Small Vehicle, greedily clinging to minor benefits, just like drinking wine and remaining unaware through the long night, like a drunken man.
At that time, a close friend had official business to attend to. This is illustrated by the princes:

the conclusion of their transformative work in this land and the ripening of conditions in another realm necessitate their departure to that other place—this is termed "official business. To leave this world and proceed to that one is termed "having to go."
He tied a priceless jewel within the hem of his garment; the seed of Buddha-nature is called a priceless jewel, which now enters the person's body as if tied beneath the clothing.
Having given it to him, he departed, meaning that after bestowing the Dharma, he proceeded to convert others in other regions.

That person lies drunk and unconscious, perceiving nothing at all. Because their faculties and powers are shallow, they lack the supernormal knowledge of past lives; how could they know former events?
It is just like a drunken person who has no awareness whatsoever.
Having arisen, they wander to other lands; that is to say, after casting off their current existence, they are reborn elsewhere.
For the sake of food and clothing, they strive and seek with great difficulty and hardship. Their bodies lack the power of endurance and they are destitute of the raiment of shame and modesty;

their minds lack the nourishment of the Dharma and are deficient in the flavor of the Deathless (amṛta). They loathe old age, sickness, and death as if they were a prison, laboring through ten thousand hardships.
They seek to study the Hīnayāna as one in the cold seeks clothing or one who is hungry seeks food; they beg everywhere for sustenance, unable to find peace within themselves.
If they obtain even a little, they consider it sufficient. Having realized the minor fruits and the provisional nirvāṇa, they claim for themselves—
Having reached his destination, he did not advance further.
Later, a close friend encountered him by chance—this is a metaphor for the meeting of teacher and disciple here on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—and spoke these words:
"Alas, O Noble One! The word "alas" is a cry of awakening; it addresses him as a "noble one."
"You who are permitted as a great vessel—
why do you concern yourself with clothing and food to such an extent? For what reason do you seek clothing and food,
even to the point of undergoing such hardships?"
In the past, I desired to bring you peace and happiness so that you might indulge yourselves in the five desires at will.
In ages long gone, because I wished for you all to obtain peace and happiness, I provided you with abundant food and clothing so that you might enjoy them to your heart's content.
On such-and-such a day and month of such-and-such a year, I tied an invaluable jewel within the lining of your garment; it remains there even now.

On such-and-such a day and month of such-and-such a year, during the time of the Great Penetration, throughout eighty thousand or more kalpas, the analogy of the invaluable jewel refers to the Buddha-nature.
When the Prince preached this sutra, he spoke of planting the great seeds below, just as one ties a precious jewel beneath one's clothing, which remains there even now. This means:
Although the seeds of goodness exist constantly within you, you are unaware of them;
thus, you do not know to strive with diligence and endure hardship and distress in order to sustain yourself.

Furthermore, you are unaware that the seed of the Mahāyāna exists within your own body, yet you instead study the Hīnayāna, needlessly undergoing the suffering of worldly movement to seek your livelihood.
This is truly foolish; it is truly a pity, for you are utterly deluded.
You may now trade this treasure for what you require. This treasure is the Buddha-nature;
that which is traded for is the transformation into what is required—namely, the garment of forbearance and the food of dhyāna-joy.
One may always have one's wishes fulfilled and lack nothing; one may always be wealthy and prosperous according to one's heart’s desire, with no deficiency at any time.
The Buddha is also like this. The Buddha is also like that person who is a close friend.
When he was a bodhisattva, while formerly on the causal ground practicing as a bodhisattva,
he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience; he instructed, transformed, and guided our assembly,
causing us to resolve upon the mind of all-encompassing wisdom.
Yet they soon fall into forgetfulness, unaware and unperceiving; subsequently, they become lax and negligent, failing to comprehend or even to reflect upon it.
Having attained the path of Arhatship, they claim to have reached extinction (*nirvāṇa*); having realized the four fruits, they claim to have already achieved ultimate realization.

Having finally attained parinirvāṇa, one finds the means of livelihood difficult to obtain; thus, one considers it sufficient to have acquired even a little. One cuts off evil and cultivates goodness through myriad forms of diligent toil, yet the requisites for livelihood remain extremely difficult to secure.
Upon realizing the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one then deems this sufficient.
The vow for omniscience remains intact and has not been lost. That great mind formerly resolved to seek omniscience still endures, and until now it has not been lost.
Now the World-Honored One awakens us; now the World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One of this sacred mountain, rouses and opens our understanding.
He enlightened those of us who were like this, speaking these words and declaring:
"O bhikṣus, that which you have attained is not ultimate cessation; that which you have realized is not the fruit of arhatship."
This is merely the Lesser Vehicle and not true extinction.
For a long time I have caused you all to plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood; indeed, since kalpas past, I have caused you all to plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood.

By means of skillful means, he manifests the appearance of nirvāṇa; for those whose faculties fear the Great [Vehicle], he uses the power of skillful means to manifest the appearance of quiescence in the Lesser Vehicle.
Yet you claim that this is the actual attainment of extinction, and you recognize it as the ultimate, true cessation.
“World-Honored One, we now truly know that we are indeed bodhisattvas. They addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, we now realize that our own selves were originally bodhisattvas;
we have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and we have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood through the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).”
The Record.

Because of these causes and conditions—because of this being the causal condition for receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood—he was filled with immense joy, experiencing what he had never known before;
in his heart, he became deeply aware of a great joy arising, having attained what was previously unattained.

It was so. At that time, the five hundred arhats, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "We have heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prophecy."
Having heard the voice of the Buddha’s prophecy— which grants us the assurance that we shall attain unsurpassed bodhi and bring peace to our minds—
we experienced a joy never known before. With hearts full of delight at having attained what was previously unattainable,
we prostrated at the feet of the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom, the World-Honored One endowed with immeasurable wisdom and myriad virtues.

Now, before the World-Honored One, I repent of all my transgressions. Now, before the Buddha, I repent of the immeasurable faults of clinging to the Small Vehicle and being deluded regarding the Great Vehicle.
Having obtained only a small portion of *nirvāṇa* from the immeasurable Jewel of the Buddhas, I have [only] [regarded] the immeasurable great wisdom-jewel of the Buddha...
Having attained a partial and one-sided nirvāṇa of emptiness,
they are like ignorant fools who consider themselves sufficient; just as those ignorant and deluded people consider themselves satisfied with a minor dharma.
For example, it is like a poor man who goes to the house of a kinsman. The poor man represents oneself, and the kinsman represents the Buddha;
in the past, one went to rely upon the Buddha just as one would go to a relative's home.
That house is exceedingly great and wealthy, fully prepared with various delicacies and dishes. This true reward land is the house of the Buddha, for it is the fruit of his merit.
The perfection of virtue is called "great wealth," and its characteristics are fully displayed.

Just as various delicacies are called *yāo* (dishes) and fine foods are called *shàn* (meals), so too is the priceless jewel tied within one's inner garment. This priceless jewel is precisely the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra*).
He then accepted the Dharma, which is likened to the "pearl fastened within his inner garment"—this refers to the physical body as the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
While he was sleeping and unaware, a close friend secretly fastened the pearl beneath his garment and departed for another land;
this is called "departing. At that time, [the man] was deluded and oblivious, like one who has been intoxicated, not realizing it himself.
Once this person has arisen and set out on a journey to another country, they die and are reborn; like one who awakens from intoxication, they resolve to practice cultivation—this is called "arising.
Forgetting what is great and practicing what is minor is likened to wandering in another country.
Seeking food and clothing to sustain their lives is extremely difficult; they search everywhere for the Dharma to adorn their physical and mental natures,

seeking nirvana for themselves without arising to transform and guide others— just like those poor people who beg for food to sustain themselves, for whom the means of livelihood are exceedingly difficult to obtain.

Having obtained a little, they consider it sufficient and no longer aspire to what is excellent. Regarding these meager teachings, they consider themselves satisfied and do not further resolve their minds to seek the true Path.
Unaware, they do not realize that within the garment of their inner being there is a priceless jewel; they do not perceive for themselves the retribution of form and mind within.
An invaluable treasure was hidden within it.
Later, a close friend of the one who possessed the jewel saw this poor man. When the Buddha appeared in the Sahā world, he again beheld those whom he had previously transformed.
Having rebuked him with harsh words, he showed him the jewel he had been wearing all along. For twenty years, he had constantly made him clear away filth;

only after severing the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*) through the *Vaipulya* teachings and being refined by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, was he called "harshly rebuked.
Upon arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha-nature was revealed and manifested, like drawing out the bright pearl from beneath one's robe.
When the poor man saw this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy. Just so, when the śrāvakas perceive the Buddha-nature, their joy at having obtained this treasure is beyond words.
While they may possess various material wealth and indulge themselves in the five desires, their immeasurable wisdom and the dharma-wealth of merit are all [present].

Because he is fully endowed with all these qualities, it is said that he possesses wealth; because his application of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch through the power of samādhi is vast and sovereign according to conditions, it is said that he may indulge himself at will in the five desires.

We are also like this. We śrāvakas who have regressed from the Great Vehicle, entered the Lesser Vehicle, and turned our minds back toward the Great Vehicle are no different from that poor man. World-Honored One, throughout the long night you have always looked upon us with compassion and taught us. In the past, when we were lost in delusion, it was like a long night. World-Honored One, now that we have encountered the Buddha, the sun has risen. We have attained the fruit of the Path; how could we not rejoice? We have obtained the most rare and supreme benefit. World-Honored One, we now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. May the World-Honored One accept us as lay followers; from this day forth until life ends, we shall refrain from taking life, refrain from taking what is not given, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from false speech, and refrain from intoxicants. May the World-Honored One accept us. At that time, the World-Honored One accepted their request. Having received the precepts, they were filled with joy and departed. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: “These five hundred śrāmaṇeras will, in a future age, become Buddhas named *Vimalaprabhā* (Pure Light) Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugatas, world-knowers, unexcelled leaders, teachers of devas and humans, and Buddhas. Their lands, kalpas, and lifespans will all be equal, and they will perform the same deeds. At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and put them into practice. This concludes the Chapter on the Five Hundred Śrāmaṇeras, the twenty-ninth chapter of the Lotus Sutra, the Dharma Blossom. Part Two. Chapter Thirty: The Former Deeds of Bhadrapāla. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “In the distant past, innumerable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named *Dīpaṃkara* (Lamp-Maker) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, world-knower, unexcelled leader, teacher of devas and humans, and Buddha. His land was called *Mahāvyūha* (Great Array). The kalpa was named *Mahāpuṇya* (Great Merit). That Buddha-Dharma remained for twelve small kalpas. At that time, there was a king named *Mahādeva* (Great God). He had a son named *Bhadrapāla* (Good Protector). The prince was wise, intelligent, and possessed great power. He deeply respected his parents and was compassionate toward all sentient beings. He gave generously to those in need and provided for the poor. He served the sages and honored the virtuous. He was filial to his parents and respectful to his elders. He was kind to his younger siblings and loved his kinsmen. He was gentle and harmonious with his neighbors and friends. He was diligent in his duties and never negligent. He was skilled in governing the state and managing the people. He was well-versed in the arts and crafts of the world. He was learned in the various treatises and commentaries. He was proficient in the calculations of the five branches of mathematics. He was skilled in the methods of the four Vedas. He understood the origins of all things. He was well-versed in the prognostications of the eight signs. He knew the sounds of all birds and beasts. He understood the cries of all wild animals. He was skilled in the sounds of all musical instruments. He knew the voices of all spirits and deities. He understood the cries of all ghosts and spirits. He was skilled in the sounds of all dragons and serpents. He understood the cries of all yakṣas and rākṣasas. He was skilled in the sounds of all heavenly beings. He understood the cries of all humans. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-human beings. He understood the cries of all beings in the six realms of existence. He was skilled in the sounds of all hells. He understood the cries of all hungry ghosts. He was skilled in the sounds of all animals. He understood the cries of all asuras. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-self. He understood the cries of all non-dharma. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-realm. He understood the cries of all non-attachment. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-obstruction. He understood the cries of all non-hindrance. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-impediment. He understood the cries of all non-barrier. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-obscuration. He understood the cries of all non-covering. He was skilled in the sounds of all non-concealment. He understood the cries of all non-secrecy. May the Honored One, out of compassion, constantly manifest and teach us, causing us to plant the supreme vow. May you cause us to plant the vast vow for unexcelled bodhi.
Because we are ignorant, we have neither awakened to nor known this; because our wisdom is inferior, we do not know our past vows.
Furthermore, they are unable to realize that they possess the Buddha-nature;

having attained a small portion of nirvana, they consider themselves sufficient and do not seek anything further. Having attained this partial nirvana of emptiness, they claim it is enough and do not seek the great benefit.
Now the Buddha has awakened us, saying that what we called extinction was not real. Now the World-Honored Buddha has awakened us, saying that the Dharma we attained was not ultimate extinction.
To attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha is what constitutes true extinction; to achieve the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is it.
This is what is called true parinirvāṇa.

We have now heard from the Buddha the matters concerning the adornment of the prediction [of our future enlightenment]. We have now personally heard from the Buddha the prediction of our attainment of Buddhahood and the adornment of our buddha-fields.
As they were successively conferred with the prediction of enlightenment and received the sequential prophesies one after another, their bodies and minds were filled with universal joy;
because their minds were joyful, that gladness suffused their entire bodies.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nine: Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
The five hundred arhats and the twelve hundred persons have all already received predictions that they shall attain Buddhahood in the future.
Among the great disciples, Ānanda, foremost in much learning, and Rāhula, foremost in secret conduct, have not yet received their predictions; they are [the Buddha’s] emanation bodies.

Furthermore, two thousand individuals, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who had attained Buddhahood, also wished in their hearts to hear the sound of the prophecy.
Because the Tathāgata responded to their needs, he preached this chapter.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula were as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
And they formed this thought. The two great disciples both formed this thought:
"We each constantly reflect; we each constantly reflect within our own minds."
"Would it not be a joy even to receive a prediction of enlightenment? If one were to receive a prediction from a Buddha, would that not be a source of great happiness?
Having said this, he rose from his seat and approached the Buddha; desiring to make a request, he left his place and stepped forward.
They prostrated with their heads at his feet and addressed the Buddha together, saying: "We prostrate with our heads in reverence at the Buddha’s two feet and speak to the Buddha with one voice:
'World-Honored One, we too should have a share in this; we too should be included within the number of those for whom you grant the prediction [of enlightenment].'"
When the division into the Buddha-bodhi occurs,
the Tathāgata alone is our refuge; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the sole support and resort for us and our assembly.
Furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras. Moreover,
we are fully seen and well-known to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings throughout the world of devas,
humans, and asuras.

Ānanda has always served as an attendant, upholding the treasury of the Dharma. Ānanda has always served as the Tathāgata’s attendant, guarding and maintaining the treasury of all the jewels of the Dharma.
Rāhula is the son of the Buddha; Rāhula is the Buddha’s own biological son.
If the Buddha were to see and bestow upon us the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to see and bestow upon us the prediction of attaining Buddhahood through unsurpassed bodhi.
"Our vows are fulfilled and the expectations of the multitude are also satisfied. "Our own aspirational minds have attained fulfillment, and what the people hoped for is likewise fully provided.

At that time, there were two thousand śrāvaka disciples, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). These two thousand individuals, including both those in training and...

Those who had studied under the Buddha and were beyond the stage of training (aśaikṣa), numbering twelve hundred, all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and approached the Buddha. With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One;
then, like Ānanda and Rāhula, they stood to one side according to their wish. The thoughts in the minds of these people were identical to those of the two venerable ones.
He merely refrained from speaking and stood to one side.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda, "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha; in a future world, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha."
He is titled "King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Wisdom and Ocean-like Sagacity. Ānanda, his wisdom is like a mountain-treasury and his mind is like an ocean-receptacle;
