his supernatural powers are vast and great, and he possesses mastery over their manifestation and withdrawal. In the future, when he attains Buddhahood, he shall be the King of the Dharma, titled "King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Wisdom and Ocean-like Sagacity."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān;
as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
One should make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas. To comply with the Buddha’s words and make offerings to these sixty-two billion is to signify the severance of the sixty-two views.
They shall uphold the treasury of the Dharma; under the presence of all Buddhas, they shall protect and receive the entire treasury of the Dharma, and thereafter attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having fully cultivated all the perfections (*pāramitās*), they shall achieve perfect enlightenment.
He taught and transformed twenty quadrillion *koṭi-nayuta* bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges,
causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Among those beings thus transformed, there were likewise as many as the sands of the Ganges who all attained enlightenment.
The name of the land is Constantly Erected Victorious Banner (*Nityotthitavaijayantī*). As for why that Buddha-land is named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner:

according to the customs of the Western Regions, those whose arguments are superior always hold a victorious banner to signify their high wisdom and excellence; because such a venerable one of great learning is constantly victorious over all, the land where he dwells is named Erected Victorious Banner.
That land is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground. Because the mind is pure and transparent both within and without, the resulting Buddha-land is likewise so.
The eon is named Pervasive Sublime Sound; at that time, the pure and even sounds of the Buddha pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Because the human lifespan is long, the Buddha’s lifespan is also long.
If a person were to pass through such kalpas for thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas...
It cannot be known through calculation or reckoning; the long duration of the Buddha’s life is not something that can be understood by the mental power of ordinary beings.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as his lifespan, increasing by one further period.
The Semblance Dharma will remain in the world for twice as long as the True Dharma, and it will increase twofold again.
Ānanda, this is the Buddha King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain and Ocean Wisdom; such was that Buddha at that time.
He is praised together by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the ten directions— immeasurable, thousands of myriads of koṭis,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— who extol his merits. All the Buddhas of the ten directions, with one voice, praise the vast merits of that Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "I now declare within the Saṃgha that Ānanda is the upholder of the Dharma.
Thus did the Buddha, amidst the assembly, proclaim that Ānanda was the upholder of the treasury of the Dharma.

One shall make offerings to all Buddhas and thereafter attain perfect enlightenment. One shall make offerings to countless myriads of billions of Buddhas and thereafter attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
being named the Buddha King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Ocean-like Mountain Wisdom, as previously described.
That land is pure and is named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner.

As previously described, he teaches and transforms bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in that Buddha’s assembly there is no group of śrāvakas, consisting purely of bodhisattvas whose number is immeasurable.
The Buddha possesses great majestic power, and his fame fills the ten directions. That Tathāgata’s majestic power is vast and his renown is widely spread, pervading the ten directions.
His lifespan is immeasurable because he takes pity on sentient beings; it is because he desires to compassionately regard all sentient beings that [he remains].
The lifespan of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is so vast and long that it cannot be measured;

the duration of the True Dharma (saddharma) is twice that lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpakadharma) is again twice that. Thus, the periods during which the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma abide in the world are each twice as long as the Buddha’s own lifespan.
Countless sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are the assembly receiving transformation during the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma,
shall plant the causal conditions for the Buddha-way within this Buddha-dharma; they shall plant the various wholesome causal conditions for the Buddha-way within the Buddha-dharma of Sāgarabuddhi.
At that time, there were eight thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly who had newly resolved their minds for enlightenment.

When these bodhisattvas of initial resolve saw the śrāvakas receiving predictions of their future buddhahood, they all thought to themselves: "We have not even heard of the great bodhisattvas receiving such predictions. All of them...
With minds full of doubt, they thought to themselves: "In all our time since the past, we have never even heard that the great bodhisattvas receive such a prediction of the path to enlightenment.
By what causes and conditions do these śrāvakas receive such a definitive assurance? For what reason have these śrāvakas attained this?"
Recorded.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas. The World-Honored One knew that these beginner bodhisattvas had given rise to doubts.
And he addressed them, saying: "I announce this to those who have newly begun their practice:

'O sons of good family, I, along with Ānanda and others—the Buddha, Ānanda, and all the Arhats—at the time of the World-Honored One of the Distant Past, the Buddha Emptiness-King (Śūnyarāja), in ages long gone by.'"
At the same time, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; at the same time, they resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
Ānanda always delighted in much hearing; by his very nature, Ānanda always loved much hearing.
I have always practiced with diligent vigor; I have always cultivated the practice of diligent vigor.
For this reason, I have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It was solely through such constant diligence that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni first attained the Way.
Ānanda shall uphold my Dharma; he shall also protect the Dharma-treasury of the future Buddhas of the Śākya clan,
and in future ages, he shall protect and maintain the treasuries of the Dharma-jewels of all Buddhas.
He brings to maturity and transforms the assembly of bodhisattvas and teaches countless billions of kinds of sentient beings.
Because his original vow was thus, he has obtained this prediction. As in the time of the former King of Emptiness, his original vow was to extensively deliver others;
it is the same in the present world. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "As long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter nirvana from this realm."
Ānanda stood face-to-face before the Buddha; in the midst of the assembly, before Śākyamuni Buddha,
he personally heard the bestowal of the prophecy and the adornment of the land, having himself heard the Buddha grant him the prophecy and describe the pure adornment of his reward-land.
His aspirations being fully realized, his heart was filled with great joy. Having fortunately fulfilled his original vow, his mind suddenly opened up in rapture;
he experienced what he had never known before. That which he has now attained was previously non-existent.
Immediately, he recollected the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas of the past;
he recalled the various Dharma-treasuries he had heard from those Buddhas in ages long past.
They have attained unhindered penetration just as they have now heard; they have fully realized everything without obstruction,
just as they have obtained through hearing today,
and they also recognize their original vows— the great vows they originally made in the past.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses: "The World-Honored One is most rare; the World-Honored One is exceptionally superior and truly extraordinary.
He causes me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, and he causes me to remember the distant past."
The Dharma of the Buddha is just as I have heard it today; what I have heard today is equal and no different from before.
I now have no further doubt; I now have no more mind of uncertainty.
Abiding securely in the Buddha-way; with a settled mind, they dwell in the way of all Buddhas.

By means of skillful means, they act as attendants to protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas; through the power of skillful means, they serve as the Buddhas' attendants to guard the treasury of the Dharma-jewels.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula as before:
"In a future age, in the distant future, you shall attain Buddhahood under the name Dàoqībǎohuá (Trampling the Seven-Jeweled Flowers).
At that time, you will have extensively cultivated the seven virtuous merits and attained the ground of fruition."
He stands tall upon the seven-jeweled lotus flower.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān— these are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
One should make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in ten worlds.
Taking the three thousandfold world-systems of transformation and manifesting them as dust particles serves as a metaphor for the number of Buddhas to whom one should offer;
"ten worlds" here represents the ten directions.
He has always been the eldest son of all Buddhas. When future Buddhas appear in the world, Rāhula shall likewise be their eldest son, just as he is now;
there is no difference between him and the present Buddha’s time.

Such matters as the adornments of the Buddha-land of this Tathāgata Padmottara—who treads upon the seven-jeweled lotuses—as well as his lifespan, the number of kalpas, the disciples he transforms, and the duration of his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma;
that is to say, the land, the lifespan, the disciples, the True Dharma, and the Semblance Dharma, and so forth.
He was no different from the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Oceanic Wisdom and Eloquence;
he was pointed out as being identical to Ānanda, and likewise served as the eldest son of this Buddha, becoming the eldest son of the Buddha Oceanic Wisdom and Eloquence.
After this has passed, and after the end of this world,
he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a venerable one of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son.
When I had not yet left the household life and was still a crown prince, this Rāhula was my eldest son."
I have now attained the Way of the Buddha and receive the Dharma as the Son of the Dharma; receiving the Tathāgata’s Dharma, I am the Son of the Dharma.
In future ages, I shall see immeasurable billions of Buddhas; in the coming future, I shall see immeasurable Buddhas.
All were the eldest sons of those Buddhas, single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way; all served as the eldest sons of those Buddhas, single-mindedly seeking the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Rāhula’s secret practice is known only by me; indeed, Rāhula’s subtle and secret conduct is—
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to know this;
he manifests as my eldest son to demonstrate it to all sentient beings. He now descends in his traces as my eldest son to reveal it to all living beings throughout the world.
His immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of merits are beyond counting; the merits of his accumulated secret practices are immeasurable tens of billions and cannot be known by number.
He dwells securely in the Buddha-dharma to seek the unsurpassed path, and with a settled mind, he abides in the teachings of all Buddhas.
They sought the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the two thousand disciples—both those still training and those beyond training—were supple in mind, tranquil, and pure.

The Buddha conferred upon them the prediction of enlightenment, sealing their realization as being unlike the worldly views of gain and loss held by ordinary people; thus he marked these two thousand individuals.
His mind was exceptionally gentle, supple, tranquil, serene, pure, and lucid, making him a fit vessel for the transmission of the Way.
With single-minded focus he contemplated the Buddha; with undistracted concentration, he gazed up at the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Do you see these two thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training?
Since they were standing before him within the range of his own vision, why did he ask again whether he saw them? One should know that the assembly saw only their physical forms;
how could they have known their mental thoughts? It was for this reason that the World-Honored One questioned Ānanda.
"Yes, indeed, I have seen them. He replied, "Yes, indeed, I have truly seen them.
Ānanda, these two thousand śrāvakas shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds; from this time forth, they shall always...
Furthermore, he made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there would be if fifty worlds were ground into atoms;
toward them, he was reverent, respectful, humble, cautious, honoring, and profoundly devoted.
They shall uphold the treasury of the Dharma; they shall uphold the treasuries of the Buddha-jewel of all Buddhas.
In the final age, they shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood in various lands throughout the ten directions, each attaining the Way of the Buddha in their final body.
They shall all bear the same name, called Ratnākara (Jewel-Phase). These two thousand people shall all equally receive the prediction of enlightenment, sharing the same name as the Buddha Ratnākara.
[He is] the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi...
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Men, as explained in the "Introductory Chapter," has a lifespan of one *kalpa*— specifically, one small *kalpa*.
The adornments of his land constitute the characteristics of his *pariṇāmanā-saṃbhoga* (retributive environment).
The characteristics of the primary retribution of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
as well as the characteristics of the duration of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma,
are all entirely equal; their meritorious practices are of a similar nature, and the retributions they induce are likewise equal.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me;
the assembly of two thousand now stands before the Buddha, positioned to one side."
All of them were given the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood in the future. I now bestow upon all of them the prediction of Bodhi, that in a future age they shall attain Buddhahood.
The number of Buddhas they have made offerings to is as described above, as numerous as atoms; the number of Buddhas they have served is as described above, fivefold.
If ten worlds were ground into atoms, and there were as many Buddhas as those countless atoms who protect and uphold their treasury of Dharma,
one shall later attain perfect enlightenment; having protected and upheld the treasury of the Buddha-treasures of as many Buddhas as those aforementioned atoms,
one shall later achieve the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.

In each of the lands throughout the ten directions, they all possessed the same name and title. Having each attained equal and perfect enlightenment in the ten directions, they were all given the identical name of Buddha Ratnaketu (Jewel-Phase).
Simultaneously seated at their sites of enlightenment, they realized supreme wisdom and were all named Ratnaketu. These were two thousand people.
At one time they all attained Buddhahood together, sitting upon the site of enlightenment to realize unsurpassed, profound wisdom, and were named Ratnalakṣaṇa Buddha.
Their lands, disciples, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma were all equal and without difference;
their various transformative activities, lands, disciples, lifespans, and kalpas were each identical, for since their virtues were the same, there was no distinction in their retribution.

All of them deliver sentient beings of the ten directions by means of their various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). All of them deliver all sentient beings throughout the realms of the ten directions by means of the power of wisdom and supernormal powers.
Their fame is universally pervasive as they gradually enter into *nirvāṇa*. Their names and reputations are spread throughout all quarters as they gradually...
They gradually entered into cessation in successive order.

At that time, two thousand individuals—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those who had newly received their predictions—heard the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment and, leaping for joy, spoke these verses: “The World-Honored One is the lamp of wisdom; the World-Honored One...”
The light of wisdom is bright and inexhaustible; as the lamp of the Dharma continues its illumination, it shines universally upon all.
We have heard the voice of the prophecy; we have heard the voice of the prophecy bestowed upon us.
Their hearts were filled with joy, as if they had been sprinkled with nectar; their hearts were so filled with joy that it was as if they had truly received the sprinkling of nectar.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Ten: "The Dharma-preacher."
In the previous "Chapter on Medicinal Herbs," the analogy of the timely rain was taught, stating that this wondrous sutra universally benefits all beings;

although they have all been granted predictions, they were [previously] categorized as śrāvakas. Now, in this chapter, it is for the sake of the great assembly and the eight classes of beings who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this sutra, or even hear a single phrase, a single verse, or a single word.
At that time, it was prophesied that they would all attain the Buddha-way.
Then the World-Honored One, on account of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings; the Buddha, because of Bhaiṣajyarāja, spoke to the great assembly.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see within this great assembly, in the presence of this current dharma-gathering,
the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas,
humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās?
As explained in the Introduction Chapter:
those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka seek the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to become arhats;

those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha seek the Dharma of dependent origination and contemplate it as being like an illusion; those who are named "pratyekabuddhas" or "solitary buddhas" [attain their goal through these means].
Pratyekabuddhas;
those who seek the Buddha-way; those who seek the Supreme Vehicle and aspire to attain the Buddha-way—such as these, the persons of the three vehicles.
All of them heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha. Having heard the sublime Dharma in the presence of the Buddha,
even those who rejoiced in it for a single verse or a single phrase, or even for a single thought-moment— even down to those who merely heard a single phrase or a single verse,
or even for a single thought-moment upon hearing the sutra, joy arose within their hearts.
"I have bestowed upon all of them the prediction that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The Buddha predicted that these individuals shall all attain the Way.
The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja:
"Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa"—the former clarifies [the period] during the Buddha's lifetime, while the latter reveals [the period] after his passing.
If there is anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoices for even a single thought-moment;
if, upon hearing even a single verse or a single phrase of this wondrous sūtra, they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy for even a single moment of thought.
I also bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I grant all of them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if there be anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [I shall likewise grant them this prediction].

With faith, one should receive and uphold this sublime sūtra by reading it according to the text, reciting it from memory apart from the text, explaining its meaning in accordance with the sense, and transcribing it upon paper or silk—even if only a single verse.
One should regard this sūtra scroll with reverence as if it were the Buddha; one should honor the sūtra scroll as being identical to the Buddha.
They offer various kinds of worship: flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers;
canopies and banners made of fine silks;
robes and musical instruments; even up to joining their palms in respectful salutation, down to merely joining their palms to pay homage.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people—those who revere, have faith in, and make offerings to this sutra—have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas;
they have, in past lives, made offerings to various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Having accomplished great vows in the presence of all Buddhas, and having already fulfilled vast aspirations before the Buddhas,
he was born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings; indeed, it was because he wished to take pity upon all living beings that he was born here.

In this world among humans, Bhaiṣajyarāja, if someone should ask, "Which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in a future age? Bhaiṣajyarāja, when anyone asks such a question, the Buddha says: [The Buddha said:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there is another person who asks such a question at that time..."
One should indicate that these individuals will certainly attain Buddhahood in future ages;
one should show others by saying that those who respect, believe in, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to such persons will definitely achieve Buddhahood in a future life.

Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or copies even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra—the former part of which describes the transmission of the sūtra and the latter part clarifies the making of offerings.
Various offerings— sūtra scrolls, flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music—
are presented with palms joined in reverence, as previously described.
Such a person is one whom all the world should look up to and honor. Such a person is one whom all classes of sentient beings in the world should revere;
they should be honored with the same offerings as a Tathāgata. In times when there is no Buddha, such a person stands as a successor to fill that place.
The Buddha proclaimed that one should honor such a person with the offerings due to a Buddha.
One should know that this person is a great bodhisattva; since they have given rise to great faith and understanding toward this sublime sūtra, one knows that this person is a great bodhisattva.
Having accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and being already able to achieve supreme enlightenment, he out of compassion for sentient beings vowed to be born in this realm;
out of pity for sentient beings, he was born into this human world.
To speak extensively, they analyze and expound this wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, widely propagating and explaining such a sublime scripture;

how much more so for those who are able to receive, uphold, and offer various kinds of worship to it? According to their respective capacities, they receive and maintain the merit that is thus protected.
If even this is immeasurable, how much more so for one who fully receives and upholds [this teaching] and makes offerings with various kinds of exquisite incense,
flowers, silk canopies, banners, and streamers? O Bhaiṣajyarāja,
you should know that such a person— one who thus upholds and makes offerings— is to be known as such.
Having relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, they shall naturally be born in pure buddha-fields; having relinquished those superior rewards, they are born here in Jambudvīpa.
After my parinirvāṇa—that is, after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha—...
Out of compassion for sentient beings—that is, out of pity for all sentient beings—he was born into an evil world.
This Sahā world is called an "evil world" because it is filled with a multitude of unwholesome things.
Extensively expound this sutra; extensively preach this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
If there are good men or good women—those good men and good women who receive and uphold this sutra.
After my parinirvāṇa, following the passing of the Buddha,
should anyone be able to secretly preach the Lotus Sūtra even for a single phrase—
even down to the meaning of a single, most minimal phrase— for the sake of a single person.
You should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata. You should know that one who speaks this sutra in this manner is an emissary of the Tathāgata’s Lotus Sutra;
they are dispatched by the Tathāgata and are sent forth by the Tathāgata as a guide.
They perform the deeds of a Tathāgata; they perform the deeds of the transformative Dharma of a Tathāgata.

How much more so when they extensively expound it for others amidst the great assembly! Secretly practicing it for a single person produces merit that is extremely great, far exceeding the merit of its extensive exposition to the multitude. No comparison can equal it.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, the former [section] clarifies that the merit of upholding this sutra is exceedingly great, while the latter reveals that the retribution for slandering it is extremely grave.
If there are wicked people who, with unwholesome minds, give rise to poisonous thoughts toward it; if there are various evil persons who harbor such toxic intentions.
To spend such a length of time throughout an entire eon appearing before a Buddha,
and in this present life to constantly revile the Buddha in his very presence—
though the sin of such [verbal] abuse might still be considered light, the sin of reviling the Buddha with an evil heart over such a long duration of time is certainly grave.
The phrase "even slight [sins] are still slight" conversely reveals that the retribution for slandering those who uphold this sutra is extremely grave.
If a person utters even a single evil word, or at the very least, produces but a single sentence of malicious speech.
They disparage householders and those who have left the home life— virtuous sons and daughters among the laity, as well as monks, nuns, and śrāmaṇeras among the monastic community—
who recite and study the Lotus Sūtra; that is, the fourfold assembly who recite and study the Lotus Sūtra.
That offense is exceedingly grave. Because one slanders others, causing them to retreat from the mind of the Way, the teachings and methods fail to be practiced;
for this reason, the offense is heavy. O Bhaiṣajyarāja, as for those who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra—whosoever there may be who reads this sūtra.
It should be known that such a person— specifically, one who upholds this sutra—
is adorned by the adornments of the Buddha. The sutra explains that sublime conduct is called the "adornment of the Buddha," and this person adorns their own body with it.
They are those who are borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata; they are the messengers entrusted with the transmission of the Dharma by the Tathāgata.

By bearing the true Dharma of the Buddha upon their shoulders and transforming sentient beings so that they may attain right view, they are those who carry the great heavy burden of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
In whichever direction that person who upholds this sutra may go, one should pay homage toward that quarter.
One should pay homage with a sincere heart according to the direction.
With single-mindedness, join the palms; with single-mindedness and without distraction, join the ten fingers together.
They pay respectful homage and make offerings; with humility, reverence, and earnest sincerity, they make offerings.
They honor and praise them, holding them in high esteem and regarding them as precious, extolling and lauding them.
They present flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and delicacies, performing all manner of [offerings].
As for the music and dance, they are to be understood in detail as previously described.
One should make offerings to them with the supreme offerings found among humans; one should provide this person with all the most excellent and wondrous offerings available in the human realm.
One should take celestial jewels and scatter them. These diligent devas scatter flowers and offer jewels;

the accumulated treasures of the heavens should be presented as an offering to this upholder of the Dharma. All the precious objects existing in the heavens should be dedicated as offerings to this one who maintains the Dharma.
Why is this so? What is the intention behind making such offerings in this manner?
It is because this person joyfully expounds the Dharma, and one desires to diligently assist this person in their joyful exposition of the Dharma.
Because by hearing [the Dharma] for even a single *muhūrta*, one immediately attains ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Each day and night is divided into thirty *muhūrtas*; this implies that through the power of faith, even during a brief interval of hearing the Dharma, one can penetrate the profound meaning and enter the divine, thereby being able to exhaustively realize the Buddha’s *bodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "If one wishes to dwell in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom;
if one wishes to fix the mind upon the Buddha’s true path and achieve unconditioned, spontaneous wisdom."

One should always diligently make offerings to and uphold those who receive and maintain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. One should always diligently make offerings to those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

If there is anyone who wishes to swiftly attain the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), that is, anyone who wishes to swiftly accomplish the Middle Way’s correct wisdom—the omniscience of all Buddhas—[they should do so].
One should uphold this sutra and make offerings to those who uphold it; one should maintain this sutra and provide for those who maintain it.
If there are those capable of upholding the Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma, or any person who can maintain this Lotus Sutra.
One should know that such a person is an emissary of the Buddha who takes pity on all sentient beings;

one should know that whoever is able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whoever is able to maintain this scripture, is an emissary of the Buddha who extends compassion to sentient beings.
Having abandoned the pure lands, they are born here out of compassion for sentient beings. Having abandoned their own pure lands, they are born within this turbid world.

One should know that such persons are born according to their own sovereign will; one should know that these persons are not born through the retribution of karma, but are born here by the power of their own intentional desire.
One who is able to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this evil world, one who is able to preach the unsurpassed Dharma in an evil world—
such a teacher of the Dharma should be honored with celestial flowers and incense, celestial precious robes, and heaps of exquisite celestial jewels.
As previously explained:
those who are able to uphold this sutra in the evil world after my parinirvāṇa— those who uphold this sutra during the turbid and evil world after the Buddha has passed into extinction.

One should join one's palms in prostration as if making offerings to the World-Honored One; one should respectfully uphold this person who possesses the sutra, regarding them as no different from the Buddha.
By offering fine foods, various delicacies, and diverse garments to these sons of the Buddha, one hopes to hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
The reason for making these offerings is the desire to hear this sutra for even a brief moment, thereby accomplishing this ultimate great matter.
If there are those who, in future generations, can receive and uphold this sutra; if, after my parinirvāṇa, they are able to maintain this sutra.
I have dispatched them to act as Tathāgatas among human beings; the Buddha has dispatched them to be born within the human realm to perform the deeds of the Buddha on his behalf.
Even if they were to constantly harbor unwholesome thoughts for an entire kalpa, or pass through a kalpa harboring such unwholesome thoughts—
One who scorns the Buddha with a frowning countenance, one who scorns the Buddha with an expression of wrathful anger, incurs immeasurable and heavy transgression.
Such a person who reviles the Buddha incurs immeasurable sin.
If there are those who read, recite, and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
and someone should for even a moment address them with evil words, their sin would exceed that of the former; if one reviles such a person who upholds the sutra for even a moment,
their sin would further exceed that of reviling a Buddha for kalpas.
There are those who seek the Buddha-way and, for the duration of one kalpa,
join their palms before me and praise me with countless verses; there are those who, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, pass through one kalpa standing with palms joined before the Tathāgata.
They praised the Buddha with countless verses.
By thus praising the Buddha, they attained immeasurable merit; by praising the Buddha, they acquired vast blessings.
Yet the merit of one who extols the excellence of the upholder of this sutra exceeds even that; the merit of praising the upholder of the sutra surpasses that of praising the Buddha.
Praising the Buddha of the Fruit:
for eighty billion kalpas, by means of the most exquisite forms and sounds— wherein the "exquisite forms" representing the eight consciousnesses refer to objects such as fragrant flowers,
and the "exquisite sounds" refer to various kinds of music— he [praises] with that which is most supreme among all worlds.
Exquisite forms and sounds,
as well as odors, tastes, and tangibles— exquisite fragrances, exquisite flavors, and the objects of touch—
one should offer these to those who uphold the sutra; one should thus provide such offerings to the upholders of the sutra.
Having made such offerings and having performed such acts of worship as these,
if one should hear [this] for even a brief moment, or if one should hear this sublime sutra for even a brief moment.

Then you should rejoice within yourself, thinking, "I have now attained a great benefit. You should give rise to great joy and celebration in your heart, thinking, "On this very day, I have obtained a great benefit.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: the Buddha summons you, Bhaiṣajyarāja; I speak these words to you now.
Of all the sūtras I have spoken—of all the sūtras I have taught since my attainment of the Way—the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost among them.
Within this collection of the Lotus Sūtra, there is nothing equal to it; it is the most supreme.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"As explained in the 'Introductory Chapter,' the sūtras I have preached are immeasurable, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis. [The Buddha] spoke a second time to Bhaiṣajyarāja: "The Dharma-sūtras I have preached during my ordinary days are immeasurable, numbering in the tens of thousands of myriads of koṭis."
That which has been spoken, that which is being spoken now, and that which shall be spoken— in all these, whether already completed, currently being delivered, or yet to come,

this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand. One should reflect that the merit of attaining Buddhahood is so sublime as to be hard to believe,
and the meaning of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is so profound as to be hard to comprehend.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas. This Lotus Sutra is the secret, essential, and wondrous dharma-treasury of all World-Honored Ones.
It must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others; it must not be easily disseminated throughout the world or wantonly entrusted to them.
Lest people give rise to contempt or slander, which would instead result in harm and affliction, one should carefully select what is appropriate before bestowing it.
It is protected by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. The Sūtras state that wherever the Buddhas travel, they are protected by all the Tathāgatas.
Since ancient times, this has never been explicitly taught. Since I attained enlightenment in the past, because the capacities of sentient beings were inferior, I have never revealed it;
rather, I have spoken it secretly through skillful means. As the sutra says: "When sentient beings hear this, their minds will harbor doubt and confusion."
Furthermore, even while the Tathāgata was present in the world, this sutra encountered much resentment and jealousy.

While the Tathāgata was still among men, people did not believe it and harbored much resentment, anger, and hatred; as the Parable Chapter says: "Is it not Mara who has become a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?"
How much more so after his parinirvāṇa! If even during the Buddha's lifetime it was thus, how much more so after his passing?
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that this shall be so after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, following the entry into extinction of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Those who are able to write it down, uphold it, read it, recite it, and make offerings to it;
those who are able to write it down, uphold it, recite it, and make offerings to it, and further explain it for others—that is, expound it for all people.
The Tathāgata then covers them with his robe. Were it not for the power of the Way, how could one understand the propagation of the sūtra and practice patience and diligence?
Without such understanding, one would be unable to don the Tathāgata’s robe of patience.

Furthermore, they are protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions; all the Buddhas of other regions revere this sutra, and those who can uphold it shall receive the protection and mindfulness of the Buddhas.
This person possesses great power of faith; this expounder of the sutra possesses the power of vast confidence, the power of aspiration, and the power of establishing one's resolve and making vows.
By the power of all roots of goodness, and by the power of roots of goodness planted long ago in the past, it should be known that such a person dwells together with the Tathāgata.
All Tathāgatas reside within the ultimate field of the One Vehicle’s tranquility; because this practitioner now abides in the ocean-treasury of merits of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is so said.

If one stays overnight [with such a person], it is as if the Tathāgata were to stroke their head with his own hand. The hand symbolizes expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and the head symbolizes ultimate reality (*tattva*).
To enter the path of the Buddha-vehicle through the meaning of the skillful means taught by the Tathāgata is to have already received the stroking of the head with his hand.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this scripture is taught, read, recited, written down, or where its volumes are kept,
and wherever anyone circulates it— there..."
One should erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, making them as high, vast, and magnificently adorned as possible, as an act of worship.
It is not necessary to enshrine relics therein. Generally speaking, the original purpose of erecting a stupa is to reverently house the Buddha’s relics;
the reason why it is unnecessary to enshrine relics here will be understood from the following text.

Why is this so? Because within this [sūtra] already exists the entire body of the Tathāgata. The sūtra clarifies the sublime principle that the purity of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is itself the pure *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata. Wherever this sūtra is present, it constitutes a stūpa;
the text of the sūtra is itself the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha. As the sūtra says: "If a person seeks the *śarīra* of the Buddha with a sincere mind, such a person..."
Then you may explain it to them:
"This stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with offerings of all kinds of flowers, incense, garlands, silk canopies, banners, pennants, music, and songs.
This precious stūpa should be venerated with such things as these."
If there are those who see this stūpa and pay homage and make offerings to it, or if people see the stūpa and prostrate themselves in worship and make offerings,
you should know that all such persons are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; these people of reverent faith are very near to the Way.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both lay and ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path.
This is because they see others—whether lay men and women or ordained monks and nuns—who are likewise practicing the bodhisattva path.
If one is unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,

then even though the aforementioned four classes of beings may accept and practice the bodhisattva path, they shall not be able to see, hear, receive, uphold, read, or recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
One should know that such persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path; one should know that these types of people are not yet well able to practice the bodhisattva path.
Only those who hear this sutra are able to skillfully practice the bodhisattva path and attain its essential core.
The Way is indeed called "virtuous conduct.
Should there be sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way, or those who resolve their minds to seek the path of the Buddha,
and should they see or hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*— that is, seeing it with their eyes or hearing it with their ears— this wondrous sūtra:
Regarding those who, having heard [this], believe, understand, accept, and uphold it: seeing, hearing, revering, and believing are the conditions for entering the Path.
One should know that such persons draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; because the seeds of their faculties have matured, they are close to the wisdom of the Buddha.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who is parched with thirst and needs water— like a person who, being thirsty,
desires cool water and digs for it upon a high plateau. Seeking the flavor of principle within the realm of the Buddha is like digging a well on a high plateau in search of water.
It is like seeing dry earth and knowing that water is still far off. Dry earth is a metaphor for the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) within the gradual teaching of skillful means;
though there is wisdom therein, one has not yet attained the water of principle. A bodhisattva at the initial stage who wanders outside of principle is like one who sees dry earth.

If one exerts effort without ceasing, one gradually sees moist soil and eventually sees mud. By applying effort without end, one dwells in the stage of the inner ordinary person (*ārya-pṛthagjana*), which is like seeing moist soil;
upon reaching the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is like seeing hardened mud.

Their minds are resolute, knowing that water must be near. When the practitioner reaches this stage, they are adjacent to the initial stage of the Gradual Teaching, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), or for a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching, the position of the first *vihāra*. Because their mind is free from doubt, it is said to be "resolute";
because they are not far from the Sage, it is said to be "near."
The Bodhisattva is also like this; this concludes the preceding analogy.
If one has not heard, not understood, and not yet practiced this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, such a person has not even touched its surface.
One should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, like seeing dry soil. If, however,
they hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it, it is like the previous analogy where one applies effort without ceasing.
One will certainly know that one is close to attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as one gradually perceives moist soil and hardened mud.
Why is this? For what reason must the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* be propagated?
The Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all bodhisattvas belongs entirely to this sutra.

All bodhisattvas who cultivate the dharmas of enlightenment are encompassed and governed by this sutra; they shall not fail to hear the wondrous Dharma and remain stuck in the gates of expedient means.

This sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the aspect of ultimate reality. Before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was preached, the three vehicles were separated and the gate of expedient means was closed;

each followed their own practice until they reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where the Buddha-nature was revealed and manifested. This clarified that the previous provisional vehicles are themselves the Bodhisattva path.
Recognizing the servant as the son, the gate of expedient means opened, bringing together all gradual teachings to enter the same Perfect and Sudden teaching.
The true nature of all people is this treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This principle of the single reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is inherently possessed by every person;
yet, because it has not been revealed, they remain unaware of it, like a hidden treasure buried beneath the earth.
"Profound, firm, obscure, and remote. It is called "profound" because it clarifies the ultimate principle of the Buddha, the unsurpassed *bodhi*.
It is called a "firm and solid dharma" because its meaning is definitive and indestructible. It is called "obscure" because its principle is subtle and secret, hidden and difficult to perceive.
It is called "remote" because, from the perspective of ordinary beings, it is separated from the Buddha by the ten fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
No one can reach it; only Buddha after Buddha can know it. The six realms of existence and the three vehicles cannot surpass it.
Therefore, the sutra says: "No one can reach it."

Now the Buddha teaches and transforms. Now the Buddha reveals and clarifies the teaching for all, bringing them to fulfillment as bodhisattvas and accomplishing the Great Bodhisattva Path of the One Vehicle;
he thus provides instruction and reveals the characteristics of the One Vehicle.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, are startled, doubtful, or terrified;
or who, having suddenly heard it explained, find its principles profound and subtle, yet give rise in their minds to doubt, alarm, fear, and dread.
You should know that these are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, just like those eight thousand who first resolved their minds.
If a śrāvaka hears this sutra and is startled, doubtful, or terrified, they will regard this perfect and wondrous teaching as the words of Māra.
One should know that such persons are those of overweening pride, like those five thousand who withdrew from their seats.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there be sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the fourfold assembly—
this section of the scripture teaches that these sons and daughters of good family shall propagate the sūtra after the parinirvāṇa.
"How should it be explained?"—this question is raised here; the answer is found in the following text.
These sons and daughters of good family are taught to practice four dharmas:
to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and to give rise to compassion.
Clothed in the Tathāgata’s robe, you should cause them to practice patience;
seated upon the Tathāgata’s seat, you should cause them to abide in the emptiness of phenomena.
Only then should you extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly. You who possess faith and understanding, enter the room, don the robes, and sit.
Only by sitting upon this seat can one preach the Dharma.
The chamber of the Tathāgata is the heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Within the sphere of all sentient beings, by means of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one removes their sorrows and afflictions and bestows happiness; by means of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one... [proceeds to rescue them].
To thus rescue and deliver others from their suffering and distress—such a mind that can accommodate all beings is called the chamber of compassion and mercy.
The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and forbearance. Because of gentleness, one does not afflict others;
because of forbearance, one does not harbor thoughts of revenge. To possess a sense of shame and dread of blame is what is meant by "wearing the robe."
The seat of the Tathāgata is the emptiness of all phenomena. To fully realize that all phenomena are entirely empty, quiescent, and immovable is called "sitting on the seat.
To abide therein is to dwell upon the seat of loving-kindness, patience, and the emptiness of phenomena.

Thereafter, with an untiring mind, although one is able to practice compassionate forbearance and realize the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it would be difficult to propagate the sutra if one were to become indolent again;
therefore, the sutra says, "with an untiring mind."
For the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, he shall extensively preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. This is the teaching he shall proclaim.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands, I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for him a congregation to hear the Dharma; that is to say, in those other lands.

In the land of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-bhūmi*), emanated beings are sent to assemble the listeners, just as those who were secretly dispatched in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*).
He likewise dispatches transformed (*nirmāṇa*) monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi-anubhāva*), these individuals are secretly brought to come and hear the Dharma.

These emanated beings heard the Dharma and accepted it with faith, following it in accordance and never opposing it. By the power of the Buddha, these emanated beings, upon hearing it, immediately accepted it with faith, without any contradiction or resistance.
If the Dharma-preacher is in a secluded place, in terms of the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*), he dwells in a vast, quiet, and uninhabited location;
in terms of the principle (*tattva*), he gathers his mind and abides in meditative concentration, delighting in the state of emptiness, stillness, and non-arising.
At that time, I extensively dispatched devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
All those in the assembly of the eight classes who came to hear the Dharma were sent there by the power of the Tathāgata.
Although I am in a different land, and although the Buddha has manifested through transformation in other realms,
from time to time he causes those who preach the Dharma to behold my body. When these preachers of the Dharma clearly understand the flavor of the Dharma’s meaning within their hearts,
they immediately see the Tathāgata’s pure Dharmakāya abiding in the light of eternal tranquility, and his perfected Sambhogakāya residing therein.
In the realm of true retribution, his thousand billion bodies manifest in response to the Land of Common Residence, appearing before one's eyes at all times, whether by day or by night.

Should one forget or lose any of the phrases and clauses of this sutra, or should there be any omission of the phrases and clauses within this wondrous sutra while receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, or expounding it—
I further explain for them so that they may attain full completion. At that very moment, they suddenly awaken and perceive the principle of the Buddha without any omission;
this is called the Tathāgata explaining for them again so that they may attain the complete fulfillment of all phrases and meanings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra. If a person wishes to cast off all indolence, they should with a sincere heart listen to and receive this sutra."

This sutra is difficult to encounter, and those who can hear it and accept it with faith are likewise rare. Such a sutra is difficult to hear, and those who can hear it and accept it with faith are also difficult to find.
It is like a person parched with thirst who must dig for water on high ground; one who seeks the Dharma with sincere resolve is like one who thirsts for water.
When one digs a well on that high plateau and still sees only dry soil,
one knows that water is yet far off; so too, when one dwells on the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), one knows that the water of principle is still far away.

Gradually seeing moist soil and mud, one knows for certain that water is near; likewise, being situated within the stage of ordinary beings yet adjacent to the stage of the sages, gradually perceiving the principle and knowing for oneself that one will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood is called "being near the water."
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these— such bodhisattvas with their initial resolve—
who have not heard the Lotus Sūtra, are very far from the Buddha’s wisdom; those who have never heard such a wondrous sūtra as this are exceedingly remote from the Buddha’s wisdom.
If one hears this profound sutra and realizes that the Dharma of the śrāvakas is the king of all sutras;
if one hears this profound and wondrous scripture, which is the king among all sutras.
Having heard it, they contemplate it with earnest attention. Having heard this Dharma, they examine it with a mind of earnest reflection.
It should be known that such persons are close to the Buddha’s wisdom. Having heard it, they are able to reflect; having reflected, they are able to practice.
It should be known that these people are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.
If anyone should preach this sutra, or if anyone else wishes to preach this sutra,
they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, give rise to great compassion,
don the Tathāgata’s robe, and practice great forbearance.
He sat upon the seat of the Tathāgata, abiding in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Fearless among the assembly, he dwelt with a mind free from fear amidst the great multitude,
extensively analyzing and explaining, and broadly expounding and teaching for the sake of all.
Great compassion is the chamber; gentleness and patience are the robe; the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat.
To enter this chamber, don this robe, sit upon this seat, and then expound the Dharma—only then is it called teaching in accordance with the Dharma.
When this sutra is being preached, or when this sublime sutra is being preached,

there may be those who revile with foul language and attack with swords, staves, tiles, or stones; there may be those who come forward to revile with foul and impure speech and strike them with swords, staves, tiles, or stones.
One should endure because of mindfulness of the Buddha. When such adverse and vexing conditions manifest before you, you should endure these evils by means of mindfulness of the Buddha.
I manifest a pure and firm body in thousands of millions of billions of lands; how should one mindfully recollect the Buddha? One should reflect upon the Tathāgata’s past...

In immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands, he manifests a pure body that is capable of enduring all evils, remaining unshakable whether reviled or praised, and steadfast; for immeasurable billions of kalpas,
he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, just as in the "Original Chapter" regarding the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be one who can preach this sutra—should there be anyone who preaches this sutra after the Buddha’s extinction—I shall dispatch emanated members of the fourfold assembly:
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and pure laymen and laywomen; that is to say, the aforementioned fourfold assembly.
One should make offerings to the Dharma-preacher; one should respectfully honor and make offerings to the teacher who expounds the Dharma.
One should guide all sentient beings and assemble them to listen to the Dharma.

One should entice, transform, and lead all sentient beings to gather in one place to hear the sublime Dharma. As for those emanated persons sent by the Buddha, they are as described in the preceding text.
As for those who, having personally relinquished the karmic retribution of pure deeds, are born in this world out of compassion for sentient beings:
if someone should wish to inflict evil upon them with swords, staves, tiles, or stones; if people come to do them harm and inflict various poisonous injuries.
Then he dispatches transformation-beings to act as his guardians; that is, he dispatches the aforementioned transformed virtuous persons to employ skillful means and act as his guardians.
Whether the person who preaches the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, or dwelling by himself in a solitary location.

In a place of profound stillness where there is no sound of human voices, one should read and recite this sutra. In that secluded and silent place, free from the sounds of people, one should read and recite this wondrous sutra.
At that time, I shall manifest for them a body of pure radiance. In that secluded place, there is no sound of human voices.
Purifying the body means reading the wondrous sutras and beholding the Buddha’s wisdom-light body. Purity is the Dharma-body;
light is the Wisdom-body; and the merging of cultivation and nature, manifesting forms wherever one is, is the Response-body.
Through quiet recitation, one attains the vision of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body of the three virtues.
If one forgets the words and phrases, [the Tathāgata] will explain them so that they may be mastered.
If there is anything forgotten in the scriptural text, the Tathāgata’s power of compassion will secretly pervade that person, so that they naturally master it and remember it without loss.
If a person possesses these virtues— if a person possesses such pure conduct—
they may preach for the fourfold assembly, or they may preach the sublime Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
Whether one recites this sutra in an empty place, or in an empty place recites this sutra, all shall behold my body;
all shall behold the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, the radiant and wondrous body.

If there is a person dwelling in seclusion, practicing the gathering and calming of the mind in a quiet place, I shall dispatch the celestial kings, nāga kings, yakṣas, spirits, and others to serve as an assembly for hearing the Dharma.
These eight classes of beings vow to protect the Buddha-Dharma; because this Dharma master recites and expounds it, the Buddha dispatches them to form an assembly for hearing the Dharma.

This person delights in preaching the Dharma and distinguishes it without obstruction. As a Dharma-preacher, when lecturing before the assembly, they are skillfully able to distinguish and delight in teaching with unimpeded eloquence.
This is because they are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; indeed, it is because they have attained the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas.
It can cause great joy; it can cause the listeners among sentient beings to experience great joy.

If one draws near to a Dharma teacher, one will quickly attain the path of a bodhisattva. If one is able to draw near to a teacher who expounds the Dharma, one will quickly achieve the realization of the bodhisattva path.
By following and learning from this teacher, one attains the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

If one can follow and learn from this teacher, then within the sutras one will attain the vision of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without departing from the fundamental mind.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
Long ago, many kalpas past, when the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the great assembly:
"Whoever wishes to make offerings to my entire body should resolve to erect a great stupa that preaches the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Because they heard this sutra while it was being preached within my jeweled stupa amidst the flowers, they leaped forth before me to serve as witnesses;
now, because they have heard from afar what the Buddha of this land is preaching in this sutra, they have surged forth from the earth.
At that time, before the Buddha, when the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" had been finished being preached,
there appeared a stupa made of the seven precious jewels— this very stupa symbolizes the manifestation of the seven treasures of wholesome dharmas.
It is five hundred yojanas in height. That the stūpa’s representation of the Dharma-body is five hundred [yojanas] is accomplished through the cultivation of fivefold merit.
It is two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth; "length and breadth" here refers to the characteristics of the stūpa's base, both vertically and horizontally.

Its breadth is two hundred and fifty *yojanas*, which, when calculated at approximately one thousand *li* per *yojana*, amounts to ten thousand *li*. It is the Dharma-body perfected through cultivation, taking the precepts as its essence.
The precepts of the Śrāvakas number two hundred and fifty; now, by opening up the Hinayana, they are all brought to the same end of Buddhahood.

Since the three characteristics of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise from this, it is said that the dimensions of the stupa base are thus; these are fully present within all four modes of deportment.
Regarding the measurement, it is said to be two hundred and fifty [yojanas] in length and breadth.
Emerging from the earth and dwelling in mid-air, this is easy to perceive in terms of its physical appearance;
if it is taken as a representation of the Dharma, it signifies that which emerges from within the mind-ground and dwells in the emptiness of ultimate great *nirvāṇa*.
It was adorned with various kinds of precious objects and embellished with the merit of ten thousand virtues.
There were five thousand railings—those horizontal ones being called *lǎn* and those vertical ones being called *shǔn*, which are the protective devices atop the jeweled stupa;
these five thousand represent the prevention and warding off of the five realms of existence.

There are thousands of millions of niches and chambers; the number of niches, caves, and jeweled rooms atop the stupa being thousands of millions signifies the immeasurable dharma-gates wherein the practitioner dwells.
It is adorned with countless banners and streamers. The banner symbolizes tranquility, while the streamer symbolizes movement;
stillness is concentration (*samādhi*) and movement is wisdom (*prajñā*). The equalization of concentration and wisdom is called "excellent adornment."
Hanging jeweled necklaces: these necklaces, fashioned by binding together various precious gems, hang down everywhere;
they symbolize that the jewels of wisdom descend through various skillful means to transform and guide sentient beings.
Ten billion precious bells were suspended above it; made of jewels, these bells hung from the top of the stupa, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced wondrous sounds.
These exquisite jewel-sounds issued from the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*), responding to every strike to benefit sentient beings and bring them aid.
From all four sides, the stupa emits the fragrance of *tamarapa* sandalwood.
*Tamarapa* means "nature-free-from-defilement" (*amala*); this "defilement-free sandalwood" is a most exquisite fragrance.
Its substance is filled within and pure without blemish, like the nature of Mount Govinda.
The fragrance of their purification fills the entire world; because the fragrance of those whose conduct is virtuous is heard throughout the ten directions, it is said to "fill everywhere.
As for those various banners and canopies—the precious banners and precious canopies that adorn the crowns of their heads—these represent the Buddha’s merit.
Virtue. It is composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby. If these are taken as symbols of the Dharma:
the nature of gold is firm and rigid, symbolizing firm wisdom; the nature of silver is pure white, symbolizing pure conduct; lapis lazuli...

The crystal, which reflects and penetrates all, represents the mind of clear wisdom; the round-turning conch shell represents the mind of profound flexibility; the agate with its variegated colors represents the mind of myriad practices;
the lustrous pearl represents the mind of skillful wisdom; and the rose-quartz, which is like jade, represents the mind of gentle warmth.
Adorned with these manifold virtues, it is a five-part Dharma-stupa; for this reason, it is said to be composed of the seven treasures.

Its height reaches as far as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings. Because the precious stupas on the flanks of Mount Sumeru where the Four Heavenly Kings reside are so high, they are level with those celestial palaces;
their fourfold mindfulness protects the mind just like the gods.

The Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). On each of the four peaks of Mount Sumeru, there are eight [deities] with Śakra, Lord of Devas, residing in their midst, thus forming the thirty-three.

If this is taken as a metaphor for the Dharma, it illustrates the fifty-two stages of a Bodhisattva: the stages of Abiding (*vihāra*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*mukha*) are called the thirty;

the sages of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are called the thirty-one; and the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksaṃbodhi*) is called the thirty-two. The Tathāgata’s wondrous... [is the thirty-three].
The "Awakened" are named the Thirty-three [Heavenly Beings].

They rained down *mandārava* flowers to make offerings to the precious stūpa. The fact that the various devas rained down flowers to make offerings to the precious stūpa symbolizes that their virtuous conduct adorns the *dharmakāya*.

The remaining multitudes of tens of billions—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—are, from the perspective of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), these eight classes (*aṣṭa-nikāya*). If they represent the manifestation of the Dharma (*dharma-pratibimba*), how could they exist outside of the one mind?
The two classes of gods and nāgas correspond to a virtuous mind, while the remaining yakṣas and others collectively [represent other mental states].
Because these roots of goodness surpass the evil mind, they gather all evil thoughts and transform countless billions of them into goodness.
One offers all flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music to the jeweled stupa; one makes offerings to the jeweled stupa through various acts of giving and support.
They honored, revered, and praised it. Beholding its appearance, they gave rise to wholesome thoughts, conceiving a mind of reverence and honoring the precious stūpa while offering praise.
At that time, within the precious stūpa, when these devas and humans were making offerings—
A great sound issued forth. From within the stupa, a magnificent and sublime voice suddenly emerged, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent, World-Honored One Śākyamuni! Thus did it praise the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
By means of the great wisdom of equanimity; by means of the vast wisdom of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which views the fundamental nature of sentient beings and Buddhas as equal;
and by means of the sublime Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas—the supreme teaching of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for their disciples who possess the Bodhisattva faculty—
This Dharma is that which the Buddhas protectively keep in mind; this Great Wisdom is constantly protected and kept in mind within the pure minds of all Buddhas.
The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma gives rise to the wondrous fruit;
the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma is preached for the great assembly, analyzed and expounded for all the great multitude.
Thus it is, thus it is: the Honored One Śākyamuni, through his compassionate skillful means, acts thus and thus for the sake of sentient beings.
It is said:
"Whatever the World-Honored One Śākyamuni has spoken is entirely true.
Every single word spoken by the Honored One Śākya is a word of truth."
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air as before, and they also heard the sounds issuing from within the stupa, such as "Excellent! and so forth.
All attained the joy of the Dharma; all found great delight within the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma.
They marveled at what had never occurred before, and the entire assembly was struck with wonder, saying it was unprecedented.
He rose from his seat, intending to inquire about the causes and conditions of this stūpa;
thus he rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side. Having first shown respect by joining his palms in greeting, he then stepped back and stood at one side.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna. He was a preeminent great bodhisattva among the assembly;
because his wisdom was profound, he was skilled in eloquently expounding all dharmas, and thus he was named Mahāpratibhāna.
He knew the doubts in the minds of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others;

seeing the jeweled stupa, they did not know its meaning and, finding it a marvelous sight never seen before, their minds were filled with doubt. The Bodhisattva, having understood this, therefore made inquiries on their behalf.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions, and for what reasons, has this precious stūpa emerged from the earth? We wish to know its origin."
Furthermore, within that [stūpa], such sounds were produced; moreover, from within the stūpa, there issued forth a great and wondrous voice of praise.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa (Great Joyous Eloquence), answering him because of his question.

Within this precious stūpa is the entire body of a Tathāgata. When various Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, they manifest fire to cremate their bodies and distribute their śarīra relics to form karmic connections for the masses.

However, when Prabhūtaratna entered parinirvāṇa, he did not manifest his body; at the end of his life, he entrusted [the disciples] with instructions to erect a stūpa to make offerings to his remains.
It was because he wished to authenticate this sutra that the Buddha replied that the stūpa contains his entire body.
In the distant past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, long ago in an eon,
there was a world in the eastern direction named Ratnaviśuddha. That land was pure and abounded in many precious treasures.
In that realm there is a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna; in that Pure Land of Jewels, the Buddha is named Prabhūtaratna.
When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a great vow; while still on the stage of a causal practitioner, he had previously made this great aspiration.
If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa— once I have realized the unsurpassed path of the Buddha and passed away—
in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, that is, in the places throughout the ten directions where this sūtra is spoken:
My stūpas— my stūpas made of the seven treasures—
shall emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sutra, for the sake of hearing this Lotus Sutra;
that is, they shall immediately emerge before those Buddhas.
He acted as a witness and praised him, saying, "Excellent! It is because of such a mind.
After that Buddha had attained enlightenment, and having already become a Buddha, at the time of his parinirvāṇa—when his work of transformation was complete and he was about to pass away—
In the midst of the great assembly of devas and humans, he addressed the bhikṣus and spoke to the gathered disciples who had left the household life:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body—those who desire to make offerings to my entire body—"
One should erect a great stūpa to enshrine the Buddha’s body;
for that Buddha, by the power of his supernormal knowledges and vows—the power of his great supernormal knowledges and solemn resolve—sustains his own body.
Wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be this Lotus Sūtra, and wherever in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there may be one preaching the Lotus Sūtra,
that precious stupa shall emerge before them, manifesting itself in accordance with each location.
His entire body remains within the stupa, and he utters the praise, "Excellent! Excellent! That his whole body appears and praises it as excellent is to fulfill his past vow;
Mahāpratibhāna, because the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna’s stupa heard the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, it has emerged from the earth to offer this praise.
He said, "Excellent, excellent! Explain your purpose for coming so that the assembly may know.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna, by means of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power—meaning that he was able to see [the Buddha] by relying on the Buddha’s compassion rather than through his own power—[spoke].
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we wish to behold this body of the Buddha; we wish to behold the body of the ancient Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna: "The Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a profound and solemn vow. The Buddha...
He told Ānanda that those Buddhas had previously made profound and weighty vows:
"When my jeweled stūpa emerges before all the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra— at the very moment the stūpa appears to hear the Dharma— [it shall do so]."
Should there be anyone who wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly, or who wishes to show my entire body within my stupa to the fourfold assembly gathered at this assembly,
those emanations of that Buddha who reside throughout the worlds of the ten directions and preach the Dharma will appear in the present world and preach.

As for the Buddha’s emanations mentioned in the sutra who reside throughout the worlds of the ten directions extensively expounding all dharmas to deliver sentient beings—they all return and assemble in one place.
They wait until these emanations have gathered simultaneously, after which the single body manifests as hundreds, thousands, and billions of bodies;
because this current assembly gathers many back into one, it is said that they "all return."
Only then shall my body appear; only then shall my entire body appear within my stūpa.
Mahāratnaprītipūrṇa, those emanations of mine, the Buddhas who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions, should now [be regarded as such].
“Gather them! If you wish to see the body of this Buddha Prabhūtaratna, I shall assemble the emanated Buddhas.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying: “Having heard this, Mahāpratibhāna spoke again to the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One, we also wish to see the Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, so that we may pay homage and make offerings to them.
We desire to see them for the purpose of practicing such offerings.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from between his eyebrows; he emitted it from the center because he wished to assemble the Buddhas who were his emanations.
The voice proclaimed: "Behold the radiance of the white tuft of hair!
Immediately, one sees the Buddhas of five hundred trillion nayuta Ganges-sands of lands in the eastern direction.
Because of the illumination of this light, the assembly is able to see them all; these five hundred trillion [Buddhas] represent the true causes of the five stages of the Bodhisattva."
The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are themselves pure mindfulness.
Those lands all have crystal for their ground; this crystal ground is the mind of sublime purity.
The jeweled trees and jeweled garments serve as adornments; the jeweled trees are the King of Bodhi Trees, and the jeweled garments are...
This is gentle forbearance.
It is filled with countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas. These bodhisattvas are the mind of every thought-moment.
A precious canopy is spread everywhere above, and a precious net covers it; the precious canopy is that which is covered by compassion, and the precious net is...
This is the net formed by the pearls of precepts.
In that land, the various Buddhas proclaim all dharmas with a great and wondrous voice; each and every Buddha issues forth a great sound to expound all dharmas.
He also saw immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the multitudes.
In each and every land, there were bodhisattvas who filled its entirety, each expounding the Dharma for their respective assemblies.

In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—there are ten directions in total. Just as that which is seen in the eastern direction illuminated by the light is thus, so too is it in the remaining nine directions;
the characteristics of the places illuminated by the light are likewise the same.
