The places illuminated by the light of the ūrṇā-kośa mark are likewise thus, being identical to those in the eastern direction.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Śākyamuni Buddhas who are emanations from the ten directions [were present].
Each addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying to the bodhisattvas seated before them:
"Good sons, I shall now go to the world of Sahā, to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha. Since his light has already illumined that place, he knows my intention and has come here."
He simultaneously made offerings to the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and desired to make offerings to the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

At that time, the Sahā world immediately transformed into a state of purity; for the purpose of assembling all the Buddhas, Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, first purified his land through his supernormal powers.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli and adorned with precious jewel-trees; golden cords demarcate the eightfold paths.

Such is the purity of the Land of True Retribution of Śākyamuni Buddha. Yet, in order to transform and deliver stubborn and evil sentient beings, he manifests this defiled land where the five turbidities coexist.
Now, wishing to speak of the reality, he manifests this pure land, adorned with all manner of jewels.
There are no villages, hamlets, towns, or cities. What is called a "village" (*grāma*) refers to the mixed dwelling of men and women;

since this land of ultimate fruition consists solely of men and there are no women, it lacks villages, as well as the characteristics of hamlets, camps, fortresses, walled cities, prefectures, and districts—all of which are entirely absent at once.
The great ocean, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, and marshes: the ocean and the rivers are metaphors for the shallow and deep wisdoms of those who follow the various vehicles;
the mountains and the flowing streams are metaphors for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); the forests and marshes are metaphors for the branches of enlightenment.
Now, in actuality, these present retributions all return to the single reality, wherein all marks are non-existent.
One burns great precious incense; cultivating great merit is what is meant by "burning precious incense.
Mandārava flowers are strewn everywhere upon the ground, signifying that one has cultivated the causes of goodness without any omission or deficiency.
It is covered above by a canopy of jeweled nets. Because the practice of the Bodhisattva takes compassion as its primary principle, it is said to be "universally covered by a jeweled canopy.
Because the path to Buddhahood cannot be established without precepts, it is said to be "covered above by jeweled nets."
He suspended various precious bells; the sound of these bells signified the preaching of the Dharma.

He left only this assembly, leaving behind solely those in the assembly who were listening to the Dharma, while he moved all other devas and humans to other lands, using the Buddha’s supernatural power to relocate all other devas and humans.
The assembly was placed within other lands.
At that time, the Buddhas—the emanations of Śākyamuni from the ten directions—each took a great bodhisattva as an attendant; each Buddha was accompanied by only one great bodhisattva.
Acting as attendants, they arrived at the Sahā world and each reached the foot of a precious tree.
Here in this direction, beneath the trees of the manifested land, each precious tree is five hundred yojanas high; this immediately symbolizes the Dharma-body of the fivefold merits.

The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are adorned in successive order. The branches are a metaphor for the phenomena (*dharmas*); within each individual phenomenon there are further distinctions, which are likened to the leaves.
The opening of the flowers represents the cause, and the formation of the fruit represents wisdom; thus, by practicing progressively, one uses these to adorn the essence of the Dharma.
Beneath each of the jewel trees there is a lion throne five *yojanas* high. The trees represent the vows and practices, while the thrones symbolize emptiness, stillness, and serenity;
their principle is termed "sitting" (*āsanam*). That the thrones are five *yojanas* high signifies the stage of the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*).
It was also adorned with great jewels. That he sits upon this seat of emptiness yet is now described as being "adorned with jewels" signifies that it is the seat of the Tathāgata of Non-Emptiness.
At that time, each of the Buddhas sat cross-legged upon these seats. Having arrived there, they each sat upon the jewels.
He sat down.

In this manner, they successively multiplied until they filled the trichiliocosm. Thus, unfolding and spreading out one after another, they sat down and filled the entire transformed realm of the trichiliocosm.
Yet, even the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha from a single direction have not yet been exhausted;
those emanations seated alone in the eastern direction alone pervade the trichiliocosm and are still not fully accounted for.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate the various Buddhas who had manifested as his emanations, and desiring to provide seats to receive those Buddhas,
further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure. Thus it is said, "The eight..."
"Square" refers here to horizontal pervasiveness; it transforms only the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions, without extending to above or below.
This occurs likewise for two million billion sets of the eight directions, totaling one trillion six hundred billion three thousandfold world systems.
There were no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras; because it was pure, there were no four evil paths.
Furthermore, all the devas and humans were transferred to other lands, leaving behind only the assembly at the gathering while the rest of the devas and humans were moved away.
The lands to be converted and the transformed realms likewise have lapis lazuli for their ground and are adorned with jewel trees.
These trees are five hundred yojanas in height, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive tiers of adornment.
Beneath each tree there is a precious lion throne, five yojanas in height, composed of various kinds of jewels.
It is considered that even in the ornamented [world-systems] there are no great oceans or rivers; this is explained as above.
Furthermore, there is Mount Mucilinda, which is translated here as "Stone Mountain," and Mount Mahāmucilinda, which is translated here as "Great Stone Mountain."
The Cakravāḍa Mountains: outside the four great continents, there is a surrounding mountain named the Lesser Cakravāḍa;
the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains: outside the trichiliocosm, there is a surrounding mountain named the Great Cakravāḍa.
Mount Sumeru and other such kings of mountains: "Sumeru" is translated here as "Wondrous High. Outside of Sumeru, there are ten great mountains that encircle it;
these are called the kings of all mountains, and none else are like them.
They were all unified as a single Buddha-land. All those transformed lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and consisting of great trichiliocosms, were unified as one land.
The ground was made of jewels, level and even, with jeweled lattices and canopies; upon the jeweled ground, canopies were formed from precious gems.
It completely covered its surface, shielding it on all sides.
Banners and canopies were suspended as explained previously.
Great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel-flowers were strewn across the ground, as before.
In order to provide seats for the Buddhas who were to arrive, Śākyamuni Buddha manifested as emanation Buddhas;
furthermore, he transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure.
Thus, through three transformations of the pure lands of the eight directions— first a single great trichiliocosm, then one thousand six hundred billion,
and finally adding the current number— the total reaches thirty-two trillion nayutas of lands, which is just sufficient to accommodate all the emanated Buddhas from the worlds of the ten directions.
There are no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras; there are no four evil paths.
Furthermore, all devas and humans are transferred to other lands in the realms he transforms, where the ground is likewise made of lapis lazuli and adorned with precious trees.
These trees are five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive layers of adornment, and beneath every tree...
There is a precious lion throne five yojanas high, likewise adorned with great jewels; furthermore, there are no great oceans,
rivers, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Mahācakravāḍa, Mount Sumeru, or any other kings of mountains—
all together constitute a single Buddha-field, a ground of jewels that is level and even.

Canopies of interlaced jewels cover it entirely; various banners and parasols are suspended from above, and great precious incense is burned while celestial jewel-flowers are strewn across the ground—all as explained previously.
At that time, in lands as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers,

where the emanations of Śākyamuni from the eastern direction reside, there were likewise Buddhas who were emanations of his body in each of those lands, facing toward the east, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Each preached the Dharma; each expounded the Dharma in their own land and then gathered here.
Thus, the Buddhas from the eastern direction came to gather in the Sahā world.
In this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions all arrived in succession and sat in the eight directions. As for the transformations they manifested—
“Good son, at that time, in each and every direction, there were four million billion nayutas of lands filled with Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
It is said that these emanation bodies of the Buddha fill the eight directions.”
At that time, each of the Buddhas sat beneath a jeweled tree upon a lion throne, exactly as in the eastern direction.
They all dispatched their attendants to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha, and each sent a great bodhisattva they were accompanied by to pay homage,
show respect, and offer greetings to the Tathāgata.
Each carried a handful of precious flowers—filling their robes and lapels—and addressed them, saying to their attendants:
"Sons of good family, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides; send each of you there."
At the assembly on Vulture Peak,
my words were as follows: "I am to transmit the Buddha's message,
asking if he has little illness and little affliction— that is, whether he has few ailments and few mental disturbances."
"Are you physically strong and at ease? Is your strength abundant and your mind peaceful?
Are the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas all secure? Having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he next inquired after the great assembly.
He scattered these precious flowers as an offering to the Buddha; having first completed the offerings, he then transmitted the message, saying:
"That certain Buddha, although an emanation of Śākyamuni, has his own distinct name, and for this reason is referred to as 'that certain one'."
I have come to open this jeweled stūpa; my purpose in coming is to open the stūpa and reveal it to this great assembly.
It is the same with the messengers sent by all Buddhas: as it is for one Buddha, so it is for all Buddhas.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha saw that the buddhas who had been emanated as his分身 (emanations) had all assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones.
Having seen that the emanated buddhas were fully settled in their seats, the Buddha [proceeded].
All heard that the Buddhas had granted their consent and together opened the precious stupa.

Hearing that the words of all the Buddhas were identical with their own aspirations, they immediately rose from their seats and stood in mid-air. Intending to open the stupa, they realized that because it was so lofty and sublime, how could it be reached otherwise than by ascending into the sky;
thus they rose from their seats and remained standing in the air.
The entire assembly of the fourfold community rose, joined their palms, and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
At that time, because they saw the Buddha leave his seat, all those in the assembly rose, joined their palms, and looked up at the Buddha with one-pointed attention.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa with his right finger. Using the right finger symbolizes the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*).
He produced a great sound, like removing the bolt and opening the gate of a great city; as the Buddha opened the stūpa door, he made this great sound.
The sound was like turning a key to open the great city gate.
Immediately, the entire assembly, all those gathered in the congregation,
saw the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna sitting upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa, his entire body intact and undispersed, as if he had entered [the state of meditative absorption].
He entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), his entire body remaining motionless as if absorbed in *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, he heard these words: "Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni Buddha, you have skillfully preached this Lotus Sūtra."
When the stūpa first appeared, he already offered praise; now that the doors of the stūpa have opened, he praises it once again, hence the words:
"Furthermore, I have heard that praising the Buddha is for the sake of the joyfully spoken sūtra.
It is for the purpose of hearing this sūtra that I have come here. By saying "I have come for the purpose of hearing the sūtra," he indicates his reason for coming.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddhas who had entered parinirvāṇa countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago speak such words,
marveled at what they had never before experienced. Seeing that these Buddhas who had long since passed away were now uttering such speech—
something never seen before— they marveled at its rarity.
With clusters of celestial jewel-flowers— clusters of various heavenly jewel-flowers—
he scattered them over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. Because he saw Prabhūtaratna scatter flowers as a mark of respect,
and because he was above Śākyamuni Buddha, he scattered the flowers for the sake of seeing Prabhūtaratna through Śākyamuni.
He made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, within the jeweled stūpa, Prabhūtaratna Buddha offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha.
Prabhūtaratna offered the seat and invited Śākyamuni to sit upon it.
He spoke these words: "May Śākyamuni Buddha please take this seat. He invited Śākyamuni Buddha to occupy the precious throne.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stūpa and sat upon half of the seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Because of the request of Prabhūtaratna, Śākyamuni entered the stupa and sat upon half of his seat.
At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas— Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna—
sitting cross-legged upon lion thrones within the seven-jeweled stupa, visible from afar as the two Honored Ones seated there.
Regarding the jeweled stūpa:
each person should thus bring to mind that the Buddha is seated high and far away. Because he is at a distance, although one wishes to draw near to him, it is impossible;
this is why one should bring him to mind.

"We only pray that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernatural powers, will cause us all to dwell together in the void. May the multitude pray that the Buddha’s power may receive and lead them to abide in the sky.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernatural powers, received the great assembly, and they were all situated in the void.
Out of compassion, the Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, received them according to their wishes so that they all dwelt in mid-air.
With a great voice, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly. Śākyamuni Buddha produced a great and wondrous sound, proclaiming it throughout the fourfold assembly.
"Who is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this Sahā world-system? Now is precisely the right time.
As the Buddha is about to manifest his parinirvāṇa, he universally addresses the great assembly, declaring that now is the very moment to exhort and recruit others to ensure its circulation."
The Tathāgata will before long enter parinirvāṇa; his work of transformation is about to end, and he wishes to return to primordial stillness.

The Buddha intends to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who shall uphold it, and thus exhorts you so that he may entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to its proper place, lest it fall into oblivion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though long since passed away;
the Great Sage, the Master of Dharma, the World-Honored One of myriad virtues, though long since entered extinction into Nirvana."

Even within this precious stupa, one has come for the sake of the Dharma; even while within this wondrous stupa made of the seven treasures, one has traveled from afar specifically to hear the Dharma.
Why, then, do you people not strive diligently for the Dharma? For what reason, all of you, are you unable to be earnest?
They diligently seek the Great Dharma.
It has been immeasurable kalpas since this Buddha entered parinirvāṇa; it is said that the Buddha’s extinction occurred so long ago that its kalpas cannot be calculated.
Because the Dharma is difficult to encounter, they travel everywhere to hear the teachings, proceeding to various places to listen to the sublime Dharma, for the Dharma is exalted.
Because it is wondrous and difficult to encounter.
Regarding that Buddha’s original vow: "After my parinirvāṇa, that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a solemn vow that after this body of mine has passed into extinction..."
Wherever I have gone, it has always been for the sake of hearing the Dharma; wherever I have traveled, I have never had any other purpose than to hear the Dharma.
Furthermore, "my emanated bodies, the immeasurable Buddhas" refers here to the emanated Buddhas of the ten directions.
As many as the sands of the Ganges have come desiring to hear the Dharma; as many as the sands of the Ganges have come for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
and they have come to see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, desiring to behold that one who has long since passed away.
Each abandoned their wondrous lands and their assemblies of disciples; each abandoned their respective Buddha-fields and their multitudes.
The various offerings of devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, as well as the services of the fourfold assembly, were all abandoned and departed at once.
They have come here so that the Dharma may endure for a long time; they have all gathered here for the sake of abiding in the Dharma.
It is because the Buddhas of the ten directions wish to sit that Śākyamuni manifests supernatural powers through his own supernormal power.
They moved immeasurable multitudes so that their own lands were purified; they moved the hosts of devas and humans and placed them in other lands to adorn and purify those realms.
Each of the Buddhas went beneath a jeweled tree; each of the Buddhas arrived at this jeweled tree.
It was adorned like a pure pond of lotuses; the pond is used as a metaphor for the land, and the lotuses for the Buddha.
Beneath those jewel trees were various lion thrones—lion thrones beneath each of the jewel trees.

The Buddha sat upon it, adorned with radiant light. All the Buddhas sat upon lion-throne jewels, blazing with intense radiance and exquisitely adorned, like great torches lit in the darkness of night.
Sentient beings wandering in delusion are like those in the darkness of night; the light of the Buddhas [illuminates them].
He shines like a blazing torch;
from his body issues a sublime fragrance that pervades the lands of the ten directions.

The fragrance of the Buddhas' bodies fills all places, and sentient beings, being perfumed by it, cannot contain their joy. Perfumed by the scent of the Buddhas, each and every sentient being rejoices.
Overjoyed, he could not contain himself.

It was like a great wind blowing against the branches of a small tree: the wind is a metaphor for the Buddha’s fragrance, and the branches are a metaphor for the capacities and views of sentient beings.
By means of such skillful expedients, he causes the Dharma to endure for a long time; through such skillful means as these, he enables them to attain the correct [path].
"So that the Dharma may long abide in the world.
He addressed the great assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa," he told the gathered multitude, "after the Tathāgata’s extinction, who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?
Who will be able to resolve their mind to protect, uphold, read, recite, and explain it?"
Sūtra: Now, before the Buddha, he himself utters this vow: "Today, in the presence of the Buddha, I shall personally make a profound and solemn aspiration."
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa,
by virtue of his great vow he utters the lion’s roar; because of the power of his great vows from past lives, he [manifests] within the jeweled stupa.
I shall now utter the lion’s roar.
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, myself, and all the emanated Buddhas gathered here should understand this intention. The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has come from afar, and my own body is present;
that the emanations of the ten directions have all assembled in this land—what is the original purpose for this? You should know it as such.
This is a deeply earnest intention.
Among you, sons of the Buddha, who is able to protect the Dharma? Summoning this great assembly, who is able to act for me? Who will uphold the True Dharma?
One should make great vows so that [the Dharma] may endure for a long time. Practice is like the pigments and the power of the vow is like the glue;
without glue, the pigments will not be firm, and with glue alone but no pigments, the patterns and forms will not be manifest.

To have vows without practice is merely empty talk; to have practice without vows lacks firm endurance. Only when practice and vows support one another can a task be accomplished. If one wishes to protect the Dharma...
For this reason, the Buddha exhorted them to make great vows so that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.
Whoever is able to protect this sutra and its Dharma—those sons of the Buddha who are able to protect this sutra.

This constitutes making offerings to me and to Prabhūtaratna. What is taught in this sutra regarding the deeds performed by the Buddha and Prabhūtaratna—following those deeds of the Buddha is called making offerings to the Buddha.

This Buddha Prabhūtaratna dwells constantly within this jeweled stupa, traveling throughout the ten directions. This World-Honored One, residing within the jeweled stupa, constantly travels through the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
For the sake of this sutra; that is, for the sake of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
they also made offerings to all the manifested Buddhas who had come, and likewise made offerings to all the manifested Buddhas from the ten directions who had come as their divided bodies.
Regarding "adorned and embellishing the world," this refers to the transformation buddhas as the adornments;
within the buddha-fields, it is by means of these buddhas and bodhisattvas that the world is adorned and embellished, enabling those who behold them to give rise to a heart of joy.
If one preaches this sutra, it is as if one has seen me, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and all the manifested Buddhas.
If there is anyone who can read and preach this sutra and deeply understand its meaning and intent, seeing the Dharma-body of the Buddha, they shall have seen Śākyamuni, Prabhūtaratna,
and all the manifested Buddhas who have come from their various bodies.
"O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this with careful attention. I address the assembly of sons of good family:
each of you should listen attentively and reflect well upon this.
This is a difficult task; you must resolve to make great vows. To uphold this sutra is a rare and difficult matter, which cannot be accomplished without patience."
Who is capable of such profound diligence and intensified effort? One ought to be courageous and give rise to great vows, taking them as the very foundation.
As for all other sūtras, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, and the various skillful means and sūtras of the Three Vehicles, their number is exceedingly vast.
Though there be a multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
it would not yet be considered difficult; though one could explain these provisional teachings of the three vehicles of incomplete meaning,
it would still not be considered difficult.

If one were to take up Mount Sumeru with one's hand and hurl it to countless other Buddha-fields, this would not yet be difficult. Whatever is considered difficult by people in this world is not difficult for them;
however, to read and expound this sutra in this evil world—this alone is difficult.
If one were to move the great trichiliocosm with a toe and hurl it to another land, this would not yet be considered difficult.

For instance, when the Buddha pressed his finger and the entire great trichiliocosm shook, even to the point of casting it toward other lands, these were merely the peripheral matters of manifested supernatural powers;
they do not equal the propagation of the sutras.
If one were to establish the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the assembly and preach immeasurable other sutras there, it would not be difficult.
The gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are called the summit of conditioned existence within the three realms;

if a person were to fix their mind upon this summit of the conditioned and preach immeasurable sutras of the provisional meaning concerning the expedient means of the Three Vehicles to the great assembly, it would likewise not be difficult.
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to preach this sutra in an evil age, that is indeed difficult.
To preach this Lotus Sutra in the turbid world after the Buddha’s extinction is truly difficult.
Even if someone were to grasp empty space with their hand while traveling about, it would not be difficult;
for empty space is without characteristics and cannot be grasped, so even if one could grasp it, it would still not be difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one were to write it down oneself or cause others to write it down, that would indeed be difficult.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, for a person of inferior faculties to be able to propagate this sutra is superior to grasping at emptiness.
If one were to take the great earth and place it upon one's toenail to ascend to the Brahma Heaven, that would not be difficult.
Since the Brahma Heaven rests upon space, it is no more difficult now to take the great earth and place it upon one's toenail to ascend there.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, to even briefly read this sutra is difficult;
during that same brief interval in the degenerate age after his passing, one who can read this sutra surpasses one who merely upholds the stages (bhūmis).
Even if one were to carry dry grass on one's shoulders and enter into a world consumed by the fires at the end of an eon (*kalpa*), not being burned would not yet be considered difficult.
While it would indeed be difficult to enter carrying dry grass when the fires of an eon arise and not be incinerated, even that is not truly difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and preaches it for even a single person, that is indeed difficult.
In the final age, to uphold this sutra and preach it for even a single person—even if they are like blades of grass entering a conflagration at the end of the kalpa—is a supreme victory.

If one upholds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures to expound them for others—wherein the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Buddha-Dharma refer to the three hundred and fifty assemblies of the Tathāgata’s preaching, each assembly containing the six *pāramitās* (making thirty-six), totaling eighteen;
and further, five times six equals thirty, and five times thirty equals one hundred and fifty; these together total two thousand [eight hundred]... [text fragment ends].
The eleven hundred [teachings] each break down the four great elements and the six sense objects to form twenty-one thousand;
when categorized according to the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as their equal combination, each possesses twenty-one thousand, totaling eighty-four thousand.

As for the twelve divisions of the scriptures: first, prose (sūtra); second, verse (geya); third, prophecies (vyākaraṇa); fourth, independent verses (udāna); fifth, unasked teachings (nidāna); sixth...
The twelve divisions of the scriptures— namely, *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*—
though the teachings spoken by the Buddha are immeasurable, are fully subsumed within these twelve categories.
If one upholds these and expounds them for others, [one attains great merit].
To cause all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and to cause that assembly of listeners to obtain the six supernormal powers and become arhats—
even though one can do this, it is not yet considered difficult; for although the teaching is sublime and profound, the listeners merely attain the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
It is not difficult to attain the fruit.
However, after my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sūtra and inquire into its meaning and intent is what is truly difficult.
If one hears this sūtra, inquires into its meaning and intent, and practices according to the teaching, one will be able to accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi; therefore, it is difficult.
Furthermore,
if a person teaches the Dharma so that thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable and innumerable beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are benefited;
and if this teacher of the Dharma is able to deliver such innumerable beings.
They attained arhatship and were endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). The meaning of these six powers is as explained in the *Bhaiṣajyavarga*.
Although such benefits exist, they are not difficult to achieve; although such benefits of the Hīnayāna exist, they are likewise not difficult to attain.
After my parinirvāṇa, it will be difficult indeed for anyone to be able to uphold a sūtra such as this.
It will be even more difficult to uphold this sūtra and preach it for the sake of others, thereby enabling those people to attain the unsurpassed path.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras across immeasurable lands.
For the sake of sentient beings attaining the Buddha-way, I have manifested bodies that pervade the lands of the ten directions;
from the time I first attained enlightenment until now, I have extensively expounded immeasurable other sutras.
Among these, this sutra is the foremost; among all other immeasurable sūtras, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most supreme.
If there is anyone who can uphold it, they uphold the body of the Buddha; for the essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the Buddha’s Dharma-body, and one who upholds it [upholds that].
The established principles are for the purpose of seeing the Buddha.
After my parinirvāṇa, sons of good family, you shall address the assembled multitude:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? You shall ask the assembly: "Who among you is courageous enough to undertake this task?"
I take this upon myself. Now, before the Buddha, I shall personally utter a vow; I shall personally make a profound oath before the Buddha:
"If one should uphold this sutra, which is difficult to maintain, even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and all the Buddhas shall do likewise. This sutra is supreme..."
If one can uphold this even for a brief moment, the Buddha and all Buddhas will be filled with joy.
Such a person is praised by all Buddhas; likewise, those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the final age shall always be lauded by all Buddhas.
This is valor; this is diligence. To be able to perform difficult tasks is called valor; to be single-mindedly untiring is called diligence.
This is what is meant by one who maintains the precepts and practices *dhūta*. Maintaining all the various precepts is the bodhisattva path of practicing *dhūta*.
By practicing this, one enters the Buddha-vehicle;
thus one will swiftly attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, and will quickly attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
One will be able to read, recite, and uphold this sutra in future ages; one will be able to read, recite, receive, and maintain this scripture in the future.
Such a person is a true child of the Buddha, dwelling on the ground of pure goodness; they are truly a child of the Tathāgata,
abiding in the station of pure goodness characterized by compassion.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will be able to understand its meaning. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will skillfully comprehend the meaning and flavor of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
They are the eyes of all devas and humans; they are the eyes for the world, for humans, and for devas.

In this world of fear, one is able to preach for even a brief moment; in the terrifying and evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to expound the teaching for others for even a short while.
All devas and humans should make offerings to such a person; all those in the world, whether gods or men, should pay them respect.
Reverently making offerings to this person.
*The Explanatory Commentary on the Phrases of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Four;
*The Explanatory Commentary on the Phrases of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Five.
The Śramaṇa Guǎngzhào of Qiántáng, Śākyamuni Wéndá, [Translates] the Devadatta Chapter, the Twelfth, of the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra.
Devadatta is also called Tiáodá; this means "Burning Heat. This person was born when [the Buddha was] thirty-three...
"The hearts of the celestial deities are all scorched with heat because they have given birth to the desire to destroy the Buddha-dharma; thus their hearts are scorched.
An interpretation such as this is explained according to the *traces* (*jì*) of the Hīnayāna.

Now, according to the Great Teaching, which reveals the fundamental through the traces, it is sufficient to understand that the Tathāgata’s teachers in past lives attained perfect enlightenment on account of this person. This clarifies the present chapter.
This clearly demonstrates that the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost among all sūtras; if one upholds this scripture, one shall attain the path to Buddhahood.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, after the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" had been concluded.
At that time, he addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, devas, and humans:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, and during immeasurable ages in times long gone, I sought the Lotus Sutra without weariness; in my quest for the Lotus Sutra, I never grew weary."
Throughout many kalpas he constantly served as a king. Having previously been the body of a king for many kalpas, he made a vow to seek unexcelled bodhicitta without ever regressing;
he vowed to seek the path to buddhahood, and his mind never once fell back or declined.
In order to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, and for the sake of practicing to completion these six perfections,
one diligently practices giving with a mind free from stinginess. Since giving is the foremost among the six perfections and the *dāna-pāramitā* encompasses all practices,
the teaching that one should "diligently give without any stinginess" is intended to instruct the world in establishing right conduct.
The external wealth consists of elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, and attendants.
The internal wealth consists of one's head, eyes, marrow, brain, body flesh, hands, and feet— sacrificing even one’s own life— given to whoever seeks them.
He bestowed everything upon them.
At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable. Regarding those people of the past, their lifespans lasted for immeasurable kalpas;
it is said that [even such things] were difficult to relinquish.
For the sake of the Dharma, he relinquished his royal position and entrusted the administration to his crown prince;
desiring to seek the sublime Dharma, he immediately abandoned the status of king and committed all state affairs to his crown prince.
He beat the drum and issued a proclamation to the four quarters to seek the Dharma. Striking the great drum, he spread his decree far and wide to search for the subtle and wondrous Dharma:
"Who can explain the Mahāyāna for me? Who is able to teach the Mahāyāna Dharma?"
"I shall serve you as a messenger for the rest of my life. By "for the rest of my life," he meant not merely for a short time;
by "serving as a messenger," he meant providing service as an attendant. If one is not humble, how can one hear the Dharma? If one cannot endure hardship, how can one persevere?
This serves as a model for worldly people and an illustration of the sages and worthies, providing a standard for those seeking the Way.
At that time, there was a seer who came and addressed the king, saying, "I have come because of your proclamation.
I possess a Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. That seer said, "I possess a great teaching named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
"If you do not disobey me, I shall proclaim it for you; if you can indeed refrain from opposing me, I shall grant you this teaching.
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king rejoiced and leaped for joy. At that time, having heard these words of the seer, the king attained his desired goal.
His heart was filled with joy, and he leaped for joy without realizing it.
He immediately attended upon the rishi, providing whatever was required; he followed and served this rishi, supplying all that was needed according to his requirements.
Gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food—performing these tasks according to the season is the traditional custom of those on the path:
gathering fruit from the treetops, drawing spring water from the mountain ravines, collecting firewood from the peaks, and preparing meals in the kitchen; all such activities are for this purpose.
Even using his own body as a seat, he remains without weariness of body or mind.

To use the body as a seat means that, like one carrying a burden on the shoulders, he endures all hardships and tolerates fatigue for the sake of the Dharma, remaining without weariness of body or mind.
At that time, he served him for a thousand years; as the time passed, his conduct remained consistent from beginning to end.
For the sake of the Dharma, he served with diligent effort so that nothing was lacking.
Desiring to seek the Dharma from his teacher, he served and ran errands with physical and mental diligence, providing whatever was required so that there was no deficiency.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recall past kalpas, when for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma... [The Buddha recalled that] during past kalpas long ago, he desired to seek the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

Although he acts as a king of the world, he does not crave the pleasures of the five desires. Although he is a worldly monarch, he is able to remain detached from the sensual pleasures of the five desires—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
He strikes a bell to announce to the four quarters. (Whereas previously it was said he struck a drum, here it is stated he strikes a bell; this refers to the profound bell and drum of the Dharma.)

"I shall do all of this. Whoever possesses the Great Dharma, if they would explain it to me, I shall become their slave; I will sacrifice my own body for the sake of the Dharma without feeling any weariness."
At that time, the Rishi Asita came and addressed the Great King. "Asita" is translated here as "Longevity";
because the King had made a request, the Rishi came and said to him:
"I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world. This subtle and wondrous Dharma is what I uphold."

This is rare. If there are those capable of practicing it, I shall explain it for you; if there are those capable of performing it, I shall first select those who are fit and worthy, and then explain it to them.
At that time, upon hearing the words of the seer, the king’s heart was filled with great joy. Hearing the seer’s words, his mind leaped with delight;
he immediately attended to the seer, providing whatever was required, serving him and supplying all that was needed.

Whenever firewood or fruits and melons were available, he would respectfully offer them at the appropriate times; "melons" here refers to gourds, vegetables, and the like—whatever was required at the time, he provided it all.
Because his heart was set upon the wondrous Dharma, his body and mind never grew weary; with his heart fixed on the Dharma, he never succumbed to indolence.

For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently seeks the Great Dharma; his mind is set on benefiting others rather than being intent upon himself, and for this reason, he diligently seeks the Great Dharma.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of his own person nor for the pleasures of the five senses, nor is it for his own benefit or for the pursuit of sensual gratification.
Therefore, as a great king, I diligently sought and obtained this Dharma. Having previously been a king, I attained this Dharma and subsequently achieved Buddhahood;
for this reason, I now speak it for you. Because one practices according to the Dharma, one now achieves the Buddha-Dharma;
because such is its wondrous nature, I speak it for you.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying to the assembled multitude:
"The king at that time was none other than myself. The Dharma-seeking king of that time is now Śākyamuni.
The seer of that time is now Devadatta; that seer of that time is indeed the present Devadatta."
"By virtue of Devadatta as a spiritual friend, and because that Devadatta was well-acquainted with the sublime Dharma and discerned what was obstructed and what was unobstructed,
he enabled me to fulfill the six pāramitās— that is, the practice of the six perfections."
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute the various marks and characteristics of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The color of purple-polished gold; his body is like the color of gold.
The ten powers and four fearlessnesses, like the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Buddha.
The four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva gathers and transforms sentient beings.
The eighteen unique qualities: these eighteen dharmas of the Buddha are not shared with the three vehicles.

Regarding the powers of the divine faculties and the power of the Way—the Buddha’s wondrous penetrations up to his power of the Way—these characteristics of the dharmas may all be found by consulting the preceding text.
In the past, he attained perfect enlightenment and extensively saved sentient beings; now, having become a Buddha, he extensively saves all.

In both cases, it was entirely due to Devadatta as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Reflecting upon this, one realizes that the merit by which he himself attained Buddhahood is owed to his teacher.

He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas from now on, and continuing through further immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Heavenly King (Devarāja).
Because his Buddha-virtue is most great, he is the God among Gods; therefore, he is called 'Heavenly'."
O King, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—
these titles are to be understood as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).
The world is named Devamārga (Heavenly Path). It is called Devamārga because the path of the heavens is purified and cultivated therein.

At that time, the Buddha Tathāgatadevarāja dwelt in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). One cycle of increase and decrease in the receptacle world is termed one small kalpa (*kalpa*);

eighty such small kalpas—comprising the periods of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness—are termed one intermediate kalpa. The lifespan of the Buddha Tathāgatadevarāja was of such a measure.
It was so. He extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Having remained in the world for a long time, he taught the Dharma even more abundantly;
sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship. In this manner, he delivered such a multitude of śrāvakas.
Immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the path of the pratyekabuddhas; he delivered such a multitude of pratyekabuddhas.

Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression;
he delivered such a multitude of bodhisattvas. Those who had attained the patience of non-arising thoroughly understood that all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent.

The point at which the axle-pin is not seen to arise is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). Because one has attained the emptiness of phenomena and the mind is able to endure with equanimity, advancing alone without retreating, it is called "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*).
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the term *parinirvāṇa*—which in the language of India means "extinction" (*śānti*)—is used.
After the Parinirvāṇa of Devendra Buddha, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas. Following its extinction, the Semblance Dharma remained for a long time.
A stupa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire body relics; unlike Śākyamuni, whose body was fragmented for offerings, Devendra’s remains were enshrined whole.
The Buddha’s stūpa enshrines his entire body;
it is sixty yojanas high, symbolizing the six pāramitās,
and forty yojanas in length and breadth, symbolizing the forty noble stages of abiding, practice, transference, and realization within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
All the devas and human beings offered various flowers; all the roots of goodness cultivated by devas and humans are called "various flowers.
Incense for powdering, burning incense, and unguent incense were used to manifest their virtues through fragrance.

The robes, necklaces, banners, and jeweled canopies represent: the robes signify patience (*kṣānti*); the necklaces signify wisdom (*prajñā*); the banners signify concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom;
and the jeweled canopy signifies the supreme dharma (*dharmāgra*).
As for the music and songs: the music represents the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the songs represent the melody of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
They prostrated and made offerings to the wondrous stupa of the seven treasures; by prostrating and breaking the banner of pride, they made offerings and repented of their stingy karma.
Immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship and achieved the state of Śrāvaka.
Innumerable sentient beings awakened to the state of a Pratyekabuddha and attained the fruit of a solitary buddha.
Inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The number of these sentient beings was so vast that it transcended the reach of thought or verbal deliberation; they all gave rise to the mind of the unsurpassed path and attained non-retrogression.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In a future age, after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni,
if there are good men or good women who hear the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—
if these good men or good women are able to hear this 'Devadatta Chapter' of the sutra."
Those who, with a pure mind, have faith and reverence and do not give rise to doubt— those who can, with a pure mind and reverent faith,
accept this Dharma and harbor no doubts regarding this sutra—
shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. Because they believe in the sutra, they shall not fall into the three evil destinies.
They shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
wherever they are born, they will constantly hear this sutra. If, in whatever place they are born, they constantly hear this wondrous Lotus Sutra.

If one is born among humans or devas, one experiences supreme and wondrous bliss; if one is born in the heavens or among humans, one attains the enjoyment of supreme and wondrous pleasures of the five senses.
If one is before the Buddha, one is miraculously born from a lotus flower; those born in a Buddha-land do not dwell in a womb but are born from lotus flowers.
At that time, from below, there was a bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa) who had come from the presence of the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna;
he was a foremost bodhisattva who had come to this Sahā world from the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

[The Bodhisattva] addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying, "I shall now return to my own land. Having previously manifested this jeweled stupa to witness the preaching of the sutra, I have now heard the sutra and request permission to return to my native land.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñatikauṇḍinya, "Because Śākyamuni saw that Jñatikauṇḍinya wished to return, he [spoke] briefly..."
"Keep him so that he may meet with Mañjuśrī.
Good son, wait but a moment; for a brief instant, please urge him to stay a little longer.
Here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī. In this place, there is a bodhisattva of profound stage named..."
Mañjuśrī, you may go to meet him to discuss the sublime Dharma and then return to your own land.
You should meet with him for a moment to discourse upon the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, and only then return to the pure land below.
At that time, Mañjuśrī’s seat was a thousand-petaled lotus as large as a chariot wheel; the pedestal upon which he sat was likewise as large as a chariot wheel.
The bodhisattvas who had come together with him were also seated upon precious lotuses, and all those who had arrived with Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva were likewise so.
They were also seated upon precious lotus flower pedestals, having spontaneously emerged from the Sāgara Dragon Palace within the great ocean. "Sāgara" means the Salt Sea;
thus, the assembly of bodhisattvas emerged from the dragon palace of the Salt Sea.
Abiding in the midst of space, each, by means of their own supernormal power, remained suspended in the air and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.
Upon reaching Vulture Peak, they went to where Śākyamuni was;
descending from their lotuses, they arrived at the Buddha’s presence, alighting from the lotus pedestals and coming before the Buddha.
He bowed his head in reverent salutation at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones, Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna.
Having completed his acts of veneration, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One and then beheld the Bodhisattva.
He went to the place where Prajñākūṭa was, exchanged greetings with him, and withdrew to sit to one side. Each of these two great Bodhisattvas came from a different [direction].
Having arrived at this place, they paid their respects, exchanged greetings, and then withdrew to their seats.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa questioned Mañjuśrī; he asked this because he had witnessed the miraculous manifestations through which Mañjuśrī had come.
"How many sentient beings have you converted while visiting the Dragon Palace? How great is the number of those you have converted while traveling to the palace of the Great Ocean Dragon King?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Their number is immeasurable and incalculable; it cannot be weighed or calculated.
It is not that which can be proclaimed by the mouth nor fathomed by the mind; neither verbal proclamation nor mental measurement can ever know it."
"Wait but a moment and you shall know for yourself; wait a short while and you shall personally realize and understand it.
Before he had finished speaking—before even the sound of Mañjuśrī’s words had ceased—[the realization occurred].
Countless bodhisattvas sat upon precious lotus flowers and surged forth from the ocean; the emanated bodhisattvas, riding upon the flowers,
likewise surged forth from the ocean all at once and proceeded to Vulture Peak, the place where the Buddha was preaching the Dharma.
They dwell in the void; because they come by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they abide in space.
These bodhisattvas were all converted and delivered by Mañjuśrī and are fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva;
each one is complete in the conduct of a bodhisattva.
They all together discussed the six pāramitās; they all together deliberated upon the methods for practicing the six perfections.
Originally, the śrāvakas were in the void expounding the practices of śrāvakas; fundamentally, they were of inferior capacity and remained below.
While previously they were expounding the path of the śrāvakas within the midst of empty space,
they now all practice the meaning of the Mahāyāna emptiness. As these superior persons have opened themselves to the principle of pervasive emptiness and gradually entered the perfect [teaching],
they now all cultivate inconceivable emptiness.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñānākara: Mañjuśrī pointed to the assembly that had come with him and told Jñānākara, "Such was the manner of my teaching and transformation in the ocean;
the nature of the teaching I established therein was like this."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa praised him in verse: "O one of great wisdom, virtue, and valor, you have transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes.
Mañjuśrī, endowed with great wisdom and all majestic virtues, you are able to courageously transform immeasurable multitudes."
Now I have seen all these great assemblies, and I have seen all those gathered here before me.

You have expounded the meaning of the true reality (*tathatā*) and revealed the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), flowing forth and thoroughly elucidating the meaning of the true reality as it is.
He demonstrates and extensively expounds the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle,
broadly guiding all sentient beings to swiftly attain Bodhi, and widely transforming all beings so that they may quickly achieve the realization of Bodhi.
Mañjuśrī said, "In the midst of the ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
I have always used this to transform immeasurable multitudes.
Jñatikauṇḍinya asked Mañjuśrī, "This sutra is extremely profound and subtle; it is a treasure among all sutras, [unknown] by the world..."
"How rare! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is of extremely profound meaning; its words and intent are subtle and secret, wondrous beyond compare, and rare throughout all worlds.
Is there any sentient being who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor and practicing this sūtra, will quickly attain Buddhahood? There were some sentient beings...
Śāriputra asked, "If one hears this sublime sūtra and applies oneself with diligent vigor, will one not swiftly attain Buddhahood?
Mañjuśrī replied, answering the question of Prajñākūṭa:
"There is a daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara; she is the daughter of the Dragon King of the Salt Sea."
At the age of eight, he possessed wisdom and sharp faculties; being only eight years old, he had great wisdom and a nature of keen intelligence.
He was well able to know the faculties, karmic actions, and practices of sentient beings, and he was thoroughly capable of discerning the various faculties of all sentient beings.
Through various types of karmic activities,
they attain *dhāraṇī* and gain entry into the gates of total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*).
They are able to receive and uphold all the profound secret treasuries spoken by the Buddhas— the secrets spoken by all the Buddhas.
They are fully able to receive and uphold the profound Dharma-treasury of the Secret [Mantra].

They have deeply entered meditative concentration and thoroughly realized all phenomena. They are skillfully able to enter the sublime samādhis of bodhisattvas and are capable of penetrating all dharmas.
In a single kṣaṇa, they give rise to the bodhicitta; in that briefest instant of one kṣaṇa, they generate the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
They attain non-retrogressive eloquence that is unimpeded, and their minds realize the wisdom and eloquence of the stage of non-retrogression.
He is able to remain free from all obstructions and hindrances.

He regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness as if they were his own infant children; he regards all sentient beings with compassion and pity as if they were his own infant children, without any distinction.
Endowed with merit: the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with all merits.

What the mind contemplates is expressed by the mouth as subtle and vast; that which the mind conceives is expounded by the wheel of speech, its meaning profound and subtle, and its essential nature vast.
Compassionate, benevolent, and yielding, their will and mind are harmonious and refined. With thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion, they are kind, generous, humble, and yielding;
their mental disposition is soft, gentle, upright, and elegant.
They are able to reach Bodhi. By possessing the various virtues mentioned above, they are able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then the Bodhisattva Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa) said to Mañjuśrī, having heard the account of the dragon girl:
"I have seen Śākyamuni Tathāgata; indeed, I have often seen the World-Honored One Śākyamuni in the past."
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he practiced difficult asceticisms; indeed, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he performed what is difficult to do and underwent immeasurable austerities.
He accumulated merit and virtue while seeking the path to Bodhi, never ceasing for a moment. Having accumulated these merits, he sought [the state of] non-...
On this path to supreme enlightenment, he has never rested for many kalpas.
He contemplates the trichiliocosm, surveying throughout his field of transformation, the three thousandfold world system.

There was not even a space the size of a mustard seed; there was not even a patch of ground the size of a single mustard seed that was not a place where a bodhisattva had sacrificed his body and life. There was no vacant spot that was not a place where a bodhisattva had given up his body.
For the sake of sentient beings—for the sake of all sentient beings—one must first accomplish the path of a bodhisattva;
having thus cultivated [the practices] in full, one subsequently attains buddhahood.
"I do not believe that this girl can attain perfect enlightenment in a mere moment.
I truly do not believe in this matter of the young dragon girl attaining perfect enlightenment in an instant, for it is extraordinary and contrary to the common way."
Before their discourse had concluded— while the dialogue between Jñatikauṇḍinya and Mañjuśrī was still unfinished—
the daughter of the Dragon King suddenly appeared before them. By means of her supernormal powers, she manifested herself in order to bear witness to this matter.
She bowed her head in prostration, withdrew to stand to one side. Having bowed her head in respectful salutation at the Buddha’s feet, she stood to one side and praised him in verse:
"You have profoundly realized the nature of sin and merit, illuminating all ten directions. Thus did the Dragon Girl extol the Buddha’s profundity.
The light of wisdom that universally illumines the characteristics of all sins and merits;
the subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body endowed with the thirty-two marks. "Subtle and wondrous" refers to the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya); "pure Dharma" refers to the Dharma Body (dharmakāya);
and "thirty-two" refers to the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya). This single phrase encompasses and offers a comprehensive praise of the three bodies.

The Dharma-body is adorned with the eighty minor marks of excellence. If one considers the Dharma-body according to its myriad virtues and marks of physical perfection as its adornment—referring to that wondrous body of merit consisting of an ocean of marks like motes of dust—then to say that the eighty marks adorn the Dharma-body is to point out the wondrous essence within the provisional response-body;
thus, the fundamental and the manifested are non-dual, and one truly accords with the Perfect Teaching.
Worshipped and looked up to by devas and humans, and revered by all dragon deities;
whether devas or humans, they all honor and uphold him with single-minded devotion, while dragons and spirits alike all turn in reverence and admire the Buddha’s virtues.
There are no classes of sentient beings who do not revere and follow him; among all living beings in the world, there are none who do not honor and revere him as their master.
Furthermore, it is heard that he has attained *bodhi*; it is also heard that through the Buddha-dharma, he attained *bodhi*.
Only the Buddha shall bear witness; only the World-Honored Buddha himself shall bear witness:

"I have expounded the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver sentient beings from suffering; I have expounded the teaching of the single reality of the Mahāyāna to deliver immeasurable sentient beings from their afflictions."

At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: "I am skeptical because I have seen Mañjuśrī tell Zhijí that this dragon girl, though only eight years old, is compassionate, gentle, and refined, and is capable of attaining bodhi."
Your claim that you will attain the unsurpassed path before long is difficult to believe.
As stated in the preceding text, because one generates the bodhicitta in a single kṣaṇa, it is said that one attains the unsurpassed path before long; this is indeed difficult to believe.
Why is this? It is because he expressed his reasons for lack of faith:

that the female body is defiled and not a vessel for the Dharma; and that within the teachings on skillful means, it is said that women have five obstacles preventing them from attaining Buddhahood—therefore, he took hold of these points as the basis for his challenge.
How can one attain unsurpassed bodhi? It cannot be accomplished through lack of faith.
The Buddha-way is vast and remote; the path of the Buddha is far-reaching, expansive, and great.

Only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practice through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the perfections (pāramitās) can it finally be realized. One must pass through many...
Only after diligently exerting oneself through kalpas, accumulating meritorious conduct, and fully practicing the six pāramitās can one finally achieve it.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles, as listed below.
First, one cannot become the Brahmā King. Even the Great Brahmā King, the sovereign of the Form Realm, has no female consort;
how then could he be a king [in that sense]?
Second, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, likewise is not made by a woman.
Third, the Māra kings. The abodes of Māra are at the summit of the desire realm within the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
these are also not created by women. Fourth, the Cakravartin wheel-turning sage-kings. All four types of Cakravartins possess male bodies and are not created by women.
Fifth, regarding the Buddha-body: the Buddha-body is pure and sublime, whereas the female body is defiled; how could such a body possibly become a Buddha?

How then can a female body swiftly attain Buddhahood? Here, Śāriputra, grasping at provisional means to challenge the ultimate reality, seeks to dispel doubts concerning the provisional and desires to hear the true path.
At that time, the dragon girl possessed a precious jewel. The supernatural powers of the dragon were entirely contained within this jewel;
it was worth a trichiliocosm and was a most noble treasure.
She held it up to offer to the Buddha. That the dragon girl held this forth to present to the World-Honored One signified her great generosity.
The Buddha immediately accepted it. By offering the pearl, the dragon girl expressed her perfect understanding; the Tathāgata’s acceptance signified his certification of her realization.
The Dragon Girl addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prajñākūṭa and the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Having offered the jewel, she then asked Prajñākūṭa and Śāriputra:
'Was it not swift that the World-Honored One accepted the precious jewel I offered? The act of offering the jewel and the Buddha's acceptance were rapid.'"
"No," he replied, "it is extremely swift. The two men replied, "This matter is indeed extremely swift.
The woman said, "By your supernatural power; by all the power of your supernormal faculties."
Behold my attainment of Buddhahood; it shall be even swifter than this. See my attainment of Buddhahood as swift as the offering of a pearl.
At that time, the entire assembly—those present in the gathering who were listening to the Dharma.
They all saw that in an instant the dragon girl had transformed into a male, endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva; having suddenly changed her female body,

she was fully possessed of great conduct and immediately departed for the stainless world (Vimalā-loka) in the south— the land where she was to transform beings, located in the southern world, named...
The title is "Stainless" (Vimala).
Seated upon a precious lotus flower, he attains equal and perfect enlightenment; this is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are the sublime within the coarse.
At that time, throughout the Sahā world— this Sahā realm— the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas,

the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and so forth, humans and non-humans, and the great assembly of humans and devas of the three vehicles, were all universally expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings in the ten directions.

The assembly all saw from afar that the dragon girl had attained Buddhahood; they saw the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood there and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the gods and humans gathered in the assembly. They also saw that Buddha preaching the Dharma for the multitude.
Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar. With minds of great delight, the assembly all gazed toward him from afar, reverently prostrating themselves.
Immeasurable sentient beings, having heard the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression. The sentient beings of that land were able to hear the Buddha.
He declared that their minds had attained awakening and they dwelt in non-retrogression;
immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of attaining the Way, and furthermore, immeasurable Great Beings with mature faculties received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
The Stainless World shook in six ways, as explained in the Introduction Chapter.
In the Sahā World, three thousand sentient beings dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression; having heard the Dharma in that land, they gained benefit and ascended to the stage of non-retrogression.

Three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment. Seeing that the Buddha had inspired them to resolve upon the Great Way, they were subsequently granted these predictions.
The Bodhisattva Jñānākara, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence, having never before experienced such a thing.
It was because there were words to be spoken that he spoke; now that we see the actual manifestation of this matter, he remains silent. All present have gained benefit, so there is no room for doubt.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Thirteen: Encouraging the Retention.
At that time, the assembly in attendance heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, praise those who uphold this sutra within the "Chapter on the Dharma-Master";
they heard how, in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Many Treasures Buddha from the lower regions manifested various supreme events to testify to the sutra;

and they heard how, in the "Chapter on Devadatta," the traces were opened to reveal the fundamental reality, whereby the Tathāgata attained supreme perfect enlightenment, and that the master Devadatta later also became a Buddha.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with their retinues of twenty thousand beings, made a vow to propagate [this teaching].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna were present along with their retinues of twenty thousand bodhisattvas;
these two great bodhisattvas were together with their entire assembly of twenty thousand followers.
They all resolved with the same aspiration and made this vow before the Buddha. Standing before the Buddha, they took their oath:
"We pray that the World-Honored One need not be concerned; we pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, need not consider us incapable of propagating [the Dharma]."
We shall regard this as a cause for concern.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sūtra; we, all of us together, shall take upon ourselves this responsibility.
In future evil ages, the roots of goodness among sentient beings will diminish further. As the time grows distant from the Sage, those possessing roots of goodness will become increasingly rare.
Arrogance will abound;
even among those who occasionally possess superior capacity for practice, they may claim to have attained what they have not, leading them to treat others with contempt.
Arrogance, craving for gain and offerings, and attachment to material things, gain,
and offerings increase the roots of unwholesomeness; because of this, one gives rise to evil karma during practice, which instead plants the seeds of birth and death rather than increasing virtue.
Rooted in detachment, they possess the liberation of detachment and the dharma of the purity of detachment;
though difficult to transform, it is likewise difficult to teach the Dharma to such as these for their transformation.
We shall arouse the power of great patience. Toward those who are difficult to transform, we shall arouse the power of great vigor and great forbearance.

To read, recite, uphold, explain, and transcribe this sutra constitutes the five kinds of Dharma-preachers: first, reading; second, reciting; third, upholding; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing.

One should perform various offerings without begrudging one's body or life. Those who extensively uphold [the Dharma] should practice various forms of respectful offering for the sake of the Dharma, being without stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth.

At that time, among the assembly were five hundred arhats who had received the prediction [of enlightenment]. These five hundred people, all of whom had already received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we also make our own vows; we each individually resolve to make these vows."
They shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands. Regarding "other lands," it is because they fear that in this defiled and evil world, beings are difficult to transform;
thus, they wish to expound it extensively in other realms.
Furthermore, there were eight thousand learners and non-learners who had received their predictions of enlightenment; these were those from the ninth category who had received their predictions.
They rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow. Rising from their seats and joining their palms expressed their reverence.
Having performed the ritual observances, they then made this vow:
"World-Honored One, we too shall widely expound this sutra in other lands. However, these beings have weak powers and we fear they are difficult to transform."
Why is this? It is because the people in this Sahā world are for the most part corrupt and evil; they are afflicted by many ailments and are moreover stubborn and wicked.
They harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*); as soon as they achieve even a slight degree of excellence, they become arrogant toward others.
Their merit is shallow; their functional power, virtue, and goodness are all deficient.
They are turbid with anger and crooked with flattery; they are clouded by wrath and devious with sycophancy.
Because their minds are not sincere, the people of this land possess such faults; for this reason, I have made a vow to seek the transformation of others.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī— whose significance is as explained in the Preface—
was accompanied by six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training. Thus, the Buddha’s maternal aunt was together with the assembly of nuns.
Rising from his seat, he joined his palms with single-minded devotion.

First establishing his dignified deportment, he gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without averting his eyes for even a moment. As he was about to make a request, wishing to hear the reason for receiving and maintaining [the teaching], his reverence prevented him from looking away even briefly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī— here called "Leader of the Assembly" (Saṃghāṭī), because she was the foremost leader of the community of nuns—
and she was also the name of the Tathāgata’s maternal aunt, as recorded in the *Mahāvastu*.
"Why do you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful countenance? Seeing that his maternal aunt had a sorrowful expression, the Buddha questioned her:
"Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name when bestowing the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"Is it a prediction? Do you perhaps think that I have not granted a prediction because I did not mention your name among the assembly of nuns, and is that why you are grieving?
Thus, Kautamī, the Buddha spoke to his maternal aunt.

I have previously stated in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions of enlightenment. Although monks and nuns differ, they are equally termed "śrāvakas" based on the practice they cultivate;
since it was said that "all" have been granted predictions, the assembly of nuns is already included therein.
Now, if you wish to know the prophecy, and if you wish to understand the specific names of those recorded:
in a future age, at a time yet to come,
within the teachings of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas— wherein "sixty" represents the six sense faculties and "eight" the eight [thousand]— you shall [attain realization].
This signifies that when the eight consciousnesses and the six sense organs are simultaneously purified within the eight consciousnesses,
one is said to "see all Buddhas" and become a Great Dharma Master, acting as a teacher of the Dharma within the Mahāyāna.
Together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training, who were all dharma-preachers; the assembly of six thousand nuns was likewise.
"In this manner, you shall gradually fulfill the bodhisattva path; in this manner, you shall gradually practice until it is complete."

The path cultivated by this Bodhisattva shall result in his attaining Buddhahood under the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (All-Sentient-Beings-Love-to-Behold). Because he fully cultivated the practices of loving-kindness and patience during the causal stage and did not afflict sentient beings,
all sentient beings joyfully behold him upon the fruition stage.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—
these titles are explained as in the "Introduction Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).
Gautamī, the Buddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, and the six thousand bodhisattvas— that is, the six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—
were each granted successive predictions; they were bestowed with their respective prophecies one after another in sequential order.
He attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and became a supreme, perfectly enlightened Buddha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, thought to herself: "The mother of Rāhula is a close relative of the Buddha;
it is only right that she receive a separate prediction, yet I have not heard the Buddha speak of it. This was why she had this thought.

The World-Honored One alone did not mention my name during the bestowal of prophecies. Yaśodharā thought to herself, "While all the other nuns have received their individual prophecies, I alone have not heard my name being drawn forth.
The Buddha said to Yaśodharā, "In the future, within the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate bodhi..."
The practice of the bodhisattva: the dharmas of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas do not transcend the cultivation of the mind of a single thought-moment;
this pure mental dharma is called "a mere instant" (*kṣaṇika*).
As a great Dharma Master, one gradually fulfills the Buddha-way, constantly acting as a teacher who expounds the Dharma for the great assembly, and thus gradually fulfills it.
He shall fulfill the path to Buddhahood and attain the state of a Buddha in the Land of Excellence (*Sukhāvatī*). Because he cultivated virtuous deeds, his fruit corresponds to that excellent land;

his name shall be "Endowed with Ten Million Marks of Radiance. Having made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas during his causal stage, he shall be fully equipped as a Bodhisattva.
The fruit of the Way is fully endowed with thousands of millions of radiant marks, forming the Honored One of the Ten Powers:
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān— as explained in the "Introductory Chapter."
The lifespan of the Buddha was immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; his stay in the world lasted for such a long duration.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, together with their retinues—these two bhikṣuṇīs and a multitude of six thousand—[were present].
