They were all greatly delighted, having attained what they had never experienced before. Because they had all received the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood in the future, they were all joyful and attained what they had never experienced before.
Then, in the presence of the Buddha, they spoke these verses: "The World-Honored One, the Guide, brings peace and security to devas and humans. Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One..."
The World-Honored One is the Great Guide, who is well able to bring peace and security to all devas and humans.
Having heard this prophecy, our minds are fully satisfied. Having heard the sound of this bestowal of prophecy, our bodies and minds are at peace and our aspirations are fulfilled.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, and having praised the Buddha with these stanzas, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we too are able to widely proclaim this sutra in other lands;
however, because our strength is slight, we fear this turbid and evil age, and thus we wish to preach this sutra extensively in other places."
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
with eyes of compassion, the World-Honored One looked everywhere throughout the assembly at his disciples and the great bodhisattvas who were being transformed.
These bodhisattvas are all *avaivartika*, which here means "non-retrogressive. They turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma;
these bodhisattvas, abiding themselves in the stage of non-retrogression, further turn the non-retrogressive, unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

They attained various *dhāraṇīs*—here translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*)—whereby these bodhisattvas, having attained this samādhi, universally retain and protect all that is wholesome and obstruct all that is unwholesome.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and with single-minded devotion joined their palms. There were eight hundred thousand such great bodhisattvas.

Because the Buddha’s single glance was clearly understood as being in accordance with their capacities, the billion beings rose from their seats, joined their palms in formal ritual, and paid homage to the Buddha.
Then they thought thus; the minds of the assembly formed this thought.
If the World-Honored One commands us to uphold and proclaim this sutra; if we are graced by the World-Honored One’s command to receive, uphold, read, and recite this scripture.
One should widely proclaim this Dharma according to the Buddha’s teaching; one should extensively expound this sutra in reliance upon the Buddha’s teaching.
Furthermore, one should form this thought and direct the mind with such a reflection:
The Buddha now remains silent and does not issue any instruction. At this moment, the Buddha merely stays silent and does not speak to give us any command.
What shall we do? How should we proceed now?
At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intention— specifically the intent of the Tathāgata’s entrustment in the preceding "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa"—
and desiring to fulfill their own original vows as well as the fundamental practices and vows cultivated by bodhisattvas, [acted accordingly].

He then uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made a solemn vow; having thus reflected, he immediately produced the sound of a lion before the Buddha and established a profound aspirational vow.
"Bhagavān, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we, all of us,
shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions and pervade every place within the realm of the Buddha."
It enables sentient beings, and those of right faith in the final age,
to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness.
As it is said in the sūtras regarding the method of practice—practicing with a correct mind, mindfulness, and diligence—all of this is due to the Buddha’s majestic power;
all is dependent upon the vast majestic power of the World-Honored One.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, while remaining in another realm, will behold us from afar and provide protection.

Since the Buddha’s transformation in this region is now complete and he has returned to parinirvāṇa, his spiritual capacity remains ripe in other places; therefore, it is said that he should behold us from afar and graciously grant his protection.
Immediately, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices together and spoke in verse: "We pray that you do not worry;
we pray that the World-Honored One need not concern himself.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the terrifying and evil age, we shall extensively proclaim [the Dharma]. After the Buddha has passed away..."
I shall extensively explain this within the most terrifying and defiled world of the five turbidities.
There are those who lack wisdom and engage in abusive speech and insults; there are various unwholesome and ignorant people who commit acts such as foul-mouthed, filthy language, and verbal abuse.
We shall endure all those who strike us with knives and staves; even when they attack us with swords, staves, and stones, we shall endure all such evils for the sake of propagating this sutra.
In this evil age, there will be bhikṣus of crooked and deceitful minds and false wisdom; the monks of this degenerate age will be born without true wisdom.
Those with various heterodox views have minds that are not upright, being sycophantic, devious, and crooked;

they claim to have attained what they have not attained, just like the bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna who, though originally an ordinary person lacking learning, falsely claimed to have realized the state of an arhat.
Their minds are filled with pride; they are filled with the perverse mind of self-exaltation and arrogance.
Or there may be forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), which here means those who dwell in empty and quiet places—that is, some people who practice the conduct of empty and quietude.
Wearing patched robes in secluded places, he constantly wears a single layer of dharma-cloth throughout both winter and summer.

Dwelling in those quiet retreats, he cultivates emptiness and stillness, claiming that he practices the true Way and looking down upon the ways of the world; he claims that what he practices is the true and real Way.
Those who travel among the lowly masses to transform them preach the Dharma to laypeople because they are greedily attached to gain and offerings. Out of a craving for gain and offerings,
they preach the Dharma to the laity and receive the veneration of the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers, obtaining the respect of all people in the world.
There was an Arhat who had attained the same fruits and the six supernormal powers;
yet this person harbored an evil mind and constantly dwelt upon worldly matters. Although he preached the Dharma with his mouth, his mind remained intent on seeking profit.
Internally harboring such evil views, he constantly thought of the mundane affairs of the world.

They falsely claim the name of *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) while delighting in exposing our faults; they borrow the name of *āraṇya* while engaging in worldly affairs, delighting in exposing the faults of us who propagate the sutras.
To counteract such words of slander from those of false views, they speak as follows.
These bhikṣus, out of greed for gain and offerings, preach the treatises of external paths;

they slander the Great Beings of compassion who dwell among people, calling them men greedy for profit, and they revile the sublime Mahāyāna sūtras they have taught, labeling them as the doctrines of external paths.

They have composed this sūtra themselves to deceive and delude the people of the world; conversely, they slander the Buddha’s sūtras as being their own private fabrications, thereby cheating and confusing the people of the world.
It is for the sake of seeking fame that they analyze and preach this sūtra, desiring to acquire renown, reputation, and prestige.
They preach such sūtras with the intent to disparage us among the great assemblies; they do so constantly before all the congregations for the purpose of reviling us.
To kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders— to kings, as well as to ministers,
various brahmins who are practitioners of purity, and householders, that is, those who remain in the home.
Furthermore, other groups of bhikṣus slander me by speaking ill of me; they also slander us in the presence of other bhikṣus,
saying that we are people of wrong views who propound the doctrines of non-Buddhists, and that we pervert what is correct into what is false, thus giving rise to contemptuous slanders.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, we endure all these evils. Desiring to show respect and obedience to the Buddha, we endure all such harms and provocations.
To those who, out of this wrong view, insult us by saying, "You are all Buddhas," we say to them: [you...]
All such people as these are indeed Buddhas;
one should endure all such words of contempt. For the sake of the Dharma, one must endure all such forms of disparaging speech.
In the midst of the turbid kalpa and evil world, there are many terrors; that is to say, in the future age of turbidity and evil, there will be many such terrifying occurrences.
Evil spirits will enter their bodies to revile and insult me, and various wicked demons will constantly possess them.

"Seeing us reviled, slandered, and humiliated, we, who revere and have faith in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience. We, these people, desiring to speak of the Tathāgata, shall cultivate the practice of loving-kindness, patience, and great compassion;
we shall don the armor of patience to transform those who are difficult to transform."
For the sake of expounding this sutra, we endure these various hardships; for the sake of widely proclaiming this sutra, we must endure such things as are difficult to bear.
We do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only value the unsurpassed path. We do not dare to love our own bodies or lives, but only...
One should cherish the unsurpassed path.
In future ages, we shall uphold that which the Buddha has entrusted to us; in future ages, we shall uphold that which the World-Honored One has assigned to us.
"Blessed One, you yourself shall know this; my mind is such that the Buddha himself shall know it—what need is there for me to speak?
In this turbid world, evil bhikṣus do not understand the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate.

Among the bhikṣus in this turbid and evil age, none are well-versed in the Buddha’s compassionate skillful means and the various teachings of the Three Vehicles spoken according to what is appropriate."
They then give rise to doubt, clinging to expedient means while slandering the ultimate truth.
With harsh speech and a frowning countenance— frowning meaning the knitting of the eyebrows— they, due to their meager merit,
knit their brows and revile this wondrous sutra upon hearing it.
Repeatedly he was expelled; repeatedly he was seen being expelled from the assembly.
He remained far removed from the stūpas and monasteries, far removed from the places where the saṃgha and stūpas were located.
Regarding such various evils as these— indeed, regarding all such manifold evils—
one should endure them all because of the Buddha’s admonition. Recalling the Buddha’s admonition,
one should uphold and preach this sutra, and thus endure all such contrary and vexing matters.
In various villages, towns, cities, hamlets, settlements, or within walled cities and districts— wherever sentient beings dwell—
should there be those who seek the Dharma, or anyone who seeks the Great Dharma.

I shall go to all those places where the Dharma entrusted by the Buddha is being preached. We shall all go to those abodes where the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma entrusted by the Buddha is being taught.
I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; standing amidst the assembly, I am fearless. There are eight hundred billion holy sages of profound realization.
With their supernormal powers and the strength of the Path fully perfected, they shall act as messengers for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma amidst the turbid and evil final age;
dwelling among the assembly and expounding the teachings, they attain great fearlessness, unlike the bodhisattvas of initial resolve and the arhats who came before.
"I shall skillfully expound the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace and security. We shall obtain the essential points of the well-expounded Dharma;
may the Buddha remain steadfast and need not harbor any concern.
Thus I speak before the World-Honored One, before Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, and the various emanation Buddhas who have come from afar from the ten directions, have made such vows;
they have courageously brought forth the aforementioned profound and solemn vows.
The Buddha knows our own minds. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he himself knows the force of our vast and firm vows.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The "wondrous Dharma" is precisely the dharma of the mind; the mind is the substance of the dharma, and the dharma is the function of the mind.
When a thought flickers up, phenomenal appearances arise accordingly. At all times, allow them to remain calm and even; simply rely on universal principle and do not follow private sentiment.
Then, clarity will naturally emerge, and there will be no situation to which it does not penetrate. Thus, one is pure and untainted by dust; thus it is.

Impartial, free from flattery or deceit, subtle, fragrant, and pure beyond even the lotus—my Buddha has realized this and, out of compassion for beings who are deluded, appears in the world to preach such a Dharma, which is called the One Great Matter.
Through these four conditions, all Buddhas attain supreme perfect enlightenment; because this Dharma is sublime, it is called the Sublime Dharma. Abiding amidst the dust of the world yet unstained...
The title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to the Dharma. It teaches all sentient beings this eternal principle:
to turn the light back upon oneself and reflect inwardly, thereby entering the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty by imperial decree.
The vocal expressions of sentient beings differ in every place; when the Buddha appeared, he spoke the Dharma by following their respective dialects.
When these teachings reached Donghua (China), the sounds and meanings of the words were all unintelligible.

There was the country of Quci, where the Dharma Master Kumārajīva was profoundly versed in the Tripiṭaka and well-versed in Buddhist principles. The sovereign of the Yao Qin state sent an envoy to welcome him and had him translate [the scriptures].
The Central Indian *brahmā-voice* is rendered here in the language of Donghua (China).

From the fourteenth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-hon*), following the previous "Chapter on Past Deeds" (*Zaihō-hon*): Previously, due to the Tathāgata’s exhortation and recruitment, Bhaiṣajyarāja, Prabhūtaratna, and twenty thousand [bodhisattvas] [vowed to propagate this teaching].
The assembly, reverently following the Buddha’s intention, made a vow to propagate this sutra. The Buddha then looked upon the great assembly with his eyes of aspiration;
eight hundred trillion great bodhisattvas vowed to exert their utmost strength to circulate it in the evil age.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again addressed the World-Honored One on behalf of the beginner bodhisattvas of the final age, seeking the gate of skillful means, asking: "How should they practice and advance?"
At that time, there was the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī. "Mañjuśrī" is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue.
Because the Buddha is the King of the Dharma and Bodhisattvas transmit the Way, they are called "Dharma Princes."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva—here translated as "One who has perfected the Great Path-mind for the sake of sentient beings"—is so named because Mañjuśrī possesses the Great Path-mind capable of bringing sentient beings to completion.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha possesses holy virtue and is revered by the world."
These bodhisattvas are truly rare and extraordinary. One must praise those great bodhisattvas who, as mentioned in the previous Chapter on Upholding, made vows to propagate this sutra;
for they act out of reverence for the Buddha, and out of respectful compliance with the Tathāgata.
They made great vows; before the Buddha, they made profound and weighty aspirations:

that in future evil ages, in the turbid and corrupt world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they would protect, uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and cherish, maintain, read, recite, and explain such a sublime Dharma.
[Sūtra]:

"World-Honored One, how can Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—referring here to those Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds on the Path at the beginning of the final age—preach this sūtra in the subsequent evil world?
For those with a new resolve, their faculties and powers are both shallow, and the evil..."
"How can one practice within this world?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "In response to Mañjuśrī’s question, the Tathāgata answers:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to preach this sutra in the future evil age, and if there is a bodhisattva who..."
If one wishes to preach this sutra in an evil age, one should abide securely in four dharmas:
first, teaching the spheres of practice and the spheres of association, which is called the "Peaceful Practice of Body";

second, admonishing against verbal faults so as to skillfully expound the Dharma, which is called the "Peaceful Practice of Speech"; third, purifying the karma of the mind by remaining free from greed, hatred, and delusion.

The practice of mental peace and happiness is called the "Practice of Peaceful and Happy Conduct. The vow to bring all beings across through the arousal of compassion is called the "Practice of the Vow of Peace and Happiness.
First, one dwells securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity; to tread throughout the day within the Buddha-dharma is what is meant by the "sphere of activity."
Regarding the points of association: distancing oneself from evil friends and associating with virtuous people is what constitutes a point of association.
One who can expound this sutra for sentient beings, and who possesses the proper methods of practice, will be able to expound this sutra for others upon gaining such associates.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the "sphere of practice" (caryā-viṣaya) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This restates the previous topical heading to raise the question anew:
what is meant by the sphere of application for the practice of a bodhisattva?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is one who is able to practice this, they abide in the ground of patience;
they settle their mind in the ground of patience, being gentle, harmonious, virtuous, and compliant.
"Gentle" means not being forceful; "harmonious" means not quarreling; "virtuous" means staying far from evil; and "compliant" means following along.
It is appropriate that one should not be abrupt or violent, nor act with haste, agitation, or rashness;
the mind should likewise not be startled. Even upon hearing the sublime Dharma, one should not be alarmed or harbor doubts.

Furthermore, one should not engage in any activity regarding phenomena; moreover, one should always respect and accord with the Buddha’s intention within the sublime Dharma, maintaining humility and self-restraint, and never claiming that one can engage in any activity regarding the Dharma.
One should contemplate all phenomena as they truly are. One should observe that the true nature of all phenomena is primordially empty and quiescent;
yet one should neither engage in nor differentiate them, for fear that if people hear that the nature of phenomena is primordially quiescent, they might think it is like a void nothingness.
Do not engage in the conceptualization of that which is to be conceptualized; do not practice this view of non-conceptualization.
This is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. To practice in such a manner is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.

What is meant by the "places of association" for a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Since it was previously stated that they "dwell securely in places of association," this [passage] is introduced to provide a detailed explanation thereof.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate; they must not indulge their desires in associating with or drawing near to others.
Kings, princes, ministers, and high officials, as well as those who associate with the noble and powerful, should fear that by relying on their influence they may damage things or harm others.
They should not associate with non-Buddhist brahmins, nor should they associate with those who have gone forth among the non-Buddhists.

Those who practice as *brahmacārins* include the Nirgranthas and other various types of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*). In total, there are six teachers among these lineages, each with their own disciples; when considering both teachers and disciples together, they comprise ninety-six schools.

Thus, the term "and others" (*ādi*) is used. To seek the Dharma outside of one's own mind is called being a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). In the Sanskrit language, a non-Buddhist is called a *nirgrantha*.

*Kaṇṭha* is translated here as "Detachment" (*li-xi*). This refers to those among the non-Buddhist outsiders who have left the household life, so they are collectively termed "Detached from Human Ties and Kin.
Furthermore, it includes those who compose secular writings and verses to praise non-Buddhist texts; one must not associate with those who produce such mundane scriptures.
Those who record this and even praise it as an external scripture include the Lokāyata,
which is here translated as "evil treatise"— referring to the wicked and unwholesome discourses prevalent among worldly people.
"Those who oppose the *Lokāyata*" refers here to those who engage in perverse arguments that are contrary to their sovereign and parents—unwholesome discourses—and specifically to the *Lokāyatikas*.
The term "opposing the *Lokāyata*" (*pratilokāyatas*) refers to those disciples who refute their teachers;

even the single character [of this name] indicates that such people who study these doctrines must not be approached, for one fears being influenced by them and giving rise to various heterodox views.

One should not associate with those who engage in frivolous play. Furthermore, one must not approach those who indulge in dangerous games, such as boxing, wrestling, mutual sparring, or competitive grappling.
And as for the *nara* and others: *nara* here means "wrestler," referring to games of physical competition.

These various transformative performances should be understood as worldly entertainments involving the decoration of the face and head to manifest diverse appearances, such as wrestling, tumbling, and throwing, like the performances put on by those at crossroads; if one watches such spectacles, they cause the mind to become agitated and scattered.

Furthermore, one should not associate with *caṇḍālas*—here translated as "butchers," that is, those who kill living beings—nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs; for raising such creatures is nothing other than preparation for slaughter.
Hunting, fishing, and trapping—such as hunting wild beasts and catching fish—are evil practices. Those who habituate themselves to such evils damage their own aspiration for the Way.
These various evil codes of discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*), which correspond to unwholesome methods of killing and harming, are called "evil disciplines" (*akuśala-saṃvara*).
For such people as these— various kinds of wicked individuals who may come at times,
or those who come with a virtuous mind at other times—
one should preach the Dharma; indeed, one should expound the True Dharma to them.
One should have no expectations; one must not harbor a mind that harbors expectations.

Furthermore, one should not associate with those who seek the state of a śrāvaka or the fruits of the Hīnayāna, whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or members of the monastic community of renunciants.
"Upāsakas, good sons, upāsikās, and good daughters—these are the four assemblies of the Hīnayāna.
One should not inquire after their welfare; since their paths are different, such inquiry is unnecessary."
Whether in a room, within a courtyard, on a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), or in a hall for preaching the Dharma,
one does not dwell together with them; or perhaps, even if one is in a hall for preaching the Dharma, it is not necessarily so.
They dwell together with him;
or at times they come— such persons as these may, from time to time, come of their own accord out of a heart of good will.
He teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
he should simply teach the Dharma to others as is appropriate, without seeking anything for himself. He must by no means harbor a mind that seeks anything.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva—one who practices as a great bodhisattva—[should act thus].
One should not, with respect to the body of a woman, take up the signs that give rise to thoughts of desire;
one should not give rise to a mind of attachment or manifest the signs of passionate longing toward the body of a woman.
He preaches the Dharma while his inner mind is corrupt and foul, yet he manifests outward deportment as he preaches.
Such a person is not pleasing to behold; nor does one wish to see the body of a woman.

If one enters the home of another, or if one enters the home of another for some purpose, one should not engage in conversation with young girls, virgins, or widows. "Young girls" refers to those of tender age;
"virgins" refers to unmarried maidens living at home; and "widows" refers to those who have lost their husbands and remain in mourning. One should not converse with such women.
Engaging in conversation with them involves matters that invite censure and suspicion; moreover, as they may act as seducers, one fears the arising of grave transgressions.

Furthermore, one does not draw near to those of the five kinds of impotence to form close intimacies. Because their minds are upright, those who are dignified and prudent possess complete physical faculties;
whereas those who are deceitful and crooked, due to evil karma from past lives, have failed to attain the full perfection of a human body even though they have obtained it.

Regarding the statement that there are five types of those with incomplete sexual organs (*indriya-vaikalya*): first, those born so, meaning those who are born from birth with an incomplete male organ;

second, the *kliba*, meaning those whose external testicles have been removed; third, the *śaṇḍha*, meaning those who, upon seeing others engage in sexual desire, become jealous of their form and only then do their sexual organs function;

fourth, the *pandaka*, meaning those who occasionally change, being indeterminate as to whether they are male or female; fifth, the *ardhapandaka*, meaning those who are male during the first half of the month and [female] during the latter half.
Because women possess improper physical forms, they are termed "not male. The nature of such persons is largely defiled and lacks the character of a man;
therefore, one is cautioned not to associate closely with them, lest one harm one's own resolve for the Path.
One should not enter another’s house alone. One must not enter another’s secular dwelling by oneself.

However, if there is a cause or condition, or if there is an urgent matter that cannot be avoided, and it is necessary to enter alone—when one must indeed enter another’s house by oneself—[one should proceed with mindfulness].
Simply focus the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha. By doing so, one’s past evils will naturally be stilled once the Buddha appears before one.
If you preach the Dharma for women, or if there is some occasion where you must preach the Dharma for a woman:
One does not smile showing one’s teeth; smiling without showing one’s teeth is intended to maintain gravity and solemnity.
One does not expose the chest; covering the chest is intended to ensure self-restraint.
Even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not be overly familiar; even when acting with right mindfulness and sincerity for the sake of the Dharma, one should still not be improper.
If one develops intimacy with those one has met, how much more so with other matters? How much more so with other unwholesome deeds?
One should take no pleasure in keeping young disciples; for young people are generally fickle and impulsive.
"Śrāmaṇeras are young children; these śrāmaṇeras are immature and have not yet received full ordination. As children, they are arrogant and weak-willed, lacking the vessel for receiving the Way.
I do not delight in having them as my fellow disciples, nor do I wish to have them as my fellow disciples."
One should always delight in sitting in meditation. One must constantly take pleasure in peaceful sitting and meditative stillness.
Remaining in a secluded place, in a vast, quiet, and tranquil location, one should cultivate and restrain the mind.
Since the mind has long remained in delusion, it has consequently developed faults and afflictions; now, wishing to enter the Way, one must cultivate it.
The mind is restored to its original purity, and at all times one maintains right mindfulness.

Mañjuśrī, this is called the first place of approach. Regarding the four modes of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), the first clarifies the bodhisattva’s sphere of action (*gocara*) and the places of approach (*upaniṣad*).
Within the places of approach, there are further two divisions; the first begins from the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
A bodhisattva does not personally associate with kings and the like; this is the first point of association.

Second, furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that all phenomena are empty and so forth, this is the second point of association. Within the first point of association, there are again two parts.
First, not associating with kings and the like: this refers to distancing oneself from those who are not suitable persons and not associating with ordinary people at all.

Regarding the phrase "causing those who are near to go far," it is said that when one comes at times, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them; this refers to causing those who are near to become distant.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that he "always delights in sitting in meditation" and so forth, which enjoins the cultivation and restraint of the mind, this refers to the nearness within the near.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

"All phenomena" refers to all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. To examine them with a correct mind and sincere intention, in accordance with reason and with thorough scrutiny, is called "contemplation.
One understands that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent; when seeking their point of origin, it cannot be found, and thus one knows their original state.

Although emptiness is by nature empty, it does not obstruct its manifest function; furthermore, it carries the meaning of the provisional. Emptiness and the provisional are non-dual, which is precisely the Middle Way.
It is neither one nor three, yet it is three and one. This is called the "True Aspect" (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, one should know that "like" (*ru*) is the meaning of emptiness, "aspect" (*xiang*) is the meaning of the provisional, and "reality" (*shi*) is the meaning of the Middle Way. They are neither identical nor different, neither combined nor separate; their single nature is perfect and complete.
"Endowment" refers to the true mark of reality—emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle—which is non-perverted.
Its own essence is fundamentally empty and truly without perversion; when one turns away from awakening and joins with sense objects, it is called the mark of perversion.
When one extinguishes sense objects and unites with awakening, there is no perversion.
Immovable: the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and suchness is immovable.
Non-retrogressive: realizing that the nature is equal, one does not give rise to despondency or retreat.
Non-reverting: like an arrow released from a bowstring, it has no momentum to turn back.

It is like space; it is like the great void, which possesses no characteristics, has no nature of existence, and lacks any variety of delusive natures. Since delusion is fundamentally empty, the mental consciousness comes to rest and is extinguished.
All paths of language are severed; it cannot be discussed by the mouth, for the pathways of speech are cut off.
It is unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated, because its nature is empty and quiescent. Fundamentally unarisen, it is like an illusion or a transformation;
fundamentally unproduced, it has no beginning and no end; fundamentally unoriginated, both arising and ceasing are illusory, for its nature is primordially empty. III.
All that arises from the very beginning is like what is seen in a dream; its characteristics of production and emergence are entirely unattainable.
It is without name and without form. That which is "without name" is the essence of the Dharmakāya, which pervades all places yet cannot be expressed by names or words.
Just as with the names "Buddha," "Bodhisattva," "Bodhi," and "Nirvāṇa," all such designations are merely provisional establishments.
"Signlessness" means that there are no false signs of self, person, sentient being, or life-span; it does not mean that the sign of suchness, pure reality, is non-existent.
In truth, nothing exists. The Dharmakāya is pure, its illuminating essence standing alone, and in truth, there are no external objects whatsoever.

Its characteristics are immeasurable and boundless. "Immeasurable" means that the substance of the Dharma-body encompasses and pervades empty space, such that it cannot be measured by the passing of days.
"Boundless" means that its substance is fundamentally empty and quiescent, with the prior and subsequent limits severed, such that it has no boundaries.

When thoroughly investigated to their ultimate limit, they are unobstructed and unimpeded. "Unobstructed" means that their essential nature is empty and pervasive, lacking any substantiality or resistance, just as wind is unimpeded within space.
"Unimpeded" means that their essential nature is undefiled and free from all hindrances; the fundamental substance and characteristics of ignorance are [originally pure].
Since one is personally devoid of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and their self-nature is pure, evil does not arise; thus there is no hindrance of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Since birth and death are fundamentally empty, one does not undergo future existence; thus there is no hindrance of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
They exist solely through causes and conditions; though their essence is empty and quiescent, they do not obstruct arising through conditions.

This is like space, whose essence is not identical to various phenomena, yet it does not refuse the manifestation of those phenomena. With ignorance as a condition, the six realms of ordinary beings arise;
with greed, anger, and delusion, the three evil paths arise; and with non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion, the three virtuous paths arise. Thus it is through teaching and practice.
When conditions arise, one practices the four noble truths, giving rise to the realm of the Four Noble Truths; when practicing the Dharma of the Four Truths, one gives rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle;
when practicing the twelve links of dependent origination, one gives rise to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; when practicing the six perfections, one gives rise to the Bodhisattva vehicle;

and through unconditioned great compassion and inconceivable function, one gives rise to the Buddha Vehicle. Neither mind acts as cause nor objects act as condition; thus, neither mundane nor supramundane phenomena can arise.
Phenomena arise solely through causes and conditions;
they are spoken of as such because they originate from inversion. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"The various inversions of sentient beings since beginningless time all result from not knowing the two kinds of roots and practicing erroneously. What are these two? First, the beginningless cycle of birth and death.
Fundamentally, there are two aspects: first, you and all sentient beings currently take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind that clings to objects) as your own nature;

second, the beginningless essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, which is fundamentally pure, is your current consciousness-essence (*shì-jīng*), the original luminosity capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet it is that which is lost amidst those very conditions.
Because sentient beings have abandoned this fundamental luminosity, although they act throughout the day, they do not perceive it.

One should know that realizing for oneself one has mistakenly entered the various realms of existence means that the fundamental luminosity is originally the pure essence, which is the *tathatā* (suchness).
To have mistakenly undergone saṃsāra and entered the various realms refers to the six classes of ordinary beings; because they arise from inversion, it is called "revolving.

If one suddenly awakens to the fact that the nature is fundamentally empty in a single thought-moment, then the great trichiliocosm and its myriad worlds are like bubbles floating upon the water; all saints and ordinary beings are likewise [illusory].
The Vajra-Whisk:
One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena; one should always aspire to discernively observe such a reality that is empty, quiescent, inherently pure, and as-it-is.
This is called the second place of intimacy for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; it is a discussion of intimacy that is neither distant nor near.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "The Tathāgata wishes to reveal [this] after his parinirvāṇa..."
In this degenerate age, for bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve, this first gate of practice— the four abodes of peace and happiness—
reiterates the preceding meaning in verse to enable them to swiftly realize peaceful liberation and the wondrous, eternal tranquility.
If there are bodhisattvas, or sons of the Buddha, who practice the bodhisattva path in the future evil age,
in the turbid and wicked world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
they shall have no mind of fear; they shall possess no heart of dread or apprehension.
If one wishes to expound this sutra— that is, to expound such a wondrous Dharma Flower Sutra—
one should enter the sphere of practice, which is the sphere of practice of the bodhisattvas mentioned in the preceding text;
and one should approach the sphere of association, which is the sphere of association mentioned in the preceding text.

One should always distance oneself from kings, princes, ministers, and high officials; from kings who possess great power, from crown princes and regents, and from ministers who wield authority, as well as from district and county magistrates who each hold power.
This is because one might fear becoming personally attached to them, or relying on their influence to harass others, or becoming arrogant, which would impair one's virtue.

Regarding "dangerous performances": these refer to worldly heterodox arts such as those involving weapons and staves, as well as the *caṇḍālas* and various butchers and hunters; he causes all those with evil minds to abandon them entirely.
The non-Buddhist brahmins and those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist brahmin practitioners do not consult with one another because their paths differ;
nor do they associate with those of overweening pride— those who are arrogant due to their excessive cultivation.
Those who are attached to the Hīnayāna develop a mind of craving and attachment toward the teachings of the Hīnayāna.

Although those scholars of the Tripiṭaka who study the Hīnayāna Piṭakas of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma may practice and learn the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, their spiritual capacity is inferior and their wisdom is slight; thus, they are not friends of the Bodhisattvas.
A precept-breaking bhikṣu, though he is a bhikṣu, has violated the prohibitions of the Buddha;
he is a "name-Arhat," one who possesses no actual virtue but is designated by the title of an Arhat who has attained the Way.

As for bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter: if one associates closely with such nuns, it will invite public censure; since they are especially prone to frivolous laughter, one should keep them at a great distance.
Regarding those deeply attached to the five desires: they develop a profound craving and attachment toward the objects of the five sensory realms.
They seek to manifest parinirvāṇa; they seek to manifest various signs and falsely claim it to be nirvāṇa.
O upāsikās, women are not those who should be approached, much less those who, out of lustful desire, seek to manifest the appearance of pure nirvāṇa.
Do not associate with any of them. Do not associate with any of the aforementioned persons.
Even if such individuals should come with a sincere heart—even if they are not the right kind of people but come with a sincere heart—[do not associate with them].
When one approaches a bodhisattva to hear the Buddha-way, or approaches a bodhisattva desiring to hear the Way,
the bodhisattva, with a mind free from fear, first settles their own mind before ascending the high seat.
One should preach the Dharma without harboring expectations. One must not harbor a mind of expectation, but should instead preach the Dharma with composure.
This applies to widows, virgins, widows, and daughters-in-law.

As for various types of eunuchs—the *jātyapaṇḍaka*, the *pakṣapaṇḍaka*, the *āsekyapaṇḍaka*, the *sāṃvṛttika-paṇḍaka*, and the *mahāpaṇḍaka*—as previously explained, one should not associate with them or treat them as close friends.
One must not stay near them, nor harbor feelings of affection or intimacy toward them.
Furthermore, do not associate with butchers or executioners. Among those who kill, the chief is called an *kaivarta* (executioner).
This includes those who hunt wild game, those who fish, those who set fires for hunting, those who hunt using dogs, and those who catch fish with nets.
They kill for profit; they commit acts of killing for the sake of wealth and gain.
They live by selling meat; they sustain their lives by trading in fish and meat.
They peddle female beauty; that is, they work in the houses of courtesans, selling their physical charms.
One should not associate with such people at all. One must not associate with those who increase anger by killing, nor with those who give rise to desire through sensual forms.
[One should also avoid] dangerous wrestling, as well as preliminary play and boxing matches.
"Various amusements" refers to the various worldly diversions.
As for the courtesans and others who previously displayed their beauty, they sell themselves for the sake of profit; thus, they cause these courtesans to speak of those who lust after physical form.
Do not associate with them at all. All such people are not of a virtuous kind; do not associate with them in any way.

Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place. One who preaches the Dharma should do so in a public place; it is improper to speak in a secluded spot where private matters might be transacted.
When preaching the Dharma, one must not engage in frivolous laughter. At the time of preaching the Dharma, gravity is paramount;
such improper jesting is not permitted.
When entering a village for alms, one should take another bhikṣu with him. Upon entering a village, it is necessary to have one person as a companion.
Companion.
If there is no bhikṣu with whom to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and if there is truly no one who can serve as a companion,
you must single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha and not allow the mind to become distracted.
This is what is called the "proper sphere of activity" (*gocara*) and the "nearby sphere" (*upagocara*). This concludes the reference to the two spheres mentioned above:

the sphere of activity and the nearby sphere. Because these two spheres enable one to preach with ease and comfort, and because one can attain peace and joy by employing these two spheres in accordance with the Dharma, one may preach;
however, in other improper spheres, one must not preach.
Furthermore, one does not practice the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas. The Bodhisattva’s six perfections are called the superior dharma;

that which is cultivated by Pratyekabuddhas is called the middling dharma; and the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas are called the inferior dharma. Since these are all not the Buddha-way, they should not be practiced.
There are the conditioned and the unconditioned. The conditioned refers to the worldly laws of cause and effect, birth and death, suffering, karma, humans, and devas;
the unconditioned refers to the expedient methods of the two vehicles’ minor practices, which are emptiness and quiescent nirvana.
Regarding the categories of real and unreal dharmas: "real" refers to the existence school (Yogācāra), which maintains that all dharmas are substantially existent;
"unreal" refers to the emptiness school (Mādhyamika). Both the views of existence and emptiness are not the Buddha-vehicle; those who seek the path of the Buddha should not practice them.
Nor does one discriminate between male and female. The Buddha-dharma is equal and universally covers all; thus, there is no necessity to differentiate between male and female.

One does not grasp at any dharmas, being neither knowing nor seeing. Within the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there are admonitions to select the appropriate capacity, yet there are those who do attain [realization].

It is obtained such that, whereas according to the various Vinaya sections only monks and nuns are permitted [to hear] and those who have not yet received full ordination are forbidden from seeing or hearing the Dharma of the Great Bodhisattvas,
here anyone capable of understanding the words of the Dharma Master may hear it; like the ocean receiving all streams, there is no discrimination.
This is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva. To practice in this manner is what is meant by the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent. "All dharmas" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the ten... [dhātus].
The eight elements, all mundane phenomena, as well as supramundane dharmas— the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, the myriad practices,
and even the eighty-four thousand dharani gates— are all empty and quiescent, fundamentally non-existent.

There is neither permanence nor arising and ceasing. While the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna teaches that the nature of form arises and ceases, yet the true nature of form is eternal—thus dividing form into two parts, one eternal and one subject to cessation—the Dharma of the Mahāyāna holds that emptiness is itself form and there is no permanence, and form is itself emptiness and there is no arising or ceasing;
this differs from the dualistic views of the Hīnayāna regarding emptiness and form.
The two are themselves perfect and eternal;
this is called the place frequented by the wise. To understand it thus and not fall into folly is what is meant by the place frequented by the wise.
To erroneously discriminate whether phenomena exist or do not exist is to misperceive. The nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent and free from all marks;
yet sentient beings, through inversion, falsely give rise to discrimination, asserting existence or non-existence—all such claims are termed false views.
This is both real and unreal. The Real-Existence school (Sarvāstivāda) of the Hīnayāna adheres to the view that all phenomena are entirely substantially existent;
the Emptiness school (Śūnyavāda) of the Hīnayāna asserts that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, and are not substantially existent.

This is "arising" and "non-arising. In the Hīnayāna Piṭaka, it is taught that form arises from conditions and is thus called an "arising dharma," whereas the Dharma-nature is inherently existent and does not arise from conditions, and is thus called a "non-arising dharma.
In the Great Teaching of the One Vehicle, form entirely arises from the nature, just as waves arise from water;

one realizes that form is non-arising and that the entirety of the wave is nothing but water. It is not merely that foolish people are deluded regarding the truth and consequently give rise to falsehoods—this is what is called "perversion."

Those of the three vehicles who rely on teachings of incomplete meaning and cling to a single gate, unable to harmonize them into a complete whole, are all subsumed within the category of universal perversion and delusion.
To dwell in a secluded place and cultivate the gathering of the mind is the essential method of practice; it values profound stillness, for if one dwells in a state of decline...
How can a restless mind ever find peace? The Buddha exhorted practitioners to dwell in empty, secluded, and tranquil places to collect their minds.
They should abide immovably like Mount Sumeru; with a settled mind dwelling in concentration, they should remain as steady and unshakable as a fixed pillar.
He remained as still as Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains.

He contemplated that all phenomena are non-existent; through wisdom he observed that the nature of phenomena is empty, like space, lacking any solidity, and like the great void, originally empty and quiescent, without any firmness.
It is the characteristic of being solid and obstructive;
it is neither born nor produced, neither moving nor retreating. Its original nature is inherently so:
it does not emerge from causes, nor is it produced by conditions, nor does it arise from dharmas; it has never wavered, nor is there any advancing or retreating.

It is eternally abiding in a single aspect. Since the preceding passage stated that there is no eternal abiding, while this passage now speaks of "eternally abiding in a single aspect," what is the intended meaning?
The former statement of "non-existence" was intended to refute the biased view of a fixed, dead eternity;
this present "eternal abiding" refers to dwelling within the principle of the single true aspect, which is signless.
This is called the proximate sphere; this is called the sphere of intimacy for a bodhisattva.

If there is a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa, enters this sphere of practice and this sphere of intimacy—should anyone be able, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to enter these two aforementioned spheres of practice and intimacy.
When preaching this sutra, one is without timidity. What was previously called "the mind being free from fear" is here termed "being without timidity.

This exhorts the practitioner to fix their mind upon the Path: first, they should remain in stillness and concentration to contemplate phenomena and conditions, reflecting with precision and mature deliberation until the principles and meanings enter the spirit.

Their practice must rely upon the sutras, and their speech must accord with reason. Even if one should attain hundreds of thousands, millions, or tens of millions [of insights], [one must remain steadfast].
When all the assembly is present before you and you raise your voice, every word must cause their minds to open and their intentions to be resolved.

Once your power of study has reached its limit and your intellectual understanding is clear, you may speak in accordance with the truth; what fear could there be? If one does not investigate thoroughly but falsely claims to have attained understanding, how could one possibly be free from timidity and dread?
At times a bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber. When a bodhisattva has the occasion and wishes to preach the Dharma, they should first enter a chamber of stillness.
With right mindfulness, they should contemplate the teachings according to their meaning; with a mind of right concentration, they should memorize and reflect upon them in accordance with the sūtras.
He examines the meaning of the Dharma he has taught;
having arisen from meditative concentration, he reflects upon it until the principles and meanings are refined and correct, and only then does he calmly emerge from concentration.
For the sake of kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others, he opens their minds and expounds this sutra.
As stated in the preceding text: "If such persons should come at any time, he then preaches the Dharma for them."

Their minds will be peaceful and secure, free from timidity. If they practice in accordance with what I have taught, their minds will naturally become peaceful and secure, and they will be free from the fault of experiencing fear or timidity before a great assembly at the critical moment.

Mañjuśrī, this is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the first dharma; it is the gate of practice for the initial bliss and purity cultivated by a bodhisattva who dwells with a settled mind amidst fear.
One who is able to preach the Lotus Sūtra in future ages will be able to preach the Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly during the evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
from this point onward, a section of the sūtra text corresponds precisely to the second "Peaceful Practice" (sukhavihāra).
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if one wishes to preach this sutra during the period of the Final Dharma after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa— that is,
if one wishes to preach the Lotus Sutra after the Buddha has passed away—
one should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Dwelling; one should abide in the gateway of the Practice of Peaceful Dwelling.
Whether speaking aloud or reading from the sūtra— when explaining or reading this sūtra— one does not delight in speaking of the faults of others or of the scriptures,
nor does one wish to speak of the faults of others or of the scriptures.
Furthermore, one should not treat other Dharma masters with contempt. One must not, out of arrogance or pride, belittle or insult other teachers who preach the various scriptures.
One should not speak of the likes and dislikes, strengths and weaknesses of others, nor discuss the ordinary virtues found within the bodies of common people.
Regarding matters of their faults or virtues,
whether great or small, one does not mention them by name to those who are śrāvakas or followers of the Hīnayāna,
nor does one speak of their transgressions by referring to them specifically by name.
Nor does one praise them by mentioning their names or extolling their virtues. Nor does one specifically name them to praise their qualities.

This is because both disparagement and praise are unsuitable for destroying the equality of the true mind. Disparagement gives rise to contention, such that they cannot dwell in peace with one another;
praise gives rise to attachment, which may lead others into inferior teachings. Therefore, both are ceased.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion; this is especially impermissible.
Because one skillfully cultivates such a mind of peace and happiness, and because one is well able to restrain and cultivate such verbal karma, it causes the mind to attain peace and happiness.

All who listen should not oppose his intent. When the Dharma Master expounds the teaching, he should observe the capacities and conditions of the audience and listen to them in accordance with their inclinations; he must not oppose them.
If there are challenges or questions—should someone raise a difficult point or pose a question for inquiry—[he should respond].
One should not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna. If one asks about the Mahāyāna but is answered with the principles of the Hīnayāna, one misses the appropriate opportunity.

One should instead provide an explanation solely through the Mahāyāna. If one asks about the Hīnayāna and is answered with the Mahāyāna, it draws those of provisional capacity into the ultimate reality;
if one asks about the Mahāyāna and is answered with the Mahāyāna, it perfectly accords with the prior capacity. In both cases, there is benefit.
[He] causes them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). He causes all listeners to attain the Middle Way and all-knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Bodhisattva always delights in teaching the Dharma for peace and security.
Practicing as a Bodhisattva, he always desires to be free from faults so that the mind may be at peace, and he teaches the Dharma according to principle."
One should provide seats upon a pure ground; one should select a clean place free from defilement and provide a high and wide seat for preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the anointing of the body with oil: while the teachings of the Hīnayāna do not permit the fondness for anointing the body with fragrant oils, here one is now instructed to do so.
This is for the purpose of removing foul odors, not out of a craving for beauty.
Bathing removes dust and filth; washing away grime and dirt serves to purify the body.
One wears new, clean garments—either putting on new clothes or washing those already possessed until they are clean—and seeks out clothing from appropriate sources.
The Dharma is also called impure;
one must be pure both internally and externally. One's inner mind and outward demeanor must both be pure.
One should sit upon the Dharma-seat, dwelling with composure at the seat for preaching the Dharma.
He explains according to their questions; he provides exposition in accordance with what is asked.
Whether it be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, members of the monastic community of renunciants, or upāsakas—faithful laymen.
As well as upāsikās—women of pure faith;
kings and princes; sovereigns and their sons;
and the ministers, officials, and common people—the various ministers, scholars, and the populace at court.
By means of subtle and profound meanings: when the aforementioned persons approach the Bodhisattva, they should explain the subtle, profound, and most deep meanings with a gentle countenance;
they should expound them with a serene and joyful expression.
Regarding difficult questions: when someone comes to raise a difficult question, one answers in accordance with the meaning;
one answers according to the meaning of what was asked.
One employs causes and conditions and parables, either citing causes and conditions or adducing parables.
He expounds and analyzes; he disseminates, propagates, analyzes, and elucidates.
By these skillful means and through these various conditions as expedients for conversion, he causes all to resolve their minds, ensuring that every listener gives rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Gradually increasing and augmenting— while it is logical that awakening may be sudden,
the practice must be gradual in order to achieve this increase and enter the Buddha-way, the unsurpassed Buddha-way of the One Vehicle.
Eliminate the mind of indolence; remove the thoughts of laziness, dissipation, and arrogance, as well as the notions of lethargy and negligence.
Be free from all sorrow and affliction; by being careful in speech and avoiding transgressions, one will be without a sorrowful mind.
He preaches the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness; he preaches the Dharma with a mind of compassionate patience.
He constantly preaches day and night; he perpetually expounds for others the unsurpassed teaching of the Way, clarifying the doctrine of the One Vehicle of the unsurpassed Way.
By means of various causes and conditions, using both the two types of causes and conditions— wholesome and unwholesome—

they cause the unwholesome to cease and encourage the cultivation and maintenance of the wholesome through immeasurable similes and illustrations of immeasurable kinds of phenomena and characteristics.
To reveal and instruct sentient beings; to open their understanding and enlighten all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice;
causing them all to attain faith and understanding, giving rise to a heart of joy.
Regarding clothing and bedding: whether it be with respect to clothing or bedding.
Regarding food, drink, medicine, and medical treatment— namely, the two daily meals and medicinal ingredients for healing—
one’s mind should have no expectations regarding these four things;
there should be no heart that seeks, hopes for, or anticipates them.
One should simply focus the mind on the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma; one should exclusively and single-mindedly, with right mindfulness,
expound the sublime Dharma and its pure causes and conditions,
vowing to attain the Buddha-way and achieve the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
He causes the assembly to be likewise; he causes the great multitude to also attain such [attainment].
This is a great benefit, peace, and happiness, an offering; this is called the vast benefit of bestowing peace and happiness, a pure offering.
After my parinirvāṇa, after the Buddha has passed away,
if there should be a bhikṣu, a monk who preaches the Dharma,
who is able to expound this wondrous Lotus Sūtra with a mind free from envy, anger, and all afflictive hindrances, his heart being pure—
Pure as still, clear water, it is free from all jealousy and anger, nor are there any matters of mutual affliction or obstruction.
There is no sorrow, nor anyone who reviles; furthermore, there is no trace of any anxiety, deliberation, or evil.
Regarding those who speak with insults and abuse:
one who possesses loving-kindness and patience has no fear of being struck with knives, staves, or the like. Since such a person’s mind is always at peace, they do not afflict others;
and since they do not afflict others, who then would afflict them? Thus, they have no fear of matters such as knives and staves.
Nor are they expelled, nor are they expelled from the assembly by others.
Because they abide in patience and are able to dwell in the blissful practice of the Mahāyāna, such is the wise person.
If those who possess wisdom can act in this way, [they shall be so].
One who has well cultivated the mind and is well able to cultivate and restrain the mind of the Way can abide in peace and happiness;
thus, one can abide in the peaceful and happy conduct of speech,
as I have explained above and as I have proclaimed in the preceding passage.
The merit of that person— the merit obtained by one who extensively propagates this sutra—
cannot be calculated or illustrated through numbers, metaphors, or cited examples, even across ten thousand koṭis of kalpas, or throughout countless ten thousand koṭis of kalpas.
It cannot be fully described; one can never reach the end of describing its merits.
△ From this point onward, a section of the sutra corresponds precisely to the third meaning: the Practice of Peaceful Abiding.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, if there should be any bodhisattva mahāsattva during the final age when the Dharma is about to perish,
at the end of the Buddha’s era when the Dharma is about to perish—
Those who receive, uphold, read, and recite; who believe in, accept, remember, and keep in mind this sutra—namely, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—must harbor no envy.
They must never harbor hatred, jealousy, or malice.
Do not harbor a mind of flattery and deception; do not harbor a mind of sycophancy, falsehood, or unwholesomeness.
Furthermore, do not belittle or revile those who study the Buddha-way, nor should you lightly provoke or abuse those who practice the holy path of the Buddhist gate.
"To seek out their faults" means to investigate, search for, and scrutinize the faults of others.
"Bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, and upāsikā" are to be understood as explained previously.
Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka are those who seek to study the Four Noble Truths of the śrāvaka.
Those who seek the pratyekabuddha are those who seek to study the twelve links of dependent origination of the pratyekabuddha.
Those who seek the bodhisattva path are those who seek to practice the six perfections on the bodhisattva path.
Do not distress them so as to cause them doubt or regret. Do not falsely distress them so as to give rise to a mind of uncertainty, agitation, or remorse.
Speak to those people, saying: "You are very far from the Way. [And] speak to the people before you, saying: "The practice you have undertaken..."
The path to Buddhahood is exceedingly long and distant;

one will ultimately be unable to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). In the end, one cannot attain the Tathāgata’s all-knowledge—wherein "all" refers to the seeds of emptiness-wisdom, which are the seeds of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā).
The non-duality of emptiness and the provisional is precisely what constitutes perfect interfusion.
The sublime wisdom of the Middle Way of the Greatly Awakened Tathāgata.
Why is this so? Because you are a person of negligence, being indolent regarding the Path;
because you are a person of unruly nature, dissolute, wild, and unwholesome, unable to apply diligent effort toward the Path. These are the seven preceding phrases.
These are precisely words that lightly provoke others.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding phenomena (*dharma*) to the point of contention.

Moreover, one ought not forcibly generate frivolous speculation concerning all phenomena to disrupt the gates of the Dharma, establishing what should be discarded and what should be maintained, thereby giving rise to dispute.

One should conceive the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings. One should conceive the thought of great compassion, feeling pity for and seeking to uproot the suffering of all beings in the world.
One should conceive the thought of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas, and one should conceive the thought of affectionate reverence for those loving fathers.
One should conceive the thought of regarding all bodhisattvas as great teachers, and conceive the thought of regarding all bodhisattvas as great teachers from whom one receives the Dharma.
One should always, with a profound mind, pay homage and prostrate to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions;
one should not hold a superficial view of the great Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, but should instead pay them homage and prostrate with a profound mind.
He teaches the Dharma with equanimity toward all sentient beings. He preaches the Dharma to all beings with a mind of impartiality.
Because he accords with the Dharma, he neither exceeds nor falls short; because he accords with the Dharma of an impartial mind, he does not dare to diminish it.
He speaks from the perspective of the majority;

even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively. Even toward those who have profound affection and delight in the Dharma, he does not show partiality by speaking to them more than others.
Mañjuśrī, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish—
amidst that evil world at the time when the Tathāgata’s Dharma is being extinguished— will [act as follows].
There is one who achieves success; this is the third practitioner of the path of bliss. There is one capable of accomplishing this third dharma-gate of the pure practitioner.
When this Dharma is being taught, none can disturb them; when the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, no external conditions can cause disturbance.
In times of turmoil,
may they find good fellow students with whom to recite this sutra together; may they find virtuous people with whom to study, uphold,
read, and recite it.
They will also cause a great assembly to come and listen to their teachings; they will be able to inspire all such assemblies to listen with faith, receive, and accept them.
Having heard them, they will be able to retain them; having listened with their ears, they will remember and hold them in their minds.
Having retained it, one is able to recite it; once retained in memory, one can then recite it;
having recited it, one is able to explain it; once all have been recited, one is able to explain them to others;
having explained them to others, one is further able to write them down.
If one causes others to transcribe it, or even if one cannot do so oneself but hires another to write it,
and then makes offerings to the scripture scrolls while further applying the mind with sincerity to perform ritual worship,
honoring, respecting, and praising them— because of such reverence, one does not dare to treat them with contempt; because of such respect, one does not dare to look down upon them.
Because they regard it with praise, they do not dare to disparage it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra—if there is a person who wishes to expound this sutra..."
One should abandon envy, anger, pride, flattery, deceit, and a crooked or false mind;
one must cast away all unwholesome states of mind, including jealousy, malice, arrogance, sycophancy, treachery, and hypocrisy.
One should constantly cultivate straightforward conduct and never treat others with contempt;
one should always practice such simple, upright, and lawful behavior, never treating others with ease, disdain, or disparagement.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous conceptualization regarding the Dharma. Nor should one forcibly give rise to views and conceptualizations concerning the Dharma.

One must not cause others to feel doubt or regret by saying, "You will not attain Buddhahood," nor should one cause others to harbor doubts or regrets by saying, "What you have cultivated will not lead to the attainment of Buddhahood."
This is the Dharma-preaching of the Buddha’s sons. If one can thus skillfully employ the mind, this is called the Dharma-preaching of the Buddha’s sons.
They are always gentle and capable of endurance; they are constantly gentle and well able to exercise forbearance.

One should practice compassion toward all. Because one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings, one bestows happiness upon them; because one gives rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one extracts them from their suffering and affliction.
One should not give rise to a mind of indolence; one must always be diligent for the sake of the multitude, never allowing oneself to become lax, arrogant, idle, or negligent.

The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Way out of compassion for sentient beings. The great Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions practice the path of loving-kindness and compassion out of pity for sentient beings.
One should give rise to a mind of reverence; they are my Great Teachers. One ought to produce a heart of reverence toward them.
This is my Dharma-transmitting Master,
whom I regard as the unsurpassed father of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; toward all Tathāgatas, I give rise to the thought of them as the unsurpassed fathers of compassion.

Having destroyed the mind of pride, one preaches the Dharma without obstruction; having eliminated all haughty and arrogant minds, one skillfully explains the essentials of the Dharma without obstructive conditions.
A wise person should guard this third dharma in this manner. This third type is the practice of mental ease and happiness.
Such being the meaning, all who possess wisdom should carefully observe it and always cherish its protection;
they should practice with single-minded ease and joy, maintaining a unified mind in this sublime conduct of peace and happiness.
"Without peer among those most honored": he is constantly revered by immeasurable and vast multitudes.
△ From this point onward, the passage of the sutra properly constitutes the fourth vow, the Practice for Peaceful Living.
Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "There are those with the Great Bodhicitta who bring sentient beings to maturity.
In the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there shall be the periods of the True, the Semblance, and the Final Dharma of the Tathāgata’s teaching."
The people of the world are pure and easy to transform; however, during the age of the final dharma, roots of goodness diminish and it becomes difficult to bring others to transformation.
Therefore, it is pointed out that propagating this sutra at such a time is most difficult.
There are those who receive and uphold the Lotus Sutra; there are those capable of maintaining this Lotus Sutra.
One should give rise to a mind of great compassion toward those who are householders and those who have left the home life;
one should give rise to a mind of great compassion that bestows happiness among all people, including faithful laymen and laywomen as well as the monastic community of monks and nuns.

One should give rise to great compassion toward those who are not bodhisattvas; one should give rise to a mind of great compassion that uproots suffering toward those who do not cultivate the great practices of a bodhisattva and who hold wrong views.
One should form this thought; one should resolve the mind and think thus:
"Such a person has incurred a great loss. A person who lacks faith in the Mahāyāna in this way commits a grave transgression."

The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate. Why is it considered a failure? It is precisely because, although the Tathāgata expounds all dharmas through the skillful means of compassion, [beings] do not hear, do not know, and do not awaken;
they are unable to listen, unable to understand, and unable to reflect upon them.
If one does not inquire, does not believe, and does not understand— if one is unable to question, unable to accept with faith, and unable to inquire for understanding— then this is a great loss.
Although such a person does not inquire, believe, or understand this sutra, even though that person [is thus disposed toward] this wondrous sutra...
They were unable to inquire about it and unable to believe and understand it.
"When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— that is, when I awaken to the Unsurpassed Way..."
Wherever they may be, and in whatever place they reside,
by means of the power of supernormal faculties and the power of wisdom, one should employ supernormal faculties to transform and guide them, and employ the power of wisdom to instruct and lead them.
To lead them so that they may abide within this Dharma—from the thought "I should act thus" up to "abiding within this Dharma"—is precisely the fourth vow:
to deliver sentient beings through the sublime practice of peace and happiness, skillfully guiding them so that they may enter the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are beings who cultivate the mind of the sublime path of practice.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there will be those who accomplish this fourth dharma;
there will be those who accomplish this fourth single capacity for peaceful and happy practice—the power of great compassion and great vows.
When this Dharma is being taught, there is no fault; when such a sublime Lotus Sūtra is expounded, there is not a single unwholesome fault whatsoever.
It is constantly [taught] for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, and people.
The common people, brahmins, householders, and others are all to be understood as previously explained.

They offer him sustenance, respect, honor, and praise because his practice accords with the Dharma; since his power of aspiration is profound and his intellectual understanding is likewise deep, all people revere and look up to him.
The devas of the void— indeed, all the devas within the void—
also constantly attend upon him for the sake of hearing the Dharma; desiring to hear the sound of the Dharma,
they also constantly follow and guard him day and night.
Whether in a village, a town, or a secluded forest; if the Dharma-preacher is in a hamlet, a district, or in a quiet and solitary place within the mountains and forests.
When someone comes wishing to challenge with questions, or someone comes wishing to interrogate and inquire about the principles of the Dharma,
the devas constantly protect them day and night for the sake of the Dharma. Because the devas stood before the Buddha and vowed to uphold the True Dharma,
they protect those who might find it difficult to explain it.
It causes all listeners to attain joy; it enables those who hear the essential points of the Dharma to attain the bliss of profound and wondrous Dharma-joy. Why is this so?
How is it that the various devas who protect those who uphold this sutra cause the listeners to rejoice and attain greatness?
The benefit of the Dharma.
Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, it is a scripture of profound and subtle mystery;
for this reason, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time protect it with their supernormal powers.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, such a wondrous Dharma and Mahāyāna sūtra,
is such that even its name cannot be heard in immeasurable lands; in other immeasurable lands,
it is impossible even to hear the title of its opening words.

How much more so for those who obtain the opportunity to see, receive, uphold, read, and recite it! How much more so for those who personally desire to see this sutra, receiving it within their hearts and reciting it with their mouths!
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King; as a king of the golden wheel, he rules over the four continents.

Below, there is great power that overpowers all; taking the Universal Monarch as a metaphor for the Buddha, it signifies that he possesses great majestic virtue to gather and transform all various kinds of sentient beings.

He desired to subjugate various kingdoms through his majestic power; the king wished to bring the smaller kingdoms under his sway by means of his authority, just as a Buddha manifests supernatural powers to subdue the hosts of Māra.
Yet the minor kings did not obey his commands, and the small kingdoms did not submit to the Wheel-Turning King’s orders, just as [other] heterodox schools do not follow [the Buddha].

Seeing that they did not enter the True Dharma, the Wheel-Turning King then raised various kinds of armies to go forth and punish them. As for the meaning of "various" (*nānāvidha*) regarding these armies—whether elephants, horses, infantry, or cavalry;

whether hidden in ambush or displayed openly; and because their names and forms differ—they are thus called "various. This is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), which may either break [the opposition] or...
