"You all said that my disciples would naturally protect and uphold [the Dharma]; yet now we hear from below that they have all rushed to assemble in the air.

Seeing such things, the assembly immediately gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha: 'From where have they come? The World-Honored One replied, 'They are my emanations. Thereupon, they further doubted, thinking:
'The World-Honored One’s attainment of Buddhahood is near, yet the number of those he has emanated is so great; surely this was not his initial resolve.'"
For this reason, I have revealed the span of my lifespan to resolve the doubts of the multitude.

Although I truly attained Buddhahood long ago, my present claim to having attained it is merely an expedient means for the sake of sentient beings; I manifest extinction, yet in reality I do not pass into extinction—it is only a proclamation that I have passed away.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family, those among you present who harbor doubts, you should believe and understand the true and sincere words of the Tathāgata; you must have firm faith."
The Tathāgata speaks the truth; do not cling to expedient means and thereby harbor doubt concerning the Buddha.
He further addressed the great assembly, saying, "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of sincere truth. He spoke this again because he wished to strengthen their faith.
Furthermore, he addressed the great assembly, saying: "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
Because the Dharma is profound and subtle, sentient beings find it difficult to understand; thus, he spoke this up to three times to inspire deep faith.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha.
Seeing the Buddha’s repeated and earnest gravity in this manner, Maitreya and the multitude joined their palms and uttered these sincere words in response to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One, we only pray that you will explain this; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. “We say we shall faithfully accept them and dare not harbor any doubt.
Having spoken thus three times, and having addressed the World-Honored One in this manner three times, the Buddha remained silent and no [teaching] was yet received.
They gave their consent.

They spoke again, saying, "We pray only that you will explain it; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. This they requested repeatedly, four times in all, with utmost sincerity and earnestness.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the bodhisattvas had made their request three times without ceasing.

Knowing that sentient beings would not stop even after the third request, he spoke to them once more for a fourth time, saying: "Listen attentively! The Buddha is about to speak words of truth; therefore, I command you."
The assembly listened with focused minds as the Tathāgata,
out of his compassionate desire to deliver sentient beings, revealed the power of his secret and supernatural faculties; through this subtle, wondrous, profound, and secret power,
he concealed his true practice and spoke in provisional terms of having recently attained enlightenment.
All the devas, humans, and asuras in the world, and all sentient beings existing within the world,
all believe that this present Śākyamuni Buddha is the one preaching the Lotus Sūtra on the Sacred Peak.
Having departed from the palace of the Śākya clan, having left the palace of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya lineage,
not far from the city of Gayā, at that time and on that occasion,
he sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Seated beneath the tree of enlightenment, he manifested [this].
To attain perfect enlightenment is called "sitting at the site of awakening.

However, son of good family, as for me, since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has actually been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas since I first attained perfect enlightenment.
To say that I have attained Buddhahood [only recently] is merely a provisional expression.
For a long time—

indeed, for as long as five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas (an incalculable number according to the great reckoning of the Western lands)— it is like taking countless great trichiliocosms.
Suppose someone were to grind them into fine dust; to use a metaphor: suppose someone were to take all the worlds and at once grind them all finely into atoms of dust.
Passing to the east through five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeya worlds, one places a single mote of dust;
passing through countless asaṃkhyeya worlds, one then places another minute mote of dust.
Thus he travels east until all these atoms are exhausted; thus he proceeds eastward in succession until every atom as described above has been marked and exhausted.
"Sons of good family, what do you think? Sons of my own household, what do you think of this?
Can these worlds be conceived of, calculated, or known by number, as was previously described regarding the East?"
"Can the number of world-systems be calculated through thought and reckoning?
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others all addressed the Buddha together, and as the assembly received the Buddha's question, they answered him simultaneously.
World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless; they cannot be known through calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind.
Because the worlds are so numerous, they cannot be known even by means of calculation or reckoning.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— those of the two vehicles—
even with their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and by means of that untainted wisdom through which they have exhausted all afflictions,
cannot contemplate or know its limit; its numerical measure is beyond the reach of contemplation.
We abide on the stage of *avaivartika*, and all these great bodhisattvas likewise abide on the stage of non-retrogression;
yet we do not penetrate this matter, nor can we [fathom] even this matter of the number of atoms.
[It is] understood.
World-Honored One, these worlds are thus immeasurable and boundless; they are said to be limitless and cannot be known.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas, including Maitreya and the others.
"Good sons, I shall now speak clearly to you. In the past, when things were kept secret, I did not dare to speak the truth;
now, however, I shall explain it with full clarity and openness."
Regarding all these worlds—those where atoms have been placed and those where they have not, those that have been marked and those that have not—all shall be reduced to dust;
let each single atom represent one kalpa. Then, taking all the worlds to the east, grind them down entirely into fine particles.
For the worldling, one minute particle constitutes one kalpa;
yet since I attained Buddhahood, more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas have passed.
The number of kalpas since I attained Buddhahood further exceeds the kalpas of dust motes and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
From that time until now, I have constantly been in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
"constantly" means that my transformation here has been without rest.
Furthermore, in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya worlds elsewhere, he guides and benefits sentient beings.
If he were to transform only this [world], his merit would not be extensive; because it is not [limited] great compassion, he likewise guides and benefits all sentient beings in other places as well.
"O sons of good family, regarding this interval, I spoke of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others.

Because the Mahāyāna is taught through skillful means as the attainment of Buddhahood through cultivation over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I spoke of his former name as the Bodhisattva Supuṣpacandra, who met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and received the prediction:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. These were all matters of that intermediate period."
Furthermore, it is said that he has entered nirvāṇa, and it is also said that Dīpaṃkara entered parinirvāṇa;
all such statements are made through skillful means and conceptual differentiation, and are not in fact so.
"Good sons, if there are sentient beings who come to me, or if there are people who go to the Buddha's presence,
I shall regard them with my Buddha-eye and with the pure divine eye of a Buddha’s compassion."

He observes the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, such as faith and the others; those called faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are the five spiritual roots (*pañca-indriyāṇi*).
Observing whether their faculty-natures are sharp or dull, he employs whatever Dharma is appropriate for their deliverance to bring them across and liberate them.
In various places, he himself speaks of his names as being different and his ages as being greater or smaller;
in various places, he himself declares that the names and titles of his response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are each different, and their ages likewise vary.
Furthermore, he manifests the statement that he shall enter nirvana. The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space, fundamentally without beginning or end;
what is called "nirvana" is entirely a skillful manifestation for the sake of sentient beings.

Furthermore, he teaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma through various skillful means. In order to enable sentient beings to attain the wondrous Dharma, he employs provisional skillful means to expound it.
This can cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy, and can cause those with receptive capacity who hear the Dharma to understand and awaken, thereby giving rise to joy.
Mind. Good sons, when the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings— beholding them with his Buddha-eye—
he sees those who delight in inferior teachings, whose merit is meager and whose defilements are heavy, and who, due to dull faculties, take pleasure in the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle.
For those whose afflictions and defilements are shallow yet heavy,
I say that I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after leaving home for only a short time.
For such people of dull faculties and heavy obstructions, I speak of attaining the Way through leaving home at a young age.
However, in truth, since my actual attainment of Buddhahood has been for as long as this— immeasurable kalpas—
I have merely used skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, leading them into the Buddha-way by speaking in such a manner.
It is only for those of dull faculties that I employ skillful means to provide instruction, speaking of the length or brevity of my lifespan.
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of delivering sentient beings.
The Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma merely seeks to respond to their capacities, just as a physician prioritizes the removal of disease when administering medicine."
Sometimes he speaks of his own body, describing his own former body during its time on the causal ground;
sometimes he speaks of another's body, describing the body of another person during their time on the causal ground.
Whether manifesting his own body or another's body, he [describes] what was experienced by those bodies in past lives.
He reveals his karmic retribution to others;
he may reveal matters concerning himself or matters concerning others, disclosing to people the various deeds performed by himself or others in past lives.
All that is spoken is true and not false; each word accords with reality and is free from deception.

Why is this so? For what reason? It is because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are; the wisdom of the Tathāgata accords with the principle of suchness and is luminous.
One perceives the sign of the non-transmigration of the three realms;
there is no birth-and-death, whether retreating or emerging. Fundamentally, all is empty and quiescent like the great void;
truly, there is neither birth nor old age and death, neither one who comes back from retreat nor one who goes forth.
Furthermore, there is neither one who abides in the world nor one who enters parinirvāṇa. Because they are fundamentally unarisen, there is no abiding in the world;
because there is no extinction, there is no parinirvāṇa.
It is neither real nor unreal. Because it is not real, it does not share the deluded grasping at signs characteristic of ordinary beings; because it is not unreal, it is not...
It is like the Lesser Sages who extinguish form to grasp emptiness;
it is neither identical nor different, neither a single characteristic nor diverse characteristics.
It does not perceive the triple world as the inhabitants of the triple world perceive the triple world, nor does it perceive the triple world as existing as those people of the triple world do.

Just as those of the Two Vehicles perceive the three realms as empty, where emptiness and existence are non-dual, and name this "suchness" (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa), so too is it with these matters; such is the reality of these three realms.
The Tathāgata perceives with clarity and without error. Through the wisdom of the Tathāgata, there is clear knowledge and vision such that no point of error whatsoever exists.
This is because sentient beings possess various natures and their faculties and dispositions differ.
There are various desires; their inclinations and cravings differ.
There are various practices; their steps and conduct differ.
Because there are various recollections, conceptualizations, and discriminations, there arise various conjectures, various thoughts, and various distinctions.
Because each is different.
Desiring to cause the production of all roots of goodness—meaning the Tathāgata desires to bring forth the fundamental roots of all virtues—he employs various causes and conditions.
The term "various" (sankhya) is an indefinite expression; it refers to the various causes of both good and evil, as well as the virtues...
Regarding adverse conditions:

through various metaphors, expressions, and diverse teachings of the Dharma, he speaks of evil causes and conditions in order to induce reform, and speaks of virtuous causes and conditions to encourage the cultivation of correct practice.

The Buddha-works he performs have never been suspended for even a moment. Although he employs various skillful means in all his activities, his fundamental intent is always to cause all beings to attain the Way of the Buddha;
thus it is said that from beginning to now, in the interim, his Buddha-works have never for a single moment been neglected or slackened.
In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed; it is truly a vast duration since I realized the Way of the Buddha.
My lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, eternally abiding and never perishing. The attainment of Buddhahood by sentient beings is like ore being refined into gold:
once it has reached the state of pure gold, it no longer becomes alloyed again. This explains the gate of the Tathāgata’s own enjoyment, which is the Great Prajñāpāramitā.
The lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* is said to be "permanently abiding" because it has birth but no extinction.
Sons of good family, this lifespan was achieved by me when I originally practiced the bodhisattva path;
it is the wisdom-lifespan attained through the cultivation of bodhisattva practices in my former times.
Even now it is not yet exhausted; it is twice as much as the aforementioned number. Since the fruit has already been realized, it is equal to the Dharma-body—how could there be exhaustion?
It cannot be known by calculation.
Yet, this is not a true parinirvāṇa; likewise, this Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is not truly extinguished.
He then proclaimed that he would enter parinirvāṇa, skillfully declaring, "I shall enter parinirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings; by manifesting birth and proclaiming extinction, the Tathāgata employs these as skillful means to guide and transform sentient beings.

Why is this so? How is it thus? If the Buddha were to remain long in the world—if the World-Honored One were to remain for a long time in the world—those of meager virtue would not plant roots of goodness;
those of meager virtue, lacking merit and dull faculties, would be unwilling to practice.
They plant the seeds of the bodhi-virtues.
Those who are impoverished and lowly, who are greedily attached to the five desires and do not cultivate meritorious deeds, are called "impoverished.
Those who associate with evil persons are called "lowly. They are greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires of the mundane world.

They have entered the net of recollective imaginings and false views; they have entered the net of various conceptualizations, false cognitions, attachments, and cravings born of speculative deliberation.
If such people perceive the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable, these individuals truly see the Buddha’s non-extinction.

They then give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence. Regarding [the teaching] as something ordinary, they develop a mind of haughty license, harboring contempt, negligence, lassitude, and indolence;
they are unable to conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter, nor can they give rise to a heart of reverence, nor can they give rise to the realization that it is difficult to encounter.
One should conceive a mind of reverence and faith.
For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means, saying that there is arising and ceasing.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter; appearing but once after a vast interval of time, they are hard to find.
I see it.
Why is this so? For what purpose was it said:
"Those of little merit; those who are persons of little merit within the world"?
After passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, having traversed many kalpas, some may see the Buddha while others do not;
some may obtain a vision of him while others see him not at all.
For this reason, I have made this statement; for this reason, I have spoken through skillful means:
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is difficult to behold. It is because they do not see him that I speak these words.
When these sentient beings hear such words, and those who have not yet seen [the Buddha] hear these words of mine, they will certainly conceive the thought that this is difficult to encounter;
they will certainly give rise to the thought that such a meeting is difficult to find.
With hearts filled with longing and thirsting for the Buddha, they yearn to behold him;
thus they plant roots of goodness, planting the roots of all virtues that lead to seeing the Buddha.

Therefore, although the Tathāgata does not truly undergo extinction, he speaks of "extinction and deliverance" (parinirvāṇa). For the sake of sentient beings, he merely manifests birth and death within that which is without birth or death.

Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is exactly like this; it is only for fear that people might doubt that the present Buddha has newly established this teaching.
The purpose of this section is to demonstrate that all Buddhas are likewise so;

in order to deliver sentient beings, they are entirely real and not false. Since the Buddha originally has no [self-centered] mind and employs skillful means to deliver beings—unlike the unwholesome and deceptive practices of the world which may have benefit but cause harm—it is said that they are "all real."
For example, it is like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning. The Buddha is like a king of physicians, his wisdom clear and penetrating;

he thoroughly understands the origins of diseases, is proficient in prescriptions and medicines, skillfully cures all ailments, and possesses a precise and practiced knowledge of medical treatises and the natures of drugs, being well able to provide treatment.
He heals the illnesses of sentient beings.
That man has many sons, which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings in the five realms.
Whether numbering ten, twenty, or even a hundred—if ten refers to bodhisattvas and twenty to those of the two vehicles—then...
When the number reaches one hundred, this refers to the ten dharma realms.
Because there are circumstances involving material affairs, he travels far to other lands. The Buddha first transforms those here by establishing Mahāyāna conditions;
when the spiritual capacities in other regions have matured, this is called "having material circumstances. To abandon this place and proceed to that is what is meant by "reaching other lands."
Later, the sons drank another person's poisoned medicine. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples following false paths are called "drinking poisoned medicine.

When the medicine takes effect, they become dazed and confused, wallowing on the ground; as the poisonous influences of falsehood assail them, their minds are distressed and they drift through the various realms of existence.
The term "destinies" (gati) refers to wandering through birth and death without ever leaving the lower realms.
At that time, his father returns home; this is a metaphor for the ripening of conditions and the subsequent reappearance of a Buddha.
Just as some of the sons who drank the poison either lost their original minds or did not lose them, so too do I see that among sentient beings,
some enter the poisonous influence of heterodoxy and lose the great vehicle, while others retain their original minds and do not lose them.
Seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly. To look upon a Buddha with an ordinary mind is called "seeing from afar";
when sentient beings see the Buddha, it is like a child seeing its father, and as the father sees his son, the father rejoices and the son is glad.
Prostrating and kneeling, one inquires after their well-being and peaceful return. Bowing the body to pay homage, one inquires after their daily life;
when they proclaim the cessation [of suffering] and return to the source—like leaving home to enter the marketplace and extend their hands—it is called a peaceful return.
We, in our ignorance, have mistakenly consumed poisonous medicine; we repent our transgressions for having erroneously entered the stream of heterodoxy.

We pray that you will grant us healing and bestow upon us further life. We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will employ skillful means to guide and transform us, and further grant us wisdom and longevity.
The father saw his sons suffering in such a manner; likewise, the Buddha saw sentient beings undergoing these various kinds of manifold sufferings within the triple world (*traidhātuka*).

Relying upon the medical treatises (*sūtra-paddhati*), he sought out excellent medicinal herbs. The Buddha’s employment of the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) practiced by all Buddhas is called "conforming to the method" (*anupada-paddhati*).
Examining their illness with discernment and subduing it through systematic treatment is called seeking excellent medicine.
It is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor; the medicinal ingredients of conduct, form, path, fragrance, Dharma-sound, and exquisite flavor are all complete.

Pounding, sifting, and blending these together, one gives them to the child to take. "Crushing and subduing" the fierce and violent is called pounding; withdrawing the evil and advancing the good is like sifting and winnowing;
the harmonious integration of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is called blending; and entrusting [the medicine] for the student to receive and uphold is called taking the medicine.
And he spoke these words: "This is a great and excellent medicine, a truly wholesome and great medicine.
It is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor; its ingredients are complete and it is not a counterfeit medicine."
"You should take this; it will swiftly eliminate your suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments. You may take this;
once the illness is removed, all physical and mental suffering and affliction will cease to arise."
Among those sons, those who have not lost their minds—those who have not lost their original Mahāyāna resolve—see that this excellent medicine possesses both fine color and fragrance;
they hear the Dharma with faith and understanding, skillfully knowing its meaning and flavor.
Even if one takes this medicine, all illnesses will be completely eliminated; likewise, by practicing according to the Dharma, one attains liberation from birth and death.
As for others who have lost their minds, this is a metaphor for those who lack right faith and a heart that delights in the good.
Seeing his father arrive at the time when a Buddha had appeared in the world,
although he greeted him with joy and, seeing the Buddha’s arrival, asked after him with delight,
he nevertheless sought a cure for his illness and prayed for liberation from suffering.
Yet, although given medicine, they are unwilling to take it; and although granted the Dharma, they are unwilling to practice it.
Why is this? For what reason do they come seeking [it], yet are unwilling to take it?

Because the poisonous vapors have penetrated deeply, they have lost their original mind; because the habitual tendencies of perverse poisons have entered deeply into their hearts, they destroy their roots of goodness.
Thus, they claim that these fine-colored, fragrant medicines are not delicious, and they are unable to perceive the flavor of the upright Dharma.
The father thought to himself, "This son is to be pitied. Seeing that his son was ill, he felt deep compassion for him.
Being struck at the heart by poison, his mind became entirely deranged; being struck at the heart by poison, he lost right mindfulness and fell into total delusion.
Though seeing me, they joyfully seek my healing; though seeing the Buddha, they joyfully seek his protection.
Yet, they are unwilling to take such excellent medicine, and they do not practice this True Dharma.
"I shall now employ skillful means to cause them to take this medicine. By proclaiming *nirvāṇa* as a skillful means, I shall cause them to contemplate the True Dharma.
He then spoke these words: "You should all know; you, my sons, should understand this intention."
I am now old and decrepit, and the time of my death has arrived; I am about to enter parinirvāṇa.
This excellent medicine, the volume of the Great Canon (Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra), is now left here to be circulated throughout the world.
"You may take and consume it; you may take it as your standard and practice according to the Dharma.
Do not worry that you will not be cured; do not harbor doubts or anxieties that you cannot be liberated from suffering.
Having given these instructions, he departed for another country. Having entrusted his son, he proceeded once more to other regions.

He dispatched a messenger to inform your father that he had already passed away. The messenger was none other than the Bodhisattva, who, having received the Buddha’s entrustment to propagate the Dharma, returned to deliver the notification, saying: "World-Honored One, you have now entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the sons—whether ten, twenty, or even numbering in the hundreds—hearing that their father had passed away, were filled with great sorrow and distress;
hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, their hearts were likewise overwhelmed with grief and despondency.
And they formed this thought, saying:

"If our father were alive, he would have compassion for us and be able to rescue and protect us. If the Buddha were in the world, he would take pity on us and, through his skillful means, be able to provide rescue and protection."
Now you have abandoned me to perish far away in another land; now you have cast me off in this land of skillful means to manifest parinirvāṇa.
I reflect upon myself as solitary and exposed, with no further one to rely upon. I think of myself as orphaned and young, destitute and without support, for my compassionate father has already—
Having lost all reliance and support,

he constantly harbored a sense of grief and sorrow, whereby his mind finally awakened. Constantly maintaining this state of lamentation and distress, he was moved to such an extent that he regained his original mind and returned to clarity.
Thereupon one realizes that this medicine possesses exquisite color, flavor, and fragrance; one realizes that the principles and flavors of the Buddha-dharma are profound and far-reaching.
Immediately taking and consuming it, all toxic illnesses are healed; immediately taking and following the teachings, all outflows and karmic actions are completely exhausted.
When his father heard that his son had fully recovered, and when the Buddha, abiding in true stillness, heard that the deluded minds of various sentient beings had already awakened,
he immediately returned home so that all might see him. He then manifested a response, appearing once more in the world to cause all to exist [in the Dharma].
"By means of these conditions, he was able to see [the tumor] manifest. Sons of good family, what do you think?
In your estimation, could anyone say that this skilled physician had committed a falsehood? The physician used skillful means and spoke these words as a pretext."
"Is there anyone who could say that it would be an untruthful fault for one to save their child by dying?
No, World-Honored One. This response from Maitreya indicates that although the father did not actually die, his original intention was virtuous and free from falsehood.
The Buddha said, "I am also like this. What the Buddha does is just like that physician.
Since attaining Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas have passed."

In truth, he attained Buddhahood long ago; having already passed through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas without arising or ceasing, for the sake of sentient beings—just as a physician acts for the sake of his child—he speaks of "passing into extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*) by means of skillful power.
To speak of "passing into extinction" is the wisdom of skillful means.
Furthermore, there is no one capable of rightfully accusing me of the fault of falsehood;
nor is there anyone capable of rightfully charging me with the transgression of falsehood regarding my conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed; since I first achieved the Way, the number of kalpas that have elapsed."

For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—such a vast duration—he constantly preached the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions of sentient beings. He never for a moment ceased preaching the Dharma or saving living beings.
Causing them to enter the Buddha-way; causing them to attain entry into the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
From that time until now, throughout immeasurable kalpas; from that very moment, passing through immeasurable kalpas.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he employs skillful means to manifest parinirvāṇa; in the interim, he repeatedly displays birth and proclaims extinction.

Yet, in reality, he does not pass into extinction but dwells eternally here preaching the Dharma. According to the true nature of the Buddha’s dharma-body and reward-body, there is truly no time of extinction;
he dwells perpetually in the world, expounding all dharmas.
I dwell here eternally. Since the Buddha dwells eternally in the world, why do sentient beings not see him?
It is because of his various supernormal powers and the power of his skillful means regarding those supernormal powers.
It causes deluded sentient beings to fail to see [the Buddha] despite being near him.

Within the bodies of every person, the Buddha-Bhagavān sits cross-legged, fully endowed with marks of excellence; yet, because of their confusion and the arising of perverted perceptions, they do not perceive him even though he is exceedingly close.

When the multitude sees my parinirvāṇa, they extensively make offerings to my relics; when the multitude sees the Tathāgata’s physical body enter extinction, they extensively raise offerings to his remains and relics.
All of them harbor longing and affection, giving rise to a mind of thirsty aspiration; the multitude all yearns with affection, their hearts filled with thirsty aspiration.

When sentient beings have already gained faith and submission, being sincere and straightforward with minds that are supple and gentle; when sentient beings thus possess deep faith and submissiveness,
being genuine, upright, and soft-hearted within,
they single-mindedly desire to see the Buddha, not begrudging their own bodies or lives, and they joyfully and single-mindedly wish to behold the Tathāgata.
Without begrudging body, life, or wealth, I and the assembly of monks then emerged together from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; the Buddha and the monastic community appeared simultaneously.
At that time, I said to the sentient beings, "I am always here and do not perish. At that moment, I spoke thus to all sentient beings.
Abiding herein, there has never been cessation;

yet, through the power of skillful means, cessation and non-cessation are manifest. For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha, by the power of his skillful means and wisdom, manifests both cessation and non-cessation.
In other lands where there are sentient beings who are respectful, faithful, and joyful;

in other regions and countries where there are those capable of revering, delighting in, and believing in the Buddha-dharma—I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them. When the capacity [of the audience] arises, I preach; there is no fixed location for it.
"You have not heard this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa. You have not yet heard of such skillful means, and thus you merely say that my dwelling here is truly parinirvāṇa.
I see all sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering; the Buddha sees sentient beings drowning in birth and death."

Therefore, he does not manifest his body to them so as to cause them to give rise to longing and reverence. Thus, he immediately withdraws and does not manifest his body, desiring to cause their minds to give rise to longing and reverence.
Because their hearts feel such yearning and devotion, he then appears and preaches the Dharma for them; because longing and devotion have arisen within their minds, [he appears].
He immediately appeared before them and preached the Dharma to them.
Such is his power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). This is the nature of the Tathāgata’s power of supernormal knowledge;
it has been thus for as long as he has been a Buddha throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
He is always present on Vulture Peak Mountain, at the place where he preached the Lotus Sūtra,
and in all other dwelling places— in every land and region where he has taught the Dharma.
When sentient beings see the world being consumed by the great conflagration at the end of the kalpa, they behold with their own eyes this time of the kalpa’s destruction.

The blazing fires simultaneously incinerate and sweep away [all else], yet this land of mine remains peaceful, ever filled with devas and humans. "Right Nature" refers to the Buddha-nature; the two natures of conditions and fruition are termed "devas and humans.
At the moment when the flames of the fire of hatred blaze fiercely, the activity of a single thought-moment of perfect enlightenment is entirely like applying a seal.
However, that which is called "unimpeded" refers to a land where all auspicious signs are present, which is termed "fullness.

Its gardens, groves, and various halls and pavilions are adorned with manifold jewels; the lush forests of the seven factors of enlightenment and the towers of the path-factors are all embellished with the precious gems of myriad virtues.

The jewel tree abounds in flowers and fruits, where sentient beings find delight. The King of Bodhicitta is called the "Jewel Tree," virtuous deeds are its "flowers," and a good reputation is its "fruit.
Moment-to-moment thoughts of a wholesome mind are called "sentient beings," and to dwell constantly therein is called "finding delight."
The various devas strike celestial drums and constantly perform manifold music. A single thought of pure mind is called the "fourfold intersection of the devas";

when sounds are emitted from the body, it is called "striking the celestial drum," and using harmonious and elegant tones to benefit sentient beings through the four means of integration is called "performing music."

They rained down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly. Performing various virtuous deeds, they were called "the rain of jewel-flowers adorning the Buddha’s realm and his retinue.
While my own pure land was not destroyed, the multitude saw it as utterly consumed by fire. The Buddha’s pure land is fully endowed with all manner of blissful karmic fruits.
Where the fire of anger arises among suffering sentient beings, the jade and the stone are consumed together; it cannot be extinguished.
Such sorrow, fear, and various afflictions completely fill [the world]. Grief, anxiety, dread, and manifold sufferings—all such calamities are entirely pervasive.

These sentient beings with transgressions do so due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma; these sentient beings suffering from transgressions within these realms have done so because they have long practiced various unwholesome and evil causes and conditions.
For incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they do not hear the names of the Triple Gem; for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they fail to obtain the hearing of the names of the Triple Gem.
Yet there are those who cultivate merit and are gentle and upright; there are sentient beings who practice wholesome conduct and are gentle...
Those who are gentle, compliant, simple, and upright—
all such persons shall see my body here preaching the Dharma; they shall all see the Buddha constantly present in this place of tranquil extinction, preaching the Dharma with them.

At times, he speaks to this assembly of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan; at other times, he speaks to the assembly of the Buddha’s long life in order to inspire joy and reverent devotion toward the Buddha.

To those who have seen the Buddha only after a long time, he speaks of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha; to those who have seen the Buddha only after passing through many kalpas, he [speaks likewise].
By speaking of what is difficult, one causes [others] to give rise to the utmost gravity;
such is the power of my wisdom. The Tathāgata’s power of wisdom may speak of what is easy or what is difficult, and may be concise or prolix; his skillfulness is likewise thus.
The light of wisdom shines immeasurably. Because it is by nature luminous, through that light one perceives the Path; the light of wisdom is immeasurable, penetrating everything without exception.
His lifespan lasts for incalculable kalpas; the life-span obtained as the fruition of the wisdom-body he has accomplished is limitless and beyond measure.
These merits, acquired through cultivation over the course of kalpas, are all accomplished by virtue of having long cultivated pure karma during the causal stage.
"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this. You Bodhisattvas, being wise, should understand this through reason and have no doubt.
You must sever it so that it is forever exhausted; you must sever the net of doubt so that it never arises again."

The Buddha’s words are truly not false, like a physician’s skillful means. The Buddha’s words are true and do not deceive sentient beings, just as a skilled physician skillfully applies expedient means.
For the sake of curing a mad son, he speaks of death while actually being present; this is for the sake of curing a son who has lost his mind through madness. It is real.
He does not enter extinction before proclaiming *nirvāṇa*.
No one can say that he speaks falsely; for although his outward appearance may seem illusory, his mind is truly virtuous, and thus no one can say that he speaks falsely.
I am also the Father of the World who rescues those afflicted by suffering; the Buddha is likewise the Father of all worlds, the savior of sentient beings from their various hardships and calamities.
For the sake of ordinary people who, due to their inverted perceptions, speak of extinction while [the truth] actually exists, and who cling to the inverted thoughts of their minds.

It is not that they fail to perceive me; rather, it is because although the Buddha truly exists yet has entered parinirvāṇa, they give rise to a mind of arrogance and indulgence due to their perception of me as being constantly present. Because their minds are deluded, they develop a sense of pride and license from seeing the Buddha as if he were always manifest before them.

Those who are heedless and attached to the five desires fall into the evil realms. Those who are dissolute, wild, and intoxicated, being addicted to the five desires, follow their karma into the three evil paths.
I always know which sentient beings practice the Path and which do not. The Buddha constantly and fully understands the minds of sentient beings, whether...
Furthermore, he practices both the path and the non-path,
preaching various dharmas according to what is appropriate for those to be saved. Observing their capacities and adapting his teaching like a physician dispensing medicine,
he teaches whichever dharma enables them to attain liberation, causing them to rejoice.

Every time he forms this thought, "By what means shall I cause sentient beings [to attain it]? and every time such a thought arises within his mind, "By what skillful means shall I cause those sentient beings to enter the unsurpassed path and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body;
to enter the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata and swiftly [attain it]," [he acts accordingly].
One attains the fulfillment of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
In the seventeenth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,

"Distinguishing Merits," because of hearing in the preceding chapter the World-Honored One’s teaching on the long lifespan achieved in former times and the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, [one attains this].
The assembly of bodhisattvas, whose wisdom is immeasurable, all attained understanding and were able to discern the different benefits they received according to their respective levels of entry.
The Tathāgata distinguished the depth and shallowness of each individual’s merit and taught accordingly for the sake of the multitude.
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan and kalpas being so exceedingly long.

Hearing the Buddha’s teaching that the lifespan of the Saṃbhogakāya was thus enduring, immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya sentient beings attained great benefit. Hearing of the Buddha’s longevity, they opened the way to the near [path].
This reveals that those far away obtain the benefits of long-term cultivation.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; having seen that the great assembly had each obtained abundant benefit, the Buddha spoke to Maitreya so that he would know.
Ajita— this is the name of Maitreya.
When I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, and when the Buddha previously described that lifespan in the preceding chapter,
six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The "six hundred" represents the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*); the "eighty" represents the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). "Sentient beings" refers to the mind of every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*).
"Nayuta Ganges-sands" describes the quantity of those mental thoughts. If deluded thoughts are extinguished, the phenomena of birth are fundamentally empty;
one thoroughly perceives the self-nature (*svabhāva*) with perfect clarity, such that no adverse or favorable conditions can shake it, and thus one attains realization.
This principle—that the Dharma-eye is purified—is what is called attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Furthermore, there were a thousand times as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the *dhāraṇī* door of hearing and retaining.

The term "a thousand times" refers to a number of bodhisattvas a thousand times greater than the previous [number]; as for this *dhāraṇī*, it is translated here as "total retention," by which one retains whatever is heard.
Because they are able to receive and uphold all dharmas, and because all dharmas emerge from them, it is called the "gate of dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful exposition.
If one world were ground into fine dust, and each single particle of dust were a Bodhisattva who had attained great eloquence and the joy of preaching all dharmas without any obstruction;
and if there were further Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the dust motes of another world, who had attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable [qualities].
The *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (revolving dhāraṇī). It revolves and brings clear understanding of all *dhāraṇī* gates, producing immeasurable and boundless phrases and meanings within a single dharma.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm who were able to turn the wheel of the non-retrogressive [Dharma].
The Wheel of Dharma. With profound wisdom, they abide on the stage of non-retrogression and are able to turn the wheel of non-retrogression for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in two thousand medium chiliocosms who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
(Note: A single small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm; one thousand medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm. Now, these two...

A medium chiliocosm consists of two great chiliocosms; if these were all ground into dust, they would equal the number of bodhisattvas who have realized the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), dwell in the pure stages, and are able to turn the wheel of purity for the sake of the multitudes.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm— wherein one thousand sets of four continents constitute a small chiliocosm—
who shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after eight births. As for what is called "eight births," it refers to...
Those on the second bhūmi who repeatedly reach the stage of wondrous enlightenment are said to attain the unsurpassed *buddhatva* bodhi after eight births.

Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in four sets of four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*). This refers to a quantity equal to four times the number of atoms in a four-continent world.

One shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after four births. Regarding these "four births," it means that upon passing through four births in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one attains the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three or four *cāturdvīpaka* worlds who were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after three more births;
that is, they would become Buddhas in their third birth upon reaching the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in two sets of four continents, who were to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after two more births;
that is, they were to become buddhas in their second birth upon reaching the tenth bhūmi.
Furthermore, there is another four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*), where each of the four great continents is called a "world. Within it,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust who, in a single lifetime, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— that is,
they shall become Buddhas in a single lifetime upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samatā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There were also assemblies of beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved upon the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.
When the Buddha spoke thus of how these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained great benefit from the Dharma,
the assembly of bodhisattvas previously enumerated experienced a further increase in benefit through the Buddha’s sublime Dharma.
In the void, mandārava flowers rained down— small white flowers and mahāmandārava flowers,
which are large white flowers. The hosts of celestial beings, hearing the Dharma with joy,
rained flowers from the sky.
He scattered [flowers] before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees,
thereby making offerings to all the emanated Buddhas seated beneath jewel trees throughout the ten directions.
He also scattered [the flowers] over Śākyamuni Buddha, who was seated upon a lion throne within the stupa made of the seven precious substances;
he invited the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the Teacher of this land, to share his seat and sit there.
And he also scattered [flowers] over the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has long since entered parinirvāṇa and now dwells within the jeweled stūpa to bear witness to the Dharma together with them,
as well as over all the great bodhisattvas and the bodhisattvas present in the assemblies from other directions and this land.

As well as the fourfold assembly—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen present in the gathering who were listening to the Dharma—it rained down fine powders of sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses. First, the scattering of precious flowers symbolized their true practice;
this presentation of fragrant offerings symbolized their true virtue.
In the midst of the void, celestial drums resounded of their own accord with a profound and far-reaching sound. The "void" signifies the emptiness of the *dharmatā*;
the "celestial drums sounding spontaneously" signifies the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) verses spoken without being asked;
and the "exquisite Brahma-voice" signifies that its meaning is profound and far-reaching.

Furthermore, a thousand kinds of celestial garments rained down. These scattered celestial garments, numbering approximately a thousand, symbolize the robes of patience born of the principle of non-arising.
Various necklaces hung down; these hanging necklaces symbolize being adorned with the jewels of wisdom.
The pearl necklace represents the pearls of oysters and conchs, which are a metaphor for limited wisdom.
The maṇi-jewel necklace represents the great precious jewel, symbolizing great wisdom.
The wish-fulfilling jewel necklace—the king of wish-fulfilling jewels—is able to produce all manner of rare treasures, representing...
The Middle Way—the Buddha’s wisdom, the perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind—pervades the nine directions.
To pervade the nine directions means that it descends from the heavens to fill the four cardinal points, the four intermediate directions, and the center;
this signifies that the six classes of ordinary beings and the three types of sages together adorn the fruit of Buddhahood.
Various precious incense burners burn priceless incense. The burner is the treasure of the mind, and the incense is the resonance of the Way;
cultivating virtue through wisdom is called "burning incense.
Spontaneously reaching everywhere, it makes offerings to the great assembly. Since a single thought-moment pervades all, a single speck of dust likewise pervades all; this arises from sincerity.

Because the mind is not initially produced by deliberate effort, it is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*). Because that mind is universal, there is no place where it is deficient; thus it is said to be "all-pervasive.
This refers to the mind of the ten dharma-realms; when it perfumes evil to transform it into good, this is termed "making offerings."
Above each and every Buddha, and above each and every realization of the nature of goodness, there are bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies.
These bodhisattvas are the very minds that practice the causal factors; their adherence to the Dharma as adornment is what is called "banners and canopies."
Ascending in succession, they reach the Brahma Heaven. By ascending in order, free from desire and pure, they arrive at the realm of non-desire, which is called the Brahma Heaven.
These Bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, manifest their wisdom-light through light in the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven). Their light of wisdom shines forth.

Manifesting now under the name Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣavatī*), she sings immeasurable verses to praise the Buddhas. This offering of sublime song and praise for the Buddhas is not something heard by the ear;
it must be seen with the eye alone.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses.
Having seen this, Maitreya Bodhisattva—the foremost of the great assembly—was filled with joy and emerged from the multitude to praise the Buddha.
The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma never heard before. This Dharma is so rare that since the Buddha attained enlightenment, it has never been heard or spoken of.
The World-Honored One possesses great power; his lifespan is immeasurable. The World-Honored One possesses great wisdom and supernormal powers. His life—
Their lifespan is long and immeasurable.

Among the countless sons of the Buddha, those in this assembly who have heard the World-Honored One’s detailed explanation of the attainment of the Dharma have their bodies filled with joy; having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One...
As thus distinguished, the members of the assembly attained the benefits of the Dharma and experienced great joy that filled their bodies;
some dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, while others ascended to the stage of non-retrogression.
Some attain dhāraṇīs and enter the gate of total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*);
some possess unimpeded eloquence, attaining the joy of unobstructed speech that flows inexhaustibly;
they master the *daśakoṭī-parivarta-dhāraṇī* and attain the *koṭī-nayuta-parivarta-dhāraṇī*.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm, each capable of turning the wheel of Dharma of non-retrogression,
as previously described. Again,
there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a medium trichiliocosm, each capable of turning the wheel of pure Dharma.
As before, there are further bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, each of whom will attain the path of Buddhahood after eight remaining births. As before.

Furthermore, there are four, three, two, and one such sets of four-continent worlds; that is to say, four sets of four-continent worlds, three sets of four-continent worlds, two sets of four-continent worlds, and one set of four-continent worlds.

Bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms attain Buddhahood according to their respective numbers of births. "According to their numbers" means that some undergo four births, some three, or some two, gradually practicing and realizing the path before finally attaining Buddhahood.
Or there may be bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world-system, who have but one birth remaining;
even these bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment have but one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge and shall achieve the realization of the knowledge of all modes.
Such sentient beings, as well as the aforementioned assemblies,
having heard that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, and having heard the Buddha reveal that his life span is long and far-reaching,
attain immeasurable, untainted, and pure karmic fruits. As previously described, these various bodhisattvas are each distinguished.
Regarding the fruits of wisdom attained by each,
there were further sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds, and those in eight great chiliocosms, who, upon hearing the Buddha speak of his lifespan,
all resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way; and upon hearing the Buddha’s revelation that the Dharma-lifespan is long and far-reaching, they all likewise did so.
Having resolved to attain the Bodhi-mind with the aspiration to become like the Buddha, the World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable Dharmas.
The Buddha has spoken of the inconceivable lifespan, which brings vast benefit as boundless as space; its great utility is as limitless as the void.
It rained mandārava and mahāmandārava flowers. All the devas rejoiced as they rained down blossoms from the sky.

Śakra and Brahmā came from as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; Śakra and Brahmā kings, numbering like the sands of the Ganges, came to this Sahā world from immeasurable lands.
Fine powders of sandalwood and aloeswood fell in profusion and in disarray.

A rain of exquisite fragrances from fine powders of sandalwood and aloeswood drifted down from the sky, like birds flying through the air to descend and scatter offerings before the Buddhas; it was as if birds were descending from the heavens to present their offerings.
The many Buddhas, such as Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni, were dispersed.

In the midst of the void, celestial drums spontaneously produced wondrous sounds; within the void, the celestial drums resonated with exquisite tones of their own accord, without being struck by anyone.
Tens of millions of billions of celestial garments descended, swirling down from above. Tens of millions of billions of exquisite heavenly robes descended, spinning through the void.
Myriad precious incense burners burned priceless incense; within those jeweled burners, various sublime fragrances were being consumed.
Spontaneously and universally, they made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones. Their sublime voices pervaded the entire Dharma-realm, making offerings to all the World-Honored Ones.
As for the assembly of great Bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies of the seven treasures—those who hold the banners and canopies of the seven treasures refers to:
It manifests the adornment of the seven merits of goodness.
It is high and sublime in ten trillion ways; it is lofty, excellent, and beautiful in ten trillion ways.
It ascends successively to the Brahma Heaven; from its own level, it proceeds in succession up to the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha—pervading before each and every Buddha—precious banners are suspended with superior pennants;
upon these precious banners, one contemplates the most excellent and wondrous pennants.
They also sang praises of the Tathāgatas with ten million verses. The Bodhisattvas likewise praised the Buddhas with verses.
Such various matters as these had never occurred before; such excellent events as these had never occurred before.

Hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, all were filled with joy. Hearing that the Buddha’s life is long and knowing the excellence of the Buddha’s virtues, the hearts of the entire great assembly rejoiced.
The Buddha’s name is heard throughout the ten directions, widely benefiting sentient beings; the Buddha’s name is transmitted and heard throughout the ten directions.
They bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
All those endowed with roots of goodness assist the unsurpassed mind; they cause all beings to be fully possessed of roots of goodness, thereby providing support for the mind of the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. After Maitreya Bodhisattva had spoken the preceding verses, the Buddha spoke to him again:
"Ajita, there may be sentient beings who hear that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, being incalculable."
Even down to being able to give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding, or at the very least giving rise to a single thought of a mind of faith and understanding,
the merit obtained is without limit. If the merit of a single thought of faith is limitless, how much more so for one who possesses a complete and profound mind of faith and understanding?
If there are good men or good women who, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and if there are good men or good women who, for the sake of seeking the Way,
practice the five *pāramitās* for eighty quadrillion *nayuta* kalpas— eighty quadrillion being...
The eight consciousnesses and five pāramitās, excluding Prajñāpāramitā,
consist of Dānapāramitā— here translated as "generosity" (bùshī)—
and Śīlapāramitā— here translated as "ethical discipline" (chíjiè).
Kṣānti-pāramitā; this is translated as "patience" (renunciation of anger).
Vīrya-pāramitā; this is translated as "diligence. Dhyāna-pāramitā;
this is translated as "entering meditative concentration."
With the exception of the *prajñāpāramitā*. This [text] refers to "wisdom" (*prajñā*) as true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), the mother of all Buddhas;
because this scripture enumerates and compares the merits of faith and understanding, it excludes the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By these merits— that is, by the merits obtained through these five perfections—
compared with the former merit, this merit of a single moment of faith and understanding does not equal even one part in a hundred,
one part in a thousand, or one part in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions; it does not even reach a fraction of one percent.
Whether one compares ten million to one, or even a hundred thousand to one, it does not equal even a ten-thousandth part, nor a hundred-millionth part; indeed,
it is beyond all calculation and analogy, such that no mathematician could calculate it through any possible metaphor.
It cannot be known through analogies.
If a son or daughter of good family possesses such merit, or possesses such merit of faith and understanding.
It is impossible that one would fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is easy for those without faith to fall away from the Path; however, it is impossible that one who possesses this faith would give rise to regression regarding *bodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom—
should there be anyone who seeks the Buddha’s wisdom—
and practices the five *pāramitās* for eighty million *nayuta* kalpas, passing through many such kalpas..."
He practiced the five perfections.
Throughout these kalpas, he made offerings of alms to the Buddhas, the disciples of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas;
for many kalpas, he made offerings to the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas.
Rare and extraordinary foods and drinks; exquisite delicacies.
Superior garments and bedding; "superior garments" refers to precious robes, and "bedding" refers to couches and mattresses.
A sandalwood vihāra; he constructed a vihāra using sandalwood to serve as a monastic dwelling.
Adorned with gardens and groves, he gives these as superior realms adorned with gardens and groves.
Such acts of giving— namely food, drink, clothing, and bedding— are practiced through the four requisites.
All varieties were exquisite; whatever various objects were offered were refined and subtle in their intention.
This continued throughout all these kalpas—eighty quadrillion nayutas of kalpas.
They dedicate this toward the Buddha-way; they turn the merit of this giving toward the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, if they maintain the prohibitive precepts—maintaining the pure precepts of the Buddha, which are pure, without deficiency or leakage—their conduct of morality is pure, being without defect or leakage.

Seeking the unsurpassed path is praised by all Buddhas; seeking the practice praised by the Buddhas on the true path, one further practices patience and abides in the stage of gentleness, being able to exercise patience and dwell in the state of pliancy.
Even if various evils are directed toward them, their minds do not waver. Or, even if various evils descend upon their bodies, they remain peaceful and patient, never wavering at all.
Those who have attained the Dharma harbor overweening pride; those who have practiced and attained the realization of the Dharma remain inwardly [steadfast].
Conceited with the pride of self-attainment, they treat him with such contempt and affliction;
yet he is able to endure it. Though treated with such contempt and affliction by these people, he is likewise able to accept it with peaceful composure.
Furthermore, if one exerts diligent effort and maintains constant firmness in resolve; if there is someone who practices diligent effort and whose vows and right mindfulness are always firm,
remaining single-minded and untiring throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, constantly thus single-minded throughout the passage of long kalpas—
He was diligent and never indolent.

Furthermore, for countless eons he dwelt in secluded places; moreover, throughout many kalpas in empty and quiet locations, whether sitting or walking, or sometimes practicing seated meditation and walking meditation.
"Except for sleep, one should always restrain the mind. This means that, except during the time of sleep, one should constantly restrain the mind.

For this reason, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Because of these causes and conditions of seclusion and the restraint of tranquility, one is able to generate the power of various meditative concentrations.

For eighty billion *koṭi* kalpas, he dwelt with an undisturbed mind. Abiding in the peaceful mind of the eighth consciousness, he maintained this single-minded merit and vow to seek the unsurpassed path.
Maintaining this single-mindedness, he cultivated the merit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and vowed to seek the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.

"I have attained all-knowledge and exhausted the limits of all meditative concentrations. He says to himself, "I have attained the wisdom of all emptiness and exhausted every boundary of all meditative concentrations.
This person practices these aforementioned merits throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
This refers to the merits of the five perfections mentioned above.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing me speak of the lifespan, and hearing the Tathāgata speak of the long duration of his lifespan, should even for a single thought-moment believe in it, their merit will surpass that [of the former];
the merit obtained through this single thought-moment of faith and understanding is superior.

To practice the five perfections throughout successive kalpas is entirely due to the fact that these five perfections are merit, and merit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); whereas wisdom brings one out of birth and death.
How could this mindfulness of merit ever equal such wisdom?

If a person is entirely free from all doubt and regret, and if a person is entirely devoid of a doubting or regretful mind, then with a profound mind they shall for a moment believe that their merit is such as this.
To believe in the Buddha’s wondrous vehicle and vow to seek the Buddha-way is called the profound mind.
Furthermore, if there is another person who gives rise to great faith for even a moment, the merit they obtain exceeds [the former].
Regarding the five perfections:

those bodhisattvas who have practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas, and those bodhisattvas who have practiced the path for many kalpas, upon hearing my teaching on the lifespan, will be able to believe and accept it;
those of the highest faculties, having long planted roots of goodness, upon hearing it...
Those wise people who are able to believe and accept that the lifespan spoken of by the Buddha is long will receive this sutra upon the crown of their heads.
Such persons as these will receive and uphold this scripture upon the crown of their heads, just as all wise people described above, having heard this sutra,
shall receive and maintain it with reverence.
May I, in the future, live a long life to deliver sentient beings.

May I, in future ages, attain a long and enduring lifespan to liberate sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King of the Śākyas, does today; even as the Śākya World-Honored One does today.
The unsurpassed Dharma King among the Śākyas,

who roars the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment, teaches the Dharma with fearlessness; within the site of enlightenment, he utters the lion’s roar and preaches the Dharma for the assembly without any dread.
"In future ages, we shall be respected by all; when we attain the realization of the Way in the future, we shall be respected by all beings.
When seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he spoke likewise regarding his lifespan; even when seated at the site of enlightenment, he spoke of the measure of his lifespan.
Just as with Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, today,
if there is one who possesses a profound mind that is pure and upright; if there is one who possesses a profound mind that is pure, untainted,
and whose heart is upright.
Those who are widely learned and able to maintain [the teachings] in their entirety, who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning;

those whose hearing and vision are vast and who can recall and maintain them all, understanding the Buddha’s words well according to the meaning of the sūtras—such people as these have no doubt regarding this. Such people as these are then deeply [established] in this sūtra.
Their minds will have faith and understanding, free from doubt.

Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, they will understand the purport of his words; they will be well able to comprehend the meaning and intent of his speech.
The merit obtained by such a person is without limit; their benefit is profound.

They are able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata. As clarified in the sutra, through faith and understanding of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one then gives rise to unsurpassed wisdom.
How much more so for one who hears this sutra extensively! The preceding text merely states that the merit of even a single thought of faith and understanding is such;
it goes without saying that the benefit of hearing it extensively is even more superior.
Whether by teaching others so that they hear it, or by instructing others so that they may hear it;
whether by upholding it oneself, personally receiving and maintaining it,
or by teaching others to uphold it, or by otherwise transforming others so that they receive and maintain it.
Whether one writes it oneself with one's own hand,
or instructs another to write it, or instructs others to transcribe this sutra;
or whether one makes offerings to the scroll of the sutra with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, ghee lamps, and flowers.
Incense represents virtue; necklaces and other ornaments are used to adorn the Dharma-body. A lamp that continues its light represents the radiance of wisdom.
By not departing from material offerings, one manifests the true and eternal.

The merit of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Through the mind, one initiates practice; through practice, [one realizes the fruit].
Practicing and entering the Way can give rise to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
Ajita, if good sons or good daughters hear me speak of the long duration of my life-span, or hear the World-Honored One speak of the long duration of the Buddha’s life-span.
With a profound mind of faith and understanding, and with a pure mind, one gives rise to deep faith and understanding;
this constitutes seeing the Buddha constantly on Vulture Peak. This sutra is the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
to understand this sutra is to see the Buddha constantly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, never having vanished.

He preached the Dharma surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. This sutra records in full detail how the various great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, with deep-seated faith and understanding, were no different from having heard it directly from the Buddha’s own mouth;
thus one sees the great multitude surrounding him all at once.
Furthermore, he saw that the ground of this Sahā world was made of lapis lazuli, level and even.

Because the sutras discourse on the true nature (*dharmatā*), whose essence is translucent and pure, it is like lapis lazuli; because the mind is free from divergent thoughts, it is level and even, utterly devoid of difficulty or peril—hence it is called "level and even."
The eight paths are demarcated by Jāmbūnada gold. This firm and correct Dharma is called the "Golden Rope," and the gold produced from the Jāmbūnada River is of the most supreme color.
Using gold as ropes, the Eightfold Noble Path is divided so that its boundaries may be known;
when one perceives these Eightfold Paths, it is called "seeing the essence of the Dharma."
Rows of jewel trees are arranged; these jewel trees, which are the successive manifestations of the King of Bodhi-vows, are called "rows.

All the terraces and towers are entirely made of jewels; the various features of these terraces and towers are metaphors for the successive stages of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Its tiers are majestic, brilliant, and beautiful to behold; because it is accumulated by all that is wholesome, it is named "Jeweled Achievement.
The assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell within it. Since all the great bodhisattvas cultivate the factors of the path, the great multitude likewise dwells therein.
If there is anyone who can contemplate in this way—if there is anyone who can observe with such discernment—one should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.
This is the reason for attaining the vision of the adornments of the true fruition; therefore, it is called the mark of profound faith and understanding.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, during the period of the turbid world following his passing,

if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy— meaning that upon hearing the sutra, one neither slanders it nor fails to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
One should know that this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding; these are also called the marks of profound faith.
How much more so for those who read, recite, and uphold [this teaching], and how much more so for those who are able to read, recite, and uphold it!
Such a person is one who bears the Tathāgata upon their crown. The Sūtra reveals that the Buddha’s wisdom and the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata are received upon the crown;
thus, to receive this Dharma is called "bearing the Tathāgata.
Ajita, these good men and good women need not build stūpas or temples for my sake. There is...
Wherever this sutra resides, that place is itself a stupa; therefore, there is no need to construct another stupa.
Furthermore, one should build monasteries and provide the four requisites to support the Sangha.

If every thought is virtuous and beyond calculation, and the mind is in accord with the Dharma such that the mind and the Dharma are non-dual, this is called the Sangha. To serve them with a profound heart of reverence is true worship.
Therefore, it is unnecessary to further construct monasteries or provide the fourfold requisites for the Sangha.
Why is this? It is because these good men and good women who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra [attain these benefits].
If good men or women read and uphold this sutra, it is as if they have already erected a stupa;
they have already constructed a precious stupa for the Buddha and established monasteries to make offerings to the Sangha.
Having been revealed and made manifest, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas are of one and the same reality.
The roots of the Path, whether great or small, all abide therein; this is the Sangha’s dwelling place. To cultivate reverence in every thought-moment is to make offerings to the Sangha.
This is equivalent to erecting a stupa of the seven treasures for the Buddha’s relics. This scripture is the Dharma-body and is called the Buddha’s relics; it is upon this that one relies.
By practicing the cultivation of the seven wholesome dharmas as prescribed in the sutras, one establishes a stupa for the śarīra made of the seven treasures.

It is high and vast, gradually diminishing in size up to the Brahma-heaven; it is called "high" because it extends vertically through the three periods of time, and "vast" because it pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions.

As it becomes increasingly expansive and increasingly lofty, becoming ever more refined and sublime, it is called "gradually diminishing"; it reaches its ultimate limit at the Fundamental Heaven (Mūla-deva).
The wondrous principle of true purity is named "Reaching the Brahma Heaven.

Hanging various banners and canopies along with many jeweled bells: the fluttering and waving are named "banners," the protective covering is named "canopies," and the insentient preaching of the Dharma is called "jeweled bells."
Flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense: flowers represent the virtuous mind; incense represents virtuous merit;
necklaces represent the exquisite adornment of patience; powdered incense represents subtle conduct; ointments represent the refinement of the body’s ornaments to make them sublime;
and burning incense represents the process of fumigation that transforms evil into good.
With various drums, musical instruments, flutes, pipes, and *konghou* lutes, he constantly performs harmonious and joyful music day and night;
his body is itself a musical instrument and his speech is the sound of music, causing all who hear it to find delight in their ears and clarity in their minds.
Performing various dances and using the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to incite all beings like a place of entertainment in order to entice them;
singing hymns of praise with wondrous sounds; and reciting the words of the Buddha with the mind of a Buddha—this is called "wondrous sound" (*svara*).
To chant and sing *brahman* hymns in praise of the Buddha’s Dharma-body is called "extolling his virtues.
