This constitutes having already performed such offerings for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
All matters from the distant past, through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, are fully proclaimed and revealed within this sutra; reciting it even once is itself a vast journey.
After making offerings to the buddha-fields for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas,
Ajita, if one hears this sutra after my parinirvāṇa— having heard this Lotus Sutra after my parinirvāṇa.

If there are those who can receive and uphold [this teaching], whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it—where one's own action and instructing others are equal in merit—then this constitutes the construction of a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma); thus, to write and uphold it is itself the founding of a monastery.
With red sandalwood— which is to say, red bone—
one constructs various halls, which represent the body.
The thirty-two [features] represent the physical marks of the body.
It is eight *tāla* trees high; its majestic stature of eight feet refers to the measurement of the body itself.
If one calculates according to physical dimensions, one *tāla* tree is seven feet long, totaling over five *zhang*.

Tall, vast, majestic, and beautiful; within a single body, it encompasses the workings of creation, rising vertically and extending horizontally to equal the expanse of space, with all the marks and signs of excellence fully and perfectly adorned.

One hundred thousand bhikṣus reside therein. The nature of awakening is called the Buddha; the rules of conduct are called the Dharma; the non-dual harmony of the Buddha and the Dharma is called the Saṅgha.
One hundred thousand collections of right mindfulness gathered within a single body are termed "residing therein."
Gardens and bathing pools: the gardens are the groves of the seven factors of enlightenment, and the precepts are called the pool in which the assembly of noble ones bathe.
Walking paths and meditation caves: treading upon them all day long is called "walking," while remaining constantly tranquil while moving is called "meditation."
The cave;
clothing and food and drink: gentleness and patience are called clothing, while the joy of dharma and the delight in meditation are called food and drink.
Regarding bedding and medicinal decoctions: the seat of the Dharma-emptiness is called "bedding," and the treatment of the sickness of the mind is called "medicinal decoction.
All instruments of pleasure are fully contained therein; various precious musical sounds delight the eyes and gladden the heart, along with all other forms of enjoyment.
All things are fully contained within it.
Thus, there are hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of such monastic dwellings, halls, and pavilions, their number being immeasurable.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are arrayed in successive layers, which are called "pavilions. A single thought-moment and a single practice constitute one location, which is termed "Juo" (If).

Gan. By means of this, one makes an offering to me in person. As stated in the sūtras, to initiate practice based upon this and to act in accordance with the Buddha’s words is called making an offering to the Buddha.
And as for the community of bhikṣus, to abide in wholesome mindfulness through the three types of action in accordance with the Dharma is called making offerings to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, I say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—this is why the Buddha spoke of the period after his passing.
If one upholds, recites, and reads it for oneself, and explains it to others— reading and reciting the sūtras constitutes self-benefit,
while explaining them to others constitutes benefit for others—
if one writes it oneself or instructs others to write it, writing it oneself or instructing others to transcribe the sūtras is beneficial for both seeing and hearing.
Therefore, the merit is great.
By making offerings to the sutra scrolls— through various forms of worship such as flowers, incense, banners, and canopies— one is able to see the Buddha because of this reverence for the Dharma.
There is no need to further erect stupas and temples or construct monasteries to provide offerings to the Sangha.
To single-mindedly abide in the Way and lead one’s own conduct into practice is itself the offering of Dharma; it does not reside in external conditions.
How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom;
and how much more so for one who can uphold the sutra while simultaneously practicing the six perfections with a single mind—that is, concentration and wisdom, which is prajñā.
Its virtue is most supreme, immeasurable, and boundless. Cultivating internal contemplation while supported externally by ritual acts, the merit obtained is incalculable.
It is, for example, like space—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—which is immeasurable and boundless; space is vast.
It is great, immeasurable, without beginning or end, and its limits are unknown;
the merit of this person is likewise thus—immeasurable, boundless, and equal to empty space.
One swiftly attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Because one cultivates the contemplation of principles, one accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
because one cultivates the practice of phenomena, it is called the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*). Since the principles and phenomena are thus, one swiftly attains all-encompassing wisdom.
If a person reads, recites, upholds, and explains this sutra to others, whether copying it themselves or instructing others to copy it—
whereas previously they only upheld the sutra, now they explain it to others as well as write it down.
Furthermore, they are able to erect stupas and construct monasteries;

moreover, they are skillfully able to build stupas and temples, making offerings to and praising the assembly of śrāvaka monks, and making offerings to the assembly of monks while praising their sutras.
Furthermore, one praises the merit of the Bodhisattva with hundreds of thousands of millions of methods of praise.
The Bodhisattva is indeed the Sangha of the Mahāyāna; such praise must accord with reality, praising what is worthy of praise, for it can generate merit.
If one were to praise someone who is not truly such a person, one would not even avoid sin, let alone obtain blessings.
Furthermore, to explain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others through various causes and conditions according to its meaning is the practice of giving;
by means of these various causes and conditions, one explains the principles of this sūtra for other sentient beings according to their significance. This is the perfection of giving.
Furthermore, one is able to purify the observance of precepts; this is the practice of the noble precepts (*śīla-ārya-caryā*).
One dwells together with those who are gentle, practicing patience and freedom from anger; this is the practice of patience (*kṣānti-caryā*).
With firm resolve and mindfulness, one always values sitting in meditation to attain various profound concentrations;
with firm aspiration, one constantly cultivates refined meditation to attain the profound and wondrous concentrations of the bodhisattvas—this is the practice of meditative concentration.

Vigor is the courageous gathering of all wholesome dharmas; it is the constant, diligent application of vigor and great strength to cultivate and collect the mind through all wholesome dharmas—this is the practice of vigor.
Those of sharp faculties and wisdom skillfully respond to questions and challenges. Because their faculties are sharp, their wisdom is lofty and brilliant;
whatever is asked, they respond with joy, faith, and submission, following along—this is called "skillful response," which is the practice of prajñā.
Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra;
or if, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sons or daughters of good family who propagate this sutra.
Furthermore, there are such virtuous merits as these: namely, in addition to propagating the sūtras, they practice the six perfections and cultivate the aforementioned various virtuous merits.

It should be known that such a person has already set out for the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it should be known that this is the bodhisattva practice of propagating the sūtras and cultivating merit.

When a person has already headed toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, being not far from the Buddha and having drawn near to awakening, they sit beneath the tree of enlightenment.
At all times their mind remains constantly upon the Path without ever wavering; this is called [the state of]...
The great bodhicitta generated by a seated Bodhisattva is called the Tree of Enlightenment (*bodhivṛkṣa*).
Wherever this good man or good woman sits, stands, or walks— to that place, which has been their habitual resort throughout their lives— [the Buddha will come].
In this regard, a stūpa should be erected. Wherever this sūtra exists, there is the Buddha; therefore, a stūpa should be erected.
All devas and humans should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha. To respectfully uphold and expound [this teaching] is to revere the Dharma;
and one who reveres the Dharma knows that the Buddha exists. Because of faith in the Buddha, one is liberated from birth and death; therefore, let them be respectful.
Such a person is like a stūpa of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, one can uphold this sūtra; if, after the Buddha’s extinction, one can maintain this sūtra."
The merit of such a person is immeasurable, as has been described above. Having approached the site of enlightenment, they shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree;
this constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings—offering to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha in their entirety.
To erect a stūpa for the *śarīra* and adorn it with the seven treasures—upholding this sūtra is precisely such an erection of a *śarīra*-stūpa;
practicing the sevenfold wholesome conduct is called "adornment with treasures.

Its spire is exceedingly high and broad, gradually tapering until it reaches the Brahma-heaven. Generating the resolve for enlightenment and practicing the path is like the construction of this stūpa, which gradually...
Progressing gradually from a broad base to a fine tip is called "gradually diminishing"; reaching the bliss of nirvana is called the "Brahma Heaven.
Thousands of millions of billions of jeweled bells, moved by the wind, produce wondrous sounds. Expounding all dharmas through these wondrous sounds is like shaking jeweled bells;
when thoughts arise, it is called being "moved by the wind," and when the lips and tongue emit resonance, it is called "producing wondrous sounds."

Furthermore, one may make offerings to this stupa for immeasurable kalpas; yet in a single thought-moment, reverently reciting the name of an ancient Buddha’s sutra is called "making offerings to the Dharma-stupa for immeasurable kalpas. The jeweled necklace represents the bright pearl of wisdom; the robe represents patience; and the music represents the joy of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the fragrant oil and ghee lamps constantly illuminate all around. The oil is the water of wisdom and the lamp is the light of insight;
that which shines everywhere without exception is called "surrounding illumination."
One who is able to uphold this sutra during the evil age of the final dharma has, after my parinirvāṇa,
already provided all the aforementioned offerings; to be able to uphold this sutra is itself to have fully provided all those offerings.
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present. This sutra remaining in the world is no different from the Buddha himself.

To construct a monastery for offerings using ox-head sandalwood and to bear the Dharma upon one’s person while maintaining right mindfulness is what is meant by "building a temple with sandalwood to provide for the Sangha."

The hall was thirty-two [feet] high and eight *tāla* trees in height; the Buddha manifesting his body within the hall possessed the thirty-two marks and secondary characteristics of a Great Man, being eight feet tall, perfectly full, upright, and straight like a *tāla* tree.
The finest delicacies and exquisite garments, along with beds and couches, are all fully provided. The food of the joy of Dharma is called the finest delicacy;
the garment of forbearance is called the exquisite robe; and the seat of the emptiness of phenomena is the throne—walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one is always within it.
The abodes of hundreds of thousands of beings; the six perfections and the myriad practices are the dwelling places of all bodhisattvas.

Therein are gardens, groves, various bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves. They sit beneath the forest of the seven factors of enlightenment, bathe in the pool of the eight virtues, walk upon the right path, and rest upon the bed of cessation.
All things are adorned and excellent; all manner of enjoyments are entirely adorned and excellent.

If there are those with a mind of faith and understanding who receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe [this], and who with a mind of faith and understanding read, recite, transcribe, and uphold it.
Furthermore, if one teaches others to write [the scriptures] or to make offerings to the scrolls, or teaches others to copy them and offer flowers,
incense, and powdered incense to the scrolls— this constitutes making offerings to the Dharma-jewel through form and fragrance.
With *sumana* and *campaka* flowers—the *sumana*, here translated as "pleasing to the mind," being yellowish-white with an exquisite fragrance;
and the *campaka*, here translated as "golden flower," having fine petals and a fragrant scent.
*Atimuktaka* refers to the sesame plant; its flowers are red, its leaves are green, and its seeds can be made into oil.
One should constantly burn *dhūpa* (incense); *dhūpa* is fragrant grass, and its seeds can be made into oil—meaning one uses this fragrant oil to light lamps as an offering.
One who makes such offerings attains immeasurable merit. By making such offerings to this sutra, one gains infinite blessings.
Just as space is boundless, so too is that merit. Just as the great void has no limits, so too is the merit of the person who offers this sutra.
How much more so for one who upholds this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, maintaining the precepts, enduring patience, and delighting in meditative concentration;
the merit of merely upholding the sutra is already immeasurable, let alone for one who also cultivates the practice of the six perfections.
Being without anger and without harsh speech; having no wrath in the mind and no evil words in the mouth.
Paying respect to stupas and shrines; when seeing a stupa or shrine, giving rise to a heart of reverence.

He humbles himself before all bhikṣus, remaining far removed from a sense of self-exaltation. Upon seeing a bhikṣu, he bows with humble reverence, remaining far removed from a mind of self-importance and arrogance.
He constantly contemplates wisdom; when questioned or challenged, he does not become angry, but explains in accordance with the truth. His mind is ever-contemplative.
Possessing profound wisdom, when faced with those who come to challenge or question one, they do not give rise to anger, but instead provide explanations in accordance with their intentions.
If one can practice this, the merit thereof is immeasurable; if one can practice such conduct in accordance with the Dharma, the blessings thereof are immeasurable.
If one sees such a Dharma-preacher who has accomplished these virtues, or if one sees such a teacher who propagates the sutra and has accomplished the various wholesome merits mentioned above,
one should scatter celestial flowers and cover their body with celestial robes; one should scatter upon them the precious flowers of the heavens.
He covered his body with celestial precious robes;

he performed the head-to-feet prostration, generating a mind that regarded him as a Buddha. He performed the head-to-feet prostration of taking refuge, generating a mind of reverence as if regarding him as a solid Buddha.
Furthermore, one should form this thought: "Before long, he will proceed to the site of enlightenment. Moreover, one should form this thought within the mind:
"This person will, before long, go forth to the site of enlightenment and sit beneath the precious tree."

Having attained the untainted and unconditioned state, they bring vast benefit to all devas and humans; they shall attain the fruit of the untainted and unconditioned, extensively benefiting all beings among devas and humans.
Whether in their place of residence, while walking, or while sitting or lying down—even when reciting a single verse—the Dharma-preacher who propagates it...
Wherever one walks, stands, sits, or lies down, even at the place where a single verse of a sutra was spoken, one should erect a stupa there,
adorning it so that it is exquisite and making various offerings to it. In such locations, one should erect a stupa,
decorating and embellishing it until it is most magnificent, and worship the Dharma-stupa with various kinds of offerings.

The Son of the Buddha dwelling in this stage is the very enjoyment of the Buddhas. In future generations, the Son of the Buddha who dwells in this ground of mind will likewise obtain the enjoyment of the Buddhas.
Constantly remaining therein, whether walking, sitting, or lying down—throughout the four modes of deportment of body: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—he remains [in that state].
Treading upon the path within the place of enlightenment.
From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen, "The Merit of Rejoicing," Maitreya Bodhisattva,
having heard from the preceding chapter the World-Honored One’s teaching on receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, and transcribing [the sutra]...
The merit of transcribing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is immeasurable and surpasses that of constructing stupas, building monasteries, or making offerings to the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, it is heard that if one can concurrently practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and engage in correct cultivation, the merit is even more superior. Therefore, [the questioner] asks the Tathāgata:
"If there are beginners who, upon hearing this sūtra, are able to merely rejoice in it (*anumodanā*), how much merit will such persons obtain?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha. Since Maitreya was the guiding master, he spoke to the Buddha regarding what ought to be asked.
Blessed One, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and if those sons and daughters of good family,
upon hearing this sublime sūtra,
give rise to faith in the Dharma and cultivate a mind of sympathetic joy;
How much merit will be obtained? To what extent does that merit amount?
Thus, having first expressed his intention, he asks in verse:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One," meaning after the passing away of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Should there be anyone who hears this sutra— should there be anyone who hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—
and is able to rejoice in it, or is able to give rise to even a single thought of sympathetic joy;
"How much merit will they obtain? What kind of karmic reward for their merit will these people receive?
At that time, the Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: "These two lines of text were recounted by Ānanda."
Ajita, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, ordained monastics who have received the full precepts,
or upāsakas and upāsikās, lay men and women who receive and uphold the five precepts and the eight precepts;
As for other wise persons: apart from the four types mentioned above, there are those who do not receive the precepts but possess wisdom and understanding.
Whether they be old or young, the essential requirement for entering the Path is awakening and understanding; this applies regardless of age.
Having heard this sutra and rejoiced in it, having heard this sutra and given rise to sympathetic joy, they depart from the assembly;
having departed from the assembly, they go to other places;
having reached those other locations.
Whether in a monastic dwelling or within a monastery;
whether in a secluded place or a quiet location;
whether in the streets and alleys of a city, or indeed within those very streets and alleys.
Villages and fields; places where people gather and settle, as well as gardens and lands—just as they have been heard, and as they were heard at that particular assembly according to the Dharma.
For the sake of one's parents, kinsmen, and relatives— namely, one's biological parents, family members, and kin;
as well as virtuous friends and spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)— those who delight in goodness and are one's regular associates—
one should expound the teaching according to one's capacity, preaching to others in accordance with the power of one's own wisdom.
When these people have heard it, they rejoice; when others hear it, they likewise all rejoice.
They further propagate the teaching, and thus, as they have heard it, they pass it on to one another in succession.
Having heard it, other people likewise rejoice and teach it in turn; others who hear these teachings further transmit them to others according to their ability.
In this manner, it is passed down in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person. Thus, through this sequential dissemination, one person transmits it to another.
Ānanda, as for the merit of the fifty-first good man or good woman who rejoices— this refers specifically to the very last person among those fifty,
who merely hears of the rejoicing but has not yet been able to teach it to others.
I shall now speak of this; you should listen well. The Buddha, wishing to reveal the merit of rejoicing belonging to those who are the very last of his followers, spoke thus to Maitreya:
"Suppose there were four hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, used as a mere illustration."
Sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth—namely, those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation.
As for the six destinies: devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; these six follow their respective actions and each proceed along its own path.

As for the four modes of birth: birth from eggs and birth from wombs are the two that are easy to understand. [Birth from] moisture and birth by transformation are so named because they arise from vapor and dampness, respectively, according to their true nature.
It is said that moisture-born beings include insects, ants, and the like; those that undergo metamorphosis and fly are called transformation-born (*upapāduka*).
If there is form, then among the six realms of existence, all except for the Formless Realm possess form and color.
"Formless" means that in the formless realm there are only four aggregates: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Possessing perception" means that—with the exception of those in the cycle of delusion and the Heaven of No-Perception—all others possess perception.

Non-conception (*asaṃjñā*). Just as when one enters meditative absorption in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), mental activity ceases because of the absence of worldly delusions and inverted views;
thus the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, and is called "non-conception."

It is not "having perception. When worldly appearances are mutually deceptive and inverted, leading to confused perceptions—such as the *yīchóng* (a type of insect) and the *wéng* (a wasp), which form a different substance from one another—the *mínglíng* (the caterpillar) originally lacks the perception that it is a *guǒluó* (the wasp). This is called "not having perception."
It is not that they lack consciousness. For example, creatures such as the earth-owl (kukkuta) attach clods of earth to serve as their offspring;

due to this perverted attachment to insentient objects, they produce what they perceive to be conscious children, yet once these are fully formed, they instead harm their own parents—thus they are called "not lacking consciousness."
Footless: such as snakes, earthworms, and others who are entirely without feet.
Biped: all classes of sentient beings who have two feet.
Quadruped: such as various animals that have four feet.
Many-footed: this category is not uniform and encompasses all those with multiple feet.
Such beings as these are included within the count of sentient beings—that is, among the ten classes of beings within the aforementioned six realms.
There are those who seek merit, and there are those who desire to obtain the retribution of merit;
according to their desires for articles of enjoyment, he provides them all, and according to what they delight in, he gives it all to them.

To each and every sentient being, he gives as much gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and amber as would fill Jambudvīpa— that is, as would fill this continent of South Jambudvīpa. The meaning of these seven treasures is as explained in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Various exquisite treasures, articles for play and enjoyment,
as well as elephants, horses, and carriages— vehicles for transport— and palaces, towers,
and pavilions made of the seven precious gems, which are their dwelling places.
This great donor practiced such giving for a full eighty years. These "eighty years" refers to practicing giving based on the eight consciousnesses of the out-flowing realm (*sāsrava*).
He then formed this thought: "I have already bestowed upon sentient beings all manner of articles for their enjoyment, according to their every desire. Following that—
Whatever the mind and heart desired, he granted it all to them.

Yet these sentient beings were all already aged; that is to say, those who received the gifts were all aged, their years exceeding eighty, their hair white and their faces wrinkled, with death not far off. The signs of decay had appeared before them, and the time of death was imminent.
"Having arrived,
I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. Thinking thus, he further resolved to transform them through the Buddha-dharma,
and immediately gathered the assembly of sentient beings who had been offered to him.
He proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them. He expounded and disseminated it, using the Dharma to transform, benefit, and bring joy.
At that moment, they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. This is translated as "Stream-enterer," meaning one who has first ascended to the fruit of the Path; the first stream-entry.
Ascending to the fruits of the Path, one joins the ranks of the noble ones.

Regarding the stage of *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner): this is translated as "One who returns once. Having realized the second fruit, one returns to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) one more time to undergo birth, thereby repaying past karmic debts.

The path of the *anāgāmin* (Non-returner). This is translated as "not returning. Having realized the third fruit and abiding in the fourth dhyāna, one no longer returns to take birth in the desire realm.

The path of the *arhat* (Worthy One). This is translated as "one beyond training. Having severed the delusions of views and thought, one realizes entry into the fourth fruit; the holy life has been lived.
The Perfect One has no dharma to learn;
he has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), exhausted all worldly, triple-world conditioned outflows and karmas,

attained mastery over all profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and has skillfully entered the bliss of the various meditative concentrations within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Obstruction is termed mastery.
To possess the eight liberations is to be liberated from the coarse and turn toward the subtle, and to abandon evil and follow the good; these are called the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa).
What do you think? In your view, how would you judge it?
Would the merit obtained by this great donor be much or not? "Not" (no) is a term of uncertainty;
[the question is] whether the resulting benefit and merit would be much or not.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "In response to the World-Honored One’s question, Maitreya has answered him.
'The World-Honored One possesses a vast multitude of human merits, immeasurable and boundless'—this means that his blessings are many."
If a donor merely bestows all manner of articles of pleasure upon sentient beings, their merit is immeasurable;
with the intention of producing much blessings, the merit of merely bestowing articles of pleasure is already boundless.

How much more so, then, to cause them to attain the fruit of arhatship? How much more so, to transform them through the Dharma and cause them to attain the qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—such merits are immeasurable.
The Buddha told Maitreya: "I now speak to you clearly. It is called "clearly" because he intends to explain it openly and manifestively.
This person bestows all manner of articles of pleasure upon four hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds.
These four hundred trillion are a metaphor for the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), wherein each individual sentient being possesses their own distinct world.
To all sentient beings of the six realms, he bestows virtue;
furthermore, he causes them to attain the fruit of arhatship and to realize the four fruits of arhatship.
The merit thus obtained is equal to the merit gained from the aforementioned practice of the two kinds of giving—material and Dharma.

The merit obtained from such giving does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the merit gained by the fiftieth person who hears a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoices in it;
the former is surpassed by the latter to such an extent that it cannot be compared. This reduction continues in sequence until—
Even one part in ten billion would not equal it;
indeed, it cannot be known even through calculation or analogy. This is because the merit of those who rejoice is so superior.
Ajita, in this way, the fiftieth person hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission from one to another.
The merit of rejoicing is already immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*); it is said that such merit is vast and beyond limit.
How much more so for those who first hear [this teaching] within the assembly and rejoice! This refers to the very first person at the Dharma assembly.

If one hears [this teaching] as it is transmitted in succession down to the fiftieth person, their merit will be even more superior—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and beyond comparison.
This is because the merit obtained by each subsequent person is exponentially greater than that of the preceding one; thus it is said to be "even more superior" and "beyond comparison."
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, and desiring to hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
goes to a monastery or a temple— whether sitting or standing— and listens and receives it for even a brief moment; or whether sitting or standing within the temple,
listens and receives it with a sincere mind for even a brief interval.
By virtue of these merits, by virtue of the merit of listening to this sutra with such sincerity,
in whatever place one is reborn after casting off this life,
one shall obtain excellent and sublime elephants, horses, carriages, precious palanquins, and celestial palaces; [one shall obtain] excellent elephants and horses.
Those who possess wealth and nobility use precious palanquins and carriages, which are the implements of kings; when the various devas travel, they likewise have palaces to serve as their vehicles.
Furthermore, if there is a person who sits at a place where the Dharma is being taught, their body is present within the assembly for the Dharma.
Furthermore, if someone else comes and encourages one to sit and listen— encouraging them to join in hearing the sound of the Dharma—
one should either share one's seat to let them sit, or, if there is no place to sit, divide one's own seat to give to them.
The merit of this person, the merit obtained through such exhortation and conversion,

is such that upon changing bodies they will attain the seat of Śakra; after casting off this body, they will be reborn in the heavens and attain the seat occupied by the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
If one sits in the place where Brahmā, King of Gods, sits, one will, upon rebirth, attain birth in the first dhyāna of the form realm and sit in the place of Brahmā,

King of Gods. If one sits in the place where a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King sits— the place where the four types of wheel-turning kings, of gold, silver, copper, and iron, rule over the four continents—
[one will likewise attain such a status].
Ajita, if there is another person who says to someone else, "If there is a place where a Dharma teacher preaches the Dharma, inform others so that they may know:
there is a sutra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; we should go together to hear it," and praises going to hear it together—[this person shall attain merit].

If one immediately accepts their instruction and hears it for even a brief moment, and the person who heard it likewise accepts the instruction and goes together with them to hear the teaching for even an instant,
the merit of that person is the merit obtained by one who exhorts others to listen.
Upon turning back from this life, one shall be born together with the Bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs.

These Bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs have already attained total retention (saṃdhāraṇa) and are Great Beings who have opened the Dharma; thus, being born as their "co-natives" (sahaja) manifests the excellence of the karmic retribution.
They possess sharp faculties and wisdom; their faculties are superior, keen, and acute, and their wisdom is clear and lucid.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they never suffer from muteness. Because they have exhorted, transformed, and instructed others with wholesome teachings when those people were mute due to slandering others, they are free from the affliction of muteness in every lifetime.
The breath does not smell foul. Because the breath is emitted through mindfulness and sound is produced through that breath, the breath is wholesome and therefore does not smell foul.
The tongue is always free from disease; for one who slanders others, the tongue becomes curled and shriveled, but now, because of praising what is good, it remains so.
The mouth is also free from disease. False speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words are great evil karmas;
by truly instructing others to distance themselves from these four transgressions, the mouth is then free from disease.
If one’s speech is unwholesome, the teeth become stained and black; by teaching others what is wholesome, the teeth become pure white.
They are neither yellow nor sparse. That the teeth turn yellow is due to fondness for discussing vulgar matters, which is not their true nature; that they are sparse is caused by emptiness.
If one is truthful and sincere, the teeth will be even and closely set, and they will not be missing. If one speaks improper words to deceive and delude others, the teeth will be missing.
If one’s speech is uneven or crooked, the teeth will be uneven. If one’s speech is not straightforward, the teeth will be curved.
Now, because this sutra of praise encourages people to listen with intelligence and because there are no faults in his speech, all [his features] are beautiful.
His lips do not hang down. Those whose lips hang down have the appearance of blowing on a fire; because of his virtuous speech, his do not hang down.
Nor are they drawn back or shriveled. A shriveled lip is a sign of premature death; now, by the power of this sutra, they do not shrivel.
They are neither coarse nor rough. When lips are coarse, speech is stammering; when lips are beautiful, speech is eloquent.
To have no sores or blisters, and for no eruptions or rashes to arise, is the retribution for wholesome speech.
Furthermore, the lips will not be defective or impaired; it is through unwholesome [speech] that they become defective, whereas with the wholesome, such things do not exist.
Nor is it crooked or askew. One whose speech is improper has lips that are distorted; one who speaks with rectitude has lips that are upright and well-proportioned.
They are neither too thick nor too large. If they were thick or large, they would not correspond to their form; being free from excess or deficiency, they attain their proper measure.
Furthermore,
it is neither dark nor black. Those with a corrupt vocal faculty have lips that are dark and black, whereas those who teach others well have lips that are red and beautiful.
He is free from anything loathsome; there is not a single sign of anything loathsome to be seen.

His nose is not flat or sunken. The nose is the gateway through which the breath enters and exits; because he delights in what is wholesome and possesses a well-proportioned, prominent nose, it is not flat or sunken.
Nor is it crooked or distorted. Because one’s mind was not upright, the nose was then warped and curved; now, through the retribution of goodness, the nose is round and straight.
One’s facial complexion is not dark. Because those who perform good deeds have clean and bright countenances, they are not ugly or black.
Nor is it narrow and long. When one looks at one's face in a mirror with a blade, one sees it as narrow and long; yet when the heart is like a sword-thorn, the face appears likewise.
Now, because the mind is square and even, the face is upright and dignified.
Nor is it sunken or crooked. When the mind is not level, the face becomes sunken and crooked; because the mind is broad and even, the face is likewise full and level.
There is not a single unpleasant feature; his countenance is perfectly rounded, with nothing that is not beautiful.
The lips, tongue, and teeth are all perfectly adorned; the nose is long, high, and straight, and the facial features are full and rounded.

Each of these qualities is twice as excellent as those previously described. The nose is intended to be elongated like a mountain peak, without being sunken; the remaining meanings are easy to understand.
The eyebrows are high and long. Those with low eyebrows are dull-witted; those with short eyebrows are narrow-minded. High eyebrows signify nobility; long eyebrows signify refinement.
The forehead is broad and level. Those with a narrow forehead are base; those with a slanted forehead are biased. A broad forehead signifies nobility; a level forehead signifies...
The forehead is settled and upright, and the features are perfectly formed; the marks of human dignity are all fully possessed.
In every lifetime one is born, and in every place where one receives retribution, these characteristics are complete.

Having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, they faithfully accepted his instructions; because of these present virtuous causes, they will obtain their future retribution, whereby they shall again see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and with faith listen to and receive the Buddha’s teachings.
Ajita, you should observe this; you should observe this: such is the merit of encouraging even a single person who delights in what is wholesome to go and listen to the Dharma.
If the merit of encouraging just one person is thus great, [how much more so for many].

How much more so for those who listen with a single-minded focus; how much more so for those who, from beginning to end, maintain a single-minded focus on the Path while listening to the Dharma Master’s exposition,
receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it,
and then analyzing and explaining it for others among the great assembly— this is the benefit of benefiting others.
Furthermore,
as for practicing according to the teaching: if a person practices their mind as described in the sutras and thus reverently follows the instructions,
the merit gained by those who encourage them is beyond measure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person, having attended a Dharma assembly, hears this sutra;
or even if they hear but a single verse and, with a heart of sympathetic joy, explains it to others, or at the very least understands the meaning of a single phrase—"
In the interim, they rejoice and explain it to others.

In this manner, the teaching is transmitted successively until it reaches the fiftieth person. Starting from one individual and passing through to fifty, the merit obtained by the final person shall now be analyzed.
By taking the fiftieth person as the reference point, we may infer the initial state from the end.
Suppose there were a great donor who provided immeasurable requisites for eighty full years, satisfying every desire according to one's wishes.
To provide for immeasurable beings is a great matter; to do so for eighty full years is a long duration;
and to bestow everything according to their desires is a vast merit.
Seeing that person’s signs of old age— the white hair, the wrinkled face, the gaps between the teeth, and the withered body— he reflects that death will not be long in coming.

Seeing that person before him whose years have declined, whose hair is white, whose face is wrinkled, whose body is withered, and whose teeth are sparse and fallen out, he realizes that his time in this world is not long and that the hour of death is approaching.
"I should now instruct them so that they may attain the fruits of the Path. Thinking thus, he intended to train them through the Dharma so that they might cultivate and attain the Path;
he immediately employed skillful means to preach the true Dharma of Nirvana, and promptly used skillful means to preach the true Dharma of world-transcending cessation.
All worlds are as unstable as foam, bubbles, and mirages. All that exists in the world is not solid;
it is like a mass of foam, a bubble of water, or a shimmering heat haze.
You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment. Such are the characteristics of the world; you should swiftly distance yourselves from them.
Upon hearing this Dharma, all those people attained arhatship. Having heard the Dharma, they practiced according to the teachings and all realized the four fruits of the śramaṇa,

becoming fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), the three knowledges (trividyā), the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), and the divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of past lives.
When the six faculties are unimpeded regarding their objects and the exhaustion of outflows, it is called "supernormal knowledge" (*abhijñā*).

Knowing the future is "knowledge of the future," knowing past lives is "knowledge of past existences," and knowing the exhaustion of outflows—which brings liberation from birth and death—is called the "three knowledges" (*trividyā*). Developing wisdom through the four dhyānas and four concentrations to sever delusions is called the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Finally, the merit of one who hears a single verse and rejoices in it surpasses that of the former; it cannot be compared to it.
The merit of hearing a single verse of this sutra and rejoicing in it surpasses the teaching of many who have realized the four fruits of arhatship.

If the merit of those who hear [the teaching] through successive transmission is thus immeasurable, how much more so for those who hear it at the very beginning of the Dharma assembly and rejoice in it?
When comparing the person at the very end with the initial rejoicer who taught others, how can their respective merits be adequately recorded?
If there is one who exhorts another person to lead them to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, saying, "This sutra is profound and subtle,

difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas," or if there is one who exhorts another person to lead them to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, saying, "Because this sutra is profound, subtle, and difficult to encounter."
He immediately accepted the instruction and went to listen; having heard it for even a brief moment, he thought, "The meritorious retribution of this person shall now be explained in detail.
Having received the instruction and gone there, he obtained a brief hearing of such meritorious retribution as should now be explained in detail.
In every lifetime, he is free from oral ailments; his teeth are neither sparse nor yellowish-black; his lips are neither thick nor upturned and cleft;
and he possesses no loathsome features, as previously explained.
His tongue is not dry, black, or short; his nose is high, long, and straight; his forehead is broad and even; and his countenance is entirely dignified and majestic.
As previously explained:

one is pleasing to others to behold because one’s breath is free from foul odors. Since it is impossible for one to be pleasing to others to behold unless one’s mouth is virtuous, there is no foul odor.
The fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issues from his mouth, and his mouth perpetually produces the scent of the blue lotus.
If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling wishing to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and upon hearing it for even a moment feels joy, I shall now describe the merit thereof.
Having gone to the monastery to listen to the sutras, one hears them briefly and rejoices; now I shall describe the merit thereof.
In future lives, among gods and humans, one will obtain exquisite elephants, horses, chariots, precious jeweled litters, and palaces of the heavens upon which to ride.
In future lives among humans, one will obtain elephants, horses, and carriages; if born in the heavens, one will obtain celestial palaces to ride upon.

Furthermore, by encouraging others to sit and listen to the sutras at places where the Dharma is preached, through these causes and conditions of merit, one will obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Wheel-Turning King.
To encourage others to sit and listen brings forth such merit that it is equal to the seats occupied by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Universal Monarch (cakravartin);
how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, understands its meaning and intent, and practices according to the teaching— their merit would be beyond measure.
With a concentrated mind, listen attentively as the principles and meanings are explained; practice according to what is taught in the sutra, and the merit you shall obtain will be immeasurable.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nineteen: "The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher."
There are five ways for a Dharma teacher: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing.
As briefly mentioned in the preceding Chapter on Rejoicing, the merit of even hearing this sutra or speaking a single verse of its meaning to others is vast and immeasurable.
If one receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes it, the conditions are already exceptionally sublime.
Because that which is experienced will necessarily be great, it is next appropriate to explain the merits of the Dharma teacher.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent: "The accomplishment of merit depends upon diligence;
therefore, by means of this person, I shall inform the great assembly."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and maintains this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, keeping it in mind,
whether by reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing— performing these five superior acts.
This person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye. When observing with the eyes, one perceives a hundred matters;

regarding the four directions and discussing them in terms of the three periods of time, this constitutes thirty-four times twelve, totaling one thousand two hundred. The front direction is fully seen, thus possessing three hundred merits;
the rear direction is not clear, thus lacking three hundred; and the left and right sides possess only half of each, thus obtaining the remainder.
Furthermore, if one lacks one hundred, one obtains the number of eight hundred, which can be discussed in terms of merit.

As for the twelve hundred merits of the ear: when listening with the ear, all one hundred ears simultaneously hear the three periods of time and the four directions without anything not being clearly perceived; thus, it possesses twelve hundred merits.
There are eight hundred merits of the nose. When smelling with the nose, one perceives a hundred kinds [of odors] simultaneously;

throughout the three periods of time and the four directions, inhalation and exhalation each possess four hundred merits, together constituting eight hundred merits. In terms of the breaths themselves, there is no lack of inhalation and exhalation, yet the four hundred [merits] are deficient.

There are twelve hundred merits of the tongue. When tasting with the tongue, one distinguishes all a hundred flavors simultaneously; as there is nothing throughout the three periods of time or the four directions that is not clearly perceived, it is thus endowed with twelve hundred merits.
There are eight hundred merits of the body. When the body makes contact with objects, it perceives all one hundred things;

when the three periods of time and the four directions are combined, it can respond to both favorable and adverse conditions, each possessing four hundred merits, thus totaling eight hundred. When separated from these conditions, perception does not arise, and therefore four hundred merits are lacking.
There are twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty (*manas*). When one contemplates with the mind, a hundred kinds [of objects] are simultaneously accessible;
because it can encompass all three periods of time and the four directions, it possesses twelve hundred merits.
By means of these merits, one adorns the six sense faculties, causing them all to become pure.
In the bodies of ordinary people, those who possess the six sense faculties all have six thousand functional capacities; they differ only according to whether they are good or evil.
Wherever there is attachment, it is called turbid and defiled; by means of wholesome merit, the holder of this sutra is able to remain far removed from the objects of the six sense-dusts.
Because they are free from [defilements], they obtain six thousand pure merits as adornments.
These good sons and good daughters possess the pure physical eyes born of their parents.

Regarding these eyes, there are five kinds—namely, the physical eye, the wisdom eye, the divine eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye—which are not different in essence, but are divided into five according to their respective functions.

The verse states: "The supernormal power of the divine eye is unobstructed; the fleshly eye is obstructed and not a supernormal power. The Dharma-eye observes only the conventional; the wisdom-eye clearly realizes emptiness.
The Buddha-eye is like the thousand suns shining—different in form yet identical in essence. The Sūtra says that what is produced by one's parents is the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).

It further states that "purity" refers to the purity of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); it is the eye as a superior sense organ (*indriya*) formed from derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and not the superficial [eye].
The "dusty faculty" refers to the physical eye-flesh.

It perceives the trichiliocosm and is able to see the entire realm of a single transformation within the Sahā world, including all that exists internally and externally—mountains, forests, rivers, and seas.
"Internal and external" here refers to both the retributive rewards of the environment and the person; "internal body" refers to [the practitioner's own] body.
The mountain bristles are the veins of the forest, the rivers are its blood, and the internal organs are the lands beyond the seas;
these four meanings need not be stated explicitly, as they can be understood by virtue of the power of upholding this sutra, which purifies the faculty of the eye so that one may see them.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above— Avīci being translated here as the "Uninterrupted" Hell because the prisoners therein suffer without interruption,
and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception being called the "Peak of Existence" because it is the ultimate summit of the contaminated world within the three realms—
the Sūtra cites these upper and lower limits to encompass everything in between; there is nothing that is not seen through with complete penetration.
One also sees all sentient beings therein. What was previously called the hells and celestial palaces refers to the *pariṇāmanirmita* (the environment or external retribution);
what is now called "all sentient beings" refers to the *sattva-nirmita* (the primary retribution or the beings themselves).

He fully sees and fully knows the places where rebirth occurs through the causes and conditions of karma, as well as the places produced by the two causes of good and evil and the two conditions of good and evil, resulting in the retributions of good and evil.
He sees with the eye of the mind and knows with the wisdom of the mind; it is because he upholds this sutra that he is able to see all of this.
[He] understands the karmic causes, conditions, and retributive fruits of both good and evil deeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, amidst the great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sūtra with a mind free from fear, listen now to its merits. Furthermore, if there is another person who, in the great..."
Among the assembly, with a mind of fearlessness born from the wisdom that understands the Dharma, he expounds the sutras for the multitude; listen now attentively as I describe his merit.
This person attains eight hundred meritorious and preeminent eyes; because they are thus adorned, his vision is exceedingly pure.
Because they are adorned with these merits, they attain a preeminent eye that is exceedingly pure.

With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entire trichiliocosm. Although the fleshly eye originally sees only what is before one's face, now, through the power of the sūtra, it sees the trichiliocosm.
The inner and outer Mount Meru mountains. "Inner and outer" refers to the primary and secondary Mount Merus; "Meru" here means "Radiance," which refers to the seven golden mountain ranges.
[There are also] Sumeru and Cakravāḍa. "Sumeru" here means "Wondrously High," rising eighty-four thousand yojanas above the waters.
The Iron Encircling Mountains (Cakravāḍa) refer to the Iron Encircling Mountains outside the great trichiliocosm.
Together with all other mountain forests, great oceans, rivers, and streams, they are all clearly revealed and present before one’s eyes, as explained in the sutra.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, he sees the hells below and the celestial palaces above;
he perceives all things across the horizontal plane with complete clarity.
Within this, he sees every single sentient being; all sentient beings within the great trichiliocosm are seen by him.
By the power of the sūtras, they are all able to see; though they do not move their bodies, they travel throughout the dharma-realm.
Although they have not yet attained the divine eye, the power of their physical eyes is such that the divine eye—though the name is the same—the realization differs for each:
the divine eye of a śrāvaka sees a trichiliocosm, while a bodhisattva of the first bhūmi sees a hundred buddha-fields; from the second bhūmi onward, it doubles.
The divine eye of the Buddhas increases manifold, such that the lands within the atoms of the voids of the ten directions are all clearly perceived;
now, although those who uphold this sutra are ordinary beings, by virtue of this sutra, what they see with the power of their physical eyes is as follows.
Furthermore, Constant Vigor, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains,
or transcribes this sutra, they are indeed a Dharma teacher of the five kinds.
One attains the merit of twelve hundred ears. The meaning is as explained previously.
By means of these pure ears, the meaning of "purity" is also as stated before.
One hears within the three-thousandfold world system, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above.
[The commentary] says: "Within it" refers to the great trichiliocosm.
All the various kinds of speech and sounds therein—the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots; the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and sighing;
the sounds of conch shells, drums, bells, and gongs; the sounds of laughter and conversation; and the voices of men, women, and boys—[are all included].

The sound of a boy, the sound of a girl, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of non-Dharma, the sound of suffering, the sound of pleasure, the sound of ordinary persons, the sound of noble ones, the sound of joy,
the sound of lack of joy, the sound of devas, the sound of nāgas, the sound of yakṣas, the sound of gandharvas, the sound of asuras, the sound of garuḍas,
the sound of kiṃnaras, the sound of mahoragas, the sound of fire, the sound of water, the sound of wind, and the sound of hell.
The sounds of animals, the sounds of hungry ghosts, the sounds of bhikṣus, the sounds of bhikṣuṇīs, the sounds of śrāvakas, the sounds of pratyekabuddhas,
the sounds of bodhisattvas, and the sounds of buddhas— in short, all internal and external sounds whatsoever within the trichiliocosm, as listed in the verse.

Although he has not yet attained the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), being by nature an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has not yet attained the divine ear, he hears with his physical ear (*māṃsa-śrotra*) possessing pure function.
With the pure, constant ears born of his parents, he hears and knows all things. The term "constant ears" refers to the superior [ears].
The faculty of meaning is not a physical, fleshy organ subject to arising and ceasing or impermanence.
Thus, one may discriminate among various sounds without damaging the ear-faculty; yet, if one hears them and gives rise to attachment, the ear-faculty is damaged.
Discriminating without obstruction does not damage the ear-faculty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity or defilement;
though they are ears of flesh, they are pure and lucid, without any attachment."
By means of this constant faculty of hearing, one hears the sounds of the trichiliocosm.

This sentence provides a general heading. One hears the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers; the sounds of flutes and pipes;
and pure, beautiful songs—yet one listens without attachment. These sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and beautiful songs constitute the internal retribution.
Sounds such as those of bells, gongs, conchs, drums, lutes, flutes, and pipes are external sounds of retribution; though heard, they leave no attachment and do not impair the purity of the ears.
One hears the voices of countless kinds of people and is able to understand them all, for through the clarity of wisdom, one skillfully understands the intentions of others upon hearing them.
From their speech and sounds, one immediately knows their virtue.
Furthermore, one hears the subtle and wondrous songs of the various devas. By practicing the ten wholesome paths and the five precepts, one is reborn in the heavens of the desire realm;

by attaining the four dhyānas and the four concentrations, one is reborn in the form and formless realms. One who understands this meaning is one who, having heard the sounds of the devas, will receive birth in the heavens.

Regarding the matters of the five celestial desires, songs, music, and so forth, one who understands this meaning is said to "hear celestial songs and music," as well as to hear the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls.
The voices of men and women refer to the voices of husbands and wives; the voices of boys and girls refer to the voices of those who are naturally pure.
The voice of the *kalaviṅka* amidst the mountains, rivers, and steep valleys. "Mountains, rivers, steep valleys" refers to secluded and tranquil places;
*kalaviṅka* is the name of a celestial bird with exquisite song. Hearing this wondrous name in such a tranquil place, one obtains this sound.
The jīvaṃjīvaka and other various birds all hear its sound. As for the jīvaṃjīvaka bird, it is also called "co-life" (*gòngmìng*);

having one body and two heads, it is termed a "co-life" bird. If this represents the Dharma, then hearing the sutra and skillfully understanding that phenomena and principle are non-dual, being of one identical, perfect, and eternal nature, and attaining this wisdom—this is what is meant by "hearing."

The various sounds of suffering and manifold agonies in the hells—caused by a mind of anger, one falls into the hells among mountains of knives, forests of swords, iron grinders, fire pits, rivers of ash, and boiling excrement; these are immeasurable in number, their painful venom and bitter acrimony unbearable to endure.
To hear such things and thereby give rise to the bodhicitta is true hearing.
The hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, cry out as they seek food and drink. Because of their greedy minds, they fall among the hungry ghosts;
at all times they do not hear of any beverages, and as the fire of hunger burns their bodies, their cries of lamentation shake the earth. To hear such sounds is called "hearing the voices of ghosts."
When the various asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves, they produce a great sound.
Driven by a mind that seeks strength, victory, and the swallowing up of others, they are called asuras.

Dwelling on the shores of the ocean of out-flowing birth and death, with greed and anger as their fierce enemies and delusion and craving as their mutual afflictions, when these two powers encounter one another in battle, they speak thus to each other:
They utter great sounds.
Thus, the one who preaches the Dharma dwells here and hears those various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired.
This person who preaches the Dharma abides in the ground of pure loving-kindness and patience; this is called "hearing from afar while remaining in this place."
When evil and unwholesome sounds become increasingly intense, it is better to maintain right mindfulness and let the faculty of hearing be destroyed.

When birds and beasts in the worlds of the ten directions call out to one another, or when evil companions associate closely and habitually commit evil like those malevolent birds and beasts calling to each other;
whereas when virtuous people love one another and together cultivate all manner of goodness, they are like those beautiful flying creatures and running beasts.
They call out to one another by name, and the person preaching the Dharma hears them all clearly. By this means, the preacher immediately verifies whether the voices are good or evil;
as they are heard, there is nothing that is not discerned with certainty.
Regarding the sounds of speech from the various Brahma heavens, including Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra):
the four dhyānas of the Form Realm are collectively termed the Brahma heavens; specifically, Ābhāsvara is the Second Dhyāna, Śubhakṛtsna is the Third Dhyāna, and Bhavāgra is the Fourth [Dhyāna].
Being at the summit of conditioned existence, those who have cultivated dhyāna free from desire are born in the eighteen Brahma heavens of the Form Realm.
Practicing the concentration of empty tranquility and wearying of the realm of form, one proceeds toward emptiness and is reborn in the four levels of the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Those who hear this sound are called the "Heavenly Beings of Renown" (*Śabdavatsara-deva*);
when the Dharma Master dwells here, he hears them all. As the teacher of the Dharma dwells in this place of form...
They shall hear the meaning of formlessness in its entirety.
Whether it be the assembly of bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who recite the scriptures or explain them to others;
whether it be those in the monastic community who recite the sutras and possess the virtue of upholding the Dharma, or those who explain the teachings to others—[all shall hear this].
By observing ritual one knows governance, and by hearing music one knows virtue; one understands them at the first sight without waiting for further explanation.
The Dharma Master, while residing here, hears them all. This teacher of the Dharma possesses such clear wisdom that there is no matter, whether near or far, that he does not hear.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who read and recite the sūtras and dharmas, or explain them for others, or compile commentaries to interpret their meaning.
As for those called "bodhisattvas," they are not defined by physical form, but simply by having resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) to benefit all fourfold assemblies;
such individuals may be called bodhisattvas whether they read and recite the sūtras, explain them to others, or compile sub-commentaries and glosses to interpret their meaning.
All such sounds and voices can be heard. Whatever bodhisattva practices they perform, such as cultivating the six perfections, the Dharma Master hears all such sounds here.
The Great Holy Sages, the Buddhas who teach and transform sentient beings, expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma within the great assemblies.

All the Buddhas, the Great Holy World-Honored Ones, out of compassion for and instruction of all sentient beings, preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma within the great assemblies, manifesting birth and proclaiming extinction through the two gates of provisional and ultimate truth; all wisdom is fully contained herein.
Sūtra: Those who uphold this *Lotus Sūtra* shall hear them all; indeed, those who uphold the *Lotus Sūtra* will not fail to hear the deeds of all Buddhas.
All sounds within and without the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above;
all sounds of the two types of retribution— wholesome and unwholesome— within and without the great trichiliocosm,
from the Avīci Hell below to the summit of existence above.

They all hear those sounds without their faculty of hearing being impaired. Although they hear various kinds of good and evil sounds, because they are undefiled, their faculty of hearing is not impaired.
Because their hearing is keen and sharp, they are able to discern and know them all. By virtue of upholding this sutra, their faculty of hearing becomes keen and sharp.
One who is able to discern and know as described above—

even if they have not yet attained the divine ear— will, by the power of upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, be able to hear from afar those currently in the ninth stage, whereas only one who has attained the divine ear is capable of such hearing.
Such is the merit of merely using the ear faculty born of one's parents;
such is the merit of being able to hear universally by means of the pure ear faculty of the body born of one's parents.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or copies this sutra,
they will accomplish eight hundred merits of the nose, as explained previously.

By means of this purified nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), which is the faculty in the ultimate sense (*paramārthendriya*), one perceives the various fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm—above, below, and within and without.

Regarding the fragrances of the trichiliocosm, from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) above down to the Avīci hell below, these refer to both internal and external retributions; internally, they refer to [the faculties of] men.
The scents of the female body; externally, there are the scents of grasses and trees, such as the scent of the sumanā flower—
which is called "the flower that accords with one's wishes" (chēngyì cǎo) in Chinese, being yellowish-white in color and possessing an exceedingly beautiful fragrance—
and the scent of the jāti flower— which is called "the golden coin flower" (jīnqián huā) in Chinese.
The fragrance of the *mallikā* flower;
the fragrance of the *campaka* flower, which in this region is called the "yellow flower" or also the "golden flower";
and the fragrance of the *pāṭala* flower, which in this region is called the "reborn flower."
The fragrance of red lotuses, the fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses, the fragrance of flowering trees, the fragrance of blooming flowers,
the fragrance of fruit-bearing trees, and the fragrance of ripening fruits.
Candana (sandalwood) incense comes from Mount Gośīrṣa on this side of the ocean.
Agaru (aloewood) incense is so called because its substance is heavy and it sinks when it encounters water.
Tamālapatra incense is translated here as "nature without defilement" or "coriander."
Tagara incense— this refers to the root-fragrant wood-tree—
and ten million kinds of blended incense, which are made by mixing ten million different varieties together to form the incense.
Whether as powder or as pills— referring to fine powdered incense and round pellet incense—
or as ointment for the body or incense for smearing upon the ground,
those who uphold this sutra can distinguish all these while dwelling in this very world, just as a single mind may manifest as ten thousand.
Goodness is like powdered incense; combining myriad virtues to adorn one's person is like ball incense.
Adorning the internal retribution (the body) is like body-anointing incense; adorning the external environment (the dwelling place) is like ground-anointing incense.
Cultivating every kind of goodness to perfect one’s virtue is like the blending of thousands of varieties of incense. To distinguish them in this way without error is called "being able to know all."
Furthermore, they separately discern the odors of sentient beings; that is, the breath within their bodies is called "odor.
They know the odors of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth; knowing these bodily emanations is called "smelling odors."

The fragrance of men, the fragrance of women, the fragrance of boys, and the fragrance of girls—men and women represent the vital breath of husband and wife, while boys and girls represent the appearance of infants.
Furthermore, there is the fragrance of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests. When flowers possess fragrance, people love them; when a person possesses virtuous qualities, the world [cherishes them].
Then one reveres them.
Whether near or far, all various fragrances are perceived and distinguished without error. "Near" refers to the fragrances of the six realms of ordinary beings as worldly retribution;
"far" refers to that which transcends the three realms, and further beyond that, to the liberation from the two deaths and ultimate nirvana.
"Pan" means "extremely far away.
Although those who uphold this sutra dwell here on earth, these upholders of the sutra, while remaining in this place,
also smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens— the fragrances enjoyed within the celestial realms.
Pārijātaka is the king of celestial trees in the garden of Śakra; its fragrance pervades fifty yojanas.
The Kovidāra tree—translated here as "Great Play"—is likewise the fragrance of a tree.
as well as the fragrance of māndārava flowers, the fragrance of small white flowers,
the fragrance of mahāmāndārava flowers, the fragrance of large white flowers,
the fragrance of mañjūṣaka flowers, and the fragrance of small red flowers.
The fragrance of mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, the fragrance of great red flowers,
various powdered incenses such as sandalwood and aloeswood, and the fragrances of diverse miscellaneous flowers— these are the myriad types of wholesome deeds cultivated by the devas,
each distinct in kind, collectively termed "miscellaneous flower fragrances."
There is no fragrance produced by the combination of such celestial incenses that he does not perceive.
Because he has attained a celestial body as the retribution for combining ten thousand virtues, it is called "the fragrance produced by combination."
Furthermore, one smells the bodily fragrances of the various devas— the individual fragrances of the bodies of each of those devas—
and that of Śakra-devānām-indra (which means "Lord of Devas," i.e., Indra).

The fragrance experienced while enjoying the pleasures of the five desires in the Palace of Victory is the fragrance of the retribution for being a Lord of Devas, dwelling in a celestial palace and enjoying the five celestial desires; this is precisely the retribution for the ten wholesome actions.
When he preaches the Dharma for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven upon the Hall of Sublime Dharma, there is the fragrance [of that occasion].
When Śakra, Lord of Devas, preaches the sublime Dharma—namely, the ten wholesome paths of action—for the assembly of devas in the Hall of Good Dharma, there is likewise that fragrance.

When playing in various gardens, one enjoys the fragrance [of those places]. By means of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), one multiplies the body to sport within the celestial palaces of the devas and experience all manner of delights.

Furthermore, there is the fragrance of the bodies of other devas, both male and female; the males possess a vigorous and masculine scent, while the females possess a pleasant, subtle, and tranquil scent, cultivating the causes for masculinity.
Those who are male devas and female asuras, and those who are female devas and male asuras, all hear from afar.

As with the aforementioned fragrances and so forth, they are able to smell and know them; this phrase summarizes that because one dwells here and hears what is there, it is called "hearing from afar."

In this manner, they proceeded successively up to the Brahma Heaven. From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they ascended successively until reaching the Brahma Heaven, and further upward to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra).
Again, from the Brahma Heaven, they reached the Formless Realm (Ārūpyadhātu).

The fragrances of the bodies of the various devas are also all smelled. One likewise smells the fragrance of the moral virtue (*dharma-gandha*) resulting from the karmic retribution of the bodies of all the celestial hosts;

yet, since the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks physical bodies, how could there be fragrance? It is simply that while bodily form is absent, it is not that the fragrance of the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the sphere of infinite space is absent.
They also smell the incense burned by the various devas; just as when devas cultivate themselves through successive stages of ascent,
they become perfected through the perfuming of incense,
so too do they smell the fragrance of the śrāvakas and the fragrance of the Path of the Four Noble Truths.
The fragrance of the pratyekabuddhas; the fragrance of the twelve links of dependent origination;
the fragrance of the bodhisattvas; the wondrous fragrance of the merit of the six perfections and myriad practices;
the fragrance of the bodies of all buddhas; and the fragrance of the fruit of ultimate liberation and bodhi.

They likewise all hear from afar and know where [the person] is located. Because they now dwell among humans while looking toward the various heavens and the four stages of holiness, it is said that they "hear from afar" and penetrate their causes and effects; this is called "knowing the location."

Although they smell these fragrances, their olfactory faculty is neither impaired nor deluded. Although they smell the celestial fragrances and experience the resulting pleasure, they hear them without attachment;
therefore, their pure olfactory faculty is not impaired. They are able to discern all known and perceived characteristics, and for this reason, they are not deluded.
If one wishes to analyze and explain it to others so as to remember it without error— referring to what was previously heard by oneself—
if one wishes to speak to others about that which has been apprehended by this faculty of the nose, one will remember it clearly and without any mistake.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The nose of this person is pure;
within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives all varieties completely. He compares fragrance with the good and compares foulness with the evil."

There are various fragrances of sumana, jāti, tamāla, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon; there are the fragrances of various flowers and fruits, consisting of various causal flowers and various resultant fruits.
Furthermore, they know the scents of sentient beings, the scents of men and women, and the scents of the physical bodies resulting from the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
A teacher of the Dharma who dwells at a distance can perceive their location by smelling these scents.

Because such a teacher remains far removed from worldly attachments and abides in right mindfulness, they are said to "dwell afar," yet they fully hear and know the whereabouts of all sentient beings.
The Great Universal Monarch (Mahāsammata) and his successors;
the four types of Wheel-Turning Kings and their sons; the minor kings of scattered principalities and their various princes;
the ministers and palace attendants; and the various officials and those within the inner court.
By smelling a fragrance, one knows its location; by smelling various fragrances, one knows where they have fallen. By cultivating such causes, one obtains such fruits:
the precious jewels worn upon the body, the treasures hidden in the earth, and the jewels of a wheel-turning monarch—all their locations are known by smelling their fragrance.
Wearing precious robes is the merit of patience; the treasure-trove within the earth is the Tathāgatagarbha within the minds of sentient beings;
the precious woman of the wheel-turning king is the "precious consort," who represents the desire-love among the seven treasures of the wheel-turning king.
When such a person smells a fragrance, they know its place of origin entirely.
When people adorn themselves with garments, ornaments, and various types of fragrant unguents, one knows their bodies by smelling them.
