Both the auspicious and inauspicious signs are called "adornments. From the auspicious ones, one obtains a good retribution:

the garments represent propriety (*li*), the ornaments represent wisdom (*zhi*), and the fragrant unguents represent the purification of the body. By smelling these fragrances, one comes to know their original selves.
Whether the various devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing miraculous transformations, those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* can know them all by their scent.

Walking is the application of movement; sitting is profound stillness. To traverse everywhere is called "sporting. By practicing the meditative concentration on phenomena (*dharmasamādhi*), they attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
By upholding the sutra and smelling the fragrance, they fully know the source from which these states arise.
The fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as those of ghee and oil—those who uphold this sūtra dwelling here shall know their locations entirely.
Such matters as these are fully elucidated in the sūtra; by upholding the sūtra and understanding its meaning, one knows their causes.
In the deep and precipitous places of the various mountains where sandalwood trees are in full bloom, those beings dwelling therein can all perceive the fragrance upon smelling it.
Likewise, those who delight in the Way, even when situated in remote mountain depths like sandalwood incense produced in secluded valleys, can all perceive it upon smelling it.
All sentient beings dwelling within the Iron Ring Mountains, the great oceans, and the earth— those who uphold this sutra shall hear their fragrance and know their locations.

As for those outside, in the regions below the Iron Ring Mountains and the great oceans, or those dwelling within the earth, even those whose bodies are wrapped in skin-sacs containing blood and vital energies,
with their conscious spirits (*vijñāna*) abiding in their physical forms— if they skillfully uphold this sutra, they shall all be found.
Yuan: When the male and female asuras and their various retinues engage in combat, strife, or play, they can know it all by smelling [the fragrance].
Asuras possess the mind of a fierce wolf; males and females represent the two thoughts of movement and stillness, and when one thought arises—

When among a multitude, they contemplate their mutual conformity; the primary thought serves as the leader, while the others are called its retinue. Good is termed "devas" (gods), and evil is termed "asuras" (titans).
When good and evil oppose one another, it is called "combat"; taking this as pleasure is called "sport."
In the vast wilderness and perilous defiles, lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, and water buffaloes know their locations by scent.
In the vast wilderness of birth and death, within its dangerous, narrow, and difficult-to-cross places, the lions, tigers, and wolves represent the predatory mind;
the wild oxen and water buffaloes represent the dull and stubborn mind that thinks only of grass and water. Upon hearing the sutra, they all come to understand.
If there is one who is pregnant, and it is not yet discerned whether it is male or female, or if there is no physical basis [for conception] or if it is a non-human being,

by smelling the fragrance, one can know all of this. If there is a person who harbors intentions and undertakes various actions, but has not yet discerned the signs of good or evil, movement or stillness, or if they lack a fundamental nature and their mind is in doubt and indecision—
whether it be a non-human being, such as one conceiving a "demon-womb" (*grahagarbha*)— if they uphold this sutra and understand its meaning, then for them, good and evil will be clearly revealed.
One can immediately discern [the truth] through the power of smelling scents;
by the power of smelling scents, one knows whether the initial conception will be successful or unsuccessful, and whether there will be a peaceful birth and the blessing of a virtuous child.
By the power of smelling scents, one knows the thoughts initially conceived at that time: that progress leads to success, whereas retreat leads to failure.

If one does not commit evil, there will be danger; if one practices goodness, there will be peace and joy. By cultivating wholesome thoughts and planting wholesome seeds, one gives birth to children who bring merit.
Through the power of perceiving fragrances, one knows the thoughts of men and women—whether they harbor lust, delusion, or anger—and likewise knows those who cultivate virtue.
It was previously stated that there is the womb; this clarifies that once born, male and female are themselves the two minds of movement and stillness.
Male is yang and female is yin; yang is movement and yin is stillness. By observing their actions, one immediately knows their thoughts:
if they harbor lustful desire, it is greed, anger, and delusion; these three poisons mean they are not practicing goodness. Those who lack these three poisons are practitioners of the Way.
Within the earth there are various hidden treasures—gold, silver, and all manner of precious jewels contained in copper vessels; by smelling their fragrance, one can know them all.
Within the minds of sentient beings exists the nature of the Tathāgata’s treasury of merit; because they are deluded, they do not perceive it, and thus it is called a "hidden treasure.
All the gold, silver, and precious jewels therein are precisely the merit of the six perfections, wisdom, and the untainted purity.
The mind is called a copper vessel; by hearing the Lotus Sūtra, one knows this hidden treasure.
Among various kinds of necklaces, none can recognize their value; yet by smelling the fragrance, one knows their worth, their origin, and their location.
The various wisdoms of the five vehicles, the three vehicles, and the single vehicle are each distinct from one another, like a necklace strung with many precious jewels.

Who, lacking wisdom, could know them? It is only those who do not recognize their value [who fail to understand]; yet by upholding this sutra and explaining its meaning, one distinguishes each in detail:
the ten wholesome paths of humans and devas, the four truths of the śrāvakas, the dependent origination of the pratyekabuddhas, and the six perfections of the bodhisattvas.
The Buddha of Deliverance displays his wondrous enlightenment; upon picking it up, one immediately knows the distinctions between noble and base, and that their origins differ.
Having attained its proper place, one can perceive all the celestial flowers, such as the *māndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and the *pārijātaka* tree, by merely smelling their fragrance.
This is explained as before.
One can fully know, by smelling their fragrance, the distinctions among the various celestial palaces—superior, middling, and inferior—and how they are adorned with myriad precious flowers.

This refers to the fact that while the causes cultivated by these devas are not equal, resulting in differences of high and low, their resultant states are likewise distinct; thus, the "precious flowers" are [the fruits of those causes].
Because one gathers the fruits of accomplishment through the causes of their practice, it is called "adornment.
Within this are celestial gardens, excellent palaces, various pavilions, and sublime Dharma halls, wherein they enjoy themselves; by smelling the fragrance, they are able to know all of them.
The factors of dhyāna are its groves, the body is its palace, and preaching the Dharma from the face is called its Dharma hall;
dwelling therein and enjoying themselves, these people can all be known by their fragrance.
When the various devas either listen to the Dharma or indulge in the five desires, their coming and going, walking, sitting, and reclining, as well as their smelling of fragrances, can all be known.
When the assembly of devas listens to the sound of the Dharma, they do not fall back or descend; this is called "walking.

When they indulge in the five desires and their merit is exhausted, they immediately fall; this is called "coming. When one cultivates goodness in the human realm and attains birth in the heavens, this is called "going."
When one dwells in a tranquil mind, abiding in goodness without advancing or receding, it is called sitting; when the mind is dissipated and goodness is abandoned, it is called lying down.
When the celestial maidens wear fine garments and are adorned with exquisite flowers and perfumes as they move about and play, he can perceive them all by their fragrance.
By cultivating wholesome deeds among humans, one is reborn in the heavens of the desire realm; because of attachment to form, one receives a female body.
The enjoyment of flowers, perfumes, and garments—namely, the enjoyment of tainted wholesome states—is termed "play."
In this manner, progressing upward through successive stages, even those who enter and emerge from dhyāna as far as the Brahmā world can all know [the source] by smelling the fragrance.

From the desire realm up to the Brahma-world is called "progressing upward"; focusing the mind toward concentration is called "entering," and arising from meditative concentration is called "emerging."
From the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), one can perceive through the scent of those who are first born there or who are passing away.

Since the second dhyāna is the Ābhāsvara heaven, the third dhyāna is the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, and one transcends the fourth dhyāna as well as the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness to reach the Peak of Existence,
it is said that "up to" those first born in the heavenly realms and those falling away from them, all are known by their scent.
The assembly of bhikṣus always applies themselves with diligence to the Dharma, whether sitting, walking in meditation, or reciting the sūtras.

As for those in the renunciant community who constantly practice diligence within this Dharma—whether through seated meditation, walking meditation, or the recitation of scriptures—those who are able to do so are all due to past conditions;
by examining the fruit, one knows the cause and thus understands their place of origin.
By observing the roots of goodness currently being cultivated, one may infer from cause to effect that their future rebirth will surely be superior to the present life.

Alternatively, when those who sit in meditative concentration or uphold the sutras with single-minded diligence beneath forest trees are perceived, he knows their locations by means of their fragrance.
Whether dwelling beneath the trees in secluded forests, focusing the mind with diligence in meditative concentration,
or abiding in the joy of emptiness, tranquility, and cessation—
when a Bodhisattva is firm in resolve, whether sitting in meditation, reciting scriptures, or preaching the Dharma to others, [the Buddha] can know it all by smelling their fragrance.
If there is a bodhisattva whose resolve is firm, whether sitting in meditation to cultivate the Way, reciting the sutras,
or preaching them for others among the great assembly— when they smell this fragrance, one knows that they are a Great Bodhisattva with the mind of the Way.
Wherever the World-Honored Ones are, revered by all and preaching the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings— one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
In every place where the Buddha-World-Honored Ones are, honored by all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma for the sake of compassion toward living beings—
one hears within this sutra the sublime merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions.
By virtue of upholding this sutra, one is able to know all fragrances.
Sentient beings who hear this sutra in the presence of the Buddha will all rejoice and practice according to the Dharma; by smelling their fragrance, one is able to know them all.
In this sutra it is said that sentient beings of the ten directions, standing before the Buddha, hear the Dharma with joy and practice according to the Dharma;
by hearing this sutra, they come to know the affairs of the ten directions.
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) faculty of the nose, those who uphold this sutra first obtain this mark of the nose.
That which arises from untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) to produce the pure nose of a bodhisattva belongs to the noble ones (*ārya*) on the stages (*bhūmi*);
those who now uphold this sutra are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), yet by virtue of the power of the sutra, they possess this functional efficacy.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue. Because the tongue is able to speak with fullness and perfection,
such merit is attained.
Whether beautiful or ugly, whether exquisite or unrefined; whether delicious, foul, sweet, or bitter;
and as for all things that are acrid or astringent—those tastes that are bitter or astringent and unfit for consumption.
Within their tongue-roots, all things are transformed into the supreme flavor. Those who uphold this sutra focus their single mind on the Way;
regarding worldly flavors, they make no distinction between them, for even the bitter and astringent are turned into truly delicious tastes.
Just as there is nothing that is not delicious about celestial ambrosia, so too, this celestial ambrosia is the deathless medicine of the devas;
entering this Dharma-gate is like drinking ambrosia—there is nothing about it that is not delicious.
If one uses the faculty of the tongue to deliver a discourse within a great assembly, at the time of speaking before the multitude,
the tongue produces a profound and wondrous sound that penetrates their hearts, causing them all to feel joy and happiness; the principles discussed thoroughly [penetrate].
The source of the Dharma is called "profound" because it enables those who hear it to reach the realization of the Buddha's vision;
it is called "wondrous" because the flavor of the Dharma enters the spirit, bringing joy to all.
Furthermore, while the previous statement described the delight of humans, this clarifies the delight of the devas—the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and all other celestial beings.
Hearing this profound and wondrous sound, all those who were expounding teachings and engaging in discourse came to listen in succession.
Because the exposition of the Dharma was delivered with clear language, logical argumentation, and systematic explanations of its various branches,
all the devas came to hear and receive it.
As well as the nāgas and nāgīs, yakṣas and yakṣīs, gandharvas and gandharvīs,
asuras and asurīs, garuḍas and garuḍīs, kiṃnaras and kiṃnarīs, and mahoragas and mahoragīs—
the explanations of the names and meanings of these eight classes of beings are as in the Introduction Chapter (Nidāna-parivarta).
In this context, it is not stated that the male members of the eight classes [of supernatural beings] are included within their respective positions;

rather, they all come to attend upon, venerate, and make offerings [to the Buddha] for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Because the Dharma being taught is profound, subtle, and sequential, they approach to listen and give rise to a mind of offering.
As well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—the fourfold assembly gathered at the Buddha’s assembly;
the kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues; and the monarchs, princes, hundreds of officials, various ministers, and the royal attendants.
A minor wheel-turning monarch (kṣudra-cakravartin) is one who rules as a king over the realms of sentient beings within a single wheel-turning domain;
such a ruler is called a wheel-turning monarch, while the multitude of minor kings scattered throughout are called minor wheel-turning monarchs.
A great wheel-turning monarch; an iron-wheel-turning monarch rules over one continent, excluding those to the east, west, and north;
a copper-wheel-turning monarch rules over two continents, excluding those to the northeast; a silver-wheel-turning monarch rules over three continents, excluding only the northern continent;
and a gold-wheel-turning monarch rules over all four continents.

The seven treasures and the thousand sons. As for the seven treasures, they are the wheel treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the military treasure, and the steward treasure.
As for the thousand sons, it means he has a thousand sons.
His inner and outer retinues— innerly his parents, brothers, queen, and court ladies, and outwardly his kinsmen, ministers, and the masses of the people—
mounted their palaces and came together to hear the Dharma. The palaces they mounted were chariots, for the sake of the Dharma.
Therefore, they all come to listen and receive [the teaching].
This is because these bodhisattvas skillfully expound the Dharma; it is because these bodhisattvas who uphold the path of the sutra are well able to explain the profound and subtle Dharma.
The brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom attended upon and made offerings to him for as long as they lived.
As for the brahmins, being of the lineage of pure conduct, out of reverence for the Dharma, they attended upon and made offerings to him throughout their entire lives without ceasing.
Furthermore, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing them. This clarifies that these are the ones whom the four types of noble beings delight to behold.
In whichever direction such a person may be, that is the direction and location where the holder of this sutra dwells.

All Buddhas preach the Dharma toward that place. Regarding the Buddhist scriptures, when one looks at them with the eyes, holds them in the hands, recites them from the mouth, and understands them in the mind, it is no different from hearing them directly from the Buddha’s own mouth. At no time do the Buddhas fail to preach toward them;
these yellow scrolls are indeed the presence of the Sages and Worthies.
One is able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas. All matters pertaining to all Buddhas are proclaimed and expounded within this sutra;
one who upholds this sutra is, in fact, receiving and upholding all the Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, they are able to produce the sounds of the profound and wondrous Dharma. By understanding the Buddha’s intention, they are able to rely upon the sūtras to produce the profound, wondrous, and pure sounds of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure; it will never..."
They experience bitter tastes; yet because their faculties are pure, bitter tastes do not enter them.
Whatever they eat or consume all becomes nectar. All bitter tastes that enter this person's mouth become nectar.

He preaches the Dharma to the great assembly with a voice that is profound, pure, and wondrous. With various deep, far-reaching, and pure, sublime sounds, he expounds all dharmas within the great assembly.
He guides the minds of sentient beings through various causes, conditions, and parables, employing all manner of analogies for the causes and conditions of both good and evil.
The parables explain and guide the minds of the sentient beings who listen;

those who hear them all rejoice and provide various supreme offerings. What is taught is profound and subtle; those who hear it enter into its spiritual essence, and their hearts all rejoice as they provide various pure offerings.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others all come together with hearts of reverence to listen to the Dharma.
If the teaching were not sublime, who would come to hear and receive it? It is because of its profound sublimity that the nāgas and spirits hold it in awe and honor.
If this person who preaches the Dharma wishes to fill the trichiliocosm with a sublime voice, they can do so at will.
Although the preacher of the Dharma remains here, if they wish to pervade the great trichiliocosm with a sublime voice, it is because the mind pervades that the voice likewise pervades accordingly.
Furthermore, one should know that the realm of the trichiliocosm is merely a provisional designation for the five aggregates and the land.
Because the name is not separate from even a single thought or a momentary state of mind, it can reach everywhere at will.
Great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons, constantly come with palms joined in reverence to listen to and receive the Dharma.
The king and his retinue also approached with reverence, joining their palms to listen and receive [the teaching] through this wondrous Dharma.
There were also devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas. "Rākṣasa" is translated here as "fierce and evil ghost," and "piśāca" is translated here as "ghost that devours vital essence."
They also constantly delight in coming to make offerings with a joyful heart; that is, the aforementioned eight classes of beings, out of a mind of Dharma-joy, raise up offerings.

These include Brahmā Devānām Indra and Māra Rājā. Brahmā Devānām Indra is the lord of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), while Māra Rājā dwells at the summit of the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātu) and wields power there.

The "real" is not different from the real; it refers to the celestial Māra and those with true false views. The "provisional" refers to Bodhisattvas manifesting transformed bodies to test practitioners and cause them to strengthen their power on the Path.
As for Maheśvara and Īśvara: "Īśvara" refers to the Nirmanarati Heaven, which manifests through its own power and experiences [the results] itself.
The realm of *Nirmāṇarati* is called "Mastery" (*Vaśavartin*) because its inhabitants exercise great mastery;

furthermore, it is called "Mastery over Others' Creations" (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) because their emanations are produced through the power of others. Moreover, the Akaniṣṭha heaven is also called "Great Mastery," which refers to Maheśvara.

In this way, the hosts of devas constantly come to his dwelling. As described above, the devas of the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness—constantly come to the place of the Dharma-preacher for the sake of the Dharma.
The Buddhas and their disciples— the Buddhas being the World-Honored Ones of Wondrous Enlightenment, and the disciples being the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles—
hear the sound of their preaching the Dharma and constantly mindfully protect them; whenever they hear the sound of the Dharma, they constantly come to guard and mindfully sustain them.
At times, he manifests his body. When the manifestation of his body is all-encompassing, this is seeing the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*).
When the principle is manifested, this is understanding the Buddha’s Dharma-sound; this is called seeing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains,
or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain eight hundred merits of the body. The number eight hundred has already been explained as before.
One attains a pure body like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings joyfully behold. By the power of upholding this sutra, one obtains the supreme faculties and a body as pure as lapis lazuli;
among all sentient beings who see it, there are none who do not feel love and delight.

Because his body is pure, the births and deaths, the high and low, the beautiful and the ugly, and the rebirths in good and evil realms of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm appear entirely within it. The trichiliocosm penetrates both the internal and external retributions;

internally, within one's own mind and single body, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) contains the lands of the three thousandfold world-system, as do the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Birth consists of various names, such as the provisional designations of the five aggregates (skandhas), twelve bases (āyatanas), and eighteen elements (dhātus).
Externally, there are all the various names of the insentient world of the environment and the sentient world of beings. From the perspective of principle, when thought arises, it is called birth;
when thought ceases, it is called death. "Good" refers to the superior and beautiful; "evil" refers to the inferior, ugly, and foul. When good arises, it is called good.
The path of evil leads to falling into the three miserable realms; this can be seen clearly by observing one's own body.

Speaking in terms of phenomena, regarding lands, sentient beings, titles, and names—among the various classes of sentient beings, who is without birth and death, or distinctions of high and low, beauty and ugliness?
The retributions for good and evil are fully recorded in the scriptures, and manifest responses before our eyes are not limited to a single instance. Therefore, the Buddha...
It is said that all these appear within it,
including the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Meru Mountains, Mahāmeru Mountains, and other such kings of mountains.
The meanings of these names have already been explained as before, and the metaphors for the Cakravāḍas and so forth are also to be understood as previously interpreted.
Furthermore, all sentient beings within it appear therein; even all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm manifest their forms within his body,
reaching down as far as the Avīci Hell, the place of ultimate suffering.
Reaching upward to the Peak of Existence, it is the realm of ultimate bliss.
All things and all sentient beings appear therein. Within it, all mountains, rivers, lands, realms of suffering and joy, and all sentient beings of the six destinies appear within his body.
Regarding the preaching of the Dharma by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas: if one perceives the principle of emptiness, it is the teaching of a Śrāvaka;
if one perceives [all things] as being like an illusion, it is the teaching of a Pratyekabuddha; if one perceives wondrous existence, it is the teaching of a Bodhisattva;
and if one perceives wondrous awakening, it is the teaching of the Buddhas. The meaning of this single dharma of the One Body is thus; if a person listens well, they will understand it accordingly.
All their forms and images appear within the body. As they arise in succession through the mind, the body is produced by karma;
how could all these forms and images exist outside of a single body?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, its..."
The body is exceedingly pure. The mind of one who upholds this sutra does not incline toward evil; being internally free from transgression, it is most pure.
Like that pure lapis lazuli which all sentient beings joyfully behold, it is like lapis lazuli, transparent and radiant both within and without.
For one who gives rise to such vision,
there is no lack of wholesome joy. Furthermore, just as a pure, bright mirror clearly reflects all forms and images, because the mind’s vision is pure, there is nothing it does not know with clarity,
just as all forms and appearances manifest within a mirror.

The Bodhisattva perceives all that exists in the world within his pure body. Because the body and mind of a Bodhisattva who upholds this sutra are pure, he perceives all matters existing in the world;
he alone clearly understands them while others do not see them. He alone sees them with his own eyes with perfect clarity, while others...
Those who have not studied cannot perceive all the various sentient beings within the three thousandfold world system. These "various sentient beings" are precisely the beings of the triple world;
the arising of their wholesome and unwholesome thoughts is termed "sprouts."
The forms of devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—all such images appear within the body.
The beings of the six realms each possess their own bodies; these do not come from without, but are created solely by the mind.
For one who contemplates thus, all these things manifest within the body.
The palaces of the various devas up to the Peak of Existence— from the heavens of the desire realm to the palatial towers of the formless realms—
as well as the Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, and all the great oceans, all appeared within his body.
Viewed with the correct eye, how could it not be so?
Whether alone or in a multitude, the Buddhas, the Śrāvakas, the sons of the Buddha, and the Bodhisattvas all manifest when preaching the Dharma.
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the aforementioned four classes of noble ones— whether dwelling in solitude or amidst the great assembly—
manifest within the body of this person as they preach various dharmas.
Although this upholder of the sutra has not yet attained the wondrous body of the untainted dharma-nature, they nevertheless [possess it] fundamentally.
There is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is devoid of a subtle body; yet, because it is the pure and eternal essence, everything manifests within it.

By means of the supreme sense-faculties (paramārtha-indriya), which are the pure and eternal essence, one contemplates, according to reality, all forms—whether good or evil, noble or ordinary—within a single body. There is nothing that does not appear therein.
They do not all appear.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds this sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—
upholding this sutra during the final age after the Buddha’s passing—
Whether reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it, one will attain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty (*manas*). The enumeration is as explained previously.
By means of this purified mental faculty, one eliminates the superficial dust and the physical mass of the four great elements, correctly grasping the pure and superior [mind].
This refers to the faculty of meaning (*arthendriya*). Even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings.

Within a single phrase of the profound and wondrous Buddha-dharma, many meanings are contained; by skillfully understanding these verses and phrases, and by revolving and penetrating them, one attains the immeasurable.
Regarding the meaning of the boundless:

having understood this meaning, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse; having understood it oneself, one is able to expound the meaning of a single phrase or a single verse for others.
As for periods ranging from one month, four months, or even one year; from a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or a day, up to a month—
there are some lands where there are three seasons in a year, each season lasting four months, such that one year consists of twelve months.

All the teachings that are expounded follow their respective meanings and intentions. For those who perceive the principle, whatever they say follows the direction of the literal meaning and the underlying intent;

all such speech is never in contradiction with the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). For those who do not perceive the principle, every word they utter becomes a source of affliction; there is never a time when this is not so.
Regarding those who perceive phenomena in contradiction with correct reasoning: first, one whose mind is set on correctness spontaneously accords with the Sūtras.
As for the worldly scriptures and secular treatises that they may speak of—
"Worldly discourse" refers to all speech that governs the world;
"occupations for sustaining life" refers to all activities that support one's livelihood.

These are all in accordance with the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Worldly speech is nothing other than instruction, the punishment of evil, and the encouragement of good; occupations for sustaining life are likewise so.
To say that karma is nothing other than wholesome deeds and to prohibit all manner of evil is to speak in constant accord with the Buddha’s True Dharma.
The "three thousandfold great world" refers to the six realms of existence, which are the six paths of rebirth.
The range of the mind; whatever the mind thinks or practices, whether good or evil;
the movements and activities of the mind; its shifting and performing of deeds;
the conceptual proliferations of the mind; and the mind’s false discursive elaborations regarding all phenomena.
They know them all completely. The Bodhisattvas who uphold this sutra, by means of the standards of the Dharma, fully understand the workings of their minds.
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), their mental faculties (*manas-indriya*) are thus pure; even though they are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Those who have not yet attained the noble, untainted liberation and the true wisdom that purifies the faculty of mind can naturally act in this way—like an image reflected in a sharp mirror;
how could there be any deliberate thought? Whatever such a person contemplates, calculates, or speaks, it is the mind of one who upholds this sutra that performs such contemplation and calculation.
Dushuo explained:
"All these are the Buddha-dharma; there is nothing that is not true. Because the mind is correct, every thought and every word accords with the Dharma and is without exception true."
This is also what was spoken in the sūtras of former Buddhas. His mental and verbal expressions are likewise words of truth spoken in the sūtras of former Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The mind of this person is pure and clear."

The faculties are free from turbidity and defilement. This means that the mental ground of one who upholds this sutra is pure, clear, lucid, and sharp, being entirely devoid of turbidity and defilement.
By means of these wondrous faculties of mind, one knows the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas; because the mind is wondrous, one penetrates the principles of the Buddha and understands them.
The teachings of the Three Vehicles are provisional methods (*upāya*).

Even hearing a single verse can lead to the thorough penetration of immeasurable meanings. Through a hundred efforts one may achieve a single contemplation, and through understanding a thousand [teachings], one follows [the truth].
This sequential exposition according to the Dharma proceeds from months and four-month periods to a year; following the sequence of these meanings, it is spoken in accordance with principle.
From a single phrase or verse up to one month, four months, and even one year, there is a sequential progression in speech whose principle is inexhaustible.
All sentient beings within and without this world— wherein "within and without" refers to the basis of self and others— are [encompassed].
Regarding the various sentient beings who receive retribution for their actions, there are the six realms, the three vehicles, the fourfold assembly, and the eight classes of beings.
These eight classes include devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth.
Regarding the various kinds of thoughts entertained by beings within the six realms of existence— indeed, the many varieties of mental inclinations held by sentient beings throughout the six paths—
the one who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* knows them all at once as a result of that merit. The person who upholds this sutra seals their own mind with the seal of the sutra, and thus...

The seal of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* stamps the dharmas within the minds of all sentient beings, such that they are all simultaneously and clearly understood, with nothing remaining unknown.

The countless Buddhas of the ten directions, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; [the practitioner] hears it all and is able to receive and uphold it.
The various marks and signs of excellence, as well as the hundred kinds of supreme merit that adorn the Buddhas of the ten directions,

all arise from their virtues and wisdom; and regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings, they are able to receive and uphold it all according to what they have attained.
He contemplates immeasurable meanings; within his mind he contemplates immeasurable principles and purposes.
His preaching of the Dharma is also immeasurable, and the dharmas he expounds are likewise immeasurable.
From beginning to end, they do not forget their practice; from beginning to end, they maintain mindfulness without any lapse or mental confusion.
Because they uphold the Lotus Sutra, they fully know the characteristics of all dharmas. The Lotus Sutra is the king of all sutras;
to understand the meaning of the Lotus Sutra is to understand all dharmas completely.
One follows the sequence according to the meaning; one skillfully discerns the sequence according to the meaning of the text.
One masters names and language; one thoroughly understands the various names for the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and all forms of expression as they are taught in the sūtras.
He expounds according to what is known; he is well able to understand and expound according to what is appropriate.
Whatever this person says is all the Dharma of the former Buddhas; whatever this upholder of the sūtras says is likewise the Dharma within the sūtras of the former Buddhas.
Because he expounds this Dharma—because he expounds such subtle and profound teachings that accord with the capacities of beings and conform to reason—he is fearless among the assembly;
he speaks with composure amidst the great multitude, free from all fear.
The mental faculty of one who upholds the Lotus Sūtra is purified in this way. By the power of upholding the sūtra, the mental faculty becomes clear and pure to such an extent that,
although they have not yet attained the untainted state— despite not having attained the pure mind free from outflows— [it is so].
First there were such signs; first there were such signs of auspicious response.
This person, upholding this sutra, dwells in a state of rarity. This person, with a pure mind, is able to uphold this sutra and dwell in the rare state of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
They cause all sentient beings to rejoice and feel love and reverence; they cause all sentient beings who see them to give rise to joy and a heart of love and reverence.
This is because they are able to analyze and expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through thousands of myriads of skillful modes of speech.
The ability to analyze and explain the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma through thousands of millions of skillful modes of speech is due to the merit of upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
*Commentary on the Verses of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Six.
Commentary on the Sentences of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
By the Śramaṇa Guāngzhào of Qiāntáng, Śākya Míndá.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: Chapter Twenty, "The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging."
The preceding chapter elucidated that the merit of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers who propagate this sutra is immeasurable;

yet, though one may hear of this sutra, such persons have not been seen. Now, by citing the verified account of how the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, in a past age, practiced this path with patient endurance and tireless diligence until attaining perfect enlightenment, we seal the previous teaching so that deep faith may arise.
"Exert yourselves to propagate this in the defiled and evil world.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta—whose name also signifies "Great Power Attained"—the meaning of which is as explained in the Preface Chapter.
The reason the Buddha addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta was that propagating this sutra in the defiled world is the most difficult task; it cannot be accomplished by anyone other than [him].
Because one must attain great forbearance and reach a state of great power before being able to practice this, it is said to this bodhisattva:
"You should now know that if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
they are just like the aforementioned fourfold assembly who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
If one uses harsh speech to revile and slander those who uphold this sutra,
they will incur a retribution for great sin as previously described; that is, as stated in the Parable Chapter, those who slander the sutra shall receive all manner of karmic punishments.
The merit they obtain is as previously described regarding the purification of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The merit acquired by those who uphold this sutra is as explained earlier in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master."
Regarding the attainment of great power: in the remote past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
The Buddha told Śrītīrtha: "In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago."
There was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja). Because he was a Dharma King whose fame spread afar and whose majesty shook the ten directions, this title was established for him.
He was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi.
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, is as explained in the "Introductory Chapter.
The kalpa was named "Free from Decline" (Vivarta), so called because the era was auspicious and free from all sorrows and afflictions.
The land was named "Great Achievement" (Mahāsaṃbhava), so called because it was fully equipped with everything, including ritual, music, law, and governance.
That Buddha King of Majestic Sound preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras within that world. Regarding the capacities of those devas, humans, and asuras who listened to the Dharma:
for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths. These śrāvakas, being of inferior capacity, were weary of suffering and sought happiness.
The Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is taught because it is that with which one should be associated.
It delivers one from birth, old age, sickness, and death; it liberates one from the four kinds of suffering-characteristics in the world;
and it leads to ultimate nirvana and the ultimate accomplishment of pervasive emptiness and quiescence.
For those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.

This is taught because those with the faculties of a Pratyekabuddha enter the Path by contemplating conditions, and it corresponds to the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the twelve factors of dependent origination.

For the sake of all bodhisattvas, by reason of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the capacity and aspiration of bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way are rooted in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is said that the teaching of the Dharma corresponding to the six pāramitās culminates in the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because it is associated with the dharmas of the six perfections, the teaching of the bodhisattva pāramitās is expounded so that the wisdom of a Buddha may be attained.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lifespan of that Buddha King of Majestic Sound was forty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand eons;
such was the lifespan of that Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The number of kalpas for which the True Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of atoms in one Jambudvīpa;
the duration of the True Dharma’s presence in the world is illustrated by the analogy of reducing one Jambudvīpa to dust-like atoms.
The number of kalpas during which the Semblance Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of atoms in the four continents.
This is illustrated by the analogy of grinding the four continents into atoms to represent the duration of the Semblance Dharma’s existence.
That Buddha, having brought great benefit to sentient beings, subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.
After dwelling in the world for forty trillion *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings, he finally entered nirvana.

After the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have been extinguished— specifically, after the extinction of the Dharma for a number of kalpas equal to the dust motes of one Jambudvīpa and the four continents— in this land,
which is the Great Accomplished Kingdom (Mahāsiddha), [the teaching shall flourish].
Furthermore, another Buddha appeared, also named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*). His name was no different from that of the first Buddha mentioned above:
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
This is as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
In this sequence, there were twenty trillion Buddhas, all bearing the same name: King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja).
After the first Tathāgata, King of Majestic Sound, had entered parinirvāṇa and his body had passed away, [the others followed].
After the extinction of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the kalpa of the True Dharma has likewise been completely exhausted.

Within the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), the flavor of the Dharma becomes somewhat thin and the conditions for its practice gradually grow rare; that which roughly resembles the period of the True Dharma is called the Semblance Dharma.
Arrogant bhikṣus possess great power; as the Dharma endures for a long time, people become weak and those who practice in accordance with reality are few.
At this time, those arrogant individuals who have not attained realization yet claim to have attained it gain influence.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). During the period of the Semblance Dharma, he took the body of a bhikṣu and practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva, and was thus named Constantly Not Disparaging.
As for why Mahāsthāmaprāpta was named "Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta*), this is an inquiry into the origin of his name intended to cite a past circumstance.
Whenever that bhikṣu saw anyone—whenever he encountered anyone at any time—[he would always pay homage].
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—the fourfold assembly of the Semblance Dharma—they all pay homage and offer praise; seeing others prostrate, they speak words of commendation.
And they spoke these words: "We deeply revere you all and do not dare to treat you with contempt. With their mouths they said:
"We have conceived a profound respect for you all and do not dare to give rise to a heart of casual disdain."
Why is this? It is because you all practice the path of the bodhisattva. Since you all practice the path of the bodhisattva, you shall attain Buddhahood.
The path is the cause of Buddhahood, and the Buddha is the fruit of the path; by practicing the path of the bodhisattva, one will certainly become a Buddha.

As for this bhikṣu, the Constantly Non-Disparaging, he did not exclusively recite and chant the sūtras but practiced only prostrations; nor did he exclusively recite the sūtras and perform prostrations.
Even when seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, he would intentionally go forward to pay homage and offer praise;

even when seeing the fourfold assembly from a distance, he would likewise intentionally go forward to pay homage and praise them. If such was the case even when they were far away, it can be known that he would do so all the more when they were near.
And he spoke these words: "I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Whenever he encountered anyone, he would immediately say this.
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to a mind of anger and impurity, and some whose minds of anger were defiled by the world.
Regarding those with impure conditions:
they revile others with harsh speech. Out of habitual custom, they in turn revile upright persons, saying, "From where has this ignorant bhikṣu come? and "From where has this fool come?"
He himself said, "I do not slight you; I bestow upon you the prediction that you shall become Buddhas.
This recounts the words from the mouth of Viśākha (Not-Light).
We do not require such false predictions. The minds of worldly people suppose that only a Buddha can grant them.
He bestowed a prediction upon this foolish bhikṣu, saying, "How can we accept such a person’s prediction as mere empty words?
Thus they passed many years, yet whenever they saw him, he would always say, "You shall become a Buddha."
Though constantly reviled, they do not give rise to anger. Though constantly reviled by the masses, they have never once conceived a mind of resentment.
They always say, "You shall become a Buddha. Even when encountering such abuse, they do not alter their original resolve.
When these words were spoken, the crowd struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones.
Because the people held such evil views and constantly spoke in this manner, they struck and pelted him with sticks and wood.
Even when fleeing to a distant place and living far away, he still cried out in a loud voice; even when struck and forced to avoid him from afar, he still spoke aloud:
"I do not dare slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. To remain unchanging in the face of peril is the mark of a true man.
Because they constantly speak these words, those bhikṣus who constantly speak such words—
those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of overweening pride (adhimāna)— at that time, the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride.
He was named Constantly Not Disparaging; this bhikṣu was called by the name Constantly Not Disparaging.
When that bhikṣu was about to reach the end of his life—that is, when the time of death for that bhikṣu’s worldly lifespan had arrived—
In the midst of the void, he heard in its entirety the Lotus Sūtra previously preached by the Buddha King of Majestic Voice.

Because he had long observed the emptiness of the nature of phenomena and was thus able to perform difficult deeds, at the time of his death, he heard the voice from the sky proclaiming the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
He was able to receive and uphold twenty quadrillion verses; although the scriptural texts were numerous, by the power of the Path, he was able to maintain them all.
He immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the eye faculty, as well as the purity of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties, through his ability to endure.
By virtue of having respectfully upheld this sutra, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties as described in the preceding chapter.
Having attained this purification of the six sense faculties and having cleansed them, one subsequently does not die.
His lifespan was further increased by two hundred trillion nayutas of years; he again increased his life-span by the same number as mentioned above.
He extensively preached this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of others, and furthermore, he extensively preached this wondrous sūtra for the sake of others.
At that time, there were the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who possessed overweening pride— namely,
the fourfold assembly during King Bhaishajyaraja’s period of the Semblance Dharma—
who treated this person with contempt and gave him the name "Not-Disparaging," thereby making "Never-Disparaging" his title.
He saw that they had attained the power of great supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), such that they were able to hear and fully retain the Dharma taught in mid-air;
he saw their power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) in joyful exposition, as they extensively preached the Dharma for others with joyful eloquence.
The power of great, sublime tranquility (*mahā-śubha-śānti-bala*). To not become angry when reviled and not to feel resentment when struck is "great, sublime tranquility.
Upon hearing what is said, all believe, submit, and follow along. Because they see his excellence, upon hearing his teachings, faith arises in their hearts;
they respectfully submit and comply with his transformative instruction.
This Bodhisattva was none other than Sadāparibhūta.
He further transformed thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He further transformed many others, causing them to dwell in the Buddha-way.
After his life ended, he encountered two thousand koṭis of buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Having cast off that previous body, in his subsequent birth, he again encountered two thousand koṭis of buddhas named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Within that Dharma, within the Buddha-dharma of Candrasūryapradīpa, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and constantly preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others.
By these causes and conditions, he further encountered two thousand billion Buddhas, all equally named Meghasvaradīparāja. Day and night...
After Dīpaṃkara, he again encountered the aforementioned Sovereign King of Lamps (Vairocanaraśmipratimaṇḍitaguṇasāgaravajranārāyaṇabimbaśrīkūṭarāja).
Within the teachings of these Buddhas, he upheld, recited, and studied them;
internally he purified his mind, and externally he practiced transformative guidance for the fourfold assembly.
By virtue of expounding this sutra—specifically, by reason of preaching such a Dharma Flower Sutra—one attains this constant eye of purity.
One attains the purity of the eyes born of one's parents, as well as the purity of the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; all six sense faculties simultaneously attain complete purity.
When preaching the Dharma among the fourfold assembly, his mind is free from fear. When one’s perspective is unclear, the mind is full of dread;
but since the six sense faculties are already purified and one has penetrated the profound depths of the Dharma, how could there be anything to fear when teaching in accordance with conditions?
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Never Disparaging made offerings to as many Buddhas as these:
namely, twenty-two thousand koṭis of King of Majestic Sound, two thousand koṭis of Sun Moon Lamp Brightness, and two thousand koṭis of Cloud Sovereign Lamp King.
They honored, revered, and praised [the Buddhas], planting various roots of goodness. With a profound mind, they served the Buddhas and cultivated many roots of goodness.
Thereafter, they again encountered ten million billion Buddhas; following the Buddha Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (Meghasvararāja), they encountered ten million billion more.

They have attended countless Buddhas and likewise preached this sutra within the teachings of those Buddhas. Having begun with this wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they shall achieve the perfection of merit and attain Buddhahood;
having achieved the adornment of the merit of the six sense faculties, they shall subsequently become Buddhas.
The Buddha said, "Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Was that Bodhisattva Never Disparaging at that time anyone else? It was none other than myself.
That Bodhisattva Never Disparaging during the era of the Tathāgata King of Majestic Voice was none other than I, Śākyamuni Buddha, here and now."
It is so. If I had not, in previous lives, received, upheld, read, and recited this sutra; if, in past lives, I had not upheld this Lotus Sutra.
Those who preach it for others, or preach it to the multitude,
will not be able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they will not be able to attain Anuttara-bodhi.
Because I received, upheld, recited, and explained this sutra for others under previous Buddhas, I quickly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it was by virtue of reciting, reciting, and explaining it that I swiftly achieved success.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
the fourfold assembly during the Semblance Dharma period of King Vimalasvara—
out of a mind of anger and malice, treated me with contempt, reviling me with harsh words and even striking and throwing things at me; such was their contempt.
For two hundred billion kalpas, throughout such a length of time,
they will never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṃgha; because they have disparaged the Saṃgha, they do not believe in the Dharma.
Because he was arrogant toward the Dharma and did not revere the Buddha, due to these karmic conditions, he did not encounter the Triple Gem for two hundred billion kalpas.
For one thousand kalpas, he underwent great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell as the retribution for his slandering and striking [the Buddha].
When these offenses were completed, his time in hell was finished.

He then encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Because he had previously heard [the teaching], when his offenses were finished, he encountered [the Bodhisattva] once again.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Were those members of the fourfold assembly who constantly disparaged this bodhisattva at that time anyone else?
They were none other than those who, at that time, treated the bodhisattva with contempt and arrogance due to their overweening pride.
Now, within this assembly— within this Lotus Sūtra assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—
there are five hundred bodhisattvas, such as Bhadrapāla; "Bhadrapāla" is translated here as "Good Protector," and the name of one representative is cited for these five hundred bodhisattvas.
There were five hundred bhikṣus, including Siṃhacandra. Regarding Siṃhacandra: in terms of his majestic presence, he was like a lion;
in terms of his wisdom, he was like moonlight.
There were also five hundred upāsakas, including Niṃsibuddha. As for Niṃsibuddha, the Sanskrit term is not clearly understood.
The five hundred others, such as Arthavargiya and the rest,
were all those who had attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, these fifteen hundred bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and upāsakas had all attained non-retrogression from bodhi.

You should know that those who were then characterized by overweening pride are now those who have attained great power; this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings immense benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, enabling them to reach unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It was through the propagation of this sūtra by the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging that he has now ascended to wondrous awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
All others who were transformed thereby attained bodhi; even those with overweening pride were included among the ranks of the noble ones.
For this reason, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—namely, the great bodhisattvas present in this assembly.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, following the passing away of the Buddha-Bhagavān,
one should constantly uphold, recite, explain, and transcribe this sutra, just as the five kinds of Dharma-preachers were described in the preceding chapter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"In the past there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-svara-rāja*), whose divine wisdom was immeasurable and who led all beings. In ages long past, the World-Honored One, the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, possessed infinite supernatural powers and wisdom, and he guided and led all sentient beings."
It is venerated by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits; the eight classes of beings all look up to it with reverence.
This is during the time when the Dharma is about to perish after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the era of the Semblance Dharma following the extinction of the True Dharma.
There was a bodhisattva named Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). Because he was highly agreeable, he was called "Not Disparaging" by the fourfold assembly.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was attached to dharmas; monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen clung to the characteristics of dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging went to where they were, approaching those in the fourfold assembly who were attached to the Dharma, and said to them:
"I do not disparage you; all of you who practice the Way shall surely become Buddhas.
The reason I do not disparage you is that, by practicing the Way, you shall all surely become Buddhas."
When the people heard this, they reviled and abused him. Because the people did not believe him, they scolded him;
yet the Bodhisattva Viśvantara was able to endure it, remaining entirely calm and patient throughout.
When those karmic offenses have been exhausted, [the person is purified]. Since the Bodhisattva’s original intention was to teach with a virtuous mind, what offense could there be?

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If there are those who read and recite this sūtra and are treated with contempt by others, these people’s karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are extinguished because they are now treated with contempt by others; this is due to their upholding of the sūtra."
Therefore, by means of this very act of contempt, their karmic retribution is immediately eliminated.

At the time of death, they shall hear this sutra and attain purity of the six sense faculties. At the moment of passing away, hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* preached from the air, they shall attain purity of the six sense faculties.
By means of his supernormal powers, he increased his lifespan; by means of his supernormal powers, he further extended his lifespan.
He then extensively expounded this sutra for all people, and again preached this Lotus Sutra to the assembly.
The various assemblies who were attached to dharmas, including the fourfold assembly who clung to the characteristics of phenomena,

were all brought to maturity through the Bodhisattva’s instruction and established in the Buddha-way. They were all brought to maturity through the instruction of Viśārada and established in wisdom upon the Buddha-way.
Not disparaging others, he passed away and encountered innumerable Buddhas, such as the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpamegha and Svayambhūpradīparāja.
Because he preached this sutra, he obtained immeasurable merit; because he preached this sutra, he was moved by it to receive manifold blessings.
Gradually perfecting his merits, he swiftly attained the Buddha-way; gradually fulfilling the merits of a bodhisattva, he swiftly achieved the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
At that time, "Not-Disparaging" was none other than myself; the present Śākyamuni is he.
At that time, among the fourfold assembly, those who were attached to the Dharma—such as Bhadrapāla and others—heard the words of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging:

"You shall become Buddhas. Although they originally had no such intention, through the power of his earnest encouragement, he forcibly administered a potent medicine to them, establishing the conditions for their future attainment and planting the seeds of the Mahāyāna.
By these causes and conditions, they encountered countless Buddhas. By virtue of these causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma, they encountered countless tens of billions of Buddhas.
The assembly of five hundred bodhisattvas in this gathering, together with the fourfold assembly of pure-faith laymen and laywomen, were all like lions.
Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī and the others who are now listening to the Dharma before me are those very people whom I exhorted in previous lives— namely,
the aforementioned individuals who are now listening to the Lotus Sutra before Śākyamuni.
To hear and receive this sutra is the foremost dharma. Because this sutra is the most supreme among all sutras, it is called "foremost.
It reveals and instructs people, causing them to abide in nirvana; it explains, demonstrates, and teaches all people, causing them to dwell therein.
Regarding the Great Parinirvāṇa, may I, in life after life, receive and uphold such sutras as these. May I, in life after life, uphold this sutra;
only after billions of billions of kalpas, until an inconceivable time has passed, shall I finally hear this Lotus Sutra. By means of billions...

Even if ten thousand become one, an eon may pass before this can be conceived or attained; it is only when the conditions of sentient beings ripen that they are able to hear this subtle and wondrous sutra.
One must know that such a teaching is difficult to encounter and must not be treated lightly.
Throughout billions upon billions of kalpas, even unto inconceivable numbers, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have preached this sutra at such times.
It is likewise rare for a Buddha to appear in the world and preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; it was only after forty years that Śākyamuni now begins to preach it.
Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, practitioners who hear such a sutra as this must not give rise to doubt or confusion.
Since doubt constitutes an obstacle, I exhort you not to doubt.
You should single-mindedly and extensively expound this sutra; you should collect your thoughts and always maintain a unified mind, teaching it widely for the sake of others.

It is said that by encountering Buddhas in every lifetime, one quickly attains the path of Buddhahood; thus, one shall constantly encounter all Buddhas in every life and swiftly achieve the unsurpassed fruit of Bodhi.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-One: "The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata.

The bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth, having heard that Śākyamuni Buddha had revealed such a vast and remote span of life and his original majesty, and further hearing the distinctions regarding the merits of the Dharma-preachers and how the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging had propagated this sutra until its fulfillment, [were filled with joy].
The Perfectly Awakened One, with palms joined in unison, addressed the Buddha, vowing to propagate and transmit this sutra after his parinirvāṇa.
It was for this reason that the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) amidst the great assembly to bear witness and protect him;
the Buddhas of his emanations did likewise, emitting light and manifesting signs to serve as witnesses. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Supernatural Power of the Tathāgata."
Furthermore,
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the dust motes of a thousand worlds who emerged from the earth at that time were none other than the bodhisattvas dwelling in the space below.

They all, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms before the Buddha, gazed up at his venerable countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "The entire assembly, with single-minded devotion, joins our palms and addresses the Buddha:
'World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, within this Sahā world-system following the Buddha's passing...'"
Wherever the emanations of the World-Honored One reside, and in whatever lands they pass into parinirvāṇa, this sutra should be preached extensively.
In those places where these emanations of Śākyamuni dwell, this sutra shall be preached extensively in the future.
Why is this? It is because we ourselves also wish to attain this truly pure Great Dharma.
The reason for this is that we do not seek it solely for the sake of others, but also for our own sake, desiring to realize this wondrous sutra of eternal truth and the pure Great Dharma.
One should uphold, recite, explain, copy, and make offerings to it; such is the nature of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and an immeasurable number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have long resided in the Sahā world—
these bodhisattvas are all former residents of this Sahā world, disciples of Śākyamuni.
And before all the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
before the entire multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth— before this great assembly of the eight classes of beings.
He manifests great supernormal powers. As will be explained below regarding the power of great miraculous transformations, he extends his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.
This tongue-attribute is so long and wide that it spans horizontally across the trichiliocosm and reaches vertically to the Brahma-world.
He who speaks falsely has a tongue that is curled and shriveled; by extending this tongue-attribute so that the multitude may behold it, he demonstrates the truth.
Truly giving rise to a mind of faith and understanding,

he emits immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors from every pore. The emission of these innumerable rays of light from the pores signifies that the Buddha has perfectly realized the wisdom-eye of the Dharma.
They all universally illumined the worlds of the ten directions, signifying that the Buddha’s great compassion shines equally upon all.

It was likewise so for the Buddhas beneath the jeweled trees and upon the lion thrones; the emanations of Śākyamuni seated beneath the jeweled trees and upon the lion thrones throughout the worlds of the ten directions also appeared in this same manner.

He extended his broad and long tongue and emitted immeasurable light; just as in previous lives the World-Honored One had extended his tongue-mark to reach the Brahma Heaven, he now likewise emitted countless rays of light from every pore of his body.
When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifest their supernatural powers, they do so for a full hundred thousand years;
yet the power of these Buddhas, though spanning the events of a hundred thousand kalpas, does not depart from a single kṣaṇa, being universally pervasive at that very moment.
Thereafter, they withdrew their tongues and simultaneously cleared their throats, snapped their fingers, and together manifested these auspicious signs.

Once the World-Honored Ones had displayed these portents, they withdrew their tongues and restored them to their original state; they then simultaneously cleared their throats, snapped their fingers, and praised [the teaching] as excellent.
That they acted thus without distinction was to manifest their identity with the Buddhas; it was for this reason that they appeared and spoke of these matters.
The Buddhas who are emanations throughout the worlds of the ten directions likewise praise this excellence.
These two sounds— the sound of coughing and the snapping of fingers— are the two kinds of sounds produced by Śākyamuni Buddha and all his emanations.
It reached all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; the sound pervaded the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, resonating everywhere, and the earth shook in six ways.
That all the great earths of the worlds in the ten directions shook signifies:
The six phases of movement, in which ignorance is destroyed, hindrances are transformed, and virtues are perfected,
are as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta). Among them, the names of the eight classes of beings— devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter."

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, and by the power of the miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One, all sentient beings throughout the ten directions behold this Sahā world. They all see this land.
The Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees were visible because of the Buddha’s light; likewise,
he saw Śākyamuni Buddha together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, both seated upon lion thrones within the jeweled stupa.
The emanated Buddhas are arrayed throughout the eight directions; therefore, one first sees them from the outside moving inward, then sees Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna.
Furthermore, one also beholds immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. This is what is seen.
The assembly gathered here,
as well as the fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
respectfully surrounded Śākyamuni Buddha; they all beheld both ordinary beings and sages respectfully surrounding him.
Having seen this—having seen the light, the signs, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly—they all experienced great joy, attaining what they had never before.
They were filled with great joy because they beheld such a rare and marvelous thing.
Immediately, the devas in the void raised their voices and proclaimed aloud. The devas in the sky announced to the great assemblies in all directions who witnessed it:
"Beyond this immeasurable, boundless hundred-thousand-myriad-ten-million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, from the place where they were seen from afar..."
Beyond that many lands,
there is a world named Sahā, which refers to this "Endurance" realm.
Within it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who refers to the Honored One Śākya.
Now, for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and for this great assembly,
he preaches the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
The twelve characters beginning with "Wondrous" (*miao*) constitute the full title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
"You all should, with deep resolve, rejoice in this. The devas exhort the great assembly to give rise to a deep resolve and rejoice in the sublime Dharma;
you should also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and further exhort you to increase your reverence for the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni."
When those sentient beings heard the voice in the void, and when the sentient beings within those worlds of the ten directions heard the proclamation of the devas in the void,
they all joined their palms toward the Sahā world and spoke these words: "All together join our palms toward this Sahā world."
They spoke these words:
"Namo Śākyamuni Buddha! Namo Śākyamuni Buddha! Through hearing this, they gave rise to faith and recited and held the name of the Buddha.
They prepared various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, and canopies,
as well as ornaments for adorning the body and rare, precious objects— specifically those precious items used to adorn the body.

They all together scattered [offerings] from afar toward the Sahā world. Because they were able to behold it from a distance due to the Buddha’s radiance, they scattered flowers and other items from afar toward this direction.
The various objects thus scattered arrived from the ten directions like a gathering of clouds; they transformed into a precious canopy, for the quantity of the objects was vast.
Thus, they gathered like clouds and transformed into jeweled canopies,
covering all the Buddhas of this world-system, as well as Śākyamuni Buddha and the jeweled seats of all his emanations.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions are unimpededly accessible as if they were a single buddha-field. This is easily understood in terms of phenomena;
if expressed in terms of the Dharma, it means that the minds of the ten dharma-realms share a single true nature, and because one penetrates this according to principle, it is called "unimpeded."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Superior Progress and the others—the very bodhisattvas who had come from the lower direction—saying:
"Such is the spiritual power of all Buddhas; such are the signs of the miraculous transformations manifested above."
It is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; its infinite auspicious signs are beyond the reach of thought.
If I were to employ this supernatural power—the majestic spiritual power manifested above—[it would be so].
For immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas— having passed such a duration of time—
for the sake of entrustment, and desiring to consign this sublime sūtra to the fourfold assembly after his parinirvāṇa.
The merit of expounding this sutra cannot be fully exhausted; its merit is so profound that it is impossible to describe it completely.
To state the essentials in brief, let me attempt to speak of them by way of their core points.
All the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata—namely, the gradual, sudden, partial, and complete teachings; the three vehicles and the one vehicle;

and the twelve divisions of the scriptural canon—as well as all the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual powers, his manifestations of birth and death, coming and going, and skillful means, appear in accordance with the minds [of sentient beings].
Within the power of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the treasury of all the secret essentials of the Tathāgatas;

it is the treasury of the most profound and essential dharmas of all Tathāgatas, which is spoken only after forty years have passed. Prior to that, it was not revealed and is therefore called "secret."
The Treasury:

All the profoundly deep matters of the Tathāgata—namely, the events of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the two gates of the remote origin and the proximate trace—are such that no sentient being is able to know them; therefore, they are called "profoundly deep."
All of these have been proclaimed and expounded within this sutra. What was previously not discussed is called the "Secret Treasury";
that which is now spoken of clearly is what is meant by "manifest."
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you should with single-minded devotion receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe [this sutra],
so as to ensure the transmission of the Dharma;
and practice according to what is taught, so as to give rise to its realization.
In whatever land there may be those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, or practice according to the teaching—
meaning, wherever anyone reads, explains, or practices,
or wherever the physical volume of the sutra resides— in whichever place this sutra is located.
Whether in a garden, within a park, in a forest,
beneath a grove, or at the foot of a tree, or beneath a solitary tree.
Whether in a monastic dwelling— a place where the Sangha resides and is called a "monastery for cultivating the Way"—
or in the house of a layperson, a home of a worldly person,
or in a hall, such as a temple building within a monastery;

Whether in mountain valleys or wildernesses, or within those mountain valleys and wildernesses, one should erect stupas for worship in all such places; in all these locations, stupas should be established.
Why is this? For what reason do they exhort others to erect stupas and make offerings?
You should know that such a place is itself a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). You should know that wherever this sutra exists in the world, there is a Buddha.
It is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the place where the Tathāgatas achieve the Way.
