It is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma. This single word "here" refers to this very sutra upon which the Buddha relies.
The Dharma turns the wheel of the Dharma;
herein all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, and it is also by means of this sūtra that all Buddhas realize great nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The Buddhas, saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The Buddhas, out of compassion, are saviors of the world who abide in supernormal powers and the treasury of great merit."
For the sake of gladdening sentient beings, he manifests immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

To cause sentient beings to see them with joy, he manifests such immeasurable supernormal powers as the tongue reaching up to the Brahma-heaven and the body emitting countless rays of light. The manifestation of these signs is precisely what constitutes supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
For those seeking the Buddha-way, he manifests this rare event; for all who study the Buddha-way, he manifests this miraculous feat of supernatural power.
The sound of the Buddhas’ clearing their throats and the snapping of their fingers resounds throughout the lands of the ten directions. [The clearing of throats and the snapping of fingers.]
These two sounds were heard pervasively throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The earth shook in six ways; it was because of the manifestation of supernatural powers that the great earth quaked in six ways.
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and because various bodhisattvas have made vows to propagate the sutra after the Buddha’s passing,
all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers; at one time, they cough and clear their throats together, simultaneously emitting a sublime sound.
Together they played instruments and praised his virtues.

Because they were entrusting him with this sutra, they extolled those who receive and uphold it; desiring to entrust him with this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they spoke words of praise for those capable of receiving and upholding it.
Even throughout immeasurable kalpas, one would still be unable to exhaust it; even if one were to spend as many kalpas as there are motes of dust in praise, one could not reach its end.
The merit of such a person is boundless and inexhaustible; the merit obtained by this person who upholds the sutra has no limit and is never-ending.
Just as the boundaries of the empty space of the ten directions cannot be found, so too are the merits of upholding this sutra boundless.
One who is able to uphold this sutra has already seen me; what this sutra elucidates is the vision of the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature is the seeing of the Buddha-body;
it is also the seeing of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his manifested bodies. When one sees the fundamental nature, one sees Prabhūtaratna;
when one sees the differentiated natures, one sees the manifested Buddhas.

Furthermore, seeing me today teaching and transforming these bodhisattvas, who perceive the Buddha-nature and advance in their practice moment by moment with the aspiration to attain the path of Buddhahood—
these very bodhisattvas who are able to uphold this sutra shall cause me, my emanations, and the parinirvāṇed Prabhūtaratna Buddha to all rejoice.
Śākyamuni appeared in the world to preach this sutra; Prabhūtaratna appeared to preach this sutra;
and the emanated Buddhas gathered from the ten directions for the sake of this sutra. Seeing one who is able to uphold it, they uphold the Buddha-body themselves, and thus all rejoice.
The Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions; the Buddhas presently dwelling in the world throughout the ten directions;
as well as those of the past and future, including those who have already passed away into *nirvāṇa* and those who are yet to attain Buddhahood in the future.

One both beholds and makes offerings [to them]. At that time, the holder of this sutra also beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time by means of this mind, and thus also makes offerings to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
It shall also cause them to attain joy, and it shall cause all Buddhas to experience great delight.

It is the secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when they sit at the site of enlightenment; it is the secret, essential, and wondrous Dharma attained by all Buddhas when they sit at the site of enlightenment.
Those who are able to uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long. Those who uphold this sutra practice the path of the Buddha;
those who practice the path of the Buddha shall also before long achieve the path of Buddhahood.
Those who are able to uphold this sutra [attain mastery] over the meanings of all phenomena; over all the principles and meanings contained within all phenomena;
and over names, expressions, designations, and terminology.
Their eloquence is inexhaustible. Within a single name there are infinite dharmas; within a single dharma there are infinite meanings.
How could their verbal explanations and analytical discourse ever come to an end?
Just as wind has no obstruction anywhere within space, so too, by seeing the principle, one thoroughly understands the meaning of the Dharma and attains universal penetration without any doubt.
This is like a pure breeze moving through the great void; the wind has no material form and space has no characteristics, for both subject and object are empty, and thus there is no obstruction.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one shall know the sūtras spoken by the Buddha;

after the Buddha’s extinction, one shall know the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, and explain its causes, conditions, and sequence according to their meaning as they truly are. All sūtras take causes and conditions as their primary principle.

The partial, the biased, and the perfect each have their own sequential order. Now, the causes and conditions of this sutra constitute one great matter. In this sutra, through three successive stages of revelation, the gradual is integrated with the sudden;

the partial is pointed out as being identical to the perfect; and the near precedes the distant. Regarding the primary and secondary, the fundamental and the manifested, there is nothing outside the Great [Vehicle], nor does it exhaust the Buddha-nature.
Its nature is inherently capable of skillful means regarding causes, conditions, and sequential order; thus, it is explained according to what is appropriate. Is this not so?
The confusion regarding the fundamental principles of the net [of teachings] is here addressed one by one;

these names accord with reality and are thus called "expositions according to truth. Just as the light of the sun and moon can dispel all darkness, so too, for example, the great radiance of the sun and moon is able to eliminate all obscurity in the world.

Such a person, walking through the world, is able to extinguish the darkness of sentient beings. This person who upholds this luminous sutra, walking through the world, is able to remove all obscurations of darkness for sentient beings.
They teach immeasurable bodhisattvas to ultimately abide in the One Vehicle. By means of this wondrous sutra, they instruct immeasurable multitudes to reach the ultimate end.
They shall ultimately abide in the Buddha-way of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom, upon hearing of these merits and benefits, and for this reason, all wise ones,
having heard of these great benefits of the merit of upholding this sutra, [should practice it].
After my parinirvāṇa, you should receive and uphold this sutra; after the Buddha’s extinction, one should maintain this sutra.

Such a person will be certain and free from doubt regarding the Buddha-way; such a wise person will possess a mind that is resolute and free from any uncertainty concerning the holy path of the Buddha.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-two: Entrustment.
The countless bodhisattvas dwelling in the regions below have vowed that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will exert all their strength to propagate this sutra.

Thus, this great matter has been entrusted to worthy recipients. The Buddha and his manifested bodies were all greatly delighted; they displayed various signs, emitted light, and cleared their throats with a cough.

By snapping his fingers to praise this person, the Tathāgata strengthened their resolve. At that time, the Tathāgata rose from his seat within the jeweled stūpa and again manifested supernatural powers;
extending his right hand, he stroked the heads of the bodhisattvas twice or thrice, entrusting them with the task of widespread dissemination.
This "entrustment" (*niyojana*) carries the sense of a burden—that is, the meaning of a laborious responsibility. It was for this reason that the Buddha [acted].
This is called the "Chapter on Entrustment" because it involves the entrustment of the Dharma to the future, relying upon the power and practice of the various bodhisattvas.
At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha had finished speaking the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers,"...

He rose from the Dharma-seat—rising from within the Dharma-seat of the Stūpa of Many Treasures—and manifested great supernormal powers by stroking the crowns of the heads of immeasurable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas with his right hand.

Were it not for the manifestation of such supernormal power, who could possibly stroke the crowns of all those immeasurable Bodhisattvas with his right hand? (The right hand symbolizes skillful means.)
The one of wisdom rubs his crown; the crown represents true wisdom.

He then speaks these words: "Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—from my first generation of the mind until the attainment of perfect enlightenment—I have passed through such *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
The cultivation of this dharma for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is difficult to achieve. One must practice, train in, and study such a bodhicitta that is so difficult to attain.
I now entrust it to you; I now transmit this dharma to you.
"You all should single-mindedly propagate this Dharma so that it may increase and flourish extensively.

If the mind is not single-minded, how can one accomplish such a task? Therefore, I exhort you Bodhisattvas to single-mindedly propagate this rare resolve, so that the seeds of the Dharma may gradually increase and flourish."
In this way, he stroked the heads of all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas three times; wishing to make them firm and steadfast, he spoke these words:
"I have practiced this for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The attainment of the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* has the same meaning as before.

[The Buddha] commands that it be entrusted to you: "You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma, and widely proclaim it. Thus he entrusts it to them, commanding that they maintain its recitation and cause it to be widely disseminated.
May all sentient beings everywhere hear and know this. It is because I wish for sentient beings to hear it and give rise to faith and understanding. Why is this? How can it be expanded?
The Tathāgata possesses great compassion; he is able to uproot the suffering of sentient beings and bestow upon them happiness.
Free from all stinginess, they possess no mind of parsimony whatsoever.
They are without fear, nor do they harbor any sense of dread.

They are able to bestow upon sentient beings the wisdom of the Buddha—the wondrous wisdom of ultimate enlightenment, in which the three delusions have been utterly extinguished, resulting in the fruit of the final fruition.
It is wisdom. The Tathāgata’s wisdom is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*), in which the one and the three are mutually identical, and cultivation and nature are non-dual.
It is spontaneous wisdom; it does not arise from cultivation or effort, but is the originally existing, truly pure, and equal Great Wisdom.
The Tathāgata is the great donor to all sentient beings. By means of the wisdom of suchness, he illuminates the realm of suchness;
since realm and wisdom are non-dual, he abides therein. Furthermore, by teaching this Dharma to all beings, he is called the Great Donor.
You all should likewise study the Dharma of the Tathāgata and not give rise to stinginess.
You should also instruct the bodhisattvas to study such Dharma accordingly, bestowing it upon sentient beings without harboring any stinginess.
In future ages, if there are good men or good women who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom—
those who are able to believe in and accept the Tathāgata’s true wisdom.
I shall expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* so that they may hear and know it;
I shall expound this sublime sūtra so that they may hear, understand, and realize its meaning and flavor.
It is for the purpose of causing that person to attain the Buddha-wisdom; it is desired that those who hear it may enter the wisdom of the wondrously enlightened Buddha.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept it, or if there are sentient beings whose conditions are shallow regarding this wondrous [teaching]...
If they are unable to believe the sūtras and receive them as taught,
one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound dharmas of the Tathāgata;
one should reveal and teach them within the profound dharmas of the Tathāgata’s other skillful means so that they may obtain benefit and give rise to great joy.
If you are able to act in this way, and if you can bestow the Way upon others according to their individual capacities,

then you will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas. Since it was the original vow of the Buddhas to deliver all sentient beings, to be able to accord with the Buddhas' intent is to repay the debt of gratitude to the Buddhas.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— those great bodhisattvas who had received the Buddha’s touch upon their heads—
having heard these words spoken by the Buddha and having heard the World-Honored One’s discourse on repaying kindness, [were filled with joy].
Great joy filled their entire bodies; the assembly was all filled with joy that pervaded their very beings.
Increasing their reverence, they bowed their bodies and lowered their heads, joining their palms toward the Buddha and speaking in unison.
Their veneration and admiration deepened as they bent their bodies and lowered their heads, all together raising their voices.
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall fully carry it out. As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has instructed, we shall prepare to practice accordingly.
Indeed, World-Honored One, please do not have any concern; we take this responsibility upon ourselves and shall not worry."
The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having thus repeated this three times, spoke with one voice, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall fully carry it out. Indeed, World-Honored One, may you have no further concern. Thus they requested that he have no concern three times.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded the various emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands.

This was because he wished for the bodhisattvas to see Prabhūtaratna, and because the task of assembling the emanated Buddhas to witness the sutra had been completed; thus, he ordered them to return each to their own original realms of transformation.
And they spoke these words: "May the various Buddhas each return to their respective abodes, and may the Stupa of Prabhūtaratna return to its former state.

May the Buddhas who have manifested as emanations each return to the abodes of their own original lands; the Stupa of Prabhūtaratna has already fulfilled its long-held vow and requests to return to the lower regions."
When these words were spoken, the countless Buddhas of the ten directions who were seated upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees,

as well as the emanated Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath bodhi trees in the four million billion nayutas of lands transformed in the eight directions during the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter, [all responded].
And as for Prabhūtaratna Buddha— the Buddha who emerged from beneath the earth and dwells within the jeweled stupa in the space below, as described in the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter—
and the vast assembly of boundless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, such as Urdhvaṅgama and others, these constitute the fifteen chapters from below.
There emerged from the earth an infinite number of *asaṃkhyeya* monks, such as the bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra who had long resided in this Sahā world and vowed to uphold this sutra,

as well as Śāriputra and the other members of the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas— namely, those great śrāvakas and their fourfold assemblies who were currently dwelling in the Sahā world and had received their predictions regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
As well as all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and the eight classes of beings,
having heard what the Buddha spoke, were all greatly filled with joy. Having heard the Tathāgata’s words regarding the various Buddhas returning to their own lands to listen to the Dharma,
and because each had attained clear realization within their own minds, they were all joyful.
In other sutras, after the entrustment (*parindanā*) has been heard, the great assembly immediately disperses.
However, at this Dharma Flower Assembly, following the entrustment, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña encounters [the Buddha] and inquires:
"For what reason does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja roam here? We wish to hear of his ascetic practices; please explain them."
The Buddha of the Body immediately vanished and did not appear again, yet Prabhūtaratna remained and the assembly likewise did not disperse.

Previously, in the "Entrusting" chapter, the Buddha rose from within the stupa, and Prabhūtaratna’s seat stood in mid-air; now, in this "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter, he is once again preaching upon the Dharma-seat at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the meaning of 'Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumita' is not yet clear to me.
How does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel through this Sahā world? Regarding 'Bhaiṣajyarāja,' the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states [that he is] without..."
From the beginning, he has come to serve as a skilled physician for the world; the World-Honored One has certified him, naming him Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The intention behind the questions of Sarvaratnapuṣpadhvaja is that he desires the World-Honored One to clarify past events and inspire the minds of those present.
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja has performed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of difficult and painful practices.
It is said, World-Honored One, that there are many painful practices among humans that are difficult to perform, which this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja has carried out.
Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this briefly. We do not dare to hear it in its entirety;
we pray that you will provide a concise exposition for the eight classes of beings: devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who had come from other lands, great bodhisattvas who had traveled from distant regions,
as well as this assembly of śrāvakas and the followers of the Hīnayāna in this land.
Upon hearing this, everyone was filled with joy and said as before, "The assembly all rejoices and wishes to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Śrīkūṭarāja): "In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
In the distant past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. This name was given because, in meaning, his Buddha-wisdom was as luminous as the sun and moon,
and his merit was pure and stainless.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—
these are as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
That Buddha had eight billion great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as Mahāyāna disciples,
and a great assembly of voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*) numbering seventy-two *gaṅgā*-sands as disciples of the two vehicles.
The Buddha’s lifespan shall be forty-two thousand kalpas; the lifespan of the Bodhisattvas dwelling in that world shall also be equal to his. Their lives will be equal to the Buddha’s.
That land shall have no women, for it is free from sexual desire.
There are no four evil realms—namely hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras—nor are there any of the various difficulties; there are no eight adversities.
The ground is level like the palm of a hand, for by leveling the mind-ground, the world-ground is also leveled.
It is composed of lapis lazuli; because the mind is luminously pure, the ground is also luminously pure.
It is adorned with jewel trees, with the practices and vows for enlightenment serving as the Bodhi tree.
A jeweled canopy covers it from above, representing the wisdom of the Buddha’s crown that cultivates the Buddha’s merit to universally cover its summit.
Hanging jeweled flower banners: the banners represent the form-body (*rūpakāya*), taking the sense of movement and vibration.
There are jeweled vases and incense burners: the jeweled vases signify that one guards the mouth like a vase so as not to let it tilt, thereby nurturing the various precious flowers;
the incense burners signify burning the incense of the mind to represent faith.
Throughout the entire realm, there were terraces made of the seven treasures; these terraces were themselves jeweled seats.
There was one terrace for each tree, with a jeweled terrace beneath every single tree.
Each tree stood at a distance of one arrow-shot from its terrace, and the jeweled trees were separated from one another by intervals of one arrow-shot, numbering one hundred and two.
It is ten paces away.
Beneath all these jewel trees sit bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; they are trees named Great Vows and seats named Abiding in the Dharma.
Upon each of the jeweled terraces dwell ten billion devas. All those who possess virtuous thoughts are called devas.
They perform celestial music and sing praises of the Buddha; the harmonious and joyful sounds of this music are termed "celestial music," extolling and praising the virtues of the Buddha.
He regarded this as making an offering. To act in accordance with the Buddha’s mind is called making an offering to the Buddha.
At that time, that Buddha [spoke] for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (Joyful-to-beheld-by-all-beings);
he was named Bhaiṣajyarāja in a previous life, and because of his compassion, he was one whom all beings delighted to behold.
As well as the assembly of bodhisattvas, the assembly of those of the Mahāyāna,
the assembly of śrāvakas, and the assembly of those of the Hīnayāna—
to them he preached the Lotus Sūtra; that Buddha also preached this wondrous sūtra for the sake of the assembly.
This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana delighted in practicing asceticism and desired to study and learn the path of rigorous austerity.
Within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he took refuge in that Buddha’s Dharma and established himself therein.
Exert oneself in walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). With single-minded cultivation and progress, one practices the Way day and night, coming and going straight as a thread on a loom;
this is called walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), which is the constant practice of *samādhi*.
He sought the Buddha with single-minded devotion; his heart was free from distracting thoughts as he resolved to seek the path of the Buddha.
After twelve thousand years had passed, having undergone such diligent and arduous practice for that length of time.
He attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies. Through diligent effort, he immediately realized the Universal Manifestation of Physical Bodies.
Having attained this samādhi, his heart was filled with great joy; because he had seen the Dharma, he obtained the bliss of samādhi.
He then thought to himself: "I have attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
That I have attained this concentration is entirely due to the power of hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. How is it that by merely hearing the sutra, one immediately attains samādhi?
The sutra enables one to direct the mind toward the universal transformation of all beings, such that before each and every sentient being, there appears my own body. Thus it is.
Therefore, I have been able to manifest my body everywhere by the power of this sutra.

I shall now make offerings to the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Bright Virtue and to the Lotus Sutra; for it is by hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and entering the Way through the Dharma that I have attained the Way, and having attained the Way, I contemplate making offerings to the Buddha and the sutra.
Immediately he entered this samādhi and manifested his body everywhere throughout space.
"Throughout space" signifies that from within emptiness and quiescence, he gives rise to the functional application of skillful means.
It rained *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers— two kinds of white flowers, large and small,
which signify pure conduct—
and fine, hard, black sandalwood powder; being of a solid black quality, it fell as a fine powder.
They descended like clouds, filling the entirety of space, signifying subtle practice.

Furthermore, they rained down the fragrance of *candana* from this shore of the ocean; for in Jambudvīpa, on this shore of the ocean, there emerges the most exquisite fragrance known as *gośīrṣa-candana*.
Six *zhū* of this incense is worth as much as the entire Sahā world. Two, two, and four *zhū* constitute one *liǎng*;
thus, six *zhū* is one-quarter of a *liǎng*. That the price of these six *zhū* equals the value of the Sahā realm signifies that it is most precious.
To make offerings to the Buddha—raining down flowers and presenting incense—is precisely to offer to the Buddha of one's own inherent nature (*svabhāva-guṇa-buddha*).
Having performed these offerings, he arises from samādhi; manifesting great supernormal transformations and having completed extensive offerings, he emerges once more from meditative concentration.
He then thought to himself: "Although I have made offerings to the Buddha through my supernormal powers, all the offerings previously manifested were external objects.
It would not be as good to make an offering with my own body; the body is an internal treasure and constitutes a truly great gift."
He then consumed various incenses, such as candana and agallochum— whose form resembles peach resin and whose leaves are like those of the pear tree— as well as tūlīpa,
white kuśa grass, pippalī, and clove.
Agallochum, aloeswood, resinous incense, and cypress-resin incense;
furthermore, they drink the yellow flowers of the *campaka*.

Various flower-essence oils: having infused the oil with various flower-fragrances so that it becomes fragrant, after twelve hundred years have passed, one likewise purifies the body for twelve hundred years.
He anointed his body with fragrant oils, such as osmanthus oil and other substances suitable for application to the body;
before the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he wrapped his body in celestial precious robes and poured over himself all kinds of fragrant oils.
First, he wrapped his body in cloth and then drenched it with oil until it resembled a candle.

By the power of his supernormal abilities (*ṛddhi*) and his vows, he manifested this natural body; through the power of his supernormal abilities and the force of his great vows, he set his own body ablaze—a body endowed with a hundred merits.

The light shines universally throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers. By means of his supernormal powers, he is able to illuminate these worlds numbering eighty billion times the sands of the Ganges;
this signifies the illumination and destruction of the afflictions of the eight consciousnesses.
Therein, all the Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Wherever the light shone, the Buddhas likewise praised him:
"Good son, this is true diligence. If one were to offer material gifts, it would not be considered difficult; however, to offer one's own body as an offering is indeed difficult."
This is true diligence.

This is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. To renounce body, life, and wealth while practicing giving according to the Dharma—yet if one does not understand that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and the four great elements do not exist, how could one truly renounce? Because one perceives the emptiness of phenomena, it is called the "Dharma."
To offer gifts that accord with true emptiness is therefore called the true dharma-offering.
If one offers flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, celestial silks, banners, and canopies, these are offerings of the sense-object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
And even the sandalwood incense from this side of the ocean—
such various substances for making offerings as these cannot equal it. All of these external objects fall short of the gift of one's own body.
Even the giving away of kingdoms, cities, wives, and children does not equal it.
The gift of kingdoms and cities is an external reward, while the gift of wives and children is an internal reward; yet both fall short of the gift of one's own body.
Good son, this is called the foremost gift; among all gifts, it is the most honored and supreme, surpassing all other gifts.
Because one makes an offering of the Dharma to all Tathāgatas, and because such a person perceives the emptiness of phenomena, they are able to relinquish their body.
Having spoken these words for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgatas, they each became silent. After the Buddhas had praised them, they then remained silent. Now, [the question arises]:
"The body is a foul substance; its entire form is impure. Even if one pours fragrant oil over it and burns it, it still reeks. Why would the Buddhas take pleasure in this?"
These offerings are all praised as "excellent" and are called the true Dharma-offering; one should know this meaning:

if one can empty the body, then there is no object whatsoever that is not empty. One who perceives emptiness is then able to be unimpeded; because the mind is unimpeded, all obstructions are immediately empty.
When even emptiness itself is emptied, and emptiness reaches its ultimate limit, awakening is fulfilled—this is true liberation.
His body burned for twelve hundred years; it is said that it lasted for such a long time.
After this period had passed, his body was finally consumed.
Having thus completed the task of burning his body, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed such a Dharma-offering, he relinquished his life.
After his life came to an end, he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Sun-and-Moon Pure Bright Virtue;
there, he again manifested in the world, taking birth in the family of King Pure Virtue.
He sat cross-legged. Through the power of his supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), he manifested a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) by means of miraculous birth.
Having suddenly manifested through transformation, he spoke this verse to his father: "Since you have been born through transformation, how can there be a father?
It is merely because you were entrusted to a royal house that you are called the father of a king."
"Great King, you should now know that I practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) at that place.

As stated in the passage above, 'through diligent walking meditation,' I immediately attained the *Sarvakāyapratibhāsa-samādhi*. Because I gave rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) from this samādhi of diligence, I am able to universally manifest all physical bodies."
Exerting great diligence, he sacrificed his beloved body. This summarizes how his previous bodies were able to renounce what they cherished and attain the path.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Sun-Moon-Pure-Virtue-Brilliance is still currently present. O Bodhisattva...
While the Tathāgata, who previously practiced austerities and attained *nirvāṇa*, has a lifespan as long as he still exists in the present world,
I first made offerings to that Buddha and attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings;
I am able to fully comprehend all the various sounds and voices of all sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions, and thus I am named "One Who Understands All Sentient Beings."
The Samādhi of Eloquence.
Furthermore, he heard eight hundred thousand million billion nayutas of *khaṅkāra*, *bimbara*, and *akṣobhya* verses from this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
"Eight hundred thousand million" means eight hundred times one thousand million. (West)
The great numbers of the earth consist of fifty-two types: *viṃvara* is the sixteenth, *bimbara* is the eighteenth, and *akṣobhya* is the twentieth;
since there are thirty-two more types following these, it is said "and so forth."
"Great King, I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha. He then proceeded to make offerings to the Buddha Pure Bright Virtue.
Having finished his address, he sat upon a terrace of the seven treasures; that is, the precious throne.
He ascended into the void, leaping into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees—each *tāla* being approximately seven feet, totaling about five zhang.

He proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet; he went to that Buddha’s presence and paid reverent homage by bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet.
He prostrated himself, joining his ten fingers and toes together, and praised the Buddha’s countenance with a verse: "The Buddha’s blessed countenance is most wondrous;
how marvelous is his appearance!"
The light shines throughout the ten directions. [He] praises the Buddha’s wisdom-light as it illuminates the worlds of the ten directions.
"I have already made offerings"—that is to say, in a previous life, he had already made offerings.
Now, "returning once more to behold him in person" means that he encountered the World-Honored One again upon his re-appearance in the world.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
[This is the narrative of the sutra-author, recorded by Ānanda.]
"World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world. Because this Bodhisattva has been reborn and is once again able to see the Buddha, he speaks these words.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, saying: "Because of his joy..."
Seeing that he had asked why the Buddha was still emerging, [the Buddha] told him:
"Good son, the time for my nirvāṇa has arrived. This means that my work of transformation is finished and I am about to return to the truth.
The moment of cessation has come; this means I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"You should prepare a seat for me at the place where I am to enter parinirvāṇa.
This very night, I shall attain parinirvāṇa. All Buddhas are born during the day to signify the light of the sun;
all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa at midnight to signify the darkness. The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of the multitude."
When the World-Honored One, who was born as the Eye, entered parinirvāṇa, the ten directions were all plunged into darkness.
Furthermore, he commanded the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Son of good family, I entrust the Buddha-dharma to you.
That is to say, I consign to you the treasury of the Buddha’s meritorious Dharma, charging you to maintain and propagate it in future generations."
He entrusted his disciples to the various bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas, charging them to instruct and guide them,
as well as the dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. While it was previously stated that the Buddha-dharma was universally entrusted to the Tripiṭaka,
this present dharma of *bodhi* refers to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*).
Furthermore, the great trichiliocosm world of the seven treasures is the land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*).
Therein, the various jewel trees and jewel terraces are such that the trees represent the King of Vows and the terraces represent the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

As well as the attendant devas: those who served and protected the Buddha while he was in the world, and now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, those who have been entrusted to transmit the Dharma—all these I entrust to you;
I commit them all to you, He Who Sees with Joy.
"After my parinirvāṇa, all my relics are also entrusted to you. These relics are the Buddha’s bone-body, refined through the cultivation of morality, concentration, and wisdom;
they are exceedingly difficult to obtain and constitute the supreme field of merit. Therefore, I entrust them to you, Priyadarśana;
you must protect and uphold them well."
One should cause it to be widely circulated and establish extensive offerings; one should cause sentient beings to circulate and offer worship.
One should erect several thousand stūpas, and further cause stūpas to be erected to enshrine the śarīras.
After the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had thus instructed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana,
and after the Buddha Vimalaprabhāsa had given his final charge as described above,
he entered parinirvāṇa in the latter part of the night; that is, he passed away immediately following midnight.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana saw the Buddha pass into parinirvāṇa. Witnessing with his own eyes the Tathāgata entering extinction, he was moved by grief and distress, longing for the Buddha;
his sorrowful lamentation was so profound that it stirred him to yearn for the Buddha’s virtues in deep anguish and attachment.
Mou immediately used the sandalwood from this side of the sea to form a pyre; the sandalwood from this side of the sea was *gośīrṣa-candana*,
which he gathered together to form the pyre.
He made offerings to the Buddha’s body and cremated it, using incense as fuel to burn the Buddha.
After the fire had been extinguished, he collected the śarīras and gathered the remains of the body.

He fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars; using these jewels as vessels, he enshrined the śarīra within them and erected eighty-four thousand stūpas, establishing one stūpa for each precious jar.
The three high worlds represent the culmination of the three periods of time.

The adornment of the *kṣetra* represents the establishment of the *kṣetra*-pole; by establishing the *kṣetra*-pole, it signifies that the Buddha reveals the *kṣetra* so that all who are deluded may know the direction toward which they should proceed.
Banners and canopies were hung down, and various precious bells were suspended, each symbolizing something as explained in detail previously.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana again thought to himself. After the stupa had been constructed, he further reflected:
Although I have made these offerings, my heart is still not satisfied; my aspiration remains unfulfilled.
I shall now make further offerings to the relics. This is my intention.
He then addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and all others present, informing the great multitude:
"You should all maintain single-minded mindfulness. He exhorted them to collect their minds, become tranquil, and abide in right mindfulness with a focused mind.
"I now make offerings to the relics of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. I shall now make offerings to the relics of the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, he immediately set ablaze his arm—adorned with the hundred blessings—in front of the eighty-four thousand stupas. Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva’s arm was adorned by the cultivation of a hundred merits, yet he offered it to the Buddha.
He made this offering for seventy-two thousand years; here, "seventy" represents the seven meritorious virtues, and "two thousand" represents the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
He causes countless seekers of the Śrāvaka vehicle and those seeking the Lesser Vehicle to be taught so that they enter the Great Vehicle.
Immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people who have newly entered the Path resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and give rise to the mind of the Great Way.
They caused all to dwell in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies. They caused the multitude to dwell in the concentration of manifesting physical bodies.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and so forth—the eight classes of beings consisting of humans and devas—[all attained this state].
Seeing him without arms, they were distressed and filled with sorrow. Seeing that the Bodhisattva lacked the hundred-fold blessed arms, they all took pity on him and said:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher; he is the one upon whom we rely."
"The one who has taught and guided me is now burning his arm, so that his body is no longer complete; because he has burned his arm, his physical marks are incomplete.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made this vow before the great assembly: "O Buddha..."
Seeing that the assembly did not understand that form is empty, the Bodhisattva made a vow to manifest its illusory nature:
"I shall give up both my arms and shall surely attain the golden body of a Buddha. The Bodhisattva considered this principle to be naturally so.
"If it is true and not false—if this matter is indeed real and not false—may my two arms be restored to their former state. Having spoken thus before the great assembly, he said:
Having made this vow, his two arms naturally returned to their original state as before.
This was brought about by the fact that the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom were pure, profound, and thick. Why did his arms return to their former state after being burned?
It was because they were summoned by the Bodhisattva’s dedication to reality through merit, and his pure, deep, and profound understanding of emptiness through wisdom.
At that moment,
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; such was the manifestation induced by the power of his supernormal knowledges and vows.
Heavenly rain fell of precious flowers; the devas, seeing this, rejoiced and scattered flowers as an offering.
All humans and devas attained what they had never experienced before. Once burned, the incense returned to its original state, a marvel unprecedented in the world.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña: "What do you think? What is your opinion?
Is the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana anyone else? It is none other than the present Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja."
The one who was then named Priyadarśana is none other than the present-day Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The number of times he has thus sacrificed his body as an act of giving is immeasurable—countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
Not only once did he perform such ascetic practices; the instances from which he has come, sacrificing his body in worship, are beyond counting.
Sudhana-śrīkusuma, if there is one who resolves their mind to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
or any person who resolves their mind to seek enlightenment,
and is able to burn a finger or even a toe as an offering to a Buddha-stūpa— with no other intent than this— Buddha alone [will know it].
It is essential that a person have some awareness of pain and pleasure;
yet, compared to [the merit of] giving away one's kingdom, cities, wife, and children— wherein the kingdom and cities are what one dwells in and the wife and children are what one loves—
even such giving does not equal the sacrifice of one's own body.

Furthermore, as for the mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds of the trichiliocosm, the lands upon which they depend, and all manner of rare treasures and objects of pleasure—these are external things; how could they compare to the sacrifice of one's own body?
Regarding those who make offerings: offering material wealth does not equal the sacrifice of one's own body.
Furthermore, suppose there were someone who filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures to offer to the Buddha;
or suppose another person likewise filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures to offer to the Buddha.
As well as great bodhisattvas and pratyekabuddhas— these being the "solitary realizers"—
and arhats, which is translated here as "non-arising," referring to those who have attained the four fruits of sanctity:
the merit obtained by such persons is the merit acquired by the person who practices giving.
It is not as meritorious as receiving and upholding even a single four-line verse of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for its merit is the greatest.
While giving results in conditioned merit, upholding the sūtra enables one to attain untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*);
thus, even the merit of upholding a four-line verse cannot compare with it, let alone that of one who upholds the entire sūtra.
Ratnakusuma, it is like this: for example, among all the streams, rivers, and torrents of water, the ocean is foremost;
all currents flow toward the ocean.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this; it is just like the great ocean.
Among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, this is the most profound and vast. It is called "profound" because it speaks most extensively of the Buddha’s wisdom;
it is called "vast" because there is no capacity for which it does not provide a means, and no phenomenon that it does not encompass.
Furthermore, there are the Earth Mountains, the Black Mountains, and the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains that encircle the four continents;
the Great Iron Ring Mountains that encircle the great trichiliocosm;
and the Ten Jewel Mountains, which are the ten great mountain kings outside of Mount Sumeru.
Among all mountains, Mount Sumeru is the foremost. Mount Sumeru arises from the great ocean and rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the surface of the water.
This Lotus Sūtra is also like this. It is like Mount Sumeru, being the most supreme among all sūtras, the king of all sūtras.
It is also like the Moon Deva-son, who is the foremost among the many stars, the king of the constellations.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this.
Just as the Moon Deity is the most illuminating among the thousands of millions of various sūtras and dharmas, so too do the lights of other skillful means illuminate the three vehicles,
whereas the light of wisdom from this sūtra illuminates ultimate awakening.
Furthermore, just as the Sun Deva is able to dispel all darkness— when the sun's rays emerge,
they shatter all gloom— so too is this sutra: it can destroy the darkness of all that is unwholesome, exhaustively eliminating the three delusions to bring about the path of the single reality.
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the most supreme;
while other lesser kings each rule over a single country, the Wheel-Turning Sage King governs the four continents under heaven.
This sutra is likewise so; among all sutras it is the most honored, the king of kings of sutras that governs all.
It is also like Śakra, the king of the thirty-three heavens, who has eight heavenly kings on each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
Among the gods dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Śakra alone is supreme, while the remaining thirty-two all honor Śakra as their lord.
This sutra is likewise so: it is the king among all sutras, the most honored among the multitude of scriptures.

Furthermore, just as the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings, and the Honored Heaven of Great Brahmā, as the lord of the three realms, is regarded by all sentient beings as their father; so too is [the Buddha].
This sutra is likewise so for all noble ones, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
"All noble ones" refers here to those within the three vehicles up to the third fruit, who are called those in training; the arhats of the fourth fruit are called those beyond training.

Furthermore, he is the father of those who have resolved to attain the bodhicitta; for while the Bodhisattva belongs to the stage of causes, the Buddha represents the fruit, and thus he is the father.
Moreover, among all ordinary persons, the Srotāpanna—here translated as "Stream-enterer"—is one who has first attained the fruit of sainthood.
They are included among the noble ones (*ārya*).
The *Sakṛdāgāmin*—here translated as "Once-returner"—having realized the second fruit, returns once more to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to undergo birth one final time.
The *Anāgāmin*—here translated as "Non-returner"—having realized the third fruit, dwells in the heavens of the fourth dhyāna and does not return to the desire realm.

Arhat. This is translated as "one who does not arise," meaning that because the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted, one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning and is no longer born within the three realms.
The Pratyekabuddha is the foremost; this is translated as "Conditionally Enlightened One" because they contemplate the principle of emptiness through the twelve links of dependent origination.

They are also called "Solitary Enlightened Ones" because they dwell alone on remote peaks and can awaken to realization by themselves. As for the Śrāvaka at the stage of fruition, they merely sever the manifest outflows (*āsrava*).
One who has attained awakening further subdues their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and dwells above the four fruits of the śrāvaka path; therefore, they are called "foremost.
This sutra is likewise so: it is the skillful means (*upāya*) and provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) spoken by all Tathāgatas.
Whether spoken by a Bodhisattva or by a Śrāvaka, these sutras and dharmas are the most supreme among all.
Because the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) of the Supreme Vehicle subsumes all provisional and Hinayana teachings, it is called "supreme."
It is likewise for one who is able to receive and uphold this sutra; among all sentient beings, such a person is also foremost.
Those who uphold other sutras have their station within the three vehicles, but if one upholds this sutra, they shall attain the path of Buddhahood and be the most supreme among all people.
Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is foremost; among the three vehicles, the bodhisattva stands at the pinnacle.
This sutra is likewise so, being the most supreme among all sūtras and dharmas. Among all...
Among the sūtras, this sūtra is the most supreme.
Just as the Buddha is the King of all Dharmas, so too is this sūtra the king among all sūtras. First it is compared to ordinary beings;
next to those of the Two Vehicles; thirdly to Bodhisattvas; and fourthly to the Tathāgata. Thus, by comparing it to increasingly superior levels, the excellence of this sūtra is revealed.
1. O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this sutra is able to save all sentient beings; this Lotus Sutra is able to act as a protector and refuge for sentient beings.
This sutra can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction; it can cause them to be free from all the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death.
This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations. Those who uphold this sutra...
The aspirations for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood are all fulfilled.
Just as a cool pond can satisfy all who suffer from thirst, so too when those who are parched with thirst obtain water they are rescued;
when sentient beings obtain the water of the Dharma-principle and it enters their hearts, they are freed from all withered desiccation.

It is like one who is cold obtaining fire; when the cold person obtains fire, they are freed from the suffering of freezing, and sentient beings obtain the warmth of the Dharma and gradually draw near to it.

It is like one who is naked obtaining clothing; when the naked person obtains clothing, they are freed from the shame of baring their form, and sentient beings enter the Dharma and attain patience (*kṣānti*).
It is like a merchant who has found his master; just as a merchant seeks refuge with his master, so too must a student prioritize the realization of their true nature.
It is like a child finding its mother; when the child finds its mother, it is freed from orphanhood and exposure. When sentient beings obtain this sutra, they achieve the body of a sage.
It is like a traveler finding a boat; when the traveler finds a boat, they pass through rivers and streams without hindrance. When students obtain this sutra, all obstacles are completely eliminated.
It is like a sick person finding a physician; once the patient finds a physician, the body becomes peaceful and recovers. When a student obtains this sutra, their mind is free from sorrow and fear.

It is like obtaining a lamp in the darkness; when a lamp is obtained in a dark place, all things become visible, and for sentient beings who attain liberation, the obscuring barriers are secretly eliminated.
It is like a poor person obtaining treasure; once a poor person obtains treasure, they are freed from destitution, and so too does the student manifest wisdom and become fully endowed with it.
It is sufficient.
It is like subjects obtaining a king; only when the subjects obtain their king can they survive. So too, only when a student realizes their nature can their mind find peace.

Just as a merchant gains access to the sea, so too does a traveler reach the ocean; as a vessel crosses the waters to reach its destination, so too does a student awaken their nature and perceive the principle with clarity and precision.
Just as a torch dispels darkness, so too can a torch destroy the gloom; likewise, the Sūtra can eliminate delusion.
This Lotus Sūtra is likewise so. It refers to the various parables mentioned above;

it is able to cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering—namely, the three types of suffering, the five types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, the two types of death, and other such sufferings.

All illnesses and pains—the illnesses and pains of the world arise from karmic retribution; by cultivating the body with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one will be free from sickness and affliction, and will be able to untie all the bonds of birth and death.
Those who do not perceive the principle are bound by birth and death; yet if they awaken to the principle...
At that time, one attains mastery.
If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*— whether hearing it with their own ears that such a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* exists,
or hearing it through its exposition— [they shall attain mastery].
Whether one writes it oneself with one's own hand,
or causes another to write it by hiring someone else to do so,
the merit obtained is the very merit acquired by the person who has written the scripture.
Even by measuring its extent with the wisdom of a Buddha, one cannot find its limit; even with the Buddha’s insight, it cannot be fully known, let alone by other sages and worthies.
If one were to write out this sutra scroll, it is because one desires to make offerings while writing this sutra.
With flowers, incense, necklaces, burnt incense, powdered incense, and unguents— using these fragrant flowers as offerings—
and with banners, canopies, and robes— using these as offerings.
"Various kinds of lamps": this phrase provides the general heading.
"Ghee lamps and oil lamps" refers to lamps made of ghee, clear oils, various fragrant oils, and oils infused with various fragrances.
The *campaka* oil lamp—this is translated as "yellow flower"; originally there was no oil, so the flower itself was used for immersion.
The *sumanā* oil lamp—this is translated as "flower that accords with one's wishes."
The *pārala* oil lamp; this is called the *punarnavā* flower.
The *bharisaka* oil lamp; this is called the *utpala* flower.
The *nāvamālī* oil lamp; *nāva* here means "various flowers," and *mālī* is also called *mallikā*.
One should now perform offerings.
By offering various fragrant oils to light lamps as an offering, the merit obtained will likewise be immeasurable.
This concludes the section on making offerings of banners, canopies, robes, incense, flowers, and oil lamps.
Those who roll up [this sutra] shall also obtain immeasurable merit.

Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there be anyone who hears this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," it is equivalent to having previously performed acts of asceticism such as burning one's body, arms, or fingers.
One shall also attain immeasurable and boundless merit. By hearing even a single virtuous word, the mind follows toward goodness; thus, one is able to likewise obtain boundless merit.
If there is a woman who hears this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," and that woman hears this [chapter], she shall... [the woman] who hears this Bhaiṣajya...
Chapter on the King:
Those who are able to receive and uphold [this teaching] do so by hearing it, revering it with faith, and upholding it with a firm mind.
After exhausting this female body, they shall no longer receive one; after exhausting this retribution as a woman, they shall subsequently receive a male body.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years— which refers to the present age of the Dharma’s decline—
there should be a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teaching; that is, having heard the sutra,
she relies upon and acts in accordance with what is taught therein.
Having ended their life here, after the conclusion of this retributive life in this Sahā world,
they shall immediately go to the Land of Peace and Bliss— the Western Pure Land of Amitābha.

Amitābha Buddha—here translated as the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—is the place where he dwells surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas; it is the place where the Buddha resides encircled by the great assembly of bodhisattvas.
They are born upon jeweled thrones within lotus flowers—referring here to the precious lotus pedestals of the nine grades of rebirth—and are no longer afflicted by desire.
For what reason does one hear this *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* Sūtra and immediately cast off the female body to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss?
It is because of craving that one receives a female body; now, having heard of the self-sacrifice of Bhaiṣajyarāja, [one abandons it].
By awakening to the fact that the nature of form is empty, one does not give rise to craving or attachment, and thus is able to be liberated.
Furthermore, one is no longer afflicted by anger or delusion. When one feels envy toward forms and gives rise to anger, now knowing that form is empty, one stills the mind of anger.
When craving and anger are not abandoned, and one fails to distinguish between the noble and the lowly, as well as different species, this is the mind of delusion. Now...
Because of this sutra, hatred and delusion are also extinguished;
furthermore, one is no longer afflicted by the defilements of arrogance, jealousy, and the like. When there is a mind of arrogance, one looks down upon those who are inferior;
when there is a mind of jealousy, one harbors resentment toward servants and concubines. These defilements pollute one's own mind; now, because of this sutra, one turns the mind back toward [virtue].
When all illnesses are naturally eliminated, one is no longer afflicted.

One attains the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This clarifies that once the mind has awakened and been born in the Pure Land, one has already attained the causes for supernormal powers and realization;
because of non-attachment, one abides in the samādhi of empty stillness and thereby brings forth sovereign supernormal powers. By virtue of this...
Through patient endurance (*kṣānti*), one realizes that all phenomena are empty and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, the faculty of the eye becomes purified. Because form destroys the eye, it makes one a slave to craving and affection;
when the eye does not cling to form, the faculty is then purified.

By means of these purified faculties of the eye, one beholds as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in seven million two thousand *koṭis* of *nayutas* of Ganges Rivers. "Seven million" signifies the correspondence with the sevenfold merits;

"two thousand *koṭis*" signifies the manifestation of the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional; and because the faculty of the eye is pure, all seven branches of both emptiness and existence [are perceived].
Regarding the objects of perception, through the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the aggregates, one perceives that all marks are none other than the Buddha.

At this time, all Buddhas praise him from afar. They are said to "praise from afar" because, although his essence is fundamentally [Buddha], he is still far removed from the state of fruition when viewed from the perspective of his causal stage.

Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able [to do so] within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha—since this present "Chapter on the Medicine King" was spoken by the Buddha—it is said that you are able [to do so] within the Dharma of Śākyamuni.
To uphold, recite, and contemplate this sutra is self-benefit;
to explain it for others is the benefit of others. One who thus benefits both self and others is called a bodhisattva.
The merit obtained is immeasurable and boundless; its benefit is profound.
Fire cannot burn it, for by the power of patience, one cannot be consumed by any fire of anger.
Water cannot wash it away. Because you have severed craving, the waters of all greed cannot sweep you away.

Your merits could not be exhausted even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of them together; even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of the merits you have attained simultaneously, they still could not exhaust them.

You have now been able to defeat the various demonic marauders. There are four kinds of demons: namely, the demon of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the celestial demon (*devaputra-māra*).
The first three are internal demons; the fourth is the external marauder. There are six kinds of thieves:

the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) act as men, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) act as women, and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) act as go-betweens. They plunder the treasures of one's own home; yet, when one realizes that their nature is empty and quiescent, the sense organs and sense objects become pure.
When one purifies external demons so that they do not create internal obstacles and eliminates them in secret, this is called "destroying the demonic marauders.
It means destroying the army of birth and death. When greed, hatred, and delusion give rise to karma of body and speech, one undergoes birth and death;
however, when objects are no longer perceived by the sense faculties, there is nothing with which to pair, and thus the army of birth and death is destroyed.

All other enemies shall be utterly crushed and destroyed. Once the great array is broken, remaining delusions will vanish of their own accord, just as frost and dew are entirely dried up when the sun rises.
Son of good family, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas shall together protect you with their supernormal powers; all discursive thoughts [shall likewise cease].

All these are transformed into goodness; these wholesome thoughts constantly protect the single mind, which is called being protected by the combined supernatural powers of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
Among all the devas and humans in every world, there is none like you. A Bodhisattva who has attained patience abides in their own [nature].
In terms of spiritual penetration, how could humans or devas possibly compare?

Only the Tathāgata is an exception; with the single exception of the Tathāgata, none among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even bodhisattvas possess wisdom and meditative concentration equal to yours.
Among the three vehicles, the Bodhisattva is the most supreme. Compared to the present person of perfect [enlightenment], the provisional teachings of the Bodhisattvas cannot reach this level.
O Śrīmalanemi, this Bodhisattva has accomplished such power of merit and wisdom. This is the power of merit.
Therefore, by virtue of having accomplished the power of merit, retribution, and wisdom, one extinguishes all birth and death.
If there are those who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," can rejoice and praise it as good;
or those who, upon hearing this sutra, comply with it with joy and praise it, saying, "Excellent! (sādhu).
In this person’s present life, their mouth constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses; as they speak of virtuous matters, fragrance issues from their mouth.
From the pores of their body, the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood constantly emanates; because their body is pure, the fragrance flows from within.
Fragrance issues from the pores of his body;
the merit he thereby attains is as previously described—referring to the passage cited above.
For this reason, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" to you.
The practice of austerities was entrusted to King Śubhavyūha with the exhortation that people should perform them.
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years" refers to the first five hundred years of the ten-thousand-year period of the Final Dharma (mappō),
which is the present time.
"Proclaim and disseminate it widely; entrust it so that it may be extensively taught and spread throughout the world.
Let it not be severed within Jambudvīpa. Jambudvīpa is named after the *jambu* tree; "dvīpa" refers to the Southern Continent.
Ensure that the seeds of the Dharma always continue without interruption.
The evil Māra and his subjects; the Māra-king himself who slays, and his subjects who are his followers;
as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth—these are all non-Buddhist māras and not the devas, nāgas, or kumbhāṇḍas who protect the Dharma.
As for the kumbhāṇḍas, they are the ghosts of malevolent enchantments.
They seek such opportunities; do not allow Māras or outsiders to find common ground for their advantage.
Suvarnapuṣpa, you should protect this sutra through the power of your supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
By means of the great supernormal powers you have realized, you must constantly provide protection for this scripture.
Why is this? For what reason is such a solemn entrustment made?
This sutra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa; it can cure both the diseases of the physical body and those of the mind.
If a person who is ill hears this sutra, their illness will immediately be extinguished. By knowing the practice of this sutra, one naturally recovers from illness and shall neither age nor die.
How is it that by upholding this sutra one attains non-aging and non-death? It is as in the case of Sadāparibhūta, whose lifespan was further increased.
Life itself is its proof.

Śrīgarbhapuṣpa, if you see anyone who upholds this sutra, or if you encounter such a person, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them over them. Blue is the color of the eastern direction.
The incense at the end represents benevolence, and the fine conduct represents the practice; because the upholder of the sūtra acts with a compassionate mind, he scatters it.
Having scattered it, he forms this thought: "Having made this offering of flowers, I should form this thought."
Before long, this person will surely take grass and sit upon it at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The Buddha of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), Śākyamuni Tathāgata, observed that all Buddhas of the three periods of time attain enlightenment beneath trees;
seeing the one who was cutting grass, he stood before him. That person asked, "Do you not wish [to do so]? The World-Honored One remained silent. The man then gathered [the grass].
Because he took grass offered by a grass-cutter to serve as his seat beneath a tree, where he sat in peaceful meditation and attained unsurpassed enlightenment,
it is said that before long he would surely take grass and sit beneath a tree at the Bodhi-maṇḍa.
He shall vanquish the armies of Māra. Manifesting the attainment of enlightenment, he causes the palaces of Māra to tremble; since Māra comes to wage war, he must be defeated.
One should then blow the Dharma conch. When the sound of the conch resounds, it marks the change of title for all Buddhas as they preach the Dharma and transform the mundane into the sacred.
The Sage then changed his title to "One Who Blows the Conch" (Yimyeong Chwirwa).

He beats the great Dharma drum. The time of beating the drum is precisely when the assembly gathers and the Buddha proclaims the sound of the Dharma; as the assembly gathers to listen attentively, it is called "beating the Dharma drum."
To deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of old age, sickness, and death;
to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death—for this reason, those who seek the Buddha-way, and indeed all who seek the Way, [should do so].
If one sees a person who upholds this sutra, or sees one who holds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one should give rise to a mind of reverence in this manner;
one should give rise to a mind of respect as described above.

When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being spoken, and as the Buddha spoke these words, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
They realized that all phrases are but a single phrase. What is this single phrase? It is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Those who attain this realization are called [possessors of] the *dhāraṇī*.
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, within the jeweled stupa, because the Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha had not yet departed, praised the Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śubhavyūha! It is well that you have asked such an excellent question."
Because your mind was sufficiently encouraged by your practice of austerities, I praised your goodness.
You have accomplished inconceivable merit; the merit of raising this question is difficult to fathom.
That you are able to ask Śākyamuni Buddha about such matters as these— that is, the aforementioned matters of ascetic practice—
which benefit immeasurable and all sentient beings— how could those who hear of them not see the worthy and strive to emulate them? What benefit is there [in this]?
The ultimate reaches have no limit or measure.

From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-four, "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," onwards, the preceding chapters follow one another in sequence, each having its own beginning and conclusion. Following the section on the Entrustment (*parindanā*), it proceeds because of the *Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña*.
In the "Chapter on the Past Deeds Spoken by Bhaiṣajyarāja," Mañjuśrī questions Bhaiṣajyarāja regarding his past conduct;

in the "Chapter on the Praise of Austerities for the Sake of Transforming Others," it is told how this Sudarśana (Wonderful Sound) arrived from afar due to the Buddha’s emission of light; having previously made offerings with music to the Buddha Ghanagarjitasvara (Cloud-Thunder-Sound), he now obtained this name, as explained in detail below.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted light from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the protuberance on the crown of the head among the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Upon the summit of the Buddha’s head was a mass of flesh shaped like a topknot;
the emission of light from this *uṣṇīṣa* symbolizes the foremost Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle.

Then he emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows. At the *yintang* (the point between the two eyebrows), there was a single white tuft of hair one zhang and five chi in length, its color like white jade or snow; it curled between the brows and had eight facets on the outside, being hollow inside like a tube.
Whenever he emitted radiance, it issued from the center of this tuft, appearing in the space between the two brows, which represents the middle way between the two truths.
The white tuft of hair symbolizes the ultimate truth of the Middle Way;
it shines universally throughout the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, numbering as many as one hundred and eight million billion nayutas of Ganges sands.
The eastern position of the trigram Zhen represents the earth of movement; its measure of one hundred and eight myriads of koṭis signifies the eighteen *dhātus*.
Beyond this number lies a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-alaṃkāra*).

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the Buddhas of the ten directions each cultivate within these eighteen realms and all attain perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*); to transcend these eighteen is the state of all Buddhas.
Pure Radiance Adornment.
In that land there is a Buddha named Pure Lotus Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Viśuddhapadmanakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña*). As the sutra states:

"Because he is pure and upright like a lotus flower in water, he is called 'Pure Lotus Flower'; because his wisdom is perfected like the Moon Deity, the king among the constellations, he is called 'Constellation King Wisdom.'"
Because his brilliance is like that of the moon, he is called "Wisdom of the Constellation King" (Sukhāvatī-vyuha).
He is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
These titles are explained as in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidānaparivarta).

He was respectfully surrounded by an immeasurable and boundless assembly of bodhisattvas as he preached the Dharma for them; the Buddha, surrounded by the assembly’s reverence, preached the Dharma for them.
As for Śākyamuni Buddha: "Śākya" means "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren), and "Muni" means "Silent Sage" (Jimo).
The radiance of his white tuft of hair shines universally throughout that land. The radiance from the tuft of Śākyamuni’s hair illuminates the Land of Pure Adornment.

At that time, in the Land of Universal Adornment of Pure Light, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara who had long since planted the roots of all virtues and had long since practiced and cultivated the roots of goodness for Buddhahood.
They have made offerings to and drawn near hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
they have already served a multitude of Buddhas and have fully accomplished profound wisdom. This profound wisdom is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha.

One attains the Samādhi of the Sublime Banner Mark (*Sudarśana-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*). "Samādhi" is here translated as "right concentration. Attaining this profound and wondrous concentration and abiding therein immovably is called the "Sublime Banner Mark.
As for the *Dharmapada-samādhi* (Lotus Samādhi):
the mind and dharmas are perfectly clear and pure, free from defilement, like a king of lotuses blooming and reflecting in water.
The Samādhi of Pure Virtue (*Viśuddhaguṇa*): Cultivating all forms of goodness while remaining detached from all signs is called "Pure Virtue.
The Samādhi of the Play of the Constellation King (*Jyotirāja-vikrīḍita*): With a mind luminous and unimpeded, one wanders in ultimate emptiness like the king of the constellations.

He dwells in the *asamāhita-samādhi* (the concentration of non-concentration). The Tathāgata’s great compassion is of three kinds: first, compassion with sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), which gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness by taking the realm of sentient beings as its condition;
second, compassion with phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), which contemplates all phenomena as entirely empty and quiescent, and does not perceive [them as real].
Arising from the great mind of compassion that transcends all obstructions, this is the threefold objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*);

without mental objects or conceptual thoughts, it responds to all sentient beings as soon as they have a need, reaching everywhere without hindrance, like the reflection of the pure lunar disc appearing in ten thousand bodies of water.
The Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom: by means of the seal of true wisdom, one realizes that all phenomena are true within their very falsity.

The Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings: regarding the diverse speech uttered by the various classes of sentient beings, the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration and wisdom are fully capable of understanding them all.
The Samādhi of Gathering All Meritorious Qualities is able to gather all boundless merits within right concentration.
The Samādhi of Purity realizes that the nature is fundamentally empty, transcending dust and leaving behind defilement.
The Samādhi of Playful Supernatural Powers: by means of supernatural power, one manifests various forms and travels throughout the entire dharma-realm to transform all sentient beings.
The Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom: one attains the great illumination of wisdom, which, like a torch, dispels darkness.
The Samādhi of the King of Adornments: one adorns oneself with the adornments of the Buddha.
The Samādhi of Pure Radiance: one illuminates all things with pure and wondrous light.
The Samādhi of Pure Treasury; the Samādhi of the Unshared Buddha, which abides in the Tathāgata’s secret treasury with a pure mind and is not shared with the three vehicles;
and the Sun-Turning Samādhi, in which pure wisdom is as clear and pervasive as the revolving sun.
Because there are many such samādhis, I have briefly indicated them;
there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. It is said that what this bodhisattva has realized is profoundly deep.

The light of Śākyamuni Buddha illuminated his body. As the Buddha’s light shone from afar upon that bodhisattva’s body, he addressed the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Śubhavyūha), saying: "Because I have seen this light shining, I have come to inform the Buddha."
“World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world.
Desiring to come from that land to this region, I wish to pay homage, draw near, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha. My purpose in coming is to draw near to and serve Śākyamuni.”
As for the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, he is explained as in the "Introductory Chapter.
