As for the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, he is explained as in the preceding chapter.
As for the Bodhisattva Sūradatta, he is a bodhisattva who is well able to practice giving with heroic vigor.
The Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña: "Nakṣatra-rāja" (Star-King) refers to the moon; "saṃkusumita" (fully blossomed) is a metaphor for the pure mind.
The Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritramati: he has resolved upon the Great Vehicle mind and cultivates the supreme practices.
The Bodhisattva King of Adornment (Vyūharāja) adorns himself with the various kingly samādhis of the Buddha’s merits.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata bestows supreme and wondrous medicines upon all people; he is designated as the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata by the seal of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara: "Gadgadasvara, as you are about to depart, that Buddha has entrusted you with this charge:
'Do not hold that land in contempt or conceive thoughts of it being inferior. As you now wish to go there, do not regard the Sahā world as lowly.'"
Regarding inferior perceptions:
"Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with high and low places; the minds of people are not level, and the earth is likewise so.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If you level the mind-ground, then the ground of the world will naturally become level and upright."
The various mountains of earth and stone stand like great peaks due to the grasping at delusion as "self" and "person";

they are filled with filth and impurity. Internally, the physical body composed of the four elements is pervaded by defilement; externally, the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are overflowing.
The Buddha’s body is short and small; according to the capacity of sentient beings, his inferior response-body (hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya) is sixteen feet tall.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise small in stature; these bodhisattvas who assist in the transformation follow the size of the Buddha.
Your body is forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height; the figure of forty-two thousand symbolizes the constant pouring of forty-two thousand rivers of merit as clarified in the Vinaya.
My body is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas* in height; the six hundred symbolize the six *pāramitās*, and the eighty...
The "ten thousand" represents the Eightfold Noble Path.
Your body is foremost in its perfection, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of blessings;
the merit of your precepts and meditative concentration is radiant and sublime, as is the merit of your wisdom.
Therefore, when you go there, do not disparage that land. This concludes the preceding admonition:

if one conceives of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their lands as inferior, then compared to those Buddhas who manifest pure lands to gather in superior beings, Śākyamuni—who manifests an impure land to subdue the ignorant—appears inferior in both the characteristics of his environment and his physical body.
The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying: "In response to the Buddha’s exhortation, I, the Bodhisattva, answer you:
'World-Honored One, I shall now go to the Sahā world; I am now proceeding to that Land of Endurance.'"
All this is through the power of the Tathāgata. All is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness of kindness and compassion.
It is the Tathāgata’s sport of supernatural powers; all is performed through the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers of wandering and transforming.
The adornments of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom consist entirely of the adornment of the merit of the five perfections, such as *dāna*,
practiced by the Tathāgata, and the adornment of the profound *prajñā* wisdom; may my mind be thus adorned, and let there be no anxiety.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara did not rise from his seat; he did not even rise from his seat in that Land of Pure Light.
Without moving his body, he entered samādhi, for he first enters meditative concentration in order to manifest supernatural powers.
By the power of samādhi, he was on Vulture Peak— here called Lingjue—
which was not far from the Dharma seat, nor very far from the seat where Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma.
They manifest as eighty-four thousand [lotuses], symbolizing the destruction of this same number of defilements and afflictions;
these precious lotus flowers represent the transformation of delusion into wisdom, thereby accomplishing the path to Bodhi.
The stem is made of Jāmbūnada gold; the golden stem and stalk represent the wisdom of the Middle Way.
The leaves are made of white silver; the silver lotus leaves represent all pure conduct (brahmacarya).
Its filaments are made of vajra. The subtle and dense wisdom within is like the filaments of a lotus.
Its pedestal is made of *cintāmaṇi* (jambūnada) jewels; *cintāmaṇi* here means "red-colored flower," as the red color of the lotus pedestal is like that of the *jambūnada*.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying: "I see these lotus flowers appear;
I ask the Buddha for the reason why.
World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen first appeared? For what causes and conditions has this sign of a portent first been manifested?"
There were several tens of millions of lotuses with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and pedestals made of karkoṭaka gems;
he described in detail the various features perceived by the eyes of the multitude.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara has manifested.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Mañjuśrī regarding this manifestation of Gadgadasvara.
He wished to depart for the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña; thus he spoke of his place of origin.
Surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he spoke of his accompanying assembly.
They have come to this Sahā world, desiring to approach, make offerings to, and pay homage to me.

Their intention is to make offerings to the Buddha, and they also wish to make offerings while listening to the Lotus Sutra; furthermore, they do so to make offerings to the assembly and to listen to the sutra.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "I wish further to question the Buddha regarding his practice and what he knows.
World-Honored One, what roots of goodness does this bodhisattva cultivate? I ask about his past roots of merit."

"What merit has been cultivated?"—this asks about the virtue practiced that enables such great supernormal power (*abhijñā*). "Pointing to the manifested phenomenon"—this asks about the samādhi practiced;
since it is through the power of samādhi that supernatural faculties arise, one asks about the samādhi as the cause of the correct concentration.
We pray that you will tell us the name of this samādhi.
We seek to inquire after its name, for we also wish to diligently practice it; seeing the worthy, we aspire to emulate them.
Only by practicing this samādhi can one perceive the physical form, dimensions, and dignified deportment of this bodhisattva;
by attaining that samādhi, one may know his body.
We pray that the World-Honored One will employ his supernatural powers, and we pray to receive the Buddha’s power.
"That Bodhisattva has come so that I may behold him; I have beheld the Wondrous Sound.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying to Mañjuśrī: "Know this, Mañjuśrī!"
"This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has been in parinirvāṇa for a long time, shall manifest his form for your sakes. It rests entirely with Prabhūtaratna.
Then, at Śākyamuni’s request, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas, "Good sons, come! It was because of Śākyamuni’s request that he spoke these excellent words.
[The Buddha said:
“Ghoṣa. Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, wishes to see your body. Because Mañjuśrī desires to see such signs, at that time the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land;
having first manifested supernatural powers, he now arrives by moving his own body.”
He arrived together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas. When a single thought moved, all thoughts turned along with it, just as when one person moves, the entire multitude follows.
As they passed through various lands, the earth shook in six ways; the ground trembled wherever the bodhisattvas traveled, signifying the shattering of ignorance.
The eighteen realms were clearly transformed, and they all rained down seven-jeweled lotus flowers. The rain of these seven-jeweled flowers symbolized the seven virtuous karmas.

Hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; such speech that requires no conscious effort is called "celestial music," for it arises from non-action (*akṛta*).
The reason it is called "sounding without being struck" is that this Bodhisattva’s eyes are like the petals of a vast blue lotus; his vast eyes of compassion are like a deep azure lotus.
Even if one were to combine hundreds of thousands of millions of moons, or even gather hundreds of thousands of billions of pure lunar discs,
his countenance would be more upright and handsome than these; yet even such a comparison would be insufficient to describe the uprightness and beauty of his face.

His body is of true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits; the marks of his purple-golden body are all the result of adornments through the accumulation of merit over many kalpas.
His majestic virtue is blazing and intense; his majesty, power, and virtuous goodness are all three intensely blazing.
His radiance shines brilliantly; the light of his body shines immeasurably.
He is endowed with all the marks, fully possessing hundreds of thousands of primary and secondary characteristics.
His body is as firm and solid as that of Nārāyaṇa; Nārāyaṇa is a metaphor for the Vajrapāṇi, which here represents the Bodhisattva.
With a body thus firm and solid,
he entered a pavilion of the seven treasures, sat upon a lotus throne,
ascended into the void, and came through the air.
It was seven *tāla* trees above the ground, at a height of about five *zhang*.
It was reverently surrounded by the assembly of bodhisattvas, who followed as its retinue.
He came to this Sahā world, to Vulture Peak Mountain.
Having arrived at Gṛdhrakūṭa, he descended from his seven-jeweled terrace and alighted from the lotus.
Taking a necklace worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces] as a gift for an audience,
he carried it to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was and arrived before the Buddha.
He prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet as a mark of respectful audience, and presented him with a necklace.
This necklace was composed of precious jewels; the use of such a necklace signifies that they met one another through the jewel of wisdom.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Having completed all formal salutations, I then transmit this message:

The World-Honored One, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom, inquires after the World-Honored One’s health, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction. This inquiry concerns whether the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) has experienced any slight illness or affliction."
Are your daily activities light and easy? Are you agile and swift in both motion and stillness?
Are you dwelling in peace and happiness? Is your body and mind at ease, and are your actions effortless?
Are the four great elements harmonious? Are the physical body composed of these four elements well-regulated and compliant?
Can the affairs of the world be endured? Can one’s conduct in the world be patiently borne?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Is it easy to liberate the various classes of sentient beings?
Are they free from excessive greed, anger, delusion, envy, stinginess, and pride? Greed, anger, and delusion are the three poisons;
envy toward others, stinginess, and arrogance make it difficult to transform sentient beings. However, if these are not excessive, it is sufficient for them to receive the Way.
Is there no one who is unfilial toward their parents? If one is unfilial toward one's own parents—the closest of kin—how can such a person enter the Way?
Is there no one who lacks reverence for śramaṇas due to wrong views? If one lacks reverence for śramaṇas, they possess wrong views; such a person is not a vessel for the Way.
Are there none among you who are like this?
Is there a wholesome mind? Mindfulness of the wholesome mind is the root of the Path.
Are the five sensory faculties restrained? Although it is commonly said that there are six faculties, now we ask specifically about the mind and then about the five faculties:
are they all capable of being restrained?

"Blessed One, can sentient beings subdue the various māras and enemies? Can they subdue the internal māras of the five aggregates, the māra of afflictions, and the māra of death, as well as the external celestial māras, so that these do not arise?"
"Has the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, come from within his seven-jeweled stupa to listen to the Dharma?

Because of his past vow to listen to the sutras wherever they are preached, he asks this question. Regarding the arrival of Gadgadasvara, it was because Prabhūtaratna called out, "Come, son of good family," that [Gadgadasvara] came;
why then do you ask now whether he has come? This is because Gadgadasvara transmits the message of his original teacher, Viśuddhapuṣpadhvaja.
The Buddha, by means of his wondrous voice, went to inquire after Śākyamuni’s welfare;

he also inquired whether the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was at ease and free from affliction, for although Prabhūtaratna had already entered extinction, his body remained in a state of tranquil meditative concentration.
"Are you able to endure and remain for a long time? Are you able to withstand worldly conditions and dwell for a long duration within this jeweled stupa?
"World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. [This is because, prior to the *Parīndanā-parivarta*, Śākyamuni had risen from his seat while the jeweled stupa was closed;
now that Gadgadasvara has arrived, he wishes to see it.]
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me so that I may see him. I pray that you will manifest him through the power of the Buddha so that I may behold him.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet with you."
This is for the purpose of introduction.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna said to Gadgadasvara, "Excellent, excellent! These are words of praise.
"You are able to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, listen to the Lotus Sutra, and behold Mañjuśrī."
They have come here for the sake of benefit and so forth. This journey of Gadgadasvara has three purposes:
first, to make offerings to the Buddha; second, to hear the sutra; and third, to see the various bodhisattvas. For this reason, Prabhūtaratna praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower-Virtue— so named because his wondrous, bright merit and fragrant reputation were like those of a flower—
addressed the Buddha, saying: "Previously, when Mañjuśrī questioned the Tathāgata Many-Jewels, he was able to see his physical marks, yet he had not yet heard [his voice]."
Because of the merit of his roots of goodness, he asks this question once more:

"World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara planted, and what merits has he cultivated? He thus inquires into both the cultivation and the planting of that bodhisattva.
He possesses such supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). These supernormal powers are so vast and his manifestations are thus;
the realization he has attained must be profound. The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*).
His response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) was like a cloud covering the trichiliocosm, and his compassionate voice was like thunder shaking all things universally; he was the king among those of the Dharma."
*Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (Rúlái).
*Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (Yìnggòng).
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Perfectly and Fully Awakened One" (Zhèngděngzhèngjué).
The name of the land was Manifestation of All Worlds; all matters pertaining to every world were fully manifested therein.
The eon was named Joyful Vision; at that time, the world was peaceful and prosperous, and was joyfully beheld by all people.
For twelve thousand years, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara used a hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments; throughout this period,
he made offerings with these various musical performances to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja, cultivating such offerings for the sake of the Buddha.
He also presented eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious substances. These eighty-four thousand represent the gates of the Dharma;
the seven precious substances serve as a metaphor for the seven types of goodness, and the bowls being capable of holding and storing things serves as a metaphor for the various virtuous vows.
By these causes and conditions of karmic retribution: a virtuous mind is the cause, and diligently offering a bowl is the virtuous condition;
that one now obtains a superior reward is the virtuous fruit.

That you are now born in the land of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom and possess such supernormal powers—this is the answer regarding the cultivation and planting of virtues by Flower Virtue.
Wen-zhi asked, "Guo-hua,
what do you think? At that time, under the Buddha King Cloud-Thunder-Sound, was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound—
who performed music as an offering and presented the precious vessel— anyone other than this present Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wonderful Sound?"
"Sa" refers to this present Gadgadasvara; "this" indicates that he was formerly Huade.

This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas, having long planted the roots of virtue—that is, having long cultivated the fundamental roots of merit and goodness.
Furthermore, he encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. His accumulation of merit is profound.
Flower Virtue, you see only that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is here in this body; do not think that by seeing only this, you know nothing else.
Yet this bodhisattva manifests various bodies, which are in fact boundless bodies;
in every place, he preaches this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings, manifesting forms and preaching the Dharma according to those who are to be saved.
Sometimes he manifests in the form of Brahmā; for those seeking to transcend desire, he manifests in the form of a Brahmā deity.
Sometimes he manifests in the form of Śakra; for those practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, he manifests in the form of a deity of the desire realm.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of Īśvara; for those who attain mastery through meritorious deeds, they manifest in the body of Nirmāṇarati-deva.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of Maheśvara; for those with great merit who have attained the enjoyment of sovereign power, they manifest as Maheśvara.
Some manifest in the form of a Paranirmita-vaśavartin deity;
others manifest in the form of a celestial general, such as the valiant great generals among the heavenly kings,
like Vaiśravaṇa and Viṣṇu.
Sometimes he manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, appearing in this form for those who wish to protect the world;
sometimes he manifests the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, appearing in this form for those who wish to become a Wheel-Turning King and govern a realm.
Sometimes he manifests the body of various minor kings or the bodies of kings and people of various small kingdoms;
sometimes he manifests the body of an elder (*śreṣṭhin*), manifesting this body because that elder is profound and steadfast in nine matters.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of a layperson; they manifest this body because they dwell in purity without seeking wealth or emolument.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of a high official; they manifest this body because they wish to adjudicate right from wrong as an official.
Sometimes he manifests the body of a brahmin; for those among the worldly who practice purity, he manifests this body for them.
Sometimes he manifests as a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī; for those with a desire for the male order, he manifests as a bhikṣu, and for those with a desire for the female order, he manifests as a bhikṣuṇī.
To those laymen and laywomen who wish to observe the five or eight precepts, he manifests this body;
or he manifests the body of an elder, a householder, or a woman. To those who wish to become the wives of elders or householders, he manifests this body.
Sometimes they manifest as the wives of officials; for the sake of appearing as wives to officials, they manifest as female bodies.
Sometimes they manifest as the wives of brahmins; for the sake of transforming such types, they are seen again in their female forms.
They may manifest in the form of boys or girls; that is, they may appear as boys who have not lost their male organs, or as girls who have not lost their female organs.
Or he may manifest the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth;
these eight classes of beings are explained in detail in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
He then preached this sutra; as manifested above, it was primarily for the sake of preaching the sutra to them.

"All those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals"—the term "all those" refers collectively to the three realms. He sports within these hells out of great compassion, taking their suffering upon himself;
he manifests as a hungry ghost to provide milk and relieve hunger, and transforms into an animal to teach and bestow wisdom.
With wisdom,
one should be able to rescue and deliver all those in places of difficulty and hardship; that is,
one should be able to save all those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions.
Even unto the king’s inner palace, he transforms his body into that of a woman and preaches this sutra;
for those who are to be saved by appearing in the form of a queen, a concubine, or a woman, he manifests himself accordingly.
Huade is the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, who is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
The reason why Gadgadasvara is able to rescue the sentient beings of this land is as follows:
In this manner, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifests various transformations of his body;
being thus able to appear in response to conditions, he preaches this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings in this Sahā world-system. All such manifestations are...

He preaches the sūtras for them, yet his supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom suffer no diminution. Supernormal powers and transformations are the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while wisdom is the power of *prajñā*.
Through wisdom, he transforms and emanates, just as one lamp is used to light another lamp, beginning from a single lamp.
Because it has been transmitted through immeasurable fundamental lamps without loss, it is without diminution.
This bodhisattva, with various forms of wisdom-light, illuminates the Sahā world; as a bright lamp for the world, he destroys the darkness of sentient beings.
May all sentient beings each attain what they know; may each, according to their own faculties and natures, achieve understanding and liberation.
It shall be thus throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, not only for this [world], but likewise for all others.
If there are those who are to be delivered through the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
For example, Pūrṇa was originally one of great expedient power who secretly concealed his great practice while outwardly manifesting as a śrāvaka.
To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a Pratyekabuddha and teaches them the Dharma;
that is, he manifests the body of a Pratyekabuddha or a Solitary Realizer.
To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a Bodhisattva and teaches them the Dharma for those of great faculties.

To those who should be saved by the manifestation of a bodhisattva’s form, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva; to those who should be saved by the form of a Buddha, he immediately manifests the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

From the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*) onward, possessing the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he is able to manifest the form of a Buddha and transform according to the capacities of sentient beings.
In this manner, he manifests various forms according to those who are to be saved; whatever is appropriate to manifest, he manifests it all.
Even for those who are to be saved through parinirvāṇa, he manifests parinirvāṇa, proclaiming his entry into extinction.
They conceived a sense of reverence and admiration.
Such was the manner in which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Flower Virtue Wondrous Sound accomplished the power of great supernormal faculties and wisdom.
Summarizing the purport of his answer, he spoke thus to Flower Virtue.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have already heard of the miraculous transformations, but I do not yet know the names of the supernatural powers and samādhis by which he dwells.
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has deeply planted roots of goodness, as has been described above."
"Blessed One, in what samādhi does this bodhisattva abide? Within what kind of right concentration does he dwell,
such that he is able to manifest transformations in this manner to deliver sentient beings, and is so skillfully adept at manifesting these transformations to save living beings?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue: "Good son, this samādhi is named 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is able to manifest all physical bodies in accordance with need.
The Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound dwells within this samādhi; he abides in this right concentration."
To be able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings— manifesting forms wherever they may be to preach the sublime Dharma so that they attain awakening—
is what is called "benefiting.
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being spoken, eighty-four thousand [beings] who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara were present.
The people and the assembly traveling with him all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies. They, like Miaoyin, realized this samādhi.
The immeasurable bodhisattvas of this Sahā world also attained this samādhi. When the bodhisattvas of this realm heard [this],...
It is said that he likewise enters into the samādhi in which Subhūti abides,
as well as the dhāraṇī, which is the samādhi of skillfully understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, having made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha,
had completed his service of honoring the Buddha and listening to the sutra.
He returned to his native land and once again went before the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Śubhavyūha-rāja-saṃkusumitābhijña).
As he passed through the various countries, the earth shook in six ways, signifying the successive overcoming of the six grades of ignorance and delusion.
A rain of precious lotus flowers fell, signifying the cultivation of wholesome causes.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music were played, signifying the attainment of immeasurable dhyāna-bliss and the joy of the Dharma.
Having arrived in his own land, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he went to the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have come before the Buddha's seat to declare my intention to take refuge.
World-Honored One, I have come to the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings; I have come to the Sahā world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
He beheld Śākyamuni Buddha; having seen Śākyamuni, he also saw the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
Next, he beheld the precious stūpa, prostrating and making offerings.
Thus he paid homage and presented offerings to these two Great World-Honored Ones.
Furthermore, he saw the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja, Vīryadatta, Sūradatta, and others; and he also beheld all those great Bodhisattvas.
He also caused these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies,
and he reported to the World-Honored One the matters concerning the benefits derived from his travels and returns.
When this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being taught— that is, when Śākyamuni Buddha spoke of the benefits resulting from the coming and going of Gadgadasvara—

forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the various devas, having heard the Dharma, entered the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).
They abide in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). The Bodhisattva Puṣpadhvaja attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Having heard this, Puṣpadhvaja immediately realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, thoroughly understanding that the nature of things is fundamentally empty and unstained by worldly phenomena, just as a lotus flower remains unsullied while in the water.
An Exegesis of the Phrases of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Scroll Seven;
An Exegesis of the Phrases of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
By the Śramaṇa Guāngzhào of Qiántáng, Śākyamuni Wéndá.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Universal Gate of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

The World-Honored One, with great compassion, relying on wisdom as it truly is, expounds the supreme vehicle—the perfectly integrated and wondrous Dharma—pure, upright, and like the king of lotuses, in order to instruct all bodhisattvas in the final age; therefore, it is called the "Wonderful Dharma."
The Lotus Sutra explains this meaning by the name "Sūtra. Avalokiteśvara was originally the King of Righteous Dharma (Dharmaprabhāsa-rāja);
in order to deliver sentient beings, he relied on the gate of expedient means, concealing his true nature and manifesting power through provisional means to appear in the form of a Bodhisattva.

As for "Inexhaustible Intent," it is not that he does not know this; rather, he desires to reveal the inconceivable great kindness and great compassion of Avalokiteśvara’s universal manifestation through the various gates.
Out of this power, he joined his palms and questioned on behalf of sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati was well able to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, having attained mastery over inexhaustible,
profound, and wondrous intent.
He immediately rose from his seat; he rose from his seat because he desired to request the Dharma.
He bared his right shoulder, signifying that when serving a teacher, one should attend to their tasks.
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these words; joining his palms in salutation, he addressed the Buddha with his sincere petition.
World-Honored One, as for this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in this assembly, by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?
This name has not been obtained in vain; it must surely have its origin.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. Because of the Bodhisattva’s question, the Buddha replied:

"Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions—when those sentient beings are undergoing such suffering and affliction..."

If one hears of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly calls upon his name, or hears the name of Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly recites it, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara will immediately perceive their cries and they shall all attain liberation.

While sound belongs to the ear and is heard, the term "perceive" (*guan*) used here refers to mental hearing; the Bodhisattva’s compassion perceives and hears through the mind, thereby uprooting their suffering.
If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and if a person holds this Bodhisattva’s name,
even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them. When the fire of anger arises and incinerates the three realms, in a single thought they turn toward goodness,
and the fire becomes a cool pool.
By virtue of this Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power— indeed, through the power of this Bodhisattva’s majesty—

if one is being swept away by great waters when the floods of greed swell and the world is submerged, in a single thought-moment the ocean of karma is dried up and exhausted through the attainment of contentment.
By invoking its name, one immediately finds shallow waters; by hearing its sound and examining its principle, one gradually reaches the shore.

If there are hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, and pearl—wherein the lapis lazuli, a treasure found within stone, originates from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in this region—[they shall find them].

Some are produced by burning medicinal substances to form them; there are those like the *śukti* (ear-ornament) of precious gems, conch shells from the ocean, and *musāragalva* (agate) which grows within stone, its color red and lustrous like a horse's brain. *Vaidūrya* (coral) grows in the sea and is shaped like a small tree;
*aśmagarbha* (amber) is that which has been transformed over a thousand years from *fuling* (tuberous fungus); and *muktikā* (pearl) is the pearl of a bivalve shell.
They enter the great ocean to trade for wealth.
Suppose a black wind blows their ship and it is cast adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons. This land is near the base of Mount Sumeru;
if a person enters there, they will be harmed. This is easy to understand in terms of the literal event. If expressed as a metaphor for the Dharma, it is as follows:

Because of greed for wealth, they enter the ocean of desire; blown by the winds of ignorance, they drift like leaking shells, falling into the rākṣasa land of the three poisons where they flow on without returning, drowning in the sea of suffering.
If among them there should be even a single person who calls upon the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
or if within the ship there should be even a single person capable of invoking the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

All these people attained liberation from the peril of the rākṣasas; because one person held their name, the multitude were all freed from suffering—this is what is meant by "a single good deed can eliminate a hundred evils."
For these reasons, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Because he can hear sounds and observe the time to rescue those in distress, he is called Guanyin (Avalokita).
Furthermore, if there is a person who is about to be harmed—meaning one who is facing execution at the moment their life is ending—

Those who invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva when oppressed by suffering—those who call upon the Bodhisattva’s name—find that the swords and staves held against them are instantly shattered into pieces, and they attain liberation. This is evidenced by many accounts, such as that of Sun Jingde, who was in prison and invoked the name at the moment of execution, whereupon his blade was destroyed.
To express this through the symbolism of the Dharma: wherever an evil thought arises, at the very moment it is about to manifest...
If one loses their life in a single thought, yet can turn the light inward and practice patience, the swords and halberds within the breast will all be destroyed without exception.
Even if yakṣas and rākṣasas fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems and come to harass people;
or if the various evil spirits, yakṣas, and rākṣasas throughout all lands conceive malicious intent and come to cause harm—whether manifesting outwardly... [the aforementioned power shall prevail].

The Dharma states that the three thousand [worlds] are nothing but the deluded mind; their evil poison is like that of yakṣas and rākṣasas, arising from the mind and in turn afflicting one's own body.
Upon hearing the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva invoked, even these malevolent spirits cannot cast an evil eye upon them.

As for looking at them, how much more so regarding inflicting harm upon them? Although the ghosts are fierce and evil, upon hearing the name of the Bodhisattva, their malicious eyes immediately close and they dare not harbor anger, let alone inflict killing or injury.
If this is expressed in terms of the Dharma, although the poison may be blazing intense, when one contemplates the Bodhisattva, the evil views immediately cease;
how much less would they arise again to cause harm?
Furthermore, suppose there is a person, whether guilty or innocent, whose body is bound by cangues, shackles, stocks, and fetters;
if they are indeed guilty, they are imprisoned in a jail, or if they are innocent, they are falsely entangled in calamity.

Those who invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara—if they are able to recite the Bodhisattva’s name—all their [restraints] shall be broken and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.
Shackles (nīdha) refer to wooden cuffs; fetters (khalī) refer to cangues, stocks, neck-irons, and drills for the feet.

By recollecting the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, all these shall be cast off and shattered. If this is interpreted as a metaphorical teaching, it refers to the arising of evil thoughts.
At that time, his body being bound and lacking self-mastery, he reflects on the bodhisattva’s evil thoughts as being like ashes,
distancing himself from afflictions as if casting off shackles.
Even if the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with enemies and bandits— the six internal thieves and the external adversaries and robbers— [he remains unshaken].

There was a caravan leader who, together with his merchants, carried heavy treasures as they passed through a perilous road. The caravan leader is a metaphor for the mind-king; the merchants are a metaphor for the mental factors (*caitta*);
carrying heavy treasures is a metaphor for the Buddha’s teachings; passing through the perilous road is a metaphor for traversing birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

To explain this according to the conventional characteristics of phenomena: the place of bandits and robbers represents the [perilous path]; the leader and his companions traveling together represents the [Buddha and his followers]; and carrying wealth to cross the danger represents [the practice of the Dharma].
Among them, one person raised this cry; from within that assembly, one person proclaimed:
"O virtuous sons, do not be afraid! To comfort the multitude and dispel their fear, there is a gateway of skillful means."
You all should single-mindedly invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Encourage the assembly to single-mindedly invoke this sacred name together.
This Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings; this Avalokiteśvara is able to grant peace and happiness.
He bestows sovereignty and fearlessness upon all.
If you invoke his name—if you can call upon the Bodhisattva’s name—you shall attain liberation from these enemies and bandits. By the power of the Bodhisattva, you may escape this calamity.
Upon hearing this, all the merchants cried out in unison, "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva! Hearing these words, they all invoked his name.
Because they called upon his name, they immediately attained liberation. Although the three thousandfold world system was filled with the six robbers, by obtaining but one—
If one takes goodness as the sovereign and draws forth other states of mind so that they all become wholesome thoughts,
then one can preserve the heavy burden of the Tathāgata and the precious treasures of wisdom— the wealth of all wholesome dharmas.
Such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Inexhaustible One.

"Majestic" (*wei*) refers to his ability to repel adversaries; "sublime" (*shen*) refers to his responsive resonance. "Power" (*li*) refers to his capacity to liberate beings from suffering. "Sublime" (*weiwei*) describes his state of manifest glory.
In the preceding text, he was shown to be able to rescue others from all calamities and enable them to attain liberation; therefore, it says, "such is [his power]."
If there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, by constantly recollecting and reverently honoring Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from desire.
When one has much desire, if one can constantly contemplate and revere Avalokiteśvara while practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
that person will then be able to leave behind lustful desire.
If one who is prone to much anger constantly recollects and reverently honors Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately be freed from anger.

When anger is prevalent, by always practicing reverence, reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, and cultivating the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, one brings an end to harmful intent and is thus able to leave anger behind.

If one who is greatly deluded constantly recollects and pays homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately be freed from delusion. When one fails to distinguish between good and evil and is mired in great ignorance,

by constantly recollecting Avalokiteśvara and practicing the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one will skillfully understand what is open and what is obstructed, thereby being able to leave delusion behind.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Lord of Infinite Intent, possesses such great majestic spiritual power that he brings benefit to many;
he can extinguish the three poisons and attain pure wisdom, and is thus named "Great Majestic Power Who Benefits All."
Therefore, sentient beings should constantly maintain this thought in their minds. Because it is beneficial, sentient beings should always single-mindedly fix their attention upon it.
If there is a woman who wishes to obtain a son, or a woman who desires to be reborn as a male, [she should do so].
By prostrating and making offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—prostrating to extinguish transgressions and making offerings to cultivate merit—one gains the causes for obtaining a son.
Thus, a son endowed with merit and wisdom will be born. Because of these prostrations and offerings, one is moved by sincere devotion to give rise to merit and virtue.
Therefore, the merit that gives rise to wisdom is derived from the mother’s virtue and should reside within the child’s body.
If one desires a daughter, a beautiful girl endowed with auspicious marks will be born. Because the mother’s mind is upright, the daughter is also upright;
because the mother’s mind is compassionate, the daughter’s feet possess the marks of excellence.

Having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, he is loved and respected by all. He has brought forth as his daughter one who, in a previous existence, had cultivated meritorious deeds and was likewise loved and respected by others.
Such is the power of the Bodhisattvas Akṣayamati and Avalokiteśvara; according to people's wishes, whatever they seek, it is all fulfilled.
It is so. If there are sentient beings who pay homage and prostrate to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, their merit shall not be in vain.
If they can pay reverence, they will certainly obtain its blessings; there shall be no waste or loss.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; because the merit is so great, they should all receive and uphold it.
Ajita, if there were someone who received and upheld the names of sixty-two billion *gaṅgā*-sands of bodhisattvas, [the merit would be even greater].
If a person upholds and recites the names of the various bodhisattvas,

and further provides them with offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for as long as they live, and is moreover able to provide these four types of requisites throughout their entire life.
What do you think? Is the merit of these good men and good women great? What do you think?
Is the merit of these good men and good women who uphold the name and make offerings to many bodhisattvas great?
Akṣayamati said, "Very much so, World-Honored One; the merit answering the Buddha's question is very great.
The Buddha said, "If there is another person who receives and upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even for a single moment, prostrating and making offerings;
if a person receives and upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara, even for a short time, paying homage and presenting offerings."
The merit of these two persons is exactly equal and without distinction. One person upholds the names of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Buddhas and makes offerings to them for their entire lives;
another person upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara and makes offerings at a single time.
The merit obtained by these two persons is truly equal and there is no difference between them. Why is this so? As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names; through my cultivation, I have attained true and perfect penetration.
It cannot be exhausted throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; the merit of even a single moment is enjoyed without end."
If the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati upholds the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, he shall obtain such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit.
This demonstrates that the merit of upholding [the name] is infinite, and it exhorts others to take refuge in and single-mindedly recollect Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "The preceding passage asked how the Bodhisattva is named Avalokiteśvara;
this present inquiry asks by what causes and conditions he wanders here, and by what means he delivers sentient beings.
This question is raised in order to reveal the Bodhisattva’s great sovereign power manifested through the Universal Gate."
"Bhagavān, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara travel through this Sahā world? For what reason does he travel through the Sahā world?
How does he preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? By means of what Dharma does he preach for sentient beings?"
What is the nature of the power of skillful means? Wandering and preaching the Dharma is its manifestation;
transforming the ordinary person into a sage is called the power of skillful means. What are the characteristics of these two matters?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who should be delivered by means of a Buddha-body;
if there are sentient beings within a land who ought to attain liberation through the form of a Buddha."
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then manifests in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma for them, or manifests in the likeness of a Tathāgata to lead them into the Way.

For those who should be saved by the body of a Pratyekabuddha— whether they delight in cultivating the path of a *saṃyaksambuddha-pratyekabuddha* (fully enlightened solitary buddha) or a *pratyekabuddha* (solitary awakened one)— [he manifests accordingly].
He immediately manifested the body of a pratyekabuddha and preached the Dharma for them. He manifests in accordance with the various types of beings to accord with their individual capacities.
For those who should be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka, if there are those who delight in cultivating the path of the Four Noble Truths, [he appears as such].
He immediately manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them; he manifests the appearance of an arhat to suit their capacities.
For those who should be delivered by the body of a Brahmā King, or those who have abandoned desire and delight in purity, [he appears accordingly].
He immediately manifested the body of Brahmā and preached the Dharma for them; he manifested the body of a Brahmā deity and taught the Dharma of detachment from desire.
For those who should be delivered by the body of Śakra, or those who wish to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [he likewise appeared].
He immediately manifested the body of Śakra and preached the Dharma for them. He manifested a body within the desire realm and taught the ten wholesome dharmas.
For those who were to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, or those who desired to travel freely through the ten directions with a body of the desire realm, [he manifested accordingly].
He immediately manifests the body of Īśvara and preaches the Dharma for them; he manifests the body of Nirmāṇarati and preaches the Dharma of sovereign bliss.
To those who are to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, he desires to exercise mastery over his body, flying through the void.
He immediately manifested the body of Maheśvara and preached the Dharma for them. He manifested the body of Akaniṣṭha Heaven and taught the methods of various dhyānas and samādhis.
For those who should be liberated by means of the body of a Heavenly General, or those who wish to command spirits and deities to protect the land, [he manifests accordingly].

He immediately manifested the body of a celestial great general and preached the Dharma for them. He manifested the body of a celestial great fierce general, such as the Great General Vajrapāṇi (Saṃjñeya), and preached the Dharma for the protection and salvation of sentient beings.
To those who should be saved by the body of Vaiśravaṇa, and for those who wish to govern the world and protect sentient beings,
he immediately manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the methods for governing the world and protecting living beings.
To those who should be saved by the body of a minor king, or those who wish to become kings of men to govern states and cities,
he immediately manifests the body of a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the methods for securing the state and governing the people.
For those who are to be liberated through the form of a householder, and whom he wishes to inspire with gravity and the respect of the world,
he immediately manifests the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the Dharma of gravity and respect.
To those who should be liberated through the form of a layperson, and to those who delight in discussing metaphysical principles and dwell in pure conduct,
he manifests in the body of a layperson and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the methods for practicing the discipline of purity.
For those who are to be saved by means of the body of a high official, he manifests in the form of a high official to preach the Dharma for them—
those who, out of affection for their subjects, adjudicate between right and wrong— and for them he preaches the Dharma of justice, impartiality, and clarity.
To those who should be saved by means of a brahmin body— those who rely on the arts of love and divination to maintain themselves in peace—
he manifests in the form of a brahmin and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the methods for nourishing life and sustaining vitality.
Those who are to be delivered by means of the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās— among them,
there are those who have left the household life and delight in maintaining the full precepts, and those who remain in the household life and delight in the five or eight precepts.

He immediately manifests the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to preach the Dharma for them. For those who are to be saved by manifesting the bodies of elders, lay devotees, officials, brahmins, or women, he does so accordingly.
He preaches the dharmas of the full precepts and the five or eight precepts.
If there are those who are to be saved by [manifesting] the bodies of elders, lay devotees, officials, brahmins, or women... [he manifests such forms].
Among the four superior types of women, he establishes their conduct through domestic governance so as to cultivate the family and the state;
appearing in the form of a woman, he preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the methods for assisting within the home and cultivating one's person.
For those who are to be liberated through the bodies of a boy or a girl— if there is a man whose male organ is intact,
or a woman who delights in staying within a chamber—
he immediately manifests in the body of a boy or a girl and preaches the Dharma for them, teaching the pure dharma of youthful innocence (*kumārabhūta*).

Those who are to be liberated by means of the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—[the text continues: "Deva" refers to the various devas, deva-kings, and deva-sons;
"nāga" refers to the various great nāga-kings and their retinues; "yakṣa" [is translated here] as "swift spirits" (捷疾鬼); "gandharva" [is translated as] "fragrance-eaters" (香神).
*Pakṣa* is translated here as "pleasure deity" (*gandharva*). *Asura* is translated as "non-upright," because their physical forms are ugly.
*Garuda* is translated as "golden-winged bird. *Kiṃnara* is translated as "song deity. *Mahoraga* is translated as "great serpent. "Humans" refers to worldly people;
"non-humans" refers to the various devas, asuras, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts, who are not the same as ordinary humans.

Because they belong to these categories, it is said that for those among the eight classes of beings who delight in liberation from their respective kinds and seek to enter the Way, [the Buddha] manifests himself in their likeness and preaches the Dharma to them; he teaches various dharmas according to each of their specific types.

To those who should be delivered by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity who protects the Dharma by wielding the precious vajra-pestle and preaches the Dharma to them, teaching the methods for courageous and resolute protection and upholding.
"Akṣayamati, it is through the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara [is so named].
The two characters "thus" (rúshì) refer back to the aforementioned meritorious virtues consisting of the functional capacities for accomplishing all matters.

By assuming various forms, he travels through all lands; this refers to the thirty-two types of bodies used for entering lands to deliver and liberate sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, responding to their cries and coming to them according to their needs. Regarding the meaning of the power of his skillful means in traveling to various regions to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, as asked by Akṣayamati in the preceding text concerning Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: [The Buddha said: "Good son, if there are those who practice the Way as śrāvakas, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifests himself in the body of a śrāvaka to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as pratyekabuddhas, he manifests himself in the body of a pratyekabuddha to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as bodhisattvas, he manifests himself in the body of a bodhisattva to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as Buddhas, he manifests himself in the body of a Buddha to teach and transform them. Furthermore, if there are gods among the devas, he manifests himself in the body of a deva to teach and transform them. If there are dragons among the nāgas, he manifests himself in the body of a nāga to teach and transform them. If there are yakṣas among the yakṣas, he manifests himself in the body of a yakṣa to teach and transform them. If there are gandharvas among the gandharvas, he manifests himself in the body of a gandharva to teach and transform them. If there are asuras among the asuras, he manifests himself in the body of an asura to teach and transform them. If there are garuḍas among the garuḍas, he manifests himself in the body of a garuḍa to teach and transform them. If there are kiṃnaras among the kiṃnaras, he manifests himself in the body of a kiṃnara to teach and transform them. If there are mahoragas among the mahoragas, he manifests himself in the body of a mahoraga to teach and transform them. If there are humans among humans, he manifests himself in the body of a human to teach and transform them. If there are non-humans among non-humans, he manifests himself in the body of a non-human to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as Brahmā kings, he manifests himself in the body of a Brahmā king to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as Śakra-devānām-indra, he manifests himself in the body of Śakra-devānām-indra to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as the Four Heavenly Kings, he manifests himself in the body of one of the Four Heavenly Kings to teach and transform them. If there are those who practice the Way as Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests himself in the body of Vaiśravaṇa to teach and transform them.
