Therefore, you all should with one mind make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Because this Bodhisattva’s virtue is profound and his compassion deep, he exhorts you to single-mindedly practice the Dharma and make offerings.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terror and urgent distress;
he is able to grant fearlessness to sentient beings in their terror and urgent distress, enabling them to attain great peace and happiness.
For this reason, all in this Sahā world call him the Bestower of Fearlessness.
Sentient beings whose minds are treacherous and evil fear him, yet those who behold his compassionate forbearance obtain peace.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Having been exhorted by the Tathāgata to practice offerings, I address the World-Honored One:
'World-Honored One, I shall now make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Having addressed the Buddha, he intended to set out."
He then untied from his neck a necklace of various precious jewels worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and gave it to him;
he took off the most precious ornaments adorning his neck and offered them to Avalokiteśvara.
He spoke these words: "Virtuous one, accept this jewel necklace as a gift of Dharma. When giving through the characteristics of phenomena, there is a giver, a receiver, and an object given;

because one clings to the reality of these three—internal, external, and intermediate—as having marks, the merit is limited and constitutes a tainted karmic retribution within the realms of humans and devas. However, the one who gives the gift of Dharma perceives the emptiness of all phenomena."
There is no giver, no receiver, and no object given; these three spheres are empty and tranquil, free from all marks.
When giving to one person, it is as if giving to all; giving to all persons is equal to giving to one.
To offer this Dharma with a mind that makes no distinctions is called the pure and impartial gift of Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was unwilling to accept it. By the power of his compassion, he declined the offering.
Ajita-kṣaya-mati addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again, saying: "Because you have not accepted it, I address you once more."
"O Benevolent One, out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace. The dharma of giving is intended to manifest a mind of renunciation;
yet if one gives without receiving, no merit is generated. We urge you to show compassion for us and accept it."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "The Buddha perceives that the donor’s words and intentions are exceedingly earnest;
yet, Avalokiteśvara declines and does not accept them, which is why I speak to you."
"You should out of compassion for this Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, as well as for the fourfold assembly—
monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— and for the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, accept these necklaces. Thus did the Buddha exhort Avalokiteśvara to take them out of compassion for the multitude.
Thereupon, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, as well as for the devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans, accepted the necklace.
Out of reverence for the Buddha’s intention and out of pity for sentient beings, he accepted the necklace bestowed by Akṣayamati.
He divided it into two portions: one portion he offered to Śākyamuni Buddha, and one portion he offered to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna.
By giving and not taking, he manifested contentment and the refusal to accept what is improper.

Having received [the offerings], he further gave them away to honor the Buddhas, manifesting that he has no stinginess regarding worldly wealth. Dividing it into two portions manifests impartial giving without partiality. Thus he bestowed them.
"Buddha" signifies the unsurpassed giving that turns causes toward the fruit to achieve the Buddha-way.

The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent possesses such sovereign spiritual power. All that has been cited previously is, in its entirety, the power of the Bodhisattva’s sovereign and unimpeded supernormal faculties.

He wanders through the Sahā world. Since the previous section contained the question from Akṣayamati as to how Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva wanders in this Sahā world, this passage concludes by providing the answer for the sake of those present.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati questioned [the Buddha] with verses. In the translation by Master Kumārajīva, there are no *geya* (repeated verses);
these verse passages were added later by someone who incorporated verses from the Guptaka version of the sutra into this present text, which has been handed down through tradition.
To the World-Honored One, who is endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask again of him. The first phrase praises the Buddha; the second phrase poses a further question:
"O Son of the Buddha, by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara? This asks from where the name Avalokiteśvara is derived.
The Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, answered the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati in verse. Because the Bodhisattva questioned the Buddha, he replied in verse:
"Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, who appropriately responds to all quarters; through thirty-two manifestations, he skillfully transforms all regions."
His great vows are as deep as the ocean, inconceivable throughout incalculable kalpas. His vast and profound vows are like the great sea;
even throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they remain beyond the power of thought.
Having attended upon many thousands of billions of Buddhas, he has made great, pure vows; having served countless thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, he has brought them forth.
Regarding these vast and pure vows, I shall briefly explain them for you.
Grant me permission to speak exhaustively of the practices of Avalokiteśvara.
Whether one hears his name or beholds his physical form—whether one hears that name or sees his bodily appearance.
"Mindfulness does not pass by in vain. This means that with single-minded focus, one's mindfulness never passes away fruitlessly.

It can extinguish all suffering of existence; it can extinguish all the afflictions of the three realms of existence. This phrase provides a general heading, while the following text provides a detailed exposition.
Even if someone were to give rise to a malicious intent and suddenly push another into a great pit of blazing fire,
through the power of Avalokiteśvara’s mindfulness,
that fiery pit would be transformed into a pond; all burning afflictions would be converted into a pool of cool clarity.
Or drifting upon the vast ocean, encountering the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts; being driven by black winds and tossed by great waters;
facing the dangers of venomous dragons, malevolent fish, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and the myriad perils of the great sea.
By recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one cannot be submerged by waves; through the power of the Bodhisattva, one escapes from imminent peril.
Or, if one is pushed off a peak of Mount Sumeru and falls from the summit of that high mountain, [one is saved].
When one calls upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, it is like the sun abiding in the void;

as the sun remains in the sky without being harmed, so too [the practitioner] may be pursued by evil people and fall onto the Diamond Mountains, yet even if pursued by evil people and losing their footing, they shall not fall into the mountains.
By the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed; it is through the power of such mindfulness that not even a single hair is damaged.
Or, if one encounters hostile bandits who disturb [the peace] and each brandishes a blade to inflict harm—hostile enemies and wicked thieves wielding weapons to cause injury.

By recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a mind of compassion. By recollecting the power of the Bodhisattva, even when enemies and bandits arise, they develop compassion and refrain from inflicting harm or killing.
Or, if one encounters the suffering of royal punishment and faces execution at the end of life—having committed a crime punishable by death—[one is saved].
By the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, the sword is instantly broken into pieces; the sword is naturally shattered into fragments.
Or, one may face the hardships of imprisonment, shackles, and fetters upon the hands and feet within a prison cell.
By recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one obtains liberation with ease; encountering a pardon or clemency, one is released and spared.
As for curses, various poisons, and those who wish to harm the body—when verbal slanders, curses, and toxic drugs descend upon one—[one is freed].
The power of contemplating that Avalokiteśvara returns to strike the person themselves. It is like a person who spits upward into the sky;
since the sky will not accept it, it falls back into one's own face.

Or, should one encounter evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, or other such malevolent beings who wish to harm one’s body—[by contemplating the Bodhisattva, these threats shall be averted].
When they call upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, at that moment none dare to harm them; they all turn their hearts at once and do not venture to inflict injury.
Even if surrounded by fierce beasts with terrifying sharp teeth and claws, such as tigers, wolves, and other fearsome creatures—
By recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, one flees swiftly to boundless regions; by recollecting the power of the Bodhisattva, one quickly runs away for oneself.
Even when the venomous breath of vipers, snakes, and scorpions blazes like smoke and fire—the poisonous vapor of these insects blazing like smoke and fire—one escapes.

By recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall return of their own accord upon hearing the sound; by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall depart of their own accord upon hearing the sound.

When clouds gather, thunder rolls, lightning flashes, hail falls, and heavy rain pours down—when clouds arise, thunder shakes, lightning bolts flash forth, hail descends, and torrential rain falls, causing damage to things.
By recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, [the calamity] shall be dispersed at that very moment; immediately the skies will clear and brighten, and one shall be spared from such afflictions.

When sentient beings are beset by distress and immeasurable suffering oppresses their bodies—when sentient beings are caught in poverty and hardship, and immeasurable multitudes of sufferings press upon their persons.
The subtle power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from suffering. Amidst the calamities of the world, there is no means of liberation other than wisdom;
only through wisdom can one avoid misfortune and pursue auspiciousness. Therefore, it is said that the power of wisdom can rescue one from all sufferings.

Endowed with the power of supernatural faculties and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom, they are fully possessed of both supernatural powers and wisdom, and extensively cultivate skillful means to benefit sentient beings.
In the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm where they do not manifest their bodies; throughout the oceans of lands in the ten directions, there is nowhere they do not universally respond.
The various evil destinies—those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—are what are known as the three miserable realms (*tricāṭaka*).

Regarding the phrase "gradually causing all suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death to be extinguished": because birth, old age, sickness, and death cannot be eliminated instantaneously, it is said that they are "gradually caused to be entirely extinguished."
True contemplation is pure contemplation. Illuminating the true principle with true wisdom is called true contemplation;
realizing that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, like the great void, is called pure contemplation.
The contemplation of vast wisdom: because one universally contemplates all things with vast wisdom until there is nothing not clearly understood, it is called the contemplation of wisdom.

The contemplation of compassion and the contemplation of loving-kindness: because one contemplates the suffering of sentient beings with a heart of great compassion and uproots their afflictions and hardships, it is called [the contemplation of compassion].

The contemplation of compassion involves bestowing happiness upon sentient beings with a mind of great loving-kindness; regulating the meaning according to the occasion is called the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-vipaśyanā*).
"Constantly aspiring and constantly gazing upward" refers to the exhortation to practice by always making vows to attain such gazing.
The sun of stainless, pure light and wisdom destroys all darkness; with its unobstructed, pure, and radiant wheel of wisdom, it shatters all deep obscurity.
It is able to subdue the winds of calamity and the fires of passion, shining universally upon the world; it is well able to overcome the winds of delusion and the fires of anger.
Universal radiance and wisdom illuminate all worlds.

The thunderous roar of the precepts, which are the essence of compassion—since the Bodhisattva’s precepts begin with non-killing and initial compassion protects living beings, the essence of these precepts is pure;
thus their name and fame are heard afar like the resonance of thunder.
The wondrous great cloud of a compassionate mind— this compassionate heart that bestows happiness upon sentient beings through wisdom is like a great cloud that universally covers all,
pouring down the nectar-rain of the Dharma. The wheel of speech preaches the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, like the falling of sweet rain that universally moistens all.

All [of these] extinguish the flames of the afflictions. Like clouds, rain, and thunder, the flavor of the Dharma of compassion extinguishes the flames of the afflictions and bestows the bliss of coolness.
In the midst of legal disputes before government officials or amidst the terrors of military arrays— when one faces litigation before officials or fears in the presence of armies—

if one recollects the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies will completely retreat and disperse; by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies will naturally and entirely withdraw and scatter.
Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara, who awakens all through subtle and wondrous sounds, and observes the world with sounds that respond to the needs of beings;
Brahma-sound, ocean-tide sound— pure, exquisite, like the voice of Brahmā, and like the great ocean tide, universally resounding.
This sound surpasses all worldly sounds; it far excels every sound in the world.
For this reason, one should constantly keep it in mind; for this reason, one should always recite and contemplate it.
Do not give rise to doubt in every thought-moment. A single thought of doubt can act as an obstruction to the Way; you should have deep faith and not harbor any suspicion or confusion.
Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One—the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, the pure and most holy one.

He is able to act as a refuge for those facing the calamity of painful death; he is able to provide protection and serve as a great refuge for all sentient beings suffering through the calamity of death.
Possessing all virtues, he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion, endowed with supernatural powers, wisdom, and skillful means.
With eyes of compassion, you regard all sentient beings with impartiality;
as an ocean of immeasurable masses of merit, you are therefore worthy of prostration.
The body of a Bodhisattva is itself a mass of wisdom and merit, profound and vast beyond measure like the great ocean; therefore, one should respectfully prostrate to it.

At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (*Dharaṇīdhara*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he was once a bhikṣu who leveled the ground to await the Buddha and thereby received his seal of approval.
With the dust of afflictions eliminated and wisdom perfected, he attained supreme enlightenment and was named Earth-Holder.
He immediately rose from his seat, came forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "The host who requested this chapter was originally Akṣayamati;

that he has now risen from the Earth-holding Bodhisattva to address the Buddha is because, having heard in this assembly the discourse on the Bodhisattva’s universal manifestation, he has offered praise."
World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear this chapter on the Sovereign Activities of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—
wherein the operation of the three karmas is unimpeded in all its movements and is thus called "sovereignty"— [they shall attain liberation].

Regarding "the power of spiritual transformations manifested through the Universal Gate": it refers to the opening of the gate of skillful means and the universal manifestation of bodies that all beings joyfully behold—the wondrous function and great power of spiritual transformations.

One should know that the merit of such a person is not small. If, upon hearing this chapter, one relies upon it and puts it into practice, one will give rise to the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate;
therefore, it is said that the merit of such a person is not small.
When the Buddha spoke this "Universal Gate" Chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings among the assembly— those who had heard the Dharma at that time in the gathering—
[attained realization] according to the dispositions of those eighty-four thousand sentient beings.
They all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is "unequaled" (*asama*).
It is called "unequaled" because the wisdom of the Buddha is supreme and most honored, transcending all things; thus there is nothing equal to it.
Yet, it is not that it does not accord with the ultimate fruit, for the Buddhas are entirely equal. Because this is the most wondrous equality of the unequaled, it is called "unequaled."
This refers precisely to the mind of the unsurpassed path.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-six, "The Dharani," following the conclusion of the "Universal Gate" chapter, Bhaiṣajyarāja asks: "If one upholds this sutra, how much merit will be obtained? The Buddha then explains it for him.

The *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* is so named because it describes how the Bodhisattva Bhaisajyarāja (King of Medicine) joyfully expounds a dhāraṇī to protect and uphold [the teaching], and how Vīradatta as well as various devas and devīs likewise recite incantations and prayers out of a desire to provide such protection.

Regarding these dhāraṇīs, there are both exoteric and esoteric forms; the exoteric refers to the scriptural text itself, as stated in the *Bodhimaṇḍagata-buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*): "There is a dhāraṇī called..."
The *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment) is essentially mantra; as in this present chapter, it is provided for the sake of protecting the one who preaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, *dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). It encompasses both extremes, obstructs evil and protects good, and sustains the Middle Way—the true principle of the Buddha.
Within a single dharma, it contains manifold meanings; it is able to retain and...
"Holding the name" means to maintain the *dhāraṇī*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Rising from one's seat and leaving it, baring the shoulder and joining the palms while facing clearly toward the Buddha, he then spoke these words."
Blessed One, if there are sons or daughters of good family who are able to receive and uphold the Lotus Sūtra, or sons or daughters of good family who,
upon hearing the Dharma, believe and accept it and remember and maintain it.
If one reads and recites until they are thoroughly mastered— reading from the original text and reciting from memory without any loss or forgetfulness— this is called "thorough mastery.
If one transcribes the sūtra scrolls, whether transcribing them oneself or instructing others to do so.
"How much merit does one obtain? How much merit does the aforementioned person obtain?

The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja: "If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million nayutas of Ganges Rivers, if one were to compare the merit of those offerings to that of upholding this sutra..."
What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this person who makes offerings to many Buddhas truly great? Is it not much?
"Very much, World-Honored One," replied Bhaiṣajyarāja, "the merit of the Buddha is very great.

The Buddha said: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse from this sutra—'upholding a four-line verse' being used here as the absolute minimum—"
To recite and explain the meaning— reciting the verses and explaining their principles—
and to practice according to what is taught: even if the text is not extensive,
the merit of such understanding and practice surpasses that of the former person who made offerings to the Buddha.

The merit is exceedingly great. While making offerings to sustain life produces blessings, upholding this sutra generates wisdom; when compared with that merit, the merit [of upholding the sutra] is far greater.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have heard that the merit of hearing this sutra is superior, and for this reason I address the Buddha."

The *Manojñā-tārā-dhāraṇī* is the secret speech and silent mystery of all Buddhas; it subdues evil so that evil naturally dissipates, and it cannot be fully explained.
World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers.
One who can uphold this mantra is able to transform those sixty-two kinds of views regarding self and person into the meritorious virtues of the sixty-two Buddhas;
because this mantra has been transmitted from all the Buddhas, it is called "spoken by the Buddha."
If there should be anyone who violates or destroys this Dharma-preacher, or anyone who violates or disparages those who uphold the Dharma,
they have thereby violated and destroyed these Buddhas; they have already harmed these World-Honored Ones.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, speaking these words of praise because he had recited a protective mantra:
"Excellent, excellent!"— these are words of high commendation.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, out of compassion for you and in order to protect this Dharma-preacher— and for the sake of the Dharma-preacher who expounds this Lotus Sūtra—
I shall now recite this dhāraṇī, which is the aforementioned mantra.

He brings great benefit to all sentient beings. By means of this dhāraṇī, the Dharma Master dwells in peace and joy, skillfully expounding all dharmas to guide and benefit all sentient beings of the final age; his benefits are manifold.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūradatta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Having spoken with courage and seen the Buddha praise the Medicine King, I also address the Buddha, wishing that he protect and uphold this sutra.
World-Honored One, I too shall proclaim a dhāraṇī for the sake of those who read, recite, accept, and uphold the Lotus Sutra."
To protect the Dharma Master, he speaks this secret mantra.
If this Dharma Master obtains this dhāraṇī, or if the upholder of the sutra obtains this divine spell, then as for the yakṣas—
here translated as "the valiant and strong"— [they shall not cause harm].
*Rākṣasa*—here translated as "swift demon" (*suqiji guǐ*).
*Pūtana*—here translated as "stench-hungry ghost" (*chou egui*), who is the master of febrile diseases.
*Kiṭava*—here translated as "that which is produced," referring to the *vetāla* or reanimated corpse-demon.
If it be a kumbhāṇḍa— here translated as "jar-shaped," referring to a spirit that causes malevolent possession—
or if it be among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) who lack food and drink,

they may watch for a weakness to exploit, yet they will find no opportunity; should such demonic spirits seek to harm a person, they enter through a point of vulnerability, and if there is even a slight [deficiency], [they may succeed].
The Dragon King could not cause any harm. He then spoke this incantation before the Buddha:
*Te le | mahā-te le | u-kī mu-kī | ā-le | a-ra-pa-ti | ni-le-ti | ni-le-da-pa-ti*
Icchini, vecchini, jicchini, nilethinī, nilethipati. World-Honored One,
this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom likewise rejoice in it.
This divine mantra was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; its transmission has its own origin. When this mantra was being recited, all the Buddhas likewise rejoiced in it.
If there should be anyone who invades or destroys this Dharma-master, or anyone who harms or damages the Dharma-master.
This would constitute an offense against and destruction of all these Buddhas; it would be as if one had already harmed Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, the World-Protecting King Vaiśravaṇa—namely, the Northern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra—addressed the Buddha, saying: [as above].
"Bhagavān, I too shall out of compassion for sentient beings protect this Dharma-preacher.

O Heavenly King, World-Protector, if you take pity on sentient beings and protect the Dharma-preacher, the sutra will be able to circulate, and thus all classes of sentient beings will obtain great benefit."
Having spoken this dhāraṇī, he protected it with a mantra, speaking the mantra as follows: *A-ri, na-ri, tsa-na-ri,
a-na-lu, na-li, ku-na-li*.
The World-Honored One uses this divine mantra to protect the Dharma Master; by reciting this mantra, he acts as a guardian for the Dharma Master.
I, too, shall personally protect those who uphold this sutra. Previously, he protected them through the mantra; now, he protects them with his own person.
He causes all decline and affliction within a hundred *yojana*s to cease; he causes all malevolent spirits and demons to depart far beyond a hundred *yojana*s, free from all decline and distress.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was present in this assembly. The Eastern World-Protector, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, likewise—
In this assembly,
surrounded by and respectfully attended by a multitude of ten million billion nayutas of gandharvas— here translated as "deities of music"—
he approached the Buddha, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too, by means of the dhāraṇī..."

The goddesses’ divine spells for the protection of those who uphold the Lotus Sutra: The Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying, "I and my retinue also vow to protect the Dharma Master with these spells.
He then spoke the spells, saying: *Agaṇe gaṇe kauri gandhāri cāṇ*.
Dhāri | Maṇḍaki | Saṃkuli | Pūruṣaṇi | Adhi. This dhāraṇī-mantra of the World-Honored One was spoken by forty-two billion Buddhas.
The number forty represents the stages of abiding, practice, and dedication (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*);
the two represent the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vimala-saṃbodhi*).
If anyone should injure or defame this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby injure and defame all these Buddhas.

To destroy one who upholds the sutra is to cause the Dharma not to be practiced and the Dharma not to circulate in the world; who then would know that there is a Buddha? Thus, to destroy a Dharma-preacher is to have already destroyed the Buddha.
At that time, there were rākṣasīs, namely: first, Lambā; second, Vilambā;
third, Kūṭadantī; fourth, Puṣpadantī; fifth, Kṛṣṇadantī; sixth, Bahuruci; seventh, Atṛptā;
eighth, Mālādharā; ninth, Gautamī; and tenth, Sarvasattvaujohārī. As for the rākṣasīs, they devour [living beings].

The "human-hating ghosts" (ren-è-gui) are *rākṣasīs*, which are female ghosts (*nǚguǐ*). Regarding the ten types [of these beings], their names and meanings may derive from their physical appearance or from their activities;
however, as I have not seen the source from which they were extracted, they cannot be fully explained.
These ten rākṣasī women, along with Hārītī— the goddess Hārītī—
her sons, her retinue, the five hundred ghost-sons, and the ghost-folk.
They all went together to where the Buddha was and addressed him with one voice, saying: "We wish to protect those who uphold the Lotus Sutra.
World-Honored One, we also wish to protect those who read, recite, receive, and uphold the Lotus Sutra, removing their misfortunes and afflictions."
I wish to protect them through mantras so that their decline and afflictions may be eliminated;
should anyone seek out the faults of this Dharma Master, let them find no opportunity;
should anyone seek out the Master's weaknesses with intent to harm, let them find no opportunity.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke this mantra: Itiri | Itimin | Itiri-Atiri | Itiri | Niri | Niri | Niri | Niri-Niri | Lohi | Lohi | Lohi | Lohi | Tahi | Ta...
He-he, ta-he, tou-he, tu-he. May you not trouble the Dharma Master.
It would be better for you to alight upon my head than to harm or trouble the teacher who preaches the Dharma.
Whether they be yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, pūtanas, or kumbhāṇḍas— the meanings of these terms have already been explained above.
As for *vidyādhara*, this is translated as "red-colored ghost."
If it is a *khandha*, this is translated as the "yellow ghost.
If it is an *ummalaka*, this is translated as the "black ghost.
If it is an *abhamara*, this is translated as the "blue ghost."
Whether it be a yakṣa-kiṭibha or a human-kiṭibha—here "human" refers to a person and "yakṣa" refers to a ghost;
both possess the appearance of such a spirit.
Whether it be a feverish illness lasting one day, two days, three days, four days, or up to seven days.
This refers to the aforementioned ghosts who bring about calamities for people;
whether it be constant fevers or the frequent outbreak of fevers to harm people,
if they are male in form, the ghosts manifest in male forms.
Whether in the form of a woman, a female ghost manifesting in the form of a woman,
or in the form of a young boy or a young girl, they manifest various transformations to delude and bewilder people.
"Furthermore, do not cause disturbance even in dreams. Even those who rely upon dreams to harass and harm others are likewise not permitted.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke these verses: "If one does not comply with my mantra and disturbs the speaker of the Dharma;
if one does not follow my mantra-prohibitions and recklessly harasses the speaker of the Dharma..."
Their heads shall be split into seven pieces like the branches of an *ari* tree; let their heads be shattered into seven fragments like those of the seven-pronged *ari* tree.
This transgression is as grave as the crime of killing one's father or mother, equal in its severity to the five heinous acts (*ānantarya*).
It is also like the calamity of pressing oil. In foreign lands, when making oil, they first crush the hemp until it ferments and produces worms;

they then press it all at once with the worms, striving to obtain as much oil as possible and ensure its richness. Because this involves the destruction of life, the karmic retribution for such a crime is especially grave.
The calamity of slandering the Dharma is likewise like that person.
Deceiving others with weights and measures refers to the sin of using light scales and small measures in marketplaces to defraud and delude others.
As for Devadatta’s sin of schism: Devadatta’s sin of causing a schism in the Sangha resulted in his being cast alive into the Avīci Hell. This is that sin.
It is likewise.
One who offends this Dharma-preacher shall incur such calamity; whoever violates this Dharma-preacher shall incur the profound and heavy calamity described above.

When the rākṣasīs had spoken this verse, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "We have previously provided protection through mantras; we now further address the Buddha that we shall personally provide protection and support.
World-Honored One, we ourselves shall also personally protect those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra."
To uphold, maintain, read, and recite this is to study the Dharma; to practice it according to the sutra is called cultivation.
It brings about peace and security, causing one to be free from all decline and affliction, and to eliminate all poisonous medicines.

For those who uphold this sutra, their minds shall attain tranquility, remaining far removed from all decline, distress, sorrow, and calamity. All poisonous medicines that enter the mouths of these people shall be transformed into ambrosia.

The Buddha said to the rākṣasīs, "Excellent, excellent! You rākṣasīs, who formerly devoured humans and consumed their vital essence, have now given rise to the aspiration to protect this Great Teaching and those who uphold the Dharma; you are truly like lotuses born from within a fire.
Therefore, the Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
If you are able to protect and uphold those who receive and maintain the name of the Lotus Sutra, their merit will be immeasurable.
If you can merely protect and uphold the name of this sutra, the merit you obtain is already beyond measure.

How much more so for those who fully receive and uphold it; how much more so for those who can protect those who uphold the entire work, as well as the sūtra scrolls themselves and the persons who honor and protect the sūtra scrolls.
Flowers, incense, and necklaces; whether flowers, incense, or necklaces;
powdered incense, unguents, and burning incense; fine aromatic powders and scents for anointing the body.
Banners, canopies, music, and dance: one may offer banners and canopies, present musical performances, and light various kinds of lamps—namely those listed below:
ghee lamps, oil lamps, and lamps of various fragrant oils—offering worship by lighting lamps with these fragrant oils.
The *sumarā* flower oil lamp; here it is called the "flower that skillfully gathers the mind. The *campaka* flower oil lamp;
here it is called the "golden flower. According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is translated as the "yellow-flowered tree," which is tall and large in form.
The *vāsika* flower oil lamp—this is called the "summer-blooming flower," which is yellowish-white in color and fragrant.
The *utpala* flower oil lamp—this is called the "blue lotus"; although the lotus itself contains no oil, it is perfumed with lotus blossoms.
There are hundreds of thousands of such kinds of offerings. There are likewise those who offer such things to the upholders of this sutra.
Gautama, you and your retinues—your retinues being the ten rākṣasīs and the retinues of Hārītī and the others.
"You should protect such Dharma-preachers as these. You should protect those who are able to uphold this sutra and perform offerings to you.
When the Buddha spoke this chapter on the *dhāraṇī*, he said these words at that time.

Sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If expressed in terms of the phenomena of representation, the six sense organs and eight consciousnesses all became pure;
they thoroughly understood that sentient beings and insentient phenomena are ultimately and fundamentally empty, thereby entering the patience of non-arising.
The Twenty-seventh Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Past Deeds of King Suśobha.
Regarding this chapter, "The Past Deeds of King Suśobha," it describes the original deeds performed by King Suśobha during a previous life as a monarch.
As no one had requested this teaching, the Buddha spoke of it himself; its purpose is to manifest [the truth].
The two kinds of inconceivable merit from propagating this sutra and making offerings to its upholders are such that they encourage its circulation.
That king had a wife named Pure Virtue (Jingde) and two sons, Pure Treasury (Jingzang) and Pure Eye (Jingyan).

These four individuals were originally fellow practitioners in past lives; because the path of cultivation is difficult to accomplish, they provided one another with food and clothing. One of them resolved...
It was because they sought to provide for these three men that they diligently practiced and attained the fruits of sainthood;
one of them, through the merit of his administrative service, became a king. These three, remembering their kindness and wishing to lead him to liberation, said to one another:
"This king is attached to sensual desires and furthermore believes in false doctrines; were it not for his wife and children, by what means could he be moved?"

Thereupon, he made use of expedient means to manifest one person as his wife and two persons as his sons, according to his will, in order to entice them away from heterodoxy and lead them into the Right Path.
As explained in the subsequent text, the former King Wondrous Adornment is now the Flower Virtue [Bodhisattva]; the former Lady Pure Virtue is now the Bodhisattva Adorned Appearance;
and the former sons, Pure Treasury and Pure Eye, are none other than the Bodhisattvas Medicine King and Medicine Master within this very assembly.
"This is the Bodhisattva of the highest rank.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: "In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago...
The Buddha told the assembly: "In the remote past, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas] ago..."
In that kalpa, there was a Buddha named Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña. In terms of meaning, his Buddha-body was like a cloud that universally covers all;

his sublime voice was like thunder that universally resounds; he was fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, and his countenance was as dignified and majestic as the moon-god.

The constellation of the Son (Putra) is a king among stars, beautifully adorned by a multitude of virtues, like flowers spread everywhere; with delusions exhausted and wisdom fully realized, his insight is boundless.
Tathāgata—here translated as "Thus-Come One"—is the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
Arhat; this means "one who should receive offerings," as he is worthy of receiving the world's offerings.
Samyaksaṃbuddha; this means "Rightly and Fully Awakened.
The land is named Radiant Adornment, for it is adorned by the radiance of the Buddha.
The kalpa was named Priyadarśana; the world was peaceful and prosperous, and all people delighted in beholding it.
Within that Buddha’s Dharma, amidst the True Dharma of the King of Constellations and Flower-like Wisdom, there was a king named Subhavyūha, who was adorned with many kinds of wondrous virtues.
The king’s queen was named Śuddhāśaya; she was called Śuddhāśaya because her virtue was truly pure.
She had two sons: the first was named Śuddhagarbha, who was able to comprehend the boundless treasury of pure dharmas.
The second was named Viśuddhanetra, who was able to penetrate and clearly behold the ocean of great wisdom.
These two sons possessed great supernormal powers, merit, and wisdom;
they were originally bodhisattvas who, fully endowed with great supernormal powers, merit, and wisdom, manifested through skillful means as prince sons.
For a long time he has cultivated the path practiced by Bodhisattvas; for many kalpas he has diligently refined the pure path practiced by Bodhisattvas,
namely the *dānapāramitā*— here translated as "giving"— which serves to destroy stinginess and greed.
Śīlapāramitā is here translated as "the perfection of ethical discipline," which serves to cease all evil.
Kṣāntipāramitā is here translated as "the perfection of patience," which serves to subdue the violent and fierce.
Vīrya-pāramitā; this is translated as "diligence" for the purpose of eliminating indolence and laxity.
Dhyāna-pāramitā; this is translated as "meditative concentration," which is free from both withdrawal and distraction.
Prajñāpāramitā: this is translated as "wisdom" (prajñā), which serves to sever ignorance and delusion.
Upāyapāramitā: skillfully cultivating oneself for the benefit of others according to their capacities is called "skillful means" (upāya).
Because it is cultivated well, one attains liberation from birth and death and reaches the other shore; thus it is named pāramitā.
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). By means of loving-kindness, one bestows happiness upon all;

by means of compassion, one uproots all suffering; by means of sympathetic joy, one rejoices upon seeing others happy; and by means of equanimity, one grants whatever is sought according to their needs.
This extends even to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). Within the Hīnayāna, these thirty-seven factors are called the "Right Path" (*samyag-mārga*);
within the Mahāyāna, they are called the "Aids to the Path. This is because the nature of the path is inherently complete and does not arise through artificial fabrication.

The cultivation of various path-practices merely serves as an aid to its fulfillment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these thirty-seven in total are called the factors of the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). To avoid prolixity, they are not explained here;
he has clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated them all, and is able to understand and penetrate them all without obstruction.
Furthermore, one attains the Bodhisattva’s Pure Samādhi; being internally and externally stainless and pure like lapis lazuli, it is the samādhi of clarity.
There is also the Sun and Constellations Samādhi; with great understanding like the sun and subtle wisdom like the stars, illuminating everything without omission, it is called a samādhi.
The Samādhi of Pure Light: the light of pure wisdom is quiescent yet constantly illuminating.
The Samādhi of Pure Form: realizing that the nature of form is empty, one does not dwell upon appearances.
The Samādhi of Pure Illumination: purity is the essence of concentration, while illumination is its function.
The Samādhi of Long Adornment: constantly cultivating right concentration as an adornment without interruption.

The Samādhi of the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue: possessing great majesty that subdues all and great benefit for living beings, it is called the Treasury of Great Jewels, arising from meditative concentration.
He has also attained complete mastery of this samādhi; indeed, he is able to master all forms of right concentration.
At that time, that Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha—out of compassion for the king’s adherence to heterodox views and desiring to lead him toward the Right Path—[acted accordingly].
Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings— and specifically out of compassion for all sentient beings who are lost in delusion—
he preached this Lotus Sūtra, expounding this sūtra within the great assembly.
Then the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra, went to their mother’s presence before Viśuddhaśīla;
with their ten fingers and palms joined together, they spoke, joining all ten fingers and both palms simultaneously.
"I pray that my mother will go to the presence of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom. I exhort my mother to see the Buddha;
we too shall attend upon, draw near to, make offerings to, and prostrate before him. I shall serve my mother and, together with her, draw near to, make offerings to, and prostrate before the Buddha."
Why is this? It is because he has generated the intention to go forth and exhort others;
he believes that this Buddha, amidst the assembly of all devas and humans, is preaching the Lotus Sutra and it is fitting that it be heard and accepted.
For this reason, he exhorts his mother to go.
The mother said to her son: "Your father has faith in and accepts the heterodox paths; he has faith in and accepted the teachings of heterodox teachers.
He is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma and has developed a profound fondness for the practices performed by the Brahmins."
"You two should go and inform your father; whether he goes with you or not, you must go. Since the father did not believe them, how could they allow themselves to leave?
They went to inform their father and transformed him so that he would go along with them.
Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra joined their palms with ten fingers together and informed their mother. Their mother told them to exhort their father, so they informed him once again.

We are sons of the Dharma King, yet we have been born into this family of false views. We are originally children of the Dharma King, but by misfortune we have been born into this family of false views.
The mother said to her sons, "You should feel concern for your father and manifest a supernatural transformation for him.
Knowing that her two sons possessed great supernormal power, she commanded them to manifest a supernatural transformation in order to move his heart.
If they should behold us, their minds will surely become pure. Since it is difficult for wholesome dharmas to enter them, they must see our supernormal powers before they can be transformed.
Either permit us to go to the Buddha’s presence, or grant us leave to go to the Buddha together with you.
Thereupon, because the two sons were mindful of their father, their mother asked why they were so filled with anxious concern.
They leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees— each *tāla* tree being seven feet high— and remained suspended there.
Measuring five *zhang* in height within the void,
he manifested various divine transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), displaying manifold supernormal powers and metamorphoses.
He walked, stood, sat, and lay down within the void, manifesting the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) as they depend upon space.
Water flows from his upper body and fire from his lower body; water above and fire below.
Fire flows from his lower body and water from his upper body; fire below and water above.
Or he manifests a massive body that fills the void of space, then again manifests as small, and then again as large. Such is the power of the Bodhisattva.
Having realized mastery over supernormal powers, they encompass the great void while entering the subtlest interstices.
They vanish from mid-air and suddenly appear upon the ground; they disappear from the earth and manifest their bodies in the sky.

Entering the earth as if it were water and treading upon water as if it were earth; entering the earth as if it were water without perceiving any obstruction, and treading upon water as if it were earth without perceiving any floating or instability—
manifesting such various supernormal transformations, namely the eighteen transformations.

He caused his father, the king, to attain pure faith and understanding. The purpose of manifesting these signs was to enable the king’s mind to become purified and to give rise to right faith and understanding.
At that time, seeing his son’s supernatural power thus displayed, the father’s heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before. He was born [into this state].

Having come to see what he had never seen before, he joined his palms and said to the sons: "Who is your teacher, and whose disciple are you? Having witnessed your spiritual wonders, I know you must have a teacher;
I ask who your disciple is, for I desire to know this."

The two sons said to the Great King: "That Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom, whom he pointed out as his teacher, is now seated upon the Dharma throne beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious substances. He has pointed out that place where he resides."
In the midst of all the world’s multitudes of devas and humans, he pointed to the entire assembly and extensively preached the Lotus Sūtra; he pointed to the Dharma he had taught, saying,
"He is our teacher and we are his disciples," thereby answering his father's question.
The father said to his son, "I also wish to see your teacher now; let us go together.
Because he had witnessed the divine wonders and recognized the majesty of that virtue, he desired to go with his son to meet him.
Thereupon, the two sons descended from mid-air; they withdrew their supernormal transformations and returned to their original forms.
Arriving at their mother’s side, they joined their palms and said to her, "Our transformed father has come with us to inform you."
"His Majesty the Father King has now attained faith and understanding and is capable of resolving to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

To say that the father has understood and is capable of generating the mind for the Way means that we have performed the work of a Buddha for our father. As manifested above through supernatural powers, this is what is called performing the work of a Buddha."
"May our mother grant us leave to leave the household life and practice the Way under that Buddha. May our mother permit us to go there to practice the Way.
At that time, the two sons, wishing to restate their intention, addressed their mother with verses, speaking once more from the heart.
"May our mother grant us permission to leave the household life and become śramaṇas. They entreated their mother to release them so they might renounce the world and join the saṅgha, saying:
"It is extremely difficult to encounter the Buddhas; we shall follow the Buddha to train. It is exceedingly rare to meet a Buddha appearing in the world;
we wish to follow the Buddha and study the Path."
It is even more difficult to encounter a Buddha than it is for the udumbara flower to appear. This "udumbara flower" is translated here as "Auspicious Response.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa there is a great king of trees named Udumbara; it has fruit but no flowers.
When the Udumbara tree bears golden blossoms, only then does a Buddha appear in the world. Thus, it is said that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, just like the udumbara.

"O Flower, it is difficult to escape from all calamities; likewise, may you grant us permission to leave the household life. To be liberated from all the afflictions and hardships of the world is also difficult;
may you grant us permission to leave the household life and practice the Way."
The mother then said, "I grant you permission to leave the household life; I allow it according to your wish.
Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter. She granted her consent because a Buddha is hard to meet.
Thereupon, the two sons said to their parents: "Since you have granted us permission and encouraged us to go together to see the Buddha,
how wonderful it would be, O parents, if you would also go at this time to the place of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom to behold him in person,
make offerings to him, and with reverence and intimacy practice the Dharma and offer worship."
Why is this so? Because it is as difficult to encounter a Buddha as it is for the udumbara flower to bloom; it is said that he is difficult to see.
Furthermore, it is like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole of a floating log drifting upon the great ocean:

for a turtle with but one eye, adrift in the vast sea, to encounter a floating log and find its hole to settle itself within is exceedingly difficult to achieve. So too is it for those who harbor biased views and are submerged in the ocean of birth and death.
To encounter the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and attain liberation through the Dharma is likewise extremely difficult.
Yet we, owing to the profound depth of our past merit, have been born at a time when the Buddha-Dharma exists; with our great fortune, we have encountered the World-Honored One.
Therefore, parents, you should grant us permission to leave the household life, for our resolve is set upon the Path.
Why is this? Because Buddhas are difficult to encounter and their times are difficult to meet. First, a Buddha is hard to find; second, the right time is hard to encounter.
At that time, the eighty-four thousand women in King Susīma’s harem were all capable of receiving and upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Because the king was attached to desire, those eighty-four thousand deluded persons who resided in the harem developed a single thought of wholesome intent, through which every evil was transformed; thus, all the palace ladies vowed to uphold the sutra.
The Bodhisattva Pure Eye has long since attained mastery in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. As the sutra says:

"He is unstained by worldly dharmas, like a lotus in water; he is widely learned, possesses the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*), and skillfully understands the Buddha’s words"—this is precisely the right concentration of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha has already, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, attained mastery in the samādhi of transcending all evil realms.
As the sutra says: "Furthermore, one sees a son of the Buddha whose mind is unattached; by means of this wondrous wisdom, he seeks the unsurpassed path.
This is precisely the right concentration for transcending all evil realms.
Because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all evil destinies, the Bodhisattva’s mind places others before himself as he cultivates this right concentration;
wishing for all sentient beings to leave behind the evil destinies, when this concentration is perfected, the sentient beings of the dharma-realm are liberated simultaneously.
The king’s consort attained the Samādhi of the Gathering of All Buddhas. While abiding in right concentration, the Buddhas of the ten directions gathered before her eyes.
She was able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas; though its nature is fundamentally empty, it does not hinder its constant use, and while being used, it remains eternally so.
It is empty and does not abide in any form; it cannot be seen when looked at, nor heard when listened to. Though present within all movement and function, it cannot be grasped;
thus it is called the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

The two sons were thus; having attained samādhi, they skillfully transformed their father through the power of expedient means. Their manifestation of supernatural powers and other such deeds were entirely expedient means, by which they were well able to thus convert and guide the King, their father.

He caused their minds to have faith and understanding, and to take delight in the Buddha-dharma. He caused the king’s mind to have faith and understanding, to comprehend the Buddha-dharma, and to give rise to love and joy.
Thereupon, King Subhavyūha, together with his ministers and retinue—the king, his ministers, and his wife—[all followed].
He gathered all his kinsmen and retinue.
Lady Pure Virtue, together with her attendants and the women of the inner palace, joined the lady and her assembly of female attendants.
The king’s two sons, together with forty-two thousand people, followed their mothers in requesting to leave the household life to receive and uphold the precepts;
the forty-two thousand rivers of merit flowing together symbolize the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
At one time, they went together to the place where the Buddha was; they went as one group to see the Buddha.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Having reached the Buddha’s presence, the act of performing a respectful prostration and circumambulating three times expresses a heart of longing and devotion, while standing to one side indicates the desire to hear the Dharma.
At that time, that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king. For King Āditya, the Buddha preached the Dharma according to his capacity, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him;
he revealed and taught the path, bringing benefit and joy.
The king was greatly delighted. Hearing the sound of the Dharma, he believed and understood it with profound sincerity, giving rise to great joy.
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment and his queen took off from their necks pearl necklaces worth hundreds of thousands and scattered them over the Buddha.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, they gave away these precious ornaments and costly articles to practice generosity.
As for "bestowing":
within the void of space, it transforms into a precious four-pillared pavilion. Because one has realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), one abides in space;
through the four great vows, these manifest as four pillars, and this station upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena is called a "precious pavilion."
In the center of the dais is a great precious throne spread with hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial garments (*devavastra*).

It is called a "precious throne" because it is securely situated upon the principle of empty stillness; it is called "celestial garments" because they are adorned with the robes of boundless patience, endurance, shame, and remorse.
Upon it is a Buddha seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*). The Buddha upon the seat represents the *zhengyin* (direct cause) nature;
his sitting without movement signifies immovability.

He emits a great radiance; this manifestation of the light of wisdom represents the *liaoyin* (penetrating cause) nature. The appearance of these auspicious signs represents the *yuanyin* (conditional cause).
At that time, King Subhavyūha thought to himself: "The Buddha’s body is rare, upright, dignified, and extraordinary.
Seeing these auspicious signs, the king further reflected: "The Buddha’s body is seldom seen; it is upright, exquisite, and sublime."
He has attained the foremost and most subtle of forms; the Tathāgata has perfected a subtle physical body that is supreme, such that no other sentient being can equal it.

At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja-pūrvayugaśrīcūḍabuddhi addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "The fourfold assembly has received the Dharma and are all disciples of the Buddha; this is why I address you.
Do you see this King Subhavyūha standing before me with palms joined? Thus the Buddha questioned the fourfold assembly.
"O King, do you still understand my intention as I stand before you?
This king shall become a bhikṣu within my Dharma;
he shall renounce the world and diligently cultivate the dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood. The Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment is called the Right Path, wherein one practices all paths."
The title of this chapter is "Aids to the Path.
You shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śāla-Tree King. As for the śāla tree, its nature is firm and solid;
it does not wither in winter or summer and is thus the king among trees. Because your mind is firm and you practice the path with diligent effort, you shall therefore become a Buddha named Śāla.
Rāja, the kingdom is named Mahāprabha. It is called Mahāprabha because it is the land upon which those who enter the Way from liberation rely.
The eon is named Mahocchrayarāja; its seasons are so excellent that they surpass all other eons, hence it is named Mahā.
"O High King,
that Sāla-tree King Buddha had an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas and an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas;
it is said that the number of those he transformed was exceedingly great."

The land was level and upright, its merit being thus. Because his mind was even, simple, and straightforward, free from partiality, the regions where he should transform beings were broad, level, and upright.
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and renounced his status as a human monarch to dwell [in seclusion].
Together with his two sons, his wife, and all his retinue and followers,
he left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma; amidst the True Dharma of that Buddha’s assembly,
he took pure ordination and cultivated the bodhisattva path.
After the king had renounced the world, he remained in the monastic life for eighty-four thousand years;

throughout his entire life as a monk, he constantly applied himself with diligent vigor to practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, meaning he constantly cultivated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
After this, one attains the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits.

The previous bestowal of the prediction concerned future events, whereas this realization of samādhi pertains to present-life cultivation; because one cultivates all merits through pure faith, one obtains this samādhi within meditative concentration.
He immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and addressed the Buddha, his entire body soaring through the sky five *zhang* above the ground:
"World-Honored One,
these two sons of mine have already performed the work of a Buddha— that is to say, the work of a Buddha manifested by these two noble sons."

Through supernatural transformations, he turned back my perverse mind. The King, who originally believed in the sons of false views, now manifested his knowledge of the Buddha’s excellence and immediately turned away from his perverse mind.
He caused me to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma and to behold the World-Honored One, thereby enabling me to attain the Buddha-dharma.
Abiding with a mind focused within, one shall behold me, the Buddha.
These two sons are my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); these two sons are truly my spiritual friends.
It is because they wish to arouse the roots of goodness from past lives that they act as described above, until the completion of their joint practice.
"Out of a desire to benefit me, he has been born into my family. The king diligently cultivated his practice and attained the knowledge of past lives;
thus he understood that his wife and children were former good friends who had intentionally taken birth through skillful means in order to benefit him.
At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed King Subhavyūha, saying:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said. The Buddha told King Vyūha: 'It is indeed as you have said; the matter is truly so.'"
If a son or daughter of good family plants roots of goodness, and because that son or daughter of good family is able to plant such roots of goodness,
they will obtain spiritual friends life after life, and encounter various spiritual friends in every successive birth.
Such spiritual friends are able to perform the work of Buddhas; these spiritual friends are well able to perform all the works of Buddhas,
instructing, benefiting, and gladdening others so that they enter into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and revealing and guiding them so that they enter into perfect enlightenment.
Great King, you should know that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition. Internally there is a latent cause, and externally one encounters a virtuous condition;
the significance of these causal conditions encompasses both the Great and the Small Vehicles. A spiritual friend is no small causal condition.
That is to say, to transform and guide others so that they may behold the Buddha and resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To transform them so that they behold the Buddha and resolve their minds upon the Great Way is why it is called the causal condition for a great matter.
"Great King, do you see these two sons? Do you see the past causes and conditions of these sons?
These two sons have already made offerings to, approached, and revered sixty-five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* Ganges-sands of Buddhas.
The number 'sixty' represents the six *pāramitās*, and the number 'five' represents the five stages."
Regarding the "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions" of virtuous causes: within each individual practice, one possesses boundless practices;
by skillfully cultivating the mind and abiding in the True Dharma, this is called drawing near to, revering, and making offerings to immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

To uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from all Buddhas, and to cultivate wisdom according to reality with a mind that accords with reality, is called "upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* as sustained by the Buddhas.
It is to compassionately regard sentient beings of wrong views and cause them to abide in right view; it is to compassionately regard sentient beings who are attached to wrong views.
He transformed them, causing them to return to the Right Path.
King Subhavyūha then descended from the midst of the void and addressed the Buddha, withdrawing his supernormal powers and returning to the ground to speak thus to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is most rare. Regarding this rarity: first, he is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in an age;

second, his marks and signs of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are peerless due to his merit and wisdom. It is because of these two aspects that he is thus: first, he has fully cultivated the five...
The perfection of the two aspects of merit and virtue constitutes the practice of profound *prajñā*, thereby accomplishing the virtue of wisdom.
First, the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his head is praised as being peerless; second, the radiance issuing from this crown-protrusion is praised for illuminating all things.
His eyes are long and wide, and deep blue in color. That the eyes are long and wide is a mark of wisdom;
that they are the color of deep lapis lazuli is a mark of compassion.
Between his eyebrows is the *ūrṇā* mark, white as a conch shell or the moon. The color of the *ūrṇā* mark between the two eyebrows is like that of a conch shell.
His teeth are as pure as the full moon;
they are white, even, and closely set, always radiant. They are neither yellow nor black, nor are they uneven;
they are bright white and clean, closely set and perfectly aligned, always emitting light.
The color of his lips was as beautiful and red as the *bimba* fruit— this refers to the fruit of the *cassia fistula*, whose vermilion-red,
lustrous hue serves as a metaphor for the lips. At that time, King Subhavyūha praised the Buddha in such ways, [extolling] the aforementioned rare and marvelous qualities.
Having performed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of meritorious deeds, and having completed the merit cultivated and the virtue accomplished,
he joined his palms with single-minded devotion before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha once more, first praising the Buddha and then recounting his own [deeds].
It is marvelous, World-Honored One! It is truly unprecedented.
Such is the Dharma of the Tathāgata; such is the true, pure, and great Dharma realized by the Tathāgata.
They are fully endowed with inconceivable and subtle merits; there is no dharma that does not possess these inconceivable and subtle merits, all of which they have completely accomplished.
The conduct governed by the precepts is secure, peaceful, and wholesome; the training and restraint of the bodhisattva’s conduct brings peace, happiness, and the swift attainment of beneficial merit.
From this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims, nor shall I follow the impulses of my own mind.
One does not give rise to wrong views, arrogance, anger, or any other evil thoughts. When wrong views do not arise, one enters the right path;
when arrogance does not arise, one is able to show respect; when anger does not arise, compassion is born.
Thus, one makes a vow before the Buddha to eliminate all evil thoughts.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated to the Buddha and departed. Having heard the Dharma, received his prediction [of enlightenment], praised the Buddha, and fulfilled his vows, his task was complete;
he then paid his respects, took his leave, and withdrew.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "What do you think? Is the King Subhavyūha anyone else? He is none other than the present Bodhisattva Puṣpadatta."
"Sā" refers to the Lady Pure Virtue (Śuddhāśaya), who is now the Bodhisattva Radiant Adornment (Prabhāsa-vyūha) before the Buddha;
this very Radiant Adornment in the present Lotus Assembly was the Lady Pure Virtue in a former life.
Out of compassion for King Subhavyūha and his retinue, he was born there; that is, he manifested birth out of pity for King Vyūharāja and the king’s followers.
As for those two sons, they were Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra.
These are none other than the present Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. These two sons,
having already accomplished such great merits as these, had long ago, throughout many kalpas,
been able to accomplish numerous and immeasurable great merits.
In the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and again in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
they have planted the roots of all virtues. The Great Bodhicitta and the Four Great Vows, as well as the Six Perfections, are the roots upon which these Bodhisattvas plant their virtues.
They have accomplished inconceivable and manifold virtuous merits; by planting roots of goodness, they have achieved these various virtues.
If there are those who know the names of these two bodhisattvas, or even those who merely know the names of these two bodhisattvas, they too may enter through the gateway of the Buddha.
All the devas and people of the world should also pay homage to them. To respectfully uphold their names and perform prostrations is the primary expedient for entering the Path.
When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha," eighty-four thousand people were freed from dust and removed from defilement;
eighty-four thousand afflictions and delusions were all completely severed, and they were liberated from all obstructions and impurities.

Among all phenomena, one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When both the conceptual marks that serve as dust and the cognitive consciousness that serves as defilement are distanced from each other, then your Dharma-eye will immediately become lucid and refined."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, originally from the pure and wondrous land of the Buddha Ratnatejas in the eastern quarter, heard from afar that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was being preached on Vulture Peak.
Together with a great multitude, he arrived here at that very moment, desiring to hear the Dharma and to offer his encouragement.
The Mind of the Way.

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s transformation reaches all sentient beings and his compassion encompasses all; because his virtue borders upon the ultimate sages, he is called Samantabhadra (Universally Good).
By the power of sovereign supernormal faculties—through the unimpeded power of supernormal faculties manifested by the excellence of his virtuous deeds—and by his majestic virtue and renown:

because of his awesome power, he is able to subdue the enmity of Māra; because of his virtuous merit, he universally transforms all beings, and his fame spreads afar, reaching throughout the ten directions.
Together with great bodhisattvas who are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable;
because they are so numerous, they have no limit or measure, cannot be fully reckoned, and cannot be known by number.
Coming from the east, they have come from that eastern land to this region.
All the countries they have passed through and all the places they have traversed have been universally shaken.
The great shaking of the earth signifies the shattering of ignorance.
It rains precious lotus flowers; from the nature of true emptiness, a single thought of goodness arises like rain falling flowers from the void.
It produces immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music; the mind is like a musician, and its harmonious resonance is called music.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas— here translated as "swift spirits"—
gandharvas, gandharvarājas, asuras—
here translated as "the ill-favored," meaning those who delight in strife— and so forth.
*Garuda*: translated here as "Golden-Winged Bird.
*Kinnara*: translated here as "Singing Deity"; the Lord of the Gods employs this class when performing music.
*Mahoraga*: translated here as "Great Python."
"Human beings" refers to those of the human world.
"Non-humans" (*amanuṣya*) and so forth—namely, devas, asuras, pretas, and hell-beings—are collectively termed non-humans.
They surrounded him in a great assembly; the multitude gathered around Samantabhadra.
Each manifested their own majestic power and supernormal abilities; each displayed their own awesome spiritual efficacy.
They arrived at the Sahā world—Sahā meaning "Endurance," so called because its sentient beings are capable of enduring all manner of suffering.
On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa— here translated as "Spiritual Vulture Peak"—
he prostrated with his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, bowing his head to the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet in reverent salutation,
and circumambulated him seven times; such circumambulation signifies respect.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "First I prostrate, and then I say:
'World-Honored One, I come from the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja. As for its location, it is called 'Jewel Splendor' because the Buddha-nature is noble and precious;
it is named 'Supreme King' because it is the most excellent among them.'"
From afar, he heard that in this Sahā world the Lotus Sūtra was being preached. With his divine ear, he heard it from a distance;
together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, he came to listen and receive the teaching.
He said that the reason for his coming was his desire to hear the Dharma.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us; I pray that the Buddha will speak it.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—that is, after the Buddha’s passing—should seek the essentials of the Dharma, this is precisely the intention of Samantabhadra for the sake of sons and daughters of faith during the Age of Dharma-Decline.
"How can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*? By what skillful means can one obtain this sūtra?
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family accomplishes four dharmas, they shall obtain it.
These four skillful means are explained below."
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one shall obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Through skillful means and wisdom, one may attain this sūtra.
First, one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; when the mind takes refuge in the Buddha, one is then protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Second, planting the roots of all virtues: for those who practice, taking virtue as the foundation and cultivating various wholesome roots is called "planting the roots of virtue.

Third, entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*): "right" serves to distinguish it from the stage of error; it encompasses all concentrated minds that have entered the hidden state of the Buddhas.
The Buddha appears through meditative concentration.
Fourth is the arousal of the mind to rescue all sentient beings. While the preceding three dharmas are entirely for one's own benefit, this fourth is precisely for the benefit of others.

Sons and daughters of good family who thus accomplish these four dharmas and practice according to the sutra will certainly obtain this sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. This concludes the response.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One, I vow to protect and preserve the sutras during the final five hundred years. Regarding the first five hundred years, liberation shall be firm;
in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration shall be firm; in the third five hundred years, upholding the precepts shall be firm; and in the fourth..."
The fifth period, of the five hundred years of firmness in learning, and the fifth period, of the five hundred years of firmness in strife;
now, in the year Xinyou of the Jingding era, two hundred and eleven years have already passed since the end of the latter five hundred years—it is precisely at this time.

"In the world of turbid evil" refers to the five turbidities of the evil world: the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life.
"Should there be anyone who receives and upholds this sutra" means that if there is a person such as the one described above who is able to uphold this sutra.
I shall protect them, removing their decline and afflictions so that they may attain peace and stability.
Desiring to fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra, I shall protect them, removing their decline and distress so that they may obtain physical and mental tranquility.

As for those who would seek out opportunities to cause harm— such as spirits who constantly wait in ambush seeking to injure others— it is because the Bodhisattva protects them that they cannot find such an opportunity.
As for Māra, he is the King of Māras who dwells at the summit of the Desire Realm.
Whether they be sons of Māra, daughters of Māra, female followers of Māra,
or any of the hosts belonging to Māra.
If one is possessed by a māra, that person, being possessed by the māra, will further come to bewitch others.
Or it may be a yakṣa— this is translated as a "swift ghost"— or a rākṣasa—
this is translated as a "corpse-devouring ghost."
If it is a kumbhāṇḍa— here translated as a "ghost of loathing and bewitchment"—
if it is a piśāca— here translated as a "ghost that devours vital essence"—
or if it is a kiṭika— here translated as a "corpse-raising ghost."
If it is a *pūtana*—here translated as "stench-pretas"—it is one who causes feverish diseases;
if it is a *vetāla* and so forth—here translated as "wondrous-good ones"—it is a spirit that performs malevolent incantations.
None who would afflict others shall find an opportunity; all ghosts shall be unable to cause them harm.
Whether this person is walking or standing, they may read and recite this sutra; they may read and recite it at will, regardless of whether they are walking or standing.
