At that time, I mounted the six-tusked white elephant king. Samantabhadra’s mounting of the elephant symbolizes the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*); the tusks are a metaphor for the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), and the white color represents pure purity.
Together with a multitude of great bodhisattvas, I proceeded to that place. The entire assembly arrived at the location where the person was reciting the sutra.
Furthermore, they manifest themselves to provide offerings and protection. To respond without being sought is called "manifesting one's own three karmas with reverence," which is termed "offering.
To eliminate the heterodox and preserve the wholesome is termed "protection."
He comforted his mind, consoling him with gentle words to set his heart at ease;
this was both for the sake of making offerings to the Lotus Sutra and for the sake of honoring the Lotus Sutra.
If this person sits and contemplates this sutra—sitting upright and examining it with focused attention—this is called contemplation.
At that time, I shall again mount the king of white elephants and appear before that person. Previously, I protected those whose minds were distracted while walking;
now, I protect those whose minds are concentrated while sitting upright.
If that person should forget even a single word or a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra, and if the one who holds the sūtra should likewise have an omission or lapse,
I shall instruct them and read and recite it with them until they have mastered it once again; through the empowerment of my compassionate power, I shall ensure they do not forget.
[Omitted].
At that time, those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Lotus Sūtra shall behold my body; they shall behold the Bodhisattvas manifesting their physical bodies.
Filled with great joy, he became even more diligent; because his mind was joyful, his diligence increased all the more.
By seeing me, he immediately attained samādhi—herein referred to as "right concentration" (samyaksamādhi).
As for *dhāraṇī*, this is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). It comprehensively encompasses both emptiness and existence, obstructs evil, and protects the good;
it is therefore called the "Revolving *Dhāraṇī*. By revolving [in wisdom], one understands all things without anything remaining unpenetrated.
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs*. From a single dharma, countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇī* gates are manifested.
There is the *dhāraṇī* of skillful means regarding the sound of the Dharma; through this, one is well-versed in skillful means within the sound of the Dharma.
One attains such dhāraṇīs as these. Since the number of all doors of total retention (*dhāraṇīmukha*) is immeasurable, two types are briefly cited;
thus, it says "and so forth" (*ādi*).
World-Honored One, if, in a future age, during the final five hundred years of the turbid and evil world—by "future age" is meant the time after the Buddha’s [passing]—...
The "five hundred years after his parinirvāṇa" refers to the present age; as for the description of it as "defiled and evil," this has already been explained previously.
These are the fourfold assembly of disciples: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen.
Those who seek it; those who search for the sūtra;
those who receive and uphold it—those who take it to heart, remember, and maintain it;
and those who read and recite it—those who read it against the original text and those who recite it from memory.
As for the scribe: whether writing it oneself or commissioning another to write it, one desires to practice this Lotus Sūtra and wishes to cultivate the practices according to this sūtra.
During the three seven-day periods, one should practice with single-minded diligence. One must resolve to maintain a pure and concentrated mind for these twenty-one days.
Once the three seven-day periods are completed, this constitutes the fulfillment of the period of cultivation.
I shall mount a six-tusked white elephant and, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, proceed with this retinue to the place where the practitioner is.
With a body that all sentient beings delight to behold— a most sublime form-body that brings joy to all beings— I shall go there.

They appear before those people and preach the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; they manifest their forms to reveal, teach, and train them for their benefit, causing them to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, they bestow dhāraṇī mantras upon them, and also explain the dhāraṇī mantras to protect them.
Because one has obtained this dhāraṇī, no non-human being can destroy it; by the power of the divine mantra,
Māras cannot destroy it.
Nor shall they be deluded or disturbed by women; their bodies will attain the dhāraṇī of the Dharma and shall not be carried away by physical forms.
I myself shall also constantly protect such persons, and I shall likewise constantly protect them with my own body.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to recite this dhāraṇī mantra.
Thus, showing that he did not seek to act on his own authority but sought the Buddha’s permission, he spoke the mantra before the Buddha, saying: Atandi (1) Dandapadi (2) Danda...
Vate (3) dandakūśale (4) dandaśūdale (5) śūdale (6) śūdaravati (7) buddhabhāṣite (8) sarvadhāraṇī-āvartani (9) sarvavaśa-āvartani (10) śū-āvartani (11) saṃghaparivarte (12)
Kṣaṇi (12), Saṃghanirghātani (13), A-saṃkhyeya (14), Saṃghapagati (15), Tiri-ā-dve-saṃgha-troṭa-arāti-parāti (16),
Sarvasaṃghati-samādhi-kalanda (17), Sarvadharmābhyudgata-ceti (18), Sarva-sa...
Tvalūdhakauśalyātigati (19) khinābhigīrtite (20). All these divine mantras are the secret words and silent mysteries of the Buddha;
they subdue evil so that it naturally dissipates, and because they cannot be explained, they are not translated.
World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this dhāraṇī— since it is difficult to hear even through incantations,
yet they have heard it—
they should know that this is the power of Samantabhadra’s spiritual transformations and the empowerment bestowed by the power of all bodhisattvas.
If the Lotus Sūtra circulates in Jambudvīpa— Jambu being the name of a tree translated here as "Victorious Gold Tree," whose ripe fruit falls into the river near its banks,
staining the sand gold-colored and purplish-brown (the character *ti* is translated as "continent," referring specifically to Jambudvīpa in the south)—
[then this sūtra shall remain].
Those who uphold [this teaching] should form this thought: "All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra. Let them reflect on this for themselves.
If one upholds, recites, and correctly recollects it, that is itself correct reflection.
They understand its meaning and intent; they skillfully comprehend the meaning and intent of the sūtras and the path of the Buddha.
They practice according to what is taught, cultivating mental conduct as described in the sūtras.
It should be known that such a person practices the conduct of Samantabhadra; their practice is itself the conduct of Samantabhadra.
They have deeply planted roots of goodness before immeasurable and boundless Buddhas; they have already deeply planted the seeds of the roots of goodness for enlightenment before boundless Buddhas.
They shall have their heads stroked by the hands of all Tathāgatas; that is, the hands of the provisional wisdom of all Tathāgatas shall stroke the crowns of the heads of Bodhisattvas of true wisdom.
If one merely transcribes [this], yet through mere transcription is unable to memorize, recite, or understand its meaning—
When this person’s life ends, they shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. "Trāyastriṃśa" means the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
By cultivating wholesome deeds with a distracted mind, one is born into the Desire Realm.
At that time, eighty-four thousand celestial maidens will perform various musical performances to come and welcome them. [This is] by virtue of having transcribed the sutra.
By virtue of their merit, they are reborn in the heavens, where they are welcomed by the music and performances of the devaputras.
Those individuals immediately don crowns of the seven precious gems and enjoy themselves amidst the celestial maidens. The maidens entertain them so that their hearts are filled with joy and delight.
How much more so for one who receives, upholds, reads, recites, correctly contemplates, and understands its meaning and intent, and practices according to the teaching;
if there is someone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, and understands its meaning and intent, their merit is even more supreme.
When such a person’s life comes to an end, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them. At the moment of death, they shall receive the Buddhas’ hands and be led away by them;
thus they shall not be terrified, their minds shall find peace, and they shall not fall into the evil realms, remaining free from the four miserable destinies.
He immediately went to Tuṣita Heaven— Tuṣita being translated here as the "Heaven of Contentment"—
to the abode of Maitreya Bodhisattva, who is here called the "Bodhisattva of Loving-kindness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, possessing the thirty-two marks of a great being, was surrounded by a vast assembly of great bodhisattvas, including Jayamitra.
Therein, he is born together with a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial maidens;
this refers to the ordinary devas of the outer courtyard of Tuṣita. As for the inner courtyard, there are no women.
There are such merits and benefits as these; it is clear that the advantages are many.
Therefore, a wise person should single-mindedly write this themselves, or cause others to write it, or commission someone else to write it.
To uphold, recite, and correctly contemplate [the teaching], and to practice according to what is taught, means that writing it down, upholding, reciting,
and explaining it constitutes "opening the understanding," while practicing according to what is taught constitutes "arousing practice."
World-Honored One, by means of my supernatural powers, I shall now protect this sutra;
may you likewise protect it through your supernormal powers during the age of the final dharma after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
Within Jambudvīpa, wherever this [teaching] circulates,
cause it to be widely disseminated so that it shall not be interrupted. By causing the sūtra to be broadly distributed and its practice and realization to remain unceasing,
the lineage of the Buddhas will attain continuity without interruption.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, commending his power of aspiration:
"Excellent, excellent, Samantabhadra! You are able to protect and assist this sutra. To eliminate demonic afflictions is called 'protecting';
to encourage the cultivation of goodness is called 'assisting.'"
It brings peace, happiness, and benefit to many sentient beings. By one person upholding this sutra, no one is troubled, and many beings all attain peace and happiness.
You have already accomplished inconceivable merit; you have long since perfected inconceivable power.

Profound and great compassion: "Compassion" (maitrī) is able to bestow happiness, while "pity" (karuṇā) is able to extract one from suffering; to extract one from the suffering of the two deaths and to bestow the happiness of the three virtues is what is meant by "profound and great.
Since time immemorial, they have generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have long since initiated it.
With the resolve for the unsurpassed path,
they are able to make such vows of supernormal power to protect this sutra; making vows of supernormal power, they protect the Dharma and take birth [for that purpose].
I shall, by means of my supernatural powers, protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
I shall likewise protect those who are able to receive and uphold your name.
Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, practice, copy, or perform these deeds regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
you should know that such persons behold Śākyamuni Buddha; the text of the sūtra is itself the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
One who perceives the Dharma perceives the Buddha;

it is as if they had heard this sutra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth. Although born in the final age, one who gains faith in the text of the scripture is no different from having heard it in person.
One should know that such a person makes offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; to accord with the Buddha’s words is called making offerings to the Buddha.
One should know that such a person is praised by the Buddha as "Excellent"; their practice is in accordance with the Dharma and is extolled by the Buddha.

It should be known that such a person has had their head stroked by the hand of Śākyamuni Buddha; it is like the hand stroking the head, wherein the Buddha’s provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) strokes the crown of the head of ultimate wisdom (paramārtha-jñāna).
It should be known that such a person is covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha; patience is called the power of the robe.
Being able to endure [adversity] so that evil is obstructed and does not arise is called being "covered by the Buddha's robe.
Such a person, like those who practice as described above, no longer craves worldly pleasures; they delight in the Dharma for themselves and do not crave worldly flavors.

He does not take pleasure in the scriptures or the calligraphy of non-Buddhist paths; his mind finds no delight in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths, nor does he appreciate their compositions or calligraphy.
Furthermore, he does not enjoy associating with such people. Because they consort with the depraved and foster evil, he takes no pleasure in drawing near to them.
As well as those who are evil— those who commit all manner of wicked and unwholesome deeds,
such as butchers and those who take life,
or those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs for profit and livelihood; from the very beginning, they are not of a virtuous class.
If one were a hunter who captures living beings, or one who traffics in female beauty—such a person who sells others for their physical form is not a virtuous person.
Yet the mind and intentions of such a person are straightforward; the mind and intentions of one who upholds this sutra are sincere, upright, simple, and honest.
They possess right mindfulness, reverently remaining silent while contemplating the Way, their minds free from delusive thoughts.
They possess the power of merit; by the power of that merit, they remain far removed from obstacles and evils.
Such persons are not afflicted by the three poisons; their minds are constantly aligned with the Way, and the three poisons do not arise.
Nor does one act out of jealousy. To harm the virtuous is called *īrṣyā* (jealousy); to covet another's beauty is called *mātsarya* (envy).

Regarding pride (*māna*) and false pride (*mithyāmāna*): to hold oneself in high esteem while looking down upon others is named pride; to be attached to what is false and to insult what is correct is named false pride.
They are afflicted by overweening pride (*adhimāna*). To hold oneself as superior and look down upon others is called overweening pride;
however, because of their merit, they cannot be afflicted by the aforementioned faults.
This person has few desires and is content. Not giving rise to longing for what has not yet been obtained is called having few desires;
being frugal according to one's means regarding what is presently possessed is called being content.

One is able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra; one is able to endure both adversity and favor, and is able to remain free from faults and evils—cultivating the mind in this way is called the conduct of Samantabhadra.
As for Samantabhadra in the period of the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it is as previously explained.
If anyone sees one who receives, maintains, reads, and recites the Lotus Sūtra, or sees such a person upholding the sūtra, they should form this thought:
"This person shall before long proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). To attain entry into the Buddha-way is what is meant by "proceeding to the site of enlightenment."

He destroys all hosts of Māras; he destroys the hostile hosts of Māras and all unwholesome objects, attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and achieves the state of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Turning the wheel of Dharma: because one successively delivers others through the Buddha’s teachings, it is called turning the wheel of Dharma.
Beating the drum of Dharma: because one expounds all dharmas with a great voice, it is called beating the drum of Dharma.

He blows the Dharma conch. Among musical instruments, blowing the conch refers to changing one's signal according to circumstances and shifting names at will; this is called "blowing the Dharma conch.

He rains down the rain of Dharma. By preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, he causes them to establish the seeds of goodness, just as a drenching sweet rain causes sprouts and stalks to grow.
When seated upon the lion Dharma throne amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, the "lion throne" symbolizes that just as the King of Beasts,
with a single roar, strikes terror into all other creatures, so too does the sound of the Dharma, with a single resonance, reach the ears of all living beings.
Samantabhadra, if there are those in future generations who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra— those people in the final age who uphold the sutra and practice the Way—
they shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food, drink, or the necessities of life. As stated in the preceding text:
Being clear regarding external objects, one does not give rise to greedy attachment; now, being clear regarding the enjoyment of experiences, one does not give rise to a greedy mind.
One's aspirations are not in vain; whatever is wished for truly accords with one's heart.
One also obtains the retribution of merit in the present life. The preceding section clarified rebirth in future lives; this explains the present retribution.
If there is someone who treats one with contempt, saying, "You are merely a madman," they are slandering the name of one who upholds this sutra by calling them a madman.
To practice in vain results in obtaining nothing at all. To act fruitlessly and thereby slander the existence of cause and effect brings this retribution:

one shall be blind life after life. Because such a person treats others with contempt, disparages the Dharma, and destroys the right view of others, they experience blindness as a manifestation of their profound transgression;
it does not pertain to a single lifetime alone, which is why it is said to occur "life after life."
If there are those who make offerings and offer praise, or if one sees others upholding this sutra and making offerings and offering praise, they shall obtain manifest retribution in this very life;
that is to say, the response of the karmic fruit is swift in this present world.
Furthermore, if one sees someone who receives and upholds this sutra, and seeing such a holder,
exposes their faults and magnifies their shortcomings—
whether those faults be real or unreal— one incurs sin even if they are real; how much more so if one slanders another?
Such a person will suffer from leprosy in their present life. By inflicting evil upon others and causing them to encounter the physical affliction of leprosy, they bring this sin upon themselves.
Furthermore, if there are those who treat with contempt or deride those who uphold this sutra, mocking them with disdain, [they shall likewise incur such retribution].
In every successive life, one's teeth will be sparse and missing. One will be ridiculed for having gaps between the teeth and mocked for missing teeth.
One will have ugly lips and a flat nose; the lips will hang down like a blowing fire while the upper lip recedes, and the bridge of the nose will fail to rise, remaining flat and sunken.
The hands and feet are contorted; their gait is not upright, and they perceive their own hands and feet as diseased.
The corners of the eyes are sunken, and the eyes become triangular or the pupils roll upward.
The body is foul-smelling and impure; the poisonous breath harms others, resulting in the foul stench of the body.
There are malignant sores and pus-blood: the poison of the mind results in malignant sores, while the poison of speech results in pus-blood.

Water-bellies and shortness of breath: the cause is anger during the time-element, and the result is water-bellies during the time-element, while the cause is shortness of breath during the time-element.
It hastens various severe and grievous illnesses. Because one slanders the Dharma and slanders others, committing grave transgressions, such conditions for these evil diseases are brought about;
they do not descend from heaven, nor well up from the earth, nor are they bestowed by humans—they are caused by karma.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra— knowing that the offense of disparaging it is profound while the merit of honoring it is vast—
you should rise to welcome them from afar; upon seeing them, you should immediately rise and go out to receive them.

One should revere them as one would the Buddha. Since there is no Buddha at present, this person propagates the sutra and acts as the Buddha’s successor; therefore, one should revere them as one would the Buddha.
When the "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being spoken, and when the Buddha spoke these words, [the earth shook].
There were bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—immeasurable and boundless. The sands of the Ganges are as fine as flour;
using the number of these grains of sand as a metaphor for the bodhisattvas is intended to express their vast multitude.
They attain hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *vartanī-dhāraṇīs*. This is translated as "revolving dhāraṇī.
Because wisdom is generated through reverent faith, one understands immeasurable meanings within a single dharma; this is called the revolving dhāraṇī.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm— just as one might grind a trichiliocosm into dust to serve as a metaphor for the number of bodhisattvas who have attained the Way.
They are endowed with the path of Samantabhadra. By hearing this sublime Dharma, all these bodhisattvas attain the complete fulfillment of the path of Samantabhadra.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the assembly of great bodhisattvas, including Samantabhadra and others, [was present].
Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas, the great assembly of śrāvakas,
as well as the eight classes of beings— including devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans—
all in the great assembly were filled with great joy; having heard the Dharma and gained its benefit, their hearts were exceedingly glad.
They received and upheld the Buddha’s words; that is to say, they received them through the power of faith and upheld them through the power of mindfulness.
Having paid homage, they departed. Having heard the Dharma in its entirety, they joined their palms in reverent salutation, withdrew by retreating backward, and retired.
An Exegesis of the Phrases of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Eight (End)
